# Romans

## 1:1 Introduction
[Philipp Melanchthon, Commentarii in Epistolam Pauli ad Romanos (Strasbourg, 1540). English: machine translation, The Faith Received (Mere Orthodoxy); the original follows each comment.]
ARGUMENT OF PAUL'S EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS.

But with the signs of things changed, the things themselves have also been lost, and manifold delusions have followed. I see, however, that even now many depraved minds are arising, which, either out of curiosity or out of ambition, will strive to disturb and overwhelm again with new illusions those things which are now rightly delivered in our Churches and explained with the best faith and simply. Wherefore, for Christ's sake, I pray and beseech all the pious who are engaged in studies to love and defend the simple truth revealed in our Churches, which indeed I desire to illustrate and fortify as much as I can, so that it may be propagated to posterity. But since I have recited the argument of the Epistle to the Romans in some way, and have admonished that certain things concerning the meaning of words should be observed, it seemed good to add an interpretation of certain terms, and to set forth the entire controversy concerning justification. For these προλεγόμενα will add some light to the argument. And when the reader has grasped the whole cause in his mind at once, he will more easily perceive that it is true, firm, and necessary for the Church, and will notice more correctly how the members of the disputation cohere in Paul, when he has first conceived as it were the idea of the building in his mind.

The sum of the doctrine delivered in the prophetic and apostolic writings concerning justification before God.

I have attempted elsewhere in my Theological commonplaces to explain with as much simplicity and clarity as I could the doctrine of justification, handed down in the prophetic and apostolic writings. Nor shall I say anything else here. But since this matter is proper to this Pauline Epistle, I shall repeat the same things, and perhaps somewhere I shall say something in plainer words. Among the philosophers, universal justice is called obedience according to all virtues, that is, an external honest discipline, which a man can effect by his own powers. This also Paul calls the justice of the law and the justice of works. However, we have often said that God demands that all men be restrained by external honest discipline, just as Paul says: The law is laid down for the unjust, and God punishes those who violate discipline, such as perjured men, those speaking contumeliously about God, the seditious, murderers, adulterers, thieves, liars. But it is true what Aristotle says, That neither the Evening Star nor the Morning Star is more beautiful than justice, that is, honest discipline. For it is an excellent ornament of man, nor can this weak nature of man effect any other more excellent grace. But nevertheless, it must be known that this discipline by no means satisfies the law, but is a certain thin shadow of the law, just as Paul learnedly teaches2. Corinth. 3.when he says that the Jews look upon Moses with a veiled face, that is, that they are not suffused with the splendor of the law, that is, that they do not shine in them the knowledge of God, and perfect obedience, but external works of whatever kind are performed. But the law of God demands, not only external works, but perfect obedience. It can therefore be easily understood that no one is righteous before God, that is, accepted on account of external discipline, as Paul clearly says: By the works of the law shall no flesh be justified. That statement takes away the praise of justification not only from ceremonies, but also from moral works, and speaks of the whole discipline. Furthermore, philosophy and human laws discourse about this external discipline, about that veiled face of Moses, they do not seek how we may be righteous, that is, accepted before God. Nor are the opinions of philosophers to be mixed with the Pauline. Let its own place be attributed to this carnal righteousness, that is, let the impious be restrained by this discipline, let philosophers wander in the assembly of the people, and let them gaze upon the veiled face of Moses, let them not ascend in mind to God. Let both Origen and the others who follow him remain in this crowd, and let them gaze upon the veiled face of Moses, since they teach no other righteousness except the carnal. Since, therefore, reason does not see how we are reckoned righteous before God, the Gospel preaches another righteousness, not known to reason, but revealed to the Fathers by God, and afterwards made more and more manifest through the prophets, and finally through Christ and the Apostles stolos scattered into the world. Therefore John says, No man hath seen God at any time. But the son of God who is in the bosom of the father, he hath declared him unto us, as if he should say, this will of God, that God is willing freely to forgive, and to give eternal life for the sake of the son, no creature, no human reason could comprehend. But only through the son has this will been revealed. Concerning this admirable benefit Paul preaches, which I shall explain briefly. Christ also, as befits an artisan, has most aptly embraced the sum and method of the Gospel, when he commands to preach repentance and remission of sins in his name. Therefore the ministry of the Gospel first convicts sins, just as Christ says: The holy spirit will convict the world of sin etc. Here when the mind acknowledges sin and the wrath of God, and is terrified by true terrors, the Gospel proposes consolation, and that voice which is proper to the Gospel itself, namely the promise of the benefit of Christ, shows the mediator the son of God, just as John was showing him, saying: Behold the lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world, it commands to establish that for the sake of this mediator the son of God, our lord Jesus Christ, the remission of sins and the imputation of righteousness are certainly given to us, not for the sake of any of our works or merits, but freely by faith, that is, when we believe those things truly and certainly for the sake of Christ to be given. With this faith we raise and sustain ourselves looking upon Christ, we truly obtain the remission of sins, and are accounted righteous, that is, accepted before God, and are gifted with the Holy Spirit, and are made children of God, and heirs of eternal life, as it is written in John chapter one: He gave them power to become the children of God, to them that believe in his name. These things are plain and clear and accommodated to the use of consciences, and can be seen in examples. David, guilty of adultery and murder, when he was accused by the prophet, was oppressed by huge terrors. Afterwards he is raised up by the voice of absolution, when the Prophet says: The Lord has taken away your sin. You shall not die. Hearing this voice, he believes that his sin is remitted to him, not on account of his own dignity or merits, but freely through mercy, and he knows that liberation from sin and from death is promised on account of the coming liberator, he knows that Christ will be the sacrifice for the sins of the human race, as he says in the psalm: You are a priest forever etc. Sustaining himself with this faith, he becomes righteous, that is, accepted before God unto eternal life. ThusLuke 7the woman comes weeping to Christ, acknowledging her sins, afterwards Christ says to her: Go in peace, your faith has made you safe. Thus these two movements are described in conversion, terrors and faith. Commonly they call terrors contrition, but it must be known that terrors do not merit the pardon of sins, indeed, unless there should approach faith, the mind oppressed by terrors would rush into eternal death, just as Saul and Judas perished, since they did not raise themselves up by faith and the acknowledgment of mercy amidst the terrors. And this is what the saying of Paul about the law means: The law works wrath, that is, it strikes in horrible terrors, such as are often described in the psalms, and Hezekiah says: As a lion he has crushed all my bones. Therefore these dreads bring about destruction and eternal death, unless faith were to approach, gradually raising up the spirits, looking into the promises of Christ, and thus apprehending Christ. The psalms warn how great these struggles are. How we see David struggling with himself, when he cries out: O Lord, rebuke me not in thy fury. Have mercy on me, O Lord. For there is no one in death who is mindful of thee, nor in hell who shall praise thee. Do not cast me away among the damned, who are burned with a horrible and eternal hatred of thee, and curse thee. Do not cast me into this assembly of thy enemies. Andpsalm 41.Why art thou sad, O my soul, and why dost thou disquiet me? Hope in God, for I shall yet praise him. Concerning these such great struggles Paul also preaches here, and he does not merely dispute about swine's flesh, or similar rites. He cries out that all are under sin. This sentence preaches about terrors, then it shows Christ, he says we are justified freely by faith etc. And so that we may know that he is speaking not of idle thoughts, but of faith struggling with dreads, he says: Being justified by faith we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ. we have, likewise access to God &c. Likewise by faith we acknowledge that we are loved by God. Since therefore these words of Paul so aptly agree with the rest of the prophetic scripture, what perversity is it to attribute another meaning to Paul? But I proceed. Since this opinion, which I have recited concerning the conversion of man, and justification, is clear and plain, and has use in life, and is a ratified and immutable opinion of the Gospel, revealed to the Fathers, the blindness of the adversaries is partly to be deplored, and their pertinacity partly to be detested, who condemn our interpretation. And here I adjure all the pious through Christ, that they weigh what is said on both sides. The adversaries confess that terrors ought to exist, but they speak otherwise concerning faith; they wish for the knowledge of history to be present, but they command one to doubt concerning the remission of sins, and if it happens to anyone, they say it happens on account of merits. Thus they simply abolish the Gospel, which teaches that this benefit happens on account of Christ, and that it may be certain, the promise was published, and God commands that we believe the promise, and assent to it, and determine that it pertains to us. That this is the true and perpetual opinion of the Gospel, it is necessary to confess. And Paul refutes the error concerning doubt, when he teaches that the promise ought to be received by faith.Rom. 4.Therefore by faith freely, that the promise may be firm. And he commands, that we attribute to God the praise of truth. as Abraham did not doubt through distrust. And1. John 5.He who believes in the Son of God has the testimony in himself; he who does not believe God, makes him a liar, etc. Therefore, when we say that the benefits of Christ are obtained by faith, it must necessarily be understood that they are obtained on account of Christ, and one must assent to the divine promise, and believe that the things promised are truly granted to us. Wherefore faith does not only signify knowledge of history, but it signifies trust in the promised mercy on account of Christ, assenting to the divine promise. Paul requires such a faith, which believes all the articles of the Creed, namely, which believes that on account of the Son of God who suffered and was resurrected, the remission of sins is given to us. For to this article, as to the final cause, the preceding ones are to be referred. When in their prayers the adversaries recite this article: I believe in the remission of sins, they fight against themselves; they command to doubt, and yet they hear it commanded that they should believe in the remission of sins. And I know some whom this very article admonished to admit consolation, and to think that one must assent to the promise of God, and to cast away the doctrine of the monks concerning doubt and merits.

But why is the particle freely added, not on account of works, but on account of Christ? Indeed, truly, concerning this particle freely, the adversaries and consciences especially contend, and the prophets and apostles. It comprises two things. It excludes our merits, and it proposes the merits of Christ. For here especially can be discerned, first, the magnitude of the wrath of God against sin, because no sacrifice could appease God except the death of the Son. Again, the magnitude of love shines forth, because He gave His Son for us. But it is necessary to hold both in the agony of conscience, namely, that the merits of Christ are to be proposed to God, and that grace is to be sought and expected on account of Christ, not on account of our merits. For this is the climax of that struggle: the terrified mind does not ask whether God wishes to be propitious to others who are well-deserving and worthy. It agrees that God is good and merciful, but to those who are worthy, who do not have sins, or who have greater merits. For the knowledge of the law, born with us, teaches that God is good, but toward the worthy. But that mind asks whether God wishes to be propitious to me, the unworthy one. Here the particle, freely, must be looked at, so that we may truly establish that God remits sins on account of Christ freely, not on account of any of our works or merits. And this particle, freely, shows the distinction between the Gospel and the law. The law also preaches that God is good, merciful, but it adds the condition of worthiness, or merit; it says that God is propitious to those who are without sin. But the Gospel removes the condition of our worthiness or merits. He testifies that God is reconciled to us freely for the sake of Christ's merits, not for the sake of any of our merits, since this faith, that is, trust in mercy, relies upon Christ. We are accustomed, however, sometimes to use this formula instead of the exclusive, we are justified freely by faith. We are justified by faith alone, where this particle does not exclude other virtues from being present, but it excludes the opinion of merit, or the condition of worthiness, or it excludes them from the cause of justification, that is, of acceptance, as I shall say more copiously later. And in itself it is entirely the same thing to say, we are just by faith, and we are just freely by faith, and we are just by faith alone. For faith can in no way exist, if trust must rely upon our worthiness, or merits, or partly upon Christ, partly upon merits, as some imagine. Faith is shaken, if it must be thought, God will be so propitious, when you will have enough merits. Therefore faith cannot rely except upon the promise of God, showing Christ, for whose sake the Father has promised that He will certainly be propitious to us. And when Paul asks, whether we are justified by faith or by works, he understands by faith, trust in the mercy promised for the sake of Christ, and he opposes this in its entirety to our worthiness, as if he were asking: Whether you ought to determine that your sins are forgiven you, and that you are a son of God for the sake of your own worthiness, for the sake of any of your virtues, qualities, or actions, or whether you ought to determine that to you sins are forgiven, and that you are a son of God through mercy alone, on account of Christ. Therefore, the very thing is an Exclusive, when it says: We are justified by faith, that is, not on account of our worthiness. Wherefore if anyone truly wishes to judge, he will acknowledge that the same thing is signified in reality, we are justified by faith, and we are justified freely by faith, and we are justified by faith alone. I have added these things in passing concerning the formulas of speech, so that the meaning may be diligently weighed. Furthermore, in whatever way we may speak, that must be seen to, that the matter is not overwhelmed. The exclusive sentence must be retained, concerning gratuitous acceptance. For this makes the distinction between the law and the Gospel, as has been said. I have spoken concerning the particle freely, concerning which let the pious also consider this, that merits are taken away and rejected, not because we do nothing, but so that the promise may be certain for us, which would become uncertain if it depended on the condition of merits, likewise so that due honor may be attributed to Christ, likewise because, even if we do something, nevertheless we are far removed from the perfection of the law. Moreover, faith arises from the word of God, namely from the Gospel, which properly is a promise, in which the benefits of Christ are both promised to us and exhibited. For the human mind could establish nothing concerning the remission of sins, if God had not revealed this will of His by a certain word, or by a certain promise. Moreover, it must be known that this Evangelical promise is universal, which is why it is necessary for the pious to be admonished of this, because timid minds are concerned about these two questions they dispute most, namely about dignity, and about election. First we ask whether he receives the unworthy, then even if we were worthy, we nevertheless think that God has chosen certain friends of his own, to whom he wishes to impart these benefits, we doubt whether it pertains to us also, we fear that we are not in the number of those. Thus human reason wavers concerning the will of God. For philosophers also agree that God favors a few certain ones, namely Heroic men, and governs their outcomes, but they think that the remaining men are neglected by God. The mind thinks about predestination, as they call it, in this very way. But the heavenly voice censures human opinion. This is how the Gospel differs from philosophical opinions and from the law, because it shows the will of God otherwise, it shows that God truly wishes to receive even the unworthy, and to offer grace to all, provided that they believe the promise. Therefore let the pious learn that the promise is universal, as innumerable sayings testify, such as Come to me all, who labor, and are burdened.Ro. 3.The justice of God through faith of Jesus Christ unto all and upon all who believe. ItemRo. 10.The same Lord of all is rich unto all etc. Let us individuals include ourselves in these universals, and let us determine that the promised benefits truly pertain to us. Therefore in the question concerning justification, let disputes about predestination be set aside for a little while. One must begin from the Gospel, which also convicts all, And he offers to all the promised grace on account of Christ, and indeed he offers it freely, provided that they receive it by faith. Let us therefore look into the word which is universal, and let us not allow ourselves to be torn away from the promise by speculations about predestination. For one must not judge concerning the will of God without his word. And as the promises are universal, so I understand this saying: God wills all men to be saved, just as in the promises he offers salvation to all. But the human will in those who do not wish to believe resists the promises. Those, however, who sustain themselves with the promise should truly establish that the benefits of Christ are attributed to them, lest they accuse God of a lie. And when they receive the voice of the Gospel and sustain themselves, at the same time the Holy Spirit is effective through the voice of the Gospel, according to that: Faith is from hearing. And to Galat 3. that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith. Thus, when minds cast down to the earth are raised up by faith, they conceive the Holy Spirit. This is the conversion which in the Gospel is called regeneration, which embraces these three things: the remission of sins, justification or the imputation of righteousness, and the gift of the Holy Spirit and of eternal life. I have spoken, however, about the movements which can be understood by the pious, about terrors and consolation, which will come about through faith. Wherefore this Pauline sentence is neither absurd, nor intricate, nor does it contain idle quibbles, but is perspicuous and consistent with the remaining sermons of the prophets and the Gospel. He proposes the greatest things, which the pious experience in life, and the knowledge of which is necessary for the Church. Now I will add a brief explanation of the terms, Law, Gospel, Sin, Justification, Grace, Faith.

The law and the Gospel differ greatly. For the law is a doctrine by which God commands what sort of people we ought to be, and what things are to be done, and what are to be avoided. And although the Mosaic polity has been abolished, nevertheless the moral law remains, which is one and the same for all times, since the knowledge of it is born with us. For God willed that there be some knowledge in man, which would judge sin. And always in all times sin is reproved by the voice of the law in the preaching of repentance. Therefore Paul says: Through the law is the knowledge of sin. Nor does he speak only of ceremonies, as some imagine, but especially of the Decalogue or moral law. For this always accuses everyone. For one must think far differently about the divine law than about the customs of civil life. In civil life only external discipline is demanded. But the law of God requires perfect obedience, interior and exterior. As the commandment testifies: You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart etc. And thusMatthew 5.Christ interprets the law. Since, however, this nature of men, corrupted by the disease of origin, cannot provide perfect obedience, the law shows the wrath of God against sin, accuses and condemns all men except Christ, who, as Paul says, delivered us from the curse of the law. He delivered, however, not only the Jews or the others who were saved after the Mosaic law was issued or abolished, but also the Fathers before Moses. Therefore, they too were under the law, that is, they were accused and terrified by the judgment of the natural law, and would have perished, had they not held to the promises concerning Christ, on account of whom they knew that deliverance from sin and from death had been promised. Perhaps political men laugh at these things, when we say that the divine law demands perfect obedience, and that no one can satisfy the divine law, because ignorance and contempt of God cling to the nature of man; these things seem inept to philosophers and those judging according to human custom. But the prophets and apostles do this very thing; they want men to acknowledge the magnitude of sin, because they do not truly acknowledge and glorify God; they teach that this sin is the cause of the greatest miseries and calamities by which this weak nature is oppressed, and to seek true righteousness, and deliverance from sin and from death, granted through Christ. As for the rest concerning the law, let the students who are to read these things for the sake of learning take them from the commonplaces which I have published. The Gospel preaches repentance and the promise of grace, and of eternal life. The promise, however, must be diligently distinguished from the law. And although the law has certain promises of its own, nevertheless even those differ from the promise which is proper to the Gospel. And the promises of the law require the condition of perfect obedience as it is said in the first commandment: I will do good to those who love me, but the Evangelical promise concerning the remission of sins, justification, and the gift of eternal life, is gratuitous, offered on account of Christ, without the condition of our merits or our dignity. No human voice can express the magnitude of this benefit, which God imparts to us through his son our Lord Jesus Christ, namely that with sin deleted, and death abolished, we may enjoy the sight of God in eternal life, justice, and joy. The promise of this benefit has been revealed only divinely, as John says: The Son who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared him to us. For although some knowledge of the law is born with us, yet the knowledge of the Gospel is by no means born with us. Human reason by itself by no means sees this will of God, namely that God was to send his son, that he might become a victim for the Church, that God wills to remit sins gratuitously. These things are placed far outside the sight of human reason. Therefore the sayings of the laws must be diligently distinguished from the Evangelical promise. Among Phocylides, Hesiod, and the like, some sayings of the laws are read. But the Evangelical promise concerning gratuitous remission, or concerning the Son of God, is nowhere read in those who followed only the judgment of reason or the light of human nature, indeed although a certain knowledge of the law is born with us, the mind itself in us accuses sins, and thinks of nothing else, except God to punish and cast away the unjust. For this is the judgment of the law, and according to the law it is true. But in a great struggle in repentance, the gratuitous promise of mercy ought to be opposed to the voice of the law and to our natural judgment, to be preferred before the law, because Christ frees from the law, so that when Adam had fallen and was being accused, he could judge nothing else except what the law showed, that he would perish because he had not obeyed God. But God comes forth, and although he subjects the human race to the death of the body and to other miseries, nevertheless he proposes consolation, he promises liberation from sin and from death, and the restoration of the human race. For he says that it will come to pass that the seed of the woman shall crush the head of the serpent. With this voice spoken, the Son of God moved the heart of Adam and instilled in him new light and life. For then the Son of God was constituted the guardian, governor, and savior of the Church, then he began to wage war with the devil. And as the devil rages with immense cruelty against the human race, destroys very many, and especially out of hatred for God attempts to blot out the church, and fixes his poisonous teeth into our heel, as we often experience, so in turn the Son of God is effective in believers, and represses the fury of the devil, restores and frees the Saints. The world does not see this struggle, but the horrible falls of very many, and the saddest and most tragic calamities, and then the glorious liberations, as of David and others they show what kind of struggle this is. Nor do the words in Genesis signify anything else: The seed shall crush the head of the serpent, than this very thing which John says: For this the Son of God was manifested, that he might destroy the works of the devil. Thus Adam understood the promise, thus subsequently all the Fathers believed that on account of this promised seed their sins were forgiven them, and that they were to be freed from sin and from eternal death. By this faith they were righteous, not by the fulfillment of the law; by this faith they were raised up in all dangers and terrors. And indeed they knew that this Lord was present with them, just as Jacob clearly says.Genesis 48.The Angel who delivered me from all evils, let him bless these boys, for he proclaims him to be the Lord, through whom he was delivered from all evils, and from him he asks that he bless his descendants. These things cannot be understood otherwise than of the Son of God. And Paul says that the Son of God accompanied the camps of the people of Israel. John also says that all things were made through this Son, and that the light shone in the darkness. All triumphs against the devil were won through this Son. Noah was saved, Abraham was defended, Joseph was raised up, the people were delivered out of Egypt, Daniel even speaks with him. Thus the Gospel of the Apostles preaches about Christ, testifies that he is the victim, the deliverer, and the savior, and commands us to trust in this leader and deliverer. Just as also very many sentences in the prophets teach, as the psalm The second says: Kiss the son: Blessed are all who trust in him. And without this faith, that is, the confidence of the mercy promised on account of the son, there is no true invocation of God, no true worship. For through this High Priest we have access to the Father, as it is often written. Therefore, the blindness of those is to be execrated who imagine the Gospel to be a law containing certain precepts about mutual love, but that faith is required, that is, the knowledge of the history concerning Christ, and that he is to be held as a teacher, just as Socrates or Phocylides handed down good precepts, and that men are to be imagined to be righteous on account of those duties of love, but that it is nevertheless to be doubted whether God forgives us, whether he hears us, or whether he has any business with us. Thus monks and now certain philosophasters transform the Gospel into Academic philosophy, that is, a doctrine about works, and they command to doubt concerning divine promises, nor do they teach that faith, that is, confidence, which relies on Christ the liberator, and seeks and expects the promised benefits on his account, is necessary. I ask, therefore, all pious readers, if they love Christ, that they here consider the distinction between the law and the Gospel, Moses and Christ, and diligently think about what glory is to be attributed to the Son of God, what are the true honors which the fathers, Adam, Jacob, the prophets, and the Apostles attributed to him. From these let us learn that Christ is present to his Church as leader, governor, liberator, savior, and defender against the devil.

that the benefits of Christ are to be received by faith, and let us remember that the Gospel is a voice promising and exhibiting these benefits, just as Paul says: The Gospel is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth, that is, the Gospel offers to us grace and eternal life freely on account of Christ, not on account of the law. And through this Gospel God is truly efficacious, He gives the Holy Spirit, He begins in us a new light and eternal life.

Sin does not signify only vicious actions, as the philosophers judge concerning the term. But it also embraces a huge weakness, which is born with us, which is called original sin, which although secure men judge to be a light evil, nay, the philosophers do not even think it to be an evil, yet it must be judged far otherwise. Darkness and doubt concerning God, whether He cares for human affairs, whether He punishes, whether He nourishes, whether He helps, whether He hears men, likewise to be void of fear, of the love of God, to love ourselves, with God neglected, to admire our own wisdom, to play with opinions fashioned about God, Epicurean or superstitious, to have impulses variously wandering, turned away from God, and fighting with the law of God, are not light evils. That these are huge evils, punishments show. For on account of these evils God subjected the human race to death, He punishes and restrains it with huge calamities. Furthermore, since God was unwilling to be appeased by any victim, except by the death of His Son, it is necessary that the evil be huge, which had to be redeemed at such a price.

it is such a great astonishment in human souls, that they do not recognize this disease. Wherefore God willed it to be revealed by his own voice and doctrine. Let us assent to this, nor let us listen to the cavils of the Sophists, who laugh a sardonic laugh, and extenuate the disease, treat the victim Christ lightly, or even despise him entirely. It behooves us to abhor that impious philosophy with our souls and ears.

To justify in the Hebrew phrase is customarily to pronounce or reckon as just, as it would be said in Hebrew, the Roman people justified Scipio, who was accused by the Tribunes, that is, acquitted, or pronounced him just. Thus in these disputations of Paul let us know for certain that justification signifies the remission of sins, and acceptance to eternal life, as the chapter 4 to the Romans testifies quite clearly, where he defines justification as the remission of sins. Therefore, we are justified by faith is the same as we are reckoned just by God on account of Christ, when we believe. And the word justice, does not here signify the justice of the law, or universal obedience, or our own qualities, when it is said, justice is given to us by faith. But it signifies the imputation of justice, or acceptance. And let just in this way be understood relatively, for one accepted to eternal life. But it must be known that in the remission of sins the Holy Spirit is given at the same time, as I said above, when we raise ourselves up by faith.

Thus, joined with justification is the gift of the Holy Spirit, who initiates not only one virtue, faith, but also the others: fear, the love of God, love of the truth, chastity, patience, justice toward one's neighbor, as I shall speak of works later. But these virtues do not merit the remission of sins, nor are they the justice on account of which a person is accepted, which still has much infirmity. Furthermore, when a terrified conscience seeks how we may be justified, it does not seek what virtues we have, but how we may obtain the remission of sins and reconciliation with God. It is anxious about the will of God toward us; it does not contemplate its own virtues, it does not set them against the judgment of God. Therefore, those who interpret justification as the infusion of virtues do not attend to the fact that here the question is about the remission of sins and about the peace of the conscience toward God, or about reconciliation. We are asking how we may be justified, that is, from where we may have the remission of sins, why it must be established that God is propitious to us. It is necessary, therefore, that justification be understood as the remission of sins and divine acceptance, or the imputation of justice.

Grace signifies gratuitous acceptance, or the mercy promised on account of Christ, with whom is joined the gift of the Holy Spirit, asRom. 5.Paul says: When the grace of God, and the gift in grace. Where when he names grace, he understands gratuitous reconciliation, then the gift in grace, he understands the donation of the holy spirit and the beginning of eternal life. For in the remission of sins, as I have said, the holy spirit is given. And the profane philosophy of Pelagius is to be execrated, who contended that without the action of the holy spirit men become sons of God and heirs of eternal life. Often, therefore, by the name of grace is signified the help and action of the holy spirit. But the principal signification is gratuitous acceptance, as when we say: Paul through grace obtained the remission of sins, that is, Paul gratuitously on account of Christ obtained the remission of sins. And the exposition of the monks is to be repudiated, who fashioned an interpretation diametrically opposed to Paul: Through grace we obtain remission, that is, we obtain it on account of our virtues. That grace signifies principally gratuitous acceptance promised on account of Christ, many sayings testify: as, You are not under the law, but under grace. For he means that the righteous, even if they have sins, are nevertheless not accused, because they are under grace, that is, accepted and pleasing on account of Christ. For he does not wish them to feel that they are pleasing on account of their habits.

Rom. 4.Therefore it is of faith, and according to grace, that the promise might be firm. Furthermore, the conscience is not certain on account of our habits or our virtues, but on account of the gratuitous mercy promised. Wherefore to this place the interpretation of the monks, who interpret grace only as our virtues, will by no means be suitable.

Romans. 5.Where sin abounded, grace did much more abound, that is, gratuitous mercy is more clearly seen when the magnitude of our sin is seen, and we understand that we obtain the remission of sins gratuitously, not on account of any merits.

To the Ephesians. 2.Predestinating us through Jesus Christ, according to the good pleasure of his will, to the praise of the glory of his grace. Here he certainly wishes not our virtues to be celebrated, but the gratuitous mercy of God.

To the Galatians. 2.I do not frustrate the grace of God; for if righteousness is by the law, then Christ is dead in vain. He does not say this, I magnify my virtues, but I magnify the gratuitous mercy, by which I determine for myself that God is appeased on account of the death of Christ.

2. Thessalonians 2.He gave us good hope in grace, he does not command us to hope on account of our virtues, but on account of the gratuitous mercy promised on account of Christ.

To the Hebrews. 4.Let us approach with confidence to the throne of grace, that is, of promised mercy. For it is sufficiently clear that grace cannot be understood here as our virtues.

Finally, the phrase of the Hebrew language is known to the learned. These things being observed, it will be easy to judge concerning the meaning of the word. Furthermore, no one is ignorant that Paul for this very reason inculcates the word of grace, so that we may establish that we are pleasing to God on account of Christ, not on account of our virtues. The interpretation of the monks completely inverts this, when they command us to believe that we are justified by grace, that is, on account of our virtues.

There is, however, in the word of grace an exclusive, which, as I said above, must be diligently observed. For the particle of exclusion, freely on account of Christ, chiefly makes the distinction between the Law and the Gospel. But, as I said, it is not repentance or other virtues that are excluded, but the condition of worthiness or merit, so that terrified minds may have firm consolation. Nor do the promises grow sweet to souls, unless we always include in them the particle, freely: Everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved; if I add, if he is worthy, the mind will be terrified. Therefore the Gospel cries out concerning the particle freely, even if you are unworthy, because on account of Christ those calling upon the Lord will be saved freely. Thus in the Psalm: Because with the Lord there is mercy; if I add, toward the worthy, the conscience recoils. But the Gospel commands that gratuitous mercy, certainly promised on account of Christ, be understood, as if it were saying: Do not recoil, but approach God, receive the gift proposed by faith. For on account of Christ God wishes to forgive you freely. And that decree is certain and immutable. If anyone thinks it is uncertain, he offers an insult to the Son of God, who is the pledge of this promise. But it is necessary that the gift be received by faith.

I have repeated these things for this reason, because it matters a great deal that this exclusive be diligently illustrated, so that the distinction between the Law and the Gospel may be rightly perceived, and so that pious minds may think that a firm consolation is set before them, and may rouse themselves to faith and invocation in all business and dangers. For in daily miseries this faith must be exercised. Nor can the Gospel be understood without these exercises, nor does true invocation exist without this faith, of which we now speak so often, just as Christ says: Whatever he shall ask the Father in my name, that is, in confidence of my name, this I will do. This distinction must necessarily exist between Ethnic invocation and Christian. The Ethnics invoke while doubting whether God cares for human prayers and is affected by our miseries. To invoke in such a way is to offer an insult to God. And yet such are those cries of the impious in the temples, and the monks command one to doubt in invocation. But against these errors must be opposed the sentencesRom. 5.Through him we have access in faith.Ephe. 3.Through whom we dare to approach confidently, through faith in him. AndRom. 8.Who sits at the right hand of God and intercedes for us. Therefore no one can approach God, except through this mediator, and high priest bearing our prayers. Just as it is alsoRom. 10.said: How shall they call upon him, in whom they do not believe? James says: Let him ask in faith, nothing wavering.Matt. 21.Whatsoever you shall ask in prayer, believing, you shall receive. Therefore, that we may be able to offer to God the chief, true, and pleasing worship, namely invocation, it is necessary that this doctrine concerning faith and gratuitous mercy be held and known.

I come to the term faith, about which in the first place many dispute with us. It is, however, a wonder that there has been such darkness in the Church, that the genuine meaning of this word, which has always been in everyone's mouth, with which the ears of all resound, has been almost lost. To that evil is now added another, worse one. It is difficult to root out an inveterate error from the minds of men, and certain sycophants, such as Cochlaeus and others, attempt to defend it. But since sycophants do not seek the truth, but serve their own disease, I have not thought it necessary to wrangle with them now. Nor, indeed, do I flee the judgment of the pious and learned. For the prophetic and apostolic sayings show so clearly what faith signifies, that no sane person can gainsay it. Therefore, faith signifies not only knowledge of history, but trust in the mercy promised on account of Christ, or to assent to the promise of grace. It is, therefore, an assent in the intellect, and to will this divine consolation, and to acquiesce in it, when we hear that God is propitious to us on account of the Son Jesus Christ. Wherefore when it is said, We are justified by faith, it is not to be imagined that we are righteous by faith on account of the dignity of the virtue itself. But this statement ought to be understood correlatively: We are justified by faith, that is, through mercy on account of Christ we are pleasing to God. But we apprehend or acknowledge this mercy by faith, and apply it to ourselves. For faith or trust, even if I assent that they are qualities, nevertheless, as other names of affections become relative, as Love relates itself to that which we love, fear to the object which is dreaded, so trust to its object upon which it relies. These dialectical matters are known even to boys, which Mensinger, an unlearned and impure buffoon, has slandered with Thersitic impudence. But I appeal to the judgments of the sound and learned, who understand relatives according to what they are called, and notice what is the use of these childish precepts in more serious controversies. As therefore this statement is understood correlatively: Trust is rich in its treasure with a tranquil mind in the difficulty of the grain supply, that is, on account of its treasure it is rich with a tranquil mind. So when you hear: We are justified by faith, let the correlative immediately come to mind, through mercy on account of Christ we are reckoned righteous, for therefore it is said by faith, that is, by trust in Christ, or by trust in the mercy promised on account of Christ, we are righteous. And I remember that I have been asked several times, why it must be said:

We are righteous by faith, if we wish for man to be righteous through mercy. To that I respond, that these are correlative statements, we are righteous by faith, and we are righteous through mercy. But it is necessary that mention of faith be made, because it is fitting that there be some movement, by which we receive the gift, and apply it to ourselves. And when we name faith, let the mind gaze upon Christ, and consider the gratuitous mercy promised on account of him, and determine that you are reckoned righteous, not on account of any of your virtues, or actions, but on account of another outside of us, namely on account of Christ the mediator, sitting at the right hand of the father, interceding for us. Meanwhile, this very movement of faith in our souls is not an idle thought, but it struggles with the terrors of sin, with death, it fights with the devil, who in horrible ways attacks weak minds, so that he may drive them either to the contempt of God, or to despair, just as Cain, Saul, Judas, and innumerable others, after they determined that they were cast off by God, furiously hated God, others become atheists or Epicureans, like Pharaoh, when in great miseries they spurn the word of God, and divine consolation, nor do they sustain themselves by faith, but broken in spirit they yield to the devil, just as the impious cry out in adverse circumstances: There are truly no Divinities for us, since the ages are snatched away by blind chance. But those who hear the Gospel, who know that it is the work of God to lead down to the underworld and to lead back, in such an agony sustain themselves by faith, they take refuge to Christ the leader. They know him to be the victor, who crushes the head of the serpent, or as it is said elsewhere, destroys the works of the devil, and has always been present with his own from the very beginning. Wherefore, aided by the Son of God, they conquer the devil, nor do they fall away from God. For the struggle is about this matter; the devil urges souls to fall away from God. On the contrary, faith struggles so that it may not lose God, so that it may not be torn away from God; it establishes that there is a God, who although he punishes, nevertheless added a gratuitous promise of mercy on account of his Son, gave the Son as a helper, and promised eternal salvation. Therefore, God is discerned in his word, and the mind, looking into the word and confirmed by faith, does not fall away from God, but acknowledging his mercy, calls upon him, awaits liberation, and submits itself to the will of God, nor does it allow itself to be torn away from him. And the praise of the victory belongs to Christ the leader, who helps his own, just as he himself says: Without me you can do nothing. Those who experience these things in life and in invocation are able to understand the doctrine concerning faith, and at the same time know how to judge that we are righteous, that is, accepted by God on account of Christ, and yet in the meantime it is necessary that faith be kindled in us, which is the true knowledge of God, nor can it be retained without the most bitter struggle.

Now therefore I shall add testimonies which show that faith does not only signify knowledge of history, but trust in mercy, struggling with despair and contempt of God.

I. Romans 4.Paul compares the promise and faith, as correlatives, teaching that the promise must be received by faith, therefore faith signifies trust, which relies upon the divine promise. This testimony is so clear that it cannot be shaken by any calumnies. Therefore it is by faith and according to grace, so that the promise may be firm, that is, I demand faith, by which the promise of reconciliation may be received.

II. Ephesians 3.Through whom we dare to approach confidently through faith in him. What more illustrious testimony do you require, reader? For now I do not litigate with sycophants, but I address pious and candid readers, I exhort them, and for the sake of Christ's glory I beseech them, that they may diligently weigh these testimonies. Paul here declares the nature of faith with three notable words, he says that we have by faith παῤῥησίαν προσαγωγην καὶ πεποίθησιν . These do not befit a knowledge of history, which rather deters, if it must be thought that we will then approach Christ when we are worthy. It is necessary, therefore, that faith be understood as trust in mercy. Nor will this interpretation be able to be shaken by the cavil of Cochlaeus, who says: If faith and trust were the same, he would not add, as an effect, trust through faith. O Carneadean sharpness. One movement in the heart is described with several words. And since faith is here the movement by which we approach God, it certainly cannot be only a knowledge of history, which rather deters minds, as I said. So alsoRom. 5.he speaks: Through whom we have access by faith.

III. Romans. 5.Being justified by faith we have peace. Knowledge of history by no means brings peace of conscience, but rather increases terrors, when the opinion of the law is retained. For what sign is more terrible of the wrath of God against sin, than that God did not wish to be appeased by any other victim, except by the death of his son. This thought increases terrors, when we think that the benefit of Christ does not pertain, except to those who bring enough merits. Therefore when faith raises up terrified minds and consoles them, it is necessary that trust in mercy be understood. And since Paul sufficiently shows that he is speaking of faith struggling with terrors, his sayings cannot be understood concerning the mere knowledge of history.

IIII. Colos. 2.In whom also you have been raised through faith of the efficacy of God. He says that we have been sanctified by faith, that is, by trust, that God is efficacious in us.

V. John. 5.He who does not believe God, makes him a liar, because he does not believe the testimony, that God has given eternal life &c. He refers faith to the promise, and demands that the promise be believed, to which if anyone does not assent, he accuses God of a lie, as if he does not perform what is promised. Furthermore to assent to the promise, is trust in mercy.

VI. Romans. 4.Who against hope believed in hope. I ask you, Christian reader, is it not necessary in this place to interpret the word, believed, as trust? There is no need to seek the meaning from afar. Abraham is praised because he believed that God would fulfill his promises, even though nature resisted. Thus it is fitting for the pious to be instructed concerning faith, so that when we are destitute of human supports, we nevertheless expect help from God, and do not lose God. And somewhat later in the same chapter he opposes faith to doubting: Abraham did not doubt through distrust. He speaks, therefore, of faith struggling with doubt, in receiving the promise.

VII. Mark. 9.I believe Lord, help my unbelief. Here it is not a matter of knowledge of history, but of trust, by which the father expected the liberation of his son. Thus in the Evangelical examples faith for the most part signifies trust seeking and expecting benefits, as in the history of the Canaanite womanMatt. 15.who, twice repulsed by Christ, and indeed with a reproach, nevertheless does not omit her prayers, and with admirable wisdom refutes the saying of Christ, confesses herself to be unworthy of the benefit, but nevertheless on account of the Lord's goodness expects the gift. Christ adorns the faith of this ethnic woman with a weighty testimony, saying: O woman, great is your faith, let it be done to you as you ask. Why should we doubt here and in similar histories, that by faith is signified trust seeking and expect ing those benefits, which since it ought to shine in every invocation, it is necessary that the pious be rightly taught concerning it. But the monks command us to remember the history, then they say that it must be doubted whether God is propitious to us, or whether He regards our prayers. This doctrine fights entirely with that most praiseworthy example of the woman and similar ones and abolishes true worships of God, true invocation.

VIII. Description of faith, ad Ebreos. 11. shows and there by faith is signified trust, because he says: Faith is ὑπόστασις , that is the expectation of things to be hoped for. This is truly the grammatical explanation of the word, as all learned men know. Furthermore, that expectation is trust in the promise.

IX. Actorum. 15.Purifying their hearts by faith. It is certain, however, that hearts are not purified by the knowledge of history. And there he soon interprets the saying, he says that neither the fathers, nor any others had pure hearts on account of the righteousness of the law, but he says that hearts are thus purified, if they believe that they are purified through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore he testifies that by faith is signified trust, which relies on the mercy promised on account of Christ.

X. Roman. 10.Everyone who believes in Him will not be put to shame. Here Paul himself distinguishes the benefit of the Gospel from the law, and he speaks not of the mere knowledge of history, but of trust, by which we determine certainly that God is propitious to us on account of Christ, not on account of the law. The same sen This sentiment is often repeated in the prophets.Psal. 2.Kiss the son. Blessed are all who trust in him. Here it is necessary that trust be understood. For he commands the son of God to be acknowledged, he commands us to trust in this Lord. Since, however, the condition of the law cannot be stitched on, for faith cannot partly rely on Christ and partly on the law, it is necessary that faith be understood as trust, which establishes that we are freed through the son of God from sin and from the tyranny of the devil.

XI. 1. Paralip. 20.Believe in the Lord your God, and you shall be secure. The army was standing in readiness, and was commanded to seek and certainly expect help from God. Wherefore it is not a matter there of the knowledge of history, but trust is commanded, which seeks help from God. These testimonies show quite clearly that by the word of faith, trust is signified. And diligent students will discover more examples in the reading of the prophets. I am not ignorant, however, that tricks can be found to elude these testimonies. And there is now a wonderful petulance of minds; some will criticize these out of ambition, others out of malevolence, others out of hatred of true piety. But I pray and beseech pious readers that they diligently weigh this interpretation, and consider that, if it is deleted, huge inconveniences follow, firm consolation is snatched away from consciences, true invocation is abolished, the benefit of Christ is obscured. Sophistry must be removed from all life, but most of all it must be warded off from the Churches, nor are the games of minds to be endured, which fashion, in the manner of painters, whatever they please. Simple truth necessary to the church should be retained, and let us take care that this be transmitted uncorrupted to posterity. God demands this duty from all, and especially from the governors of doctrine or of the republic, and it is a debt of the Church. Nor is any worship more pleasing to God. Thus, therefore, let the sentences cited by Paul also be understood: Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him for righteousness, that is, Abraham acknowledged that he was not righteous on account of the law, or his own virtues, he acknowledged the infirmity of nature, which produces many vices, doubts about God, and variously wandering desires, he also remembers his errors committed among the Chaldeans, where he was contaminated by impious cults. But because he afterwards heard the promise concerning the seed, and God had said to him: I will be your protector, he determined that the remission of sins was granted to him through mercy, and that he had a propitious God, a defender, and a savior. Thus he is pronounced righteous by faith, that is, by confidence in divine mercy, even if he sees that nature is infirm and vicious. Often, however, faith not only struggles concerning the remission of sins, or concerning acceptance, but is also occupied with external objects, as the faith of David concerning the single combat with Goliath. These examples also pertain here, for faith receiving the remission of sins always precedes this faith expecting bodily help. The mind does not determine that we are helped by God, unless it first determines that He is propitious. By this rule He shows that Paul correctly cites testimonies concerning faith, and he instructs us in invocation.

I shall add sayings from the ancient writers. Augustine says: From the law we fear God, by faith we flee to mercy. Augustine is correct, nor can this be understood concerning the mere knowledge of history.

Chrysostom in the commentary on the Epistle to Rom. chapter 4. says: By faith, we not only love God, but we also believe that we are loved by Him, although we are manifoldly guilty, and that our sins are forgiven us. And this worship is more excellent than the others, and glorifies God more than the other worships of works, such as not stealing, not killing. Although Chrysostom often runs off the path, yet this saying is rightly celebrated. For he illustrated the nature of faith clearly, and so to speak, in vivid colors when he says that it must be believed that we are loved by God, although ὑπεύτυνοι, and we receive the remission of sins. καυχᾶται γὰρ πάλιν ὅ πιστὸς, οὐχ ὅτι τὸν θεὸν ἐφίλησε μόνον γνησίως ἀλλ' ὅτι κὰι πολλῆς παρ' αὐτοῦ τιμῆς ἀπήλαυσε κὰι ἀγάπης. ὥσπερ γὰρ αὐτὸς αὐτὸν ἠγάπησε, μεγάλα περὶ αὐτοῦ φαντασθεὶς, τοῦ το γὰρ ἀγάπης δεῖγμα, ὅυτω κὰι θέος αὐτον ἐφίλησε μυρίοις ὑπευθυνον ὄντα, οὐχί κολάσεως ἀπαλλάξας μόνον, ἀλλὰ κὰι δίκαιον ἐργασάμενος.

The voice of Bernard is worthy to be celebrated, whose words in the sermon on the annunciation are these: It is necessary first of all to believe that you cannot have the remission of sins, except through the indulgence of God. But add still that you believe also this, that through him sins are forgiven TO YOU. This is the testimony which the Holy Spirit bears in your heart, saying: your sins are forgiven you. For thus the Apostle judges, that a man is justified freely through faith. There exist also some similar sentiments in this writer, although a recent one, but yet not unskilled in spiritual exercises, in which he learned that the conscience cannot find rest, unless it determines by faith that sins are forgiven freely on account of Christ. He understands faith, therefore, as we do, as trust. I said, however, above that we include the knowledge of history, or all the articles of faith, and when faith contemplates this article: I believe the remission of sins, it is necessary that trust be conceived, that we truly receive this benefit. For the others, who understand faith only as the knowledge of history, do not believe this article: The remission of sins, just as they also openly command one to doubt concerning the remission of sins.

I think I have said enough concerning the term, which I hope will satisfy the pious, the candid, and those who love the truth. Now the sophistry of Origen, of the monks, and of many others must be censured, who κατὰ συνεκδοχὴν they think it is said: We are justified by faith, that is, on account of the knowledge of the history concerning Christ, or profession, and other virtues, or universal obedience, we are righteous. Thus they understand faith, and they think that profession is praised by Paul, because even if the profession is common with the wicked, yet without it other virtues, as in the Turks, would not please God. Thus this synecdoche transforms the Gospel into law, transfers the glory of Christ to our virtues, deletes the consolation of consciences, abolishes the true doctrine concerning faith, that is, trust in mercy. Indeed, the monks even command one to doubt concerning the remission of sins. For they see that doubts concerning the will of God naturally cling in human minds. Therefore they confirm them, nor do they think these vices are darkness born with us, just like the Academic philosophers or Pyrrhonists. More copiously, therefore, below in the commentary I will refute this synecdoche, which fights with the whole disputation of Paul. We retain τὸ ῥητὸν among Paul: We are justified by faith freely, that is, we obtain the remission of sins and the imputation of righteousness before God, not on account of any of our merits, but by faith, that is, by trust in the mercy promised on account of Christ. Therefore we do not attach a synecdoche to Paul, we do not change his sermon, but we learn from him, we retain the sentiment, which both the propriety of speech and the series of the disputation effect. I hope With the words narrated, the proposition is to be understood, We are justified by faith freely. But it is very profitable for the pious to have certain testimonies and confirmations of this proposition at hand and in sight, both for instructing minds and for exciting faith and invocation. Therefore, elsewhere I have gathered many sentences from Paul concerning this proposition. Here it may suffice to have pointed out the principal passages. At the end ofchapter 3 to the Romans Paul delivers this proposition clearly and at length, then he adapts to the proposition, as the series of the disputation demanded, the most weighty and most learned confirmations, which indeed are to be fixed in the minds, so that they may kindle faith and shine before us in all dangers.

I have spoken concerning justification and concerning faith. Now I shall briefly add the doctrine concerning good works or concerning new obedience, which ought to follow faith. But these four things are asked: What works are to be done? How can they be done? How do they please, and whether the regenerate are just on account of new obedience, that is, accepted by God for eternal life, or whether they are without sin and worthy of eternal life on account of their own purity. Fourthly, it is asked concerning the distinction of sins, which cast out grace, faith, and the Holy Spirit. Which are called venial.

On the first question, What works are to be done. It is right to lead minds to the word of God, so that they may know that their whole life, in the struggle of conscience, and in actions, must be governed by the word of God, as the prophet says: Lucerna pedibus meis verbum tuum. I answer therefore, that the works to be done are those commanded to us by God. And let a certain word be proposed, namely, the decalogue as it is repeated and explained in the New Testament, and if there are any other precepts concerning morals in the sermons of Christ and the Apostles. This must be said for this reason, lest men think it permissible for worship and works to be fashioned by our own judgment without a command from God, just as the Enthusiasts in all times, that is, formerly the monks and now the Anabaptists, having omitted and cast aside the word of God, chose works by their own judgment, afterwards pretending that they were thus incited by the Spirit, and that the spirit should not be hindered by the law. Hence followed the horrible ἀνομία of the Anabaptists. Furthermore, it will be said below what it is to be freed from the law; now I say this briefly, that those reborn by faith, as has been said, receive the Holy Spirit, so that a new obedience, light, and eternal life may be begun in them, which is a certain beginning of the divine law within us. Therefore it is said in the prophet: I will put my law in their hearts. This beginning must necessarily follow faith, as many sentences testify: If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments. Item, Unless your righteousness shall abound &c. Item. Fornicators, adulterers, shall not inherit the kingdom of God. And the Holy Spirit moves hearts through the word of God. Therefore obedience must be governed by the certain word of God, to which we ought to submit, as Paul says: We are debtors, not to live according to the flesh. Nor can faith exist without repentance, because the remission of sins must be received by faith. But he who delights in wickedness against his conscience does not seek remission. Nor is merely external discipline demanded, but the beginning of interior obedience. Namely, the pious motions of the heart consenting with the law of God. Clearly, our Adversaries, when they shout about good works, clamor about childish discipline, about modesty in dress, in food and drink, and sometimes they say something about alms. Meanwhile, there is silence regarding the works of the first table, about which, since they are ignorant of the doctrine of faith, they can say nothing. But God demands the duties of both tables. He wants us to be terrified, recognizing His wrath against our manifold infirmity and our infinite errors. He wants us, reconciled through the Son, to believe that He has received us into grace, that He wishes to save us, to help us. By this faith He wants to be invoked, He wants help to be sought from Him and expected according to the psalm 49. Call upon me &c. He wants us to depend on Him by faith, not to seek protections against His will. These are the secret acts of worship, and proper to Christians, which it behooves us to understand, and

whose examples are seen in those excellent men, whom God has set before us as teachers in Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, Samuel, David, Jeremiah, Daniel, and the like. He also wishes us to burn with a desire for knowing, propagating, and adorning the Gospel. He teaches that all are especially created, reborn, and called for this worship. As Peter says: Called out of darkness, that you may declare and celebrate the benefits of God. And in Psalm 34. I will confess to you in the great Church. And in Psalm 115. I will pay my vows to the Lord before all his people, in the courts of the house of our God. He wishes us to show constancy in the profession of the Gospel, obedience in afflictions, and to seek and expect help from Him. He wishes us to take care, lest we stir up scandals by our errors or bad examples, He wishes us to refute and hate impious dogmas, not to collude with the instruments of the devil, which attempt to destroy the Gospel. But I have not instituted here an exposition of the decalogue, into which, however, it is always fitting for the pious to look, and to consider how many, great, and arduous duties it embraces.

Concerning the second question. But in this our infirmity how can such great works, interior and exterior, be effected? Although exterior discipline can in some way be performed by human diligence, yet spiritual motions cannot be effected without the Holy Spirit, therefore with faith hearts are raised up, the Holy Spirit is given, so that He may kindle a new light in souls, and stir up pious motions, agreeing with the law of God, according to that of Paul: that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith. And of Zechariah. 12. I will pour out upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem the Spirit of grace and of supplications. Most beautifully the Prophet signified the chief offices of the Holy Spirit in the hearts of the pious, and the chief acts of worship. He names the Spirit of grace, because when we are raised up by faith, we are helped by the Holy Spirit, so that we may establish for ourselves that God is propitious, and that we in turn are acceptable to Him. Therefore, first He signifies that faith is stirred up by the Holy Spirit, in which motion He gives us testimony, as Paul says. With faith we now acknowledge the mercy and presence of God, we call upon Him, and we subject ourselves to Him, and we begin to perform the other true acts of worship, all of which he embraces under the name of supplications. For this is the highest honor. Therefore it can be sufficiently understood that the faith of which we speak is also the beginning of the remaining interior obedience, and as it is called, of a good purpose. Nor could the first commandment be begun, which preaches of the wrath of God against sin, not of gratuitous forgiveness, unless, having first heard the Gospel, we established that we through faith on account of Christ freely obtain the remission of sins.

Faith, however, looks upon the Son of God reigning, and I know that He is not idle, but is assiduously waging war with the Devil, so that he does not cease to rage against the members of Christ with the greatest savagery and cunning; he entices them with snares into sins, into sad misfortunes, so that from there he may drag them into despair; he pours out errors, he confirms Epicurean opinions, which flatter gentle minds; he incites tyrants, so that with giant-like audacity they may attempt to erase the name of Christ, and exercise the most unjust cruelty. Since, however, it is sufficiently evident that human nature is far too weak to be able to overcome such a vigilant and rabid enemy without heavenly aid, therefore faith remembers the kingdom of Christ; it knows that He, after the first promise, has always been present to the pious, when it was said, Semen mulieris conteret caput serpentis, which sentence John renders with these words: Christus apparuit ut destruat opera diaboli. He was present to Jacob and blessed him, and confirmed him with the Holy Spirit; He was present to Daniel, and indeed speaks with him. Thus He reigns, therefore, so that He may be present to His members, confirm them with His Spirit, and protect them against the snares and attacks of the devil. What kind and how glorious such victories are, the examples of David, Hezekiah, Daniel, and the like signify, and Christ will show these triumphs in the resurrection of the dead, even if the world now neglects and mocks such great things. But the pious are not altogether ignorant of these battles, and individuals ought to exercise faith in their own dangers, and to acknowledge, and to invoke Christ as leader, and to do battle with the devil by trust in him, nor to forget the words of John: For this purpose the Son of God appeared, that he might destroy the works of the devil. From this it can be understood that faith is not an idle speculation, but a light governing all actions and all dangers. We can therefore begin obedience, aided by the reigning Son of God, who is present with us as a leader, and imparts the Holy Spirit. For it must not be thought that Christ reigns idly, just as poets imagine Jupiter to be leading banquets idly in heaven. Such are the darknesses in the minds of men concerning God. But these errors are to be corrected by the light of the Gospel and by faith. Concerning these exercises of faith, and concerning true invocation, what can our adversaries say, who instead of the Gospel concerning faith teach us the philosophy of the Pyrrhonists concerning doubt?

Concerning the third question. This is less explained in the Ancients than the former ones, although it is most necessary. There remains in the reborn a huge weakness, they fear God less than they ought, they do not burn with faith and love, sometimes they seek human protections otherwise than is permitted, they err, they are negligent in duty, they become insolent in favorable circumstances, they have immoderate affections, loves, hatreds, they desire unconceded pleasures, they rage in afflictions against God, they doubt the mercy of God, they are tormented by diffidence, they are inflamed by an unjust desire for vengeance, they do not ardently strive to declare their gratitude to God, they do not give thanks with a burning heart for so many benefits, they do not value the Gospel highly enough, they coldly assist the propagation of the Gospel, they are not affected by the public calamities of the Church and the republic, they do not make vows for the Church, for princes, they are inflamed by unjust pursuits of seeking wealth, honors, power, they envy others whom they see excelling in virtue, or in other goods, and by emulation they sometimes excite scandals, just as emulation produced contumacy in the sister of Moses and Aaron. These are not to be considered light evils, but are vices fighting against the law of God, and worthy of eternal death, and they arise from great plagues, from the sin of origin, namely from the ignorance of God, and the aversion of the human will from God, concerning which vices, when Paul says: The sense of the flesh is enmity against God, he does not describe a light deformity, but a huge and atrocious evil. It is evident, therefore, that no one satisfies the law of God except Christ, and that in the saints remain vices fighting against the law of God, which are sins worthy of eternal death, unless they are forgiven. Since this is so, not only in the schools, but in the minds of all the pious, this question is perpetually agitated, and it stirs up no common dangers and struggles: Whether imperfect and contaminated obedience pleases God, and how it pleases. Therefore, it is necessary for the pious to be rightly taught concerning this question on both sides. Hypocrites, as is the infirmity of nature, please themselves, admire their own virtues, extenuate the infirmity of nature, and think that they are without sin, and satisfy the law of God, that they are worthy of eternal life, and merit eternal life. Such are not only the thoughts of hypocrites, but of all men judging according to reason. Thus Plato, thus Cicero argue concerning the immortality of the soul, that purer souls which have less contagion from bodies, that is, which have lived more modestly, fly up into the ether, but the more sluggish ones which have more contagion from bodies, that is, which have defiled themselves with the pleasures of the body, wander on the ground around the tombs. What else do monks say in reality, when they boast of their merits. Although human reason judges no otherwise by its own light, yet the word of God testifies that no one satisfies the law, it accuses men trusting in their own righteousness, and he proposes the mediator, the Son of God. It is necessary, therefore, that the arrogance and security of hypocrites be rebuked. Again, for fearful consciences there is need of true consolation, that they may learn that diffidence does not please God, but faith; they may learn also how life, morals, or works please, for these also must please. Peter, terrified in the boat, says: Depart from me, O Lord, for I am a sinner. Although in that consternation of mind he did not attend to what he was saying, yet, as happens in sudden movements, he expressed without simulation what his mind was feeling; he was fleeing from God, looking upon his own unworthiness. Thus all men, having beheld their own unworthiness, flee from God, and think they are doing rightly because, being unworthy, they do not wish to approach God. This error, fixed in human minds, the voice of the Gospel rebukes, which commands us to approach even though we are unworthy, but relying on the mediator, the Son of God. Although, therefore, a new obedience is necessary, as has been said, and the righteousness of a good conscience, yet the regenerate do not satisfy the law, and there remains in them the disease of origin, which, as has already been said often, should by no means be considered a light evil, and this disease begets innumerable depraved affections. Since these are vices worthy of eternal death, the regenerate, even after conversion, are not righteous, that is, accepted by God for eternal life on account of their own virtues, but through mercy freely by trust in the mediator Christ. Item not they merit eternal life by their own works or virtues. But they must establish that they are made heirs of eternal life on account of Christ freely by faith, and if faith, as has been said, must always be followed by new obedience. But that the saints do not satisfy the law, and that sins remain in them, the following sentences testify.

I. Psalm 142.Enter not into judgment with thy servant, for in thy sight shall no man living be justified.

II. 1 John 1. If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.

III. Romans 7.I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind, and bringing me into captivity to the law of sin. And often there Paul repeats the word sin, signifying that that disease is a vice truly fighting against the law of God, and worthy of eternal death, unless by faith he sought pardon. And he speaks not of the light titillation of the body, but of the most bitter motions of a mind doubting concerning the will of God, abhorring the cross, not erected with confidence and joy in God, as we are erected with joy, and acquiesce, when we see bodily protections. And from this diffidence arise many wicked counsels etc. Therefore he used two very illustrious words. ἀντιστρατευόμενον he says the disease rages in a hostile manner, wounding the mind, with diffidence, terrors, pride, confidence in one's own wisdom and just ciae, security, and to kindle flames with a variety of desires. And let not the enemy be seen as contemptible. αἰχμαλωτίζοντα , he oppresses weak souls, and captures them, and if the captured are freed through Christ, as Moses was captured, when he hesitated at the rock and lacked faith. David was captured, when he ordered the people to be numbered, by some human error, either because he was moved by glory, because he had increased the kingdom by his own deeds, or for other causes. But I omit examples, for there is no lack of many domestic examples for the pious, we ourselves experience how assiduous the enemy is, and how often he oppresses souls beyond our expectation. For the devil also attacks the pious at the same time.

IIII. 1. Corinthians. 4.I am conscious of nothing in myself, yet I am not justified by this, as if he were saying, even if the righteousness of a good conscience is necessary, nevertheless on account of it I am not just, that is, accepted before God for eternal life, but by faith in Christ.

V. Christ commands the saint to ask for the remission of sins: And forgive us our debts. Likewise he says: Say, we are unprofitable servants etc.

VI. Psalm. 129.If you, O Lord, should mark iniquities, Lord, who shall stand. He acknowledges that he has sins, and yet he determines that he pleases God through mercy, and he awaits salvation, therefore he adds: My soul has waited in his word, that is, I sustain myself with his divine promise, I approach him, I await salvation, and I rest in him, trusting in his goodness, that he is about to save me.

VII. Psalm. 18.Who understands his faults? Cleanse me from hidden ones. It is evident, however, that the prophet there, as elsewhere, speaks both of himself and of the other saints. Those very ones whom he calls servants of God, sanctified by the Holy Spirit, adorned with excellent gifts, occupied in the exercises of faith, in the governance of the greatest matters, such as Abraham, Joseph, Moses, Samuel, David, Isaiah, with one voice cry out thus: Who understands his faults? Cleanse me from hidden ones. Wherefore the arrogance of hypocrites is to be detested, who boast that they merit eternal life by their own works, and indeed, as they themselves say, by condignity.

VIII. Psalm. 31.I said I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord, and you forgive the sin of my heart. For this, every saint will pray to you in an opportune time. He openly testifies that the saints must seek the pardon of present vices and errors.

IX. Job. 9.I feared all my works.

X. Exodus. 34.And the innocent is not innocent before you, that is, even if he cannot be accused by human judgment, nevertheless he can be accused by you.

XI. To You, O Lord, belongs righteousness, but to us confusion of face, that is, I acknowledge that we have sins, and are justly punished by You. Then he adds: To us confusion, but to You mercy and propitiation, that is, I acknowledge that we are sinners, but You, on account of Your promised mercy, hear us again and deliver us.
