He repeats the same sentiment a little later, and proposes to us an example of faith and invocation: We do not ask on account of our righteousness, but on account of Your great mercy. These proclamations are repeated with great consensus in the sacred books; our infirmity is always accused, and we are commanded to flee by faith to mercy on account of the promised mediator, the Son of God. Thus also Paul does not accuse some part of men, but simply affirms that all men except Christ are guilty before God. Therefore he says: that every mouth may be stopped, and the whole world may thus be guilty before God. Item: He has concluded all under sin, that He might have mercy upon all. Item: He who glories, let him glory in the Lord. Let the pious propose these sentences to themselves, so that they may acknowledge that our infirmity is truly sin, and may tremble with fear of the wrath of God against sin. Thus let repentance grow in us. In the first proclamation concerning the final judgment, it is said in Genesis: Sin will rest until it is revealed. Here is described the security of the whole human race, neglecting the judgment of God. Sin, he says, will rest, that is, because God will defer punishments, all men will be of idle minds, they will despise threats, but yet at length sin will be brought forth, there it will not rest, but will strike eternal terrors into minds, it will bring horrible punishments. There is therefore a security fixed in the minds of all. This is the reason why all men extenuate their own infirmity, nor are they moved by the magnitude of the evil, even though the most grievous falls of the saints, and the huge calamities of men ought to admonish us, that we might determine that God is truly angry at this vice, and we might be moved by the voice of the Holy Spirit, reproving this sin.

That therefore begun obedience may please, let these three concur, First it must be determined that the person pleases freely by the faith of Christ, then let us acknowledge our infirmity to be truly sin, and let us truly grieve that we have these vices, but again let us raise ourselves and believe that they are pardoned to us on account of Christ after we have been made sons by faith, and that begun obedience pleases, not on account of its own cleanliness or dignity, but on account of the mediator Christ who since he is our high priest, now carries our prayers and worships to the father, thus Peter teaches: Offer spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God through Jesus Christ. He adorns good works with an honorific appellation, when he calls them sacrifices, for this word is suitable to the proper worships of God. And indeed he calls them spiritual sacrifices, that is, motions awakened in the heart by the Holy Spirit. And yet he says that these acts of worship are not accepted otherwise than through Jesus the redeemer and high priest continually interceding for us. In this way the pious are to be taught, and stirred up to do good works. God founded the human race for society especially for this reason, that He might become known among men, that they might be able to hand down the doctrine concerning God and the Son of God to one another, as Stigellius says rightly and elegantly:

That others might teach others about religion, piety commanded us to have contiguous houses.

And so He also attributed various duties to men, the government of the Church, of schools, marriage, the education of children, political government, wars, contracts. Furthermore, He subjected the Church to huge afflictions. For what purpose was this great variety of works instituted? For this very thing, that faith might shine and grow in these difficulties and dangers. Let him believe that we were not created by God for destruction, but that He wishes to receive and save us on account of Christ. Let him call upon Him, and let him determine that Christ the leader is present, who may restrain the Devil, and help us in private and public life. Let the governor of the Church cry out: O Lord, you will open my lips, and my mouth shall announce your praise. Let the teacher of youth consider how atrociously Christ has threatened those who stir up pernicious scandals for children; let him pray that Christ may rule their studies and morals. Let heads of families understand their dangers. Let good princes consider that they ought to rightly establish Churches, rule the morals of the people, punish Epicureans, robbers, the unchaste, thieves, liars, and administer justice, so that each may keep his own. Moreover, the devil studies especially to disturb Churches and empires; he arms tyrants against the Church; therefore, let faith burn in princes, which believes that Christ will help them and will destroy the works of the devil. Finally, as with invocation, so faith ought to shine before all actions. Although the virtues or works of the pious do not merit the remission of sins, nor eternal life, or rather are not the price of eternal life—for no one satisfies the law, and the merit of Christ ought not to be transferred into our works, and the promise would become uncertain if it depended on the condition of our worthiness—nevertheless, new obedience must necessarily follow faith, and indeed it is begun when we receive the Holy Spirit with faith. And faith and the Holy Spirit are cast out, with new obedience lost, when the commandments of God are violated against conscience. For faith and the purpose of acting against conscience cannot coexist. to be at the same time. To this pertain very many sayings about works. With the heart one believes unto righteousness, with the mouth confession is made unto salvation. Universal obedience ought to be a confession, that is, to be referred to celebrating the glory of Christ, and to propagating the Gospel. Although therefore we are righteous and heirs of eternal life on account of Christ, nevertheless this obedience must be present, and it is pleasing as has been said, nor could faith exist without that obedience. Therefore also elsewhere Paul says: we shall be clothed upon, if so be that we shall not be found naked. On account of Christ eternal life is given, but it is given to the believer, in which faith eternal life is begun, which beginning is new obedience. Our dignity is excluded, so that its own honor may be attributed to Christ, and so that the promise may be certain, and we may have firm consolation against despair. There was therefore also in the thief converted on the cross new obedience, repentance was present, for he seeks himself to have sinned. And a wonderful light of faith arose in this cast-off man, and God shows by this example that He wonderfully preserves and restores the Church in extreme difficulties. The apostles having slipped away were doubting about the master, they had seen the magnitude of the calamity, wherefore they were thinking him to be deserted by God. But the thief is not deterred by this appearance from seeking salvation from him, he had heard a little before this voice: Father forgive them, he had heard also certain of his deeds and the kind of profession. He was seeing the nature of things, with the sun darkened, and the earthquake to bear witness concerning him. With great force, therefore, he invokes him, saying: Remember me, O Lord, when you shall come into your kingdom. How great was this light of faith, that he recognizes this companion in punishment and one already dying to be the Messiah who forgives sins, and who will give eternal life once death is abolished, and who will reign after this life. The apostles had previously thought in prosperous times that he would be king, once the Romans were driven out. But this man, while dying together with him, proclaims that he will reign after death. In turn, therefore, Christ also testifies that he will reign, that he is the giver of eternal life, and he proposes to the thief absolution and the Gospel concerning eternal life, so that he may kindle and confirm his faith. Today you shall be with me in Paradise. Confirmed by this voice, the thief recognizes that he does not have eternal life on account of his own merits, but on account of this Lord. And simultaneously with this faith and consolation, eternal life is begun in him, which is new obedience toward God. See, I pray, for this apostle, while hanging, preached from on high not only to that assembly which was then present, but to the entire future Church. How illustrious an image is proposed, from which it must be learned that we are saved freely on account of Christ through faith, and yet that repentance and other good fruits must be present. In this thief are seen: repentance, faith, invocation, confession or preaching. It is certain, however, that these are the principal good works and the highest acts of worship of God. He added also another notable work, and one especially necessary, whenever Christ is treated badly it is said, he harshly chastises the slanderer, and defends the glory of Christ. Thus we too ought to tax with true ardor of spirit the impious teachers, tyrants, and their satellites, who speak insults to Christ. And it often comes to my mind that this preacher is especially signified in the last times of the Church, wherefore let us listen to him diligently, and consider his example attentively, and imitate it.

But after it pleases in this way, as I have said, new obedience, although eternal life is given freely on account of Christ, nevertheless it also compensates our labors, actions, and miseries. Therefore Christ says: your reward is abundant in the heavens. And although they do not merit eternal life, nevertheless they merit their own corporal and spiritual rewards, which happen both in this life and after this life. For since God wishes to preserve the Church among men, he imparts many corporal benefits. There is need of sustenance, civil peace, and other comforts of life. There is also need of spiritual benefits, prudence, erudition, fortitude, successes in one's vocation. Therefore Christ says: Seek first the kingdom of God, and the rest shall be added unto you. And Paul: Godliness has promises of the present and future life. AndMark 10.He shall receive a hundredfold in this life, but with persecution. And the fourth commandment says: that you may be long-lived upon the earth. And Christ: Give, and it shall be given to you. AndMatt. 10.Whoever shall have given a drink of water to one of the least, on account of doctrine, shall not lose his reward. Finally Promises concerning bodily and spiritual benefits are extant throughout the sermons of the prophets, as it is said in Esaiae. 33. concerning the pious: Bread shall be given to them, and they shall see the king flourishing, that is, they shall have sustenance, tranquil commonwealths, etc. The widow of Sarepta received the prophet Elijah into hospitality, when the grain supply was most scarce. Here, first consider the faith of the woman, then the work, finally the admirable rewards. The prophet commands that the little bit of food that remained be offered to him, and he adds a promise, as the reading of the history shows. The woman obeys this voice, even though she saw that nothing remained beyond these remnants. The woman would not have exercised this liberality, unless, raised by faith, she had thought that God must be obeyed, the prophet must be helped, and in turn a benefit must be expected from God. She receives, therefore, the reward of faith and almsgiving; the family is nourished divinely until the grain supply became more abundant; the dead son is also restored, by which miracle the faith of the mother was more confirmed, and the youth was called to piety, who indeed Epiphanius writes was the prophet Jonah, who afterwards preached to the Assyrian king in Nineveh, and propagated the word of God widely and happily. Thus, in all times the Saints received not only spiritual benefits, but also very many bodily ones, for the preservation of the Church, and others were adorned with other gifts, as it seemed good to God. He keeps Paul safe for a time, while He wishes him to perform his ministry, and meanwhile He provides for him hospitality and other comforts of life. Thus also Paul to the Corinthians he writes concerning the pestilence, that they are chastised with that punishment on account of their vices, and that if they were to perform penance, the punishments would cease. Just as Zechariah also says: Turn to me, and I will turn to you, that is, I will mitigate the calamities and punishments, if you perform penance. Nor does he speak of one work only, but of true conversion and fruits. From these it can be sufficiently understood, both how begun obedience is pleasing, and what rewards it has. Moreover, many things ought to kindle the zeal for working well: the commandment of God, likewise that faith is extinguished when obedience is lost, likewise that they are punished with present and eternal punishments, both the loss of faith, and other offenses. Likewise, offenses are often punished by blindness and sins. Again, not only does the promise invite one to believe, and to retain faith, but also the commandment of God. For He commands that we believe in the Son. Let it invite one to exercise faith in good works, because without exercises faith does not grow, as the parable of the talent shows. And rightly that of Augustine, love merits the increase of love, for he is not speaking of imputation, but of gifts. Gifts grow by use, and merit increases. Let the greatness of the mercy of God also invite one, that this miserable, beggarly, and so variously contaminated obedience, He nevertheless approves and indicates that He is affected with honor through it. Let other rewards necessary for life and the Church, and to be sought in their own place, which are proposed for the exercises of faith, also invite one, as Life, peace, good success in vocations, in studies, in the government of the Church and the republic, the piety, virtue, and happiness of children. These are huge rewards, but such is the blindness of the world, that it is not only lightly affected by the command of God, and the mention of eternal punishments and eternal salvation, but also does not sufficiently understand how much need there is for bodily benefits, and how much it matters to use them rightly. Let us therefore pray to God for the sake of our Lord Jesus Christ, who intercedes for us, that He may rouse us to true piety, instruct and govern us by giving the Holy Spirit. Just as He promised that He would give the Holy Spirit to those who ask.

Concerning the fourth question. Concerning the distinction of sins. For when we say that the remnants of sin remain in the reborn, and at the same time faith exists, it is necessary that sins be distinguished so that no one may think that adulteries and similar outrages can exist with faith. I have spoken, however, in the common places, somewhat more lengthily about the distinction between mortal and venial sin. Therefore, here I will admonish the reader in a few words. Since we have been justified by faith, there must follow in works the righteousness of a good conscience. The doctrine of Christ openly and often establishes this degree. As 1. Timothy 1. The sum of the commandment is love from a pure heart, and a good conscience, and faith unfeigned. And again in the same chapter: Wage a good warfare, having faith and a good conscience. And 2. Corinthians 1. This is our boasting, the testimony of our conscience. And.1. John 3.If our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence toward God, for he teaches that those who have the purpose of violating the commandment of God against conscience cannot call upon God. And1. Peter 3.With modesty and fear, having a good conscience. Therefore also to the Galatians. 5. it is said: The works of the flesh are manifest, adultery, fornication, uncleanness, idolatry, etc. They who do such things shall not possess the kingdom of God. For he calls them manifest for this reason, because he condemns the deeds which those who know them commit against conscience. Wherefore also PaulRom. 8.distinguishes sins: If you live according to the flesh, you shall die. If you mortify the actions of the flesh by the Spirit, you shall live. There are actions of the flesh in the saints, that is, vicious affections; when these are resisted by the Spirit, that is, not with hypocrisy, but when vicious affections are restrained with the true fear of God and true faith, the saints remain in grace, they retain the Holy Spirit and faith. Nor are these things done without a great struggle in the souls. Various are the allurements of the world, turbulent are the impulses in our flesh. And the devil is intent upon the occasions through which he might be able to impel souls. Therefore we have need of vigilance, and of faith and invocation. For the victory is of Christ conquering the devil in us. But nevertheless our discipline ought to be added, and help must be sought by faith, just as Peter says: Watch, because the devil as a roaring lion goes about, seeking whom he may devour. And concerning discipline: I chastise my body, and

I bring into servitude. Let the fear of God resist depraved desires and allurements, let faith seek help and the pardon of infirmity, let it gather arguments which show the magnitude and the punishments of sin, both perpetual and present. As Joseph, solicited by the allurements of his mistress, resisted not without a struggle both the fury of the woman and the snares of the devil. He saw that the devil was doing this, first so that, polluted by the crime, he might tear him away from God, despoil him of the gift of prophecy and other divine ornaments, and excite a scandal to weaken the doctrine which Joseph professed, so that God might be cursed and true religion, which had recently shone forth, might be extinguished there. This one little pleasure would have dragged along such a great ruin. For the devil looks far ahead and weaves webs for us that are afterwards inextricable, as David experienced and many pious people experience. Gathering all these arguments, Joseph raised himself by faith against the allurements and dangers, and while he restrained himself by discipline, he truly sought heavenly help. Thus our Leader, the Son of God, through Joseph overcame and broke the attempts of the devil. When in this way the pious resist infirmity and by faith seek help and pardon, they do not lose grace, the Holy Spirit, and faith. And such infirmity is commonly called venial sin in the saints.

There are other lapses against conscience, which they call The Greeks φονικὰς ἁμαρτίας . And Paul says: The works of the flesh are manifest, namely, when someone violates the commandments of God against their conscience, either by indulging a depraved affection and not resisting it, as Saul hated David, or by adding an external crime, as David snatched another man's wife. Those committing such offenses lose grace, grieve and cast out the Holy Spirit, and cast away faith, and unless they do penance and are converted again to the faith, dying they are cast into eternal torments. Nor is there need for disputes about predestination to be brought here. We ought to pronounce upon our deeds, and upon the will and judgment of God, according to the expressed word of God. If David had not repented, he would have been cast into eternal torments, just like Saul. Security is deeply fixed in the minds of men, especially the idle. Therefore, we must beware lest we indulge this evil, which is confirmed by various pretexts. Let us set before ourselves the word of God, according to that: Thy word is a lamp to my feet. That testifies that grace is lost, and the Holy Spirit is cast out through such falls. asRom. 8.If you live according to the flesh you shall die.Matth. 12.Concerning the devil returning to those from whom he had been cast out. He goes and takes seven other spirits more wicked than himself, and entering they dwell there, and the last state becomes worse than the first.Matth. 13.concerning the seed which is choked by worldly things allurements.1. Corinth. 6.Do not err, neither fornicators, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor thieves, shall possess the kingdom of God. And he testifies that he is preaching to those who had previously obtained the benefits of Christ. He commands these to beware lest they lose them. Item1. Corinth. 10.Do not become idolaters, let us not commit fornication, as some of them committed fornication, and twenty-three thousand men perished in one day.Ad Galatas. 5.Those who do such things shall not obtain the kingdom of God. And then. He who sows in the flesh, shall reap destruction, He who sows in the Spirit, shall reap eternal life.1. Themoth. 5.If anyone does not have care for his own, he has denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel.Ad Ebreos. 13.God will judge fornicators and adulterers.2. Petri 2.If, when they had escaped the pollutions of the world through the knowledge of the Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, they are again entangled in them and overcome, the latter state becomes worse for them than the former.Matth. 10.Whoever shall deny me before men, I will deny him before my heavenly Father.Matth. 24.He who shall have persevered to the end, this one shall be saved.Matth. 25.Depart from me, you cursed, into eternal fire. I was hungry and you did not give me to eat, etc.1. Corinth. 13.If I should have all faith, but do not have love, I am nothing. Although we are not justified, that is, accepted by God, on account of our virtues or works, nevertheless it is necessary that an incipient obedience exist in us, according to that saying. He who by the Spirit They are led by God, these are the sons of God.1. John 3.In this the sons of God are manifest, and the sons of the devil. He who does not do justice is not of God. He who does not love his brother, remains in death. Little children, let no one deceive you. He who does justice, is just. He who commits sin, is of the devil. Human security diminishes the magnitude of our falls, but see how atrocious these threats are, what could be said more terrible, than what he says: He who commits sin, is of the devil, that is, he is a captive of the devil, he is agitated and driven by him, deserted by the Holy Spirit, cast away from God. Just as events also testify. How many crimes and calamities did one fall of David produce? After lust conquered, with another's wife snatched away, he orders the husband to be killed, and together many citizens, holy and strong men perish, the name of God is afflicted with insult. Afterwards the son stirs up sedition, the wives of the father are snatched away for rape by the son, with a nefarious and more than tragic crime, many thousands of citizens are killed. Finally, sedition cannot but produce innumerable scandals and crimes. From the idolatry of Solomon what evils arose? The kingdom of Israel was torn apart, and perpetual idolatry followed, and internal wars. The fall of Adam what evils did it then produce? The devil does this, so that he may weave such webs, when he notices us diminishing sins, and flattering ourselves, and loosening the rein on desires. Thus faith is extinguished. For the faith which He seeks the remission of sins, he cannot be among those who take pleasure in sin knowingly, and are without repentance, according to that saying: Where shall God dwell? In a contrite spirit, trembling at my words. For they do not wish to be freed from sin, who knowingly take pleasure in it. Let the saying of John therefore admonish us, whence sin arises, how great an enemy we have, whither it looks, and let us learn to exercise faith, so that Christ may conquer this enemy in us.

Thus far I have set forth the sum of the doctrine of the Gospel, concerning justification, as it is called, or concerning grace, concerning reconciliation, concerning faith, and concerning good works. Since, however, this opinion is plain and clear, since it has nothing of absurdity, or perplexity, or sophistry, since it speaks of movements which are known to pious minds in the Church, does not dispute about idle subtleties, since it illustrates the glory of Christ, since it uncovers the magnitude of human infirmity, finally since it best agrees with the perpetual consensus of the entire scripture, of the old and new testament, since all the pious in all times in the Church experience this consolation to be true and necessary, it is a wonder in the adversaries, partly that there is such darkness that they do not approve it, partly such fury that they do not cease to attack it with every wickedness. But the devil manifoldly pours errors into human minds, so that he may obscure the glory of Christ. Therefore let the pious pray that Christ may preserve his Gospel, and not allow it to be blotted out everywhere, and may govern us with his light, and show the truth to as many as possible, having driven away the clouds which the devil pours forth. Let our diligence also invite Christ, let the learned apply themselves, so that they may set forth this great cause diligently and clearly, so that they may take care that it be transmitted to posterity, without sophistry, and let them not shrink from labor in learning and teaching, or from struggles in confession. For this cause cannot be explained clearly enough without erudition. And a certain greatness of soul is needed to endure the hatreds of the powerful and the wise, who disapprove of these disputations, some for one reason, some for another. But it behooves the pious συναγωνίζεσθαι τῶ εὐαγγελίω , as Christ says: In this is my heavenly father glorified, if you shall be my disciples, and bring forth abundant fruit. Therefore let us set forth the doctrine in good faith, simply and rightly, and let us pray that God may add the holy spirit, and grant, as Paul calls it, the increase. I will add, however, a few arguments by which the adversaries attempt to weaken our opinion. The chief testimony is in James: Not by faith only, but by works. The answer is very easy, James calls faith the knowledge of history, for he says that the demons believe. But Paul calls faith something far different, namely, the trust in mercy promised on account of Christ. He therefore reproves the error of those who thought themselves to be righteous on account of their professio not the history. This is a work that is indeed necessary, like other good works, but it is not that confidence by which we receive the remission of sins, as is evident. Furthermore, when he says, he was justified by works, the phrasing must be observed. For he does not mean that Abraham was reconciled on account of works, but that the works of one already reconciled afterwards pleased God. For works in those who are reconciled are pleasing, as has been said, and are a certain justice of the law, but they do not merit the remission of sins or acceptance unto eternal life. Thus, therefore, he spoke. That Abraham was also justified by works, that is, that his works were also pronounced just. That is true, concerning one who is reconciled and believing. And indeed it is necessary, as I have said, for works to follow, in which faith may live and be exercised; let us act candidly, without sophistry. James does not treat the cause of Paul, but speaks incidentally about the faith which is the knowledge of history. Wherefore his sayings are not to be opposed to Paul, or to the rest of the prophetic scripture. Another.

If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments. Therefore, eternal life is given on account of works, it is not given freely to the believer. There is a plain and perpetual answer to such sayings. The sayings of the law and of the Gospel must be distinguished. Here the voice of the law is proposed, which to interpret from the law would be to judge. He who keeps the commandments will enter into life, for no one satisfies the law, no one is without sin. Add, therefore, the Gospel to that saying. If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments, namely according to ἐπιεικειαν the Gospel, which promises the remission of sins and the imputation of righteousness on account of Christ, afterwards it begins new obedience, and approves it, although it is imperfect, and is not the price of eternal life. Thus it is true, that the commandments must be kept, and it is necessary that the law be proposed, so that repentance and faith may grow in us. But not only the law is to be taught, but the promise of the Gospel is to be added, without which the law is only a ministry of wrath and eternal death. And it is established that Christ is the end of the law. Wherefore one must not stop in the law, but when we hear the law, and are terrified, let us think that we are accused, not that we may perish, but that we may seek the mediator the Son of God, let us know that this one has been given to us, so that through him we may be freed from sin, from the tyranny of the devil, and from death. Therefore when eternal life is begun in us, we obey the law, and the commandments are fulfilled, as it is said: I will pour out upon the house of David the spirit of grace, and of prayers. Another.

1. Corinth. 13If I have all faith, but do not have love, I am nothing. The answer is the same. I confess that love is necessary, but love of God can neither exist, nor please, unless we have first received by faith the remission of sins, and the imputation of righteousness. It is easy for the idle to feign love of God, but these things ought to be referred to the true struggle in the minds, and true motions in invocation in dangers. Here others doubt whether God cares for human affairs, or whether prosperous and adverse things truly happen by chance. Others, sensing the wrath of God, like Saul, succumb in afflictions and rage against the judgment of God. The heavenly voice preaches about these huge storms of the soul, and among these waves it raises up minds with the Evangelical promise. When the soul sustains itself with faith and acknowledges mercy, there follows love. It is necessary, therefore, for faith to precede, which receives the remission of sins. And this faith cannot rely on our dignity; therefore, although love follows, nevertheless it stands that we are not righteous on account of love, but on account of Christ. Commonly they interpret love as the love of God and neighbor, therefore I have responded concerning the love of God. But Paul here speaks properly of the love of neighbor, which it is more certain does not merit the remission of sins: Forgive, and it will be forgiven you; therefore by our pardoning we merit justification for ourselves as well. The response is plain. This is a sermon of repentance, such as many are in the prophets, as Isaiah. 1. Cease to do evil, and learn to do good. Then your sins will be wiped away, etc. The former part commands concerning our repentance, the latter contains the promise. Nor does Christ say: It will be forgiven you on account of your pardoning, but he only commands that we forgive, then he admonishes concerning the promise, which depends elsewhere, not from the dignity of our work. What kind of consternation of consciences would there be, if it had to be felt that divine pardoning depends on the purity and the dignity of our forgiveness, toward those with whom we had enmity, for scars remain even in reconciled minds, as he says. Therefore it is necessary to seek another cause of remission. The sentence of the Gospel concerning gratuitous forgiveness must therefore be held. Such is the offense in Daniel. A part is the sermon concerning repentance. Love justice and do good to the wretched who are unjustly oppressed. Defend the Church against tyrants, for that is what Daniel wanted. The other part is the promise. And there shall be a healing of your offenses. It is necessary that repentance exist and yet forgiveness is gratuitous, and to be received by faith. For if the promise depended on the condition of our dignity, it would become void, as Rom 4. it is said. Another.

Love is the greatest of virtues. Therefore on account of love we are reckoned righteous. I deny the consequence, and the reason is manifest, for it would follow more correctly: Love is the greatest, therefore since we perform it least, we are least righteous on account of this virtue. If we had the virtues which the law of God demands, and were without sin, we would rightly be called righteous on account of love and other virtues: But because human nature is far from the perfection of the law, it does not burn with love, therefore the Gospel proposes another righteousness, it teaches us that we are not reckoned righteous on account of our virtues, but on account of something else outside us, namely the mediator the Son of God, but in such a way, if by faith we establish that we have a propitious God on account of him. We are therefore righteous by imputation not on account of our virtues, although these also must be begun in us. Furthermore, if anyone seeks a distinction of virtues. Faith receives in the present the remission of sins. Hope is the expectation of a future event, or of future liberation. Faith is the assent by which the will wills and receives the promise, and acquiesces on account of the mediator, the Son of God. And when the will thus acquiesces, the heart becomes tranquil, and conceives consolation and joy, which is the beginning of a new life. Hope and love follow these movements. Because faith establishes that God is propitious to us, it dares to seek and expect other benefits. And love arises, because we now recognize that God is not idle, as reason imagines, nor is He an enemy, such as the law showed, but is a Father, who is affected by the magnitude of our calamity, and desires to deliver us, who swears: I live. I do not desire the death of the sinner, etc. In this way, when we recognize that we are received into grace, and are heard, we in turn submit ourselves to Him, and a certain reverence is kindled, or a certain desire, by which we prefer God to other things. Such is love in this life, not burning as it ought, but weak. Another.

They also object the name of reward. Eternal life is called a reward, therefore good works merit eternal life. I shall not seek subtle interpretations of the word, let the sources of the cause be considered. The Psalm says: Enter not into judgment with thy servant, for in thy sight shall no man living be justified Psalm 143:2. Item. Who can understand errors Psalm 19:12.

Wherefore we cannot establish that we merit eternal life by our virtues, or that our virtues are the price of eternal life. And above I collected many testimonies which show that sin remains in the reborn, which must be contemplated here in the mind. And let each one consult his own conscience, whether he prefers that eternal life be given on account of Christ, or indeed be paid for merits. The zeal for doing right languishes, you will say, if it is said that eternal life is given freely. Nay, rather, despair weakens the zeal for doing right more. For it is necessary that those who imagine that eternal life is given for merits should despair. The wiser fathers also saw that danger. Therefore Augustine and Bernard expressly say that eternal life is given freely to the believer on account of Christ. Just as Paul also says: The gift of God is eternal life through Christ Jesus our Lord. Nor is the gift uncertain. But God commands that we believe that we shall certainly receive eternal life on account of Christ, according to thatJohn 6.This is the will of the Father, that everyone who believes in the Son may have eternal life. However, this faith does not exist without repentance, and faith contemplates both voices, namely, I live, I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he may be converted and live. How? Through the Son, as he says here: This is the will of the Father, that everyone who believes in the Son may have eternal life. Although, however, it is necessary that repentance be present, yet a condition of our worthiness is not to be attached. Nay, rather, confidence in merit fights with repentance, as the saying warns: He who glories let him glory in the Lord. Why therefore is it called a reward? I answer. Even if eternal life is given on account of Christ, yet at the same time it compensates for our labors and miseries. That is sufficient for the reason of the term, just as an inheritance at the same time compensates for the duties of the heir, even if it happens for another reason. But there is another answer, simpler and truer. The phrases of the law are, He will render to everyone according to his works. Likewise, Great will be the reward in heaven. For scripture speaks after the manner of the law concerning justice, as if concerning our own dignity. Likewise concerning faith as if concerning our own virtue. And it says that a reward is given to our virtues. But meanwhile it must be known from the gospel that we are just not by our own dignity, but by imputation. And that the benefits of Christ are received by faith, not on account of the dignity of the virtue itself, but because it relies upon another's merit, namely that of Christ. This is an expeditious and true answer and without sophistry.

Another. I will also add certain scholastic objections, which when explained add much light to this disputation. And sometimes they exercise the sharp-witted. Justice is obedience toward the whole law, Good works are obedience toward the whole law, Therefore we are justified by good works. I answer. First, the minor premise must be denied. For good works are not perfect obedience toward the law, because human nature resists the law of God. Then I answer to the major premise. The major premise is true concerning the justice of the law. For the justice of the law is obedience toward the whole law. But because we do not perform this, therefore the Gospel offers gratuitous imputation of righteousness, just as Paul also admonishes us concerning the word of imputation. This objection is very useful, for it shows the distinction between the righteousness of the law and of the Gospel. It shows that the term righteousness is used differently elsewhere. This deceived the Sententiaries, who, when they had read in Aristotle that righteousness signifies universal obedience, dreamed that it signifies the same thing everywhere in the prophets and apostles. The Psalm says: They shall exult in thy righteousness. Here it does not signify Aristotelian virtues, but relatively, thy righteousness, that is, by the imputation of righteousness, by which thou through mercy accountest us righteous, that is, accepted. The righteousness of the law signifies obedience, as when it is said, I have done judgment and righteousness. But the righteousness, concerning which the Gospel properly preaches, signifies relatively the imputation of righteousness, that is, gratuitous acceptance unto eternal life, even if the gift of the Holy Spirit is joined with it. Thus, when you hear the word, to be justified, you should think of the Hebrew phrase, by which it signifies to be accounted or pronounced righteous, or an accused person to be absolved. And righteous signifies accepted by God unto eternal life.2. Corinth. 5.Him who knew no sin, he made sin for us, that we might be made the righteousness of God through him. That is, Christ was made guilty for us, that we might be made accepted on account of him. This is the simple grammar and the true explanation of the words. In other places the term is used differently; at one time mention is made of the righteousness of the law, at another of imputation. It is necessary to observe these distinctions.

Works against the law of God are sins, therefore good works are righteousness. Let the consequence be valid from the nature of contraries. Wherefore it follows, that men are also justified by good works, since they are righteousness. I answer. The consequence would be valid, if good works were perfect obedience. But since they are far from perfect obedience, it can easily be understood that the argument is not valid, because there is no true contrariety. Vicious things are entirely vicious. To good works, a great deal of vice is admixed, by which they themselves are also contaminated. Pomponius Atticus is modest, just toward citizens, but he doubts whether God cares for human affairs, he is without the fear of God. The magnitude of these interior vices is not discerned. Therefore the argument deceives those who are not warned. But the consequence must be denied, because there is no true contrariety. I answer the same to the following argument. Another.

Evil works condemn, therefore good works save. I deny the consequence, and the reason is, because there is no contrariety. Evil works are entirely vicious. To good ones, a great deal of evil is admixed, so that even if David has good works, nevertheless he has many vicious impulses, he has doubts about God. And this darkness draws with it a great army of vices, security, confidence in one's own wisdom and righteousness, nor does the breast burn with fear, nor with love of God, nor with faith, as it ought. I know there were some who proclaimed that our opinion had been greatly shaken by this argument, but how empty and futile it is, a moderately attentive reader can easily judge. Another.

Sin is hatred of God, therefore love is righteousness.

I remember Eck celebrated great triumphs when he attempted to show with this argument that men are not justified by faith alone. But the answer is easy. I agree that perfect love is the righteousness which the law demands. But as was said above, we are not righteous by the law. For love cannot exist unless we are first reconciled by faith. Afterwards a certain beginning follows, and yet a huge infirmity remains, resisting the law of God, indignant and raging against the judgment of God, as the psalm signifies: Be angry, and sin not, etc. Therefore, there is need of another righteousness, namely, gratuitous imputation. Another.

Righteousness is in the will, Faith is in the intellect, Therefore faith is not righteousness. I answer. The major premise is true concerning the righteousness of the law, which signifies our virtues and qualities in our will. But when Paul preaches about the righteousness of faith, righteousness signifies the imputation of righteousness. For he teaches that men are reckoned righteous, that is, accepted not because of their own quality, but because of something else extrinsic, namely, because of the mediator, the Son of God, through mercy. And yet this mercy must be received by faith. And faith is not only knowledge, but assent, for which a movement of the will is also required, as the learned know, which is to will and to receive the promise, and to acquiesce in it. Moreover, this faith is conceived when we assent to the Evangelical promise, by which, when the terrified mind sustains itself, the Holy Spirit at the same time moves hearts through the word to believe. Another Faith is the righteousness of the just, Faith is a work, Therefore by works we are just. To the major it must be answered, that when it is rightly understood, the argument can be explained and dissolved. And so that the matter may become clearer, the speech must be transformed into a correlative, we are just by faith, that is, we are just through mercy on account of Christ, but nevertheless it must be established by faith that that mercy pertains to us. The minor is true. Faith is a work, namely, like other virtues, love, patience, chastity. And as other virtues are imperfect, so also faith is weak, wherefore we are not just on account of the dignity of the virtue itself, but because it apprehends mercy. For it is necessary that there be some, so to speak, instrument by which mercy is apprehended, it is necessary to look upon Christ, and to establish that He forgives us. Let it therefore be answered to the minor, Faith is a work but we are not just on account of the dignity of the work itself, but because it apprehends mercy. Therefore it cannot follow that we are just on account of works. This can also be learnedly said, that there is more in the conclusion than in the premises.

Another. We are just by grace, Grace is love infused into souls, Therefore we are just by love. I answer to the minor. Grace primarily signifies relatively favor, or mercy, or gratuitous acceptance on account of Christ. Therefore the apt interpretation of the word must be held. Furthermore, with this acceptance is joined the gift of the Holy Spirit. But those who thus explain, We are just by grace, that is, we are just on account of infused virtues, these invent an interpretation diametrically opposed to Paul, and altogether removing from sight the true consolations of pious minds. If in invocation we ought to look at ourselves, and imagine that we shall approach God in such a way when we are sufficiently adorned with these virtues, and that eternal life is to be hoped for when we shall see in ourselves this new purity, minds would flee, and would despair of help and salvation. And the more minds are terrified, the more closely they look at the impurity and infirmity of our nature. Paul, however, for this very reason, because we see that we cannot bring merits and dignity to God, proposes grace, that is, free forgiveness and acceptance on account of Christ. Even if you do not bring dignity to God, nevertheless approach with confidence in the mediator Christ, as he says: Having this high priest, let us approach the throne of grace.

I have added these refutations both so that I might satisfy, as much as I could, the learned, who dispute about the propriety of speech. For we also desire to say true and right things, and to avoid ἀκυρολογίας, and so that I might instruct learners, so that they might be able to dissolve scholastic cavils with greater dexterity. And I hope these examples are useful, first for the clarity of the cause, then also for sharpening the care of learning in students. For these refutations show that there is a need for erudition and a certain exercise for those who attempt to explain such controversies dexterously. Let those who wish to profess the explanation of Christian doctrine not think that they are taking up a light burden for study. But I pray to God that He may govern the studies of the pious, and not allow the light of the Gospel and the true knowledge of Christ to be extinguished in the Church.

Latin:

ARGUMENTUM EPISTOLAE PAULI AD ROMANOS.

Mutatis autem rerum notis, etiam res amissae sunt, & secuta sunt delyria multiplicia. Video autem & nunc exoriri multa prava ingenia, quae vel propter curiositatem, vel propter ambitionem, ea quae nunc in Ecclesiis nostris recte traduntur & optima fide ac simpliciter explicata sunt, rursus novis praestigiis conturbare & obruere studebunt. Quare propter Christum oro & obtestor omnes pios, qui in studiis versantur, ut simplicem veritatem patefactam in Ecclesiis nostris ament ac tueantur, quam quidem quantum possum illustrare & munire cupio, ut ad posteros propagetur. Cum autem argumentum Epistolae ad Romanos utcunque recitaverim, & quaedam de vocum significatione observanda admonuerim, visum est adiicere interpretationem vocabulorum quorundam, & integram controversiam exponere de iustificatione. Nam haecπρολεγόμεναaliquid lucis is addent argumento. Et cum lector totam causam simul animo complexus fuerit, facilius perspiciet veram, firmam & necessariam Ecclesiae esse, ac animaduertet rectius, quomodo in Paulo membra disputationis cohereant cum prius quasi ideam aedificii in mente conceperit.

Summa doctirnae in propheticis & apostolicis scriptis traditae de iustificatione cotam Deo.

Conatus sum alibi in locis communibus Theologicis quanta potui simplicitate & perspicuitate doctrinam de iustificatione, traditam in scriptis propheticis & apostolicis, explicare. Neque hic alia dicam. Sed quoniam propria est huius Epistolae Paulinae haec materia, repetam res easdem, & fortassis alicubi aliquid dicam verbis planioribus. A pud philosophos iusticia universalis vocatur obedienta iuxta omnes virtutes, id est, externa disciplina honesta, quam homo suis viribus efficere potest. Hanc & Paulus vocat iusticiam legis ac iusticiam operum. Saepe autem diximus Deum postulare ut externa disciplina honesta coherceantur omnes homines, sicut Paulus inquit: Lex est posita iniustis, ac punit Deus violantes disciplinam, ut homines periuros, contumeliose loquentes de Deo, sediciosos, homicidas, moechos, fures mendaces. Verum est autem quod inquit Aristoteles, Nec Hesperum nec Luciferum formosiorem esse iusticia, id est, honesta disciplina. Est enim egregium ornamentum hominis, nec aliud prestantius decus efficere haec infirma natura hominis potest. Sed tamen sciendum est, hanc disciplinans nequaquam sacisfacere legi, sed esse tenuem quandam umbrà legis, sicut Paulus erudite docet2. Corinth. 3.cum ait, Iudaeos intueri Moisen velata facie, idest non perfusos esse fulgore legis, hoc est non lucere in eis noticiam Dei, & perfectam obedientiam, sed externa opera qualiacunque effici. At lex Dei flagitat, non tantum externa opera, sed perfectam obedientiam. Facile igitur intelligi potest neminem esse iustum coram Deo, idest acceptum propter disciplinam externam, sicut clare inquit Paulus: Ex operibus legis non iustificabitur omnis caro. Id dictum detrahit laudem iustificationis notantum ceremoniis, sed etiam moralibus operibus, ac loquitur de tota disciplina. Porro de hac externa disciplina, de illa velata Moisi facie, philosophia & leges humanae disserunt, non querunt quomodo coram Deo iusti, idest accepti simus. Nec commiscendae sunt philosophorum sententiae cum Paulina. Tribuatur suus locus huic carnali iusticiae, hoc est coherceantur impii hac disciplina, vagentur philosophi in coetu populi, & velatam Moisi faciem intueantur, non ascendant in mentem ad Deum. Maneant in hac turba & Origenes & caeteri qui eum sequuntur, & velatam Moisi saciem intueantur, cum non aliam iusticiam, nisi carnalem doceant. Cum igitur ratio non videat, quomodo coram Deo iusti reputemur, Evangelium praedicat aliam iusticiam, non notam rationi, sed Patribus revelatam à Deo, & postea per prophetas magis magisque patefactam, ac tandem per Christum & Apo stolos sparsam in mundum. Ideo Iohannes inquit Deum nemo vidit unquam. Sed filius Dei qui est in sinupatris, ipse enarravit nobis, quasi dicat, hanc voluntatem Dei, quod Deus gratis velit ignoscere, & dare vitam aeternam propter filium, nulla creatura nullaratio humana deprehendere potuit. Sed tantum per filium haec voluntas patefacta est. De hoc admirando beneficio concionatur Paulus, quod exponam breviter. Est & Christus, ut convenit artifici, aptissime complexus Evangelii summam ac methodum, cum iubet praedicare paenitentiam et remissionem peccatorum in suo nomine. Itaque ministerium Evangelii primum arguit peccata, sicut Christus inquit: Spiritus sanctus arguet mundum de peccato &c. Hic cum mens agnoscit peccatum & iram Dei, ac veris terroribus expavescit, Evangelium proponit consolationem, et eam vocem quae est ipsius Evangelii propria, scilicet promissionem beneficii Christi, monstrat mediatorem filium Dei, sicut Iohannes eum monstrabat, inquiens: Ecce agnus Dei, qui tollit peccata mundi, iubet statuere quod propter hunc mediatorem filium Dei, dominum nostrum Iesum Christum certo nobis donentur remissio peccatorum, & imputatio iusticiae, non propter ulla nostra opera seu merita, sed gratis fide, idest, cum credimus illa vere nobis ac certe propter Christum donari. Cum hac fide nos erigimus & sustentamus intuentes Christum, consequimur vere remissionem peccatorum, et reputamur iusti id est, accepti eoram deo, et donamur spiritu sancto, et efficimur filii dei, ac haeredes vitae aeternae, ut Iohannis primo scribitur Dedit eis potestatem filios Dei fieri, credentibus in nomine eius. Haec sunt plana & perspicua & ad usum conscientiarum accommodata, ac conspici in exemplis possunt. David reus adulterii & cedis, cum à propheta accusaretur, oppressus est ingentibus terroribus. Postea erigitur voce absolutionis, cum ait Propheta: Dominus abstulit peccatum tuum. Non morieris. Hanc vocem audiens credit sibi peccatum remitti, non propter suam dignitatem aut merita, sed gratis per misericordiam, ac scit promissam esse liberationem à peccato & à morte propter venturum liberatorem, scit Christum fore hostiam pro peccatis humani generis, sicut in psalmo ait: Tu es sacerdos in aeternum &c. Hac fide se sustentans fit iustus, id est, acceptus coram Deo ad vitam aeternam. SicLucae 7mulier venit lachrymans ad Christum, agnoscens sua peccata, postea illi inquit Christus: Vade in pace, fides tua salvam te facit, Ita hi duo motus in conversione decribuntur, pavores & fides. Vulgo pavores vocant contritionem, sed sciendum est pavores non mereri condonationem peccatorum, imò nisi accederet fides, mens oppressa terroribus rueret in aeternam mortem, sicut Saul, Iudas, perierunt, cum non erigerent se fide & agnitione misericordiae inter terrores. Et hoc vult dictum Pauli de lege: Lex iram efficit, id est incutit horribiles terrores, quales saepe describuntur in psalmis, & Ezechias inquit: Sicut Leo contrivit omnia ossa mea. Adserrent igitur hi pavores exitium & aeternam mortem, nisi accederet fides paulatim erigens animos, intuens in premissiones Christi, atque ita Christum apprehendens. Haec certamina quanta sint monent psalmi. Quomodo videmus luctantem secum Davidem, cum clamitat: Domine ne in furore tuo arguas. Miserere mei Domine. Quoniam non est in morte qui memor sit tui, neque in inforno qui laudet te. Non abiicias me inter damnatos, qui uruntur horribili & aeterno odio tui, & tibi maledicunt. Ne in hunc coetum hostium tuorum abiiciar. Etpsalmo 41.Quare tristis es anima mea, & quare conturbas me? Spera in Deum, quoniam adhuc laudabo eum. De his tantis certaminibus hic quoque Paulus concionatur, nec tantum litigat de suilla carne, aut similibus ritibus. Clamitat omnes esse sub peccato. Haec sententia de terroribus concionatur, deinde monstrat Christum, inquit nos gratis fide iustificari &c. Et ut sciamus eum loqui non de ociosis cogitationibus, sed de fide luctante cum pavoribus, inquit: Iustificati fide pa cem habemus, item accessum ad Deum &c. Item fide agnoscimus nos diligi à Deo. Cum igitur adeo apte ad reliquam scripturam propheticam haec Pauli dicta congruant, quae perversitas est aliam sententiam Paulo affingere? Sed pergo. Cum haec sententia, quam recitavi de conversione hominis, & instificatione, perspicua & plana sit, & in vita usum habeat, et sit rata & immutabilis sententia Evangelii, patefacta Patribus, adversariorum partim deploranda est coecitas, partim detestanda pertinacia, qui nostram interpretationem damnant. Atque hic obtestor per Christum omnes pios, ut expendant quid in utraque parte dicatur. Adversarii fatentur, oportere existere terrores, sed de fide aliter loquuntur, volunt adesse noticiam historiae, sed iubent dubitare de remissione peccatorum & si cui contingit, aiunt contingere propter merita Ita simpliciter abolent Evangelium, quod docet propter Christum contingere hoc beneficium, & ut sit certum, edita est promissio, & mandat Deus ut promissioni credamus, ac assentiamur, eamque ad nos pertinere statuamus. Hane esse veram & perpetuam Evangelii sententiam, fateri necesse est. Et refutat Paulus errorem de dubitatione, cum docet promissionem oportere fide accipi.Rom. 4.Ideo ex fide gratis, ut sit firma promissio. Et iubet, ut Deo tribuamus laudem veritatis, sicut Abraham non dubitavit diffidentia. Et1. Ioannis 5.Qui credit in filium Dei, habet testimonium in se ipso, qui non credit Deo, mendacem facit eum &c. Ergo cum dicimus fide contingere beneficia Christi, necesse est intelligi, quod contingant propter Christum, & assentiendum est promissioni divinae, ac credendum vere nobis praestari promissa. Quare fides non tantum significat historiae noticiam, sed significat fiduciam promissae misericordiae propter Christum, assentientem promissioni divinae. Talem fidem requirit Paulus, quae credat omnibus articulis Symboli, Videlicet quae credat propter filium Dei passum, resuscitatum, dari nobis remissionem peccatorum. Nam ad hunc articulum, tanquàm ad causam finalem, superiores referendi sunt. Cum in precationibus adversarii recitant hunc articulum: Credo remissionem peccatorum, secum ipsi pugnant iubent dubitare, & tamen audiunt praecipi, ut credant remissionem peccatorum. Ac scio quosdam, quos hic ipse articulus admonuit, ut consolationem admitterent, & cogitarent adsentiendum esse promissioni Dei, & abiicerent doctrinam monachorum de dubitatione, & meritis.

Sed quare additur particula gratis, non propter opera, sed propter Christum? Imo vere de hac particula gratis praecipue dimicant & conscientiae, & prophetae ac apostoli. Complectitur autem duo. Excludit merita nostra, & proponit Christi merita. Hic enim vel praecipue cerni potest, primum magnitudo irae Dei adversus peccatum, quod nulla hostia placare Deum potuit, nisi mors filii. Rursuslucet amoris magnitudo, quod filium pro nobis dedit. Utrumque autem in agone conscientiae tenere opus est, videlicet Deo proponenda esse Christi merita, propter Christum petendam et expectandam esse gratiam, non propter nostra merita. Nam & certaminis illius Epitasis haec est, Non querit mens perterrefacta an aliis benemeritis ac dignis Deus velit esse propicius. Adsentitur Deum bonum & misericordem esse, sed dignis qui non habent peccata, aut qui maiora habent merita. Nam legis noticia nobiscum nata, docet Deum bonum esse, sed erga dignos. Illud vero querit, an Deus mihi indigno velit esse propicius Hic intuenda est particula, gratis, ut statuamus vere deum remittere peccata propter Christum gratis, non propter ulla nostra opera aut merita. Et haec particula, gratis, monstrat discrimen Evangelii ac legis. Lex etiam concionatur, Deum esse bonum, misericordem, sed addit conditionem dignitatis, seu meriti, ait Deum propicium esse his, qui sine peccato sunt. At Evangelium remonet conditionem nostrae dignitatis seu meritorum, testatur Deum propter Christi merita gratis nobis reconciliari, non propter ulla nostra merita, cum haec fides, idest fiducia misericordiae nititur Christo. Solemus autem interdum pro exclusiva, gratis iustificamur fide, uti hac formula. Sola fide iustificamur, ubi haec particula non excludit caeteras virtutes ne adsint, sed excludit opinionem meriti, seu conditionem dignitatis, seu excludit illas à causa iustificationis, hoc est acceptationis, ut postea copiosius dicam. Acre ipsa prorsus idem est dicere, fide sumus iusti, & fide gratis sumus iusti, & sola fide sumus iusti. Nam fides existere nulla potest, si fiducia debeat niti dignitate nostra, seu meritis, aut partim Christo, partim meritis, ut fingunt aliqui. Excutitur fides, si cogitandum erit, ita propicius erit Deus, cum satis meritorum habebis. Ergo non potest niti fides nisi promissione Dei, monstrante Christum, propter quem pollicitus est pater certo se nobis fore propicium. Et cum Paulus querit, utrum fide an operibus iustificemur, fidem intelligit, fiduciam misericordiae promissae propter Christum, & hanc opponit in universum dignitati nostrae, quasi interroget: Utrum statuere debeas tibi remitti peccata, & te filium Dei esse propter tuam dignitatem, propter ullas virtutes tuas, qualitates aut actiones, an vero statuere debeas tibi remitti peccata, & te esse filium dei per solam misericordiam, propter Christum. Proindereipsa est Exclusiva, cum ait: Fide iustificamur, idest non propter dignitatem nostram. Quare si quis vere volet iudicare, agnoscet reipsaidem significari, fide iustificamur, & gratis iustificamur fide, & sola fide iusti ficamur. Haec obiter adieci de formulis sermonis, ut significatio diligenter expendatur. Caeterum quoquo modo loquemur, illud videndum erit, ne res obruatur. Sententia exclusiva retinenda est, de gratuita acceptatione. Haec enim discrimen inter legem et Evangelium efficit, ut dictum est. Dixi de particulagratis, de qua & hoc considerent pii, merita tolli ac reiici, non quia nos nihil agamus, sed ut promissio nobis sit certa, quae fieret incerta, si penderet ex conditione meritorum, item ut debitus honos Christo tribuatur, item quia, etiamsi quid agimus, tamen procul absumus à perfectione legis. Oritur autem fides à verbo Dei, videlicet ab Evangelio, quod proprie est promissio, in qua beneficia Christi nobis tum promittuntur, tum exhibentur. Nihil enim posset mens humana statuere de remissione peccatorum, si deus non revelasset hanc suam voluntatem certo verbo, seu certa promissione. Sciendum est autem hanc Evangelicam promi ssionem universalem esse, quod eò necesse est admoneri pios, quia pavidae mentes de his duabus quaestionibus maxime disputant, videlicet de dignitate, & de electione. Primum querimus an indignos recipiat, deinde etiamsi essemus digni, cogitamus tamen Deum suos quosdam amicos elegisse, quibus haec beneficia velit impertire, dubitamus an ad nos quoque pertineat, veremur nos non esse in numero illorum. Ita ambigit humana ratio de voluntate Dei. Nam & philosophi adsentiuntur, deum paucis quibusdam, videlicet Heroicis viris favere, & eorum eventus gubernare, sed reliquos homines negligi à Deo cogitant. Prorsus hoc modo cogitat mens de praedestinatione, ut vocant. Sed humanam opinionem taxat vox caelestis. Hoc differt Evangelium à philosophicis opinionibus & à lege, quia aliter monstrat Dei voluntatem, ostendit Deum vere & indignos velle recipere, & omnibus offerre gratiam, modo ut credant promissioni. Quare discant pii, promissionem esse universalem, sicut testantur innumera dicta, ut Venite ad me omnes, qui laboratis, et onoratiestis.Ro. 3.Iusticia Dei per fidem Iesu Christi in omnes et super omnes credentes. ItemRo. 10.Idem dominus omnium dives in omnes etc. In has universales includamus nos singuli, et vere ad nos pertinere beneficia promissa statuamus. Itaque in questione de iustificatione, seponantur aliquantisper disputationes de prae destinatione. Exordiendum est ab Evangelio, quod et arguit omnes, & offert omnibus gratiam promissam propter Christum, & quidem gratis offert, modo ut fide accipiant. Intueamur ergo in verbum quod est universale nec sinamus nos à promissione avelli speculationibus de praedestinatione. Non enim iudicandum est de voluntate Dei, sine ipsius verbo. Et ut promissiones sunt universales, sic intelligo hoc dictum: Deus vult omnes homines salvos fieri, sicut in promissionibus offert omnibus salutem. Sed humana voluntas in his, qui nolunt, credere, repugnat promissionibus. Illi autem qui se promissione sustentant, vere sibi tribui beneficia Christi statuant, ne Deum accusent mendacii. Cumque vocem Evangelii accipiunt, & se sustentant, simul efficax est spiritus sanctus per Evangelii vocem, iuxta illud: Fides ex auditu est. Et adGalat 3.ut promissionem spiritus accipiamus per fidem. Ita cum per terre factae mentes fide eriguntur, concipiunt spiritum sanctum. Haec est conversio quae in Evangelio vocatur regeneratio, quae haec tria complectitur, remissionem peccatorum, iustificationem seu imputationem iusticiae, & donationem spiritus sancti, ac vitae aeternae. Dixi autem de motibus qui à piis intelligi possunt, de terroribus & consolatione, quae fiet fide. Quare haec Paulina sententia nec absurda, nec intricata est, nec ociosas argutias continet, sed est perspicua, consentanea reliquis prophetarum & Evangelii concionibus, &res maximas proponit, quas pii in vita experiuntur, & quarum cognitio Ecclesiae necessaria est. Nunc adiiciam brevem vocum enarrationem, Legis, Evangelii, Peccati, Iustificationis, Gratiae, Fidei.

Plurimum differunt lex & Evangelium. Nam lex est doctrina, qua Deus praecipit quales nos esse oporteat, & quae facienda, quae vitanda sint. Et quanquam politia Mosaica deleta sit, tamen manet lex moralis, quae est una & eadem omnium temporum, cum eius noticia nobiscum nascatur. Voluit enim Deus aliquam esse noticiam in homine, quae iudicaret peccatum. Ac semper omnibus temporibus voce legis arguitur peccatum in praedicatione paenitentiae. Ideo Paulus dicit: Per legem cognitio peccati. Nec tantum loquitur de caeremoniis, ut quidam fingunt, sed praecipue de Decalogo seu lege morali. Haec enim semper, & omnes accusat. Nam longe aliter de lege divina sentiendum est, quam de moribus vitae civilis. In vita civili tantum flagitatur externa disciplina. At lex Dei requirit perfectam obedientiam, interiorem & exteriorem. Ut testatur praeceptum: Diligas Dominum Deum tuum ex toto corde &c. Et sicMathaei 5.Christus legem interpretatur. Cum autem haec natura hominum morbo originis viciata non possit praestare perfectam obedientiam, lex ostendit iram Dei adversus peccatum, accusat & damnat omnes homines praeter Christum, qui, ut inquit Paulus, liberavit nos à maledictione legis. Liberavit autem non tantum Iudeos aut caeteros qui post editam vel abolitam legem Mosaicam salvati sunt, sed etiam Patres ante Moisen. Ergo illi etiam fuerunt sub lege, hoc est, sunt accusati et perterrefacti iudicio legis naturalis, & periissent, nisi tenuissent promissiones de Christo, propter quem sciebant promissam esse liberationem à peccato & à morte. Rident fortassis homines politici haec, cum dicimus legem divinam flagitare perfectam obedientiam, neminem legi divinae satisfacere posse, quia in natura hominis ignoratio et contemptus dei herent, videntur haec inepta philosophis et humano more iudicantibus. Sed hoc ipsum agunt prophetae et apostoli, volunt homines agnoscere magnitudinem peccati, quod non vere agnoscunt et glorificant Deum, docent hoc peccatum esse causam maximarum aerumnarum et calamitatum quibus haec infirma natura oppressa est, & querere veram iusticiam, et liberationem à peccato ac à morte, per Christum donatam. Caetera de lege, studiosi qui discendi causa haec lecturi sunt, sumant ex lòcis communibus, quos edidi. Evangelium praedicat paenitentiam et promissionem gratiae, ac vitae aeternae. Diligenter autem à lege discerni debet promissio. Et quanquam lex habet suas quasdam promissiones, tamen et illae differunt à promissione, quae est propria Evangelii. Et promissiones legis requirunt conditionem perfectae obedientiae ut in primo praecepto dicitur: Benefaciam diligentibus me, sed Evangelica promissio de remissione peccatorum, iusti ficatione, et donatione vitae aeternae, est gratuita, oblata propter Christum, sine conditione meritorum nostrorum seu dignitatis nostrae. Nulla vox humana eloqui potest magnitudinem huius beneficii, quod Deus per filium suum dominum nostrum Iesum Christum nobis impertit, scilicet ut deleto peccato, et abolita morte, fruamur conspectu Dei in aeterna vita, iusticia et laeticia. Huius beneficii promissio tantum revelata est divinitus, sicut Ioannes inquit: Filius qui est in sonu patris, ipse enarravit nobis. Etsi enim aliqua legis noticia nobiscum nascitur, tamen Evangelii noticia nequaquam nobiscum nascitur. Ratio humana per sese nequaquam videt hanc Dei voluntatem, videlicet Deum missurum esse filium suum, ut fiat victima pro Ecclesia, Deum velle gratis remittere peccata. Haec longe extra conspectum humanae rationis positasunt. Ideo diligenter discerni debent dicta legum à promissione Evangelica. Apud Phocyllidem, Hesiodum, & similes leguntur aliqua legum dicta. Sed Evangelica promissio de gratuit a remissione, vel de filio Dei, nusquam legitur in his qui rationis iudicium seu lumen naturae humanae tantum sequebantur, imo cum quaedam noticia legis nobiscum nascatur, mens ipsa in nobis accusat peccata, nec aliud cogitat, nisi Deum punire & abiicere iniustos. Hoc est enim legis iudicium, ac iuxta legem verum est. Sed ingenti certamine in paenitentia voci legis, & naturali iudicio nostro opponi debet promissio gratuita misericordiae, anteserenda legi, quia Christus liberat à lege, ut cum Adam lapsus esset, & accusaretur, nihil aliud iudicare potuit, nisi quod lex ostendebat, se periturum esse, quia non obtemper asset Deo. Sed prodit Deus, & quanquam subiicit genus humanum morti corporis & caeteris aerumnis, tamen proponit consolationem, pollicetur liberationem à peccato & à morte, ac restitutionem generis humani. Ait enim fore, ut semen mulieris conterat caput serpentis. Hac voce dicta, filius Deimovit cor Adae & novam illi lucem ac vitam indidit. Tunc enim filius Dei constitutus est custos, gubernator, & servator Ecclesiae, tunc belligerari cepit cum diabolo. Et ut diabolus immani sevicia grassatur in genus humanum, perdit plurimos, & odio Dei praecipue conatur delere ecclesiam, & calcaneo nostro venenatos dentes infigit, ut saepe experimur, ita rursus filius Dei efficax est in credentibus, & reprimit diabolifurorem, restituit & liberat Sanctos. Non videt mundus hoc certamen, sed plurimorum horrendi lapsus, & tristissimae ac tragicae calamitates, & deinde gloriosae liberationes, ut Davidis & aliorum ostendunt quale sit hoc certamen. Nes aliud sinificant verba in Genesi: Semen conteret caput serpentis, quàm hoc ipsum quod Iohannes inquit: Ad hoc exhibitus est filius Dei, ut destruat opera diaboli. Sic intellexit Adam promissionem, sic deinceps omnes Patres crediderunt propter hoc promissum semen sibi remitti peccata, se liberandos esse à peccato & à morte aeterna. Hac fide erant iusti, non legis impletione, hac fide erigebantur in omnibus periculis & terroribus. Et quidem norant hunc Dominum sibi adefse, sicut Iacob diserte inquit.Genesis 48.Angelus qui liber avit me de cunctis malis, benedicat pueris istis, praedicat enim eum Dominum, per quem à cunctis malis liberatus est, & ab hoc petit ut benedicat posteris. Haec non possunt aliter nisi de filio Dei intelligi. Et Paulus ait, filium Dei comitatum esse castra populi Israel. Io annes etiam inquit, omnia per hunc filium facta esse, & lucem in tenebris fulsisse. Omnes triumphi adversus diabolum parti sunt per hunc filium. Noe servatus, defensus Abraham, excitatus Ioseph, liberatus populus ex Aegipto, Daniel etiam cum eo colloquitur. Sic Evangelium Apostolorum concionatur de Christo, testatur esse victimam, liberatorem, & salvatorem, & iubet nos confidere hoc duce & liberatore. Sicut et Plurimae sententiae in prophetis docent, ut psalmus Secundus inquit: Osculamini filium: Beati omnes quam confident in eo. Ac sine hac fide idest fiducia misericordiae promissae propter filium, nulla est vera dei invocatio, nulli veri cultus. Nam per hunc Pontificem habemus aditum ad patrem, ut saepe scriptum est. Execranda est igitur caecitas illorum, qui fingunt Evangelium esse legem continentem praecepta quaedam de mut va dilectione, requiri autem fidem, id est noticiam historiae de Christo, et hunc habendum esse pro doctore, ut Socrates aut Phocylides tradiderunt bona praecepta, & imaginandum homines esse iustos propter illa dilectionis officia, sed tamen dubitandum esse, an deus igno scat nobis, an exaudiat nos, an aliquid sit ei negocii nobiscum. Ita monachi & nunc quidam philosophastri transformant Evangelium in Academicam philosophiam, id est, doctrinam de operibus, & iubent dubitare de promissionibus divinis, nec docent fidem id est fiduciam, quae nititur Christo liberatore, petit & expectat propter ipsum beneficia promissa, necessariam esse. Rogo igitur omnes pios lectores si amant Christum, ut hic considerent discrimen legis & Evangelii, Moisi, & Christi, & diligenter cogitent, quae gloria tribuenda sit filio Dei, qui sint veri honores, quos eitribuerunt patres, Adam, Iacob, prophetae & Aposto li. Ab his Christum adesse suae Ecclesiae ducem, gubernatorem, liberatorem, salvatorem, defensorem adversus diabolum, discamus &

fide accipienda esse beneficia Christi, et meminerimus Evangelium esse vocem promittentem et exhibentem haec beneficia, sicut inquit Paulus: Evangelium est potentia Dei ad salutem omni credenti credenti, id est Evangelium offert nobis gratiam et vitam aeternam gratis propter Christum non propter legem. Et per hoc Evangelium deus vere est efficax, dat spiritum sanctum, inchoat in nobis novam lucem & vitam aeternam.

Peccatum non significat tantum actiones viciosas, sicut philosophi de vocabulo iudicant. Sed complectitur etiam ingentem imbecillitatem, quae nobiscum nascitur, quae vocatur peccatum originis, quod etsi securi homines iudicant leve malum esse, imò philosophine malum quidem esse arbitrantur, tamen longe aliter iudicandum est. Non sunt levia mala tenebrae ac dubitatio de deo, an curet humana, an puniat, an alat, an iuvet, an exaudiat homines, item vacare metu, amore dei, amare nosipsos, neglecto Deo, mirari nostram sapientiam, ludere opinionibus fingendis de deo, Epicureis, aut supersticiosis, habere impetus varie errantes, aversos à Deo, et pugnantes cum lege dei. Haec esse ingentia mala, ostendunt poenae. Nam propter haec mala deus subiecit genus humanum morti, punit et cohercet ingentibus calamit atibus. Deinde cum Deus nulla victima placari voluerit, nisi filii morte, necesse est ingens esse malum, quod tanto precio redimendum fuit.

-irum est tantum in animis humanis stuporem esse, ut hunc morbum non agnoscant. Quare Deus patefieri eum sua voce ac doctrina voluit. Huic assentiamur, nec audiamus cavillationes Sophistarum, qui rident Sardonium risum, & morbum extenuant, leviter curant hostiam Christum, aut etiam prorsus contemnunt. Ab illa impia philosophia decet nos animis atque auribus abhorrere.

Iustificare Ebraica phrasi usitate, est iustum pronunciare vel reputare, ut Ebraice diceretur, populus Romanus Scipionem accusatum à Tribunis iusticavit, id est absolvit, seu iustum pronunciavit. Ita in his Pauli disputationibus certo sciamus iustificationem significare remissionem peccatorum, & acceptationem ad vitam aeternam, sicut satis perspicue testatur caput 4. ad Romanos, ubi definit iustificationem esse remissionem peccatorum. Est ergo fide iustificamur, idem quod reputamur iusti à Deo propter Christum, cum credimus. & vocabulum iusticia, non hic significat iusticiam legis, seu obedientiam universalem, seu nostras qualitates, cum dicitur, fide donatur nobis iusticia. Sed significat imputationem iusticiae, seu acceptationem. Et iustus hoc modo relative intelligatur, pro accepto ad vitam aeternam. Sed sciendum est in remissione peccatorum simul donari spiritum sanctum, ut supra dixi, cum fide nos erigimus.

Ita cum iustificatione coniuncta est donatio Spiritus sancti, qui non tantum unam virtutem, fidem. sed etiam caeteras inchoat, timorem, dilectionem Dei, amorem veritatis, castitatem, patienciam, iusticiam ergà proximum, ut postea de operibus dicam. Sed hae virtutes non merentur remissionem peccatorum, nec sunt iusticia, propter quam persona sit accepta, quae adhuc multum habet infirmitatis. Porro cum conscientia perterrefacta quaerit, quomodo iustificemur, non hoc quaerit quas habeamus virtutes, sed quomodo consequamur remissionem peccatorum & reconciliationem cum deo. De volunt ate Dei erga nos angitur, non contemplatur proprias virtutes, non opponit illas iudicio Dei. Ideo qui iustificationem interpretantur infusionem virtutum, non attendunt hic, quaeri de remissione peccatorum, et de pace conscientiae erga Deum, seu de reconciliatione. Quaerimus quomodo iustificemur, id est unde habeamus remissionem peccatorum, quare statuendum sit, deum nobis propicium esse. Necesse est igitur, iustificationem intelligi, remissionem peccatorum, & acceptationem divinam, seu imputationem iusticiae.

Gratia significat gratuitam acceptationem, seu misericordiam promissam propter Christum, cum quo coniuncta est donatio Spiritus sancti, utRom. 5.inquit Paulus: Quando magis gratia Dei, et donum in gratia. Ubi cum nominat gratiam, intelligit gratuitam reconciliationem, deinde donum in gratia, intelligit donationem spiritus sancti et inchoationem vitae aeternae. Nam in remissione peccatorum, ut dixi, datur spiritus sanctus. Estque prophana philosophia pelagii execranda, qui contendebat sine actione spiritus sancti homines fieri filios Dei & haeredes vitae aeternae. Sepe igitur gratiae nomine significatur auxilium et actio spiritus sancti. Verum principalis significatio est gratuita acceptatio, ut cum dicimus: Paulus per gratiam consecutus est remissionem peccatorum, id est, Paulus gratis propter Christum consecutus est remissionem peccatorum. Ac repudianda est monachorum enarratio, qui finxerunt interpretationem ex diametro pugnantem cum Paulo: Per gratiam consequimur remissionem, id consequimur propter nostras virtutes. Quod. n gratia significet praecipue gratuitam acceptationem propter Christum promissam, testantur multa dicta: ut, Non estis sub lege, sed sub gratia. Sentit. n. iustos, etsi habent peccata, tamen von accusari, quia sint sub gratia, id est, acceptiiam & placentes propter Christum. Non enim vult eos sentire, quod placeant propter suos habitus.

Rom. 4.Ideo ex fide, ac secundum gratiam, ut firma sit promissio. Porro conscientia non est certa propter nostros habitus seu virtutes nostras, sed propter gratuitam misericordiam promissam. Quare huic loco nequaquàm conveniet monachorum interpraetatio, qui gratiam tantum interpretantur nostras virtutes.

Romanos. 5.ubi abundavit peccatum, magis exuberavit gratia, id est, gratuita misericordia magis conspicitur, cum magnitudo peccati nostri conspicitur, & intelligimus nos gratis, non propter aliqua merita, consequi remissionem peccatorum.

Ad Ephesios. 2.Praedestinans nos per Iesum Christum, iuxta beneplacitum suae voluntatis ad laudem gloriae gratiae suae. Hic certe vult celebrari non nostras virtutes, sed gratuitam misericordiam Dei.

Ad Galatas. 2.Non sperno gratiam Dei, si enim ex lege est iusticia, frustra Christus mortuus est. Non hoc dicit, magnifacio meas virtutes, sed gratuitam misericordiam magnifacio, qua mihi propter Christi mortem statuo, Deum placatum esse.

2. Thessalonicenses 2.Dedit nobis spem bonam in gratia, non iubet sperare propter nostras virtutes, sed propter gratuitam misericordiam promissam propter Christum.

Ad Ebreos. 4.Accedamus cum fiducia ad thronum gratiae, idest promissae misericordiae. Satis enim liquet hic intelligi non posse gratiam de nostris virtutibus.

Denique nota est eruditis phrasis Ebraici sermonis qua observata, facile erit iudicare de significatione vocabuli Deinde nemo ignorat Paulum hanc ipsam ob causam inculcare vocabulum gratiae, ut statuamus nos placere Deo propter Christum, non propter nostras virtutes. Id interpretatio monachorum prorsus invertit, cum iubent sentire, gratia nos, id est, propter virtutes nostras iustificari.

Inest autem in vocabulo gratiae exclusiva, quae ut supra dixi, diligenter observanda est. Nam discrimen legis & Evangelii praecipue facit particula exclusiva, gratis propter Christum. Excluditur autem, ut dixi, non paenitentia seu caeterae virtutes, sed conditio dignitatis seu meriti, ut mentes perterrefactae habeant firmam consolationem. Nec dulcescunt animis promissiones, nisi illis semper includamus particulam, gratis: Omnis qui invo caverit nomen Domini, salviis erit, si adiiciam, si dignus erit, deterrebitur animus. Ideo Evangelium clamitat, de particula gratis, in voca etiam si es indignus, quia propter Christum gratis salvabuntur invocantes dominum. Sic in psalmo: Quia apud Dominum misericodia, si adiiciam erga dignos, refugit conscientia. Sed Evangelium iubet intelligi gratuitam misericordiam certo promissam propter Christum, quasi dicat: Ne refugite, sed accedite ad Deum, accipite fide propositum munus. Nam propter Christum gratis vult Deusuobis ignoscere. Idque decretum certum, & immutabile est. Si quis cogitat incertum esse, contumelia filium Dei afficit, qui est pignus huis promissionis. Sed fide accipi munus oportet.

Haec ideo repetivi, quia plurimum refert, hanc exclusivam diligentur illustrari, ut discrimen legis & Evangelii recte conspici possit, & ut piae mentes cogitent sibi firmam consolationem propositam esse, & se exuscitent ad fidem & invocationem in omnibus negociis & periculis.
