Ac Episcopus est vocatus per omnes homines ad docendum Evangelium, certo loco, & potest errare, nec necesse est certum esse, quod habeat spiritum sanctum. Ex his descriptionibus multa iudicari possunt. Ut enim prophetae in populo Israhel longe antecellebant sacerdotibus, & multa agebant heroica, quae non concedebat lex caeteris sacerdotibus, ita Apostoli vocationem habent longe superiorem caeteris Episcopis, legem abrogant, vocant gentes ad societatem populi Dei, enarrant obscuros articulos de Messia, quod sit filius Dei, quod non fuerit habiturus regnum politicum. Expresse impertiunt remissionem peccatorum, quod Sacerdotes Levitici nequaquàm fecerant. Enarrant articulum de iusticia fidei, quem pauci in populo Legis antea audierant. At Episcopi dictata ab Apostolis accipere debent, non inchoare novum aut aliud doctrinae genus. Ut igitur Paulus admoneret omnes de autoritate suae doctrinae, facit mentionem suae vocationis, inquiens: Servus IESU Christi, vocatus Apostolus.

Origenes hic ineptè rhetoricatur de liberatione & caeremoniis, & de servitute Pauli, qua caeremoniis fuerat obnoxius ante conversionem. Hae declamationes non pertinent ad hunc locum. Paulus enim hic non de privata servitute loquitur, sed de officio, vocat se servum, id est, ministrum gerentem officium pertinens ad regnum Christi.

## 1:1
Called.

That can be better understood from the Galatians, where he adds that he was not called by men nor through men, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father. That signifies, when he calls himself here not a common preacher, but κλητὸν ἀπόστολον. And these sentences are to be opposed at this time to the Papists, whose impudence is so great that they openly dare to say that one is to believe Paul no more than the Roman Pontiff, or the Bishops. They imagine Paul to be some Irus or vagabond, who wandered without authority, and obstinately quarreled about religion. We, however, upon hearing the mention of the Apostle, should think that he preaches with prophetic authority, and let us accept his sayings as the voice of God sounding from heaven.

If we think on this, it will greatly confirm us in his opinion.

Latin:

Vocatus.

Id ex Galatis melius intelligi potest, ubi addit se non ab hominibus neque per homines vocatum esse, sed per Iesum Christum & Deum Patrem. Id significat, cum hic se vocat non vulgarem concionatorem, sed κλητὸν ἀπόστολον. Et hae sententiae opponendae sunt hoc tempore Papistis, quorum tanta est impudentia, ut apertè ausint dicere, non plus esse credendum Paulo, quàm Romano Pontifici, aut Episcopis. Imaginantur Paulum esse Irum aliquem aut erronem, qui sine autoritate vagatus, & pertinaciter de religione rixatus sit. Nos autem audita Apostoli mentione, cogitemus prophetica autoritate eum concionari, et eius dicta tanquàm vocem Dei de caelo sonantem accipiamus.

Hoc si cogitabimus valde nos eius sententiae confirmabunt.

## 1:1
Set apart for the Gospel of God.

He names the kind of business which was entrusted to him; he says that he was chosen to propagate the Gospel. Now, in this place, it behooves the reader to remember that there is a very great difference between these two kinds of doctrine, between the Law and the Gospel. Concerning that distinction, it has been spoken of above in the preface, and it will have to be spoken of below in the third chapter. He himself also adds a description of the Gospel. The Gospel is a promise made divinely, handed down in the holy scriptures, concerning the Son of God, Jesus, born of the seed of David according to the flesh, but declared the Son of God, powerful through the sanctifying spirit, raised from the dead, who is the Messiah, or the king through whom there is liberation from sin and from eternal death.

This definition will become more illustrious if the antithesis of the Law and the Gospel is established. The Law is a doctrine commanding what kind of people we ought to be, and what we ought to do, requiring perfect obedience, not promising the remission of sins freely, not liberating us from sin and from death, but rather arming sin, when it accuses us and oppresses us with lethal terrors. But the Gospel is a promise, which promises to us the remission of sins freely, and liberation from sin and from death through the Son of God, born from the posterity of David according to the promises, and by divine power sanctifying us and quickening us with eternal life.

These members will be declared more copiously below. Paul, however, proposed the definition immediately at the beginning for this reason, that we might know what he has professed, and might diligently distinguish the Law from the Gospel, as if he were saying, Paul divinely called to teach the Gospel concerning Christ, not to teach the law or philosophy.

Latin:

Segregatus ad Evangelium Dei.

Nominat genus negocii, quod ei mandatum fuit, inquit se delectum esse ad propagandum Evangelium. Iam hoc loco meminisse lectorem oportet, plurimum interesse inter haec duo doctrinae genera, inter Legem & Evangelium. De eo discrimine & supra dictum est in praefatione, & infra dicendum erit capite tertio. Ipse etiam addit descriptionem Evangelii. Evangelium est promissio divinitus facta, tradita in scripturis sanctis, de filio Dei Iesu, nato ex semine David secundum carnem, declarato autem filio Dei, potente per spiritum santificantem, resuscitato ex mortuis, qui est Messias, seu rex per quem sit liberatio à peccato & à morte aeterna.

Haec definitio fiet illustrior, si antithesis legis & Evangelii instituatur. Lex est doctrina praecipiens quales esse nos, & quid agere oporteat, requirens perfectam obedientiam, non promittens gratis remissionem peccatorum, non liberans nos à peccato & à morte, sed potius armans peccatum, cum nos accusat, & terroribus letalibus opprimit. At Evangelium est promissio, quae pollicetur nobis remissionem peccatorum gratis, & liberationem à peccato & à morte per filium Dei, natum ex posteritate David iuxta promissiones, ac divina potentia nos sanctificantem & vivificantem vita aeterna.

Haec membra copiosius infra declarabuntur. Ideo autem Paulus initio statim proposuit definitionem, ut sciremus quid professus sit, et diligenter discerneremus Legem ab Evangelio, quasi dicat, Paulus divinitus vocatus ad docendum Evangelium de Christo, non ad docendam legem aut philosophiam.

## 1:2
Through the Prophets in the holy scriptures etc.

He inserts this, therefore, so that he may tacitly meet an objection. When he was professing a new kind of doctrine, the Pharisees were undoubtedly clamoring. Since there has always been some Church of God from the beginning of the world, it is necessary that it held the doctrine necessary for salvation. The Pharisees were therefore asking whether they also held the doctrine of the Apostles. If they did not hold it, the Pharisees cry out that it is new and fictitious. Paul responds, on the contrary, it is one and the same Gospel concerning the Messiah, which was promised to the Fathers, and shown to the Prophets, and is now exhibited. We do not bring forward a doctrine unknown to the Fathers and Prophets, but one buried by us through human opinions concerning the justice of the law, concerning the political kingdom of the Messiah. You execrate this kind of doctrine as if it were new and fabricated, because you do not understand of what liberation the fathers and prophets preached. You imagine that we are righteous by the law, that the Messiah is to come so that he may occupy the empire of the world, that he may give you provinces to be ruled, so that you may abound in riches and pleasures. This is the liberation which you, drunken, dream of. But they were expecting a Messiah who by divine power would abolish sin and death, who would destroy the kingdom of the devil. That was what the promise intended, in which is promised the seed which would crush the head of the serpent. In the same way now the Papists oppose the Church to us. They shout that we bring forward a kind of doctrine unknown to the Church. We protest, and testify that our doctrine has shone in the Church of the fathers, of the prophets, of the Apostles, and subsequently among the pious. We allege the testimonies of the Church, namely of the prophets, of the Apostles, and of other pious men. For no kind of doctrine ought to be received which was always unknown to the true Church of Christ. But For many centuries now the opinion of the true Church has been obscured. For the pontiffs, the mass-priests, and the monks have scattered false and Pharisaical opinions in the Church concerning the righteousness of works, they have devised ἐθελητρησκείας, they have heaped up pagan superstitions, the invocation of the dead, manifest idolomania, and with horrible impiety they have profaned the Lord's Supper.

These things were devised partly out of superstition, partly for the sake of gain, and partly for the sake of fortifying tyranny. This assembly of impious pontiffs and monks is not the Church of Christ, wherefore they unjustly arrogate this most honorable title to themselves, and they oppose to us their fictitious authority, not the authority of the true Church. Therefore, Paul warns in this place that dogmas should not be received without the testimonies of divine scripture; he also warns that we should seek the opinions of the true Church, and distinguish the true Church from the false.

Latin:

Per Prophetas in scripturis sanctis &c.

Ideo inserit, ut tacite obiectioni occurrat. Cum novum genus doctrinae profiteretur, haud dubie obstrepebant Pharisaei. Cum semper ab initio mundi aliqua fuerit Ecclesia Dei, necesse est eam tenuisse doctrinam necessariam ad salutem. Querebant igitur Pharisaei an & Apostolorum doctrinam tenuerint. Si non tenuerint, clamitant Pharisaei novam & commenticiam esse. Respondet Paulus imo unum & idem Evangelium est de Messia, quod Patribus promissum, et Prophetis monstratum, & nunc exhibitum est. Non adferimus doctrinam ignotam Patribus & Prophetis, sed à nobis obrutam per humanas opiniones de iusticia legis, de regno politico Messiae. Vos execramini hoc genus doctrinae tanquam novum & commenticium, quia non intelligitis, de qua liberatione patres & prophetae concionati sint. Fingitis nos esse iustos lege, Messiam venturum esse, ut occupet mundi imperium, vobis det provincias regendas, ut opibus & voluptatibus adfluatis. Haec est liberatio quam vos temulenti somniatis. At illi expectabant Messiam, qui divina potentia aboleat peccatum & mortem, qui destruat regnum diaboli. Id volebat promissio, in qua promittitur semen quod conterat caput serpentis. Eodem modo nunc nobis opponunt Papistae Ecclesiam. Vociferantur nos adferre genus doctrinae ignotum Ecclesiae. Nos reclamamus, & testamur fulsisse doctrinam nostram in Ecclesia patrum, prophetarum, Apostolorum, ac deinceps apud pios. Allegamus Ecclesiae testimonia, videlicet prophetarum, Apostolorum, & aliorum piorum. Nullum enim genus doctrinae recipi debet, quod verae Ecclesiae Christi semper ignotum fuit. Sed multis iam seculis obscurata fuit verae Ecclesiae sententia. Nam pontifices, sacrificuli, monachi, sparserunt in Ecclesia falsas & Pharisaicas opiniones, de iusticia operum, excogitaverunt ἐθελητρησκείας, cumulaverunt ethnicas superstitiones, invocationem mortuorum, idolomaniam manifestam, & horribili impietate prophanaverunt cenam domini.

Haec partim superstitione, partim questus, partim muniendae tyrannidis causa, excogitata sunt. Hic coetus impiorum pontificum & monachorum non est Ecclesia Christi, quare iniuste hunc honestissimum titulum sibi arrogant, & suam autoritatem commenticiam non verae Ecclesiae autoritatem nobis opponunt. Monet igitur Paulus hoc loco, ne sine testimoniis scripturae divinae dogmata recipiantur, monet etiam ut verae Ecclesiae sententias requiramus, & veram Ecclesiam à falsa discernamus.

## 1:3
Concerning his Son.

He also opposes this clause to the common persuasions of the Jews. The Jews were expecting a Messiah who would not be the Son of God by nature, but only a man similar to the other prophets, that is, excelling the common people in wisdom, righteousness, and happiness in the conducting of affairs, so that easily he would occupy the empire of the world. But the Fathers and the Prophets knew that the Messiah was the Son of God, then also governing and helping them. Jacob says: The Angel who delivered me from all evils, let him bless these boys, where he signifies that he is speaking of the deliverer, whom he knew to have been promised. For it is the proper office of this one to deliver from all evils. And Jacob, Moses, and Daniel saw him. Therefore John, that he may testify that the Messiah is the Son of God, and that he was always present to the Fathers, says: In the beginning was the Word, all things were made through him, etc. Signifying that all the glorious victories of Noah, Abraham, Joseph, Moses, Samuel, David, Isaiah, Jeremiah were obtained by this leader and our champion against the devil. Wherefore also in this place Paul discourses concerning the two natures in the Messiah, he calls him the Son of God, that he may tax the error of the Jews, just as Christ himself also taxed John 5 and often elsewhere. Paul speaks, however, about the person, and aptly attributes to the person the appellation of the Son of God. For this appellation is not to be attributed only to the divine nature, but to the person of Christ. He testifies, however, that this one consists of two natures, he says that this Son was born according to the flesh from the seed of David. He affirms, therefore, in Christ has a human nature. And this passage refutes the Manichaeans and very many others, who stripped a human nature from Christ, or denied that it was received from the blood of the virgin mother. Then he preaches about the divine nature, when he says: Who was declared to be the Son of God, powerful through the sanctifying spirit, by the resurrection of the dead.

There is a singular emphasis in the word ὁρισθέντος, which the Greeks explain by the term ἀποδειχθέντος. And the meaning is that this Son of God was certainly acknowledged through these testimonies, because he rose from the dead, because he showed his immense power by many miracles, as when he raised Lazarus, because he now gives the Holy Spirit to the Church, who both strengthens minds against the devil and produces many huge miracles, for Paul also raised a dead listener, and all things then were full of miracles, which were done by the Apostles, requesting those gifts from the Son of God. Therefore Paul speaks about the testimony toward us. For on account of these testimonies this Jesus is pronounced certainly καὶ ὁρίξεται to be the Son of God by nature, since he has divine and immense power. The word ὁρίξεσθαι signifies this, to be pronounced certainly. Moreover, he opposes all these things to the Jewish opinions, who were expecting a Messiah who was indeed an excellent man, but having only a human nature, flourishing with heroic victories, who would give wealth, not a new nature, and eternal life. But Paul, he says, declares this Messiah to be powerful, and to give the sanctifying spirit, through whom a new light, righteousness, and eternal life are begun in believers, and the devil is conquered. This, he says, is the true liberation, which the Fathers both understood and experienced in the exercises of faith, struggling with the devil, with death, in various dangers, and it is far greater than the liberation which you expect, you who think that the Messiah is going to distribute provinces, just as Alexander distributed kingdoms to his fellow soldiers. Paul rebukes these errors with this although brief description. But when he names this Christ, let us contemplate in our mind all the ancient promises in the prophecies, so that we may see them truly agree with this proclamation of the Gospel, and so that by the thought of the benefits of Christ we may kindle faith in ourselves, and call upon him. For unless faith is exercised in invocation, the kingdom and presence of Christ cannot be understood.

It would be a long task to explain these such great matters, as their magnitude demands. Since, however, there ought to be a certain limit to commentaries, I will not linger any longer on this Inscription, especially since the same matters often recur. And the pious reader, having been admonished concerning the intention of the author and concerning the sum of the opinion, will contemplate the magnitude of the matters with assiduous meditation, and will learn how this knowledge of Christ ought to shine in life, in invocation, in dangers, in every action, so that the Son of God may be for us also powerful, a liberator from sin, from death, and from the devil, so that he may be for us a high priest interceding for us before God, and may be our leader, who helps us in our calamities, just as he promises help to the weak, saying: Come to me all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you.

Let adolescents diligently observe the syntax of the words, by the noticing of which much light is added to the sentence. Paul the Apostle, called to teach the Gospel concerning Jesus Christ, who was born from the posterity of David according to the flesh, and was declared to be the Son of God through the resurrection, and by the Holy Spirit having been given, wishes salvation to the Romans.

Latin:

De filio suo.

Opponit & hanc particulam vulgaribus Iudaeorum persuasionibus. Iudaei expectabant Messiam, qui non esset natura filius Dei, sed tantum homo caeteris prophetis similis, hoc est, antecellens vulgus, sapientia, iusticia, & felicitate in rebus gerendis, ut facile orbis imperium occuparet. At Patreset Prophetae norant Messiam esse filium Dei, tunc quoque ipsos gubernantem & iuvantem. Iacob inquit: Angelus qui eripuit me ex omnibus malis, benedicat his pueris, ubi significat se loqui de liberatore, quem norat promissum esse. Nam huius proprium munus est, liberare ex omnibus malis. Ac viderunt eum Iacob, Moises & Daniel. Ideo Iohannes, ut testetur Messiam esse filium Dei, & semper adfuisse Patribus, inquit: In principio erat verbum, omnia per ipsum facta sunt &c. Significans omnes gloriosas victorias Noae, Abrahae, Ioseph, Moisi, Samuelis, Davidis, Esaiae, Ieremiae partas esse hoc duce & propugnatore nostro adversus diabolum. Quare & hoc loco Paulus de duabus naturis in Messia concionatur, vocat filium Dei, ut Iudaeorum errorem taxet, sicut & Christus ipse taxavit Iohannis v. & saepe alias. Loquitur autem Paulus de persona, & apte tribuit personae appellationem filii Dei. Non enim tantum divinae naturae tribuenda est haec appellatio, sed personae Christi. Hunc autem testatur constare duabus naturis, ait hunc filium secundum carnem natum esse ex semine Davidis. Adfirmat igitur in Christo esse humanam naturam. Et hic locus refutat Manicheos & plaerosque alios, qui humanam naturam Christo detraxerunt, aut negarunt acceptam esse ex sanguine matris virginis. Deinde concionatur de divina natura, cum ait: Quis declaratus est esse filius Dei, potens per spiritum sanctificantem, ex resurrectione mortuorum.

Singularis est emphasis in voce ὁρισθέντος, quem enarrant Graeci per vocabulum ἀποδειχθέντος. Estque sententia, certo agnitum esse hunc filium Dei per haec testimonia, quod resurrexit à mortuis, quod potentiam suam immensam multis miraculis ostendit, ut cum Lazarum resuscitavit, quod iam dat spiritum sanctum Ecclesiae, qui & mentes confirmat adversus diabolum, & multa ingentia miracula edit, nam & Paulus resuscitavit mortuum auditorem, & omnia tunc plena erant miraculorum, quae fiebant ab Apostolis, petentibus ea munera à filio Dei. Loquitur ergo Paulus de testimonio erga nos. Nam propter haec testimonia pronunciatur certo καὶ ὁρίξεται, hic Iesus esse filius Dei natura, cum potentiam habeat divinam & immensam. Hoc significat verbum ὁρίξεσθαι, certo pronunciari. Opponit autem haec omnia Iudaicis opinionibus, qui expectabant Messiam praestantem quidem virum, sed tantum humanam naturam habentem, florentem victoriis heroicis, daturum opes, non novam naturam, & aeternam vitam. At Paulus, inquit, hunc Messiam esse potentem, & dare spiritum sanctificantem, per quem in credentibus inchoatur nova lux, iusticia, & vita aeterna, & vincitur diabolus. Haec inquit est vera liberatio, quam Patres & intellexerunt & experti sunt in exercitiis fidei, luctantes cum diabolo, cum morte, in variis periculis, ac longe maior est liberatione, quam vos expectetis, qui Messiam arbitramini partiturum esse provincias, sicut Alexander distribuit regna suis commilitonibus. Hos errores reprehendit Paulus hac quanquàm brevi descriptione. Cum autem nominat hunc Christum, animo intueamur omnes veteres promissiones in prophetiis, ut videamus eas vere cum hac Evangelii concione congruere, & ut cogitatione beneficiorum Christi accendamus fidem in nobis, eumque invocemus. Nisi enim fides exerceatur in invocatione, non potest regnum & praesentia Christi intelligi.

Longum esset has tantas res explicare, ut earum magnitudo postulat. Cum autem modus quidam esse commentariorum debeat, non immorabor prolixius huic Epigraphiae, praesertim cum eaedem res saepe recurrant. Et pius lector admonitus de consilio autoris, ac de summa sententiae, assidua meditatione magnitudinem rerum contemplabitur, & discet quomodo haec Christi noticia lucere debeat in vita, in invocatione, in periculis, in omni actione, ut sit nobis quoque filius Dei potens, liberator à peccato, à morte, & à diabolo, ut sit nobis pontifex pro nobis interpellans apud Deum, sit dux noster, qui in calamitatibus nostris adiuvet nos, sicut pollicetur infirmis auxilium, inquiens: Venite ad me omnes, qui laboratis & onerati estis, & ego reficiam vos.

Adolescentes Syntaxin verborum diligenter observent, qua animadversa multum lucis accedit sententiae. Paulus Apostolus vocatus ad docendum Evangelium de Iesu Christo, qui natus est ex posteritate David secundum carnem, & declaratus est esse filius Dei per resurrectionem, & dato spiritu sancto, optat Romanis salutem.

## 1:5
Through whom we have received.

Although above, when he calls himself an Apostle, and says that he was set apart, or chosen for the office of teaching the Gospel, yet he had not said by name that he was called by Christ. Wherefore here he adds this by name: through whom we have received grace, that is, reconciliation with God, and the office of Apostle, for the obedience of faith, that is, that obedience may be rendered to the faith, or to the Gospel preaching about faith, among all nations. He adds this, that he may incidentally testify that the nations also are to be called to the Gospel. Furthermore, I said above that the authority of the mandate of the office is alleged, so that we may know that this preaching of Paul must necessarily be believed. So read Paul, that you may think that you are not reading a human disputation, but hearing God himself speaking with you.

Latin:

Per quem accepimus.

Etsi supra, cum se nominat Apostolum, ac dicit se segregatum, seu delectum esse ad munus docendi Evangelii, tamen non dixerat nominatim se à Christo vocatum esse. Quare hic nominatim hoc adii cit: per quem accepimus gratiam, id est, reconciliationem cum Deo, & munus Apostoli, ad obedientiam fidei, id est, ut obediatur fidei, seu Evangelio concionanti de fide, apud omnes gentes. Id adiicit, ut obiter testetur & gentes vocandas esse ad Evangelium. Porro dixi supra allegari autoritatem mandati muneris, ut sciamus necessario credendum esse huic concioni Pauli. Sic legas Paulum, ut existimes te non humanam disputationem legere, sed ipsum audire Deum tecum loquentem.

## 1:7
Grace to you and peace.

First, he wishes them grace, that is, reconciliation and the gift of the Holy Spirit. Then peace, that is, the other goods of which there is need. For the word peace generally signifies in the Hebrew custom prosperous and joyful things. Moreover, there is need also for the Church of many gifts, purity of doctrine, increase of virtues, concord, constancy, food, hospitality. The word peace embraces all these things. Moreover, he joins God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, first, that he may remind us that grace and other things are given by God on account of the Son, the mediator. Then, that we may know how these things certainly come to us, namely, if we ask on account of the Son. Thirdly, he signifies that Christ is God by nature, reigning with equal power with the Father, helping us by divine power, as is promised in the Psalm: The Lord lifts up all who are falling, and raises up all who are bowed down Ps. 145:14.

Exordium.

The members of the prayer must be diligently distinguished, for one thing is treated in one place, another in others. Here he prepares the minds of the readers, so that it may be in the exordium; he is not yet disputing, he is not yet engaged in the citadel of the cause. But he puts forward certain rhetorical devices, he congratulates them on the knowledge of the Gospel, he signifies his benevolence toward them, he says that he desires to help their study. Then he adds αἰτιολογίας taken from the function of an Apostle. Learned men know that such a dwelling upon our will is customary in exordia, nor is it difficult to apply the parts of the exordium to common precepts: It consists of four members, I congratulate you on the knowledge of the Gospel, and I desire that that knowledge may grow in you. Then follows the proposition of the Exordium: I desire to teach you in person. To which he immediately attaches an adversative: but until now the Churches of these regions have detained me, so that I have not been able to set out to you. Thirdly follows the reason for the proposition, why he desires to teach them in person, because, he says, I owe it to assist the studies of the Gospel among all the learned and the unlearned. All these things pertain to the topics of conciliating benevolence. The other αἰτιολογία renders the reader attentive, taken from the dignity of the Gospel: I am not ashamed of the Gospel. He opposes this voice to the judgments of all the impious. For the Epicureans in the world, of whom there is a huge multitude, despise the Gospel, and think it to be a fictitious and foolish poem of barbarian men. Most governors of the Republic also cruelly hate this kind of doctrine, by which they think the tranquility of cities and empires is disturbed, they desire to extinguish it as a torch of seditions and civil discords. Besides these, hypocrites fascinated by superstitions, as the Jews then and at this time the monks and these likewise, they hate the Gospel much more bitterly than others, because they judge it to be insulting toward God, when it censures superstitious cults, which they admire as the height of piety and the religions of angels. And the devil, burning with immense hatred for Christ, increases and confirms these furies in the impious, intent upon the occasions by which he can irritate, impel, and inflame the minds of individuals. For he holds these captive, and incites them by presenting various occasions, just as the power of the devil is seen in Idolomania and other horrendous lapses. Lucian narrates that a certain man had furiously loved a statue of Venus, and was accustomed to embrace it while weeping, and to kiss it. And many things could be narrated from histories that are horrendous to hear, which, since they are foreign to the common custom of nature, it appears sufficiently that they have arisen properly from the devil; when we read these, let us think that the devil does not have an idle tyranny, but he horribly impels the impious to nefarious crimes. Wherefore let us not wonder at all that he can inflame hatreds and savagery in hypocrites and tyrants. The Pharisees saw the ceremonies of the Law and their own traditions being abolished. Therefore they raged and complained that God was being insulted, and that works pleasing to God were being prohibited. license to sin is granted. Then they saw that with the law abolished, their Republic was changed, the distinction between priests and people was confounded, and the chief glory of the Republic, namely ἀξίωμα ἱερατικὸν, was taken away. Such a change brings great grief to the wise. The devil was increasing these flames of hatred, he was inciting princes to cruelty, to the killing of the Apostles. Thus also at this time we are most proudly mocked by the Epicureans, because we feel that the Gospel is not a fabrication, because we feel seriously that it must be obeyed. Kings and princes rage that the tranquility of states is disturbed by a dissimilarity of doctrine. Pontiffs do not want Idolatry to be reproved, lest their authority be shaken, monks fear for their gain, a few, fascinated by superstition, contend that good works are forbidden. From so many causes arises the enormity of hatreds against the Gospel. But let us, on the contrary, determine with a great spirit that the profession of the Gospel is not to be cast aside. Let us not be ashamed of this doctrine. For it is not an empty fable, it is not a barbaric superstition, but it is the sentence of God, revealed divinely, by which He wishes to impart eternal salvation to men. God is the creator of all things and of the human race, He did not wish the race to perish entirely. human, which He had created, so that the knowledge of God might shine in it. Wherefore from the beginning He revealed Himself to the Fathers by certain testimonies, and delivered the Gospel to them. Nor is there any other doctrine anywhere concerning this will of God, accepted by certain authority or confirmed by true heavenly testimonies, except this doctrine of the Gospel. Wherefore let us not despise it, but let us obey it, and let us know that God truly performs what He promises. Let us therefore fix in our minds this saying of Paul: I am not ashamed of the Gospel, so that it may raise us up against the judgments of the impious.

Although Paul is not yet disputing in the beginning, nevertheless these ἠθικὰ contain five useful topics: The first is concerning spiritual worship. He says that he serves God in spirit, through the office of preaching. Here he teaches that the chief worship is to teach and learn the Gospel, which the studious and pious ought to remember, so that they may perform these acts of worship to God with greater care.

The second is concerning mutual confirmation. Paul desires to teach and confirm them, and in turn to be stirred up by them. Concerning this mutual confirmation Christ says to Peter: And you, when you have turned, confirm your brothers. It is profitable for the pious to hear the testimonies of the pious and the learned concerning doctrine.

The third is concerning the Apostolic office. I am a debtor He says, I am debtor both to the wise and to the unwise. Truly, it seems a glorious voice. The Apostle dares to profess that he can teach even the wise. What kind of arrogance this seemed to the Roman nobles, that a wandering Jew should promise that he is a teacher even of the wise. For the most part, those who are excellent in intellect and learning, especially if a persuasion of holiness about themselves is added, admire themselves too much, and demand that divine honors be attributed to them, such as I have seen some receive. Such men look down upon Paul from on high, and mock this voice, by which he says that he is a teacher of the wise. But let us remember that he is an apostle, who brings not human doctrine, but heavenly; as Elijah, Elisha, and Isaiah were teachers and governors of kings and high priests, so let us also hear Paul, nor let the wise be ashamed to learn from God, since we so often experience human wisdom to hallucinate shamefully and to wander far astray, as all wise men have complained. And God says: I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, as the histories of all times truly show, and daily life testifies. Moreover, it pertains to the Apostle's office to teach both, the wise and the unwise; he ought to adapt himself even to the grasp of the weak, as Paul says. 1. Cor. iii. As to carnal men, as to infants in Christ, I have preached; I have fed you with milk Thus let the teachers and governors of the Churches propose useful things, and accommodate themselves to the capacity of those learning. When the unskilled and unlearned do not hear things explained clearly, they sometimes conceive false persuasions, as I have often observed. Now let the pontiffs and monks be compared to the image of Paul. Paul says that he is a debtor, that he may teach; he is obligated by the command of God to this duty. But the pontiffs do not even wish to teach, but only to maintain domination in a tyrannical manner. They have confirmed the Idolatry that arose in the Church from the devil, namely the profanation of the Lord's supper, the invocation of saints, monasticism, and similar things; they have confirmed lusts by the nefarious law of celibacy. Now, having been admonished, they tenaciously retain the foulest errors and turpitude, and they do not even pretend to have doctrine; they confess that they are in error, but they say that wealth, power, and authority must be defended. Therefore, they defend their crimes only by the cruelty of punishments, just as Nebuchadnezzar ordered all who would not adore the statue to be thrown into the kindled furnace. There is the greatest dissimilarity between the Apostle and the Tyrant, as between pious Angels and devils. For both good teachers are called Angels of God in Malachi, and the tyrant is truly an instrument of of the devil in the world. Therefore let us diligently weigh these words of Paul, which indeed testify that pontiffs opposing the Gospel are not to be held as Bishops and successors of the Apostles, but are to be avoided as tyrants cast out of the true Church. A Bishop is a debtor to the conscience of his subject, wherefore he ought not to impose a law upon him, such as is the law concerning celibacy, which he cannot obey without crimes and offense to God. Furthermore, whom do the satellites of Tyrants, the writers and monks, teach? To the wise they propose childish traditions, concerning clothing, concerning foods, concerning the pomps of ceremonies. These they adorn and now begin to paint with eloquence. Just as now indeed they invent allegories of gestures, for the sake of excusing superstition in the temples. What does this doctrine contribute to the wise? By which they are recalled to childish discipline, and πτῶχα στοιχεῖα κόσμου, when they ought to hear doctrine unknown to reason, concerning interior vices, concerning doubt, concerning diffidence, concerning security, concerning the admiration of our own wisdom and justice, concerning the infirmity seeking human protections against the commandments of God, just as the kings of Judah used to flee now to the Assyrians, now to the Egyptians, when they distrusted God. Again, they were to be raised up by true with spiritual consolations, so that they do not succumb when human counsels or human errors have deceived them. This is the doctrine of the wise, in which the knowledge of God grows. How do they instruct the foolish? Two kinds of doctrine reign among the adversaries: the Labyrinths of questions on the Lombard, which not even the professors themselves understand, and the summaries excerpted from Canon Law, which collect sins against human traditions. Both things are infinite, full of errors, and of perplexity. Wherefore many good men before these times have desired an amendment of Ecclesiastical doctrine. What is more, there are many things that are idolatrous, than are the futile disputes in the fourth book of the Sentences: whether a mouse gnawing the bread of the Sacrament gnaws the body of the Lord. I shudder to relate it. There it should have been warned that Sacraments are actions, and that Sacraments are not spectacles alien to their instituted use. I could recite many examples of futile questions, but the books are at hand, which sufficiently show that there was a need for an amendment of doctrine. The little verse of Ovid is known: And what he knows little, no one can teach. Let it therefore be the first care of one teaching the Gospel, that he himself rightly holds the sum of the doctrine Christian, from which he will then be able to choose useful things for teaching both, for instructing the more unlearned, and for admonishing and correcting the wise, just as Paul corrected Peter, Isaiah Hezekiah, etc.

The fourth point is consolation, for he confirms us by his own example, saying: I am not ashamed of the Gospel, so that we may not be deterred from the Gospel by the judgments of the world. Even if Epicureans mock us as mad, because we believe the Gospel is not an empty fable. Even if tyrants and hypocrites attempt to erase the name of Christ with the immense bitterness of punishments, nevertheless let us not allow ourselves to be drawn away from this kind of doctrine, and let this profession be glorious to us before God, his son, the pious angels, and the universal Church. Let us look to these judgments, and let us know that through this doctrine the promised benefits are truly exhibited to us, namely reconciliation and eternal life.

The fifth point is a distinguished and memorable saying about the ministry of the word, namely that the remission of sins, the Holy Spirit, and the beginning of eternal life are given through the voice of the Gospel heard, read, or pondered: When the minds are sustained by the voice of the Gospel in terrors, the Holy Spirit is at the same time effective, as is said below: Faith comes by hearing He thinks the same thing, saying: The Gospel is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth, that is, it is an instrument through which God is efficacious, He gives the Holy Spirit, not as the Pharisees imagine, by the work performed, without the thought of the mind, but God commands the Gospel to be received by faith. And when the mind receives it, it struggles with terrors and distrust. Therefore it is said to the Galatians: That we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith. He adds, moreover, the sum of the Gospel, which is the proposition of the whole disputation which follows. The righteousness of God is revealed therein from faith to faith. This is the sum of all the benefits of Christ. For God being reconciled is present, He endows them with new light, and eternal life, He hears and defends them in all calamities. Wherefore when he names the righteousness of God, he has embraced all the benefits of Christ. Furthermore, let the kind of speech be observed: The righteousness of God, that is, divine acceptance, by which God receives and approves us, this is revealed in the Gospel. And the antithesis is to be observed, as if he were to say: You indeed have the law, in which the righteousness of the law is revealed, but because of the law you did not yet have the righteousness of God, that is, you were not accepted by God. But in the Gospel the righteousness of God is revealed, that is, the acceptance by which God is now certainly propitious to us, remits sins, and reckons us righteous.

Therefore it follows: it is revealed from faith to faith. That also is opposed to the justice of the law. As if to say: The Law taught that there is justice, to satisfy the Law. But now justice is revealed from faith, that is, justice imputed through mercy. For when we read the word of faith, let there immediately come to mind the correlative, namely, the promised mercy. The Pauline discourse smells of the Hebrew phrase, for Cicero speaks otherwise when he says concerning Caesar, your right hand excelling in faith. Wherefore the phrase in Paul is to be observed, where faith signifies trust in the mercy promised on account of Christ. Wherefore when he names the justice of faith, he understands the justice which is imputed through mercy. And this he opposes to the justice of the law, which ought to be perfect obedience according to the law. But since no one can provide this, since this miserable nature of men is captive to sin, a new justice is revealed in the Gospel, namely, justice imputed through mercy. But nevertheless this must be received by faith, that is, by the acknowledgment and trust of Christ, as Isaiah says: The knowledge of Christ shall justify many, as if to say: Since by the law men are not just or accepted by God, but have sins, God wills to remit sins to them in this way, and to be propitious, if they have acknowledged him to wish to impart these benefits on account of the Son, who is the victim and the propitiator. This is the simple and native explanation. He says, however: From faith into faith, that is, from imperfect faith into more perfect faith. Mercy is indeed revealed, but it does not happen to all, because God wills it to be received by faith, but since many do not wish to receive it, and spurn this ineffable goodness, they perish. Nor is faith an idle knowledge, but it is necessary that it grow in constant struggle, in invocation, in all business and dangers. Let it always shine in hearts, that God is propitious to us on account of the mediator Son, about to help. And by this faith let us invoke him, and let us seek the governance of all business and dangers. Thus faith and the true knowledge of God grow in the hearts of the pious. But that the opinion which he proposed is true, namely that men are just by faith, he soon adds a testimony, so that the hearer may know that the Pauline sermons truly agree with the prophetic ones, and that the apostles renew the doctrine of the prophets.

Latin:

Gratia vobis & pax.

Primum optat eis gratiam, id est reconciliationem, & donationem spiritus sancti. Deinde pacem, id est, caetera bona quibus opus est. Nam vocabulum pacis generaliter significat Ebraica consuetudine res secundas & letas. Est autem opus etiam Ecclesiae multis donis, doctrinae puritate, virtutum augmento, concordia, constantia, victu, hospitio. Haec omnia complectitur vocabulum pacis. Coniungit autem Deum patrem & Dominum Iesum Christum, Primum, ut moneat nobis gratiam, & caetera donari à Deo propter filium mediatorem. Deinde ut sciamus quomodo haec certo nobis contingant, scilicet si propter filium petamus. Tertio significat Christum natura Deum esse, pari potentia cum patre regnantem, adiuvantem nos divina potentia, sicut promittitur in psal. Allevat Dominus omnes qui corruunt, & erigit omnes elisos.

Exordium.

Membra orationis diligenter discernenda sunt, aliud enim aliis locis agitur. Hic praeparat animos lectorum, ut sit in exordiis, nondum disputat, nondum versatur in arce causae. Sed rhetorica quaedam praeponit, gratulatur illis cognitionem Evangelii, significat suam erga illos benevolentiam, ait se cupere illorum studium adiuvare. Deinde subiicit αἰτιολογίας sumptas à functione Apostoli. Eruditi norunt talem commorationem nostrae voluntatis in exordiis usitatam esse, nec difficile est partes exordii ad vulgaria praecepta conferre: Quatuor membris constat, Gratulor vobis cognitionem Evangelii, et opto, ut ea cognitio in vobis crescat. Deinde sequitur Exordii propositio: Cupio vos coram docere. Cui attexit statim adversativam: sed hactenus detinuerunt me harum regionum Ecclesiae, ut ad vos proficisci non potuerim. Tertio sequitur ratio propositionis, cur illos coram docere cupiat, quia, inquit, debeo iuvare Evangelii studia apud omnes eruditos & ineruditos. Haec omnia pertinent ad locos conciliandae benevolentiae. Altera αἰτιολογία reddit lectorem attentum, à dignitate Evangelii sumpta: Non pudet me Evangelii. Hanc vocem opponit impiorum omnium iudiciis. Nam Epicurei in mundo, quorum est ingens multitudo, contemnunt Evangelium, & arbitrantur commenticium & stultum poema barbarorum hominum esse. Plaerique gubernatores Reipublicae etiam crudeliter oderunt hoc doctrinae genus, quo existimant turbari civitatum & imperiorum tranquillitatem, cupiunt extinguere tanquàm facem seditionum, & discordiarum civilium. Praeter hos hypocritae fascinati superstitionibus, ut tunc Iudaei & hoc tempore monachi & horum similes, multo acerbius oderunt Evangelium, quàm alii, quia iudicant esse contumeliosum adversus Deum, cum vituperat superstitiosos cultus, quos isti tanquàm summam pietatem & religiones angelorum admirantur. Et hos furores in impiis diabolus immani odio Christi ardens auget & confirmat, intentus in occasiones, quibus irritare, impellere, & accendere animos singulorum potest. Hos enim habet captivos, & incitat obiiciens varias occasiones, sicut in Idolomania, & aliis horrendis lapsibus conspicitur diaboli potentia. Lucianus narrat quendam furenter amasse statuam Veneris, & solitum complecti lachrymantem, & deosculari. Ac possent multa narrari ex historiis horrenda auditu, quae cum aliena sint à commuvi consuetudine naturae, satis apparet proprie à diabolo orta esse, quae cum legimus, cogitemus diabolum non habere ociosam tyrannidem, sed horribiliter impellit impios ad nefaria scelera. Quare nihil miremur eum posse accendere odia & sevitiam in hypocritis, et tyrannis. Videbant Pharisaei aboleri caeremonias Legis, & traditiones suas. Fremebant igitur & quaerebantur Deum contumelia adfici, prohiberi opera Deum placantia cantia, concedi licentiam peccandi. Deinde videbant abolita lege mutari Rempub. suam, confundi discrimen sacerdotum et populi, tolli & Reipub. praecipuum decus, videlicet ἀξίωμα ἱερατικὸν. Talis mutatio ingentem dolorem adfert sapientibus. Has flammas odii augebat diabolus, incendebat principes ad crudelitatem, ad interficiendos Apostolos. Ita & hoc tempore superbissime deridemur ab Epicureis, quod Evangelium non esse commenticium sentimus, quod serio sentimus ei obtemperandum esse. Reges et principes sremunt turbari tranquillitatem civitatum dissimilitudine doctrinae. Pontifices nolunt reprehendi Idolatriam, ne autoritas eorum labefiat, monachi metuunt questui, pauci superstitione fascinati, contendunt prohiberi bona opera. Ex tot causis existit immanitas odiorum contra Evangelium. Sed nos contra ingenti animo statuamus non esse obiiciendam Evangelii professionem. Non pudeat nos huius doctrinae. Non est enim inanis fabula, non est barbarica superstitio, sed est sententia Dei, patefacta divinitus, qua vult hominibus impertire salutem aeternam. Est Deus conditor omnium rerum ac generis humani, is non voluit prorsus perire genus humanum, quod condiderat, ut in eo luceret Dei noticia. Quare se ab initio certis testimoniis patefecit Patribus, eisque Evangelium tradidit. Nec alia est usquàm doctrina de hac voluntate Dei, certa autoritate accepta aut confirmata veris testimoniis caelestibus, nisi haec Evangelii doctrina. Quare non aspernemur eam, sed ei obtemperemus, ac sciamus Deum vere praestare quae pollicetur. Infigamus ergo animis hoc dictum Pauli: Non pudet me Evangelii, ut nos adversus iudicia impiorum erigat.

Etsi autem in exordio nondum disputat Paulus, tamen haec ἠθικὰ continent quinque utiles locos: Primus est de cultu spirituali. Ait se servire Deo in spiritu, per munus concionandi. Hic docet praecipuum cultum esse, docere & discere Evangelium, quod meminisse studiosi & pii debent, ut hos cultus maiore cura Deo praestent.

Secundus est de mutua confirmatione. Paulus cupit illos docere & confirmare, ac vicissim ab eis excitari. De hac muta confirmatione inquit Christus ad Petrum: Et tu conversus confirma fratres tuos. Prodest piis audire piorum & peritorum testimonia de doctrina.

Tertius de Apostolico officio. Debitor inquit sum sapientibus & insipientibus Gloriosa profecto vox videtur. Audet Apostolus profiteri se etiam sapientes posse docere. Qualis haec arrogantia visa est proceribus Romanis, erronem Iudaeum polliceri se etiam sapientum magistrum esse. Plerumque excellentes ingeniis & doctrina, praesertim si accedat persuasio sanctitatis de se, nimium se ipsi admirantur, ac sibi divinos honores tribui postulant, quales vidi aliquos. Tales ex alto despiciunt Paulum, ac derident hanc vocem, qua se magistrum esse sapientum dicit. Sed nos meminerimus apostolum esse, qui affert non humanam doctrinam, sed caelestem, ut Elias, Eliseus, Esaias, erant Regum & pontificum doctores & gubernatores, sic audiamus et Paulum, nec pudeat sapientes à Deo discere, cum toties experiamur humanam sapientiam turpiter hallucinari ac procul deerrare, ut omnes sapientes questi sunt. Et Deus inquit: Perdam sapientiam sapientum, ut prosecto omnium temporum historiae ostendunt, & quotidiana vita testatur. Pertinet autem ad Apostoli officium utrosque docere, sapientes & insipientes, attemperare se etiam ad imbecillium captum debet, sicut Paulus inquit. 1. Cor. iii. Ut carnalib. ut infantibus in Christo concionatus sum, lacte vos potavi Ita doctores & gubernatores Ecclesiarum proponant utilia, & se ad discentium captum attemperent. Imperiti & rudes cum non audiunt diserte explicata, interdum falsas persuasiones concipiunt, ut saepe animadverti. Iam ad imaginem Pauli conferantur pontifices, & monachi. Paulus ait se debitorem esse, ut doceat, est obligatus mandato Dei ad hoc munus. At pontifices ne volunt quidem docere, sed tantum tyrannico more dominationem tueri. Confirmaverunt Idolatriam in Ecclesia ortam à diabolo, videlicet prophanationem cenae Domini, invocationem divorum, monachatum, & similia, confirmaverunt libidines nefaria lege de caelibatu. Nunc admoniti, mordicus retinent teterrimos errores & turpitudinem, ac ne quidem pretexunt doctrinam, fatentur se errare, sed aiunt opes, potentiam, autoritatem propugnandam esse. Ideo tantum crudelitate suppliciorum defendunt sua scelera, ut Nabugdonofor iussit in fornacem accensam iniici omnes, qui nollent adorare statuam. Summa dissimilitudo est inter Apostolum & Tyrannum, ut inter pios Angelos & diabolos. Nam & boni doctores vocantur Angeli Dei apud Malachiam, & tyrannus est vere organum diaboli in mundo. Ideo haec verba Pauli diligenter expendamus, quae quidem testantur, pontifices adversantes Evangelio, non esse habendos pro Episcopis, ac successoribus Apostolorum, sed vitandos tanquàm tyrannos eiectos extra veram Ecclesiam. Episcopus est debitor conscientiae subditi, quare non debet ei legem imponere, qualis est lex de caelibatu, cui sine sceleribus & offensione Dei obtemperare non potest. Deinde satellites Tyrannorum, scriptores & monachi quos docent? Sapientibus proponunt pueriles traditiones, de vestitu, de cibis, de pompis caeremoniarum. Has ornant & pingere iam eloquentia incipiunt. Sicut nunc quidem allegorias gestuum comminiscuntur, ad in templis excusandam superstitionem. Haec doctrina quid conducit sapientibus? qua revocantur ad puerilem disciplinam, & πτῶχα στοιχεῖα κόσμου, cum audire deberent doctrinam ignotam rationi, de interioribus viciis, de dubitatione, de diffidentia, de securitate, de admiratione nostrae sapientiae & iusticiae, de infirmitate quaerente praesidia humana contra mandata Dei, sicut reges Iuda confugiebant iam ad Assyrios, iam ad Aegyptios, cum Deo diffiderent. Rursus erigendi erant veris consolationibus spiritualibus, ne succumbant, cum fefellerunt eos humana consilia, aut humani errores. Haec est sapientum doctrina, in qua crescit agnitio Dei. Quomodo erudiunt insipientes? Duo genera doctrinae regnant apud adversarios, Labyrinthi questionum in Longobardum, quos ne ipsi quidem professores intelligunt, & excerptae summae ex Iure canonico, quae colligunt peccata contra traditiones humanas. Utraque res est infinita, plena errorum, & perplexitatis. Quare multi boni viri ante haec tempora optaverunt emendationem doctrinae Ecclesiasticae. Quid quòd multa sunt Idolatrica, quam sunt futiles disputationes in quarto sententiarum: an mus rodens panem Sacramenti, rodat corpus Domini. Horresco referens. Ibi illud erat monendum, Sacramenta actiones esse, nec spectacula aliena ab instituto usu Sacramenta actiones esse, nec spectacula aliena ab instituto usu Sacramenta esse. Possem multa exempla recitare futilium questionum, sed libri sunt in promptu, qui satis ostendunt, opus fuisse doctrinae emendatione. Notus est Ovidii versiculus: Quodque parum novit, nemo docere potest. Sit igitur prima cura docentis Evangelium, recte ut ipse teneat summam doctrinae Christianae, ex qua deinde poterit eligere utilia ad utrosque docendos, ad erudiendos rudiores, & ad admonendos, ac corrigendos sapientes, sicut Paulus corrigebat Petrum, Esaias Ezechiam &c.

Quartus locus consolatio est, confirmat enim nos suo exemplo, inquiens: non pudet me Evangelii, ne deterreamur ab Evangelio iudiciis mundi. Etiamsi Epicurei derident nos tanquam amentes, propterea quod Evangelium sentimus non esse inanem fabulam. Etiam si tyrañi & hypocritae delere nomen Christi ingenti acerbitate suppliciorum, conantur, tamen non sinamus nos abstrahi ab hoc genere doctrinae, & hanc professionem nobis gloriosam esse coram Deo, filio eius, piis angelis, & Ecclesia universa. Haec iudicia respiciamus, & sciamus nobis per hanc doctrinam vere exhiberi promissa beneficia, scilicet reconciliationem & vitam aetarnam.

Quintus locus est insigne & memorabile dictum de ministerio verbi, quod videlicet dentur, remissio peccatorum, spiritus sanctus, & inchoatio vitae aeternae, per vocem Evangelii auditam, lectam seu cogitatam: Cum voce Evangelii sustentantur animi in pavoribus spiritus sanctus simul est efficax, ut infra dicitur: Fides exauditu est. Idem hic sentit, inquiens: Evangelium est potentia Dei ad salutem omni credenti, id est, est instrumentum per quod Deus est efficax, dat spiritum sanctum, non ut fingunt Pharisaei, ex opere operato, sine cogitatione mentis, sed Deus iubet fide accipi Evangelium. Et cum accipit mens, luctatur cum pavoribus & diffidentia. Ideo ad Galat. dicitur: Ut promissionem spiritus accipiamus per fidem. Addit autem summam Evangelii, quae est propositio totius disputationis, quae sequitur. Iusticia Dei in eo revelatur ex fide in fidem. Haec est summa omnium beneficiorum Christi. Nam reconliatis Deus adest, donat eos nova luce, & aeterna vita, exaudit & defendit eos in omnibus calamitatibus Quare cum nominat iusticiam Dei, complexus est omnia beneficia Christi. Porro genus sermonis observetur: Iusticia Dei, id est, acceptatio divina, qua nos Deus recipit & approbat, haec patesit in Evangelio, Estque antithesis observanda, quasi dicat: An rea legem habetis, in qua patesit iusticia legis, sed propter legem nondum habebatis iusticiam Dei, id est, non eratis accepti Deo. At in Evangelio patesit iusticia Dei, hoc est, acceptatio, qua nunc Deus nobis certo propitius est, remittit peccata, & reputat nos iustos.

Ideo sequitur: patefit ex fide in fidem. Id quoque opponitur iusticiae legis. q. d. Lex docebat esse iusticiam, satisfacere Legi. At nunc patefit iusticia ex fide, id est, iusticia per misericordiam imputata. Nam cum vocabulum fidei legimus, statim veniat in mentem correlativum scilicet misericordia promissa. Sermo Paulinus redolet phrasin Ebraicam, aliter enim loquitur Cicero, cum ait de Caesare, dextram tuam fide praestantem. Quare phrasis in Paulo observanda est, ubi fides significat fiduciam misericordiae propter Christum promissae. Quare cum nominat iusticiam fidei, intelligit iusticiam quae imputatur per misericordiam. Et hanc opponit iusticiae legis, quae esse debeat persecta obedientia iuxta legem. Hanc autem cum nemo praestare possit, cum haec misera natura hominum sit captiva peccati, patefit in Evangelio nova iusticia, scilicet iusticia imputata per misericordiam. Sed tamen hanc side, hoc est, agnitione & fiducia Christi accipi oportet, ut inquit Esaias: Noticia Christi iustificabit multos, quasi dicat: Cum lege homines non sint iusti seu accepti Deo, sed habeant peccata, Deus vult eis ita remittere peccata, & esse propitius, si agnoverint eum haec beneficia velle impertire propter filium, qui est victima & placator. Haec est simplex & nativa enarratio. Ait autem: Ex fide in fidem, id est, ex imperfecta fide in perfectiorem. Patesit quidem misericordia, sed non omnibus contingit, quia Deus vult eam fide accipi, sed cum multi nolint accipere, & aspernentur hanc ineffabilem bonitatem, pereunt. Nec fides est ociosa noticia, sed crescere eam in assidua lucta, in invocatione, in omnibus negociis & periculis oportet. Semper luceat in cordibus, quod Deus propter filium mediatorem nobis sit propitius, opitulaturus. Et hac fide invocemus eum, & petamus omnium negociorum & periculorum gubernationem. Ita crescunt in cordibus piorum fides, & vera agnitio dei. Quod autem vera sit sententia, quam proposuit, videlicet fide homines iustos esse, mox addit testimonium, ut auditor sciat Paulinas conciones vere congruere cum propheticis, et renovare apostolos prophetarum doctrinam.

## 1:17
The just shall live by faith

The antithesis is clear in Galatians, where he says: But that no one is justified by the law is manifest, because the just shall live by faith. The law, however, is not of faith, but he who shall have done them shall live in them. Here he clearly defines the righteousness of the law to be doing the law, that is, to render perfect obedience to the law. But no one renders this, therefore another righteousness is proposed, namely, righteousness imputed through mercy, to the believer, to the one fleeing to mercy. When therefore the Prophet says, the just shall live by faith, he teaches that we are finally just in this way, not when we look at the law, not when we set our virtues and deeds before God, but when by faith, that is, by confidence in mercy, we determine that God is propitious to us, that He hears us, that He wills to save us, and we await salvation. This is the meaning of the prophetic saying. You will observe, however, that two huge praises are attributed to faith, namely, that by faith we are both justified and quickened. For God gave His Son for us for this reason, for this reason He is propitious to us, that we might not perish. As He says swearing: I live, I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he be converted and live. When the terrified mind by faith determines that sins are remitted to it, it is at the same time freed from terrors, and conceives true consolation, which is the beginning of eternal life in us, as Christ says: This is eternal life, that they may know Thee the true God, and Jesus whom Thou hast sent to be Christ. Wherefore let us know that together with the remission of sins and reconciliation, the gift of the Holy Spirit is joined, Let us know that the kingdom of Christ in the Church, that is, in the righteous, is not idle, but that the Son of God is truly present with us, truly destroys the works of the devil, defends, assists, and preserves believers. The voice of the prophet embraces all these things when he promises life, that is, joy, victory, and eternal salvation to the believer. But certain sycophants slander the maxims cited by Paul; they say they have been wrongly twisted to the Pauline cause. This, they say, was what Paul was doing: that men are reconciled to God through faith in Christ. But the Prophet did not speak of Christ in that place. Likewise, when elsewhere he cites the saying about the faith of Abraham. Abraham believes that he will have descendants propagated from himself. What, they say, does this faith pertain to the Pauline cause? I answer, the rule must be held that even when faith is concerned with corporal objects or benefits, nevertheless, faith, which is trust in mercy and receives the remission of sins, always precedes the expectation of the corporal benefit in the believer. Jacob expects defense against enemies, David expects victory, but they expect it for this reason, because they feel that they have a propitious God. For the conscience cannot seek or expect other benefits from God if it feels that He is angry with us, us not to hear. It is necessary, therefore, that confidence in mercy always precede. And statements about faith in general always include the article concerning the remission of sins. Thus, in the daily prayer, when we ask for daily bread, let it come to mind that this petition of ours is heard if God is propitious to us, and that He is propitious on account of Christ. Therefore, it immediately follows: And forgive us our debts. But someone might ask, whence did the Fathers know this doctrine concerning confidence in mercy and concerning the remission of sins? I answer, concerning this article the Prophets were contending with the teachers of the law. Therefore, so many psalms, so many sayings of the prophets cry out that men are not righteous by the law, and they inculcate sermons about mercy. And Isaiah clearly says that the Messiah would come as a victim for sin. They were, therefore, renewing the promise made first to Adam, afterwards to Abraham, concerning the liberator who was to come; they understood that God had promised reconciliation on account of that liberator and benefactor of whom it was said: He shall crush the head of the serpent. They were looking into this promise and knew that the promise was to be believed; on account of this they were expecting all other benefits. To this promise concerning the liberator who was to come they were referring to the other promises. The prophets prophesy that the people would return from Babylon, because they knew that the Messiah had to be born from Judah, and openly publish the Gospel in Zion. Let them look to this principal promise, when they promise other benefits, just as we too must now believe that God will preserve the ministry of the Gospel, for which reason He will save some ministers, and will supply them with defense, and other necessary inconveniences of life. Thus we shall include other comforts in the promise of grace. Since God is propitious to us on account of Christ, we ask for other benefits. For the life of ministers, with food and civil peace, is a work of the Church.

These things I have answered in general concerning the sayings in which there is mention of faith. Furthermore, the sayings which Paul cites also speak by name concerning the promised deliverer; Habakkuk speaks about expecting that deliverer who was promised to the Fathers, as the text shows. And Abraham believes not only that he would have children, but that seed by which all nations were to be blessed. I know that many cavils can be devised by the crafty to evade and overwhelm these testimonies. For human wisdom, because it does not understand the righteousness of faith, does not rightly accept the sayings of the Prophets, but twists them in various ways. But the pious, looking at the consensus of the whole prophetic scripture and the true exercises of faith, will easily understand that these sayings are rightly applied by Paul to the present cause concerning the remission of sins.

Latin:

Iustus ex fide vivet

Perspicua est antithesis in Galat. ubi inquit: Quod autem lege nemo iustificetur, manifestum est, quia iustus ex fide vivet. Lex autem non est ex fide, sed qui fecerit ea, vivet in illis. Hic manifeste definit iusticiam legis esse, facere legem, hoc est, praestare perfectam obedientiam legi. At nemo hanc praestat, ideo proponitur alia iusticia, scilicet, iusticia per misericordiam imputata, credenti, confugienti ad misericordiam. Cum igitur Propheta inquit, iustus ex fide vivet, docet ita nos demum iustos esse, non cum legem intuemur, non cum virtutes nostras & facta proponimus Deo, sed cum fide, id est fiducia misericordiae statuimus nobis Deum propitium esse, nos exaudire, velle servare, & expectamus salutem. Haec est sententia dicti prophetici. Observabis autem fidei duas laudes ingentes tribui, quod videlicet fide & iustificemur, & vivificemur. Deus enim ideo filium suum pro nobis dedit, ideo nobis sit propitius, ne pereamus. Sicut inquit iurans: Vivo, nolo mortem peccatoris, sed ut convertatur & vivat. Cum mens perterrefacta fide statuit sibi remitti peccata, simul liberatur à pavoribus, & concipit veram consolationem, quae est inchoatio in nobis vitae eaternae, sicut Christus inquit: Haec est vita aeterna, ut agnoscant te deum verum, et quem misisti Iesum esse Christum. Quare sciamus simul cum remissione peccatorum & reconciliatione coniunctam esse donationem spiritus sancti, sciamus regnum Christi in Ecclesia, hoc est, iustis, non esse ociosum, sed vere adesse nobis filium Dei, vere destruere opera diaboli, propugnare, adiuvare, & servare credentes. Haec omnia complectitur vox prophetae, cum promittit vitam, id est leticiam, victoriam, aeternam salutem credenti. Sed Sycophantae quidam calumniantur gnomas à Paulo citatas, dicunt male detortas esse ad Paulinam causam. Hoc inquiunt, agebat Paulus, homines reconciliari Deo per fidem in christum. At Propheta non dixit in eo loco de Christo. Item cum alibi citat dictum de fide Abrahae. Abraham credit se habiturum posteros ex se propagatos. Quid haec fides, inquiunt, ad Pauli causam pertinet? Respondeo, tenenda est regula, quod etiam cum fides versatur circa corporalia obiecta seu beneficia, tamen semper expectationem corporalis beneficii in credente praecedit fides, quae est fiducia misericordiae, & accipit remissionem peccatorum. Iacob expectat defensionem contra hostes, David expectat victoriam, sed ideo expectant, quia sentiunt se habere Deum propitium. Nam conscientia non potest alia beneficia à Deo petere aut expectare, si sentiat eum nobis iratum esse, nos non exaudire. Necesse est igitur semper praecedere fiduciam misericordiae. Et dicta de fide in genere semper complectuntur articulum de remissione peccatorum. Sicin oratione quotidiana, cum petimus panem quotidianum, veniat in mentem, hanc petitionem nostram exaudiri, si Deus sit nobis propitius, & esse propitium propter Christum. Ideo statim sequitur: Et remitte nobis debita nostra. Sed querat aliquis, unde norant Patres hanc doctrinam de fiducia misericordiae, & de remissione peccatorum. Respondeo, De hoc articulo pugnabant Prophetae cum doctoribus legis. Ideo tot psalmi, tot dicta prophetarum vociferantur, homines non esse iustos lege, & inculcant conciones de misericordia. Et Esaias diserte inquit, Messiam venturum victimam pro peccato. Renovabant igitur promissionem, primum Adae, postea Abrahae factam de venturo liberatore, intelligebant Deum promisisse reconciliationem propter illum liberatorem, & benedictorem de quo dictum est: Caput serpentis conteret. In hanc promissionem intuebantur & norant promissioni credendum esse, propter hanc expectabant omnia caetera beneficia. Ad hanc promissionem de venturo liberatore referebant caeteras promissiones. Vaticinantur prophetae rediturum esse populum ex Babylone, quia norant oportere Messiam nasci ex Iuda, & palam edere Evangelium in Sion. Hanc principalem promissionem intueantur, cum promittunt alia beneficia, ut nunc quoque credere debemus Deum conservaturum esse ministerium Evangelii, quare servabit aliquos ministros, & suppeditabit eis defensionem, & alia necessaria vitae incommoda. Sic nos includemus in promissionem gratiae caetera commoda. Cum Deus nobis sit propitius propter Christum, petimus caetera beneficia. Est enim opus Ecclesiae vita ministrorum, victu, pace civili.

Haec in genere respondi de dictis, in quibus sit mentio fidei. Caeterum dicta, quae citat Paulus, etiam nominatim de liberatore promisso concionantur, Abacuc loquitur de expectando liberatore illo, qui erat Patribus promissus, ut ostendit textus. Et Abraham credit non tantum se habiturum liberos, sed illud semen, quo benedicendae erant omnes gentes. Scio ab astutis multas cavillationes excogitari posse, ad eludenda & obruenda haec testimonia. Nam sapientia humana, quia iusticiam fidei non intelligit, non accipit dextre dicta Prophetarum, sed variè detorquet. Pii vero consensum totius scripturae propheticae & vera exercitia fidei intuentes, facile intelligent haec dicta recte à Paulo ad praesentem causam de remissione peccatorum accommdari.

## 1:18
For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven.

It is a dreadful beginning and a thunderbolt with which he begins the disputation, such as are the beginnings in prophetic sermons, as in Isaiah the first: Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth, woe to the sinful nation, etc. For there is one form of prophetic and apostolic sermons, which Christ embraced in these words: Go preaching repentance and remission of sins in my name. Thus Paul, when he indeed establishes a most suitable κέθοδον of Christian doctrine, first sets forth a proposition, which is the doctrine of repentance, or arguing sins. For above he finished the exordium, now he begins to explain the controversy. And he hands down two propositions, of which the one opens the way to the other. The first proposition is: The Gospel argues all men and pronounces all to be under sin, that is, guilty of sin and eternal death, and not able to be freed from sin and eternal wrath through their own righteousness.

In this proposition he dwells for two chapters. For he wishes to call all to repentance, he wishes us to truly dread the judgment of God, so that we may seek salvation, and acknowledge the liberator, through whom reconciliation and salvation are promised. Therefore, the principal proposition follows in the third chapter, that men obtain the remission of sins, and are reckoned righteous, and are freed from eternal death, not on account of their own righteousness, but through mercy on account of Christ freely. And this is done by faith, when we believe that the Father is appeased and propitious to us on account of the Son of God. And this is the principal proposition of this Epistle, and the state of the disputation and the sum of the Gospel. But before he arrives at this proposition, another is treated first. For consolation cannot be delivered, unless sins are first reproved. And God demands repentance, just as both John and Christ begin their sermons: Repent. And Christ says: The Holy Spirit reproves the world of sin, of righteousness, and of judgment. And Isaiah: Where shall the Lord dwell? In a contrite spirit and one trembling at my words. And Paul used atrocious words, when he says the wrath of God is revealed from heaven. He threatens eternal punishments for all who do not tremble, nor flee to the Son of God. You see, therefore, that the opinions of Paul agree, and the order in teaching agrees with the sermons of the Prophets and of Christ.

The Gospel, however, convicts not only external offenses, which reason can judge, but also the uncleanness of the heart in all men; therefore it says thus: The wrath of God is revealed from heaven, that is, it is preached in the Gospel delivered by God, against all impiety and injustice of men. It is a Hebraism, with the particle, all, transposed, since the meaning is, upon the impiety and injustice of all men, for afterwards he will clearly and expressly say that he accuses all men.

Impiety, however, signifies properly the vices fighting against the first table, ignorance of God, to be void of fear, love, trust in God, to have security and contempt of God, indignation, and raging against God in afflictions, trust in one's own wisdom, justice, works, to seek human protections against the command of God, to prefer to the commands of God our fortunes, pleasures, reputation, glory, life, just as those prefer these things who flee the dangers of confession, to play by inventing false opinions about God, by taking pleasure in Epicurean or Academic errors, and by not truly assenting to the word of God. Finally, the mass of vices fighting against the first table is immense, which embraces all things under the name of impiety. Injustice is a general name, embracing all sins, against God and men, for it signifies universal disobedience.

Latin:

Revelatur enim ira Dei de caelo.

Horrendum est initium ac fulmen quo inchoat disputationem, qualia sunt initia in concionibus propheticis, ut Esaiae primo: Audite caeli & auribus percipe terra, vae genti peccatrici &c. Una est enim concionum propheticarum & apostolicarum forma, quam Christus complexus est his verbis: Ite praedicantes paenitentiam, & remissionem peccatorum in nomine meo. Ita Paulus cum quidem aptissimam κέθοδον doctrinae Christianae instituat, primum ponit propositionem, quae est doctrina paenitentiae, seu arguens peccata. Supra enim absolvit exordium, nunc incipit controversiam explicare. Et duas propositiones tradit, quarum altera aditum ad alteram patefacit. Prima propositio est: Evangelium arguit omnes homines ac pronunciat omnes sub peccato esse, id est, reos peccati & aeternae mortis, nec posse liberari à peccato & aeterna ira per propriam iusticiam.

In hac propositione commoratur per duo capita. Vult enim omnes ad paenitentiam vocare, vult nos vere expavescere iudicium Dei, ut queramus salutem, ac agnoscamus liberatorem, per quem promissa est reconciliatio & salus. Sequitur ergo in tertio capite principalis propositio, quod homines consequantur remissionem peccatorum, & reputentur iusti, & liberentur ab aeterna morte, non propter propriam iusticiam, sed per misericordiam propter Christum gratis. Et hoc fide fit, cum credimus nobis propter filium Dei patrem placatum & propitium esse. Et haec est principalis propositio huius Epistolae, & status disputationis ac summa Evangelii. Sed priusquàm ad hanc propositionem pervenit, altera prius tractatur. Non enim potest tradi consolatio, nisi prius arguantur peccata. Et Deus postulat paenitentiam, sicut & Iohannes & Christus suas conciones inchoant: Agite paenitentiam. Et Christus inquit: Spiritus sanctus arguit mundum de peccato, de iusticia, & de iudicio. Et Esaias: Ubi habitabit Dominus? In Spiritu contrito & tremente sermones meos. Et usus est Paulus atrocibus verbis, cum ait revelari iram Dei de caelo. Minatur aeternas poenas omnibus qui non expavescunt, nec confugiunt ad filium Dei. Vides igitur congruere Pauli sententias, & seriem in docendo congruere cum concionibus Prophetarum & Christi.

Arguit autem Evangelium non tantum externa delicta, quae ratio iudicare potest, sed etiam immundiciem cordis in omnibus hominibus, ideo sic dicit: Revelatur ira Dei de caelo, hoc est prae dicatur in Evangelio divinitus tradito, auduersus omnem impietatem & iniusticiam hominum. Ebraismus est, transposita particula, omnem, cum sit sententia, super impietatem & iniusticiam omnium hominum, postea enim diserte & expresse dicet se accusare omnes homines.

Significat autem impietas propriè vitia pugnantia cum prima tabula, ignorationem Dei, vacare metu, dilectione, fiducia Dei, habere securitatem & contemptum Dei, indignationem, & fremitum adversus Deum in adflictionibus, fiduciam propriae sapientiae, iusticiae, operum, quaerere praesidia humana contra mandatum Dei, anteferre mandatis Dei, fortunas nostras, voluptates, existimationem, gloriam, vitam, sicut haec antem ferunt, qui fugiunt pericula confessionis, ludere fingendis opinionibus falsis de Deo, delectari Epicureis aut Academicis erroribus, & non vere adsentiri verbo Dei. Denique immensa est moles viciorum pugnantium cum prima tabula, quae omnia complectitur nomine impietatis. Iniusticia generale nomen est, complectens omniapeccata, contra Deum et homines, significat enim universalem inobedientiam.

## 1:18
Who hold the truth in injustice.

He calls the knowledge of God, or the law of nature, the truth. For when sins are argued in the preaching of repentance, the law is cited, just as Paul says: Through the law is the knowledge of sin. Thus here he alleges the law of nature, he says all men have some knowledge of God. Through this he accuses and condemns all, for because we know the law, and yet we do not obey, the Law, which is the judgment of God, accuses and condemns all. Therefore, students must first be admonished to diligently distinguish between the Law and the Gospel. Some knowledge of the law is born with us, and if in this depravity of human nature it is more obscure, it is not, however, entirely obliterated. Moreover, these are the knowledges about God: That there is one God of immense power, wise, just, good creator and the preserver of nature, punishing the unjust and the wicked, hearing and saving, not freely, not those guilty of sin, but the just and the clean, that God must be obeyed, that He commands honorable things and forbids base things, that He has implanted in our souls a distinction between honorable and base things. These are natural notions, which we hear perpetually preaching to us in our conscience. Natural reason does not know of free forgiveness or reconciliation on account of Christ, but is a knowledge of the law requiring the condition of our obedience, judging that only those please God who are without sin. This is the natural voice of conscience. But the Gospel promises free forgiveness and reconciliation on account of the Son of God. This knowledge is not born with us, but is revealed divinely, as John says: The Son who is in the bosom of the Father, he declares him to us. And because it dissents from the natural voice of conscience, and from the handwriting written against us in our minds, therefore it is difficult to assent to the promise of free reconciliation. It is necessary for the reader to remember this at the beginning, that natural knowledge about God is a certain knowledge of the law, lest he untimely confuse the Law and the Gospel. Wonderful, however, is the discourse of Paul, and

far surpassing the thoughts of the philosophers. He says that there is in us a knowledge, which he calls truth. But the Epicureans and Academics have overwhelmed these very knowledges. But they are lying and fighting against the very nature of man. For some knowledge of God clings within us, as has been said. Then Paul adds that this very knowledge is held back in injustice, that is, the will of man or the heart does not assent to these knowledges nor obey them. He looked into human minds much more deeply than the philosophers. Here he collected huge vices. The mind establishes that God exists in some way, but because it sees the wicked flourishing, and the good being harshly exercised, and indeed being cruelly killed by criminals, by tyrants, it begins to doubt whether God cares for human affairs, whether He punishes the wicked, or does good to the good. It judges that God either does not care for human affairs, or is cruel, who has burdened such a weak nature with such great calamities. From this doubt and darkness arise many vices. The heart is void of fear, of trust, of the love of God. And since it is without a bridle, it obeys desires against natural knowledges. Even if Paris knows it is unjust to snatch another's spouse, yet he indulges his lust, with God despised. Learnedly, therefore, Paul described human infirmity, he attributes to man some knowledge, and yet he testifies that the will or heart does not assent to, nor obey, this knowledge, which is turned away from God, and without divine motions, loves itself, not God, therefore it is carried away by wandering and various motions against the commandment of God. Paul signifies all these things, saying that the truth is detained, as if captive in injustice, that is, in the depravity of the will or heart, which is, as is said below, enmity against God.

For insofar as God can be known, he is known to them.

This is an exposition of the previous proposition, for here he alleges the Law of nature, and expressly says what that truth is in the minds of men, arguing and accusing us. There is knowledge, he says, of God, and other knowledge, which are called the Laws of nature. The syntax is to be observed, His invisible things, namely his eternal power, and divinity, are seen from the creation of the world, being understood by the works. His divinity and eternal power, that is, that he is God, eternal, powerful, wise, just, good, punishing the unjust, hearing and helping the just.

This, I say, the mind acknowledges while contemplating the workmanship of the world. For from many traces it reasons these things about God.
