Nor, however, would it reason these things, unless there were also implanted in the mind a certain knowledge, or πρόληψις, of God. Wherefore, he says, God first manifested to them, but afterwards the mind, admonished from without by the sight of the world and the order of the work, thinks that these things could not have existed or arisen by chance, but were undoubtedly founded and distributed by some eternal mind. There is no doubt that men were especially created so that the knowledge of God might shine in them. God wished to reveal Himself, and to be acknowledged and celebrated by the human race. Therefore, an admirable light and a clear and illustrious knowledge of God shone in the human mind, implanted in it at its creation. And if darkness had not approached through the disease of origin, the human mind would have been like a mirror showing, if I may say so, an image, that is, many clear knowledges of God. Therefore it is written that the mind is a certain image of God. Nor is there any doubt that this whole world was created so that it might bear witness to God. The order of the works clearly shows that these things could not have arisen by chance. And if the nature of man had remained intact, it would have been especially occupied with this philosophy; it would have considered the traces of divinity in nature, and would have proclaimed wisdom, and the goodness of the architect. But after darkness entered minds on account of the disease of origin, the image does not shine, and natural notions are quite obscure, and the heart or will, on account of the turning away from God, does not sufficiently assent to those notions, nor does it constantly defend them, and it easily allows even true notions about God to be shaken off from itself, with other persuasions being presented. Therefore, such was and remains among men the dissension concerning God. All philosophers doubted concerning providence, because even if some were moved by nature to establish that God exists, nevertheless they doubted whether He cared for human affairs, when they saw the secondary things of the wicked and the just oppressed by the wicked. Disturbed by this offense, minds afterwards rush more, and the devil pours out greater mists, so that many atheists in all times have altogether denied that there is a God, or any eternal divinity, just as the Cyclops in Homer and Euripides. But these fight with their own minds and know that they are lying. Therefore, since there is such darkness and levity of the human mind, that even true arguments are easily shaken off from us, let the chief care be that we confirm ourselves by the word of God. For the divine law also was promulgated for this reason, that the recognition of God might be renewed. But nevertheless, because natural notion has not been altogether deleted in souls, let us stir up it, and let us look at the traces of God in the nature of things. It is written in the Acts, that God is so near that He can almost be touched with the hands. Nor are so many traces of God impressed upon nature in vain. God wishes us to be admonished by these marks, He wishes them to be considered, and the author to be acknowledged. Therefore, let the studious seek these traces, but in such a way that they nevertheless hold to the rule, namely the word of God; afterwards, it certainly profits much for confirming good opinions to hold fixed in the mind true reasons, which testify that there is a God, the creator and preserver of things. And a learned physicist can aptly gather many things. Therefore, philosophers who have handled physics skillfully have thought more honestly about God, as Galen. On the contrary, the Epicureans, as they disturbed physics, so they did not wish to look at the traces of God in nature, wherefore they furiously professed those Cyclopean things about God. I will therefore briefly recite nine arguments taken from nature, which testify that there is a God, the creator and preserver of things.

First, the most illustrious testimonies about God are the human mind, and the distinction between honorable and base things impressed upon the mind. From this the argument is taken. Man has a mind, man originates from elsewhere, therefore it is necessary that he originated from some eternal mind, because it is impossible for the mind to arise from brute nature. The psalm also admonishes us concerning this argument: He who made the eyes, shall He not see? &c.

Second. The distinction between honorable and base things is naturally known to the human mind. It is impossible that this came to exist by chance, or flowed forth from brute nature. Therefore it is necessary to confess that God is the creator. No one can weaken this argument, even if Cyclopes, Giants, Epicureans, Academics, Mezentii, and all such people should gather together and attempt with joined forces to wage war against heaven. We will necessarily have to confess that the distinction between honorable and base things did not come to exist by chance, but was ordained by some mind.

Third, In atrocious crimes all men naturally grow terrified, and judge that God exists, and that He punishes crimes. Therefore both pieces of knowledge are implanted in the human mind, both that God exists, and that He punishes wicked deeds. However much Mezentius rages, nevertheless it is necessary that he be often terrified by the conscience of his own crimes. Therefore it cries out in his soul, even if he resists, that there is a God who is the avenger of crimes. Otherwise, why does the soul not truly rejoice after an atrocious crime, just as it truly rejoices in the recollection of things done rightly?

Fourth, From the order of things in all of nature. We see how certain are the laws of celestial motions, the certain number of species, and like things are propagated from like, not indiscriminately one from another. We see the final causes of things. Individual things are born for some utility. There is also a wonderful consensus of superior and inferior bodies. Celestial motions effect certain turns of summer and winter for the utility of living things. What of the perpetuity of fountains and rivers? What of the distribution of individual parts in the human body? What of the very recognition of number and order? Do they not clearly testify that this nature did not exist by chance, but has arisen from some eternal mind. It is impossible that these things always happen thus by chance, it is impossible that the notions of number and order have arisen by chance or from matter alone. O blind minds of men, who are not moved by such clear arguments, by such express traces of divinity, so that they might think better of God, and revere him.

Fifth, to the consideration of order pertains also the consideration of political order. In this also shine the wisdom and goodness of God, that human nature is founded for society, that it is associated by many bonds, contracts, pacts, judgments, empires, punishments. This whole order testifies that the human race did not exist by chance.

Sixth, from the punishments of murderers and the preservation and overturning of empires. It is manifest that murderers are drawn to punishments not by human diligence, but divinely, so that the society of life may be preserved. Thus it is manifest that empires are established, not by human strengths, but by some divinity, and again are overturned on account of tyrannies and lusts, because God punishes atrocious crimes in civil society. Just as Tarquin was driven out, and the Lacedaemonians were defeated, when certain men had by force raped the daughters of a host and afterwards had killed them.

Seventh, from the significations of future things. There are many certain physical significations, either of the stars or of inferior bodies, as most certain and perpetual experience testifies that the conjunctions of humid stars in humid signs signify rains and storms. Likewise, many prodigies appear without a certain law, and yet are signifying. Likewise true prophecies, such as that of Daniel concerning the order of empires. These significations cannot proceed except from some eternal mind.

Eighth, heroic motions, are motions above human nature, and sometimes happen to men for the sake of some great utility, such as for the establishment of empires, or for the illustration of arts useful to life. Therefore they arise from some more excellent and intelligent nature.

Ninth, from the series of causes. Causes are ordered in nature, so that it is necessary to arrive at one first cause, which is not moved by anything else, but moves the others. If there is a first, it is necessary to have from itself the power of moving: Therefore it is of infinite power. And it is necessary that there be some first cause, for otherwise there would be no order of causes, if they were scattered into infinity. This argument is treated at length in physics. And it is firm enough, but the preceding ones are more illustrious, which are taken from the nature of the mind, from the distinction between honorable and base things, from the order in nature and society, which indeed testify not only that God is the craftsman, but also the avenger, and invite us to the fear of God. Wherefore let young men strengthen their minds with such thoughts. For the more diligently we consider these arguments, the more we assent, as Plato says, and we ourselves experience. Let students know, however, that all these arguments are laws of nature, commanding that we acknowledge God to be the creator of all things, and that we owe him obedience. And thus Paul adapts it in this place. Since, however, he accuses all men above in the proposition, he now institutes a distribution, first he preaches to the Gentiles, afterwards to the Jews, he says the Gentiles are under sin, because although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God, nor did they give thanks to him.

Latin:

Qui veritatem in iniusticia detinent.

Veritatem vocat noticiam Dei, seu legem naturae. Cum enim arguuntur peccata in praedicatione paenitentiae citatur lex, sicut Paulus inquit: Per legem cognitio peccati. Ita hic allegat legem naturae, ait omnes homines habere aliquam Dei noticiam. Per hanc accusat & condemnat omnes, quia enim scimus legem, & tamen non obedimus, Lex, quae est iudicium Dei, accusat et condemnat omnes. Primum igitur admonendi sunt studiosi, ut diligenter discernant Legem & Evangelium. Aliqua legis noticia nobiscum nascitur, & si in hac depravatione naturae humanae est obscurior, non tamen prorsus obliterata est. Sunt autem hae noticiae de Deo: Quod sit Deus unus immensae potentiae, sapiens, iustus, bonus conditor & conservator naturae, puniens iniustos & sceleratos, exaudiens & servans, non gratis, non reos peccati, sed iustos ac mundos, quod Deo sit obediendum, quod praecipiat honesta, ac prohibeat turpia, quod inseverit animis nostris discrimen honestorum & turpium. Hae sunt naturales noticiae, quas audimus nobis in conscientia perpetuo concionantes. Non novit ratio naturalis gratuitam condonationem, aut reconciliationem propter Christum, sed est legis noticia requirens conditionem nostrae obedientiae, iudicat eos tantum placere Deo, qui sunt sine peccato. Haec est naturalis vox conscientiae. Sed Evangelium promittit gratuitam condonationem & reconciliationem propter filium Dei. Haec noticia non nascitur nobiscum, sed est revelata divinitus, ut Iohannnes inquit: Filius qui est in sinu patris, ipse enarrat nobis. Et quia dissentit à naturali voce conscientiae, & â Chirographo contra nos scripto in nostris mentibus, ideo difficile est assentiri promissioni gratuitae reconciliationis. Haec initio meminisse lectorem oportet, noticiam naturalem de Deo, esse quandam legis noticiam, ne intempestive confundat Legem & Evangelium. Mira est autem Pauli concio, &

longe superans philosophorum cogitationes. ait in nobis esse noticiam, quam vocat veritatem. At Epicurei & Academici has ipsas noticias obruerunt. Sed mentientes & pugnantes cum ipsa natura hominis. Haeret enim aliqua in nobis de Deo noticia, ut dictum est. Deinde addit Paulus, hanc ipsam noticiam detineri in iniusticia, id est, voluntatem hominis seu cor, non assentiri his noticiis nec obtemperare. Multo penitius introspexit mentes humanas, quam Philosophi. Hic collegit ingentia vitia. Esse Deum utcunque statuit mens, sed quia videt florere improbos, & duriter exerceri bonos, & quidem à sceleratis, à tyrannis crudeliter interfici, incipit dubitare an Deus curet res humanas, an puniat sceleratos, an benefaciat bonis. Iudicat Deum aut non curare res humanas, aut esse crudelem, qui tam imbecillem naturam oneraverit tantis calamitatibus. Ex hac dubitatione & caligine oriuntur multa vicia. Cor vacat metu, fiducia dilectione Dei. Et cum sit sine freno, obtemperat cupiditatibus contra noticias naturales. Etiamsi scit Paris iniustum esse rapere alterius coniugem, tamen gerit morem suae libidini, contempto Deo. Eruditè igitur descripsit Paulus infirmitatem humanam, manam, attribuit homini noticiam aliquam, & tamen testatur huic noticiae nec assentiri, nec obtemperare voluntatem seu cor, quod est aversum à Deo, & sine motibus divinis, sese amat non Deum, ideo rapitur motibus errantibus ac variis contra mandatum Dei. Haec omnia significat Paulus, inquiens veritatem detineri, tanquàm captivam in iniusticia, id est, pravitate voluntatis seu cordis, quae est, ut infra dicitur, inimicicia adversus Deum.

Quatenus enim Deus cogno-sci potest, notus est eis.

Expositio est superioris propositionis hic enim allegat Legem naturae, & expresse dicit, quae sit illa veritas in mentibus hominum arguens & accusans nos. Est noticia inquit de Deo, & caeterae noticiae, quae vocantur Leges naturae. Syntaxis observanda est, Invisibilia eius, videlicet aeterna potentia eius, & divinitas, conspiciuntur ab opificio mundi, animadversa ex operibus. Divinitas eius & aeterna potentia, id est, quod sit Deus, aeternus, potens, sapiens, iustus, bonus, puniens iniustos, exaudiens & adiuvans iustos.

Haec inquam agnoscit mens intuens opificium mundi. Nam ex multis vestigiis ratiocinatur ista de Deo. Neque tamen haec rotiocinaretur, nisi etiam insita esset menti noticia quaedam, seu πρόληψις de Deo. Quare prius inquit, Deus manifestavit eis, postea autem foris admonita mens conspectu mundi, et ordine operis, cogitat non potuisse haec casu existere, aut oriri, sed haud dubiè ab aliqua mente aeterna condita & distributa esse. Nihil dubiem est homines praecipuè conditos esse, ut in eis luceret noticia Dei. Patefacere se Deus voluit, & ab humano genere agnosci ac celebrari. Ideo in mente humana fulsit admiranda lux & clara ac illustris noticia de Deo, insita ei in conditione. Ac si non accessisset caligo per morbum originis, mens humana fuisset tanquàm speculum ostendens, ut ita dicam, imaginem, hoc est multas perspicuas noticias de Deo. Ideo scriptum est, mentem esse quandam dei imaginem. Nec dubium est hunc totum mundum conditum esse, ut dicat testimonium de deo. Ordo operum perspicue monstrat, non potuisse haec casu oriri. Et si natura hominis mansisset integra, hac philosophia praecipuè fuisset occupata, considerasset vestigia divinitatis in natura, & praedicasset sapientiam, & bonitatem architecti. Sed postquàm caligo subiit mentes propter morbum originis, non fulget imago, & noticiae naturales sunt admodum obscurae, & cor seu voluntas propter aversionem à Deo, non satis assentitur illis noticiis, nec constanter eas propugnat, facileque sibi excuti etiam veras noticias de Deo sinit, obiectis aliis persuasionibus. Ideo tanta fuit manetquè inter homines dissensio de Deo. Philosophi omnes de providentia dubitarunt, quia & si aliqui movebantur natura, ut esse Deum statuerent, tamen an curaret res humanas dubitabant, cum viderent res secundas sceleratorum & iustos opprimi à sceleratis. Hac offensione perturbati animi postea magis ruunt, & offundit nebulas maiores diabolus, ut multi athei omnibus temporibus prorsus negarunt esse Deum, seu aliquod aeternum numen, sicut Cyclops apud Homerum & Euripidem. Sed hi pugnant cum suis mentibus & mentiri se norunt. Itaque cum tanta caligo sit humanae mentis ac levitas, ut etiam vera argumenta facile nobis excutiantur, praecipua cura sit, ut confirmemus nos verbo Dei. Nam & lex divina ideo promulgata est, ut renovaretur Dei agnitio. Sed tamen, quia non prorsus deleta est in animis noticia naturalis, excitemus eam, & aspiciamus vestigia Dei in natura rerum. In Actis scriptum est, Deum adeo prope adesse pene ut manibus contrectari possit. Nec frustra impressa sunt naturae tot vestigia Dei. Admoneri nos Deus vult per has notas, vult eas considerari, & agnosci autorem. Ideo studiosi querant haec vestigia, sed ita, ut tamen regulam teneant, scilicet verbum Dei, postea profecto ad consirmandas bonas opiniones multum prodest, tenere infixas animo veras rationes, quae testantur esse Deum conditorem, & conservatorem rerum. Et eruditus Physicus multa apte colligere potest. Itaque philosophi qui dexterè physicen tractarunt, honestius de Deo senserunt, ut Galenus Econtra Epicurei, ut physica turbarunt, ita nec vestigia Dei in natura aspicere voluerunt, quare illa Cyclopica de Deo furenter professi sunt. Recitabo igitur breviter novem argumenta sumpta à natura, quae testantur esse Deum conditorem & conservatorem rerum.

Primum, Maximè illustria testimonia sunt de Deo, mens humana, & discrimen honestorum & turpium impressum menti. Inde sumitur argumentum. Homo habet mentem, homo aliunde oritur, Ergo necesse est cum ab aliqua aeterna mente ortum esse, quia impossibile est mentem à natura bruta oriri. De hoc argumento nos & psalmus admonet: Qui fe it oculos non videret &c.

Secund. Diserimen honestorum & turpium naturaliter notum est humanae menti. Id impossibile est, casu extitisse, aut à bruta natura profluxisse. Ideo necesse est fateri Deum esse conditorem. Id argumentum labefactare nemo potest, vel si Cyclopes, Gigantes, Epicuraei, Academici, Mezentii & similes omnes concurrant, & coniunctis viribus caelo bellum inferre conentur. Fateri nos necesse erit, discrimen honestorum & turpium non casu extitisse, sed ab aliqua mente ordinatum esse.

Tertium, In atrocibus delictis omnes homines naturaliter expavescunt, & iudicant Deum esse, ac delicta punire. Ergo utraque noticia insita est menti humanae, & quod sit Deus, & quod scelera puniat. Quantumvis furit Mezentius, tamen necesse est eum saepe conscientia suorum scelerum perterrefieri. Clamitat igitur in eius animo, vel si repugnet, esse Deum vindicem scelerum. Alioqui cur non vere letatur animus post facinus atrox, sicut verè letatur recordatione rectè factorum

Quartum, Ab ordine rerum in tota natura. Videmus quàm certae sint Leges motuum caelestium, certum numerum specierum, & propagari similia ex similibus non promiscue alia ex aliis. Videmus causas finales rerum. Singula nascuntur ad aliquam utilitatem. Est & mirabilis consensus superiorum & inferiorum corporum. Motus caelestes certas vices aestatis & hyemis ad utilitatem viventium efficiunt. Quid fontium & fluminum perennitas? Quid in corpore humano partium singularum distributio? Quid ipsa numeri & ordinis agnitio? Nonne testantur clarè hanc naturam non extitisse casu, sed ab aliqua aeterna mente ortam esse. Impossibile est ē hec semper ita fieri casu, impossibile est noticias numeri et ordinis casu aut ex materia tantum ortas esse. O coecas hominum mentes, quae tam perspicuis argumentis, tam expressis vestigiis divinitatis non moventur, ut melius de Deo sentiant, & eum revereantur.

Quintum, Ad ordinis considerationem pertinet & politici ordinis consederatio. In hoc quoque lucent sapientia & bonitas Dei, Quod natura humana ad societatem condita est, quod consociata multis vinculis, contractibus, pactis, iudiciis, imperiis, poenis. Totus hic ordo testatur humanum genus non extitisse casu.

Sextum, A poenis homicidarum & conservatione ac eversione imperiorum. Manifestum est homicidas retrahi ad poenas non humana diligentia, sed divinitus, ut conservetur societas vitae. Ita manisestum est imperia constitui, non humanis viribus, sed ab aliquo numine, ac rursus everti propter tyrannides & libidines, quia deus punit in societate civili atrocia delicta. Sicut Tarquin. pulsus est, victi Lacedemonii, cum quidam per vim stuprassent hospitis filias et postea eas interfecissent.

Septimum, A significationibus rerum futurarum. Multae sunt phisicae significationes certae, vel stellarum: vel inferiorum corporum, ut certissima & perpetua experientia testatur congressus stellarum humidarum in signis humidis, significare pluvias tempestates. Item, prodigia multa adparent sine certa lege, & tamen significantia. Item vera vaticinia, ut Danielis de imperiorum ordine. Hae significationes non possunt, nisi ab aeterna aliqua mente proficisci.

Octavum, Heroici motus, sunt motus supra naturam humanam, & magnae alicuius utilitatis causa interdum contingunt hominibus, ut ad imperiorum constitutionem, aut ad artes illustrandas, vitae utiles, Ergo oriuntur ab aliqua praestantiore natura & intelligente.

Nonum, A serie causarum. Causae sunt in natura ordinatae, ita ut necesse sit perveniri ad unam primam, quae non aliunde movetur, sed movet caeteras. Si est prima necesse est eam ex sese habere vim movendi: Ergo est infinitae potentiae. Et esse aliquam primam necesse est, alioqui enim nullus esset ordo causarum, si sparsae essent in infinitum. Hoc argumentum in physicis prolixe tractatur. Et satis firmum est, sed superiora sunt magis illustria, quae à natura mentis, à discrimine honestorum & turpium, ab ordine in natura & soceitate sumpta sunt, quae quidem testantur non solum opisicem esse Deum, sed etiam vindicem, nosque ad timorem Dei invitant. Quare adolescentes talibus cogitationibus confirment animos. Nam quò diligentius haec argumenta consideramus, eò magis adsentimur, ut Plato inquit, & nos ipsi experimur. Sciant autem studiosi omnia haec argumenta esse leges naturae, praecipientes ut agnoscamus Deum esse conditorem omnium, et nos ei debere obedientiam. Atque ita accommodat hoc loco Paulus. Cum autem supra in propositione accuset omnes homines, nunc instituit distributionem, primum concionatur gentibus, postea Iudaeis, ait gentes esse sub peccato, quia cum Deum norint, non tamen glorificaverunt, ut Deum, nec ei gratias egerunt.

## 1:21
They did not glorify him as God.

To glorify as God, is to the eternal God of things to attribute this glory, that he is God, that is, eternal, of immense power, the creator and preserver of things, wise, just, punishing the unjust, hearing and helping the just: and to obey him, and truly to fear his judgment, and truly to believe him, and to seek and expect good things from him. We all ought to attribute this honor to God, and this he calls glorifying as God.

To give thanks is to believe that God is the creator of things, that we are a care to him, that we receive life and other good things from him, to seek and expect help and defense from him, and therefore to acknowledge him as lord, and to obey him, lest we be ungrateful and contumacious against the lord, and to celebrate and preach his name, power, goodness, justice. These are the works of the first and second commandment, necessary, and for which we were especially created. But the world does not perform them. Therefore the voice of the Gospel at all times accuses the impiety of the world. For men are some ἄθεοι others are Idolaters. In these two ways men sin against the first table of the divine law. ἄθεοι , as the Cyclopes and Epicureans, entirely deny that there is a God, or that he cares for human affairs. It is sufficiently agreed that these do not glorify God, they do not fear, they do not believe him, they do not invoke him, they judge it to be an empty name. For that is to attribute to him some glory of power, of goodness, of justice. Nor is the multitude of such Cyclopes small, although it is a wonder that innate notions can be so overwhelmed. But the devil, who holds the minds of men captive, pours greater errors upon a nature otherwise weak. And now indeed some learned men, especially at Rome, think it is wisdom to be delighted by these Cyclopean opinions. But idolaters err otherwise; they transfer the honor owed to God to other things. For it is εἰδωλολατρέια to attribute divinity to that which is not God, to invoke that which is not God, to attribute the honor of redemption to another than Christ, to attribute trust to our works, which was owed to God, to bind God to certain cults and statues against his commandment, to fear or love something else more than God. This properly comprises and signifies εἰδωλολατρέια as they commonly call it. Hence it can easily be understood that the world is full of idolomania. Concerning this worship, the saying of the poet is true: Fear first made gods in the world. Cyclopes are for the most part secure. Others, seeking God in dangers, as reason shows God to be a helper, being anxious, do not seek God rightly. For since they have opinions of the law and think that God hears the just, his worshippers, those who have deserved well, they invoke who but without the promise of grace, without the knowledge of the mediator, therefore they either doubt that they are heard and regarded, or they put on a vain confidence in their own acts of worship, just as the little sacrificer says in Homer: If I have sacrificed pleasing victims to you, Phoebus, hear me. The first impiety is therefore that they either doubt that they are heard by God, or they put on a confidence in their own righteousness, and they do not know the mediator. This error having been admitted, many crimes follow. By confidence in their own acts of worship, men are moved to accumulate ceremonies, and to devise new acts of worship, and gods, as when the rustics thought that good weather could be obtained by ceremonies, they instituted a cult, so that they would make certain sacrifices at the statue of Jupiter the Thunderer. Soldiers, when they thought that victories could be obtained from God by ceremonies, instituted a cult, so that they would make certain sacrifices at the statue of Mars. Thus human audacity devised new acts of worship, by confidence in works, without the command of God, and against the command of God. Hence, the minds wandering further, even attributed a certain divinity to statues, and subsequently to other things, where the devil had driven them, or where some affection had drawn them, divinity was attributed to statues, to cattle. And let examples not be sought only from the Heathens. What is happening now, men invoke the Saints, exactly as they once did Hercules, Or the heathens invoked Romulus. And there are other deities for other people. Soldiers invoke George, sailors Nicholas, the greedy Anna. People run to statues in the manner of the nations, and either divinity is attributed to the statues themselves, or God is bound to the statues with this opinion, that he is more appeased at this statue, although God does not wish to be bound to any thing to which he does not command himself to be invoked by an express mandate. There is therefore manifest idolatry in the world, and popes and kings approve and defend this. In Paris, some had removed a wooden statue of Mary, perhaps to prevent the superstition of the people; another silver one was restored, so that εἰδωλομανέια might be confirmed. Furthermore, there is manifold idolatry in other forms of worship. They attribute to the mass and to vows the honor owed to Christ, in that they satisfy for sins, in that they merit the remission of sins.

Since, therefore, impiety remains, namely Epicurean security, and superstition of every kind, let us do penance, let us seek the word of God, and let us learn to worship and invoke God rightly with true faith; let faith and works be ruled by the word of God, according to that: Your word is a lamp to my feet. For when one departs from this lamp, infinite errors immediately creep in. Let us therefore embrace the word of God, and let us pray to God, that through his son He may deliver us from all errors and impiety, since He has for this reason exhibited His Son to us, that He might destroy the works of the devil. Let the magnitude of punishments also exhort us to repentance. Contempt of God and superstition are punished even in this life, by blindness and madness. Men deserted by God rush into every kind of wickedness, and with minds inflamed by some desire, love, or hatred, the devil offers opportunities. How foul are the things read in histories which I do not wish to recite. How foul was Alexander, who saw that he had been gifted with such a kingdom, and because he was glorious, that he was adorned with such excellence of talent, yet he killed a friend among his cups, afterwards raged against princes who had deserved the best, and finally, when he was called to a banquet by a lover, he paid the penalty there, when he had fallen into a lethal disease from intemperance. Paul embraces these and similar things, that is, the greatest part of the history of the world, saying, when they boasted that they were wise, they became foolish and vain. For in such great baseness the madness of Alexander can be sufficiently seen, than whom nevertheless there was hardly any other more excellent talent. Let us contemplate in our mind both ancient histories and the vices of present times, and let us think those things to be punishments either of Cyclopean contempt of God, or of Idolomania. Paul warns of this, when several times He repeats that men were therefore delivered into the desires of their hearts, because they did not glorify God. Furthermore, the more unlearned should be admonished here concerning the phrase: He delivered them into desires, that is, He permitted them to rush. This phrase is customary among the Hebrews. As, Do not lead us into temptation, that is, do not allow us to be led, these things are to be understood permissively, for God is by no means the cause of sin, but the devil, as it is written: He who commits sin is of the devil. And he truly is the efficient and impelling cause of these frenzies which are described here.

Latin:

Non glorificaverunt ut Deum.

Glorificare ut Deum, est Deo aeterno rerum conditori tribuere hanc gloriam, quod sit Deus, id est aeternus, immensae potentiae, rerum conditor & conservator, sapiens, iustus, puniens iniustos, exaudiens & adiuvans iustos: eique obedire, ac vere timere eius iudicium, & vere ei credere, & ab eo petere et expectare bona. hunc honorem Deo tribuere omnes debebamus, idque vocat hic glorificare ut Deum.

Gratias agere, est credere quod Deus sit rerum conditor, quod ei curae simus, quòd vitam & alia bona ab ipso accipiamus, auxilium & defensionem ab eo petere, & expectare, ac propterea eum agnoscere tanquàm dominum, eique obedire, ne simus ingrati, et contumaces adversus dominum, & celebrare ac praedicare eius nomen, potentiam, bonitarem, iusticiam. Haec sunt opera primi & secundi praecepti, necessaria, & ad quae praecipuè conditi sumus. Sed mundus ea non praestat. Ideo vox Evangelii omnibus temporibus accusat impietatem mundi. Nam homines alii sunt ἄθεοι alii sunt Idolatrae. His duobus modis peccant homines contra primam tabulam legis divinae. ἄθεοι, ut Cyclopes & Epicuraei, prorsus negant esse Deum, aut curare res humanas. Hos satis constat non glorificare Deum, non metuunt, non credunt ei, non invocant eum, iudicant inane nomen esse. Id enim est ei gloriam aliquam tribuere potentiae, bonitatis, iusticiae. nec est exigua multitudo talium Cyclopum, etsi mirum est posse innatas noticias adeo obrui. Sed diabolus qui habet captivas mentes hominum, is naturae alioqui infirmae offundit maiores errores. ac nunc quidem nonnulli literati, praesertim Romae, sapientiam putant esse, delectari his Cyclopicis opinionibus. At Idolatrae aliter errant, honorem Deo debitum transferunt in alias res. Est enim εἰδωλολατρέια tribuere divinitatem ei quod non est Deus, invocare id quod non est deus, tribuere alteri honorem redemptionis, quàm Christo, tribuere fiduciam operibus nostris, quae Deo debebatur, alligare Deum ad certos cultus, & statuas contra suum mandatum, plus timere aut diligere aliud quàm Deum. Haec proprie complectitur, & significat εἰδωλολατρέια ut vulgo vocant. Hinc facile intelligi potest mundum plenum esse Idolomania. De hoc cultu verum est dictum poetae: Primus in orbe Deos fecit timor. Securi sunt plerunque Cyclopes. Alii in periculis querentes Deum, ut ratio monstrat Deum esse opitulatorem, anxii non recte querunt Deum. Cum enim habeant opiniones legis & cogitent, Deum exaudire iustos, cultoressuos, bene meritos, invocant qui sed sine promissione gratiae, sine noticia mediatoris, ideo aut dubitant se exaudiri ac respici, aut induunt inanem fiduciam suorum cultuum, sicut apud Homerum inquit sacrificulus: Si gratus hostias tibi mactavi phoebe exaudias me. Prima est igitur impietas, quod aut dubitant se exaudiri à Deo, aut induunt fiduciam propriae iusticiae, nec norunt mediatorem. Hoc errore admisso accedunt multa scelera. Fiducia propriorum cultuum moventur homines, ut cumulent caeremonias, & excogitent novos cultus, & Deos, ut cum rustici putarent bonas tempestates impetrari caeremoniis, instituerunt cultum, ut ad Iovis tonantis statuam quaedam sacrificia facerent. Milites, cum putarent caeremoniis impetrari victorias à Deo, instituerunt cultum, ut ad statuam Martis quaedam sacrificia facerent. Ita humana audacia excogitavit novos cultus, fiducia operum, sine mandato Dei, & contra mandatum Dei. Hinc longius aberrantes animi, etiam numen quoddam tribuerunt statuis, ac deinceps alii aliis rebus, quò impellebat diabolus, aut quò ad fectus aliquis traxerat, tribuebatur divinitas statuis, pecudibus. Nec tantum ab Ethnicis petantur exempla. Quid nunc fit, homines invocant Divos, prorsus ut olim Herculem, aut Romulum invocabant Ethnici. Et alia sunt aliorum Numina. Milites invocant Georgium, Nautae Nicolaum, Avari Annam. Curritur ad statuas more gentium, & aut ipsis statuis numen tribuitur, aut allegatur Deus ad statuas hac opinione, quod placatior sit ad hanc statuam, cum Deus nolit allegari ulli rei, ad quam se non expresso mandato iubet invocari. Est igitur manisesta in mundo Idolatria, & hanc probant ac defendunt pontifices & reges. Lutetiae quidam sustulerant ligneam statuam Mariae, fortassis ut superstitionem populi prohiberent, restiuta est alia argentea, ut confirmaretur εἰδωλομανέια. Deinde multiplex est Idolatria in aliis cultibus. Tribuunt missae & votis honorem debitum Christo, quod satisfaciant pro peccatis, quod mereantur remissionem peccatorum.

Cum igitur maneat impietas, videlicet Epicurea securitas, et superstitio cuiuscunque modi, agamus paenitentiam, queramus verbum Dei, & Deum recte colere & invocare vera fide discamus, regantur verbo Dei fides et opera, iuxta illud: Lucerna pedibus meis verbuum tuum. Nam cum ab hac lucerna disceditur, statim infiniti errores obrepunt. Amplectamur igitur verbum Dei, & oremus Deum, ut per filium suum liberet nos ab omnibus erroribus et impietate, cum filium ideo nobis exhibuerit, ut destruat opera diaboli. Hortetur ad paenitentiam nos et magnitudo poenarum. Contemptus dei et superstitio puniuntur etiam in hac vita, coecitate & amentia. Homines deserti à Deo ruunt in omne genus flagicii, & accensis animis aliqua cupiditate, amore, odio diabolus offert occasiones. Quam foeda leguntur in historiis quae recitare non volo. Quam foedus Alexander, qui videbat se donatum esse tanto regno, & quod erat gloriosus, ornatum esse tanta ingenii praestantia, is tamen inter pocula interfecit amicum, postea seviit in optime meritos principes, tandem cum in convivium ab amatore vocatus ibi dat poenas, cum ex intemperantia in morbum letalem incidisset. Haec & similia, hoc est maximam: partem historiae mundi, complectitur Paulus inquiens, cum se esse sapientes gloriarentur, stulti ac vani fuerunt. Satis enim in tanta turpitudine conspici potest Alexandri amentia, quo tamen vix aliud excellentius fuit ingenium. Intueamur animo & veteres historias, & praesentium temporum vitia, eaque cogitemus esse poenas aut Cyclopici contemptus Dei, aut Idolomaniae. Hoc monet Paulus, cum aliquoties repetit, ideo traditos esse homines in desideria cordium suorum, quia Deum non glorificaverint. Caeterum hic de phrasi admonendi sunt rudiores: Tradidit eos in desideria, id est, permisit eos ruere. Usitata est haec phrasis apud Ebreos. ut, Ne inducas nos intentationem, id est, non sinas nos induci, permissivè haec intelligenda sunt, Deus enim nequaquàm est causa peccati, sed diabolus, ut scriptum est: Qui facit peccatum ex diabolo est. Et is vere est causa efficax & impellens ad hos furores, qui hic describuntur.

## 1:29
Full of all injustice.

He adds an accumulation and a great heap of sins, so that he may also convict the other vices. ἀδικία is general, signifying universal disobedience against the first and second table of the divine law, just as the justice of the Law signifies universal obedience.

πονηρία properly signifies the desire to do harm. κακία contains sins of omission, as they call them. For as for the Latins, baseness is the general opposite to virtue, so for the Greeks κακία is the opposite of τῆ ἀρετῆ. M. Antonius is κακὸς, a glutton, negligent. But Domitian is πονηρὸς, desirous of doing harm, to whom this very thing is a pleasure, to harm others. Κακοήθεια properly is malevolence Such is the case with detractors, who know how to deprave with art, simply or candidly, words and deeds. And it is truly a vice opposed to candor. κακόηθες μὴ καθαρὸν. Plutarch opposes these to one another. Malevolence is a savage plague, and often pernicious to the Republic, when malevolent natures harass others who are mediocre or even well-deserving, merely from a disease of the mind, just as Cato did not favor the praises of Cicero. For to κακοήθειαν this also is accustomed to be added, the vice is covered by a simulation of gravity. There exist little verses of Menander, in which are described certain ranks of men, in whom the powerful take pleasure especially. ὁ βίος μάλιστα τοῖς πονηροῖς ἥδεται πράττει δ' ὃ κολαξ ἄριστα πάντων, δέυτερος ὁ συκοφάντης, ὁ δὲ κακοήθης τρίτατος ὅς μηχαναν κακ' ἐστὶ τεχνικώτατος.

He assigns the first place to the flatterer, for this one is the sweetest; the next is the informer, or whisperer, who gains favor by carrying tales and by fabricating and constructing calumnies. The third place is held by κακοήθης, who knows how to allude to the affections of the Lord, to interpret deeds candidly in a different way, to inflame hatreds. θεοστυγεῖς, whether it be taken actively or passively, signifies those who are openly contumelious against God, such as are described Sennacherib and Rabshakeh in the history Isaiah, or Mezentius in Virgil, or Antiochus in the history of the Maccabees. And this age has too many examples of Tyrants, who openly profess themselves to be enemies of God. ἀσύνετοι, furious men, who blind against the judgment of common sense rush headlong into all crimes, and their own destruction, like Catiline, Thomas Müntzer, who raging had taken up arms to destroy all princes, to institute a community of goods. Likewise the scoundrel of Münster, who called himself the king of the temple of God. The prophets often say that this madness is the punishment of impiety. Thus Pharaoh, Saul, and others summoned destruction upon themselves. Both a good conscience and moderate counsel are lacking in them. ἀσύνθετοι not keeping covenants σήνθυκας, in contracts and treaties. ἄστοργοι, who cast off natural affections toward parents, children, brothers, or benefactors. For στοργὴ signifies good affections divinely implanted in the nature of men, even if now on account of the disease of origin they wander somewhat. But nevertheless God approves of them and wishes them to be rightly ruled, He commands us to love spouses, parents, children, He commands us to be grateful. These are στοργαὶ. Therefore Paul condemns those iron men, who cast off these στοργὰς, such as the brothers in the Tragedies, Atreus & Thyestes. ἄσπονδοι are implacable, just as Saul could not be appeased by any service, so that he might return into favor with David. Again, however, in the end he alleges the law of nature, and the calling of God. Let students therefore remember the rule, that the violation of the laws of nature is a violation of divine law and truly a mortal sin. I have compared in places the law of nature with the decalogue, which indeed is the best method and the sum of the laws of nature, if one understands the decalogue rightly. Paul condemns, however, not only those committing deeds against the law externally, but also those consenting. All who are not reborn in Christ consent to the impious who doubt concerning God, and they have depraved desires, and although at other times others in others show themselves more, most of all, however, impious Kings and princes consent to the impious, who, when they ought to punish Cyclopean impiety and Idolatry with the most severe punishments, especially approve, confirm, and establish it. But let them learn here that they will give an account to God. It is a wonderful saying, however, which he says, that men naturally know that they are worthy of death, both those who do depraved things, and those who consent. Whence do we know that they are worthy of death? From the true terrors of conscience. For Paul looks into minds far differently than secure men. He sees what terrors exist, when in affliction sins are more recognized.

Latin:

Plenos omni iniusticia.

Addit coacervationem & magnum cumulum peccatorum, ut caetera vicia etiam arguat. ἀδικία, generale est, significans universalem inobedientiam contra primam & secundam tabulam legis divinae, sicut iusticia Legis significat universalem obedientiam.

πονηρία significat propriè cupiditatem nocendi. κακία peccata omissionis, ut vocant, continet. Nam ut Latinis turpitudo generale oppositum virtuti, ita Graecis κακία est oppositum τῆ ἀρετῆ. M. Antonius est κακὸς, helluo, negligens. Sed Domitianus est πονηρὸς, cupidus nocendi, cui hoc ipsum voluptati est nocere aliis. Κακοήθεια proprie est malevolentia qualis est in obtrectatoribus, qui simpliciter aut candi de dicta & facta, arte depravare norunt. Estque vere opposituum vicium candori. κακόηθες μὴ καθαρὸν. Haec ē inter se opponit Plutarchus. Seva pestis est maleulentia, & saepe Reip. perniciosa, cum malevolae naturae exagitant alios mediocres aut etiam bene meritos, tantum animi morbo, ut Canto non favebat Ciceronis laudibus. Nam id quoque ad κακοήθειαν solet accedere, simulatione gravitatis tegitur vicium. Extant versiculi Menandri, in quibus describuntur gradus quidam hominum, quibus praecipuê delectantur potentes. ὁ βίος μάλιστα τοῖς πονηροῖς ἥδεται πράττει δ' ὃ κολαξ ἄριστα πάντων, δέυτερος ὁ συκοφάντης, ὁ δὲ κακοήθης τρίτατος ὅς μηχαναν κακ' ἐστὶ τεχνικώτατος.

Primum locum tribuit adsentatori, nam hic est dulcissimus, proximus est delator, seu susurro, qui init gratiam perferendis fabellis & confingendis ac instruendis calumniis. Tertium locum habet κακοήθης, qui novit alludere ad Domini adfectus, candide facta secus interpretari, odia incendere. θεοστυγεῖς, sive activesive passive accipiatur, significat palam contumeliosos in Deum, quales describuntur Sennacherib & Rapsaces in historia Esaiae, aut Mezentius apud Vergilium, aut Antiochus in historia Machabeorum. Et habet haec aetas exempla nimis multa Tyrannorum, qui apertè profitenturse esse hostes Dei. ἀσύνετοι, furiosi, qui coeci contra iudicium communis sensus ruunt praecipites in omnia scelera, & exitium suum, sicut Catilina, Thomas Monetarius, qui furens arma coeperat ad delendos omnes principes, ad communionem rerum instituendam. Item nebulo Monasteriensis, qui se vocabat regem templi Dei. Hanc amentiam saepe dicunt prophetae poenam esse impietatis. Sic Pharao, Saul & alii sibi accersiverunt exitium. Deest eis utrumquè bona conscientia, & moderatum consilium. ἀσύνθετοι non servantes pacta σήνθυκας, in contractibus ac foederibus. ἄστοργοι, qui naturales adfectus erga parentes, liberos, fratres aut benemeritos exuunt. Nam στοργὴ significat bonos adfectus divinitus inditos naturae hominum, etsi nunc propter morbum originis nonnihil aberrant. Sed tamen probat eos Deus & rectè regi vult, iubet nos diligere coniuges, parentes, liberos, iubet gratos esse. Hae sunt στοργαὶ. Damnat igitur Paulus illos ferreos homines, qui exuunt has στοργὰς, quales sunt fratres in Tragediis Atreus & Thyestes. ἄσπονδοι sunt implacabiles, sicut Saul nullo officio placari potuit, ut rediret in gratiam cum Davide. Iterum autem in fine allegat ius naturae, ac vocatius Dei. Meminerint ergo studiosi regulam, quod violatio legum naturae sit violatio iuris divini et vere peccatum mortale. Contuli in locis ius naturae cum decallogo, qui quidem est optima methodus & summa legum naturae, si quis dextre decalogum intelligat. Damnat autem Paulus non solum facta contra legem externa ad mittentes, sed etiam cnosentientes. Consentiunt autem impiis dubitantibus deDeo omnes qui non sunt renati in Christo, habent & pravas cupiditates, &si alias aliae in aliis magis se promunt, maxime autem consentiunt impiis Reges & principes impii, qui cum Cyclopicam impietatem & Idolatriam punire deberent, severissimis poenis, praecipue eam adprobant, confirmant, & stabiliunt. Sed hic discant se Deo poenas daturos esse. Mirum est autem dictum, quod ait, naturaliter homines scire dignos esse morte, utrosque qui prava faciunt, & qui consentiunt. Unde scimus esse morte dignos? ex veris terroribus conscientiae. Nam Paulus longe aliter introspicit mentes, quam homines securi. Videt qui terrores existant, cum in adflictione peccata magis agnoscuntur.

## 2:1 Argument
CHAPTER II.

Latin:

CAPUT II.

## 2:1
Therefore thou art inexcusable O man &c.

There is a need for this doctrine to exist in the Church, that external discipline or obedience does not satisfy the Law, nor justify before God. Therefore Paul now accuses those who trust that they are righteous on account of external good morals when nevertheless they have impious and unclean hearts, in this sentiment he says: Therefore thou art inexcusable every one who judgest, that is, who condemnest others and feignest thyself to be righteous. And here the universal must be diligently weighed. Every one who judgest, makes an equalization of all men, so that all may know themselves to be guilty, and may not judge, that is, may not trust in their own righteousness, may not justify themselves, and condemn others. This equalization is valid for terrifying hypocrites and the proud: And on the contrary for raising up the fearful so that they may not despair, because they recognize that they do not have merits, just as in this place an equalization is made, he has concluded all under sin, so that He may have mercy on all. There is, however, a syllogism. The major premise is at the end of the previous chapter, the conclusion at the beginning of the following one, then the minor: those doing and consenting are worthy of death, you hypocrites are consenting, therefore you also are inexcusable. As to what he says: you do the same things, he speaks not of the external work, but of the interior uncleanness: You have impious opinions and doubt concerning God, just as they do, you have depraved desires just as they do: Then he exhorts these also to repentance. And it is a notable commemoration of the goodness of God. That God defers judgment and punishment, so that He may grant space for performing repentance. Just as the parable of the fig tree also teaches Lucae xiii.

Latin:

Quapropter inexcusabilis es ô homo &c.

Opus est extare hanc doctrinam in Ecclesia, quod externa disciplina seu obedientia non fatisfaciat Legi, nec iustificet coram Deo. Ideo iam accusat Paulus illos qui confidunt se iustos esse propter externos bonos mores cum tamen habeant corda impia & immunda, in hanc sententiam inquit: Ideo inexcusabilis es omnis qui iudicas, id est, qui damnas alios & fingis te iustum esse. Ac diligenter hic expendenda est universalis. Omnis qui iudicat, facit exaequationem omnium hominum, ut omnes sciant se reos esse, nec iudicent, id est, non confidant sua iusticia, non iustificent se, & damnet alios. Haec exaequatio valet ad perterrefaciendos hypocritas & superbos: Et econtra ad erigendos pavidos ne despernet, quia agnoscunt se non habere merita, sicut in hoc loco fit exaequatio, conclusit omnes sub peccato, ut omnium misereatur. Est autem syllogismus. Maior est in fine prioris capitis, Conclusio in principio sequentis, deinde minor: facientes & consentientes sunt digni morte, vos Hypocritae estis consentientes, ergo & vos estis inexcusabiles. Quòd ait: eadem facis, loquitur non de externo opere, sed de interiore immundicia: Habes impias opiniones & dubitationem de Deo, sicut illi, habes pravas cupiditates sicut illi: Deinde adhortatur & hos ad paenitentiam. Estque insignis commemoratio bonitatis Dei. Quod Deus differt Iudiciam & poenam, ut concedat spacium ad agendam paenitentiam. Sicut docet etiam parabola de ficu Lucae xiii.

## 2:6
Who will render to everyone according to his deeds &c.

This passage is cited against the doctrine of faith, that works merit eternal life. But the answer is easy. For first, that it is necessary to mitigate τὸ ῥητὸν with some interpretation, from there it can be understood, because no one satisfies the Law, wherefore no one would be saved, if the sentence were to be accepted in such a way, that on account of the fulfillment

tion of the Law men are to be saved. It is necessary therefore to add an interpretation concerning faith, and concerning mercy. Moreover, the phrase of the law is, he will render to everyone according to his works. For when the law names works, it understands the justice or injustice of each one, as if it were saying, God will render to everyone according to his own justice or injustice. And indeed the Law is accustomed to speak of faith as if it were a work, and yet meanwhile it must be known from the Gospel, that justification is received freely by faith, which afterwards must necessarily be followed by new and begun obedience. The Law calls this whole thing works. Scripture is accustomed, however, to distinguish justification and glorification, just as Paul says: Those whom he justifies, them he also glorifies. Therefore, when it is said here and elsewhere, according to works, it is signified to what kind of persons eternal life is given. For although faith and works are not merits, nevertheless faith is the instrument by which we receive reconciliation, and by which we are made sons of God and co-heirs of Christ, and this must necessarily be followed by new obedience, which does not satisfy the Law. Wherefore it is not a merit or price of eternal life, but it pleases because we believe in Christ. Therefore it cannot be gathered from this, that our works are merits and the price of eternal life, because we do not satisfy the Law.

Latin:

Qui redditurus est unicuique iu-xta facta sua &c.

Hic locus citatur contra doctrinam de fide, quod opera mereantur vitam aeternam. Sed facilis est responsio. Primum enim quod necesse sit τὸ ῥητὸν mitigare aliqua interpretatione, inde intelligi potest, quia nemo Legi satisfacit, quare nemo salvus fieret, si sic esset accipienda sententia, quod propter imple.

tionem Legis homines salvandi sint. Necesse est igitur addere interpraetationem de fide, & de misericordia. Est autem phrasis legis, reddet unicuique iuxta opera sua. Nam cum lex opera nominat, intelligit cuiusque iusticiam aut iniusticiam, quasi dicat, Deus reddet unicuique secundum ipsius iusticiam aut iniusticiam. Et quidem Lex solet de fide tanquam de opere loqui, et tamen interim ex Evangelio sciendum est, quod fide gratis accipiatur iustificatio, quam postea necessario sequi debet nova & inchoata obedientia. Hoc totum Lex vocat opera. Solet autem scriptura discernere iustificationem & glorificationem, sicut Paulus inquit: Eos quos iustificat, eosdem & glorificat. Ideo cum hic & alibi dicitur, iuxta opera, significatur qualibus detur vita aeterna. Quamvis enim fides & opera non sunt merita, tamen fides est instrumentum, quo accipimus reconciliationem, & quo efficimur filii Dei & cohaeredes Christi, & hanc ncessario sequi debet nova obedientia, quae non satisfacit Legi. Quare non est meritum aut precium vitae aeternae, sed placet quia credimus Christo, Ergo non potest hinc colligi, quòd nostra opera sint merita & precium vitae aeternae, quia non satisfacimus Legi.

## 2:13
For not those who hear the Law are just, etc.

This is a general statement concerning the justice of the Law. For the Jews arrogated justice to themselves on account of the Law. Here Paul opposes the definition of the justice of the law. For the justice of the law is to do the law, to provide complete obedience to the Law, not only to hear the Law or to profess the ceremony of the Law; thus he says: The doers of the Law are justified, that is, they are pronounced just, they are just. Paul speaks here of the Idea and refutes the Jews, because they are not just by the Law, since no one satisfies the Law. Wherefore this passage cannot be twisted against the justice of faith, nor does Paul add here how the Law is begun and how it pleases. For he only refutes those who pretend that they are just on account of the external profession of the Law.

Latin:

Non enim qui audiunt Le-gem, iusti sunt &c.

Generalis sententia est de iustitia Legis. Nam Iudaei arrogabant sibi iustitiam propter Legem. Hic opponit Paulus definitionem iustitiae legis. Est enim iustitia legis facere legem, praestare integram obedientiam Legi, non tantum audire Legem aut profiteri Legis caeremoniam, sic ait: Factores Legis iustificantur, id est, pronunciantur iusti, sunt iusti. Italoquitur Paulus de Idaea & coarguit Iudaeos, quod non sint iusti Lege, quia nemo Legi satisfacit. Quare hic locus non potest detorqueri contra iustitiam fidei, nec addit hic Paulus, quomodo inchoetur Lex & quomodo placeat. Tantum enim refutat illos, qui fingunt fe esse iustos propter externam professionem Legis.

## 2:14
They are a Law to themselves, etc.

He had said that the impious Jews and Gentiles would perish, even if the latter did not have the Law; now he adds a correction: Nay, the Gentiles also had the Law, that is, a natural knowledge concerning morals, distinguishing between honorable and base things. Here again stands the testimony concerning the Law of nature. And Paul reasons learnedly that the Gentiles have the Law, and at the same time he declares what the Law of nature is, they have a conscience accusing and excusing, that is, discerning honorable and base things, therefore they have the Law. The consequence is known from the definition. For the Law is properly that natural knowledge, teaching honorable things and reproving base things. But it must be diligently observed what he says, by nature doing, that is, by natural knowledge and light. And Paul testifies by this word nature, that that knowledge is a work of God established in the mind, just as light in the eyes. For nature properly signifies a thing established by God. Wherefore those knowledges are true, and are divine law as was said above: In this place Augustine sweats greatly although he has nothing obscure, First he disputes what Paul means when he says the Gentiles have done the Law, whether he speaks of some saints as of Job and the like. Secondly he disputes about the particle nature, since the law cannot truly be done without the holy spirit, why Paul says the Gentiles have done it by nature. Augustine brings these difficulties to Paul. For the text itself is not so very obscure. For first nature signifies principally natural knowledge. For Paul he reasons, concerning knowledge and judgment. Then it is also manifest that the unregenerate can perform the external works of the Law by natural powers, and provide discipline or civil works. It is enough for Paul here to show that the Gentiles understand the distinction between honorable and base things. Discipline shows this, from which he reasons that they have the Law. He speaks, therefore, of those doing external works and of discipline, and indeed he compares the Jews and the Gentiles. He signifies that the Gentiles have progressed as much from the Law of nature as the Jews have from the Law of Moses. For he does not say that the Gentiles were righteous before God by the Law, but he signifies that both performed external civil works. Fabius, Scipio, Atticus, and many others excelled in the most beautiful virtues, and perhaps surpassed many outstanding Jews in discipline and diligence in every duty. Hence Paul reasons that the Gentiles have the Law, that is, natural knowledge concerning morals. Nor does it follow from this comparison that any were righteous before God on account of that discipline.

Behold, you are called a Jew.

As he previously accused the Gentiles by name, so now he accuses the Jews by name, so that he may arrive at that execution of the Gentiles and Jews, in which it is seen that all men are under sin, and are not freed from sin by the Law. Moreover, this rebuke is to be taken in such a way that we understand both manifest sins and hypocrisy to be accused, just as it is necessary for repentance to be preached, according to that command of Christ: Go preaching repentance and remission of sins. And although some among the Jews were holy, nevertheless Paul speaks of the Jews insofar as they have nothing but the law, nor are they sanctified by faith and the acknowledgment of the promised Christ. For he wishes to effect this, that the Law does not suffice for justification. Wherefore the argument is valid. If the Law sufficed for justification, all who received the Law and observe external rites would be just. But these are not just, therefore the Law does not suffice for justification. For it must be diligently considered with what purpose Paul wrote these things; he accuses the Jews so that they may understand that there is need of another benefit for justification. Moreover, this is a grave rebuke of arrogance in hypocrites who swell with confidence in their own righteousness; such passages are to be observed both so that we may learn fear, and so that terrified minds may conceive consolation. For such passages are of very great value in both directions, as they both delay carnal security and, in turn, raise up fearful minds, according to that saying: let him who boasts, boast in the Lord.

Latin:

Sibi ipsis Lex &c.

Dixerat impios perituros esse Iudaeos & gentes, etiamsi hae Legem non habuerunt, nunc addit correctionem: Imo gentes etiam habuerunt Legem, hoc est notitiam naturalem de moribus, discernentem honesta & turpia. Hic iterum extat testimonium de Lege naturae. Ac Paulus eruditè ratiocinatur, quod gentes habeant Legem, ac simul declarat quid sit Lex naturae, habent conscientiam accusantem & excusantem, id est, discernentem honesta & turpia, Ergo habent Legem. Consequentia est nota ex definitione. Nam Lex proprie est illa naturalis noticia, docens honesta & repraehendens turpia. Diligenter autem observandum est, quod ait natura facium, id est, naturali noticia ac lumine. Et testatur Paulus hoc verbo natura, quod noticia illa, sit opus Dei conditum in mente, sicut lumen in oculis. Natura enim proprie significat rem conditam à Deo. Quare notitiae illae sunt verae, & sunt lex divina ut supra dictum est: In hoc loco valde sudat Augustinus cum nihil habeat obscuri, Primum disputat, quid velit Paulus, cum ait gentes Legem fecisse, an loquatur de aliquibus sanctis ut de Iob & similibus. Secundo disputat de particula natura, cum lex non possit vere fieri sine spiritu sancto, quare Paulus dicat gentes natura fecisse. Has difficultates affert ad Paulum Augustinus. Nam ipse textus non usque adeo obscurus est. Primum enim natura significat principaliter noticiam naturalem. Paulus enim ratiocinatur, de noticia & de iudicio. Deinde manifestum est etiam non renatos viribus naturalibus posse externa Legis opera facere, & disciplinam seu civilia opera praestare. Paulo hic satis est ostendere quod gentes intelligant discrimen honestorum & turpium. Hoc ostendit disciplina, inde ratiocinatur quod Legem habeant. Loquitur ergo de facientibus externa opera & de disciplina, & quidem confert Iudaeos & gentes. Significat gentes tantundem profecisse ex Lege naturae, quantum Iudaeos ex Lege Moisi. Non enim dicit Lege fuisse iustas gentes coram Deo, sed significat, utrosque externa civilia opera fecisse. Excelluerunt pulcherrimis virtutibus, Fabius, Scipio, Atticus, & plaerique alii, ac fortassis disciplina & diligentia in omni officio superarunt multos praestantes Iudaeos. Hinc ratiocinatur Paulus gentes habere Legem, id est, noticiam naturalem de moribus. Neque sequitur ex hac collatione quod propter illam disciplinam ulli fuerint iusti coram Deo.

Ecce tu Iudaeus.

Ut antea nominatim gentes accusavit, ita nunc nominatim accusat Iudaeos, ut perveniat ad illam exaequutionem gentium & Iudaeorum, in qua conspicitur quod omnes homines sunt sub peccato, & Lege non liberentur à peccato. Est autem haec obiurgatio sic accipienda, ut intelligamus accusari & manifesta peccata & hypocrisim, sicut necesse est praedicari paenitentiam, iuxta illud mandatum Christi: Ite praedicantes paenitentiam & remissionem peccatorum. Et quanquam aliqui inter Iudaeos fuerunt sancti, tamen Paulus loquitur de Iudaeis quatenus nihil habent nisi legem, nec sunt sanctificati fide & agnitione promissi Christi. Hoc enim vult efficere quòd Lex non sufficiat ad iustificationem. Quare valet argumentum. Si Lex sufficeret ad iustificationem, omnes essent iusti qui Legem acceperunt et observant externos cultus. Atqui hi non sunt iusti, ergo Lex non sufficit ad iustificationem. Diligenter enim considerandum est quo consilio Paulus haec scripserit, accusat Iudaeos ut intelligant opus esse alio beneficio ad iustificationem. Est autem hic gravis obiurgatio arrogantiae in Hypocritis qui tument fiducia propriae iustitiae, tales loci observandi sunt & ut timorem discamus, & ut perterrefactae mentes concipiant consolationem. Nam in utranque partem plurimum valent tales loci qui & carnalem securitatem tardant & rursus erigunt pavidas mentes, iuxta illud: qui gloriatur in Domino glorietur.

## 2:25
For circumcision indeed profits, if you keep the Law.

This is an objection. For Paul meets the objection concerning the merits of external rites, when the Jews preferred themselves to the Gentiles and objected that they had certain rites instituted by God and argued that these rites were not instituted in vain, but merited the remission of sins, etc. Paul responds with a new paradox: Circumcision profits if you observe the Law. And it is a general statement concerning all external rites, that they do not profit by the work performed, as they commonly say, nor do they merit the remission of sins, but they are pleasing in those who are righteous. However, this statement must be applied not only to Levitical rites, but also to external works and ceremonies in the Church.

Latin:

Nam Circumcisio quidem pro-dest, si Legem servaveris.

Occupatio est. Paulus enim occurrit obiectioni de meritis externorum cultuum, cum Iudaei se praeferrent gentibus & obiicerent se habere certos cultus à Deo institutos & disputarent hos cultus non esse frustra institutos, sed mereri remissionem peccatorum &c. Respondet Paulus novo paradoxo: Circumcisio prodest si Legem observes. Estque generale dictum de omnibus externis cultibus, quòd non prosint ex opere operato, ut vulgo loquuntur, nec mereantur remissionem peccatorum, sed placeant in his qui sunt iusti. Accommodandum est autem hoc dictum non solum ad Leviticos cultus, sed etiam ad externa opera & caeremonias in Ecclesia.

## 3:1 Argument
CHAPTER III.

Latin:

CAPUT III.

## 3:3
Whether their unbelief, etc.

He inserts incidentally other questions, whether the Jews therefore lost the promises and the whole nation was condemned because they did not believe but killed Christ. Paul answers that the promise of grace is not made void, but remains valid for all who believe, even if very many spurn it. This passage contains excellent consolation and warns us not to suspect, because of the huge multitude of the impious, that the promise of grace made to the Church is void, but let us know that it is truly exhibited to believers, even if they are very few.

Latin:

Num incredulitas illorum &c.

Inserit obiter alias quaestiones utrum ideo amiserunt Iudaei promissiones & tota gens damnata sint quia non crediderunt sed interfecerunt Christum. Respondet Paulus promissionem gratiae non fieri irritam, sed manere ratam omnibus quicumque credunt, etiamsi plurimi eam aspernantur. Hic locus continet egregiam consolationem ac monet ne propter ingentem multitudinem impiorum suspicemur promissionem gratiae Ecclesiae factam irritam esse, sed sciamus vere eam exhiberi credentibus, etiamsi paucissimi sint.

## 3:4
But every man a liar.

He adds an antithesis, so that it may become more illustrious that God is truthful, because He keeps His promises to the unworthy on account of His own truth and goodness. Every man is a liar, not judging rightly concerning God, not truly fearing God, not truly believing God, not thinking that He is angry at sin, or that He has mercy on those doing penance, but doubting, neglecting, distrusting God; the remnants of these sins and of these darknesses are even in the saints. Therefore he says: Every man a liar. Therefore the promises depend not on our dignity but on the fact that God is truthful.

Latin:

Omnis autem homo mendax.

Addit antithesim, ut fiat illustrius quod Deus sit verax, quia servat promissa indignis propter suam veritatem et bonitatem. Omnis homo mendax, non recte iudicans de Deo, non vere timens Deum, non vere credens Deo, non existimans eum irasci peccato, aut misereri agentium paenitentiam, sed dubitans, negligens, diffidens Deo, horum peccatorum & harum tenebrarum reliquiae sunt etiam in sanctis. Ideo dicit: Omnis homo mendax. Pendent igitur promissiones non ex dignitate nostra sed ex eo quod Deus est verax.

## 3:4
That you may be justified in your words, and overcome when you are judged.

A verse from a Psalm is cited for the same sentiment, in which the first part is a confession of sin. Then the glory of justice and truth is attributed to God: Against you alone I sin and do evil before you, that you may be justified in your words, and overcome when you are judged, that is, I am only a sinner, I acknowledge that I bring nothing to you except sins. The latter part contains a petition and the reason for the petition. Therefore, hear me, relying not on my dignity but on your promise, so that it may appear that you are just and keeping your promises because of your truth, and you may overcome when the world judges you and blasphemes, because you do not care, you do not hear men. Likewise, when hypocrites pretend that they are heard because of their own righteousness, etc. Do you now hear me, so that there may exist an example that you truly hear those fleeing to you, and you hear not because of our dignity, but through mercy. Thus this verse becomes sweeter when a petition is added to the confession of sin, which is certainly joined with the confession of sin. The verse of the Psalm proposes most abundant consolation. For it signifies that the conscience does not bring merits to God, but only the acknowledgment of sin, and that it is justified not on account of any merits, but because it apprehends the promised mercy on account of the Son and attributes glory to God, that He Himself is just and the justifier, and that He is truthful in keeping His promises. Epicureans and Hypocrites do not attribute this praise to Him, but they judge God, either because He does not hear, or because God does not judge rightly, punishes the unworthy, and does not hear except on account of merits, etc. If we transfer this to our own use and to the stirring up of faith and invocation within us, the sentence will become more illustrious. Furthermore, new questions now arise from this verse. If the mercy of God is amplified by this, that He makes alive the unworthy, and those bringing nothing but sins, Why is God angry with sinners? seeing that our sins amplify the glory of His mercy. Item, if we are not just on account of our virtues, to what end is there a need to do good? Item, The more sins mercy forgives, the more illustrious it becomes, therefore let us sin, etc. These absurdities are now also objected to those who defend the doctrine concerning grace and faith. Wherefore it is sufficiently It appears that it is the same cause which Paul argues and which we now defend according to the doctrine of Paul. Below, however, he responds to these absurdities and refutes them in the sixth chapter. Now he only breaks off. He rebukes those who, by carnal judgment, were deforming the great benefit of the Gospel with these diabolical calumnies, and were reasoning falsely from badly distorted promises. For although God justifies freely, yet He does not grant a license to sin, but He justifies in such a way that justification brings a new life and a new light, and we owe obedience to God, even though another price is proposed, on account of which He pronounces us just, because this obedience of ours does not satisfy the Law. The rebuke is set forth in atrocious words, as we are blasphemed, likewise whose condemnation is just. For he signifies that those calumnies are blasphemies against the Gospel, and he says that those who thus revile are justly condemned. Let this threat admonish us to hear and learn the Gospel reverently and to flee from blasphemers, who calumniate, deprave, or in any way attempt to deform pious doctrine.

Latin:

Ut iustificeris in sermonibus tuis, & vincas cum iudicaris.

Citatur in eandem sententiam versiculus ex Psalmo, in quo primum est confessio peccati. Deinde tribuitur Deo gloria iusticiae & veritatis: Tibi solum pecco & malum coram te facio, ut iustificeris in sermonibus tuis, & vincas cum iudicaris, id est, tantum sum peccator, agnosco me nihil afferre ad te nisi peccata. Posterior pars continet petitionem & rationem petitionis. Ideo exaudias me fretum non mea dignitate sed tua promissione, ut appareat te esse iustum & servantem promissa propter tuam veritatem, & vincas cum mundus te iudicat & blasphemat, quod non cures, non exaudias homines. Item cum hypocritae fingunt se exaudiri propter suas iusticias, &c. Tu nunc me exaudias, ut extet exemplum, quòd vere exaudias confugientes ad te, & exaudias non propter nostram dignitatem, sed per misericordiam. Sic fit dulcior hic versiculus cum ad confessionem peccati additur petitio, quae certè est coniuncta cum confessione peccati. Versiculus Psalmi proponit uberrimam consolationem. Significat enim conscientiam non afferre ad Deum merita, sed tantum agnitionem peccati, & iustificari non propter aliqua merita, sed quia appraehendit promissam misericordiam propter filium & tribuit Deo gloriam, quòd ipse sit iustus & iustificans, & quòd sit verax servans promissa. Hanc ei laudem non tribuunt Epicurei & Hypocritae, sed iudicant Deum, vel quod non exaudiat, vel quod non recte iudicet Deus, puniat indignos, & non exaudiat nisi propter merita, &c. Si ad usum nostrum & excitandam fidem & invocationem in nobis transferamus, fiet sententia illustrior. Porro iam ex hoc versiculo oriuntur novae quaestiones. Si misericordia Dei amplificatur per hoc, quod vivificat indignos, & nihil nisi peccata afferentes, Quare Deus irascitur peccantibus? siquidem peccata nostra amplificant gloriam misericordiae ipsius. Item si non sumus iusti propter nostras virtutes, quorsum opus est benefacere? Item, Quo plura peccata remittit misericordia, eo fit illustrior, peccemus igitur, &c. Haec absurda nunc quoquè obiiciuntur his, qui doctrinam de gratia & de fide defendunt. Quare satis apparet eandem esse causam, quam Paulus agit & quam nunc defendimus iuxta Pauli doctrinam. Infra autem ad haec absurda respondet & diluit ea capite sexto. Nunc abrumpit tantum. Obiurgans illos qui carnali Iudicio his dyabolicis calumniis ingens beneficium Evangelii deformabant, et ex promissionibus male detortis falsa ratiocinabantur. Etsi enim gratis iustificat Deus, tamen non concedit licentiam peccandi, Sed ita iustificat, ut iustificatio afferat novam vitam & novam lucem, & debemus obedientiam Deo, etiam aliud precium propositum est, propter quod iustos pronunciat, quia haec nostra obedientia non satisfacit Legi. Obiurgatio posita est atrocibus verbis sicut blasphemamur, item quorum condemnatio iusta est. Significat enim calumnias illas esse blasphemias adversus Evangelium, & sic convitiantes ait iustè damnari. Haec comminatio admoneat nos ut reverenter audiamus & discamus Evangelium et fugiamus blasphemos, qui piam doctrinam calumniantur, depravant, aut quoquo modo deformare conantur.

## 3:9
What therefore does the Jew have in which he excels?

It is a digression in which, as if interrupted, he meets certain objections, for a great and difficult question arises from that equalization of the Gentiles and the Jews. For if the Jews are not righteous on account of their worships, if they are not freed from sin on account of the works of the Law, why was the Law given? Why does God require it? Why does He call for worships and propitiations? Why are the Jews called the people of God, if the Law does not make a distinction between the Jews and the Gentiles? What prerogative do the Jews have? Paul answers in two ways. First affirmatively, then negatively. First he says that the Jews excel the Gentiles and have this prerogative, that they have the promises. They excel, therefore, not on account of the Law, not because they merit justification by the Law, but because they have the promises. This was a huge prerogative, to know the word of God and the promise concerning Christ, and indeed to have this right, that the promise pertained by name to this people. And so many, hearing that word, were being saved, and indeed it was certain that some from the Jews were always being saved, because the promise had been issued in such a way that it pertained by name to the descendants of Abraham. Therefore this passage now teaches concerning the principal end of the entire Jewish polity; the unlearned imagine that those Laws were given so that the people might be justified through them, but Paul strips the Law of the glory of justification and shows that the end was political. For it was necessary that there be a certain people in whom the promises concerning Christ would be revealed by certain and clear testimonies of God; therefore God set this people apart from the nations and by many evident miracles testified that they possessed the word of God. Wherefore the worship and the entire polity were external things, ordered principally to this political end, that they might distinguish this people from the remaining nations. Meanwhile, however, the miracles of the issued Law and the rest were testimonies that God had given the word to this people, and the acts of worship themselves were ordained by God so that they might admonish men that the word of God was in this people, and indeed the promise concerning Christ, and for the righteous they were exercises of faith. Likewise they admonished others, etc. Hence this passage of Paul usefully teaches that the acts of worship did not merit the remission of sins, that they did not justify.

Latin:

Quid igitur habet Iudaeus in quo praecellat?

Digressio est in qua velut interpellatus occurrit quibusdam obiectionibus, magna enim & difficilis quaestio oritur ex illa exaequatione gentium & Iudaeorum. Nam si Iudaei non sunt iusti propter suos cultus, si non liberantur à peccato propter opera Legis, quare data est Lex? quare Deus éam requirit? quare vocat cultus & propitiationes? quare Iudaei dicuntur populus Dei, si Lex non facit discrimen inter Iudaeos & gentes? quam habent Iudaei praerogativam? Paulus respondet bifariam. Primum affirmative deinde negative. Primum ait Iudaeos praestare gentibus & hanc habere praerogativam quod habeant promissiones. Praestant igitur non propter Legem, non quod Lege mereantur iustificationem sed quia habent promissiones. Haec erat ingens praerogativa nosse verbum Dei & promissionem de Christo, & quidem habere hoc Ius quod promissio nominatim ad hunc populum pertineret. Itaque multi audientes verbum illud, salvabantur, & quidem certum erat semper aliquos ex Iudaeis salvari, quia sic erat aedita promissio ut nominatim ad posteros Abrahae pertineret. Ideo hic locus iam docet de principali fine totius politiae Iudaicae, indocti imaginantur Leges illas raditas esse ut per eas iustificaretur populus, sed Paulus detrahit Legi gloriam iustificationis & ostendit finem fuisse politicum. Oportuit enim certum populum esse in quo revelarentur promissiones de Christo certis & claris testimoniis Dei, ideo Deus hunc populum discrevit à gentibus & multis evidentibus miraculis testatus est eos habere verbum Dei. Quare cultus & tota politia fuerunt res externae praecipue ad hunc politicum finem ordinatae, ut hunc populum discernerent à reliquis gentibus. Interim tamen miracula aeditae Legis & reliqua erant testimonia quod Deus dedisset huic populo verbum & cultus ip si erant â Deo ordinati ut admonerent homines in hoc populo esse verbum Dei, et quidem promissionem de Christo, & iustis erant exercitia fidei. Item admonebant alios &c. Proinde hic locus Pauli utiliter docet quod cultus non merebantur remissionem peccatorum, quod non iustificabantur.

## 3:9
What then? Do we excel them?

Here he returns to the main subject, namely to the equalizing of the Jews and the Gentiles, so that he may teach that all men are under sin, that is, are guilty of sin and of the wrath of God. You will observe, however, the dissimilar responses to the questions added in the digression. First, he responds affirmatively that the Jews have a great prerogative as far as the promise is concerned, not as far as merits are concerned. Therefore, a negative response is added here. The Jews provide nothing, namely, as far as merit is concerned. The meaning is therefore: We do not excel at all, that is, we are not righteous on account of our own dignity, on account of the works of the Law, on account of our virtues, etc.

For before, having rendered the causes, we showed, both Jews etc.

It is a repetition of the proposition: and it must be diligently observed that he now brings it forth universally and says: that all are under sin, that is, that all men are guilty of sin, of the wrath of God, and of eternal death. He speaks, however, of all men except Christ, and he includes even the saints, insofar as their nature is considered, and they are not understood as reconciled through mercy. Always, however, let this equalization admonish us, because it terrifies proud hypocrites and the secure. Again, it raises up the prostrate because it testifies that God truly wishes to forgive us freely on account of Christ. Moreover, it confirms the proposition with cited testimonies in which not only civil offenses are blamed, but interior sins against the first table. There is none who understands or seeks God, that is, all despise God, they are without fear of GOD and without faith, therefore they have impious opinions and doctrines, and impious counsels, and through pride and self-confidence they dare many things against the will of God and persecute those teaching and admonishing pious things. Thus he describes especially the secret vices of hypocrites, which the world admires as excellent wisdom and justice.

Latin:

Quid igitur? Praecellimus eos?
