Hic redit ad institutum principale, videlicet ad exaequationem Iudaeorum, & gentium ut doceat omnes homines sub peccato, id est, reos esse peccati & irae Dei. Observabis autem dissimiles responsiones ad quaestiones in digressione additas. Primum affirmative respondet Iudaeos habere magnam praerogativam quod ad promissionem attinet, non quod ad merita attinet. Ideo hic additur negativa responsio. Iudaei nihil praestant, scilicet, quod ad meritum attinet. Est ergo sententia: Nequaquam excellimus, id est, non sumus iusti propter nostram dignitatem, propter opera Legis, propter nostras virtutes &c.

Nam ante caussis redditis osten-dimus, & Iudaeos &c.

Repetitio est propositionis: ac diligenter observandum est, quod iam effert eam universaliter & ait: omnes sub peccato esse, id est, omnes homines esse reos peccati, irae Dei & mortis aeternae. Loquitur autem de omnibus hominibus excepto Christo, ac sanctos etiam complectitur, quatenus ipsorum natura consideratur, nec intelliguntur per misericordiam reconciliati. Semper autem haec exaequatio nos admoneat, quod superbos Hypocritas & securos perterrefacit. Rursus prostratos erigit quia testatur quod Deus vere gratis propter Christum nobis ignoscere velit. Confirmat autem propositionem citatis testimoniis in quibus non tantum civilia delicta culpantur, sed interiora peccata contra primam tabulam. Non est intelligens nec requirens Deum, id est, omnes contemnunt Deum, sunt sine timore DEI & sine fide, propterea habent impias opiniones & doctrinas, & impia consilia, & per superbiam & fiduciam sui multa audent contra voluntatem Dei & persequuntur pia docentes, & monentes. Ita describit praecipue Hypocritarum arcana vitia, quae mundus suspicit tanquam excellentem sapientiam, & iustitiam.

## 3:20
By the works of the Law shall no flesh be justified &c.

In the conclusion he repeats the universal again, so that every mouth may be stopped and the whole world may be guilty before God, but there are some who pretend that men merit the remission of sins and are righteous on account of good moral works, they evade this universal and say it is a synecdoche, as if PAUL were not accusing absolutely everyone, but very many, and from this universal a very few good ones are to be excepted, so that although at Rome very many are guilty, yet they imagine that a few certain ones are to be excepted from that number, Scipio, Atticus. Even if among the Jews very many sin, yet they wish a few certain ones to be excepted, such as John, Peter, etc. Against cavils of this kind, minds must be fortified, so that we may retain the simple and true meaning of Paul, and Paul himself prudently took care, lest this exception could be attached. For first, he often inculcates the universal. Then he adds a reason which shows what he accuses: For he says, because by the works of the Law shall no flesh be justified. Here he expressly accuses not only persons, but he detracts justification from those very good works, which they wish to be excepted. Then the Psalm says: Enter not into judgment with thy servant, for in thy sight shall no living man be justified. This sentence and most similar ones testify that that exception is false, because they clearly teach that our good works cannot be opposed to the judgment of GOD. Furthermore, if moral the works would justify, or would have justified, the Jews, even the ceremonies. For among them these also had the command of God. Wherefore the sentence of the Psalm and of Paul should be understood universally concerning all men and concerning all works, nor should a synecdoche be admitted which feigns that some are righteous and merit the remission of sins on account of their own dignity and their own works, etc. Moreover, he expressly adds that they are guilty before God, because he is speaking not of human judgment but of divine judgment. In that struggle, the conscience cannot be pacified by any works, but let it know that it is the command of God that it should believe that we are certainly forgiven on account of Christ through mercy, etc. And indeed the weights of the words are to be observed which exhort all to repentance. For he threatens most gravely those who are secure and confident in their own righteousness when he says: That every mouth may be stopped. Item, that the whole world may become guilty.

Latin:

Ex operibus Legis non iustifi-cabitur omnis caro &c.

In conclusione iterum repetit universalem, ut omne os obscuretur & totus mundus sit reus coram Deo, sed quidam qui fingunt homines mereri remissionem peccatorum & esse iust os propter bona opera moralia, eludunt hanc universalem & dicunt esse synecdochen, quasi PAULUS non prorsus omnes arguat, sed plurimos, & ab hac universali sint excipiendi paucissimi quidam boni, ut quamvis Romae plurimi sint rei, tamen fingunt ex illo numero excipiendos esse paucos quosdam, Scipionem, Atticum. Etsi inter Iudaeos plurimi peccant, tamen paucos quosdam excipi volunt, ut Iohannem, Petrum, &c. Adversus huiusmodi cavillationes muniendi sunt animi, ut simplicem & veram sententiam Pauli retineamus, ac prudenter cavit ipse Paulus, ne haec exceptio affingi posset. Primum enim saepe inculcat universalem. Deinde addit rationem quae ostendit quid accuset: Ait enim, eo quod ex operibus Legis non iustificabitur omnis caro. Hic disertè non tantum personas accusat, sed illis ipsis bonis operibus detrahit iustificationem, quae illi volunt excipi. Deinde Psalmus inquit: Non intres in Iudicium cum servo tuo, quia non iustificabitur in conspectu tuo omnis vivens. Haec sententia & plaeraeque similes testantur exceptionem illam falsam esse, quia clare docent nostra bona opera non posse opponi iudicio DEI. Praeterea si moralia opera iustificarent iustificassent Iudaeos etiam caeremoniae. Nam apud illos hae quoque habebant mandarum Dei. Quare sententia Psalmi & Pauli universaliter intelligatur de omnibus hominibus & de omnibus operibus, nec admittatur synecdoche quae fingit aliquos esse iustos & mereri remissionem peccatorum propter propriam dignitatem & propria opera &c. Diserte autem addit coram DEO reos esse, quia loquitur non de humano iudicio sed de divino iudicio. In illo agone non potest conscientia pacificari ullis operibus, sedsciat mandatum Dei esse ut credat nobis ignosci certo propter Christum per misericordiam &c. Et quidem pondera verborum observanda sunt quae hortantur omnes ad paenitentiam. Minatur enim gravissime securis & confidentibus propria iustitia cum ait: Ut omne os obturetur Item ut reus fiat totus mundus.

## 3:20
For by the Law is the knowledge of sin, etc.

This is an objection. For it could be objected, if we are not righteous by the Law, for what use was it given the Law? Paul answers: But more briefly, because this occupation will be repeated below, and this response seems entirely new and absurd to the world, that by the Law sin is only shown, not taken away. For Lawgivers in empires enact Laws not only to show sins, but to take them away. But here the listener must be warned that Paul is not at all preaching in this place about civil justice and external morals; another matter is being handled. How we are reputed just before God, how we obtain the remission of sins. What the Law contributes there. Therefore the uses of the Law must be distinguished, and we are speaking here not only about the Law of Moses, but about the moral Law, implanted in all men. There is, however, a double use; the one is political, namely to restrain carnal men outwardly. For God requires this external justice also, even if we are not just before God on account of it: even if it does not merit the remission of sins: he is not speaking of this use in this sentence. Elsewhere he speaks of this use, the Law is laid down for the unjust, etc. The other use is not political, but pertains to the Judgment of God and to the conscience, namely to accuse and terrify the conscience, just as he says elsewhere in Aruleus: the sin of death is, the power The Law is of sin, that is, the Law shows sin and terrifies hearts; it is of such recognition that he speaks here. For he does not understand an idle speculation, but such a recognition, in which we acknowledge the wrath of God against sin and truly tremble. And these terrors truly become eternal death in those who are not raised up by the Gospel. The meaning, therefore, is that by the Law we are not righteous before God, we do not merit the remission of sins. And when consciences are terrified, they cannot be pacified by the Law, which accuses us more and more and drives us to despair. Thus, as he says elsewhere, that sin might become exceedingly sinful and harmful, that is, killing by those terrors. From this it clearly follows that another word is needed for consolation and justification.

Latin:

Per Legem enim agnitio pec-cati &c.

Occupatio est. Poterat enim obiici, si non sumus iusti Lege, ad quem usum data est Lex? Paulus respondet: Sed brevius, quia haec occupatio infra repetetur, & haec responsio prorsus nova & absurda videtur mundo, Lege tantum ostendi peccatum, non tolli. Nam Legumlatores in imperiis ferunt Leges non tantum ut ostendant peccata, sed ut tollant. Verum hic monendus est auditor Paulum prorsus non concionari hoc loco de iustitia civili & de externis moribus, alia res agitur. Quomodo coram Deo iusti reputemur, quomodo consequamur remissionem peccatorum. Quid ibi conferat Lex. Ideo discernendi sunt usus Legis, & loquimur hic non tantum de Lege Moisi, sed de Lege morali, indita omnibus hominibus. Est autem duplex usus, alter est politicus scilicet foris cohercere homines carnales. Requirit enim Deus hanc quoque externam iustitiam, etiamsi propter eam non sumus iusti coram Deo: Etiamsi non meretur remissionem peccatorum: de hoc usu non loquitur in hac sententia. Alibi de hoc usu loquitur, Lex est iniustis posita, &c. Alter usus non est politicus, sed pertinet ad Iudicium Dei & ad conscientiam, scilicet accusare & perterrefacere conscientiam, sicut alibi inquit Aruleus: mortis peccatum est, potentia peccati Lex est, id est, Lex ostendit peccatum & perterrefacit corda, de tali agnitione hic loquitur. Non enim intelligit ociosam speculationem, sed agnitionem talem, in qua iram Dei adversus peccatum agnoscimus & verè expavescimus. Et hi temrores vere fiunt mors aeterna in his qui non eriguntur per Evangelium. Est igitur sententia, lege non sumus iusti coram Deo, non meremur remissionem peccatorum. Et cum conscientiae perterrefiunt, non possunt Lege pacificari, quae nos magis magisque accusat & ad desperationem adigit. Sic ut alibi inquit, ut peccatum fiat excellenter peccans & nocens, id est, illis terroribus occidens. Hinc clarè sequitur quòd alio verbo opus sit ad consolationem & iustificationem.

## 3:21
But now apart from the Law the righteousness of God has been manifested.

Above he made an approach to the principal proposition. For he said that all men are guilty of sin and the wrath of God, and cannot be freed from sin by the Law. Now, therefore, follows the principal proposition, which is the state of this controversy, which must be diligently observed, and because of the magnitude of the cause.

For this proposition contains the proper and principal meaning of the Gospel concerning the benefit of Christ, and because arguments will then have to be referred to this state as if to a head. Furthermore, in propositions, perspicuity is most required. Therefore, Paul delivers the proposition accurately, properly, and perspicuously. But the phrase must be considered, and the very weights of the words must be observed, the righteousness of God, namely by which He justifies us, that is, acceptance, or the remission of sins and the imputation of righteousness. And the meaning is, Now it is manifested how God justifies, how He wills to pronounce [men] righteous and to remit sins and to accept us: but he says, without the Law. This seems absurd to the world. Wherefore this particle must be diligently considered. For it shows what the Gospel properly is and what the distinction is between the Law and the Gospel. For the world has political imaginations about Christ, it thinks He is a legislator bringing a new Law somewhat more convenient than the Mosaic one, because He abolishes ceremonies, which were not convenient for all nations, and He commands many things about love. Then they collect what Laws Christ added to the Mosaic ones, and they fashion these laws into the idea that men merit the remission of sins by their observation, and are righteous, and they interpret it without the Law, that is, without ceremonies. This error must be removed from minds: For Christ did not come to bring a Law, nor is He Moses, nor Solon, but He has another much greater office, He is a victim for sin, and freely grants to us the remission of sins, and the imputation of righteousness, and the Holy Spirit and eternal life. Therefore Paul speaks when he says without the Law concerning the whole law, and he means that Christ brings the remission of sins, and the imputation of righteousness not because of any Law, nor because of ceremonies, nor because of moral works, but freely, and let us know that this statement does not pertain to civil life, or external morals, but to the conscience acting before God, and seeking how it may obtain the remission of sins and reconciliation. Hence the distinction between Law and Gospel becomes much more illustrious, or because it testifies that a gratuitous benefit is announced in the Gospel not hanging from the condition of the Law or our merit, and this passage is not only to be opposed to the Anabaptists and the like, who imagine the Gospel to be a new worldly polity, but it is also to be held in in the struggle of conscience, so that there we may truly understand the benefit of Christ to be gratuitous. And the sentence is, the justice has been manifested without the Law, that is, we obtain the remission of sins and are reputed just not on account of that law, but on account of Christ gratuitously through mercy. For although in those who have been justified by faith, a new obedience is begun, nevertheless that new obedience, or Law, is not the cause on account of which we obtain the remission of sins, and are reputed just or accepted, but these things are given gratuitously on account of Christ.

They are destitute of the glory of God.

They lack that glory which God approves, they lack that justice which God judges to be glory. Or if anyone prefers to interpret it actively, it will be the same sentence, they lack the glory of God, that is, the wisdom and justice glorifying God, that is, which truly attributes glory to God, acknowledges, loves, performs perfect obedience, they lack the glory of God, that is, the light by which God is acknowledged and glorified, and it is a repetition of the universal sentence, which teaches that all men are guilty of sin and the wrath of God, that they lack glory, that is, that they are rejected before God, and not on account of the Law to be just. This also must be observed, which diminishes the justice of the Law and those most holy cults, which the Jews certainly thought to be the glory of God, and teaches that this external justice is not the glory of God, because it is not the acknowledgment and glorification of God.

Latin:

Nunc vero absquè Lege iusti-cia Dei manifestata est.

Supra fecit aditum ad principalem propositionem. Dixit enim omnes homines esse reos peccati & irae Dei, nec posse à peccato liberari per Legem. Nunc igitur sequitur principalis propositio, quae est status huius controversiae, qui diligenter observandus est, & propter magnitudinem causae.

Continet enim haec propositio propriam & praecipuam Evangelii sententiam de beneficio Christi, & quia ad hunc statum velut ad caput deinde referenda erunt argumenta. Porro in propositionibus maximè requiritur perspicuitas. Ideo Paulus accuratè, propriè & perspicuè tradit propositionem. Sed phrasis consyderanda est, & ipsa verborum pondera observanda sunt, iusticia Dei, scilicet qua iustificat nos, hoc est, acceptatio, vel remifsio peccatorum & imputatio iusticiae. Estque sententia, Nunc manifestatum est quomodo Deus iustificet, quomodo velit pronunciare iustos & remittere peccata & nos acceptare: inquit autem, sine Lege. Hoc videtur absurdum mundo. Quare haec particula diligenter consyderanda est. Ostendit enim quid propriè sit Evangelium & quod discrimen sit Legis & Evangelii. Mundus enim habet imaginationes politicas de Christo, cogitat esse legislatorem afferentem novam Legem aliquanto commodiorem quàm Mosaicam, quia abolet caeremonias, quae non erant commodae omnibus gentibus, & praecipit multa de dilectione. Deinde colligunt quas Leges addiderit Christus Mosaicis, & fingunt harum Legum observatione homines mereri remissionem peccatorum, & esse iustos, & interpretantur sine Lege, id est, sine caeremoniis. Hic error eximendus est animis: Nam Christus non venit ut Legem ferret, nec Moises est, nec Solon, sed habet aliud multo maius officium, est victima pro peccato, & gratis donat nobis remissionem peccatorum, & imputationem iusticiae, & spiritum sanctum ac vitam aeternam. Loquitur igitur Paulus cum ait sine Lege de tota lege, ac sentit Christum afferre remissionem peccatorum, & imputationem iusticiae non propter ullam Legem, nec propter caeremonias, nec propter moralia opera, sed gratis, & sciamus hoc dictum non ad civilem vitam, aut externos mores pertinere, sed ad conscientiam agentem coram Deo, & quaerentem quomodo consequatur remissionem peccatorum & reconciliationem. Hinc discrimen Legis & Evangelii multo fit illustrius, vel quia testatur in Evangelio annunciari gratuitum beneficium non pendens ex conditione Legis seu meriti nostri, et hic locus non solum opponendus est Anabaptistis et similibus, qui fingunt Evangelium novam politiam mundanam, sed etiam tenendus est in agone conscientiae, ut ibi verè intelligamus beneficium Christi esse gratuitum. Estque sententia, iusticia manifestata est sine Lege, id est, consequimur remissionem peccatorum & reputamur iusti non propter illam legem, sed propter Christum gratis per misericordiam. Etsi enim in his qui fide iustificati sunt, inchoatur nova obedientia, Tamen illa nova obedientia, seu Lex non est causa propter quam consequimur remissionem peccatorum, & reputamur iusti seu accepti, verum haec gratis donantur propter Christum.

Destituuntur gloria Dei.

Carent illa gloria quam Deus approbat, carent illa iusticia, quam Deus iudicat esse gloriam. Aut si quis mavult activè interpraetari, erit eadem sententia, carent gloria Dei, id est, sapientia & iusticia glorificante Deum, id est, quae verè tribuit gloriam Deo, agnoscit, diligit, praestat perfectam obedientiam, carent gloria Dei, id est, Iuce qua agnoscitur & glorificatur Deus, estque repetitio sententiae universalis, quae docet omnes homines reos esse peccati & irae Dei, carere gloria, id est, reiectos esse coram Deo, nec propter Legem iustos esse. Est & hoc observandum quod extenuat iusticiam Legis & illos sanctissimos cultus, quos certè Iudaei putabant esse gloriam Dei, & docet hanc externam iusticiam non esse gloriam Dei, quia non est agnitio & glorificatio Dei.

## 3:24
But we are justified freely.

That is, we obtain the remission of sins and are reckoned just, that is, accepted, and with this reckoning is joined the gift of the Holy Spirit and acceptance to eternal life. These things, therefore, we must embrace when we dispute about justification, namely the remission of sins and the imputation of justice, that is, acceptance, with which is joined the gift of the Holy Spirit and acceptance to eternal life. Moreover, the description of Paul is clear when he says freely by grace, that is, by mercy. Here he clearly shows that he is preaching about another justice than the justice of the Law or of our works. For he excludes the condition of the Law or of merit, and testifies that we are justified freely, not on account of any dignity of ours, or our works.

Latin:

Iustificamur autem gratis.

Id est, consequimur remissionem peccatorum & reputamur iusti, id est, accepti, & cum hac reputatione coniuncta est donatio spiritus sancti & acceptatio ad vitam aeternam. Haec igitur complecti debemus, cum de iustificatione disputamus, scilicet remissionem peccatorum & imputationem iusticiae, id est, acceptationem, cum qua est coniuncta donatio spiritus sancti & acceptatio ad vitam aeternam. Est autem perspicua Pauli descriptio, cum ait gratis per gratiam, id est, per misericordiam. Hic clarè ostendit se de alia iusticia concionari, quàm de iusticia Legis seu nostrorum operum. Excludit enim conditionem Legis seu meriti, & testatur nos iustificari, gratis non propter ullam dignitatem nostram, aut opera nostra.

## 3:24
Through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.

Because God, angered by sin, demanded some victim, therefore Paul says through the redemption that is through Christ Jesus. And here let our minds resist, and let them think first of the anger of God against sin. Then of the greatness of mercy, because both are proposed here. The world does not see the greatness of the anger of God against sin, and says that sin is a light thing. But here let us learn that the anger is so great that God could not be appeased by any sacrifice, except only by the death of the son. Therefore, security in those who persevere in sins and despise the anger of God is a horrible sin: Secondly, the mercy is so great that the father gave the son for us, and willed us to be certain of mercy by such a pledge being given. Now how great a blasphemy it is to transfer the glory of the son of God to human works and to invent other victims, such as satisfactions, masses, monasticism? etc.

Reconciler.

He dwells upon the description of the office of Christ, that he is a victim, a propitiator, etc. And indeed the title of propitiator is one signifying that the benefit which is promised on account of that propitiator is certain, because this Christ was not made a propitiator in vain: but why does he add through faith? This particle must be diligently observed, because he is now speaking about application, so that we may know how we obtain the benefit of Christ.

Latin:

Per redemptionem, quae est in Christo Iesu.

Quia Deus iratus peccato requirebata, aliquam victimam, ideo Paulus inquit per redemptionem quae est per Christum Iesum. Atque hic resistant animi nostri, & cogitent primum de ira Dei adversus peccatum. De inde de magnitudine misericordiae, quia utrunquè hic proponitur. Mundus non videt magnitudinem irae Dei adversus peccatum, & dicit peccatum rem levem esse. Sed hic discamus tantam esse iram, ut nulla hostia placari potuerit Deus, nisi tantum morte filii. Est igitur horribile peccatum securitas in iis, qui perseverant in peccatis & contemnunt iram Dei: Secundo tanta est misericordia, ut pater dederit filium pro nobis, & voluerit nos tali pignore dato de misericordia certos esse. Iam quanta est blasphemia gloriam filii Dei transferre in humana opera & fingere alias victimas, ut satisfactiones, missas, monachatus? &c.

Reconciliatorem.

Commoratur in descriptione officii Christi, quod sit victima, propitiator, &c. Et quidem propitiator titulus est significans certum esse beneficium, quod propter illum propitiatorem promissum est, quia hic Christus non est frustra factus propitiator: sed quare addit per fidem? Haec particula diligenter observanda est, quia iam de applicatione loquitur, ut sciamus quomodo consequamur beneficium Christi.

## 3:25
Through faith.

The adversaries also confess that Christ is a mediator and propitiator. But they afterwards change and corrupt this very thing. For they say nothing about application, nor do they teach that Christ the mediator is to be used. And first, they say absolutely nothing about this faith, that is, about confidence in the mediator; they do not teach one to use Christ the mediator, nay, they command the conscience to doubt. This doubting manifestly fights against the faith which Paul requires here. Secondly, they imagine that Christ is a propitiator only as far as it pertains to the occasion of meriting, as when a master of a house who is angry at a servant is appeased by some friend. There that friend obtains access for the servant to the master, then he has no business there. But the servant is pleasing on account of his own duties: They attribute so much to Christ that he has earned for us this beginning and occasion of meriting. They speak thus. That Christ merited the first grace. Afterwards they bury him and pretend that he is idle, and they imagine that men merit the remission of sins and are righteous on account of their own fulfillment of the Law, etc. We, on the contrary, let us rightly understand that Christ always remains the mediator and must be applied by faith, that is, it must be established that we are pleasing, not on account of our own dignity or fulfillment of the Law, but on account of Christ. We ought not to oppose our virtues to the Judgment of God, but Christ the victim and propitiator; thus Paul speaks explicitly below concerning application, when he says: through whom we have access by faith into this grace, as if he were to say we approach God in such a way, if we use Christ as mediator, if by faith we flee to this propitiator, and think that we are forgiven on account of him.

Latin:

Per fidem.

Adversarii etiam fatentur Christum esse mediatorem & propitiatorem. Sed hoc ipsum postea mutant & corrumpunt. Nihil enim dicunt de applicatione, nec docent utendum esse mediatore Christo. Ac primum nihil prorsus de hac fide, id est, de fiducia mediatoris dicunt, non docent uti mediatore Christo, imo iubent dubitare conscientiam. Haec dubitatio manifeste pugnat cum fide, quam hic requirit Paulus. Secundo fingunt Christum esse propitiatorem tantum, quòd ad occasionem merendi attinet, ut cum paterfamilias iratus servo placatur ab amico aliquo. Ibi amicus ille aditum servo impetrat ad dominum, deinde nihil ibi negocii habet. Sed placet servus. propter propria officia: Tantum tribuunt Christo quod hoc principium & occasionem merendi nobis promeruerit. Ipsi sic loquuntur. Christum meruisse primam gratiam. Postea sepeliunt eum & fingunt ociosum esse, & imaginantur homines mereri remissionem peccatorum & iustos esse propter propriam impletionem Legis, &c. Nos econtra rectè intelligamus, Christum semper manere mediatorem & applicandum esse fide, id est, statuendum quòd placeamus, non propter nostram dignitatem, aut impletionem Legis, sed propter Christum. Non debemus opponere Iudicio Dei nostras virtutes, sed victimam & propitiatorem Christum, ita disertè infra Paulus de applicatione loquitur, cum ait: per quem habemus accessum fide in gratiam hanc, quasi dicat ita accedimus ad Deum, si utamur mediatore Christo, si fide confugiamus ad hunc propitiatorem, & putemus nobis propter ipsum ignosci.

## 3:25
For the showing of his righteousness.

The sentence will be clearer if the form of the speech is changed, for the demonstration of his justice, that is, so that God may declare that he himself is about to justify, and it is an antithesis. Above he argues against all and says that we are not just, even when we have the works of the Law. But now in Christ God reveals his justice, that is, that he himself is about to justify, just as he promised in the promises, that he is about to bestow a new justice, a new and eternal life, that he is about to restore the human race with sin abolished and death abolished. This new justice and life he now reveals in the Gospel, etc.

Latin:

Ad ostensionem iusticiae suae.

Sententia erit planior mutata forma orationis, ad ostensionem iusticiae suae, id est, ut declaret Deus, quod ipse, iustificaturus sit estque antithesis. Supra arguit omnes & dicit, nos non esse iustos, etiam cum habemus Legis opera. Sed nunc in Christo revelat Deus iusticiam suam, id est, quòd ipse sit iustificaturus, quemadmodum in promissionibus pollicitus est, quòd novam iusticiam, novam & aeternam vitam donaturus sit, quòd sit instauraturus genus humanum abolito peccato & abolita morte. Hanc novam iusticiam & vitam iam revelat in Evangelio, &c.

## 3:25
For the remission.

It is a definition of the preceding particle, for it interprets what he said by his justice. If you change it into words it will be clearer, so that he may declare that he is about to justify, namely through the remission of sins. Thus he sets forth the definition and, so to speak, the formal cause of justification. For properly justification is the remission of sins on account of Christ, with which is joined the gift of the Holy Spirit, etc. And let the remission of sins be understood not only concerning actual sins, but also concerning natural uncleanness. Justification is therefore to be accounted righteous not because of our virtues, but because God forgives sins and accepts the unclean and unworthy through mercy on account of Christ. Just as he elsewhere defines justification as the remission of sins: Blessed are they whose sins are forgiven.

Of past sins.

They say this clause was added so that we might know that in the Gospel a license to sin is not granted, but that we might know that sins are forgiven in those who perform penance in whom sin is mortified, and yet it does not follow from that that if those who have fallen after remission perform penance again, pardon cannot happen again, because always as often as remission happens, it is a remission of a preceding sin. It is therefore a description of present remission in general, it is not exclusive of subsequent remissions, but in my judgment the simplest opinion is if this clause is understood to be opposed to the Law, as if he were saying: Sin has reigned until now, not even the Law abolished sin and death, but by this faith in Christ sin is now abolished, which until now existed or reigned, because Paul speaks not only of actual sins, but also of original sin, as if he were saying, the sin which has existed until now is remitted, just as he says below: Until the Law sin was in the world, that is, not even the Law abolished sin. But now the sin of origin is abolished in two ways, namely imputatively, because the guilt is removed, and it begins to be abolished and mortified in reality, namely when true terrors, true consolation, and the beginning of a new creature exist in the heart in repentance.

Where then is boasting?

He adds an epiphonema to the proposition. For he brings forward the contrary, namely what is to be thought concerning merit. For boasting in this place properly signifies the confidence of merit or merit itself. Moreover, this passage is an excellent confirmation of our interpretation. For it clearly shows that Paul intends this very thing which we interpret and teach, that the opinion of the monks concerning merit is false, who imagine that the remission of sins happens on account of merits, not freely, and they abolish the doctrine of faith, as when they teach: if contrition is sufficient it will merit remission, and because we can never determine what is sufficient, they command one to doubt, thus then they imagine that a man is pleasing on account of the fulfillment of the law, etc. This is the sum of the imagination of the monks, which Paul openly condemns here when he says: Boasting is excluded by the Law of faith, that is, the doctrine concerning faith teaches that remission is given freely, not on account of our merits, and is likewise given to believers, whether Jews or Gentiles, that is, to those who do not have the works of the Law. This equalization, as has already been said often, terrifies the secure and consoles the fearful. That also must be observed, when Paul entirely excludes boasting, he certainly also removes from moral works the condition of merit in reconciliation. Because if remission were given on account of moral works, then there would be boasting, there would be some merit of the remission of sins; likewise, when he opposes faith to our dignity and takes away boasting, it sufficiently appears that he understands faith as trust in gratuitous mercy. The Law of works signifies the doctrine which requires works and teaches men to be righteous on account of works. Conversely, the Law of faith signifies the doctrine which preaches concerning faith, that is, it teaches men to be righteous not on account of their own dignity, or the fulfillment of the law, or works, but the trust of the mercy promised on account of Christ. For faith does not signify the Law of nature or the Decalogue, as some falsely interpret, but it signifies the trust of the mercy promised on account of Christ which Paul opposes to our dignity. For this is what he disputes, whether reconciliation happens on account of our works, or indeed on account of Christ through mercy freely. Wherefore faith does not signify any Law, but it behaves itself correlatively to the promise and is trust apprehending the promised mercy.

Latin:

Propter remissionem.

Definitio est praecedentis particulae, interpraetatur enim quid dixerit iusticiam suam. Si mutes in verba erit clarius, ut declaret, quod sit iustificaturus scilicet per remissionem peccatorum. Ita ponit definitionem & ut ita dicam formale iustificationis. Proprie enim iustificatio est remissio peccatorum propter Christum, cum qua coniuncta est donatio spiritus sancti, &c. Et remissio peccatorum intelligatur non tantantum de actualibus delictis, sed etiam de naturali immunditie. Est itaque iustificatio iustos reputari non propter nostras virtutes, sed Deo remittente peccata & immundos & indignos acceptante per misericordiam propter Christum. Sicut aliâs definit iustificationem esse remissionem peccatorum: Beati quorum remissa sunt peccata.

Praeteritorum peccatorum.

Hanc particulam dicunt adiectam esse, ut sciamus in Evangelio non concedi licentiam peccandi, sed sciamus peccata remitti in his qui agunt paenitentiam in quibus peccatum mortificatur, nec tamen inde sequitur quòd lapsis post remissionem si rursus agant paenitentiam non possit iterum venia contingere, quia semper quotienscunque contingit remissio fit remissio praecedentis peccati. Est ergo descriptio remissionis praesentis in genere, non est exclusiva sequentium remissionum, sed meo iudicio simpli cissima sententia est, siintelligatur opponi haec particula Legi, quasi dicat. Peccatum regnavit hactenus, ne Lex quidem abolevit peccatum & mortem, sed hac fide in Christum iam aboletur peccatum, quod hactenus extitit seu regnavit, quia Paulus loquitur non solum de actualibus delictis, sed etiam de originali, quasi dicat, remitti peccatum quod hactenus extitit, sicut infra ait: Usque ad Legem peccatum fuit in mundo, id est, ne Lex quidem abolevit peccatum. Iam autem peccatum originis aboletur bifariam imputativè scilicet, quia reatus tollitur, & incipit reipsa aboleri, & mortificari, scilicet quando in paenitentia existunt veri terrores, vera consolatio ac initium novae creaturae in corde.

Ubi igitur gloriatio?

Addit propositioni Epiphonema. Confert enim contrarium, scilicet quid sit sentiendum de merito. Nam gloriatio proprie significat hoc loco fiduciam meriti seu meritum. Est autem hic locus egregia confirmatio nostrae interpretationis. Clare enim ostendit Paulum hoc ipsum velle quod nos interpretamur, & docemus monachorum opinionem de merito falsam esse, qui fingunt contingere remissionem peccatorum propter merita, non gratis, & abolent fidei doctrinam, ut cum docent: si contritio fuerit sufficiens merebitur remissionem, & quia nunquam possumus statuere, quod sit sufficiens, iubent dubitare, sic deinde fingunt hominem placere propter impletionem legis &c. Haec est summa imaginationis monachorum, quam Paulus hic aperte damnat cum ait: Exclusa est gloriatio per Legem fidei, id est, doctrina de fide docet gratis donari remissionem non propter nostra merita, & pariter donari credentibus sive Iudaeis sive gentibus, hoc est, iis qui non habent opera Legis. Haec exaequatio, ut saepe iam dictum est, terret securos & consolatur pavidos. Illud etiam observandum est, cum Paulus prorsus excludit gloriationem, certe etiam detrahit moralibus operibus in reconciliatione conditionem meriti. Quia si propter moralia opera daretur remissio, iam esset gloriatio, esset aliquod meritum remissionis peccatorum, item cum fidem opponit nostrae dignitati & tollit gloriationem, satis apparet quod fidem intelligat, fiduciam gratuitae misericordiae. Lex operum significat doctrinam quae requirit opera & docet homines propter opera iustos esse. Econtra Lex fidei significat doctrinam quae concionatur de fide, id est, docet homines iustos esse non propter propriam dignitatem, aut impletionem legis, aut opera, sed fiducia misericordiae promissae propter Christum. Nam fides non significat Legem naturae aut Decalogum, ut quidam falso interpretantur, sed significat fiduciam misericordiae promissae propter Christum quam opponit Paulus dignitati nostrae. Hoc enim disputat an contingat reconciliatio propter nostra opera, an vero propter Christum per misericordiam gratis. Quare fides non significat Legem aliquam, sed habet se correlative ad promissionem estque fiducia apprehendens promissam misericordiam.

## 3:28
We conclude therefore that a man is justified by faith.

To the epiphonema he added a conclusion, in which he briefly repeats the sum of the proposition & again inculcates the exclusive, so that the sentence may be more certain, to be justified signifies to obtain the remission of sins & to be reckoned righteous, that is, accepted unto eternal life. Joined with this acceptance is the gift of the holy spirit. Faith signifies the trust of mercy promised on account of Christ. The sentence is therefore, we pronounce that a man obtains the remission of sins & is reckoned just before God, on account of Christ through mercy, not on account of the Law. And this mercy must be received by faith. Furthermore, the adversaries mutilate this opinion and interpret it as only excluding ceremonies, without the works of the Law, that is, without ceremonies. Then they imagine that a man obtains the remission of sins and is reckoned just on account of moral works, or as they say, on account of love, and they understand faith only as knowledge of history. Thus they transfer the benefit of Christ to their own dignity. But this interpretation fights against the opinion of Paul: For Paul strips the whole Law of this glory of merit, or of justification, as is evident from the things said above, so that the whole world may become guilty, etc. Item, Not every living person will be justified in your sight. These sentences exclude even moral works from the cause of justification. And this can be easily understood. In a true struggle, the conscience cannot establish that our sins are remitted to us, or that we are accepted, on account of our virtues and dignity. Therefore, another cause must be sought for why we are accepted, namely, Christ the mediator. From this it can be easily understood that Paul is preaching about the whole Law, not only about ceremonies, as his confirmation also shows below, that justification is taken away from the whole Law. And indeed he himself alleges the moral law: Thou shalt not covet, so that the dispute may not be ambiguous. Likewise in this place he says: We establish the law. Wherefore it is necessary that it be understood concerning moral things. Likewise when the term of faith is rightly understood, it sufficiently appears that justification or reconciliation is taken away from the whole Law, because to be justified by faith is to be reputed just, by trust in mercy, not on account of our own dignity. Thus this very formula, we are justified by faith, is opposed to the imagination of those who pretend that men are justified on account of their own dignity or the fulfillment of the moral Law. Therefore it excludes even moral things from the cause of justification because no one satisfies the moral Law. Furthermore, it does not exclude them from the effect. For it is necessary that new and begun obedience follow.

Do we therefore make the law void?

The objection is necessary. Because all men, as soon as they hear this new preaching, that men are reputed just through mercy and not on account of the Law, ask whether license to sin is granted. Whether the law is so abrogated that license to sin is granted. Paul answers: That the law is not abolished by faith, but much more established, that is, fulfilled. This passage teaches us to interpret all sayings concerning works and the Law. Such as is: if thou wilt enter into life keep the commandments and similar things. For here Paul testifies that the Gospel of faith must be added to the Law. Let these two rules therefore be held: without faith it is impossible for the Law to be fulfilled. Also, by faith the Law is fulfilled and is pleasing, by faith obedience is begun and is pleasing. The former rule, that it is impossible for the Law to be fulfilled without faith, should be understood in two ways. First, concerning spiritual obedience itself, when pious hearts feel the wrath of God, when they doubt, they flee from God, they despair, they do not love God, they do not call upon Him, but when the conscience, raised up by faith, has acknowledged the mercy proposed by faith, it now begins to love and to call upon Him, according to that saying of Paul: through faith we have access to God. Secondly, it should be understood concerning acceptance, that is, even this which a man does without faith, nevertheless does not please without faith. From this it can be clearly understood that the Law cannot be fulfilled without faith. Wherefore, when good works are praised, it is necessary that this be understood in such a way that we remember that the Gospel concerning Christ must be added and we know that faith is necessary for fulfilling the Law, and that the Law does not please without faith. The other rule should also be understood in two ways: the Law is fulfilled by faith first, because faith is a spiritual movement, by which we acknowledge the mercy of God proposed in Christ: therefore it produces the knowledge of God, love and other good motions, invocation, etc. Item, by faith the Holy Spirit is received, who excites good motions and new obedience in hearts. Secondly, the Law pleases on account of faith, that is, although we do not satisfy the Law, yet because we are in Christ, the new obedience now pleases, and that which is lacking is pardoned to believers on account of CHRIST. This understanding is necessary, so that consciences may hold firm consolation, and acknowledge the ineffable mercy of God approving the begun obedience, in which there is much infirmity and disobedience. Thus here Paul says we establish the Law, that is, we fulfill it by faith, and because pacified consciences acknowledge God by faith, and love and invoke Him, etc., and because that begun obedience would not please, unless we were reconciled by faith.

Latin:

Arbitramur igitur fide iustifi-cari hominem.

Epiphonemati adiecit conclusionem, in qua breviter repetit summam propositionis & iterum inculcat exclusivam, ut sententia sit certior, iustificari significat consequi remissionem peccatorum & reputari iustum, id est, acceptum ad vitam aeternam. Cum hac acceptatione coniuncta est donatio spiritus sancti. Fides significat fiduciam misericordiae propter Christum promissae. Est igitur sententia, pronunciamus hominem consequi remissionem peccatorum & reputari iustum coram Deo, propter Christum per misericordiam, non propter Legem. Et hanc misericordiam fide accipi oportet. Porro hanc sententiam mutilant adversarii & interpraetantur tantum excludi caeremonias, sine operibus Legis, id est, sine caeremoniis. Deinde fingunt hominem consequi remissionem peccatorum, & reputari iustum propter moralia opera, seu ut loquuntur propter dilectionem, & intelligunt fidem tantum de notitia historiae. Ita transferunt beneficium Christi in propriam dignitatem. Sed haec interpraetatio pugnat cum sententia Pauli: Nam Paulus detrahit toti Legi hanc gloriam meriti, seu iustificationis, sicut constat ex superioribus dictis, ut totus mundus fiat reus, &c. Item, Non iustificabitur in conspectu tuo omnis vivens. Hae sententiae excludunt à causa iustificationis etiam moralia. Et facilè hoc intelligi potest. In vero certamine conscientia non potest statuere quod propter nostras virtutes et dignitatem remittantur nobis peccata, aut simus accepti. Ergo quaerenda est alia causa quare simus accepti, scilicet mediator Christus. Hinc facilè intelligi potest Paulum de tota Lege concionari non tantum de caeremoniis, sicut etiam infra ostendit eius confirmatio, detrahi iustificationem toti legi. Et quidem ipse allegat legem moralem: Non concupisces, ne sit ambigua disputatio. Item hoc loco inquit: Stabilimus legem. Quare necesse est eam intelligi de moralibus. Item cum vocabulum fidei recte intelligitur satis apparet toti Legi detrahi iustificationem seu reconciliationem quia fide iustificari est iustum reputari, fiducia misericordiae non propter nostram dignitatem. Ita haec ipsa formula, fide iustificamur, opponitur imaginationi illorum qui fingunt homines iustificari propter propriam dignitatem seu impletionem Legis moralis. Excludit ergo etiam moralia à caussa iustificationis quia nemo satisfacit Legi morali. Caeterum non excludit ab effectu. Necesse est enim sequi novam & inchoatam obedientiam.

Legem igitur irritam facimus?

Occupatio necessaria est. Quia omnes statim cum audiunt hanc novam concionem, homines reputari iustos per misericordiam non propter Legem, interrogant an concedatur licentia peccandi. An ita sit abrogata lex ut sit concessa licentia peccandi. Paulus respondet: Non aboleri legem per fidem, sed multo magis stabiliri, id est, impleri. Hic locus docet nos interpretari omnia dicta de operibus & Lege. Quale est: si vis in vitam ingredi serua mandata & similia. Hic enim Paulus testatur Legi addendum esse Evangelium de fide. Teneantur ergo hae duae regulae, sine fide impossibile est Legem fieri. Item fide fit & placet Lex, fide inchoatur obedientia & placet: Prior regula, impossibile est sine fide fieri Legem, intelligatur dupliciter. Primum de ipsa obedientia spirituali, pia corda cum sentiunt iram Dei, cum dubitant fugiunt Deum, desperant, non diligunt Deum, non invocant, sed conscientia fide erecta cum agnovit misericordiam fide propositam, iam incipit diligere & invocare, iuxta illud Pauli: per fidem habemus accessum ad Deum. Secundo intelligatur de acceptatione, id est, etiam hoc quod facit homo sine fide tamen non placet sine fide. Hinc clarèintelligi potest Legem non posse fieri sine fide. Quare cum laudantur bona opera, necesse est id intelligi ita, ut meminerimus addendum esse Evangelium de Christo & sciamus fidem necessariam esse ad faciendam Legem, nec placere Legem sine fide. Altera regula intelligatur etiam dupliciter, Lex fit fide primum, quia fides est motus spiritualis, quo agnoscimus misericordiam Dei in Christo propositam: Ideo parit agnitionem Dei, dilectionem & alios bonos motus, invocationem, &c. Item fide accipitur spiritus sanctus, qui excitat bonos motus & novam obedientiam in cordibus. Secundo Lex placet propter fidem, id est, quanquàm Legi non satisfacimus, tamen quia sumus in Christo placet iam nova obedientia, & id quod deest condonatur credentibus propter CHRISTUM. Hic intellectus necessarius est, ut conscientiae teneant firmam consolationem, & agnoscant ineffabilem misericordiam Dei approbantis inchoatam obedientiam, in qua plurimum est infirmitatis & inobedientiae. Ita hic Paulus inquit Legem stabilimus, id est, fide implemus, & quia conscientiae pacatae fide agnoscunt Deum, & diligunt & invocant, &c. & quia inchoata illa obedientia non placeret, nisi fide essemus reconciliati.

## 4:1 Argument
CHAPTER IV.

Latin:

CAPUT IIII.

## 4:1
What then shall we say that Abraham our father has found?

There follows a confirmation, in which the arguments must be diligently distributed and referred to the proposition. For these not only confirm the proposition but also add a great deal of light to it, they also teach, fortify, console, and raise up our consciences remarkably, when they are distressed concerning the remission of sins and concerning grace. For they show the sources of this question, and most learnedly distinguish the promise of the Gospel from the Law, and they distinguish also the righteousness of the Law and of the Gospel. Furthermore, in a wonderful way Paul here diminishes and casts away the righteousness of the Law, as nowhere else. Therefore, it must be prudently seen to what this dispute pertains. For it asks concerning righteousness before God: Can our righteousness be opposed to the terrors of sin, the wrath and the Judgment of God? Do we obtain the remission of sins on account of our dignity? Does our dignity free us from sin and from death? In a true struggle, ought the conscience to rely on its own dignity? Or rather on the mercy promised on account of Christ? To this struggle these diminutions of the righteousness of the Law are to be referred, not to secure consciences, or to the outward life, or the civil life. For the Gospel preaches concerning spiritual and eternal life, it preaches concerning true repentance, and it frees from sin and from death.

The exterior life has need of discipline and Law. But it is not about this exterior life that we are disputing in this place. Therefore, Paul expressly prefaces his remarks about Abraham, who possessed many excellent and heroic virtues, and who undoubtedly excelled all the men of his age in the gifts of intellect, wisdom, and every kind of virtue. Paul does not despise these great virtues and these gifts of God, but he denies that they can be set against the wrath and Judgment of GOD, and he distinguishes them from that righteousness about which the Gospel preaches, namely, from the remission of sins, which is given on account of CHRIST. The unskilled must be warned of these things at the beginning, so that they may know to what Paul's doctrine pertains, and to what this new and wonderful extenuation of the righteousness of the Law must be referred. For the profane transfer it to the exterior life; afterwards, some interpreters, when they dream that Paul is speaking about the exterior life and righteousness, corrupt Paul's sentences and think that this is the only thing being dealt with, that the Mosaic Ceremonies in the exterior life are to be abrogated. They do not refer this doctrine to the remission of sins and the struggle of the conscience. There are, however, five arguments. The first is from example. Abraham was justified before God by trust in mercy, not on account of his virtues, therefore we also are justified by faith, the consequence is manifest, because the reason for the virtues is the same. If Abraham, when he had so many excellent and heroic virtues, was not righteous before God on account of them, how much less do inferior virtues accomplish this in others?

Second, from the definition, Justification is the gratuitous imputation of righteousness, Therefore we are not justified on account of our quality or dignity, etc.

Third, from the definition. Justification is the remission of sins: Therefore it does not happen on account of our dignity, since we always have need of the remission of sins.

Fourth, from the order of causes and effects. Abraham is pronounced righteous before circumcision: Therefore he is not righteous on account of that work.

Fifth, from the cause of the promise. A promise hanging from the condition of the Law is not certain. The promise of grace must be certain: Therefore the promise of grace does not hang from the condition of the Law, but is to be received freely by faith.

The first argument concerning the example of Abraham must be diligently inculcated into minds. For although it offends the Jews in a wonderful way, this seemingly immoderate attenuation of the justice of the Law nevertheless brings most abundant consolation to pious and fearful consciences. And let us always remember that this sermon does not pertain to the outward life, but to the remission of sins in true repentance. And here let us diligently amplify the virtues of Abraham. For there is no doubt that that heroic man possessed excellent virtues and by his character and holy works far surpassed many. And yet Paul dares to strip them of this glory of justification. He has praise, he says, but not before God, that is, those virtues cannot be opposed to the wrath and Judgment of God, they do not free from sin and from death: this example brings great consolation to the pious. Not even Abraham was justified on account of the dignity of his own virtues: Therefore let us truly establish for ourselves that we are forgiven freely, and so, having posited the negative sentence, he adds from Genesis the antithesis, which is the antecedent of the argument. To Abraham it was imputed for righteousness that he believed: Therefore we also are justified by faith, not on account of our works or the Law. But some cavil at this argument in many ways, others say it is a synecdoche, and to believe, they say, is a work and signifies universal obedience, Abraham believed, that is, he obeyed God according to a synecdoche, because obedience ought to follow faith: Therefore they say that by faith universal obedience is signified. Others say that this saying is wrongly distorted, because Genesis does not make mention there of Christ, or of this faith receiving the remission of sins. It is useful to refute these calumnies, so that the meaning of the words of Genesis may be better understood. First, therefore, this must be observed, that Paul by this saying of Genesis distinguishes the righteousness of the Law and of faith. Wherefore it is necessary that this saying be understood properly of faith. Likewise, Paul adds an interpretation, that by faith a gratuitous imputation is received. Therefore, here he properly understands faith as assent and trust, by which we receive the promised mercy, that is, by which we determine that God truly wishes to forgive us and to be propitious, through mercy freely, even if we feel that we are unworthy. The meaning, therefore, is, he believed, that is, he determined that he had a propitious God although he felt that he was unworthy, and by this trust he expected help and the promised seed, etc. Thus, he was justified by faith, that is, he was pleasing through mercy freely, not on account of his own dignity. And he determined this by faith according to the promise, because God had said: I will be your protector &c. And Abraham knew the promise made concerning that seed to come, by which God willed that sin and death be abolished. Wherefore a synecdoche is not to be feigned: Abraham was justified on account of the knowledge of the word, and his own morals agreeing with the doctrine and profession. Because faith does not lean upon the dignity of one's own virtues, but looks only at mercy. I advise these things briefly concerning the first cavil, so that the simple and true meaning of the word, he believed, may be retained. The second cavil. That the passage of Paul is badly twisted, because Genesis does not seem to speak in that sentence of faith in Christ, but of the expectation of a corporal thing, namely posterity. To this cavil I answer. Faith is the confidence of promised mercy on account of Christ, and this confidence renders the conscience peaceful, and overcomes the terrors of sin. Therefore the proper object of faith is promised mercy. Faith always looks first at this object, even if afterwards other external things are sought or expected.

In this way, in all things said about faith, let it be understood that the faith which receives the remission of sins is first included. Then, faith is otherwise occupied about other external objects. The faith of Moses at the Red Sea was concerned with the defense of the people. Meanwhile, however, he himself determined that he had a propitious God, and on that account he expected deliverance. The faith of Jacob Genesis xxviii. was concerned with the expectation of sustenance and return. Yet he could not seek or expect these things from God unless he first determined that he had a placated God. Thus, as often as we seek our daily bread, let us simultaneously determine that God is propitious on account of Christ. This faith, receiving the remission of sins, is required in every prayer. Although, therefore, external affairs are dissimilar, nevertheless the primary and proper object, namely the promised mercy, is the same in all promises and in every exercise of faith. Since, therefore, faith has a primary object, Paul rightly cites this saying. Furthermore, the fathers knew the first promise concerning Christ and knew that all promises were to be referred to this, that all things are given on account of that seed on account of which God is propitious, and indeed Abraham knew that this very promise properly pertained to the coming seed, Christ. Third cavil. To this testimony cited from Genesis they oppose another passage concerning Abraham Gen. xxii. Because you have done this thing, and have not spared your son I will bless you. From this they argue, Abraham is praised on account of a work: Therefore he was justified on account of a work, not only by faith. I answer briefly. The consequence must be denied, because a work in a believer has its own praise, and is a necessary obedience, and becomes righteousness, and yet it does not have this dignity that on account of the work itself the person has the remission of sins, and is righteous, that is, accepted for eternal life before God. Because it is necessary for the person first to have the remission of sins and justification, afterwards the begun obedience is pleasing and is a worship of God. First, because through Christ there is access. Item: Everything that is not from faith is sin. Secondly, because consciences would become uncertain, if the remission of sins depended on the dignity of works. Therefore it is necessary for the person first to have faith. And these things can easily be judged in a true struggle, because the conscience cannot oppose our work to the wrath or judgment of God, according to that: No living person will be justified in your sight. Nor did Abraham oppose his work to the judgment of God. Rather, in the work itself he acknowledged his infirmity, and overcame this by faith, and determined that he was certainly pleasing to God on account of another, namely the promised mercy, and yet afterwards it pleases God in the believing obedience, and has great rewards. For this text does not say that Abraham was therefore reckoned righteous, but bodily rewards are promised to him, even if in these also the promise concerning Christ is repeated. Therefore, both passages in Genesis must be learned. The one teaches simply concerning the imputation of righteousness. The other concerning the praise and rewards of obedience which arises from faith, and has huge rewards. Wherefore it must be discerned how Genesis has taught concerning justification, and what must be judged concerning the following obedience.

Second argument.

Justification is the gratuitous imputation of mercy: Therefore justification is not our work. The antecedent is Paul's, for Paul agitates the word of imputing, and interprets it concerning gratuitous imputation. For he opposes it to debt. Moreover, the phrase is to be observed. As now the adversaries use the term of merit, so Paul uses the correlative term of debt, so that therefore as he takes away debt, so he takes away merit in justification, and clearly affirms that the imputation is made, not on account of debt or merit, but is gratuitous and is received by faith.

Third argument.

This is the declaration and confirmation of the second point. Justification is the remission of sins: Therefore, justification does not happen on account of our dignity or merits. This argument declares much more clearly the opinion of Paul concerning gratuitous imputation, or concerning the exclusive. For Sadoleto and others imagine a synecdoche, that we are justified by faith, that is, by faith we obtain virtues, and on account of the dignity of these we are pleasing to God. Thus they imagine. But Paul excludes this merit, and says that we are sinners before God, and are thus reputed righteous, namely by the remission of sins. Therefore, this is the genuine opinion of Paul, that we are reputed righteous through mercy on account of CHRIST, not on account of our dignity, and that this mercy must be received by faith. This opinion retains the exclusive, and removes the synecdoche.

Furthermore, this must be known, that with imputation and the remission of sins is joined the gift of the Holy Spirit, when we apprehend the word by faith. Now, how great is this consolation for pious consciences to know that justification is the remission of sins? Therefore, let us not be deterred by the fact that we bring sins to God, not merits, but let us know that this itself is the voice of the Gospel, and the eternal will of the Father, and the immutable benefit of Christ, that He truly wills to justify even the unworthy who bring their sins, if only we believe. And here again observe, the exclusive is repeated to whom God imputes righteousness without works, but the adversaries cavil at this passage in this way. Other passages attribute blessedness to works. Blessed is the man who fears the Lord: Blessed are the merciful, etc. Therefore, in a similar way, we can argue that we are justified on account of works, just as Paul argues from the Psalm that we are justified by the remission of sins. I answer: The consequence must be denied. Because in all passages concerning works, this passage must be included. Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, because works do not please except in a believer or a just person. Therefore, Paul most correctly cites this passage when he speaks of the remission of sins, which is gratuitous: but someone might say: Why do you make a synecdoche in the passages of works and not in the passages of faith? I answer: Because works do not please except in a believer or a just person. Therefore, in the passages of works, we include faith. In the passages concerning faith, there is no synecdoche, because it receives remission through mercy, nor does it rely on the dignity of works, indeed it would become uncertain and would be shaken if it were to depend upon the dignity of works or merit. Therefore it is by grace, so that the promise may be firm. Furthermore, whenever it is said that works are pleasing on account of faith, by that very fact justification is already detracted from works, because faith does not rely upon works, but is a trust in mercy alone. And this very thing he says, that the person is first reconciled by faith, and afterwards the works are pleasing. The Psalm: Blessed are they whose &c. is a doctrine and a confession in which he proposes an example of doctrine. Then in the third place he adds the doctrine of the Law concerning discipline and the causes of human calamities. In the beginning he delivers a doctrine or sermon which contains two parts, namely the doctrine that all are under sin. Also the promise that God wills to remit sins, and he teaches how He remits, how He justifies, namely freely, not imputing sins &c. It is therefore a proposition. Blessed are they whose iniquities are remitted, that is, we are thus just not on account of our dignity or merits, but by God not imputing, by God remitting sins. Therefore all men have sin and to all God can impute sin, and all ought to acknowledge that they have sin. Therefore he says: Nor is there guile in his spirit, that is, He who acknowledges and confesses sin is blessed, etc. And thus we are reckoned righteous when we acknowledge and confess that we have sins, and believe that they are forgiven us through mercy on account of Christ. Then follows the confession itself, which is an example of the proposed sermon. Because I kept silent, my bones grew old, etc. He opposes silence to confession. Confession, however, is to acknowledge sin and to seek and believe in forgiveness. This is what he means when he says: I said, I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord. Conversely, to be silent is to feel sin and not to seek or believe in gratuitous forgiveness, but to remain in that doubt and dread, or to seek consolation through works, just as some seek it through monasticism, others through other works. Thus he says: I remained in dread, and I was almost consumed. Then he adds concerning confession, in which he clearly teaches that God forgives sins, and indeed forgives the one who confesses, not the one who brings the righteousness of the Law: Therefore He forgives gratuitously, he transfers the example to others: For this, every saint shall pray to You, that is, even the saints acknowledge that they have sins and seek and believe that they are forgiven: Therefore it is a gratuitous forgiveness. By this faith they will be saved, and will not be overwhelmed by the waves, they will not be oppressed by terrors. You see, therefore, that the doctrine concerning repentance and concerning remission is joined. He does not promise remission to the secure and to those not grieving, but to those where repentance exists at the same time and terrors exist. Therefore he adds a sermon to the people of the law, whom he exhorts to repentance: Do not become like the horse and the mule, that is, acknowledge the wrath of GOD against sin: and he adds concerning the punishments of sin, God burdens the world with calamities and death, so that he may restrain and punish the impious, and so that he may humble us so that we may acknowledge sins. Thus all the plagues of the world are a part of the Law and divine sermons, which testify that the world is subject to sin and that God is angry at sin. He opposes this opinion to human judgments. For men think that calamities happen by chance and without the counsel of GOD or by the unjust judgment of God, but the prophet here preaches and teaches, wisdom divinely revealed, that with GOD knowing and ordaining, calamities happen, so that GOD may restrain the impious and declare wrath against sin, so that we may acknowledge sin, and seek grace and liberation in CHRIST. Furthermore, he teaches that the saints, even if at the same time they are nevertheless afflicted to be preserved and finally delivered from death and all evils.

The fourth argument from the order of causes. Abraham is pronounced righteous before Circumcision: Therefore that work does not merit the remission of sins nor justification. This argument is illustrious because it contains a comparison of justification or reconciliation and the works that follow. Furthermore, it teaches concerning the use of the sacraments. But first the cavil must be dissolved, since Paul named a ceremony, it seems he only detracted justification from ceremonies. To that it must be answered, in Abraham, David, and the like, ceremonies had the command of God just as other good works did. Therefore there is no reason for a difference here. If other works, commanded by God, merited the remission of sins and justification, much more did ceremonies merit that with them, because they were excellent works of the first table. And so when Paul detracts merit from ceremonies, he also detracts it from other works.

Secondly, this passage contains a useful comparison of faith and the works that follow. Abraham obtained the remission of sins by faith and being justified, the person is thus pleasing. Afterwards follows his obedience. This, in such a person, already has great praise. Thus David first receives by faith the remission of sins and becomes a son; afterwards his bravely performed deeds in warfare, his diligence in command, his patience in afflictions, and other virtues are pleasing. And yet, meanwhile, he does not set these against the Judgment of God; he knows they do not satisfy the Law, nor do they please on account of their own perfection, but because he believes that he has a propitious God through mercy on account of the promised seed, as he says, what shall I render to the Lord, etc.? Thus, in the believer, good works now become sacrifices and offerings of praise, and they have great rewards.

Thirdly, this passage concerning the use of the sacraments must be observed most diligently, so that it may fortify us against Pharisaical opinions concerning the work performed. Likewise against Anabaptist imaginations. For because Paul calls circumcision the seal of the righteousness of faith, he testifies that the sacraments are signs requiring faith. Wherefore they do not justify without faith from the work performed, as the monks used to speak. Likewise, this passage teaches that the sacraments are not merely signs of profession toward men, or symbols of our morals, as the Anabaptists imagine, who diminish the sacraments. But that use and principal end of the sacraments is that they are signs of the promise and testimonies of the will of God toward us and require faith, just as the promise does. In Abraham, circumcision is a mark which always reminded him of the promise. And it was a testimony that God was propitious to him according to the promise. Thus, baptism in our body should remind us of the promise, and it ought to testify that God truly wishes to impart those things which He promised in the Gospel. The eating of the body and blood of the Lord in us ourselves is a testimony that Christ truly joins us to Himself as members, that He truly wishes to wash us with His blood. Thus, therefore, the sacraments are to be used just as the Word, and faith is to be aroused and exercised by the sacraments, just as by the Word.

The fifth argument from the cause of the promise. No promise hanging upon the condition of the Law is certain: the promise of grace ought to be certain: Therefore, the promise of grace does not hang upon the condition of the Law, but is to be received freely by faith. This is the principal syllogism to be especially agitated in this controversy. And it is the of the whole dispute. held together by a line of reasoning drawn from sources, or from the place of causes. Therefore it adds much light to this business, it explains what kind of thing a promise is, and what faith is, likewise it shows the distinction between the promises of the Law, and the promise of grace. Wherefore, in order to understand this controversy, it is necessary to agitate this argument. Furthermore, it contributes greatly not only to instructing consciences, but also to consoling them. For this passage declares most of all the particle freely, and shows why the promise is gratuitous.

Declaration of the Major Premise.

If the promise were to depend upon the condition of the Law, it would become uncertain. Paul confirms this proposition in the text, because the Law works wrath, that is, the Law always accuses and condemns us, since we never satisfy it, because the Law of GOD requires not only external civil deeds, but perfect interior and exterior obedience, the highest love of GOD. No one has performed this except Christ; the Law accuses and condemns all others. As Paul says, we are all by nature children of wrath. Therefore, if the promise had the condition of the Law, since the Law always accuses and condemns, the promise of grace would be made void, therefore Paul recites the major premise of the syllogism thus. If those who are of the Law were heirs, faith would be abolished, and the promise would be void. And he himself adds the confirmation, the Law works wrath, that is, it condemns and drives to despair. He reviewed this confirmation more briefly, however, because he will repeat it below concerning the use of the Law. But someone might say: on the contrary, certainly the Gospel is conditional, because sins are not forgiven unless repentance is added, just as the text says: Repent. Likewise, definitely to do evil. Likewise Christ says, If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments, I answer briefly. These requirements are not the condition and cause for which reconciliation is given, but rather they are affections necessarily following. And that they are not the cause for which remission or reconciliation is given, appears from this, because sin is remitted or concupiscence, even if it still clings in reality in the flesh, and concupiscence is not idle, but begets infinite depraved affections. Therefore, remission does not depend on the condition of the Law fulfilled, or to be fulfilled, or of our purity. And yet when remission is apprehended by faith, since faith is the beginning of new and eternal life, It is now necessary for a new obedience to be begun. Which, even if it is imperfect, yet it pleases on account of Christ. Likewise, since faith frees from the terrors of sin, it is necessary that terrors exist in us, but those terrors are by no means the price or cause of the remission of sins. But the conscience ought to establish that this benefit is given freely on account of the mediator and high priest Christ.

But here it can be objected, if conditional promises are void: Therefore all promises added to works are useless, such as are, Give and it shall be given to you. Break your bread to the hungry and the Lord will hear you, etc. I answer, the promise of the remission of sins and of reconciliation or justification, and of eternal life, is proper to the Gospel, and is exhibited freely on account of Christ, not on account of the condition of the Law or of works. This promise ought to be diligently distinguished from legal promises, which have the condition of works, such as are, Give and it shall be given to you. If anyone shall have given so much as a drink of water, etc. he shall not lose his reward. Honor your father and mother if you wish to be long-lived upon the earth. These promises have the condition of works, and are truly useless and void without the promise of the Gospel, because the works themselves do not please God, except in those who are reconciled. But after we have been freely accepted through mercy by faith, afterwards the begun obedience pleases, not on account of its own purity or dignity, not because it can be set against the Judgment of God, not because it satisfies the Law, not because on account of it the person is righteous, But the person is righteous, that is, accepted on account of CHRIST through mercy. Therefore, then, works please, because we are sons, as Paul says, Now you are not under the Law but under grace. Although, therefore, such works are not in reality the fulfillment of the Law, yet since they please on account of CHRIST, they are as it were a certain fulfillment of the Law. Therefore legal promises, that is, promises added to such works, now become valid and useful to the reconciled. This is the useful doctrine concerning the distinction of promises, and concerning the use of legal promises, that we may know how they are valid, and may learn also in these to exercise faith, because promises are added to works, chiefly for this reason that we may so work, that at the same time faith may seek and expect from God spiritual and bodily benefits, necessary for the Commonwealth and for us.

Declaration of the minor premise.

The minor premise of the syllogism is that the promise of grace ought to be certain and ratified. For first, what would have been the need to issue a promise and reveal remission if there were none? Yet it would be none if it depended upon the condition of the Law, because the Law is sometimes satisfied. Indeed, reconciliation was revealed for this very reason, because we could not attain it by the Law. And for this very reason the condition of the Law was removed. Secondly, doubt in souls produces despair; just as it was said above, the Law works wrath. Therefore, it is necessary for the promise to be known, certain, and ratified to us, so that it may be opposed to doubt and be an effective consolation. At this point, it is necessary to rebuke the common opinion which teaches that the conscience ought to doubt concerning the remission of sins, and whether God is propitious to us, and that this doubt is not a sin. Doubt indeed clings naturally in the souls of all. For the darkness is so great that even secure souls despise the wrath of God and doubt concerning the Judgment, and then when the conscience is disturbed, it perpetually accuses and condemns. We confess, therefore, that doubt clings in souls, but we say that that doubt is a sin and that it must be fought against, that doubt. For this reason the promise was revealed, so that it may correct that doubt, so that we may have certain and firm consolation and may certainly establish that it is remitted to us, and that we are heard, and the Gospel, just as it proposes the promise, so it expressly requires faith, that we believe that very promise, as in John 3. Faith, however, is contrary to doubt. Likewise, doubt accuses God of lying, denies that God is truthful, etc. Wherefore we ought to oppose both the promise and the commandment concerning faith to doubt, and learn that doubt is the greatest sin. The Scholastics therefore imagined that doubt is not a sin, because they saw that it naturally clings to souls. Likewise, they did not distinguish the Law from the Gospel at all, nor did they consider that faith is required or what faith is, because they imagined that faith is the knowledge of the Law. And so, by this doctrine concerning doubt, or because they command one to doubt simply, they abolish the whole Gospel, the promise, and the commandment concerning faith. Wherefore that impious imagination, which commands one to doubt, must be rejected.

Who beyond hope believed under hope.

There follows an amplification which illustrates the of faith. nature and exercise. And that must always be held, which was said above, that faith first embraces trust, which establishes that sins are remitted to us, and that God is propitious to us on account of Christ. Afterwards this same faith is occupied with various other external objects, as the faith of Abraham first looks upon this very promise, the promised seed on account of which God is about to bless the human race. Then it exerts itself and awaits the promised posterity. The faith of Moses first apprehends mercy, afterwards it awaits the liberation of the people, etc. Thus the external objects always vary, and yet there is one common principal object of faith, namely, the mercy promised on account of Christ. Wherefore let each one also stir up faith in his own danger, in his own affliction. I said, however, that the nature of faith is illustrated here, because the object is first described, the proper object of faith is the word, which fights with external appearance, as to Abraham is promised a seed and posterity which God wills to bless, meanwhile his spouse is barren, he himself is worn out, the Gospel promises peace and life. Meanwhile we are exercised by every kind of affliction, and in death life is not seen.

Therefore Paul says here: Abraham believed against hope in hope: against hope, that is, against the proposed object about which one had to despair: in hope, that is, in the word in which one had to hope. Thus faith looks upon the word and sustains itself by the word even if the external appearance resists. Deliverance is promised to the Israelites. Meanwhile the bitterness of servitude grows and other greater miseries follow. Thus we also ought to exercise faith in our dangers. I have spoken about the object, now about the formal aspect of faith. And this passage clearly shows that faith is called by Paul a confidence which assents to the promise of the Gospel, and fights against doubt.
