Therefore faith does not signify knowledge of the Law or only knowledge of history, but it signifies to assent to the promise, not to doubt that God will exhibit what is promised. And this passage is to be observed, so that it may be opposed to those who deny that faith is a confidence fighting against doubt. For here are expressly placed four descriptions. He did not doubt about the promise, through diffidence: Item he was certain, item giving glory to God, etc. Thus above Paul compares faith and the promise, and shows them to be connected among themselves as correlatives. Therefore it is certain that by faith Paul signifies the confidence which assents to the promise of the Gospel, and receives the promised remission of sins, and reconciliation. Likewise, there is no doubt that Paul is speaking of faith doing something in the terrors of the conscience and comforting consciences, as he says below: Being justified by faith we have peace. Furthermore, that consolation is not brought about by knowledge of the Law or knowledge of history alone, but by confidence in the promise fighting against doubt. All things are full of darkness and gloom in Christian doctrine, with this proper meaning of the word faith lost. Therefore these passages of Paul must be diligently observed, so that what faith properly signifies may be certainly judged and established, and so that the ravings of those who deny that faith is confidence fighting against doubt, but imagine it to be only knowledge of history, may be refuted. Then let us also transfer to use let us learn from this description proposed here that this is the true exercise of faith, to resist natural doubt and diffidence, and to oppose to it the word or promise, and to seek, and to expect that we be confirmed by God, just as he says in Mark 9: I believe Lord, help my unbelief.

Thirdly, Paul adorns faith by its final cause. For after he described what it is like and what its nature is, he adds an excellent commendation, that it is a worship rendering glory to God, that is, affirming that God is powerful and truthful, because he who does not assent to the promise doubts whether it is true, nay, denies that it is true. He therefore accuses God of a lie, just as John says: He who does not believe God, makes him a liar. On the contrary, he who assents to the promise establishes that God is truthful, powerful, etc. And so that it may be better understood that without this faith no glory is attributed to God, the antithesis must be considered. Reason either has Epicurean opinions about God, that he is idle, neither punishing nor saving. This is the first insult described in the Psalm: The fool has said in his heart, there is no God. Or it has opinions of the Law about God, namely that God saves the righteous, and because we are not just, he will have rejected us. This is also another insult, because thinking thus about God, he flees from God and rages against God. Those who judge about God in this way do not call upon God. They expect nothing from God. Therefore they do not acknowledge him to be God, but on the contrary, believing in the promise of grace, he casts away Epicurean opinions, and opinions of the Law, and attributes glory to God, that he truly cares for and loves us, that he does not wish to destroy, but to hear and to save, according to the promise, although we are unworthy. Therefore by this faith he calls upon and expects help and salvation from God. This faith therefore attributes glory to God, that he is God, that he is powerful, that is, effective, doing something with us, that he is truthful, that he is merciful, that he hears, that he saves. This is the proper glory of God, and this faith produces invocation and true spiritual worship. Here it is necessary to admonish the hearers concerning those who oppose the doctrine of faith and boast themselves to be teachers of good works. This praise those men falsely arrogate to themselves, because they only teach external and civil works, meanwhile they do not teach true and interior worship, namely the exercises of faith and invocation. These works are proper to Christians. Concerning these, churches are especially to be taught. Secondly, With the doctrine of faith omitted, other works neither please God, nor can consciences understand how they might please. Therefore, such teachers who omit the doctrine concerning this faith do not teach at all about good works, but about certain works of their own rejected by God, which, when they propose them as acts of worship and transfer to them the honor owed to Christ, they teach idolatrous things. To this pertain those sermons among the prophets, such as Esaiae 41. Behold, all are unjust and their works are vain, wind and emptiness are their idols. Therefore, in the true doctrine of good works, let us consider first that faith and the exercises of faith are required, which are acts of worship that properly attribute glory to God, and let us practice invocation in every life and all business. Thus, faith itself will grow and God will give other gifts as He promises. How much more will your Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him, from which other good works will also exist.

But it is not written for his sake alone, that it was imputed to him, but also etc.

This is a notable passage and it contains two things. First, that this righteousness about which he is preaching has been revealed from heaven, and is not known by reason or from the Law. Second, that the example of the justification of Abraham pertains to all. Each point contains excellent doctrine. For the former, concerning revelation, shows the distinction between the righteousness of the Law and imputation, and leads us to the word and the promise, and clearly teaches the same thing which John teaches in that saying: The Son who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared him to us, because neither reason nor the Law teaches or renders certain that God remits sins, especially to the unworthy. Likewise, that he pronounces them righteous although they do not satisfy the Law. Therefore, this promise, which is the Gospel, concerning the remission of sins and the imputation of righteousness, is divinely revealed, and is a different judgment than the doctrine of the law and of reason. Wherefore, it must be diligently observed in this place what he says: It is written, that it might be imputed: as if he were to say: This will concerning imputation is not known to reason as the Law is, but is a different judgment and a new revelation. Then also that must be considered, that he leads us to the word. He does not want us to seek other illuminations, but he wants us to begin with the word and to console consciences with the word and to establish that this is the certain and rare will of GOD, which is proposed in the word. Therefore, Anabaptist and Manichaean imaginations are to be rejected, which seek illuminations without the word of God and outside the word of God.

Secondly, it contains an excellent consolation that in this place he transfers the example of justification to all, and first teaches that Abraham is the form of the people of God, so that we may know that the rest are reckoned righteous, just as he himself was justified. Then it is most sweet to see that he makes all equal to Abraham, as far as it pertains to the remission of sins and the imputation of righteousness. For there is a dissimilarity of gifts. Therefore, let all know that they are so loved and reckoned righteous, just as God testifies that He loves and justifies Abraham. And that in him testimonies of true and great love are proposed, that was done for this reason, that we may know that we are similarly loved and heard. To this use this passage of Paul is to be accommodated, which transfers the example of Abraham to us. And to this it ought to be referred, that we often say that it must be inculcated into consciences that the promises are universal. Since this is so, God demands and commands that all should believe that they are equally loved and are reckoned righteous.

Finally, it is not enough to speak of faith or trust in mercy. But it is necessary to embrace the mediator: Therefore Paul added that it is reckoned to those who believe in him who raised Jesus from the dead, who was delivered up for our offenses, and was raised for our justification. Here again you have the argument that faith signifies not the knowledge of the Law, or only of history, but signifies trust, which apprehends the imputation, which is made on account of the mediator Christ who suffered and reigns. Paul distinguishes between death and resurrection, and when mention is made of the resurrection, the kingdom and priesthood of Christ are to be understood, for we are Christ's for this reason, because Christ our high priest intercedes for us before the Father, that He may reckon us righteous: Likewise because Christ lives and reigns, He gives the Holy Spirit and makes alive, He frees from wrath and eternal death, He will raise the dead. And faith apprehends both and applies them to us, namely the death of Christ, and the resurrected mediator, high priest, and life-giver. It apprehends the death of Christ, so that it may hold the victim, which it may establish as the certain price for sins of ours, because God willed there to be some final [satisfaction] for sin. And indeed He is so angered by sin, that no sacrifice pleased Him except the death of the Son. This very thing testifies both that the anger of God against sin is ineffable, and that His mercy toward us is infinite, in that He made the Son a victim for us. Moreover, it is not only the death of Christ that must be apprehended, but also that, having been resurrected, He is our high priest before the Father, so that He may truly hear us, truly be efficacious, truly give life, give the Holy Spirit, help us, deliver us from eternal death, and is about to resurrect the dead and give new and perpetual life, wisdom, and righteousness. Paul embraced all these things when he says: He rose again for our righteousness.

Latin:

Quid igitur dicemus invenis-se Abraham patrem nostrum?

Sequitur confirmatio, in qua diligenter distribuenda sunt argumenta & ad propositionem referenda. Haec enim non solum confirmant propositionem sed plurimum etiam lucis ei addunt, praeclarè etiam docent, muniunt, consolantur, & erigunt nostras conscientias, cum anguntur de remissione peccatorum & de gratia. Monstrant enim fontes huius quaestionis, & promissionem Evangelii eruditissimè discernunt à Lege, discernunt & iusticiam Legis & Evangelii. Porro mirum in modum hic extenuat Paulus & abiicit iusticiam Legis, ut nusquàm aliâs. Ideo prudenter videndum est, quò pertineat haec disputatio. Quaerit enim de iusticia coram Deo: An iusticia nostra possit opponi terroribus peccati, irae & Iudicio Dei? An consequamur remissionem peccatorum propter nostram dignitatem? An nostra dignitas liberet nos à peccato & à morte? An in vero agone conscientia debeat niti propria dignitate? An vero misericordia propter Christum promissa. Ad hoc certamen referendae sunt hae extenuationes iusticiae Legis, non ad fecuras conscientias, aut ad vitam exteriorem, aut civilem. Nam Evangelium concionatur de spirituali & aeterna vita, concionatur de vera paenitentia, et liberat à peccato & a morte.

Exterior vita habet opus disciplina & Lege. Sed de hac exteriore vita non disputatur hoc loco. Ideo Paulus diserte prae fatur de Abraham, qui habuit multas excellentes & heroicas virtutes, et haud dubie dotibus ingenii, sapientia & omni genere virtutum excelluit omnibus hominibus eius aetatis. Has tantas virtutes & haec dona Dei non aspernatur Paulus, sed negat posse opponi irae & Iudicio DEI & discernit ab illa iusticia, de qua concionatur Evangelium, videlicet à remissione peccatorum, quae datur propter CHRISTUM. Haec initio monendi sunt imperiti, ut sciant quo pertineat Pauli doctrina, & quo referenda sit haec nova, & mira extenuatio iusticiae Legis. Nam prophani transferunt ad exteriorem vitam, postea interpretes aliqui cum somniant Paulum de exteriori vita & iusticia loqui, corrumpunt Pauli sententias, & putant tantum hoc agi, ut abrogentur Caeremoniae Mosaicae in vita exteriori. Non referunt hanc doctrinam ad remissionem peccatorum & agonem conscientiae. Sunt autem quinque argumenta. Primum ab exemplo. Abraham iustificatus est coram Deo fiducia misericordiae, non propter suas virtutes, Ergo & nos iustificamur fide, consequentia est manifesta, quia eadem est ratio virtutum. Si Abraham cum tot excellentes & heroicas virtutes haberet, non fuit propter eas iustus coram Deo, quanto minus hoc praestant virtutes inferiores in aliis?

Secundum ex definitione, Iustificatio est gratuita imputatio iusticiae, Ergo non iustificamur propter nostram qualitatem aut dignitatem, &c.

Tertium ex definitione. Iustificatio est remissio peccatorum: Ergo non contigit propter nostram dignitatem, siquidem semper habemus opus remissione peccatorum.

Quartum ex ordine causarum & essectuum. Abraham pronunciatur instus ante circumcisionem: Ergo non est iustus propter illud opus.

Quintum ex causa promissionis. Promissio pendens ex conditione Legis non est certa. Promissio gratiae debet esse certa: Ergo promissio gratiae non pendet ex conditione Legis, sed fide gratis accipienda est.

Primum argumentum de exemplo Abrahae diligenter inculcandum est animis. Etsi enim mirum in modum offendit Iudaeos, haec ut videtur immodica extenuatio iusticiae Legis, tamen piis & pavidis conscientiis affert uberrimam consolationem. Ac semper meminerimus hanc concionem non pertinere ad exteriorem vitam, sed ad remissionem peccatorum in vera paenitentia. Et hic diligenter amplificemus virtutes Abrahae. Neque enim dubium est, quin ille heroicus vir habuerit excellentes virtutes & moribus ac sanctis operibus longè vicerit multos. Et tamen Paulus audet detrahere eis hanc gloriam iustificationis. Habet laudem, inquit, sed non coram Deo, id est, virtutes illae non possunt opponi irae & Iudicio Dei, non liberant à peccato & à morte: hoc exemplum magnam consolationem piis affert. Ne quidem Abraham propter dignitatem propriarum virtutum iustificatus est: Ergo vere statuamus nobis gratis ignosci, itaque posita negativa sententia addit ex genesi antithesin, quae est antecedens argumenti. Abrahae imputatum est ad iusticiam quod credit: Ergo & nos iustificamur fide, non propter nostra opera aut Legem. Sed hoc argumentum cavillantur aliqui multis modis, alii dicunt esse synecdochen, & credere, dicunt esse opus & significare universam obedientiam, Abraham credidit, id est, obedivit Deo iuxta Synecdochen, quia fidem debet sequi obedientia: Ideo fide aiunt significari universam obedientiam. Alii dicunt malè detorqueri hoc dictum, quia Genesis non faciat ibi mentionem de Christo, aut de hac fide accipiente remissionem peccatorum. Has calumnias prodest confutari, ut sententia verborum genesis melius intelligatur. Primum igitur hoc observandum est, Paulum hoc dicto Genesis discernere iusticiam Legis & fidei. Quare necesse est hoc dictum intelligi proprie de fide. Item Paulus addit interpretationem, quod fide gratuita imputatio accipiatur. Ergo hic proprie intelligit fidem assensum & fiduciam, qua accipimus promissam misericordiam, id est, qua statuimus quod Deus verè velit nobis ignoscere et propitius esse, per misericordiam gratis, etiamsi sentiamus nos indignos esse. Est ergo sententia, credidit, id est sta vit se habere Deum propitium quamvis sentiebat se indignum esse, et hac fiducia expectabat auxlium & promissum semen, &c. Ita fide iustificatus, est, id est, placuit per miser icordiam gratis, non propter propriam dignitatem. Et id fide statuit iuxta promissionem, quia deus dixerat: Ego ero protector tuus &c. Et norat Abraham promissionem factam de illo venturo semine, quo Deus vellet aboleri peccatum et mortem. Quare non est affingenda synecdoche: Abraham est iustificatus propter notitiam verbi, & suos mores convenientes doctrinae & professioni. Quia fides non nititur dignitate virtutum propriarum, sed intuetur tantum misericordiam. Haec breviter moneo de prima cavillatione, ut retineatur simplex & vera significatio verbi, credidit. Secunda cavillatio. Locum Pauli malè detortum esse, quia genesis non videatur loqui in illa sententia de fide in Christum, sed de expectatione rei corporalis videlicet posteritatis. Ad hanc cavillationem respondeo. Fides est fiducia promissae misericordiae propter Christum, & haec fiducia reddit pacatam conscientiam, & vincit terrores peccati. Itaque proprium obiectum fidei est promissa misericordia. Hoc obiectum semper primum intuetur fides, etiamsi postea aliae res externae petuntur vel expectantur.

Hoc modo in omnibus dictis de fide primum intelligatur compraehendi fides, quae accipit remissionem peccatorum. Deinde fides aliâs circa alia obiecta externa versatur. Fides Moisi ad Mare Rubrum versabatur circa defensionem populi. Interea tamen ipse statuebat se habere Deum propitium, & propterea expectabat liberationem. Fides Iacob Genesis xxviii. versabatur circa expectationem victus & reditus. Haec tamen non posset petere nec expectare à Deo, nisi prius statueret se habere Deum placatum. Ita nos quoties petimus panem quotidianum, simul statuamus Deum propitium esse propter Christum. Haec fides accipiens remissionem peccatorum in omni oratione requiritur. Quanquam igitur externa negocia sunt dissimilia, tamen primum obiectum & proprium, scilicet promissa misericordia idem est in omnibus promissionibus & omni exercitio fidei. Cum igitur fides habeat obiectum praecipuum, Paulus rectè citat hoc dictum. Praeterea patres norant primam promissionem de Christo & sciebant ad hanc omnes promissiones referendas esse, omnia dari propter illud semen propter quod Deus sit propitius, & quidem Abraham hanc ipsam promissionem sciebat proprie pertinere ad venturum semen Christi. Tertia cavillatio. Huic testimonio citato ex Genesi opponunt alium locum de Abraham Gen. xxii. Quia fecisti hanc rem, & non pepercisti filio benedicam tibi. Hinc argumentantur, Abraham laudatur propter opus: Ergo iustificatus est propter opus, non tantum fide. Respondeo breviter. Neganda est consequentia, quia opus in credente habet suam laudem, & est necessaria obedientia, & fit iustitia, & tamen non habet hanc dignitatem quod propter ipsum opus persona habeat remissionem peccatorum, & sit iusta, id est, accepta ad vitam aeternam coram Deo. Quia oportet personam prius habere remissionem peccatorum & iustificationem, postea placet inchoata obedientia & est cultus Dei. Primum, quia per Christum est accessus. Item: Omne quod non est ex fide, peccatum est. Secundo, quia conscientiae fierent incertae, si penderet remissio peccatorum ex dignitate operum. Ideo necesse est personam prius habere fidem. Et haec facile iudicari possunt in vero certamine, quia conscientia non potest nostrum opus opponere irae aut iudicio Dei, iuxta illud: Non iustificabitur in conspectu tuo omnis vivens. Nec Abraham opponebat opus suum iudicio Dei. Imo in ipso opere agnovit suam infirmitatem, & hanc vicit fide, & statuit fe certo placere Deo propter aliud scilicet misericordiam promissam, & tamen postea in credente obedientia placet Deo, & habet magna praemia. Nam textus hic non dicit, Abraham propterea iustum reputari, sed promittuntur ei praemia corporalia, & si in his quoque repetitur promissio de Christo. Ideo uterque locus in Genesi discendus est. Alter docet simpliciter de imputatione iustitiae. Alter de laude & praemiis obedientiae quae oritur ex fide, & habet ingentia praemia. Quare discernendum est quomodo Genesis de iustificatione docuerit, & quid de sequenti obedientia iudicandum.

Secundum argumentum.

Iustificatio est gratuita imputatio misericordiae: Ergo iustificatio non est nostrum opus. Antecedens est Pauli, Paulus enim agitat verbum imputandi, & interpretatur de gratuita imputatione. Opponit enim debito. Est autem phrasis observanda. Ut nunc utuntur adversarii vocabulo meriti, ita Paulus utitur correlativo vocabulo debiti, ut igitur tollit debitum ita tollit meritum in iustificatione, & clare affirmat, quod imputatio fiat, non propter debitum seu meritum, sed sit gratuita & accipiatur fide.

Tertium argumentum.

Est declaratio & confirmatio secundi. Iustificatio est remissio peccatorù: Ergo iustificatio non fit propter nostram dignitatem, seu merita. Hoc argumentum multo magis declarat sententiam Pauli de gratuita imputatione, seu de exclusiva. Nam Sadoletus & alii imaginantur Synecdochen, fide iustificamur, id est, fide consequimur virtutes, propter harum dignitatem placemus Deo. Sic illi imaginantur. At Paulus excludit hoc meritum, & dicit nos coram Deo peccatores esse, & ita iustos reputari scilicet remissione peccatorum. Ergo haec est sententia germana Pauli, quod iusti reputemur per misericordiam propter CHRISTUM non propter nostram dignitatem, & quod hanc misericordiam fide oportet accipi. Haec sententia retinet exclusivam, & tollit Synecdochen.

Caeterum illud sciendum est, quod cum imputatione & remissione peccatorum est coniuncta donatio spiritus sancti, cum fide apprehendimus verbum. Iam quanta est haec consolatio piis conscientiis scire, quod iustificatio sit remissio peccatorum? Ergo non deterreamur eo quod peccata ad Deum afferimus, non merita, sed sciamus quod haec ipsa sit vox Evangelii, & aeterna voluntas patris & imutabile Christi beneficium, quod vere velit iustificare quanquam indignos afferentes peccata, si tamen credamus. Et hic iterum observa, repeti exclusivam cui imputat Deus iustitiam sine operibus, sed cavillantur hunc locum adversarii hoc modo. Alii loci tribuunt beatitudinem operibus. Beatus vir qui timet Dominum: Beati misericordes &c. Ergo simili modo possumus argumentari quod iustificemur propter opera, sicut Paulus argumentatur ex Psalmo, quod iustificemur remissione peccatorum. Respondeo: Neganda est consequentia. Quia in omnibus locis de operibus, debet includi hic locus. Beati quorum remissae sunt iniquitates, quia opera non placent nisi in credente seu iusto. Ideo Paulus rectissime citat hunc locum, cum de remissione peccatorum loquitur, quae est gratuita: sed dicat aliquis: Quare facis Synecdochen in locis operum & non in locis fidei? Respondeo: Quia opera non placent nisi in credente seu iusto. Ideo in locis operum includimus fidem. In locis de fide non est Synecdoche, quia accipit remissionem per misericordiam, nec nititur dignitate operum, imo fieret incerta & excuteretur si penderet ex dignitate operum seu merito. Ideo gratis, ut sit firma promissio. Praeterea quandocunque dicitur, opera placent propter fidem, iam eo ipso detrahitur operibus iustificatio, quia fides non nititur operibus, sed est fiducia solius misericordiae. Et hoc ipsum dicit, fide personam prius esse reconciliatam, postea placere opera. Psalmus: Beati quorum &c. est doctrina & confessio in qua doctrinae exemplum proponit. Deinde tertio loco addit doctrinam Legis de disciplina & de caussis calamitatum humanarum. Initio doctrinam tradit seu concionem quae duas partes continet, scilicet doctrinam quod omnes sint sub peccato. Item promissionem quod Deus velit remittere peccata, & docet quomodo remittat, quomodo iustificet scilicet gratis, non imputans peccata &c. Est igitur propositio. Beati quorum remissae sunt iniquitates, id est, ita sumus iusti non propter dignitatem nostram aut merita, sed Deo non imputante, Deo remittente peccata. Ergo omnes homines habent paccatum & omnibus potest Deus imputare peccatum, & omnes agnoscere debent se habere peccatum. Ideo inquit: Nec est in spiritu eius dolus, id est, qui agnoscit & confitetur peccatum, beatus est &c. Atque ita reputamur iusti, cum agnoscimus, & confitemur nos habere peccata, & credimus nobis remitti per misericordiam propter Christum. Deinde sequitur confessio ipsius quae est exemplum propositae concionis. Quoniam tacui inveteraverunt ossa &c. Tacere opponit confessioni. Confessio autem est agnoscere peccatum & petere & credere remissionem. Hoc vult cum inquit: Dixi confitebor adversum me iniustitiam meam Domino. Econtra tacere, est sentire peccatum, & non petere aut credere gratuitam remissionem, sed manere in illa dubitatione & pavoribus, aut quaerere per opera consolationem, sicut alii per monachatus, alii per alia opera quaerunt. Ita dicit: Mansi in pavoribus, & pene consumptus essem. Deinde addit de confessione in qua clare docet, quod Deus remittat peccata, & quidem remittat confitenti, non afferenti iustitiam Legis: Ergo gratis remittit, transfert exemplum ad alios: Pro hoc oravit ad te omnis sanctus, id est, etiam sancti agnoscunt se habere peccata & petunt & credunt sibi ignosci: Ergo est gratuita remssio. Hac fide servabuntur, & non obruentur fluctibus, non opprimentur terroribus. Vides igitur coniungi doctrinam de paenitentia & de remissione. Non promittit remissionem securis & non dolentibus, sed iis ubi simul existit paenitentia & existunt terrores. Ideo addit concionem ad populum legis, quem hortatur ad paenitentiam: Nolite fieri sicut equus & mulus, id est, agnoscite iram DEI adversus peccatum: & addit de poenis peccati, Deus onerat mundum calamitatibus & morte, ut coherceat & puniat impios, & ut humiliet nos ut agnoscamus peccata. Ita omnes plagae muldi sunt pars Legis & conciones divinae, quae testantur mundum esse subiectum peccato & Deum irasci peccato. Hanc sententiam opponit iudiciis humanis. Nam homines cogitant casu accidere calamitates & sine consi io DEI aut iniusto iudicio Dei, sed propheta hic concionatur & docet, sapientiam divinitus revelatam quòd sciente & ordinante DEO accidunt calamitates, ut DEUS coherceat impios & declaret iram adversus peccatum, ut agnoscamus peccatum, & quaeramus in CHRISTO gratiam & liberationem. Praeterea docet sanctos etiamsi simul affliguntur tamen servari & tandem liberari à morte & omnibus malis.

Quartum argumentum ex ordine causarum. Abraham pronunciatur iustus ante Circumcisionem: Ergo opus illud non meretur remissionem peccatorum nec iustificationem. Hoc argumentum est illustre quia continet collationem iustificationis seu reconciliationis & sequentium operum. Praeterea docet de usu sacramentorum. Primum autem diluenda est cavillatio, cum Paulus nominaverit caeremoniam, videtur tantum caeremoniis detraxisse iustificationem. Ad id respondendum est, in Abraham, Davide, & similibus caeremoniae tam habebant mandatum Dei quàm alia bona opera. Ergo ratio diversitatis nulla est hic. Si caetera opera, mandata à Deo, merebantur remissionem peccatorum & iustificationem, multo magis cum illis merebantur id caeremoniae, quia erant praestantia opera primae tabulae. Itaque cum Paulus detrahit caeremoniis meritum, detrahit etiam caeteris operibus.

Secundo, hic locus continet utilem collationem fidei, & sequentium operum. Abraham fide consecutus est remissionem peccatorum & iustificatus ita placet persona. Postea sequitur eius obedientia. Haec in tali persona iam habet magnam laudem. Sic David primum accipit fide remissionem peccatorum & fit filius, postea placent eius fortiter facta in militia, diligentia in imperio, patientia in afflictionibus & aliae virtutes. Et tamen has interim non opponit Iudicio Dei, scit eas non satisfacere Legi, nec placere propter suam perfectionem, sed quia credit se per misericordiam propter promissum semen habere Deum propitium, sicut inquit, quid tribuam domino, &c? Ita incredente iam bona opera fiunt sacrificia & hostiae laudis, & habent magna praemia.

Tertio diligentissime hic locus de usu sacramentorum observandus est, ut muniat nos contra pharisaicas opiniones de opere operato. Item contra anabaptisticas imaginationes. Quia enim Paulus circumcisionem vocat, sigillum iusticiae fidei, testatur sacramenta esse signa requirentia fidem. Quare non iustificant sine fide ex opere operato, ut monachi loquebantur. Item docet hic locus sacramenta non tantum esse signa professionis erga homines, aut symbola nostrorum morum, ut imaginantur Anabaptistae, qui extenuant sacramenta. Verum ille usus & finis principalis est sacramentorum, quod sunt signa promifsionis & testimonia voluntatis Dei erga nos & requirunt fidem, sicut promissio. In Abraham circumcisio est nota, quae semper admonebat eum promissionis. Et erat testimonium quod Deus ei propitius esset iuxta promissionem. Ita baptismus in nostro corpore admoneat nos promissionis, & testari debet, quod vere velit Deus impartiri ea, quae in Evangelio promisit. Manducatio corporis & sanguinis domini in nobis ipsis testimonium est, quod Christus vere nos sibi tanquàm membra adiungat, quòd verè velit nos abluere sanguine suo. Sic igitur utendum est sacramentis, sicut verbo, et fides exuscitanda & exercenda est sacramentis, sicut verbo.

Quintum argumentum ex causa promissionis. Nulla promissio pendens ex conditione Legis, est certa: promissionem gratiae oportet esse certam: Ergo promissio gratiae non pendet ex conditione Legis, sed fide gratis accipienda est. Hic est principalis syllogismus in hac controversia praecipue agitandus. Estque totius disputationis synechon ductum ex fontibus, vel ex loco causarum. Ideo multum lucis addit huic negocio, exponit qualis sit promissio, & quid sit fides, item monstrat discrimen promissionum Legis, & promissionis gratiae. Quare ad hanc controversiam intelligendam necesse est hoc argumentum agitare. Deinde non solum ad erudiendas conscientias, sed etiam ad consolandas mognopere conducit. Nam hic locus maximè declarat particulam gratis, & ostendit quare promissio sit gratuita.

Declaratio Maioris.

Si promissio penderet ex conditione Legis, fieret incerta. Hanc propositionem confirmat Paulus in textu, quia Lex iram efficit, id est, Lex semper accusat & condemnat nos, cum nunquàm ei satisfaciamus, quia Lex DEI requirit non tantum externa civilia facta, sed perfectam obedientiam interiorem & exteriorem, dilectionem DEI summam. Hanc nemo praestitit praeter Christum, caeteros omnes accusat, et condemnat Lex. Sicut Paulus inquit, omnes natura sumus filii irae. Itaque si promissio haberet conditionem Legis, cum Lex semper accuset & condemnet, promissio gratiae fieret irrita, ideo Paulus maiorem syllogismi ita recitat. Si hi qui ex Lege sunt essent haeredes, abolita esset fides, & irrita esset promissio. Et confirmationem addit ipse, Lex iram efficit, id est, condemnat adigit ad desperationem. Brevius autem recensuit hanc confirmationem quia infra repeteteam de usu Legis. Sed dicat aliquis: imo certè Evangelium est conditionale, quia peccata non remittuntur, nisi accedat paenitentia, sicut inquit textus: Agite paenitentiam. Item definite male facere. Item Christus inquit, Si vis in vitam ingredi serva mandata, respondeo breviter. Haec requisita non sunt conditio & causa propter quam datur reconciliatio, sed potius sunt affectus necessario sequentes. Et quod non sint causa propter quam datur remissio seu reconciliatio, inde apparet, quia peccatum remittitur vel concupiscentia, etiamsi adhuc re ipsa haereat in carne, et concupiscentia non est ociosa, sed gignit infinitos pravos affectus. Non igitur pendet remissio ex conditione impletae Legis, vel implendae, seu nostrae puritatis. Et tamen cum apprehenditur remissio fide, cum fides sit inchoatio novae & aeternae vitae, necesse est iam inchoari novam obedientiam. Quae etiamsi est imperfecta, tamen placet propter Christum. Item cum fides liberet à terroribus peccati necesse est existere terrores in nobis, sed illi terrores nequaquàm sunt precium aut causa remissionis peccatorum. Sed conscientia debet statuere quòd hoc beneficium gratis detur propter mediatorem & pontificem Christurm,

Sed hic obiici potest, si promissiones conditiaonales sunt irritae: Ergo omnes promissiones additae operibus sunt inutiles, quales sunt, Date & dabitur vobis. Frange esurienti panem & Dominus exaudiet te, &c. Respondeo promissio remissionis peccatorum & reconciliationis seu iustificationis, ac vitae aeternae propria est Evangelii, & gratis propter Christum exhibetur, non propter conditionem Legis aut operum. Haec promissio diligenter discerni debet à promissionibus legalibus, quae habent conditionem operum, quales sunt, Date & dabitur vobis. Si quis dederit tantum potum aquae, &c. non perdet mercedem suam. Honora patrem et matrem si vis longaevus esse super terram. Hae promissiones habent conditionem operum, & verae sunt inutiles & irritae sine promissione Evangelii, quia opera ipsa non placent Deo, nisi in reconciliatis. Sed postquàm fide per misericordiam gratis accepti sumus, postea placet inchoata obedientia, non propter propriam munditiem aut dignitatem, non quòd possit opponi Iudicio Dei, non quòd Legi satisfaciat, non quòd propter eam persona sit iusta, Sed persona est iusta, id est, accepta propter CHRISTUM per misericordiam. Ideo deinde placent opera, quia sumus filii sicut Paulus inquit, Iam non estis sub Lege sed sub gratia. Quanquàm igitur talia opera reipsa non sunt, impletio Legis, tamen cum placeant propter CHRISTUM, sunt velut quaedam impletio Legis. Ideo legales promissiones, id est, promissiones additae talibus operibus, iam siunt ratae & utiles reconciliatis. Haec est utilis doctrina de discrimine promissionum, & de usu legalium promissionum, ut sciamus quomodo sint ratae, & discamus etiam in his fidem exercere, quia promissione s sunt additae operibus, praecipue propter hanc causam ut ita operemur, ut simul fides petat & expectet à Deo beneficia spiritualia & corporalia, necessaria Rei pub. & nobis.

Declaratio minoris.

Minor syllogismi est, promiffio gratiae debet esse certa & rata. Primum enim quid fuisset opus aedere promissionem & revelare remissionem si nulla esset. Esset autem nulla si penderet ex conditione Legis, quia Legi nonnunquam satisfit. Imo ideo revelata est reconciliatio, quia Lege non poteramus consequi. Et ob hoc ipsum detracta est Legis conditio. Secundo dubitatio in animis parit desperationem, sicut supra dictum est Lex efficit iram. Ideo necesse est nobis promissionem esse notam, certam & ratam, ut opponatur dubitationi & sit efficax consolatio. Hoc loco necesse est reprehendi opinionem vulgarem, quae docet quod conscientia debeat dubitare de remissione peccatorum, & an Deus sit nobis propitius, & quod haec dubitatio non sit peccatum. Haeret quidem naturaliter in omnium animis dubitatio. Nam & caligo tanta est, ut securi animi etiam iram Dei contemnant, & de Iudicio dubitent, & deinde cum conscientia perturbatur, perpetuo accusat et condemnat. Fatemur igitur haerere dubitationem in animis, sed dicimus dubitationem illam peccatum esse illi et repugnandum esse, dubitationi. Ideo enim revelata est promissio, ut corrigat illam dubitationem, ut certam & firmam consolationem habeamus & certo statuamus nobis remitti, & nos exaudiri, et Evangelium sicut proponit promissionem ita expresse requirit fidem, ut illi ipsi promissioni credamus, ut Iohan. iii. Fides autem est contraria dubitationi. Item dubitatio accusat Deum mendacii, negat Deum veracem esse, &c. Quare & promissionem & mandatum de fide debemus opponere dubitationi, & discere quod dubitatio sit summum peccatum. Scholastici ideo imaginati sunt dubitationem non esse peccatum, quia viderunt eam naturaliter haerere in animis. Item prorsus non discernebant Legem ab Evangelio, nec consyderaverunt requiri fidem aut quid sit fides, quia imaginabantur fidem esse notitiam Legis. Itaque hac doctrina de dubitatione, vel quod iubent dubitare simpliciter, abolent totum Evangelium, promissionem & mandatum de fide. Quare repudianda est illa impia imaginatio, quae iubet dubitare.

Qui praeter spem sub spe cre-didit.

Sequitur amplificatio quae illustrat fidei naturam & exercitium. Ac semper illud tenendum est, quod supra dictum est, fidem primum complecti fiduciam, quae statuit nobis remitti peccata, & Deum nobis propitium esse propter Christum. Postea hanc ipsam fidem versari circa alia atque alia obiecta exteriora, ut fides Abrahae primum intuetur in hac ipsa promissione, semen promissum propter quod Deus benedicturus est generi humano. Deinde exerit se & expectat promissam posteritatem. Fides Moisi primum apprehendit misericordiam, postea expectat liberationem populi &c. Ita variant semper obiecta exteriora, & tamen unum commune obiectum est fidei principale, scilicet misericordia promissa propter Christum. Quare unusquisque & exuscitet fidem in suo periculo, in sua afflictione. Dixi autem illustrari hic naturam fidei, quia primum describitur obiectum, fidei obiectum proprium est verbum, quod pugnat cum externa specie, ut Abrahae promittitur semen & posteritas cui velit Deus benedicere, interim coniunx est sterilis, ipse est effoetus, Evangelium promittit pacem & vitam. Interim exercemur omni genere afflictionum, & in morte vita non conspicitur.

Ideo dicit hic Paulus: Abraham credidit contra spem in spem: contra spem, id est, contra obiectum propositum de quo desperandum erat: in spem, id est, in verbum in quod sperandum erat. Ita fides intuetur verbum & se verbo sustentat etiamsi externa species repugnat. Israelitis promittitur liberatio. Interim crescit acerbitas servitutis & sequuntur aliae maiores aerumnae. Sic nos etiam debemus in nostris periculis fidem exercere. Dixi de obiecto, nunc de formali fidei. Atque hic locus clare ostendit fidem à Paulo vocari fiduciam quae assentitur promissioni Evangelii, & pugnat cum dubitatione. Non igitur significat fides noticiam Legis aut tantum noticiam historiae, sed significat assentiri promissioni, non dubitare, quin Deus exhibiturus sit promissum. Estque hic locus observandus, ut opponatur illis qui fidem negant esse fiduciam pugnantem cum dubitatione. Nam hic expresse ponuntur quatuor descriptiones. De promissione non dubitavit, diffidentia: Item certus fuit, item dans gloriam Deo &c. Ita supra Paulus confert fidem & promissionem, & ostendit ea inter se connexa esse tanquam correlativa. Ergo certum est fide apud Paulum significari fiduciam quae assentitur promissioni Evangelii, & accipit promissam remissionem peccatorum, & reconciliationem. Item non dubium est Paulum loqui de fide agente aliquid in terroribus conscientiae & consolante conscientias, sicut infra inquit: Iustificati fide pacem habemus. Porro illa consolatio non fit noticia Legis aut noticia solius historiae, sed fiducia promissionis pugnante cum dubitatione. Omnia sunt plena tenebrarum & caliginis in doctrina Christiana, amissa hac propria significatione vocabuli fidei. Ideo hi loci Pauli diligenter sunt observandi, ut, quid proprie fides significet, certo iudicari & constitui possit, & ut refelli deliramenta illorum possint, qui negant fidem esse fiduciam pugnantem cum dubitione, sed imaginantur tantum esse noticiam hostoriae. Deinde nos etiam ad usum transferamus hanc descriptionem hic propositam & discamus hoc esse verum fidei exercitium, repugnare naturali dubitationi & diffidentiae, & illi opponere verbum seu promissionem, & petere, & expectare ut confirmemur â Deo, sicut ille ait Marci nono: Credo Domine, adiuva incredulitatem meam.

Tertio ornat Paulus fidem à caussa finali. Postquam enim descripsit eam qualis sit & quae sit eius natura, addit egregiam commendationem, quod sit cultus reddens Deo gloriam, id est, affirmans quod Deus sit potens & verax, quia non assentiens promissioni, dubitat an sit vera, imo negat esse veram. Accusat igitur Deum mendacii, sicut Ioannes inquit: Qui non credit Deo, mendacem facit eum. Econtra assentiens promissioni, statuit Deum esse veracem, potentem &c. Et ut magis intelligi possit, quod sine hac fide non tribuatur Deo ulla gloria, antithesis consideranda est. Ratio aut habet opiniones Epicureas de DEO quod sit ociosus, nec puniens nec salvans. Haec est prima contumelia descripta in Psalmo: Dixit insipiens in corde suo, non est Deus. Aut habet opiniones Legis de Deo, quod scilicet Deus salvet iustos, & quia non sumus iusti, reiecerit nos. Haec etiam est altera contumelia, quia sic sentiens de Deo, fugit Deum et fremit adversus Deum. Qui sic de Deo iudicant, non invocant Deum. Nihil à Deo expectant. Itaque non agnoscunt eum esse Deum, sed econtra credens promissioni gratiae, abiicit opiniones Epicureas, & opiniones Legis, & tribuit Deo gloriam, quod vere curet & diligat nos, quod non velit perdere, sed exaudire & salvare, iuxta promissionem, quanquam indignos. Itaque hac fide invocat & expectat à Deo auxilium & salutem. Tribuit igitur haec fides gloriam Deo, quod sit Deus, quod sit potens, id est, efficax, agens aliquid nobiscum, quod sit verax, quod sit misericors, quòd exaudiat, quòd salvet. Haec est gloria propria Dei, & haec fides parit invocationem & veros cultus spirituales. Hic necesse est admoneri auditores de illis, qui adversantur doctrinae fideri & iactitant se esse doctores bonorum operum. Hanc laudem isti falso sibi arrogant, quia tantum docent externa & civilia opera, interim non docent veros & interiores cultus scilicet exercitia fidei & invocationem. Haec opera sunt propria Christianorum. De his praecipue docendae sunt ecclesiae. Secundo, Omissa doctrina fidei, nec placent Deo alia opera, nec conscientiae possunt intelligere quomodo placeant. Ideo tales Doctores, qui omittunt doctrinam de hac fide, nequaquam docent de bonis operibus, sed de suis quibusdam operibus reiectis à Deo, quae cum proponunt tanquam cultus & transferunt in eos honorem debitum Christo, docent idolatrica. Huc pertinent illae conciones apud prophetas, ut Esaiae 41. Ecce omnes iniusti & vana opera eorum, ventus & inane simulachra eorum. Ideo in vera doctrina bonorum operum, cogitemus primum fidem & exercitia fidei requiri, quae sunt cultus qui proprie tribuunt Deo gloriam, & exerceamus invocationem in omni vita & omnibus negociis. Ita crescet ipsa fides & Deus dabit alia dona sicut promittit. Quanto magis pater vester dabit spiritum sanctum petentibus, inde existent etiam alia bona opera.

Non scriptum est autem pro-pter illum tantum, imputatum fu-isse illi, sed etiam &c.

Insignis locus est & duo continet. Primum quod haec iustitia de qua concionatur revelata sit de caelo, non sit nota ratione aut ex Lege. Secundo, quod exemplum iustificationis Abrahae ad omnes pertineat. Uterque locus continet egregiam doctrinam. Prior enim de revelatione, ostendit discrimen iustitiae Legis & imputationis, & deducit nos ad verbum ac promissionem, planeque idem docet, qoud Ioannes in illo dicto: Filius qui est in sinu patris ipse enarravit nobis, quia nec ratio nec Lex docet aut certos reddit, quod Deus remittat peccata, praesertim indignis. Item quòd pronunciet iustos quanquam non satisfacientes Legi. Est igitur haec promissio, quae est Evangelium, de remissione peccatorum, & imputatione iustitiae revelata divinitus, & est alia sententia, quàm doctrina legis & rationis. Quare diligenter hoc loco observandum est, quod inquit: Scriptum est, quod imputetur: quasi dicat: Haec voluntas de imputatione non est nota rationi sicut Lex, sed est alia sententia & nova revelatio. Deinde & illud considerandum est, quod deducit nos ad verbum. Non vult nos quaerere alias illuminationes, sed vult nos à verbo ordiri & verbo consolari conscientias & statuere quod haec sit certa & rara voluntas DEI, quae in verbo proponitur. Sunt igitur repudiandae Anabaptisticae & Manicheae imaginationes, quae quaerunt illuminationes sine verbo Dei & extra verbum Dei.

Secundo illud continet egregiam consolationem quod hocloco transfert exemplum iustificationis ad omnes, & primum docet Abraham esse formam populi Dei, ut sciamus caeteros iustos reputari, sicut ipse iustificatus est. Deinde illud est suavissimum, videre quod facit omnes pares Abrahae, quod attinet ad remissionem peccatorum, & imputationem iustitiae. Nam donorum est dissimilitudo. Sciant igitur omnes sic se diligi & iustos reputari, sicut testatur Deus se diligere & iustificare Abraham. Et quod in illo proposita sunt testimonia veri & magni amoris, id eò factum est, ut sciamus nos similiter diligi & exaudiri. Ad hunc usum accomodandus est hic locus Pauli, qui transfert ad nos exemplum Abrahae. Et huc referri debet, quod saepe dicimus inculcandum esse conscientiis, quod promissiones sint universales. Hoc cum ita sit, Deus postulat ac praecipit, ut omnes credant se pariter diligi & iustos reputari.

Postremo non satis est dicere de fide seu fiducia misericordiae. Sed necesse est mediatorem complecti: Ideo Paulus addiditimputari credentibus in eum, qui excitavit Iesum à mortibus, qui traditus est propter delicta nostra, & resuscitatus propter iusticiam nostram. Hic rursus habes argumentum quod fides significet non notitiam Legis, aut tantum historiae, sed significet fiduciam, quae apprehendit imputationem, quae fit propter mediatorem Christum passum & regnantem. Paulus discernit mortem & resurrectionem, & cum fit mentio resurrectionis intelligatur regnum & pontificatus Christi, nam ideo sumus Christi, quia Christus noster pontifex pro nobis interpellat apud patrem, ut reputet nos iustos: Item quia Christus vivit & regnat, dat spiritum sanctum & vivificat, liberat ab ira, & aeterna morte, resuscitabit mortuos. Ac fides utrunque apprehendit et applicat nobis, videlicet mortem Christi, & resuscitatum mediatorem, pontificem, vivificatorem. Mortem Christi apprehendit, utteneat victimam, quam statuat certum precium esse pro peccatis nostris, quia Deus voluit esse aliquam ultimam pro peccato. Et quidem ita irascitur peccato, ut nulla placuerit hostia nisi mors filii. Hoc ipsum testatur & iram Dei adversus peccatum ineffabilem esse, & misericordiam erga nos infinitam esse, quòd filium pro nobis fecit victimam. Est autem non solum mors Christi apprehendenda, sed etiam quod resuscitatus sit noster pontifex apud patrem, ut re exaudiat, verè sit efficax, verè vivificet, det spiritum sanctum, iuvet nos, liberet à morte aeterna, resuscitaturus sit mortuos & daturus novam & perpetuam vitam, sapientiam & iusticiam. Haec omnia Paulus complexus est, cum ait: resurrexit propter iusticiam nostram.

## 5:1 Argument
CHAPTER V.

Latin:

CAPUT V.

## 5:1
Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace.

It is an epilogue of the confirmation, which repeats the proposition, and adds an excellent amplification concerning the first effect of faith or concerning the proper prerogative which faith has; afterwards he attaches a consolation full of affections of the most bitter ones, which must always be kept in sight, and accommodated to bodily and spiritual afflictions. But I return to the beginning of the Epilogue, being justified by faith we have peace toward God, through our Lord Jesus Christ. For the sentence is, By faith we are reconciled and being reconciled we thereafter please God by the same faith, and we have peaceful consciences not on account of the fulfillment of the Law, but on account of Christ. But first this saying must be opposed to the Scholastic imagination, which feigns that the reborn are thereafter just on account of the fulfillment of the Law, and as they themselves speak, that the virtues and works of the reborn merit eternal life by condignity. Thus they destroy faith, and feign that there is no need for Christ the mediator for the reborn afterwards: this is to bury Christ again. Secondly, this saying must be used, so that it may instruct and console the pious who acknowledge their own infirmity, so that namely they may be recalled to Christ the mediator, and may learn that they are reputed just on account of Christ by faith, not on account of their own dignity. And so the infirmity which still clings in them is pardoned to them, nor are they just on account of that begun and imperfect obedience.

But by faith on account of CHRIST.

Thirdly, it must be observed again the testimony concerning justification. For he says here expressly, justified by faith. Fourthly, Origen twists this passage to peace among men, and to the duties of love, and corrupts the reading. Let us have peace, that is, let us be of placid character toward others. This interpretation is entirely untimely here. For Paul expressly says we have peace toward God. He speaks, therefore, of peace, that is, the consolation of the conscience toward God or liberation from fears. And the meaning is: God is no longer angry with us: And in turn we have tranquil consciences liberated from the terrors of sin and death. Here, therefore, it must be observed that the first and most proper effect of faith is to render the conscience peaceful or tranquil, or to be liberated from the terrors of sin and death. This consolation is the vivification of which Scripture speaks when it teaches us that we are vivified, as the just shall live by his faith. Now if we are liberated by faith from terrors, it is necessary that terrors and repentance exist in the pious.

Fifthly. This passage teaches that the opinion is false which commands one to doubt concerning the remission of sins, because this text says: peace we have. But a doubting conscience by no means has peace. Therefore, it is necessary that minds be raised up by faith against doubting. Sixth. This passage teaches that the imagination is false, which tears apart the remission of guilt and the remission of eternal punishment. For since in the remission of guilt we are made alive, and we obtain peace, that is, we are freed from the terrors of sin and eternal death, it is necessary that in the remission of guilt there be simultaneously a remission of eternal punishment, and that eternal punishment is not remitted on account of compensation in purgatory. Furthermore, the remission of guilt and the remission of temporal punishment in this life ought to be distinguished, and in the pious there exists peace and consolation of conscience, even if they are outwardly oppressed by bodily afflictions, as David retains faith and peace of conscience even when driven into exile. Seventh. The argument concerning justification is to be taken from here from the effect: We obtain remission and are justified only by that thing by which consciences are rendered peaceful before God. By faith alone they are rendered peaceful. Therefore, by faith alone we obtain remission and justification: The major premise is manifest, because justification is vivification. The minor premise is Paul's in this place, by faith we have peace, and it can be declared from the things above.

If faith were to rely partly on mercy, and partly on our own worthiness, it would become uncertain and would be shaken: For the exclusive term excludes worthiness. It does not teach this, that newness, or repentance, or contrition ought not to exist in us.

Eighth, there is a notable passage which says, through whom we have access by faith: For it teaches concerning the mediator and teaches how the mediator ought to be apprehended and what faith is, namely that sins are forgiven on account of the mediator Christ, that the Law is not fulfilled, nor does it please except on account of Christ. It also refutes the opinion of the monks, who even if they say that Christ is the mediator, nevertheless do not speak of the faith by which it is necessary to apprehend the mediator in the remission of sins, they only say that sins are forgiven on account of contrition, or other works, they do not teach that faith is necessary, that is, the confidence which determines that on account of Christ the mediator sins are forgiven us freely, just as he said above, whom he set forth as a propitiator through faith, so that we may know that the benefit of the mediator is applied to us by faith. Wherefore this passage is to be observed, so that it may be opposed to hypocritical opinions, which although they speak in appearance concerning the mediator, nevertheless in reality they take away the mediator, because they do not teach concerning this faith, which is the confidence applying to us the benefit of the mediator, or which relies upon the mediator and establishes that on account of him sins are freely remitted to us, etc.

Ninth, again in this place a testimony stands, that faith signifies the confidence of the mediator, or the confidence which apprehends grace, that is, mercy, because he says, by faith we have access into this grace. These things cannot be understood concerning the knowledge of history, but concerning the confidence apprehending grace, that is, gratuitous mercy, namely the remission of sins, and the imputation of righteousness. For this properly signifies grace in this place.

Latin:

Iustificati igitur ex fide, pacem habemus.

Epilogus est confirmationis, qui repetit propositionem, & addit egregiam amplisi cationem, de primo fidei effectu seu de propria praerogativa quam habet fides, postea attexit consolationem plenam affectuum acerrimorum, quae semper in conspectu habenda est, & accommodanda ad corporales & spirituales afflictiones. Sed redeo ad Epilogi principium, iustificati fide pacem habemus erga Deum, per Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum. Est enim sententia, Fide reconciliamur & reconciliati deinceps eadem fide placemus Deo, & habemus conscientias pacatas non propter Legis impletionem, sed propter Christum. Primum autem opponendum est hoc dictum imaginationi Scholasticae, quae fingit renatos deinde iustos esse propter impletionem Legis, & ut ipsi loquuntur, virtutes & opera renatorum mereri vitam aeternam de condigno. Ita delent fidem, & fingunt renatis postea nihil opus esse mediatore Christo: hoc est rursus sepelire Christum. Secundo usurpandum est hoc dictum, ut erudiat & consoletur pios agnoscentes suam infirmitatem, ut videlicet revocentur ad mediatorem Christum, & discant se iustos reputari propter Christum fide, non propter propriam dignitatem. Itaquè infirmitas quae adhuc in ipsis haeret, condonatur eis, nec sunt iusti propter illam inchoatam & imperfectam obedientiam.

Sed fide propter CHRISTUM.

Tertio observandum est rursus testimonium de iustificatione. Dicit enim hic disertè, iustificati fide. Quarto, Origenes detorquet hunc locum ad pacem egra homines, & ad officia dilectionis & depravat lectionem. Pacem habeamus, id est, simus placidis moribus erga alios. Haec sententia prorsus intempestiva hic est. Nam paulus disertè ait pacem habemus egra Deum. Loquitur igitur de pace, id est, consolatione conscientiae egra Deum seu liberatione à pavoribus. Estque sententia Deusiam non irascitur nobis: Et vicissim nos habemus tranquillas conscientias liberatas, à terroribus peccati & mortis. Hic igitur observandum est, primum & propriissimum effectum fidei esse, reddere pacatam seu tranquillam conscientiam, seu liberari à terroribus peccati et mortis. Haec consolatio est vivisicatio, de qua loquitur scriptura, cum docet nos vivificari, ut iustus ex fide sua vivet. Iam si fide liberamur à terroribus, necesse est existere in piis terrores & paenitentiam.

Quinto. Docet hic locus falsam esse opinionem, quae iubet dubitare, de remissione peccatorum, quia hic textus in quit: pacem habemus. At conscientia dubitans, nequaquàm habet pacem. Igitur fide erigi mentes contra dubitationem oportet. Sexto. Docet hic locus falsam esse imaginationem, quae divellit remissionem culpae & remissionem poenae aeternae. Cum enim in remissione culpae vivificamur, & pacem consequimur, hoc est, liberamur à terroribus peccati & mortis aeternae, necesse est inremissione culpae simul fieri remissionem, poenam aeternam, nec remitti poenam aeternam propter compensationem in purgatorio. Caeterum remissio culpae & remissio poenae temporalis in hac vita discerni debent, & in piis existit pax & consolatio conscientiae, etiamsi foris sunt oppressi afflictionibus corporalibus, ut David retinet fidem & pacem conscientiae etiam pulsus in exilium. Septimo. Argumentum de iustificatione hinc sumendum est ab effectu, Tantum illa re consequimur remissionem & iustificamur, qua conscientiae redduntur pacatae coram Deo. Sola fide redduntur pacatae. Ergo sola fide consequimur remissionem & iustificationem: Maior est manifesta, quia iustificatio est vivificatio. Minor est Pauli in hoc loco, fide pacem habemus, & potest declarari ex superioribus.

Si fides partim niteretur misericordia, partim nostra dignitate, fieret incerta & excuteretur: Nam exclusiva excludit dignitatem. Non hoc docet, quòd non debeant existere in nobis novitas, vel paenitentia vel contritio.

Octavo, Insignis locus est quod ait, per quem habemus accessum fide: Docet enim de mediatore & docet quomodo apprehendi debeat mediator & quid sit fides, videlicet quod peccata remittuntur propter mediatorem Christum, quod Lex non fiat, nec placeat nisi propter Christum. Refutat & opinionem monachorum, qui etiamsi dicunt Christum esse mediatorem, tamen non dicunt de fide, qua oportet apprehendi mediatorem in remissione peccatorum, tantum dicunt peccata remitti propter contritionem, vel alia opera, non docent fide opus esse, hoc est, fiducia quae statuat propter Christum mediatorem nobis remitti peccata gratis, sicut supra dixit, quem posuit propitiatorem per fidem, ut sciamus fide applicari nobis beneficium mediatoris. Quare hic locus observandus est, ut opponatur hypocriticis opinionibus, quae quanquàm in speciem dicunt de mediatore, tamen re ipsa tollunt mediatorem, quia non docent de hac fide, quae est fiducia applicans nobis beneficium mediatoris, seu quae nititur mediatore & statuit propter ipsum nobis gratis remitti peccata, &c.

Nono, Iterum hoc loco testimonium extat, quòd fides significet fiduciam mediatoris, seu fiduciam quae apprehendit gratiam, hoc est, misericordiam, quia inquit, fide habemus accessum in hanc gratiam. Haec non possunt intelligi de noticia historiae, sed de fiducia apprehendente gratiam, id est, gratuitam misericordiam, videlicet remissionem peccatorum, & imputationem iusticiae. Haec enim propriè significat hoc loco gratia.

## 5:2
We glory under the hope of the glory of God.

In the Epilogue they repeat the principal proposition concerning justification, and he admonished that just as we are justified by faith, so henceforth the saints ought to establish that they are righteous by faith, not on account of their own dignity. Now it could be asked, what kind therefore is that righteousness and liberation from sin and from death, when sin still clings in us, and we are liable to death: indeed we are oppressed by all calamities? What have believers obtained over other men as many mocked the Christians preaching liberation from sin and from death, since there is no kind of men more calamitous. Indeed, even the consciences of the saints, when they acknowledge their own infirmity, grieve and struggle, disputing with doubt whether they please God, since they are so infirm, nor is it a light temptation, because since faith ought to depend upon the Word, and to establish that God is certainly propitious on account of CHRIST, our infirmity attempts to comprehend this with eyes and sense. Therefore, the Anabaptists also revile the doctrine of faith, and say that other heavenly illuminations must be sought. And there are others who dream that they already have glory, that is, perfect obedience, and that they please GOD, for the reason that they satisfy the Law, and are without sin. Paul therefore meets both, he consoles the saints, who acknowledge their infirmity and commands them to glory, but in hope, and to establish that they have glory, that is, newness and eternal life, which even if it is not yet revealed, nevertheless is certain to us. Wherefore consciences ought to acquiesce, not to doubt and despair, even if they still feel infirmity, but he commands them to glory in hope, that is, they ought not to feel that they already have perfect newness, nor ought they to seek other illuminations, but to stand firm in the word and to establish that they are pleasing by faith on account of Christ, and that this newness is not yet perfect, because sin still clings to us. The sentiment is therefore, even if the world and our reason judge that we do not have glory, that is, liberation from sin and from death, nevertheless we glory, that is, we consider ourselves to have that glory with which God will glorify us, but as hoped for. We hold it still by hope, but nevertheless this hope is certain, it does not deceive. In the same manner he speaks to the Galatians: We through the Spirit by faith wait for the hope of righteousness, that is, even if we are still unclean, nevertheless we are pleasing by faith and we await perfect newness. Thus he teaches here that the saints do not yet have perfect newness, and yet in the meantime they are pleasing by faith and glory in hope, that is, in hope they would possess a new nature, eternal life, new wisdom, new righteousness.

Latin:

Gloriamur sub spe gloriae Dei.

In Epilogo repetunt principalem propositionem de iustificatione, et admonuit quod sicut fide iustificamur, ita deinceps sancti statuere debeant se fide iustos esse, non propter propriam dignitatem. Iam poterat interrogari, qualis igitur est ista iusticia et liberatio à peccato & à morte, cum adhuc haereat in nobis peccatum, et simus obnoxii morti: imo simus oppressi omnibus calamitatibus? Quid sunt consecuti credentes prae aliis hominibus sicut multi deriserunt Christianos praedicantes liberationem à peccaro & à morte, cum nullum genus hominum sit calamitosius. Imo et sanctorum conscientiae cum agnoscunt suam infirmitatem, dolent & luctantur, cum dubitatione disputantes an Deo placeant, cum adeo sint infirmi, nec est levis tentatio, quia cum fides ex verbo debeat pendere, & statuere quod Deus certo propitius sit propter CHRISTUM, nostra infirmitas hoc oculis & sensu comprehendere conatur. Ideo & Anabaptistae vituperant doctrinam fidei, & dicunt alias caelestes illuminationes quaerendas esse. Et sunt alii qui somniant se iam habere gloriam, id est, persectam obedientiam, & placere DEO, propterea quia Legi satisfaciant, & sint sine peccato. Occurrit igitur Paulus utrisque, consolatur sanctos, qui agnoscunt suam infirmitatem & iubet eos gloriari, sed spe, & statuere quod habeant gloriam, id est, novitatem & vitam aeternam, quae etiamsi nondum revelata est, tamen nobis certa est. Quare conscientiae debent acquiescere, non dubitare ac desperare, etiamsi adhuc sentiunt infirmitatem, sed iubet spe gloriari, id est, non debent sentire, quod habeant iam perfectam novitatem, nec debent alias illuminationes quaerere, sed resistere in verbo & statuere, quod fide placeant propter Christum, & quod haec novitas nondum sit perfecta, quod adhuc haereat in nobis peccatum. Est ergo sententia, etiamsi mundus & nostra ratio iudicant nos non habere gloriam, id est, liberationem à peccato & à morte, tamen nos gloriamur, id est, ducimus nos habere gloriam illam qua Deus nos glorificabit, sed speratam. Spe adhuc tenemus, sed tamen haec spes certa est, non fallit. Ad eundem modum loquitur ad Galatas: Nos spiritu ex fide spem iustitiae expectamus, id est, etsi adhuc immundi sumus, tamen fide placemus & expectamus perfectam novitatem. Ita hic docet quòd sancti nondum habeant perfectam novitatem, & tamen interim fide placeant & spe glorientur, id est, spe possiderent novam naturam, aeternam vitam, novam sapientiam, novam iustitiam.

## 5:3
And not only that, but we also glory &c.

He adds a correction. Nay, in reality we have glory not only hoped for but present. What is that? Afflictions. This necessary consolation he opposes to the judgments of the world and of reason. The world sees us afflicted as if deserted and rejected by GOD, and by this scandal it is deterred from the Gospel. Likewise, reason itself, according to the Law, judges afflictions to be curses, that is, evil things and signs of the wrath of God. Paul, on the contrary, teaches us concerning afflictions that they are not curses, but are glorious for us, that is, that they are not signs of the wrath of God, but signs of the good will of God. The meaning, therefore, is: we glory in afflictions, that is, we consider afflictions to be good things, not ignominious, not curses, not signs of wrath and rejection, and we consider enduring them to be a good work and a worship pleasing to God, not on account of their own dignity or perfection, but because the person is already accepted by faith, just as we have said elsewhere concerning begun obedience. The meaning, therefore, is: We have a double glory, the one primary, but still hoped for, that is, a new nature and eternal life, but this glory we still possess by hope; the other glory we have present, that is, afflictions. For although the world judges afflictions to be signs of the wrath of God, nevertheless We know that they are signs of the good will of God and obedience in afflictions, that they are a new worship of God.

Latin:

Nec id solum, verum etiam glo-riamur &c.

Addit correctionem. Imo reipsa gloriam habemus non tantum speratam sed praesentem. Quae est illa? afflictiones. Hanc necessariam consolationem opponit iudiciis mundi & rationis. Mundus videt nos affligi velut desertos & reiectos à DEO, & hoc scandulo deterretur ab Evangelio. Item ratio ipsa secundum Legem iudicat afflictiones esse maledictiones, id est, res malas & signa irae Dei. Paulus econtra docet nos de afflictionibus, quod non sint maledictiones, sed sint nobis gloriosae, id est, quod non sint signa irae Dei, sed signa bonae voluntatis Dei. Est ergo sententia, gloriamur in afflictionibus, id est, ducimus afflictiones esse res bonas, non ignominiosas, non maledictiones, non signa irae & reiectionis, & fustinere eas, ducimus esse opus bonum & cultum Deo placentem, non propter propriam dignitatem aut perfectionem, sed quia fide persona iam est accepta, sicut aliâs de inchoata obedientia diximus. Est ergo sententia: Habemus duplicem gloriam, alteram praecipuam, sed adhuc speratam, id est, novam naturam & vitam aeternam, sed hanc gloriam adhuc spe possidemus, alteram gloriam habemus praesentem, id est, afflictiones. Tametsi enim mundus ludicat afflictiones esse signa irae Dei, tamen nos scimus esse signa bonae voluntatis Dei & obedientiam in afflictionibus, esse novum cultum Dei.

## 5:3
Knowing that affliction produces patience, and patience indeed probation.

Since he had said before that our present glory is afflictions, because as long as we die this life is a perpetual struggle, and the flesh is subject to afflictions so that the remnants of sin may be mortified. The Law judges these mortifications to be curses and signs of wrath, but the Gospel on the contrary teaches that they have been transferred into another form, namely, that they may be signs of the good will of God. Therefore he now speaks consolation in this sentiment, and preaches on the end and use of afflictions. Paul weaves together a gradation. Afflictions produce patience, patience probation, probation hope etc. These words in sum mean this, that afflictions are exercises of faith or hope, and that God requires obedience, and faith or hope in afflictions: Therefore they are not signs of wrath. This is the sum of this opinion, but before we treat the individual words, the doctrine concerning afflictions must first be considered. There are, however, four precepts which it is necessary to know concerning afflictions.

The first, which must be established, is that we are not afflicted by chance, but by the certain counsel and permission of God.

The second, it must not only be established that afflictions happen by the counsel of God, but it must also be added that God punishes, not that He may destroy, but that He may recall us to repentance, or that He may exercise our faith, and that afflictions are not signs of wrath, but of the good will of God, according to that: I do not desire the death of the sinner. And it is profitable in these precepts to have as many testimonies as possible at hand.

The third precept, that God requires obedience in afflictions, and that indignation and impatience are sin, and that God has especially subjected us to afflictions, and that this obedience must be performed on account of God.

Fourth, it is not enough to offer obedience, but more is required, namely faith and invocation, by which we seek and expect help, according to that saying: Call upon me in the days of tribulation, etc. These four precepts must be held in all afflictions, and the knowledge of these produces true Christian patience, which differs from philosophical patience. For philosophical patience is obedience toward reason in enduring adverse things for some honorable cause. But Christian patience is obedience which is offered on account of God, and to which is added faith or hope and the expectation of help. I have repeated these things briefly, so that the opinion of Paul might be more easily understood from them. Now I return to the text. Tribulation brings about patience. These words ought not to be understood only in the manner of the Law, that obedience is required in afflictions, but also as a consolation. For since God demands patience and hope, it is manifest that afflictions are not signs of wrath, but exercises in which God wishes to exercise our obedience and faith. For by the judgment of the Law or of reason, affliction does not bring about patience, but indignation, by which weak nature rages against God and becomes angry, because this weak nature is burdened and flees them as much as he can, but by the judgment of the Gospel affliction brings patience, when clearly the mind recognizes these to be signs of the good will of God, and that in these exercises faith and invocation must be stirred up.

Latin:

Scientes quòd asflictio patien-tiam pariat, patientia vero proba-tionem.

Cum antea dixisset praesentem gloriam nostram esse afflictiones, quia donec morimur haec vita est perpetuum certamen, & caro subiecta est afflictionibus ut reliquiae peccati mortificentur. Has mortificationes Lex iu dicat esse maledictiones & signa irae, sed Evangelium econtra docet, translatas esse in aliam formam, videlicet, ut sint signa bonae voluntatis Dei. Ideo iam ait consolationem in hanc sententiam, & concionatur define & usu afflictionum. Paulus gradationem contexit. Afflictiones patientiam efficiunt, patientia probationem, probatio spem &c. Haec verba in summa, hoc volunt, quod afflictiones sint exercitia fidei seuspei, & quod Deus requirit obedientiam, & fidem seu spem in afflictionibus: Non sunt igitur signa irae. Haec est summa huius sententiae, sed priusquam singula verba tractamus, prius doctrina de afflictionibus consideranda est. Sunt autem quatuor praecepta, quae de afflictionibus, scire necesse est.

Primum, quod statuendum est nos non affligi casu, sed certo consilio & permissione Dei.

Secundum, non solum statuendum est afflictiones Dei consilio accidere, sed etiam addendum est, quod Deus puniat, non ut perdat, sed ut revocet nos ad paenitentiam, seu ut exerceat fidem nostram, quodque affli ctiones non fint signa irae, sed bonae voluntatis Dei, iuxta illud: Nolo mortem peccatoris. Et prodest in his praeceptis habere in promptu quàmplurima testimonia.

Tertium praeceptum, quod Deus requirat obedientiam in afflictionibus, & quod indignatio & impatientia sint peccatum, & quod praecipue Deus subiecerit afflictionibus, & quod haec obedientia propter Deum praestanda sit.

Quartum, Non satis est obedientiam praestare, sed plus requiritur, videlicet fides & invocatio, qua auxilium petimus, & expectamus, iuxta illud: Invoca me in diebus tribulationis, &c. Haec quatuor praecepta tenenda sunt in omnibus afflictionibus, & horum cognitio parit veram patientiam Christianam, quae differt à philosophica. Nam philosophica, est obedientia erga rationem in perferendis adversis rebus ex aliqua honesta causa. Sed patientia Christiana est obedientia, quae prestatur propter Deum, & ad quam accedit fides seu spes & expectatio auxilii. Haec breviter repetivi, quod inde facilius intelligi possit sententia Pauli. Nunc ad textum redeo. Tribulatio affert patientiam. Haec verba non tantum more Legis intelligi debent, quod in afflictionibus requiratur obedientia, sed etiaam tanquam consolatio. Nam cum Deus patientiam & spem exigat, manifestum est afflictiones non esse signa irae, sed exercitia in quibus Deus vult obedientiam & fidem nostram exercere. Nam Iudicio Legis seu rationis afflictio non affert patientiam, sed indignationem, qua natura infirma fremit adversus Deum & irascitur, quod haec infirma natura tantis calamitatibus oneratur & fugit eas quantum potest, sed iudicio Evangelii afflictio affert patientiam, cum videlicet mens agnoscit esse signa bonae voluntatis Dei, & in his exercitiis excitandam esse fidem & invocationem.

## 5:4
Patience [brings] probation.

That is, exercise [brings] exploration, in which faith is stirred up, so that it may not be idle, not feigned, but true, nor grow languid, etc. Thus also Peter says: Your faith after it has been proved may be found unto praise, that is, after it has been exercised, so that it might be true and not feigned. Therefore the end of afflictions is described here, as if he were saying: Afflictions are not signs of wrath for this reason, because they are probations, that is, exercises in which faith is stirred up and confirmed. And we experience true consolation and true struggle. As Isaiah says: The cry in distress is your discipline to them, because in idleness and pleasures there is no struggle of faith, therefore it grows languid and is extinguished. Likewise there is no serious invocation, etc.

Latin:

Patientia probationem.

Id est, exercitium explorationem, in qua exuscitatur fides, ut non sit ociosa, non simulata, sed vera, nec languescat &c. Sic etiam Petrus inquit: Fides vestra postquam probata est inveniatur ad laudem, id est, postquam exercitata est, ut esset vera & non simulata. Describitur ergo hic finis afflictionum, quasi dicat: Ideo afflictiones non sunt signa irae, quia sunt probationes, id est, exercitia in quibus fides excitatur & confirmatur. Et nos veram consolationem & verum certamen experimur. Sicut Esaias inquit: Clamor in angustia, est eis disciplina tua, quia in ocio & voluptatibus non est certamen aliquod fidei, ideo languescit & extinguitur. Item nulla seria invocatio est &c.

## 5:4
And probation [brings] hope.

That is, in that exercise faith and hope are stirred up and confirmed. For although the movements of faith and hope are near, and are not torn apart from one another, yet there is some difference. Faith is the confidence by which we receive the remission of sins in the present, and we determine that we now have a propitious God, and in the present we console ourselves with this mercy. And the object is God apprehended in the word by which remission is exhibited, but hope is the expectation of future liberation and determines not only concerning present mercy, but also concerning the future outcome. He says these movements grow in that exercise and patience does not behave itself as a merit, upon which hope might depend, but it behaves itself as an occasion for exercise. For then faith and hope exist, when in the affliction itself they resist doubt and desperation, nor does patience precede hope, but Paul wishes hope to be in that very struggle, which struggle is patience obeying God and awaiting liberation. And faith and hope depend upon the gratuitous promise, otherwise they would become uncertain.

Furthermore, hope does not put to shame.

The phrase is Hebrew, hope does not confound, that is, it does not frustrate the one hoping. This is the genuine interpretation of the word to confound, to be frustrated, as elsewhere: No one has hoped and been confounded, that is, frustrated. Moreover, the sentiment is similar to that saying which is recounted in the ninth chapter: Everyone who believes in God will not be confounded, but someone might say: Why is hope not frustrated, what if we are unworthy? Concerning this objection it is necessary for the pious to be admonished, because this very objection is the intensification of the struggle concerning faith and hope, namely whether God wills to save the unworthy. Here the exclusive must be held that freely on account of Christ He wills to save us, although we are unworthy. And thus finally the passages concerning faith and hope aid consciences, when in them this exclusive is understood. It must also be considered that concerning the remission of sins, and concerning eternal life, there is an express command of God, that we believe in the remission and hope for eternal life. Here we ought to believe and hope without condition. Concerning bodily afflictions, liberation is sought with a condition, if it pleases God.

That the love of God has been poured out.

The reason for the consequence seems to be obscure. Hope does not confound because the love of God has been poured out. The consequence would seem less obscure if he said it thus: hope does not confound, because the promise is certain and ratified. For this reason is taken from the proximate efficient cause, namely from the nearest object, and the thing itself says this, but it adds something. For the sentiment is, hope does not confound for this reason, because God certainly loves us. And we apprehend this love by the very motion of faith, by which the Holy Spirit is efficacious. For the cause of hope is that God loves us. But this love is not apprehended except by the word. Therefore, the love of God in this place signifies the love by which God loves us. And it is the simplest and least intricate interpretation, and useful for consciences. Hope does not confound, because the promise is certain and ratified, in which we apprehend the love of God toward us. This is the plain sentiment and it contains a most grave doctrine, such as what the motions of faith and hope are, namely that they are struggles in which the conscience is raised up, and they establish that we are loved by God. For this is the highest and most difficult article, which the mind cannot retain without great conflict, because it is the very voice of the Gospel, that God loves us on account of Christ, even if we are unworthy, unclean. The Son who is in the bosom of the Father revealed this voice. But human hearts are so oppressed by diffidence, that they not only do not see this the will of the Father, but also that they greatly abhor this voice. Here, therefore, let us learn what kind of motions faith and hope are, which clearly lift up souls with this consolation, so that they may establish that we are loved by God. The sentence below teaches the same: You have received the spirit in which we cry Abba Father.

Secondly, it is also to be observed here that these motions, faith and hope, arise from the Holy Spirit. Monks invert this sentence and attach a reason for the consequence from the cause of hope in this way. Hope does not confound, because we have love, that is, because we love God. Thus they argue from merit; once merit or price is posited, the event is posited. This interpretation is foreign to the sentence of Paul, and the conscience would be overturned if it were to judge thus, that one must hope on account of merit. For the promise would become conditional and uncertain: Therefore, our quality is not the cause of hope, but it must be known that the cause of hope is the gratuitous promise, which shows the benefit of Christ and the love of God toward us on account of Christ, wherefore the interpretation of the monks is to be rejected. Furthermore, if anyone should attach it thus: Hope does not confound, because we have the earnest, the Holy Spirit, it does not displease me the connection, and it is a place of the affections of the promises, and from the helping cause, as if he were saying thus: Now we have the beginning and the firstfruits of eternal life, namely the Holy Spirit, who also consoles and helps us, and is the pledge of future glorification. But here it must be known that, nevertheless, our quality is not to be looked at, but consolation is to be sought in the word. For the Holy Spirit is effective through the word only in this way, he does not precede the word.
