And so he is present, he helps us in such a way that we apprehend the love of God, when we sustain ourselves with the word. This interpretation agrees with the first. For it is the meaning. Hope does not confound, because when we apprehend the word, the Holy Spirit is at the same time effective and helps us, so that in the word we may apprehend the love of God toward us. But it can be attached more plainly thus: Hope does not confound, because God loves you, and this you have already apprehended through the Holy Spirit, you certainly establish that he loves you: Therefore hope that he will do good to you. And it is a place from causes, because to know that he loves, is a cause for hoping. This meaning again warns that faith signifies trust in mercy, because Paul says so, through the Holy Spirit you have apprehended the love of God, that is, that God loves you: Therefore faith is the confidence that God loves us, because faith is to apprehend that. Likewise, this passage warns that those who command one to doubt concerning the remission of sins do not teach correctly.

Latin:

Probatio aute spem.

Id est, in illo exercitio fides & spes exuscitantur & confirmantur. Etsi enim sunt vicini motus fides & spes, & à se non divelluntur, tamen aliquid interest. Fides est fiducia, qua in praesentia accipimus remissionem peccatorum, & statuimus iam nos habere Deum propicium, & in praesentia consolamur nos hac misericordia. Estque obiectum Deus apprehensus in verbo quo exhibetur remissio, sed spes est expectatio futurae liberationis & statuit non solum de praesenti misericordia, sed etiam de futuro eventu. Hos motus ait crescere in illo exercitio & patientia non habet se ut meritum, ex quo pendeat spes, sed habet se sicut occasio exercitii. Tunc enim existunt fides & spes, cum in ipsa afflictione repugnant dubitationi & desperationi, nec patientia praecedit spem, sed Paulus vult in illo ipso certamine esse spem, quod certamen est patientia obediens Deo & expectans linerationem. Et fides & spes pendent ex gratuita promissione, alioqui fierent incerta.

Porro spes non pudefacit.

Phrasis est Hebraica, spes non consundit, id est, non frustratur sperantem. Haec est germana interpretatio verbi confundere, frustrari, ut alibi: Nullus speravit & confusus est, id est, frustratus est. Est autem similis sententia illi dicto quod recensetur capite nono: Omnis qui credit in Deum non confundetur, sed dicat aliquis: Quare spes non frustratur, quid si simus indigni? De hac obiectione necesse est admoneri pios, quia haec ipsa obiectio est epitasis certaminis de fide & spe, videlicet an velit Deus indignos salvare. Hic tenenda est exclusiva quod gratis propter Christum velit nos salvare. quanquam simus indigni. Atque ita demum loci de fide & spe, iuvant conscientias, cum in illis haec exclusiva intelligitur. Considerandum est etiam, quòd de remissione peccatorum, & de vita aeterna expresfum mandatum Dei est, ut credamus remissionem & speremus vitam aeternam. Hic sine conditione credere, & sperare debemus. De corporalibus afflictionibus, liberatio cum conditione petitur, si placet Deo.

Quod dilectio Dei effusa sit.

Videtur obscura esse ratio consequentiae. Spes non confundit quia dilectio Dei effusa est. Minus videretur obscura consequentia si sic diceret: spes non confundit, quia promissio missio est certa & rata. Nam haec ratio sumitur ex causa efficiente propinqua, videlicet ex proximo obiecto, ac re ipsa hoc dicit, sed addit aliquid. Est enim sententia, spes ideo non confundit, quia Deus certo diligit nos. Et hanc dilectionem apprehendimus ipso motu fidei, quo spiritus sanctus est efficax. Nam causa spei est, quod Deus diligit nos. Sed haec dilectio non apprehenditur nisi verbo. Significatigitur dilectio Dei hocloco, dilectionem qua Deus nos diligit. Estque simplicissima & minimè intricata interpretatio, & utilis conscientiis. Spes non confundit, quia promissio est certa & rata, in qua apprehendimus dilectionem Dei erga nos. Haec est plana sententia & gravissimam doctrinam continet, quales sint motus fidei & spei, scilicet quod sint certamina in quibus conscientia erigitur, & statuunt nos diligi à Deo. Hic enim est sūus & difficilimus articulus, quem retinere mens sine magna dimicatione non potest, quia est ipsissima vox Evangelii, quòd Deus diligat nos propter Christum, & si sumus indigni, immundi. Hanc vocem revelavit filius qui est in sinu patris. Sed humana corda ita oppressa sunt diffidentia, ut non solum non videant hanc voluntatem patris, sed etiam ab hac voce valde abhorreant. Hic igitur discamus quales motus sint fides & spes, qui videlicet hac consolatione erigunt animos, ut statuant nos diligi à Deo. Idem docet sententia infra: Accepistis spiritum in quo clamamus Abba pater.

Secundo etiam hic observandum est, quod hi motus, fides, spes oriantur à spiritu sancto. Monachi invertunt hanc sententiam, & attexunt rationem consequentiae ex causa spei, hoc modo. Spes non confundit, quia habemus dilectionem, id est, quia diligimus Deum. Ita argumentantur ex merito, posito merito seu precio, ponitur eventus. Haec interpretatio aliena est à Pauli sententia, & conscientia everteretur si sic iudicaret, sperandum esse propter meritum. Fieret enim conditionalis & incerta promissio: Non igitur est causa spei nostra qualitas, sed sciendum est causam spei esse promissionem gratuitam, quae ostendit beneficium Christi, & dilectionem Dei erga nos propter Christum, quare repudianda est monachorum interpretatio. Caeterum si quis sic attexat: Spes non confundit, quia habemus arrabonem spiritum sanctum, non displicet & mihi connexio, estque locus affectuum promissionum, & à causa adiuvante, quasi sic dicat: Iam habemus inchoationem & primitias vitae aeternae, scilicet spiritum sanctum, qui nos etiam consolatur & adiuvat, & est pignus futurae glorificationis. Sed hic sciendum est, quòd tamen non sit inspicienda nostra qualitas, sed quaerenda est consolatio in verbo. Nam spiritus sanctus ita demum est efficax per verbum, non praecurrit verbum. Itaque sic adest, sic adiuvat nos, ut apprehendamus dilectionem Dei, cum verbo nos sustentamus. Haec interpretatio cum prima congruit. Est enim sententia. Spes non confundit, quia cum apprehendimus verbum, spiritus sanctus simul est efficax & adiuvat nos, ut in verbo apprehendamus dilectionem Dei erga nos. Sed planius potest sic attexi: Spes non confundit, quia Deus diligit vos, & hoc iam apprehendistis per spiritum sanctum, vos certo statuitis quod diligat vos: Ergo sperate eum vobis benefacturum esse. Et est locus ex causis, quia scire quod diligit, est causa sperandi. Haec sententia rursus monet quod fides significet fiduciam misericordiae, quia Paulus ita inquit, per spiritum sanctum apprehendistis dilectionem Dei, id est, quod Deus diligat vos: Ergo fides est fiducia quod Deus diligat nos, quia fides est illud apprehendere. Item monet hic locus quòd non rectè doceant hi, qui iubent dubitare de remissione peccatorum.

## 5:6
For Christ, when we were yet weak according to the measure of time.

There follows an amplification, which gathers signs and testimonies that God loves us, namely that highest and ineffable benefit, namely that He gave His Son for us, and indeed He willed this very thing to be a certain pledge of true and immutable love. He amplifies this love with a double comparison: Scarcely for a just man does anyone die, that is, even when we ought to die, nevertheless we meet death unwillingly. As a thief dies unwillingly, even if he owes death to the Laws. Understand therefore the words of Paul for a just man, that is, for a just matter, or a just cause, or a debt. The other comparison is, for a good man perhaps someone dares to die, that is, for a good and pleasant thing, that is, incited by desire, or an opinion of utility, we more easily undertake dangers, as for the defense of a spouse, children, or dignity, a brave man meets death, etc. From these two propositions he argues and amplifies the love of God and of Christ, from a comparison of causes. If anyone does well, especially by laying down his life, when he neither owes it nor is moved by any desire of his own, it is necessary that this person be moved by a great force of love: because even those who owe penalties to the Laws die unwillingly: and others, if any meet death, are moved by some opinion of utility. Christ died for us when he did not owe it to us, nor was he moved by any utility of his own: Therefore it is necessary that there be a huge and ineffable force of love toward us, afterwards he amplifies from the lesser. If he died for the unjust, how much more will he now save the just: and it is a necessary consolation for those who, although they have been sanctified, nevertheless see that they still have remnants of sin, and are liable to terrors and fears. Also to be immersed in the harshest and most horrible calamities, and they struggle with diffidence, desperation, etc. Here they have need of this doctrine and consolation, that although they are unworthy, unclean, nevertheless they are pleasing by faith freely on account of Christ, just as he said above, justified by faith we have peace. Also we have access by faith into this grace, in which we stand. Also, then the death and resurrection of Christ are a pledge that God wills to free them.

Latin:

Christus enim, cum essemus ad-huc infirmi iuxta temporis rationem.

Sequitur amplificatio, quae colligit signa & testimonia quod Deus diligat nos, scilicet illud summum beneficium & ineffabile, scilicet quod dedit filium pro nobis, et quidem voluit hoc ipsum esse certum pignus verae & immutabilis dilectionis. Hunc amorem amplificat duplici collatione: Vix pro iustare aliquis moritur, id est, etiam cum debemus mori, tamen inviti oppetimus mortem. Ut fur invitus moritur, etiamsi debet mortem Legibus. Intellige igitur verba Pauli pro iusto, id est, re iusta, seu causa iusta, seu debito. Altera collatio est, pro bono ausit aliquis mori, id est, pro bona & suavi re, id est, incitati cupidtate, aut opinione utilitatis facilius suscipimus pericula, ut ad defensionem coniugis, liberorum, aut dignitatis, vir fortis mortem oppetit, &c. Ex his duabus propositionibus argumentatur & amplificat dilectionem Dei & Christi, à collatione causarum. Si quis bene facit praesertim vitam impendens, cum neque debet neque movetur aliqua sua cupiditate, hunc necesse est adduci magna vi amoris: quia etiam qui debent poenas Legibus inviti moriuntur: & alii si qui mortem oppetunt moventur aliqua opinione utilitatis. Christus pro nobis mortuus est cum nobis non deberet, neque aliqua sua utilitate moveretur: Ergo necesse est ingentem & ineffabilem vim esse amoris erga nos, postea amplificat ex minore. Si pro iniustis mortuus est, quanto magis iam iustos salvabit: estque consolatio necessaria his, qui cum sint sanctificati, tamen vident se adhuc habere reliquias peccati, & obnoxios esse terroribus & pavoribus. Item immergi asperrimis & horribilibus calamitatibus, & luctantur cum diffidentia, desperatione, &c. Hic habent opus hac doctrina & consolatione, quod quanquàm sint indigni, immundi, tamen placeant fide gratis propter Christum, sicut supra dixit, iustificati fide pacem habemus. Item habemus accessum fide in gratiam hanc, in qua stamus. Item, tunc mors & resurrectio Christi sunt pignus, quòd Deus velit eos liberare.

## 5:11
Glorying in God, through our Lord Jesus.

With singular counsel and emphasis the particle glorying in God, through our Lord Jesus Christ is added. For again he inculcates the doctrine most necessary of all, namely how the conscience is rendered certain. For especially in true afflictions our unworthiness clamors against us, we dispute whether we are certainly heard, whether God certainly wills to provide those things which are promised in the Gospel. &c. To these doubts Paul opposes this particle Glorying in God, &c. For to glory is to feel that we have glory, that is, righteousness, wisdom, that is, for the conscience to truly and certainly establish that it pleases God. But he adds, glorying in God, through our Lord Jesus Christ. Here he teaches concerning the cause of this glory and certainty, as if to say: We do not glory, we do not please on account of our own dignity, but we glory in God, that is, we feel that we have glory, and that we are just through the mercy of God on account of Christ. Therefore, it teaches in summary that even the reborn should conclude that they certainly please God on account of Christ freely, not on account of their own dignity or the fulfillment of the Law. Just as he also says to the Corinthians: That no flesh should glory in his sight. Likewise, He who glories, let him glory in the Lord, that is, let him conclude that he pleases God on account of His promise, not on account of our dignity. This sentiment must always be kept in view, so that its honor may be attributed to Christ, that He is always the mediator. Likewise, so that we may understand our own unworthiness, and yet the conscience may have firm consolation, namely that it is the command of God that we believe that we have the remission of sins, and that we please and are heard on account of Christ. But what he added above, we glory in afflictions, it was said elsewhere concerning begun obedience, that it is not glory, that is, justice, which can be opposed to the Judgment of God, in which there is no vice, or on account of which we are just and have the remission of sins. Therefore, this sentiment remains firm. He who glories, let him glory in the Lord. But after we have been reconciled by faith and conclude that we please through the mercy on account of Christ. Then, an initial and imperfect obedience of worship and glory is brought about, not indeed to be opposed to the Judgment of God: But God approves it, because we have been made sons.

Ανάλυσις follows.

Latin:

Gloriantes in Deo, per domi-num nostrum Iesum.

Singulari consilio & emphasi adiecta est particula gloriantes in Deo, per Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum. Iterum enim inculcat doctrinam omnium maximè necessariam, videlicet quomodo conscientia reddatur certa. Nam praesertim in veris afflictionibus obstrepit nobis indignitas nostra, disputamus utrum certo exaudiamur, utrum certo Deus velit praestare illa quae promittuntur in Enangelio. &c. His dubitationibus opponit Paulus hanc particulam Gloriantes in Deo, &c. Nam gloriari est sentire quod habeamus gloriam, id est, iusticiam, sapientiam, id est, conscientiam vere & certo statuere quod placeat Deo. Sed addit, gloriantes in Deo, per Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum. Hic docet de causa huius gloriae & certitudinis q. d. Non gloriamur, non placemus propter propriam dignitatem, sed in Deo gloriamur, id est, sentimus nos habere gloriam, ac iustos esse per misericordiam Dei propter Christum. Docet igitur in summa etiam renatos statuere, quod certo placeant propter Christum gratis, non propter propriam dignitatem seu impletionem Legis. Sicut & ad Corinthios inquit: Ut ne glorietur coram eo omnis caro. Item, Qui gloriatur in Domino glorietur, id est, statuat se placere Deo propter ipsius promissionem, non propter nostram dignitatem. Haec sententia semper in conspectu habenda est, ut Christo suus honos tribuatur, quod semper sit mediator. Item ut intelligamus nostram indignitatem, & tamen conscientia habeat firmam consolationem, quod scilicet sit mandatum Dei, ut credamus nos habere remissionem peccatorum, & placere & exaudiri propter Christum. Quod vero supra addidit, gloriamur in afflictionibus, dictum est aliâs de inchoata obedientia, quod non sit gloria, id est, iusticia, quae possit opponi Iudicio Dei, in qua nihil sit vitii, seu propter quam sumus iusti & habeamus remissionem peccatorum. Manet ergo haec sententia firma. Qui gloriatur in Domino glorietur. Sed postquam fide reconciliati sumus & statuimus nos placere per misericordiam propter Christum. Deinde ftt inchoata & imperfecta obedientia cultus & gloria, non quidem opponenda Iudicio Dei: Sed Deus approbat eam, quia sumus facti filii.

Ανάλυσις sequitur.

## 5:12
Therefore, just as through one man.

The upper part of the Epistle is contention. For a proposition was instituted and confirmed by arguments. Now there follows as it were a new book, for argumentation is not instituted here, but a certain ἀνάλυσις of the individual parts, of which mention was made above. For the previous disputation contains these propositions: All men are under sin. Item, Men are not righteous by the Law, because no one satisfies the Law. Item, By faith on account of Christ through grace we are reckoned righteous. In these propositions are simple members, sin, Law, grace. Moreover, this ἀνάλυσις is in teaching, both customary and necessary: as when a physician disputes whether veins, arteries, and nerves are born from the heart, surely it is necessary for the unskilled to be taught how differ. veins, nerves, and arteries. Such an explanation of parts is called analysis.

Thus also Paul, after the contention, now returns to the propositions, and he selects individual members and explains them, and compares them among themselves. This comparison brings a great deal of light to the preceding propositions, because definitions and causes are the sources of matters. But first he speaks here of sin. Then of the Law; thirdly, of grace. These are the principal places of Christian doctrine, which in the church it is necessary to exist, the knowledge of which is necessary for all. Paul, however, does not distinguish the designations of original and actual sin, because he embraces both the root and the fruits, even if he speaks properly about the propagation of original sin, yet sometimes he also distinguishes them, as when he names sin and the fruits of sin. There was, however, a need in the church for new designations to avoid ambiguities.

Latin:

Propterea, quemadmodum propter unum hominem.

Superior pars Epistolae est contentio. Fuit enim instituta propositio & confirmata argumentis. Nunc sequitur velut novus liber, Non enim instituitur hic argumentatio, sed quaedam ἀνάλυσις singularum partium, de quibus supra facta est mentio. Nam disputatio superior continet has propositiones: Omnes homines sunt sub peccato. Item, Homines non sunt iusti Lege, quia nemo Legi satisfacit. Item, Fide propter Christum per gratiam reputamur iusti. In his propositionibus sunt simplicia membra, peccatum, Lex, gratia. Est autem haec ἀνάλυσις in docendo, & usitata, & necessaria: ut cum medicus disputat an venae, arteriae & nervi nascantur ex corde, profecto opus est doceri imperitos quid differant venae, nervi et arteriae. Talis enarratio partium vocatur analysis.

Ita & Paulus post contentionem iam redit ad propositiones, & singula membra excerpit eaque enarrat, & inter se confert. Haec collatio plurimum affert lucis superioribus propositionibus, quia definitiones & caussae, sunt fontes negociorum. Primum autem hic de paccato loquitur. Deinde Lege, tertio, de gratia. Hi sunt praecipui loci doctrinae Christianae, quos in ecclesia extare oportet, quorum cognitio omnibus necessaria est. Paulus autem non discernit appellationes peccati originalis & actualis, quia radicem & fructus complectitur, etsi proprie de propagatione peccati originalis loquitur, interdum tamen etiam discernit ut cum nominat peccatum & fructus peccati. Fuit autem opus in ecclesia novis appellationibus ad vitandas ambiguitates.

## 5:12
Sin entered into the world.

That Paul speaks of the sin of origin is manifest, because he speaks of the sin on account of which all men are guilty, as he says a little later: In that all have sinned, that is, are guilty. Item: By the offense of one, condemnation reached unto all: Item, by the disobedience of one man, many were made sinners. Now, if there were only actual offenses, each one would only be guilty of his own offense. But here Paul testifies that all are guilty on account of one Adam. Therefore, there is another sin besides the actual one.

Latin:

Peccatum in mundum introiit.

Quod loquatur Paulus de peccato originis manifestum est, quia loquitur de peccato propter quod omnes homines rei sunt, sicut paulò post dicit: Eo quod omnes peccaverunt, id est, rei sunt. Item: Per unius delictum condemnatio pervasit in omnes: Item propter inobedientiam unius peccatoris facti sunt alii. Iam si tantum essent actualia delicta, unusquisque tantum reus esset sui delicti. Nunc testatur hic Paulus omnes reos esse propter unum Adam. Ergo est aliud peccatum praeter actuale.

## 5:13
For until the Law, sin was in the world.

He does not only mean that sin was in the world before the Law was promulgated, but he also adds this here, that sin was not abolished by the Law, therefore this statement should be understood inclusively. Until the law sin was in the world, that is, even when the Law of Moses was enacted, sin nevertheless remained. Thus he briefly warns that sin and death are not taken away by the law, because that external righteousness of the law does not yet free one from sin, nor is it the beginning of eternal life, but a certain external bodily discipline, and when the conscience is tormented and seeks justification in the law, then the law has its principal effect, it accuses and casts consciences into terrors and desperation. This is what Paul means when he adds here, but sin is not imputed, where there is no Law, that is, where there is no Law, sin is not acknowledged, it is not accused. For Paul is speaking about the judgment of our conscience. The Law was therefore enacted so that the conscience might acknowledge sin and be accused and terrified, just as he said above: Through the Law is the knowledge of sin. Afterwards, however, he will speak more copiously about the use of the Law: For now he has only touched upon it incidentally and as if in passing. But what follows: Death reigned from Adam until Moses. By this statement the preceding words are explained, just as he said before: Sin to have been until the Law, and not even by the Law to have been abolished, so he says here: that death reigned from Adam until Moses and was not even abolished by the Law. He adds, however, that death reigned even over those who did not sin according to the likeness of the transgression of Adam, that is, that even infants are subject to death, although they do not have actual sins. For Paul calls actual sin the transgression. He says this for this reason, to confirm the first proposition that all are guilty: For if infants also are subject to death, therefore they have a certain sin, because death entered into the world through sin. There is therefore another sin besides actual ones.

To the likeness of the transgression of Adam who bears the type &c.

Thus far he has preached concerning original sin, that this human nature is guilty and corrupt. Therefore it is not righteous by the Law or by works, because it does not render true obedience to the Law, but there remain in the nature of man corruption, blindness, concupiscence, and horrible impulses against the Law of God. There is need therefore of a certain other righteousness, namely the grace of Christ, therefore he now begins to preach concerning it.

He who is the form of the future, just as he spoke above concerning sin, concerning the cause of sin, concerning propagation and effect. Thus he now teaches concerning grace, concerning the cause, propagation and effect of grace, so that he may teach that sin is taken away through grace. Moreover, he joins grace and the gift through grace. The term grace signifies gratuitous mercy. Therefore, here it signifies most truly the remission of sins, and the gratuitous acceptance which is made on account of Christ. The gift through grace signifies the donation of the Holy Spirit, who begins a new and eternal life in souls and excites new motions. Therefore, first he compares Adam and Christ. This comparison greatly illuminates both members. Moreover, he declares the mode of merit, which each merited for others. Adam merited guilt for others, Christ merited reconciliation for others. This comparison clearly refutes the adversaries who imagine that men are righteous by their own dignity. For here he says clearly: just as others are guilty on account of Adam, so others are righteous on account of Christ. And this sentence is often repeated. He speaks of this mode of merit when he says: Adam is an example of Christ, namely, as far as this pertains, that each merited for others. For in a comparison it is not necessary that all things be similar. Therefore Paul himself adds a correction, so that he may warn that there are many things dissimilar in this comparison, for thus he says: But not as the offense, so also is the gift, that is, there are many things dissimilar in this comparison of the offense and the gift. First, the things are most diverse: guilt, or sin, and pardon, or grace, eternal death and eternal life. Second, there is a great difference in the manner of propagation. From Adam, a guilty, vicious, and death-liable nature is propagated, and it is propagated by carnal generation: On the contrary, from Christ, reconciliation is gifted. This is not propagated by carnal generation, but is received by faith, just as it is written in John 1: He gave them power to become the sons of God, to those who believe, etc. Likewise John 3: Unless one has been reborn, etc. This dissimilarity of propagation must be diligently observed on account of the Anabaptists, who invent prodigious delicacies here: Some entirely remove original sin: Others imagine that after the resurrection of Christ, absolutely no one is born with original sin. Against those fanatic opinions, the passages cited from John fortify us. And see how great the insanity of the Anabaptists is. If there were no original sin, all men would live without sin and death. Since this is manifestly false, it is necessary that the cause remains, namely original sin. The third dissimilarity must be diligently considered, which Paul also treats and amplifies here in the text, that grace surpasses sin. This dissimilarity must especially be inculcated, because if sin and grace had equal power, how would grace save, especially when sin is felt? Thus the benefit of the Gospel would be nothing, there would be no firm consolation. Therefore this dissimilarity must be illustrated, as Paul does afterwards: That grace surpasses sin. It surpasses, however, in two ways, both by imputation and by effect. It surpasses by imputation, because God reckons those who apprehend grace as righteous, even if in reality they still have remnants of sin. Then it also surpasses by effect, because in those very people, although they are weak, there nevertheless exist new motions that resist sin. Likewise, those very people, although they were still weak in this life, are nevertheless resurrected to eternal life. It is necessary for these things to be known, so that the benefit of Christ may be understood, and firm consolation may be held. And Paul himself subsequently treats and exaggerates this dissimilarity.

For if by the transgression of one.

He repeats the comparison in clear words, just as through the transgression of one others were made guilty, so conversely through one Christ others are reconciled to God, and are made acceptable to God. This comparison clearly shows that we are not reconciled to God and accepted by our own merit, but by another's. Here Paul joins two things, grace and the gift by grace: Grace signifies gratuitous acceptance on account of Christ, that is, the gratuitous remission of sins, and the gratuitous imputation of righteousness on account of Christ. The gift by grace signifies the donation of the Holy Spirit and eternal life. For in the remission of sins the Gospel at the same time offers the Holy Spirit, whom we indeed receive by faith, when hearts are lifted up and conceive consolation through the word. And this is the benefit of the new testament or Gospel given on account of Christ, the remission of sins, the imputation of righteousness, the donation of the Holy Spirit and eternal life. * By grace we are righteous. Grace is our love etc. Therefore by our love we are righteous. I respond to the minor premise: Even if sometimes the word grace is taken in this way, nevertheless it is done καταχρηστικῶς : But grace signifies the remission of sins.

* By righteousness we are righteous. Righteousness is our quality:

Therefore we are righteous by our own quality. I respond to the minor premise: Righteousness in these disputations signifies acceptance, and to be righteous is to be accepted.

* Righteousness is in the will: Faith is in the intellect: Therefore by faith we cannot be righteous: R. Righteousness which is our quality is in the will. But righteousness, that is, acceptance, is a relation, it does not inhere in anything. Furthermore, faith insofar as it is a will accepting, is not only in the intellect, but is also in the will.

Commonly they understand grace, the scholastic doctors, as the quality itself in us, and they call it charity. Furthermore, when it is said we are righteous by grace, men imagine that they are righteous on account of their own quality, namely the quality, that is, new obedience. Thus they do not teach how to apprehend the mediator Christ, and they leave consciences doubtful. Finally, to teach thus, that it must be felt that we are righteous on account of our own quality, is the doctrine of the Law, and it has many inconveniences: Therefore let grace be understood relatively for gratuitous acceptance, so that it may be the same, We are righteous by grace, as that: We are accepted by God freely on account of Christ, by an acceptance according to the promise in which this grace, that is, acceptance, is proposed, and the conscience will determine that we are righteous, that is, that we are accepted on account of Christ, and it will not look upon its own worthiness, but the word or promise, and according to this it will determine concerning the will of God toward us, and thus it will apprehend Christ the mediator by faith; when this happens, the Holy Spirit is given, and new motions are made in us. Therefore, let both be retained: both that it is necessary that new motions be made in us, and yet that the conscience ought to look outside ourselves to Christ the mediator, and determine that on account of him we are righteous, that is, accepted, and this is to say that men are righteous by grace, namely that they are righteous, that is, accepted freely on account of Christ, with God accepting. Thus also let that be understood: We are righteous by faith, that is, correlatively we are righteous on account of Christ, whom it is necessary to apprehend by faith. In this way the conscience learns to look upon the word, and has firm consolation, because that grace, that is, the will of God accepting on account of Christ, is set forth in the word, and it is to be known that the Holy Spirit is thus efficacious when we apprehend this word. Thus far concerning the term grace. Paul adds the gift by the grace which is of Christ. For he teaches the gift, that is, the Holy Spirit and eternal life to be given on account of Christ, just as it is written elsewhere grace for grace, that is, we are pleasing not on account of ourselves, but on account of the fact that the Son is pleasing: Item to the Ephesians. He accepts us in the beloved Son.

Not as on account of one.

The speech in the text can be completed thus: & the gift does not stand as the sin does, which through one sinning destroyed men. Paul added this sentiment most prudently and necessarily, so that he might show the dissimilarity of the kingdom of sin and the kingdom of grace, and he teaches that this is the dissimilarity, that grace is more abundant and more powerful than sin. It is necessary for this dissimilarity to be proposed, for if sin and grace had equal power, how would we be saved if sin condemned equally &c. Wherefore let the conscience know that grace is more powerful, first because it abolishes sin by the remission of sins and the imputation of righteousness, by which imputation we are accepted, although sin and infirmity cling to us: Then it is also more powerful in effect, because it resists sin, and the devil, and brings forth new and eternal life. And let the pious diligently consider this eminence of grace, so as to set it against the magnitude of sin, and set it against present infirmity. No sin, however great, ought to be preferred to grace. Likewise, although the saints are still infirm, yet let them know that grace is more abundant, wherefore they are pleasing on account of Christ: Therefore Paul exaggerates this dissimilarity and adds the judgment from one unto condemnation, that is, the one sin of Adam brought condemnation to the entire posterity. But grace abolishes many sins, that is, original and actual, the root and the fruits, etc.

Latin:

Usque ad Legem enim peccatum erat in mundo.

Non solum hoc vult peccatum fuisse in mundo ante promulgatam Legem, sed etiam illud hic attexit, Lege non esse abolitum peccatum, ideo inclusive intelligatur hoc dictum. Usque ad legem peccatum erat in mundo, id est, etiam cum lata est Lex Moisi, tamen mansit peccatum. Ita breviter admonet lege non tolli peccatum et mortem, quia illa externa iustitia legis nondum liberat à peccato, nec est inchoatio aeternae vitae, sed quaedam externa corporalis disciplina, & cum conscientia angitur & quaerit iustificationem in lege, tunc lex habet praecipuum effectum, accusat & coniicit conscientias in terrores & desperationem. Hoc vult Paulus cum hic addit, sed peccatum non reputatur, ubi non est Lex, id est, ubi non est Lex non agnoscitur peccatum, non accusatur. Loquitur enim Paulus de iudicio nostrae conscientiae. Lata est igitur Lex ut conscientia agnoscat peccatum & accusetur & perterrefiat, sicut supra inquit: Per Legem agnitio peccati. Postea autem de usu Legis copiosius dicet: Nunc enim obiter tantem & velut in transcursu attigit. Quod autem sequitur: Mors regnavit ab Adam usque ad Mosen. Hoc dicto superiora verba declarantur, sicut antea dixit: Peccatum fuisse usque ad Legem, ac ne Lege quidem fuisse abolitum, ita hic ait: mortem regnasse ab Adam usque ad Moisen ac ne quidem Lege abolitam esse. Addit autem mortem regnasse etiam in eos qui non peccaverunt secundum similitudinem transgressionis Adae, id est, etiam infantes morti subiectos esse, tametsi non habeant actualia peccata. Nam Paulus actuale peccatum vocat transgressionis. Hoc ideo dicit, ut confirmet primam propositionem omnes esse reos: Si enim infantes quoque sunt subiecti morti, ergo habent quoddam peccatum, quia mors intravit per peccatum in mundum. Est igitur aliud peccatum praeter actualia.

Ad similitudinem transgressio-nis Adam qui typum. gerit &c.

Hactenus concionatus est de peccato originis, quod haec natura humana sit rea & corrupta. Ideo non est iusta Lege vel operibus. quia Legi non praestat veram obedientiam, sed manent in natura hominis, corruptio, caecitas, concupiscentia, & horribiles impetus contra Legem Dei. Opus est igitur alia quadam iustitia scilicet gratia Christi, ideo de ea iam incipit concionari.

Qui est forma futuri, sicut supra dixit de peccato, de caussa peccati, de propagatione & effectu. Ita iam docet de gratia, de causa, propagatione & effectu gratiae, ut doceat peccatum tolli per gratiam. Coniungit autem gratiam & donum per gratiam. Vocabulum gratiae significat gratuitam misericordiam. Ideo hic significat verissime remissionem peccatorum, & gratuitam acceptationem quae fit propter Christum. Donum per gratiam significat donationem spiritus sancti, qui inchoat novam & aeternam vitam in animis & excitat novos motus. Primum igitur confert Adam & Christum. Haec collatio valde illustrat utrumque membrum. Declarat autem modum meriti, quod uterque aliis meruerit. Adam meruit aliis reatum, Christus meruit aliis reconciliationem. Haec collatio clare refellit adversarios qui imaginantur homines iustos esse propria dignitate. Hic enim clare dicit: sicut alii propter Adam rei sunt, ita alii propter Christum iusti sunt. Et haec sententia saepe repetitur. De hoc modo meriti loquitur cum ait: Adam est exemplum Christi, scilicet quod ad hoc attinet quod uterque aliis meruit. Nam in collatione non necesse est omnia similia esse. Ideo Paulus ipse addit correctionem, ut admoneat multa esse dissimilia in hac collatione, sic enim inquit: Sed non sicut delictum sic & donum, id est, multa sunt dissimilia in hac collatione delicti & doni. Primum res diversissimae sunt reatus, seu peccatum & venia seu gratia, mors aeterna & vita aeterna. Secundo plurimum interest in modo propagandi. Ab Adam propagatur natura rea, vitiosa & morti obnoxia, & propagatur generatione carnali: Econtra à Christo donatur reconciliatio. Haec non propagatur generatione carnali, sed fide accipitur, sicut Ioannis primo scriptum est: Dedit eis potestatem filios Dei fieri, his qui credunt, &c. Item Iohan. iii. Nisi quis renatus fuerit, &c. Haec dissimilitudo propagationis diligenter observanda est propter Anabaptistas, qui prodigiosa delicamenta hic comminiscuntur: Alii prorsus tollunt peccatum originis: Alii fingunt post resurrectionem Christi prorsus neminem nasci, cum peccato originis. Adversus illas phanaticas opiniones, muniunt nos loci citati ex Iohanne. Ac vide quanta sit insania Anabaptistarum. Si nullum esset peccatum originis, omnes homines viverent sine peccato & morte. Quod cum sit manifeste falsum, necesse est causam manere scilicet peccatum originis. Tertia dissimilitudo est diligenter consideranda, quam & hic in textu. Paulus tractat & amplificat, gratia superat peccatum. Hanc dissimilitudinem praecipue oportet inculcari, quia si parem vim haberent peccatum & gratia, quomodo gratia salvaret, praesertim cùm peccatum sentiatur. Ita beneficium Evangelii nihil esset, nulla esset firma consolatio. Quare haec dissimilitudo illustranda est, ut postea facit Paulus: Quod gratia superat peccatum. Superat autem dupliciter, & imputatione & effectu. Imputatione superat, quia eos qui apprehendunt gratiam, Deus reputat iustos, etiamsi reipsa adhuc habent reliquias peccati. Deinde etiam effectu superat, quia in illis ipsis quanquam infirmis, tamen existunt novi motus qui resistunt peccato. Item, illi ipsi quanquàm in hac vita adhuc fuerunt infirmi, tamen resuscitantur ad vitam aeternam. Haec sciri necesse est, ut beneficium Christi intelligatur, & teneatur firma consolatio. Ac Paulus ipse deinde tractat & exaggerat hanc dissimilitudinem.

Si enim propter unis delictum.

Repetit collationem perspicuis verbis, sicut propter unius delictum alii facti sunt rei, ita è regione propter unum Christum alii reconciliantur Deo, & fiunt accepti Deo. Haec collatio perspicuè ostendit nos non nostro merito, sed alieno reconciliari Deo & acceptos esse. Hic Paulus duo coniungit, gratiam & donum per gratiam: Gratia significat gratuitam acceptationem propter Christum, hoc est, remissionem peccatorum gratuitam, & imputationem iusticiae gratuitam propter Christum. Donum per gratiam significat donationem spiritus sancti et vitae aeternae. Nam in remissione peccatorum Evangelium simul offert spiritum sanctum, quem quidem fide accipimus, cum corda eriguntur & concipiunt consolationem per verbum. Atque hoc est beneficium novi testamenti seu Evangelii donatum propter Christum, remissio peccatorum, imputatio iusticiae, donatio spiritus sancti & vitae aeternae. * Gratia sumus iusti. Gratia est nostra dilectio &c. Ergo nostra dilectione sumus iusti. Respondeo ad minorem: Etiamsi interdum sic accipitur vocabulum gratiae, tamen id fitκαταχρηστικῶς: Sed significat gratia remissionem peccatorum.

* Iusticia sumus iusti. Iusticia est nostra qualitas:

Ergo nostra qualitate sumus iusti. Respondeo ad minorem: Iustitia in his disputationibus, significat acceptationem, & iustum esse est, esse acceptum.

* Iusticia est in voluntate: Fides est in intellectu: Ergo fide non possumus esse iusti: R. Iusticia quae est nostra qualitas est in voluntate. Sed iusticia, id est, acceptatio est relatio, non haerat in aliquo. Deinde fides quatenus est voluntas accipiens, non est tantum in intellectu, sed est etiam in voluntate.

Vulgo gratiam intelligunt, scholastici doctores ipsam qualitatem in nobis, & vocant charitatem. Deinde quando dicitur sumus iusti per gratiam, imaginantur homines iustos esse propter propriam qualitatem, scilicet qualitatem, hoc est, novam obedientiam. Ita non docent apprehendere mediatorem Christum, & relinquunt conscientias dubias. Denique sic docere, quod sentiendum sit, nos esse iustos, propter propriam qualitatem, est doctrina Legis, & multa habet incommoda: Ideo gratia intelligatur relativè pro acceptatione gratuita, ut sit idem, Sumus iusti per gratiam, quod illud: Sumus accepti Deo nos gratis propter Christum, acceptatione iuxta promissionem in qua haec gratia, id est, acceptatio proposita est, & conscientia statuet nos iustos, id est, acceptos esse propter Christum, nec intuebitur propriam dignitatem, sed verbum seu promissionem, & iuxta hanc statuet de voluntate Dei erga nos, atquè ita apprehendet fide Christum mediatorem, hoc cum fit donatur spiritus sanctus, & fiunt in nobis novi motus. Retineatur ergo utrunque, et quod fieri novos motus in nobis oportet, & quòd tamen conscientia debeat extra nos intueri mediatorem Christum, & statuere quod propter illum simus iusti, id est accepti, & hoc est dicere homines iustos esse per gratiam, videlicet quod sint iusti, id est, accepti gratis propter Christum, Deo acceptante. Sic etiam illud intelligatur: Sumus iusti fide, id est correlativè sumus iusti propter Christum, quem fide apprehendi oportet. Hoc modo conscientia discit intueri verbum, & habet firmam consolationem, quia illa gratia, id est voluntas Dei acceptans propter Christum est proposita in verbo, estque sciendum ita efficacem esse spiritum sanctum, cùm hoc verbum apprehendimus. Hactenus de vocabulo gratiae. Paulus addit donum per gratiam quae est Christi. Docet enim donum, id est, spiritum sanctum & vitam aeternam dari propter Christum, sicut alibi scriptum est gratiam pro gratia, id est, nos placemus non propter nos, sed propterea quia placet filius: Item ad Ephes. Acceptat nos in filio dilecto.

Non quemadmodum propter unius.

Oratio in textu sic absolvi potest: & non sic se habet donum sicut peccatum, quod per unum peccantum perdidit homines. Hanc sententiam prudentissimè & necessario adiecit Paulus, ut ostendat dissimilitudinem regni peccati & regni gratiae, & docet hanc esse dissimilitudinem, quòd gratia sit uberior & potentior peccato. Hanc dissimilitudinem necesse est proponi, si enim parem haberent potentiam peccatum & gratia, quomodo salveremur si peccatum pariter damnaret &c. Quare conscientia sciat gratiam potentiorem esse, primum quia abolet peccatum remissione peccatorum & imputatione iusticiae, qua imputatione sumus accepti, quanquàm haereat in nobis peccatum & infirmitas: Deinde & effectu potentior est, quia resistit peccato, & diabolo, & affert novam et aeternam vitam. Ac diligenter considerent pii hanc eminentiam gratiae, ut opponant magnitudini peccati, & opponant praesenti infirmitati. Nullum peccatum quamlibet magnum anteferri debet gratiae. Item quanquàm sancti adhuc sunt infirmi, tamen sciant gratiam uberiorem esse quare placent propter Christum: Ideo Paulus exaggerat hanc dissimilitudinem & addit iudicium ex uno in condemnationem, id est, unum peccatum Adae attulit condemnationem universae posteritati. At gratia abolet multa peccata, id est, originalia & actualia, radicem & fructus &c.

## 5:16
What is original sin?

Original sin is guilt or imputation, by which, on account of the fall of Adam, all who are propagated according to nature are guilty, and it is the corruption of human nature, following the fall of Adam, by which it comes about that human nature cannot truly obey the Law of God, but has defects and concupiscence against the Law of God. The common definition of Anselm says exactly the same thing as ours, just as he himself explains it copiously, even if commonly only a few words extracted are recited, namely that original sin is the lack of original justice which ought to have been present. For original justice was to have been not only acceptance, but also the integrity of the faculties or rectitude, which would have provided perfect obedience to the Law of God, nor would there have been in the souls of men doubt concerning the will of God, a void of fear, of trust, of the love of God, but there would have been born in souls a light or a concreated and firm knowledge of God, and inclinations consenting to the law of God. Now, on the contrary, the nature of man is guilty and corrupt. From this antithesis, the definition can easily be understood.

Why do dissensions exist concerning original sin?

Because men do not see the uncleanness of the heart, namely those sins, doubt concerning God, being void of the fear of God, of trust, of love, having horrible impulses against the Law of God. These vices they do not see, and much less do they see them to be sins. Therefore, the impious feign that there is no original sin. Then they stitch on philosophical opinions: that nature is good. Likewise, that nothing is a sin unless it is voluntary. These things are rightly said in their own place, but they are not to be twisted toward original sin. And so, darkness and blindness in human souls is the cause why many either extenuate original sin or take it away entirely, and then astutely corrupt the scriptures and elude them, as Pelagius did and many others. Against such calumnies, minds must be fortified with true and firm testimonies. The cause of original sin is the devil and the will of the first parents, which, since it was free, turned itself away from the word of God of its own accord, nor did it retain obedience toward God. Therefore Adam was made guilty and made his posterity guilty, and stripped of the integrity of nature and the gifts which God had added to nature, he subsequently procreated such as he himself was. Thus a guilty and corrupted nature is propagated.

Effects.

The Scholastics said that concupiscence is not a sin, but only a punishment, and they called it the tinder. We say that concupiscence is both a punishment in a guilty nature and a sin. The second punishment is death and all the calamities of the human race. The third punishment is that this weak nature is subject to the tyranny of the devil, who strives to destroy both by bodily evils and by terrors, and impels [men] to sins of every kind, to blasphemies, heresies, slaughters, lusts, and other sins. Philosophers have wondered whence there exists in such an excellent nature of the human race so much not only of calamities, but also of flagrant crimes, when indeed it is according to nature to do rightly, but only Christian doctrine shows the cause, namely original sin. Since, however, such horrible effects and punishments have followed, sin is not to be extenuated of origin, but such is the darkness of souls that we not only do not see sin and the wrath of God, but we do not even understand the magnitude of the calamities. Therefore, some common teachers have either removed or attenuated the sin of origin, but Scripture reveals this sin to us, so that, being humbled, we may seek grace and acknowledge the benefits of Christ, as John says: For this purpose the Son of God appeared, that he might destroy the works of the devil.

Latin:

Quid est peccatum originis?

Peccatum originis est reatus seu imputatio, qua propter lapsum Adae omnes secundum naturam propagati rei sunt, & est corruptio naturae humanae, secuta lapsum Adae, qua fit ut humana natura non possit vere obedire Legi Dei, sed habeat defectus & concupiscentiam contra Legem Dei. Vulgata Anshelmi definitio prorsus idem dicit quod nostra, sicut & ipse eam copiose enarrat, etsi vulgo tantum pauca verba excerpta recitantur, videlicet peccatum originis est carentia iustitiae originalis quae debebat inesse. Nam iustitia originalis erat futura non tantum acceptatio, sed etiam integritas virium seu rectitudo, quae praestitisset perfectam obedientiam Legi Dei, nec fuissent in animis hominum dubitatio de voluntate Dei, vacuitas timoris, fiduciae, dilectionis Dei, sed fuisset natum in animis lumen seu concreatum & firma noticia de Deo, & inclinationes consentientes legi Dei. Nunc econtra natura hominis est rea & corrupta. Ex hac antithesi facile potest intelligi definitio.

Quare existunt dissensiones de peccato originis?

Quia homines non vident immunditiem cordis, scilicet illa peccata, dubitationem de Deo, vacare metu Dei, fiducia, dilectione, habere horribiles impetus adversus Legem Dei. Haec vitia non vident, ac multo minus vident esse peccata. Ideo fingunt impii nihil esse peccatum originis. Deinde assuunt Philosophicas sententias: Naturam esse bonam. Item nihil esse peccatum nisi sit voluntarium. Haec suo loco recte dicuntur, sed non sunt detorquenda ad peccatum originale. Itaque caligo & caecitas in animis humanis est causa, quare multi vel extenuent peccatum originis vel prorsus tollant, & deinde astute corrumpant scripturas & eludant, ut Pelagius fecit & alii multi. Adversus tales calumnias muniendi sunt animi veris & firmis testimoniis. Causa peccati originalis, est diabolus & voluntas primorum parentum, quae cum esset libera, per sese avertit se à verbo Dei, nec retinuit obedientiam erga Deum. Ideo Adam factus est reus & fecit ream posteritatem, & exutus integritate naturae & donis quae Deus addiderat naturae, procreavit deinde tales qualis erat ipse. Ita propagatur natura rea & corrupta.

Effectus.

Scholastici dixerunt concupiscentiam non esse peccatum, sed tantum poenam, & vocarunt fomitem. Nos dicimus concupiscentiam & poenam in rea natura & peccatum esse. Secunda poena est mors & omnes calamitates humani generis. Tertia poena est, quod haec infirma natura subiecta est tyrannidi diaboli, qui & corporalibus malis & terroribus studet perdere, et impellit ad peccata omnis generis, ad blasphemias, haereses, caedes, libidines, & alia peccata. Philosophi mirati sunt, unde in tam praestanti natura generis humani tantum existat non solum calamitatum, sed etiam flagiciorum, cum quidem secundum naturam sit recte sacere, sed sola doctrina Christiana monstrat caussam, scilicet peccatum originis. Cum autem tam horribiles effectus, & poenae secutae sint, non est extenuandum peccatum originis, sed tanta est caligo animorum ut non solum peccatum, & iram Dei non videamus, sed ne quidem calamitatum magnitudinem intelligamus. Ideo etiam vulgo aliqui doctores vel sustulerunt vel extenuaverunt peccatum originis, sed scriptura revelat nobis hoc peccatum, ut humiliati quaeramus gratiam & agnoscamus beneficia Christi, sicut Ioannes inquit: Adhoc apparuit filius Dei, ut destruat opera diaboli.

## 5:16
What is grace?

Grace is the remission of sins and the imputation of righteousness, or acceptance, which is done by God freely on account of Christ, and joined with this acceptance is the gift of the Holy Spirit and eternal life.

Causes.

The efficient cause is the will of God, which willed that Christ be made a victim for us, and in this way to have mercy on us on account of him, not on account of any dignity of ours.

How does grace come to us?

The Word of God is the instrument, and this is to be received by faith: For when hearts conceive consolation from the promise which is revealed in the Gospel, let them determine that they truly obtain those things which the Gospel promises, namely the remission of sins, the imputation of righteousness, and the Holy Spirit, since God is truthful and wishes this glory of truth to be attributed to himself. He wishes to be worshipped by this faith, that we may assent to his word: Indeed, this is the highest and immutable commandment, that we believe that these things which the Gospel promises are given to us on account of Christ, and that we resist doubt, it must be known that the promise is gratuitous and universal, because these two things cry out against consciences, our unworthiness and particularity.

Effects of grace.

The motions of the Holy Spirit which occur when we apprehend the Gospel, and the chief one is faith by which we raise ourselves up and establish for ourselves that God is propitious to us on account of Christ. This motion is called vivification, because by this confidence the terrors of sin and death are overcome. Then follow other motions, begun obedience toward God, invocation, fear, love, patience, chastity, and the remaining motions consenting to the Law of God as it is said: I will put my Law into their hearts. There are also effects of grace, liberation from the power of the Devil, help against the devil and the infirmity of the flesh: Likewise consolation and help in present calamities, as Christ says: I will not leave you orphans. There is also the effect of liberation from the Law, namely that it may not condemn believers: The final effect is also the consummation, the newness of our whole nature and eternal life.

Of the Law.

At the beginning the reader must be warned that Paul is not speaking of the political use of the Law, or of the pedagogy, but of the use of the Law acting in the conscience with God, and seeking justification. Therefore, the uses of the Law are to be distinguished. The first is the pedagogy or political use, namely to restrain the flesh and to perform external works, the precepts of the Law: This use in those who are not sanctified, or in the oldness of the flesh, is called discipline. Although, however, it does not justify before God, yet we ought to know that this discipline is commanded by God, even to the unsanctified, and that it can in some way be performed by human powers. And it is to be known in this political or pedagogical use that the Law is necessary, that it is the highest gift of bodily life, which God both gave and preserves. There are, however, four ends to be considered, which ought to exhort us that we perform this pedagogy with the greatest care and diligence: The first is because God requires this obedience, even in the unsanctified. The second, God also adds rewards and punishments. The third end is for the sake of the peace of common society. The fourth end, because it is also a pedagogy unto Christ.

Three things, however, pertain to pedagogy: It is necessary that there be order and peace, so that men may be able to be taught. Secondly, it is necessary that men do not resist the word of God, and do not dwell in manifest crimes.

For in one who remains in sin, the word of God is not effective. Thirdly, pedagogy is not only a guardian of peace, it not only restrains, but it also teaches. That is the property of pedagogy; therefore the Law had ceremonies, and every pious head of a household has rites and exercises, so that that very habituation may teach the unlearned and the weak; we sing, we read, we meditate upon certain passages of Scripture at certain times for the sake of pedagogy, that is, so that the word may be impressed, so that, being habituated, we may understand the word of God. Moreover, the Holy Spirit is effective through the word: these utilities are not to be despised, because certainly these two things are necessary: not to remain in manifest sins, and to learn and meditate upon the word of God, and yet in the meantime men must be taught that these external exercises are not righteousness before God, but that righteousness before God is something else. Furthermore, when faith in Christ is added in those who are pious, even these exercises by which the flesh is restrained, if they are done with the due end, are good works and pleasing to God. Let this be enough to have warned about the first and political use of the Law, and it is profitable often to impress upon adolescents what the difference is between this pedagogy, between the righteousness of faith and the fruits of faith; it is also profitable to exhort to this pedagogy, so that they may learn to truly displease God with that barbaric, or Cyclopean, or Neronian life, which is led in manifest baseness. Then that they may learn to profit from the exercises and studies of the word of God. And the opinion is: The Law is a pedagogue, that is, it is an exercise by which men are accustomed and taught, so that they may understand the word. In this opinion Paul said, The Law is placed for the unjust, that is, God wills that the unjust be restrained, and in the Church there ought to exist a doctrine concerning the distinction of this discipline and the righteousness of faith. It ought also to be taught what the commandment of God is, so that the unlearned may be restrained; the pious also, who are still weak and unlearned, have need of such exercises, so that they may be restrained and learn: Just as Paul says, Bring up children in the discipline and admonition of the Lord. And so much for the first use or political use, of which Paul does not speak here in Romans. The second use of the Law is political, to accuse and terrify consciences, when it judges and condemns sin. This is the secret use, which the Law has in the conscience not understood hypocritically, but when minds are truly terrified by the recognition of sin: These terrors are often described in the Psalms. There is no peace in my bones from the face of my sins. Of this use speaks Paul in the whole epistle to the Romans, and to the Corinthians, when he says: The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the Law, that is, because of sin men are destined to death: And indeed sin brings terrors, despair, and death. But sin would not be recognized, unless the Law judged and accused us. He means the same above when he says: The Law works wrath, that is, it accuses and terrifies consciences, and here the Law increases sin, not civilly, but it increases it in the conscience, that is, it renders it more powerful, so that it may terrify and bring despair and death. Thus sin is increased within the conscience, when it is recognized to be sin, that is, when we recognize that God is truly angry, and we feel the wrath of God, terrors, and death, just as David, having heard the rebuke of Nathan, felt true and horrible terrors. And Hezekiah describes his terrors: like a lion he crushed all my bones. Therefore Paul teaches that this is the chief work of the Law, when it accomplishes the most, it accuses and condemns, it does not justify, it does not bring the remission of sins, it does not announce liberation from sin and from death. Thus Paul distinguishes the Law from the Gospel, the Law either restrains the body externally in some way, or when it does its own proper and its own work, it cites, accuses, terrifies, and condemns. Here a twofold use is signified by the type, namely, the face of Moses. The shining face of Moses, so that the people could not look upon it, signifies the Law terrifying, when the Law is truly understood concerning perfect obedience, not carnally concerning external discipline. Afterwards Moses speaks with the people with a veiled face, thus the people hear him. This figure signifies that men do not truly understand the Law by rational judgment, but only concerning external discipline. Then the related reason attaches false opinions, that that external discipline is the fulfillment of the Law, and is righteousness before God. But God uses the word of the Law to judge and condemn sin, and to accuse and terrify consciences, just as afterwards Rom. vii this whole passage is repeated: That which is good, did it become death to me? Far be it, but sin, that it might appear as sin, works death.

Latin:

Quid gratia?

Gratia est remissio peccatorum & imputatio iusticiae, seu acceptatio, quae fit à Deo gratis propter Christum, & cum hac acceptatione coniuncta est donatio spiritus sancti & vitae aeternae.

Causae.

Causa efficiens est voluntas Dei, quae Christum pro nobis voluit fieri victimam, & hoc modo propter ipsum nostri misereri, non propter aliquam nostram dignitatem.

Quomodo contingit nobis gratia?

Verbum Dei est instrumentum, et hoc fide accipiendum est: Quando enim corda concipiunt consolationem, ex promissione quae in Evangelio revelata est, statuant se vere consequi illa quae promittit Evangelium, scilicet remissionem peccatorum, imputationem iusticiae, & spiritum sanctum, qua Deus est verax, & vult sibi hanc gloriam veritatis tribui. Vult se coli hac fide, ut verbo suo assentiamur: Imo hoc est summum & immutabile praeceptum, ut credamus nobis propter Christum haec dari, quae promittit Evangelium, & ut repugnemus dubitationi, sciendum est promissionem gratuitam & universalem esse, quia conscientiis haec duo obstrepunt, indignitas nostra & particularitas.

Effectus gratiae.

Motus spiritus sancti qui fiunt cum Evangelium apprehendimus, ac praecipuus est fides qua nos erigimus & statuimus nobis Deum esse propitium propter Christum. Hic motus dicitur vivificatio, quia hac fiducia vincuntur terrores peccati, & mortis. Sequuntur deinde alii motus, inchoata obedientia erga Deum, invocatio, timor, dilectio, patientia, castitas, & reliqui motus consentientes Legi Dei sicut dictum est: Dabo Legem meam in corda eorum. Sunt effectus gratiae etiam liberatio à potestate Diaboli, auxilium contra diabolum & infirmitatem carnis: Item consolatio & auxilium in praesentibus calamitatibus, sicut ait Christus: non relinquam vos orphanos. Est et effectus liberatio à Lege, scilicet ne credentes condemner: Ultimus effectus est & consummatio, totius naturae nostrae novitas & vita aeterna.

De Lege.

Principio monendus est lector, Paulum non loqui de politico usu Legis, aut de paedagogia, sed de usu Legis in conscientia agente cum Deo, & quaerente iustificationem. Sunt igitur discernendi usus Legis. Primus est paedagogia seu politicus usus, videlicet cohercere carnem & praestare opera externa, praecepta à Lege: Hic usus in his qui non sunt sanctificati, vel in vetustate carnis vocatur disciplina. Quanquâm autem non iustificat, coram Deo, tamen scire debemus hanc disciplinam praecipi à Deo, etiam non sanctificatis, & aliquo modo posse eam praestari humanis viribus. Estque in hoc usu politico seu paedagogico sciendum, quòd Lex necessaria sit, quòd sit summum donum virae corporalis, quod Deus & dedit & conservat. Sunt autem fines quatuor considerandi, qui nos hortari debent, ut summa cura & diligentia praestemus hanc paedagogiam: Primus est quia Deus hanc obedientiam requirit, etiam in non sanctificatis. Secundus, Deus etiam addit praemia & poenas. Tertius finis propter pacem communis societatis. Quartus finis, quia est etiam paedagogia in Christum.

Tria autem ad paedagogiam pertinent: Necesse est ordinem & pacem esse, ut homines doceri possint. Secundo, Necesse est homines non repugnare verbo Dei, non commorari in manifestis flagitiis.

Nam in commorante non est efficax verbum Dei. Tertio, Paedagogia non solum pacis custos est, non solum cohaercet, sed etiam docet. Id proprium est paedagogiae, ideo Lex habuit caeremonias, & habet ritus & exercitia quilibet pius paterfamilias, ut illa ipsa assuefactio doceat rudes & infirmos, canimus, legimus, meditamur, aliqua loca scripturae certis temporibus pedagogiae causa, id est, ut verbum inculcetur, ut assuefacti intelligamus verbum Dei. Est autem spiritus sanctus efficax per verbum: Hae utilitates non sunt contemnendae, quia certe haec duo sunt necessaria, non commorari in manifestis peccatis, & discere ac meditari verbum Dei, et tamen interim docendi sunt homines, quod haec externa exercitia non sint iusticia coram Deo, sed quod aliud quiddam sit iusticia coram Deo. Caeterum cum accedit fides in Christum in his qui sunt pii, etiam haec exercitia quibus cohercetur caro, si fiant debito fine, sunt bona opera & Deo placentia. Haec satis sit monuisse de primo & politico usu Legis, & prodest saepe inculcare adolescentibus quid intersit inter hanc paedagogiam, inter iusticiam fidei & fructus fidei, prodest etiam hortari ad hanc paedagogiam, ut discant vere displicere Deo illiam Barbaricam, aut Cyclopicam, aut Neronicam vitam, quae agitur in manifesta turpitudine. Deinde ut discant prodesse exercitia & studia verbi Dei. Estque sententia: Lex est paedagogus, id est, est exercitium, quo assuefiunt et docentur homines, ut intelligant verbum. In hanc sententiam dixit Paulus, Lex est posita iniustis, id est, Deus vult coherceri iniustos, & in Ecclesia extare oportet doctrinam de discrimine huius disciplinae & iusticiae fidei. Doceri etiam oportet quod sit mandatum Dei, ut rudes coherceantur, habent & pii qui sunt adhuc infirmi & rudes opus talibus exercitiis, ut coherceantur & discant: Sicut inquit Paulus, Educate pueros in disciplina & admonitione domini. Et tantum de primo usu seu politico, de quo hic ad Rom. non loquitur Paulus. Secundus usus Legis politicus est, accusare & per terrefacere conscientias, cum iudicat & damnat peccatum. Hic est usus arcanus, quem in conscientia habet Lex non intellecta hypocritice, sed cum vere perterrefiunt animi agnito peccato: Hi terrores saepe describuntur in Psalmis. Non est pax ossibus meis à facie peccatorum meorum. De hoc usu loquitur Paulus in tota epistola ad Romanos, & ad Corinthios, cum inquit: Aculeus mortis peccatum est, potentia vero peccati Lex, id est, propter peccatum homines sunt destinati morti: Et quidem peccatum affert terrores, desperationem & mortem. Sed peccatum non agnosceretur, nisi Lex iudicaret & accusaret nos. Idem vult supra cum inquit: Lex iram efficit, id est, accusat & perterrefacit conscientias & hic Lex auget peccatum, non civiliter, sed auget in conscientia, id est, reddit potentius, ut perterrefaciat & afferat despe rationem & mortem. Ita peccatum augetur intus conscientia, cum agnoscitur esse peccatum hoc est, cum agnoscimus Deum verè irasci, & sentimus iram Dei, terrores, & mortem, sicut David audita obiurgatione Nathan sensit veros & horribiles terrores. Et Ezechias describit suos terrores: sicut leo contrivit omnia ossa mea. Docet igitur Paulus hoc esse Legis praecipuum opus, cum plurimum efficit accusat &condemnat, non iustificat, non affert remissionem peccatorum, non annunciat liberationem à peccato & à morte. Ita discernit Paulus Legem ab Evangelio, Lex aut externa disciplina utcunque cohercet corpus, aut cum suum proprium & sūum opus facit, cit, accusat, perterrefacit, & damnat. Hic duplex usus significatus est typo videlicet facie Mosi. Mosis facies fulgens adeo, ut intueri eam populus non posset, significat Legem perterrefacientem, cum verè intelligitur Lex, de perfecta obedientia non carnaliter de externa disciplina. Postea Moses velata facie cum populo loquitur, ita eum audit populus. Haec sigura significat homines non vere intelligere Legem rationali iudicio, sed tantum de externa disciplina. Deinde relata ratio affingit falsas opiniones, quod illa externa disciplina sit impletio Legis, & sit iusticia coram Deo. Sed Deus utitur verbo Legis ad iudicandum & damnandum peccatum, & ad accusandas & per terrefaciendas conscientias, sicut postea Rom. vii, totus hic locus repetitur: Quod bonum est sit mihi mors. Absit, sed peccatum ut fiat excellenter peccatum efficit mortem.

## 5:17
For if by the trespass of the one death reigned.

As he previously compared sin and grace, so now he compares the effects, death and life. But the emphasis is on the word reigned: Death remains in the sanctified but does not reign in them, that is, the sanctified overcome the terrors of sin and death by faith. Likewise, they are freed from eternal death: Likewise, they have consolation in human calamities. For by the appellation of death, other human calamities also ought to be understood. Therefore he says expressly here, death reigned, that is, the impious succumb to the terrors of sin and death, they are not freed from eternal death, they do not have consolation in great afflictions, just as Saul, Cain, they procure death for themselves. There is also an emphasis to be considered in what he says: How much more those receiving the abundance of grace, etc. For he urges the dissimilarity about which it was spoken above, that grace is more powerful than sin, how much this matters to be inculcated I have admonished above. Then follows a repetition of the comparison, in which the previous sentiments are inculcated in almost the same words. Where first this argument is to be observed concerning original sin. For because he says clearly: by the sin of one all were condemned, it is necessary that others are guilty and condemned, not only on account of their own transgression, but that of another, namely Adam's. There is therefore some original sin. That which he says righteousness to come to all men on account of the righteousness of one, should be understood concerning the promise or concerning the word, which offers grace universally to all even if not all accept it.

Latin:

Si enim propter unius delictum mors regnavit.

Utantea peccatum & gratiam contulit, ita nunc effectus confert, mortem & vitam. Sed emphasis est in verbo regnavit: Mors manet in sanctificatis sed non regnat in eis, id est, sanctificati vincunt fide terrores peccati & mortis. Item liberantur ab aeterna morte: Item habent consolationem in calamitatibus humanis. Nam appellatione mortis etiam caeterae calamitates humanae intelligi debent. Ideo disertè hic ait, mors regnavit, id est, impii succumbunt terroribus peccati & mortis, non liberantur à morte aeterna, non habent consolationem in magnis afflictionibus, sicut Saul, Cam consciscunt sibi mortem. Est & emphasis consideranda quod ait: Quanto magis accipientes excellentiam gratiae, &c. Urget enim dissimilitudinem de qua supra dictum est, gratiam potentiorem esse peccato, hoc quantum referat inculcari supra admonui. Deinde sequitur repetitio collationis, in qua superiores sententiae propemodum iisdem verbis inculcantur. Ubi primum hoc argumentum observandum est de peccato originis. Quia enim clarè dicit: unius peccato omnes condemnatos esse, necesse est alios reos & condemnatos esse, non tantum propter proprium delictum, sed alienum scilicet Adae. Est ergo aliquod peccatum originis. Quod inquit iusticiam pervenire ad omnes homines propter unius iust iciam, de promissione seu de verbo intelligatur, quod offert omnibus universaliter gratiam etiamsi non omnes accipiunt.

## 6:1 Argument
CHAPTER VI.

Before Paul weaves through the established comparison concerning Law and grace, he inserts objections and dilutes certain absurdities. For a great tumult of questions arises here. If we are not righteous by the Law and our works but through mercy on account of Christ, to what end is there a need to work well?

If the Law neither justifies nor brings eternal life, to what purpose is there need for the law, one will more easily understand these objections of Paul if he considers the controversies of this our time. For just as the adversaries now cry out, if we are not righteous on account of works, to what purpose does it pertain to work well? So the Pharisees object the same absurdities to Paul. Whence it sufficiently appears that we are engaged in that very cause about which Paul disputes, and that we are rendering the proper and genuine opinion of Paul. Let the pious also weigh this here, that not only do the adversaries object those things which I have said, but in all men there is such infirmity of nature that when we hear the doctrine concerning gratuitous imputation we become more sluggish toward working well and carnal security is confirmed. But this knowledge of mercy ought to excite the zeal of working well. For doubt deters minds. Now therefore, since we have learned how works certainly please, and with how much honor God adorns them, because He approves and calls them sacrifices, and promises rewards, this certainty ought to more kindle minds toward working well. Furthermore, to the question, If we are not righteous on account of works, to what purpose is there need to work well, we respond customarily, the benefit of justification is transferred into Christ, so that it may be certain, that is, the person is righteous, that is, accepted on account of Christ. And that this may be certain does not depend upon our dignity, but it is imputed on account of Christ to the believer, that is, to the one receiving by faith. Then, new obedience is necessary, as an effect necessarily following imputation, because with imputation comes renewal, which is the beginning of new and eternal life. But the beginning of new and eternal life is new and spiritual obedience. Therefore, new and spiritual obedience is necessary. This itself is the sum of Paul's response. But he himself distributes the two members of renewal, namely mortification and vivification, and thus he argues from the efficient causes. The first syllogism: A dead nature is not effective. It is necessary that the old and vicious nature be mortified in us. Therefore, the old and vicious nature ought not to be effective, nor must one yield to it when it fights against the will of God. The other syllogism is: A living nature ought to be effective. We conceive new life and light when faith raises up and consoles the conscience: Therefore, this new life ought to have works consistent with it, that is, obedience toward God, whom we now begin to acknowledge in this new life. These two syllogisms Here Paul recounts those things in which we see the renewal of man described, and he uses here the terms of mortification, vivification, and certain related ones. But it must be diligently considered what those terms properly signify. For the conversion of man or repentance, as it is customarily called, is described . Let us always look upon this as the principal place of the Gospel, and let us see what sentences can be referred to it, and just as the Gospel preaches repentance and the remission of sins, so both are proposed to us in the death of Christ. The wrath of God against sin: For it is necessary that there be a great and ineffable wrath, since no other sacrifice could satisfy God, and since He willed His Son to die and be crucified: Therefore there is a huge and ineffable wrath: Again, this very death is a pledge, which renders us certain of the remission of sins. Thus in our conversion or repentance, it is necessary that true terrors and sorrows exist, in which hearts truly feel that God is angry at sin: Again, it is necessary that hearts conceive true consolation by faith, when they determine that on account of Christ they certainly have the remission of sins. Nor is it to be imagined that those things only once to be done. Faith must struggle constantly with terrors in this life, and in this struggle faith and spiritual newness grow. Therefore, both words are also constantly set forth: the word reproving sins, and the promise concerning Christ announcing remission, etc. And indeed the Gospel reproves unbelief, and by the ministry of the Law declares other sins, adulteries, hatreds, etc. Moreover, God employs punishments and calamities, which are also the voice of God accusing sin. And mortification without faith is terror, such as is in the ungodly in Saul, in Judas, and brings about despair and eternal death. But terrors with faith and the knowledge of Christ are filial fear or true contrition, and they become worship of God and a good work, as the psalm calls it a sacrifice. This declaration of terms and accommodation to repentance is necessary, lest inept men imagine mortifications to be Monastic works, and observances summoned by us, or idle speculations, like Monetarius. Likewise, the Platonists ineptly imitated these terms. But let us know that mortification is true terrors and sorrows, and vivification is faith itself comforting us.

Latin:

CAPUT VI.

Priusquam Paul. institutam collationem de Lege & gratia pertexit, inserit occupationes et diluit quaedam absurda. Magnus enim tumultus quaestionum hic oritur. Si non sumus iusti Lege & operibus nostris sed per misericordiam propter Christum, quorsum opus est bene operari.

Si Lex nec iustificat nec affert vitam aeternam, quorsum opus est lege, facilius intelliget has obiectiones Pauli, si considerabit huius nostri temporis controversias. Sicut enim nunc clamitant adversarii, si propter opera non sumus iusti, quorsum attinet bene operari? Ita eadem absurda obiiciunt Pharisaei Paulo. Unde satis apparet nos in illa ipsa causa versari, de qua disputat Paulus, & nos propriam & Germanam sententiam Pauli reddere. Illud hic etiam pii expendant, non solum adversarii obiiciunt illa quae dixi, sed in omnibus hominibus tanta est infirmitas naturae, ut cum audimus doctrinam de gratuita imputatione segniores fiamus ad bene operandum & confirmetur carnalis securitas. At haec misericordiae cognitio debebat excitare studium bene operandi. Nam dubitatio deterret animos. Nunc igitur cum didicimus quomodo certo placeant opera, & quanto honore Deus ea ornet, quod approbat & vocat sacrificia, & promittit praemia, haec certitudo magis accendere animos ad bene operandum debeat. Porro ad quaestionem, Si non sumus iusti propter opera, quorsum opus est bene operari, respondemus usitate, beneficium iustificationis est ranslatum in Christum, ut sit certum, id est, persona est iusta, id est accepta propter Christum. Et ut hoc sit certum non pendet ex dignitate nostra, sed imputatur propter Christum credenti, id est, fide accipienti. Deinde nova obedientia est necessaria, ut effectus necessario consequens imputationem, quia cum imputatione fit renovatio, quae est inchoatio novae & aeternae vitae. Inchoatio vero novae & aetern ae vitae, est nova & spiritualis obedientia. Ergo nova & spiritualis obedientia est necessaria. Haec ipsa est summa respon sionis Pauli. Sed ipse distribuit duo membra renovationis, scilicet mortificationem & vivificationem & sic argumentatur à causis efficientibus. Prior syllogismus: Mortua natura non est efficax. Necesse est in nobis veterem & vitiosam naturam mortificari. Ergo vetus & vitiosa natura non debet esse efficax, nec obsequendum est ei pugnanti cum voluntate Dei. Alter syllogismus est: Viva natura debet esse efficax. Nos concipimus novam vitam & lucem, cum fides erigit & consolatur conscientiam: Ergo haec nova vita debet habere opera consentanea, id est, obedientiam erga Deum, quem iam in hac nova vita incipimus agnoscere. Hos duos syilogismos hic recitat Paulus, in quibus videmus describi renovationem hominis, & utitur hic appellationibus mortificationis, vivificationis, & quibusdam affinibus. Diligenter autem considerandum est, quid appellationes illae propriè significent. Describitur autem conversio hominis seu paenitentia, sicut usitate vocatur. Hunc tanquàm princi palem Evangelii locum semper intueamur, & videamus quae sententiae eo referri possint, & ut Evangelium praedicat paenitentiam & remissionem peccatorum, ita utrumque in morte Christi nobis proponitur. Ira Dei adversus peccatum: Necesse est enim magnam & ineffabilem iram esse, cum nulla alia hostia potuerit Deo satisfacere, & cum voluerit filium mori & crucifigi: Ergo est ingens & ineffabilis ira: Rursus haec ipsa mors est pignus, quod reddit nos certos de remissione peccatorum. Sic in conversione nostra seu pcenitentia, necesse est existere veros terrores & dolores, in quibus corda verè sentiunt Deum irasci peccato: Rursus necesse est corda veram consolationem fide concipere, cum statuunt quòd propter Christum certo habeant remissionem peccatorum. Nec imaginandum est semel illa tantum fieri. Fides cum terroribus in hac vita assiduè luctari debet, & in hoc certamine crescit fides & novitas spiritualis. Ideo etiam assiduè proponitur utrunquè verbum: verbum arguens peccata, & promissio de Christo annuncians remissionem &c. Et quidem Evangelium arguit incredulitatem, & ministerio Legis declarat caetera peccata, adulteria, odia &c. Immo Deus adhibet poenas & calamitates, quae etiam sunt vox Dei accusans peccatum.
