Ac morti ficatio sine fide est terror, qualis est in impiis in Saule, Iuda, & affert desperationem & mortem aeternam. Sed terrores cum fide & noticia Christi, sunt timor filialis seu vera contritio, & fiunt cultus Dei & bonum opus, sicut psalmus vocat sacrificium. Haec declaratio vocum & accommodatio ad paenitentiam est necessaria, ne inepti homines fingant mortificationes esse opera Monastica, & à nobis accersitas observationes, aut ociosas speculationes, sicut Monetarius. Item Platonici inepte imitabantur haec vocabula. Sed sciamus mortificationem esse veros terrores & dolores, et vivi ficationem ipsam fidem consolantem nos.

## 6:3
Whoever of us have been baptized into Christ Jesus.

In the first syllogism he wishes that mortification or repentance ought to exist in those who believe: or that faith is not in those who, secure, despise the judgment of God against sin, because he says: You have been baptized into the death of Christ and buried together, that is, on account of the death of Christ you have remission. But that death shows also the wrath of God against sin, so that in us also sin may be mortified, that is, so that acknowledging the wrath of God we may console ourselves with the benefit of Christ. Likewise, the remission of sins is so brought about that sin may be abolished. But that which has been abolished ought not to be effective.

We are buried therefore together with him &c.

Our conversion is most seriously compared to the death, burial, and resurrection of Christ. For he thus institutes the response. On account of the death of Christ you have remission, which happens in such a way that at the same time on account of the death of Christ sin begins to be abolished, or the vicious nature to be mortified, because at the same time is given. the Holy Spirit, so that He may mortify the old nature and begin the new. We are buried, however, together with Christ, because after our nature has begun to be mortified, sin is buried in two ways. First, by imputation, for although the remnants remain, yet they are forgiven. Second, as it pertains to the effect, because the vicious nature ceases to be effective, or begins to be mortified. Therefore, the remainder of life after the begun mortification is a burial; sin is indeed deleted by imputation, we are not yet glorified. Wherefore, even if we are righteous, yet we lie buried, awaiting glorification. Just as Paul says: Your life is hidden with Christ, that is, even if we have glory, righteousness, life, yet this glory lies hidden still covered with Christ, until we shall be resurrected. Second, as it pertains to the effect, we lie in the sepulcher, that is, in the cross, in afflictions of every kind; the devil disturbs and persecutes the pious in horrible ways. These calamities all, and finally death itself, are as it were a sepulcher, in which the old nature lies dead, so that it may not be effective. This comparison of burial is an illustrious picture of the death of sin, as it pertains to imputation and effect, and it warns that The Christian life is a struggle. Then he adds a third member: Not only does mortification take place, but vivification is also begun. Furthermore, the new nature is efficacious. Therefore, it is necessary for new obedience to exist. He repeats this comparison: If we are grafted into the image of his death, we shall also be grafted into the image of his resurrection, that is, Just as our old man was crucified together with him, so we who are renewed shall live together with him. But since there is a new life, or a new nature, a new light and knowledge of God, a new obedience also exists.

He who has died has been justified from sin: Nero is dead: Therefore he is justified. R. To the major premise, he speaks of actual sin. Or he is justified, that is, he has made satisfaction for sin. It is a figure taken from common speech, just as we say when a thief is hanged: now they cease to sin.

* In man there are certain good notions: God is to be obeyed, etc. Therefore the whole old man is not to be condemned. R. Those notions are in man, but the affections do not obey: Therefore the distinction between appetites and notions must be diligently noted, στόργαι they are good by their nature, but they become vicious, because they are in a vicious nature, and are not directed to the glory of God.

The old man does not signify only a part of man, namely the senses and the appetites of sense, but also reason and will. Nor do appetites alone fight against the Law of God, but also in reason there is ignorance of God, doubt whether we are heard, blasphemies. Then also appetites. Security, contempt of God, distrust, love and confidence in present things against the commandment of God, despair, etc. These vices pertain not to the sense, but to the higher part. Therefore Paul, describing a man without the Holy Spirit, says: The natural man does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God. On the contrary, the new man is called , insofar as he has new light and new motions excited by the Holy Spirit, namely the acknowledgment of Christ, confidence toward God, the fear of God, invocation, love, and similar motions. Of this newness Paul speaks in II Corinthians 3. Now with unveiled face beholding the glory of the Lord, we are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as from the Spirit of the Lord, that is, when in the Gospel mercy is shown to us, we are raised up by the acknowledgment and confidence of God and we feel that we are a care to God, we invoke. In this knowledge and these motions God is acknowledged and shines forth, and we are renewed by a certain image, that is, the knowledge of God. Nor does newness signify thoughts and motions of reason without the Holy Spirit.

Therefore let it not reign.

The conclusion is of the instituted objection, which follows from the previous argument: Because on account of Christ's death sin began to be abolished: Therefore let it not reign nor be effective.

A dead nature ought not to be effective. On account of Christ's death sin has been remitted, so that at the same time it begins on account of Christ's death to be abolished: Therefore since it is being abolished it ought not to be effective.

He says, however, expressly, Let it not reign, so that he may signify that the vicious nature has not been entirely extinguished. Sin therefore remains in nature: but it has begun to be mortified, therefore let it not reign. Paul himself interprets these words: Let it not reign so that you obey it, that is, do not yield to vicious affections, but resist: Just as he also says below: If you mortify the actions of the flesh by the Spirit you shall live. These passages and similar ones show the distinction between mortal and venial sin. Concupiscence and vicious affections remain in the saints, but when they resist these, and by faith seek and determine for themselves that these sins are forgiven, they become venial, because even when such things are present, the Holy Spirit and faith can exist simultaneously in the pious. But they are mortal in those who had been sanctified, when they obey depraved affections against their conscience: As it is said below: If you live according to the flesh you will die, and here: do not offer your members as weapons of unrighteousness. He commands, however, because the Holy Spirit is efficacious with the word of God and impels them, and we ought to comply with the one impelling and not resist, just as Paul says elsewhere: See that you have not received the grace in vain. He orders that we exercise the gift, and in this exercise the pious progress according to that: Practice these things so that your progress may appear. Thus here he significantly says: Offer your members, so that they may be weapons of righteousness. For he wishes to excite and sharpen fervor, just as he says elsewhere: fervent in spirit. For just as the members are not languid, they are not idle, insofar as they have the impulses of the old nature. But just as they are lively and have sharp impulses, so it was fitting that the members of the renewed nature should not be languid, but have sharp and true motions toward doing good, and he used the term of weapons, so that he might signify that in this warfare there must be a most sharp struggle against the devil, the flesh, and snares and temptations of every kind.

Latin:

Quicunquè baptizati sumus in Christum lesum.

In primo syllogismo vult, quò oporteat existere mortificationem seu paenitentiam in his qui credunt: seu quod fides non sit in iis, qui securi iudicium Dei adversus peccatum contemnunt, quia inquit: In mortem Christi baptizati estis & consepulti, id est, propter mortem Christi habetis remissionem. Sed illa mors osten dit etiam iram Dei adversus peccatum, ut in nobis quoque mortificetur peccatum, id est, ut agnoscentes iram Dei consolemur nos beneficio Christi. Item, Ita fit remissio peccatorum ut si, mul aboleatur peccatum. Abolitum autem non debet esse efficax.

Sepulti sumus igitur unà cum illo &c.

Gravissima collatio est nostrae conversionis ad Christi mortem, sepulturam & resurrectionem. Ita enim instituit responsionem. Propter mortem Christi habetis remissionem, quae ita fit ut simul proptermortem Christi aboleri peccatum, seu mortificari vitiosa natura incipiat, quia simul datur spiritus sanctus, ut mortificet veterem naturam & inchoet novam. Sepelimur autem una cum Christo, quia postquàm natura nostra mortificari cepit, peccatum sepultum est dupliciter. Primum imputatione, Quanquàm enim reli quiae manent, tamen sunt condonatae. Secundo, quod ad effectum attinet, quia natura vitiosa desinit esse efficax, seu incipit mortificari. Itaque reliquum vitae post inchoatam mortificationem est sepultura, peccatum quidem imputatione deletum est, nondum sumus glorificati. Quare & si sumus iusti, tamen iacemus sepulti expectantes glorificationem. Sicut Paulus inquit: Vita vestra abscondita est cum Christo, id est, &si habemus gloriam, iusticiam, vitam, tamen hace gloria latet adhuc tecta cum Christo, donec resuscitabimur. Secundo, quod ad effectum attinet, iacemus in sepulchro, id est in cruce, in afflictionibus omnis generis, diabolus horribilibus modis perturbat & persequitur pios. Hae calamitates omnes, denique & ipsa mors, sunt velut sepulchrum, in quo iacet vetus natura mortua, ne sit efficax. Haec collatio sepulturae est illustris pictura mortu peccati, quod ad imputationem attinet & effectum, & monet qua lis sit vita Christiana. Deinde addit tertium membrum: Non solum fit moritificatio, sed etiam inchoatur vivificatio. Porro nova natura est efficax. Ideo necesse est existere novam obedientiam. Hanc collationem repetit: Si sumus inserti imagini mortis eius, etiam inseremur imagini resurrectionis hoc est, Sicut vetus noster homo unà crucifixus est, ita renovati una vivemus. Cùm autem sit nova vita, seu nova natura, nova lux & notitia Dei, existit etiam nova obedientia.

Qui mortuus est, iusti ficatus est a peccato: Nero est mortuus: Ergo est iustificatus. R. Ad maiorem, loquitur de peccato actuali. Vel iustifiicatus est, id est, satisfecit pro peccato. Est figura sumpta ex communi sermone sicut dicimus, quando suspenditur fur: nunc desunt peccare.

* In homine sunt quaedam bonae notitiae: Deo est obediendum &c. Ergo non totus vetus homo est damnandus R. Sunt in homine notitiae illae, sed affectus non obediunt: Ergo diligenter not andum est discrimen appetitionum & notitiarum,στόργαιsunt bonae suanatura, sed fiunt vitiosae, quia sunt in natura vitiosa, & non diriguntur ad gloriam Dei.

Vetus homo non significat tantum partem hominis, scilicet sensus & appetitiones sensus, sed etiam rationem & voluntatem. Nec solum appetitiones pugnant cum Lege Dei, sed etiam in ratione ignoratio Dei, dubitatio an exaudiamur, blasphemiae. De inde etiam appetitiones. securitas, contemptus Dei, diffidentia, amor et fiducia rcrum praesentium contra mandatum Dei, desperatio &c. Haec vitia non ad sensum, sed ad superiorem partem pertinent. Ideo Paulus describens hominem sine spiritu sancto, inquit: Animalis homo non percipit ea, quae sunt spiritus Dei. Econtra novus homo dicitur, quatenus habet novam lucem & novos motus excitatos à spiritu sancto, videlicet agnitionem Christi, fiduciam erga Deum, timorem Dei invocationem, dilectionem & similes motus. De hac novitate loquitur Paulus ii. Corrint. iii. Nunc retecta facie gloriam Domini intuentes in eandem imaginem transformamur à gloria in gloriam, tanquàm à Domini spiritu, id est, cum in Evangelio ostenditur nobis misericordia, erigimur agnitione ac fiducia Dei & sentimus nos Deo curae esse invocamus. In hac notitia & his motibus agnoscitur & refulget Deus & nos quadam imagine, id est, notitia Dei renovamur. Nec significat novitas cogitationes & motus rationis sine spiritu sancto.

Ne igitur regnet.

Conclusio est institutae obiectionis, quae sequitur ex superiore argumento: Quia propter Christi mortem peccatum coepit aboleri: Ergo non regnet nec sit efficax.

Mortua natura non debet esse efficax. Propter Christi mortem peccatum remissum est, ita ut simul incipiat propter Christi mortem aboleri: Ergo cum aboleatur non debet esse efficax.

Dicit autem disertè, Non regnet ut signi ficet non prorsus extinctam esse vitiosam. Reliquum est igitur peccatum in natura: sed id mortificari coepit, ideo non regnet. Haec verba Paulus ipse interpretatur: Non regnet ita ut ei obediatis, id est, non ob temperate vitiosis affectibus, sed repugnate: Sicut & infra dicit: Si actiones carnis spiritu mortificabitis vivetis. Hi loci & similes ostendunt discrimen peccati mortalis & venialis. Manent in sanctis concupiscentia & vitiosi affectus, sed cum his resistunt, & fide petunt ac statuunt sibi condonari haec peccata, fiunt venialia, quia etiam cum adsunt talia possunt simul existere in piis spiritus sanctus & fides. Sed mortalia sunt in his qui fuerant sanctificati, cum contra conscientiam obtemperant pravis affectibus : Sicut infra dicitur : Si secundum carnem vivetis moriemini, & hic: non praebete membra vestra arma iniusticiae. Praecipit autem quia cum verbo Dei est efficax spiritus sanctus & impellit eos, & nos obsequi impellenti non repugnare debemus, sicut alibi inquit Paulus: Videte ne frustra gratiam acceperitis. Iubet ut donum exerceamus, & in hoc exercitio proficiunt pii iuxta illud: Haec exerce ut profectus tuus appareat. Ita hic significanter ait: Exhibete membra, ut sint arma iusticiae. Vult enim excitare & acuere fervorem, sicut alibi inquit : ferventes spiritu. Ut enim non sunt languida membra, non sunt ociosa, quatenus habent impetus veteris naturae. Sed sicut vegeta & habent acres impetus, ita renovatae naturae membra oportuit non esse languida, sed habere acres & veros motus ad benefaciendum & armorum vocabulo usus est, ut significet in liac militia acerrimam dimicationem esse debere adversus diabolum carnem & omnis generis insidias & tentationes.

## 6:11
For our sin shall not have dominion.

He answers a silent objection, for whenever we hear a sermon about obedience, the pious mind immediately asks, since we cannot satisfy the Law, how will our obedience please ? Thus here, when Paul had said: present your members as weapons of righteousness, the pious are distressed and argue, how that obedience pleases, especially since there is an infinite dissimilarity of gifts, since there is great infirmity, since our obedience is deformed by many huge scandals. Here Paul answers: sin shall not have dominion over you. For you are not under the Law, but under grace. This doctrine and consolation is necessary for the pious, so that they may know to what extent and how begun obedience pleases when it is imperfect, when there is a great dissimilarity of gifts, with innumerable scandals and terrors we may be vexed. Wherefore let this saying be understood thus, as a consolation and promise: Sin shall not have dominion over you, that is, it does not condemn you, it is not imputed to those believing in Christ, but begun obedience is pleasing on account of grace, that is, because we believe in Christ even if it is imperfect. In the same sentiment he says below: There is now no condemnation to those who walk in Christ Jesus. And therefore the reason or explanation is subjoined: You are not under the Law, but under grace, that is, under mercy accepting you on account of Christ, according to the promise, that is, believers are pleasing on account of Christ, even if they do not yet in reality satisfy the Law. Nor does the Law have the right of judging and condemning believers. Thus also to the Galatians he says: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the Law, etc. This is the simple and genuine sentiment of this passage. However, the meaning of the word grace must be prudently observed here. For the whole sentiment is corrupted and overwhelmed by those who explain it. You are under grace, that is, the moral Law, when the moral Law most of all condemns. But let grace be understood concerning imputation, by which believers they are righteous, that is, accepted on account of Christ, which imputation is announced in the Gospel, and although effect and renewal accompany the imputation, nevertheless the conscience ought to look upon the promised imputation, and the mediator Christ, not one's own qualities or habits. Thus this sentiment proposes the most ample doctrine and consolation: You are not under the Law but under grace, that is, the Law does not have the right of condemning believers. Although therefore obedience is imperfect in believers, it pleases nevertheless because the persons are reckoned righteous or accepted on account of the high priest Christ. Now here mercy is to be amplified, so that this very thing may rouse us to doing good. It is a huge and ineffable goodness of God, that God approves in believers this obedience, which nevertheless has wondrous infirmity, and dissimilarity, and is contaminated by many filthinesses and scandals. Therefore let not doubt weaken or deter minds, but let the very greatness of mercy, which approves however infirm they may be, if nevertheless they believe in Christ etc., invite us to doing good. It is necessary that this doctrine and consolation exist in the Church, so that we may know how far and where good works are to be rejected, both as to how far they are to be sought and how they are pleasing to God.

Latin:

Peccatum enim nostrum non dominabitur.

Respondet tacitae obiectioni, semper enim cum audimus concionem de obedientia statim quaerit pia mens, cum non possimus satisfacere Legi, quomodo placebit nostra obedientia? Ita hic cum Paulus dixisset: praebete membra vestra arma iusticiae, Pii anguntur & disputant, quomodo placeat illa obedientia praesertim cum sit infinita dissimilitudo donorum, cumsit magna infirmitas, cum multis ingentibus scandalis nostra obedientia deformetur. Hic respondet Paulus: peccatum non dominabitur vobis. Non enim estis sub Lege, sed sub gratia, Haec doctrina & consolatio necessaria est piis, ut sciant quatenus & quomodo inchoata obedientia placeat cum sit imperfecta, cum sit magna dissimilitudo donorum, cum innumerabilibus scandalis, & terroribus vexemur. Quare sic intelligatur hoc dictum, tanquàm consolatio & promissi: Peccatum non dominabitur vobis, id est, non damnat vos, non imputatur credentibus in Christum, sed placet inchoata obedientia propter gratiam, id est, quia credimus in Christum etiamsi est imperfecta. In eandem sententiam infra inquit: Nulla nunc damnatio est his, qui in Christo Iesu ambulant. Ideoque ratio seu explicatio subiicitu: Non estis sub Lege, sed sub gratia, id est, sub misericordia acceptante vos propter Christum, iuxta promissionem, id est, credentes placent propter Christum, etiamsi nondum reipsa satisfaciunt Legi. Nec habet Lex ius iudicandi & damnandi credentes. Sic & ad Galatas inquit: Christus redemit nos à maledicto Legis, &c. Haec est simplex & germana huius loci sententia. Est autem hic prudenter observanda significatio vocabuli gratia. Tota enim sententia corrumpitur & obruitur ab illis qui exponunt. Estis sub gratia, id est, Lege morali, Cum Lex moralis maximè condemnet. Sed gratia de imputatione intelligatur, qua credentes sunt iusti, id est, accepti propter Christum, quae imputatio in Evangelio annunciatur, & quanquàm effectus & renovatio comitatur imputationem, tamen conscientia debet intueri promissam imputationem, & mediatorem Christum, non proprias qualitates aut habitus. Ita haec sententia doctrinam & consolationem amplissimam proponit: Non estis sub Lege sed sub gratia, id est, Lex non habet ius condemnandi credentes. Quamvis igitur in credentibus imperfecta est obedientia, placet tamen quia personae reputantur iustae seu acceptae propter pontificem Christum. Iam hic amplificanda est misericordia, ut haec ipsa nos exuscitet ad bene operandum. Ingens & ineffabilis bonitas Dei est, quòd Deus in credentibus approbat hanc obedientiam, quae tamen mirificam habet infirmitatem, & dissimilitudinem, & multis sordibus & scandalis contaminatur. Ergo non debilitet aut deterreat animos dubitatio, sed ipsa magnitudo misericordiae, quae approbat quamlibet infirmos, si tamen credant in Christum &c. invitet nos ad bene operandum. Hanc doctrinam & consolationem extare in Ecclesia necesse est, ut sciamus quatenus & ubi bona opera reiicienda sint, & quatenus requirenda & quomodo placeant Deo.

## 6:11
What then? Shall we sin?

Paul inserts a necessary occupation: For that former voice: You are not under the Law seems most absurd, for good natures love nothing more than the Law. Therefore it cannot be that they are not vehemently offended by those tribunitian voices, as it were, in which they think the Law is so abrogated that license to sin is granted. But it has often been said elsewhere that this disputation of Paul pertains absolutely nothing to political life, nor does it abolish discipline or civil morals, but that an entirely different matter is being treated here. Others easily escape here, who refer liberty only to the abrogation of the ceremonies and the Mosaic polity, not to the whole Law. But it has often been said already that Paul is here preaching chiefly about the moral Law, and in sum he wants us to be liberated from the whole Law, as far as it pertains to justification, that is, another matter is proposed, on account of which we have remission of sins and are reckoned righteous before God, namely the merit of Christ. For thus we are liberated from the Law if we establish that we have the remission of sins on account of him and are reckoned righteous before God, not on account of the Law, and joined with this imputation is the renewal of nature, repentance, or begun obedience. Therefore, the Gospel does not grant a license to sin, since it preaches not only about imputation, but also about repentance, and begins a new obedience, and shows how it pleases. Meanwhile, however, the Law remains, as it pertains to discipline in the external life. Also, as it pertains to reproving and mortifying the old self, but in such a way that when faith conquers, the Law does not have the right to condemn. I simply answer thus. The Law is abrogated as it pertains to justification, not as it pertains to obedience, that is, obedience is to be performed and indeed is begun, and yet it must be known that we are meanwhile righteous on account of Christ, so that the benefit may remain certain. This response, in my judgment, has nothing perplexed or intricate, concerning which, however, I permit the judgment of the prudent.

Far be it. Do you not know?

Paul refutes the objection with two arguments, both of which are taken from the final cause or from the effect. Christ appeared, that He might abolish sin and death, and restore nature, so that the restored might have eternal life, which is new and eternal obedience and wisdom. Since therefore the end is that newness or restoration of nature, it is necessary that new obedience be begun and performed, because that very spiritual newness is that obedience, and in sum the Gospel when it grants reconciliation on account of Christ, at the same time subjects us to obedience toward God, and begins obedience. No one does not see that this argument is apt, and proper to the business and taken from the final cause. Paul renders this very sentiment with a syllogism.

Everyone obeys him to whom he is already subject.

You are not subject to sin, but freed from sin, and you have been transferred into the kingdom of God and are subject to God.

Therefore you ought not to obey sin, but God.

It can also be accommodated to the formal cause, as if you should say: A healthy body has healthy actions.

A hot body heats, so in this proposal.

The righteous have righteous actions, You are righteous: Therefore you also ought to have righteous actions. I declare the minor premise. For although we are righteous, that is, accepted by imputation on account of Christ, nevertheless it is necessary that the very virtue of justice, that is, obedience, also be begun in us. Now the virtue of justice produces righteous actions. And yet meanwhile it must be known that we are righteous, that is, accepted by God, on account of Christ the high priest, not on account of the dignity of our obedience or quality.

Latin:

Quid igitur? peccabimus?

Necessariam occupationem inserit Paulus: Nam illa prior vox : Non estis sub Lege videtur absurdissima, nihil enim magis amant bonae naturae quâm Legem. Ideo non potest fieri, quin vehementer offendantur illis velut tribunitiis vocibus, in quibus putant ita abrogari Legem, ut concedatur licentia peccandi. Saepe autem alâs dictum est hanc disputationem Pauli, prorsus nihil pertinere ad politicam vitam, nec tollere disci plinam aut mores civiles, sed prorsus aliam rem hic agi. Alii facile hic evadunt, quiliber tatem referunt tantum ad abrogationem ceremoniarum & politiae Mosaicae, non ad totam Legem. Saepe autem iam dictum est, Paulum hic concionari praecipue de morali Lege, et in summa vult nos liberatos esse à tota Lege, quod attinet ad iustificationem, id est, alia res proposita est, propter quàm habemus remissionem peccatorum & reputamur iusti coram Deo, videlicet meritum Christi. Ita enim liberati sumus à Lege si statuamus nos propter ipsum habere remissionem peccatorum & reputari iustos coram Deo, non propter Legem, & cum hac imputatione coniuncta est renovatio naturae, paenitentia seu inchoata obedientia. Non igitur concedit Evangelium licentiam peccandi, cum non solum concionetur de imputatione, sed etiam de paenitentia & inchoet novam obedientiam & ostendet quomodo placeat. Interea tamen manet Lex, quod attinet ad disciplinam in vita externa. Item quod attinet ad arguendam & mortificandam vetustatem, sed ita, ut cum fides vincit non habeat Lex ius damnandi. Ego simpliciter ita respondeo. Lex est abrogata quod attinet ad iustificationem, non quod ad obedientiam attinet, id est, obedientia praestanda est & quidem inchoatur, & tamen sciendum est nos interim propter Christum iustos esse, ut maneat beneficium certum. Haecresponsio meo iudicio, nihil habet perplexi aut intricati, de qua tamen prudentibus permitto iudicium.

Absit. an nescitis?

Paulus diluit obiectionem duobus argumentis, quae ambo sunt à causa finali sumpta vel ab effectu. Christus apparuit, ut aboleret peccatum & mortem, & restitueret naturam, ut instaurata habeat vitam aeternam, quae est nova & aeterna obedientia & sapientia. Cum igitur finis sit illa novitas vel instauratio naturae, necesse est inchoari & praestari novam obedientiam, quia illa ipsa novitas spiritualis est illa obedientia, & in summa Evangelium cum donat reconciliationem propter Christum, simul subiicit nos obedientiae erga Deum, & inchoat obedientiam. Nemo non videt hoc argumentum esse aptum, & proprium negocio & ex causa finali sumptum. Hanc ipsam sententiam Paulus reddit syllogismo.

Unusquisquè obedit illi cui iam subditus est.

Vos non estis subditi peccato, sed liberati à peccato, & estis traducti in regnum Dei & subditi Deo.

Ergo non debetis obedire peccato, sed Deo.

Potest accommodari & ad causam formalem, ut si dicas : Sanum corpus habet sanas actiones.

Calidum corpus calefacit, Ita in hoc proposito.

Iusti habent actiones iustas, Vos estis iusti : Ergo vos quoque debetis habere actiones iustas. Minorem declaro. Etsi enim sumus iusti, id est, accepti imputatione propter Christum, tamen necesse est in nobis etiam inchoari ipsam virtutem iusticiam, id est, obedientiam. Iusticia autem virtus parit iustas actiones. Et tamen interea sciendum est nos propter Christum pontificem esse iustos, id est, acceptos Deo, non propter dignitatem obedientiae nostrae seu qualitatis.

## 7:1 Argument
CHAPTER VII.

Latin:

CAPUT VII.

## 7:1
Do you not know, brethren?

The second similitude is that which also contains an argument from the final cause. We have been reconciled for this reason, that we might now obey God. Now there are two parts of the comparison; the former teaches what kind of nature is subject to the Law. The latter part of the comparison speaks of the final cause, namely, of new obedience. This is the former part: The Law pertains to the living carnal nature. But you are now mortified, that is, if you are truly in Christ. Therefore the Law does not accuse, it does not condemn us. He proves the major premise by a similitude:

Just as a woman is subject to her husband as long as the husband lives, so the Law rules over the living. The subsequent comparison is as follows: Just as when the husband is dead a woman married to another ought to adhere to him, so we, having been freed from the former servitude, have now become the liberator's, therefore we ought to adhere to and obey him. This is a simple and not a complex application. The former part, however, signifies that the liberation is not merely an imagination, but comes to pass when the old nature, which was previously under the law, is mortified. Now, therefore, since the nature is different, the right of the law does not pertain to it, that is, to this one as it did to the old one; insofar as we believe, the law does not accuse nor condemn us. The other part is more illustrious, namely that which speaks of the final cause: we have become the liberator's, therefore let us adhere to and obey him.

Latin:

An ignoratis fratres?

Altera similitudo est, quae etiam continet argumentum à causa finali. Ideo reconciliati sumus, ut iam Deo obediamus. Sunt autem duae partes collationis, prior docet qualis natura sit subiecta Legi. Posterior pars collationis loquitur de causa finali, scilicet de nova obedientia. Prior pars haec est: Lex pertinet ad viventem carnalem naturam. Vos autem iam estis mortificati, scilicet si verè estis in Christo. Ergo Lex non accusat non condemnat nos. Maiorem probat similitudine:

Sicut mulier subiecta est marito tantisper donec vivit maritus, Ita Lex dominatur viventibus. Posterior collatio talis est : Sicut mortuo marito mulier nupta alteri debet ei adhaerere, ita nos liberati a priore servitute facti iam sumus liberatoris, Ergo ei adhaerere & obedire debemus. Haec est simplex & non perplexa accommodatio. Prior autem pars significat liberationem non esse tantum imaginationem, sed fieri mortificata veteri natura, quae prius erat sub lege. Nunc igitur cum alia sit natura, non pertinet, id est ad hanc ius legis sicut ad veterem, quatenus credimus lex non accusat nec damnat nos. Altera pars illustrior est, scilicet quae loquitur de caussa finali : facti sumus liberatores, ergo ei adhaereamus & obediamus.

## 7:4
You have been mortified to the Law through the body of Christ, etc.

The conclusion, in which Paul applies the previous similitude to this very sentiment, just as I have applied it: You have died to the Law through the body of Christ, that is, you have been freed from the Law, that is, so that the Law may not condemn or accuse you, and indeed you have been freed through the body of Christ, that is, through the victim Christ, who satisfied the Law for us, and took away condemnation and eternal death. Furthermore, on account of the death of Christ, nature is restored and the old nature is mortified, just as he said above: We are buried together through baptism into death, etc.

Latin:

Mortificati estis Legi per cor-pus Christi &c.

Conclusio, in qua Paulus accommodat superiorem similitudinem in hanc ipsam sententiam, sicut accommodavi: Mortui estis Legi per corpus Christi, id est, liberati estis à Lege, id est, ne damnet ne accuset vos Lex, & quidem liberati estis per corpus Christi, id est, per victimam Christum, qui pro nobis satisfecit Legi, & sustulit condemnationem & aeternam mortem. Praeterea propter mortem Christi instauratur natura & mortificatur vetus natura, sicut supra dixit : Consepulti sumus per baptismum in mortem &c.

## 7:5
For when we were in the flesh.

He attaches an antithesis to the conclusion, so that he may describe in passing what kind of prior servitude there was under the Law, and on the contrary what kind of thing that newness is, which exists when we are freed from the Law. Such, he says, was the servitude, that the Law even increased sin, because when it accuses and terrifies, doubt is kindled, and indignation against God and despair follow. He speaks here properly of such sins, when he says: The affections of sins excited by the Law were effective in our members, namely doubt and indignation against God, they turn the heart away from God, they prohibit invocation, etc. For first that huge doubt which clings in the souls of all men, is certainly effective in the members, because on account of that doubt men rush against the will of God, so that because they do not trust in God, they do many things out of fear and distrust against the will of God, in seeking wealth, aids, etc. Now the Law increases this doubt or distrust, which, because it always accuses, causes hearts to be turned away from God, to flee from God, not to call upon Him, not to trust, not to expect help from God. These things happen much more, and are more clearly seen in the very terrors and agony of conscience, as in Saul the terrors excited by the Law were truly effective in his members, they produced indignation and raging against God, despair and death, they prevented invocation. Now this passage is to be diligently observed, so that we may learn that that doubt is a sin, so that we may resist, and raise ourselves up by the Gospel, and know that it is a worship of God, in those terrors to resist doubt and distrust. But the greatest part of men lives in that perpetual doubt and distrust, and neither calls upon God, nor asks, nor expects anything from God: Men do not discern these secret sins, but Christians ought to understand them, and console themselves with the voice of the Gospel, they conceive true faith. Paul used very significant words when he names the affections and explicitly says they are excited by the Law, and adds that they are effective in the members. These are very illustrious descriptions, just as we see in Saul how vehement is the indignation, how ardent are the motions. Thus in individual men doubt turns hearts away from God, and holds them captive. These things are not said by Paul according to common judgment, but Paul looks with spiritual eyes upon the captivity of human hearts, and the secret distrust and doubt, which afterwards brings forth infinite sins. To the same point pertains what he says afterwards: We are dead to the Law in which we were held captive, for they signify that captivity by which human hearts, oppressed by doubt, distrust, and terrors, are turned away from God, flee from God, and can neither truly call upon Him, nor are they assured that they are forgiven. But when, having heard the voice of the Gospel, they raise themselves up and conceive true faith, then they begin to acknowledge and call upon God, and are assured that they are forgiven, and that they are heard, and they expect good things from God. Thus he speaks of liberty ii. Corint. iii. And here he says that liberation from that captivity happens in such a way that now hearts liberated from distrust truly acknowledge God. Therefore, he says, that we may serve in newness of spirit.

Latin:

Cum enim essemus in carne.

Attexit conclusioni antithesin, ut obiter describat qualis fuerit prior servitus sub Lege, & è contra qualis res sit illa novitas, quae existit cum sumus liberati à Lege. Talis inquit erat servitus, ut Lex etiam augeret peccatum, quia cum accusat & perterrefacit, incenditur dubitatio, & sequuntur indignatio adversus Deum et desperatio. De huiusmodi peccatis propriè hic loquitur, cum ait: Affectus peccatorum excitati per Legem erant efficaces in membris nostris, scilicet dubitatio & indignatio adversus Deum, avertunt cor à Deo, prohibent invocationem &c. Primum enim illa ingens dubitatio quae in omnium hominum animis haeret, certè est efficax in membris, quia propter illam dubitationem ruunt homines contra voluntatem Dei, ut quia non confidunt Deo, multa faciunt metu & diffidentia contra voluntatem Dei, in quaerendis opibus auxiliis &c. Hanc autem dubitationem seu diffidentiam auget Lex, quae quia semper accusat, facit ut corda sint aversa à Deo, fugiant Deum, non invocent, non confidant, non expectent à Deo auxilium. Multo magis haec fiunt, & magis conspiciuntur in ipsis terroribus & agone conscientiae, ut in Saul terrores excitati per Legem, prosecto erant efficaces in eius membris, parebant indignationem, & fremitum adversus Deum, desperationem & mortem, prohibebant invocationem. Est autem hic locus diligenter observandus, ut discamus illam dubitationem esse peccatum, ut repugnemus, & erigamus nos Evangelio, & sciamus esse cultum Dei, in illis terroribus repugnare dubitationi & diffidentiae. Sed maxima pars hominum vivit in illa perpetua dubitatione & diffidentia, nec invocat Deum, nec petit, nec expectat quicquam à Deo: Haec arcana peccata, non cernunt homines, sed Christiani ea intelligere debent, & consolari se voce Evangelii, concipiunt veram fidem. Paulus usus est admodum significantibus verbis, cum nominat affectus & diserte dicit eos per Legem excitari, & addit efficaces esse in membris. Hae sunt admodum illustres descriptiones, sicut in Saul videmus quàm sit vehemens indignatio, quàm sint ardentes motus. Sic in singulis hominibus dubitatio avertit corda à Deo, & tenet captiva. Haec non dicuntur vulgari iudicio à Paulo, sed spiritualibus oculis intuetur Paulus captivitatem cordium humanorum, et arcanam diffidentiam & dubitationem, quae postea infinita peccata parit. Eodem pertinet quòd postea inquit: Mortui Legi qua captivi tenebamur, significant enim illam captivitatem, qua corda humana oppressa dubitatione, diffidentia, pavoribus, avertuntur à Deo, sugiunt Deum, nec possunt vere invocare, nec statuunt sibi ignosci. Sed quando audita voce Evangelii erigunt se, & veram fidem concipiunt, tunc incipiunt Deum agnoscere & invocare, & statuunt sibi ignosci, le exaudiri, expectant bona à Deo. Sic de libertate loquitur ii. Corint. iii. Et hic ait, liberationem ex illa captivitate ita fieri, ut iam corda liberata diflidentia vere agnoscant Deum. Ideo, ait, ut serviamus in novitate spiritus.

## 7:6
But now we are delivered from the Law, etc.

He described the servitude under the Law in a few words in the previous conclusion, namely that the Law holds hearts captive, and increases diffidence and doubt, which beget despair, blasphemy, and turn hearts away from God, so that they rush into various sins. Then he adds a description of liberty, and first he says that we are dead to the Law, that is, delivered from that captivity, because the Gospel brings the remission of sins. For neither can God be invoked, nor can God be obeyed, unless the remission of sins is first received, because as long as we are captives of the Law, and do not hear of the remission of sins, the goodness of God is not yet acknowledged, hearts do not feel that we are heard, they flee the wrath of God and are turned away from God. But after the remission of sins has been received through the Gospel and the acknowledgment of Christ, then obedience begins, because now we acknowledge the will of God, that He wishes to hear us, wishes to have mercy, and now we invoke Him. Therefore he says here that obedience begins only then, when we are delivered from the Law through faith, that is, when in Christ we now acknowledge the will and goodness of God. the goodness of God. This opinion therefore teaches clearly that without faith and outside of faith in Christ, no works please God, nor are they righteousness or obedience toward God, or worship of God, just as he says above: through whom we have access to God. He distinguishes, however, the new obedience from the carnal and calls the new one spiritual, but the other he calls the oldness of the letter. Moreover, it was said above that the letter signifies all thoughts, endeavors, good intentions: Likewise works, which reason performs without true fear of God, and without true trust in Christ, and without the Holy Spirit. Just as Saul has good intentions, good purposes, that he wishes to serve God: Likewise, he sacrifices and meanwhile has neither fear nor true faith. Just as contrition, when it is not true sorrow, but summoned sadness, is the letter. For it is called the letter for this reason, because it is not a true and living movement of the soul, but is an idle imitation, interior or exterior, nor can there be true invocation there, where the heart does not apprehend the remission of sins. On the contrary, the spirit signifies true spiritual movements, namely true fear of God, and true trust, which is conceived in true consolation, when, namely, hearts in terrors raise themselves up in the promise of the Gospel, and they apprehend the mercy promised on account of Christ; there, when they acknowledge mercy, they begin to truly invoke God, and truly to expect help from him, and truly to love, etc. These motions are true worship and the new obedience of which he speaks here. And they are made excited by the Holy Spirit, who is conceived in that consolation when we are raised up by faith. As Paul says Gal. iii. That we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith. Thus, therefore, the spirit and the letter are distinguished. The spirit signifies living motions excited by the Holy Spirit. The letter, however, signifies thoughts, intention, purposes, and imitations without a true motion of the heart, and yet the letter pertains to discipline. He uses the word let us serve, not because the new obedience is such a servitude as is the righteousness of the Law, but that he might teach that even the new creature is subject to God, and ordered toward obedience, even if that obedience is voluntary, as he says to the Ephesians: We are his work, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God has ordained, that we should walk in them. And Isaiah lxi. They shall be called trees of righteousness and the planting of the Lord to glorify, that is, that they might glorify God, and not affect God with reproach through scandals.

Latin:

Nunc autem liberatia Lege su-mus &c.

Descripsit servitutem sub Lege paucis verbis in conclusione proxima, quod videlicet Lex teneat captiva corda, & diffidentiam ac dubitationem augeat, quae pariunt desperationem, blaspemiam, & avertunt corda à Deo, ut ruant in varia peccata. Deinde addit libertatis descriptionem, & primum inquit, nos mortuos esse Legi, id est, liberatos ab illa captivitate, quia Evangelium affert remissionem peccatorum. Neque enim potest invocari Deus, aut obediri Deo, nisi prius accepta remifsione peccatorum, quia donec sumus captivi Legis, nec audimus remissionem peccatorum, nondum agnoscitur bonitas Dei, non sentiunt corda nos exaudiri, fugiunt iram Dei & avertuntur à Deo, Sed postquàm accepta est remissio peccatorum per Evangelium & agnitionem Christi, tunc incipit obedientia, quia iam agnoscimus voluntatem Dei, quod velit nos exaudire, velit misereri, iam invocamus. Ideo hic dicit primum tunc inchoari obedientiam, quando à Lege liberamur per fidem, id est, quando in Christo iam agnoscimus voluntatem & bonitatem Dei. Docet igitur haec sententia clarè, quòd sine fide & extra fidem in Christum, non placeant Deo ulla opera, nec sint iusticia seu obedientia erga Deum, vel cultus Dei, sicut supra inquit : per quem accessum habemus ad Deum. Discernit autem novam obedientiam à carnali & novam vocat spiritualem, alteram vero vocat vetustatem literae. Supra autem dictum est, literam significare omnes cogitationes, conatus, bonas intentiones : Item opera, quae ratio facit sine vero timore Dei, & sino vera fiducia Christi, & sine spiritu sancto, Sicut Saul habet bonas intentiones, bona proposita, quod velit Deo servire : Item, sacrificat & interea nec timorem habet, nec veram fidem. Sicut contritio quando non est verus dolor, sed accersita moesticia, est litera. Ideo enim dicitur litera, quia non est verus et vivus motus animi, sed est ociosa imitatio interior vel exterior, nec ibi potest esse vera invocatio, ubi cor non apprehendit remissionem peccatorum. Econtra spiritus significat veros motus spirituales, scilicet verum timorem Dei, & veram fiduciam, quae concipitur in vera consolatione, cum scilicet corda in terroribus erigunt se in promissione Evangelii, & apprehendunt misericordiam propter Christum promissam, ibi cum agnoscunt misericordiam, incipiunt vere invocare Deum, & vere expectare ab eo auxilium, vere diligere &c. Hi motus sunt veri cultus & nova obedientia, de qua hic loquitur. Et fiunt excitati à spiritu sancto, qui in illa consolatione cum fide erigimur, concipitur. Sicut inquit Paulus Gal. iii. Ut promissionem spiritus accipiamus per fidem. Sic igitur discernuntur spiritus & litera. Spiritus significat vivos motus excitatos à spiritu sancto. Litera vero cogitationes, intentio, proposita & imitationes sine vero motu cordis, & tamen litera ad disciplinam pertinet. Utitur autem vocabulo serviamus non quod nova obedientia sit talis servitus, qualis est iusticia Legis, sed ut doceat etiam novam creaturam subiectam esse Deo, & ordinatam ad obedientiam, etiamsi illa obedientia est voluntaria, sicut ad Ephesios inquit: Ipsius sumus opus conditi in Christo Iesu ad bona opera, quae ordinavit Deus, ut in eis ambulemus. Et Esaiae Ixi. Vocabuntur arbores iustae & plantulae domini ad glorificandum, id est, ut glorificent Deum, non afficiant Deum contumelia perscandala.

## 7:6
The Law is spiritual.

He dissolves a tacit objection, for it could be objected, what is to be thought of those who obey the law, such as are not only hypocrites, whose life is blameless, but also saints, such as Isaiah, John the Baptist, etc. Concerning these it is asked whether they are not righteous by the Law, whether the Law does not profit them for life, that is, for the remission of sins and vivification. Here Paul answers: Nay, he says, the Law is spiritual, but I am carnal, as if he were to say, neither I nor anyone satisfies the Law, because the Law is spiritual, that is, requiring spiritual and perfect obedience, which carnal nature does not provide. And it is to be diligently observed in this place what he calls spiritual. For he opposes it to political or external discipline, which is called carnal discipline and righteousness, as if he were to say, the Law is not only political doctrine, that is, to which external discipline can satisfy, but it requires spiritual obedience, that is, spiritual motions, an illustrious acknowledgment of God, fear, trust, love of God, and other pious, ardent motions without concupiscence. But because the heart of man is not such, therefore the Law is a ministry condemning sin and truly terrifying hearts. Therefore, the interpretation of Origen and those like him, who think that to signify spiritual is the same as allegorical, and afterwards understand the whole Law to be only a doctrine concerning external morals, and think that the Law can be satisfied, is foreign to this saying of Paul. But let us hold the antithesis, that he opposes spiritual to external discipline, which is carnal justice, not spiritual, because spiritual signifies motions acting with God. This antithesis, therefore, adds much light when we interpret: the law is spiritual, that is, not only political, but requiring spiritual and perfect obedience, and a ministry not only external, but by which God judges and condemns sins and terrifies hearts. Furthermore, although human reason only understands the Law concerning political morals, nevertheless the Gospel in the preaching of repentance draws away from human hearts the veil of Moses, that is, the false opinion concerning the Law and convicts the very justice of the law, that is justice is not satisfied by the Law, and he testifies that the Law requires perfect obedience, etc. Then Paul declares the proposed proposition: The Law is spiritual, but I am carnal, when he mentions that he does not satisfy the Law, but has in the flesh impulses fighting against the Law of God. He also adds a declaration of what he wishes to be understood by these words: I am carnal, because he subjoins these words: sold under sin. By which words he signifies that nature does not have spiritual obedience, but is vicious, and a slave or captive of sin, that is, corrupted. This whole passage declares what kind of corruption of nature there is, and that original sin is not only an imputation, but in reality a certain corruption in nature. These things must be taught in the Church, so that we may acknowledge sin, and from the opposite direction the magnitude of the benefit of Christ may be known. Wherefore these words must be diligently weighed: sold under sin, so that the magnitude of sin and servitude may be understood, namely that nature is truly corrupted and vicious. Some elude these things and pretend that Paul is speaking here not of his own person, not of the converted and holy, but of the impious. This cavil is to be rejected, for just as David of himself And he speaks of all the saints when he says: No living man shall be justified in thy sight, or when he says: Behold I was conceived in iniquities etc. Thus Paul speaks of himself and by his own example embraces all the saints. Since therefore this interpretation of Paul has firm and illustrious testimonies in the psalms, it is certain, nor are foreign interpretations to be feigned. Moreover, carnal nature signifies the nature of man of itself not understanding, nor desiring spiritual things, that is, doubting concerning God, empty of the fear of God and secure, and either despising the judgment of God, or being angry at the judgment of God, and on the contrary desiring carnal things, pleasures, riches, glory, trusting not in the help of God, which it does not discern, but in present things, the powers of wisdom or of justice. Such is human nature without the Holy Spirit, but when it is renewed by faith through the Holy Spirit, spiritual newness begins to struggle with carnal corruption, which is still remaining, as long as we live in this mortal body. That struggle Paul then describes: That which I work, I do not know, that is, I do not approve, as if he were to say, I feel my nature to be repugnant to the Law of God, that I do not have ardent motions of fear, of faith, of love Of God: Item, in afflictions nature resists the will of God, it desires to shake off afflictions, and seeks bodily protections; doubts about God often enter into the mind. Paul signifies such interior motions when he says: What I do I do not approve, that is, spiritual newness struggles within me against those vicious motions, and disapproves of those vices. He then describes this battle in more words: Not what I will, the good, that I do, that is, although I have an incipient fear, yet it is hindered by natural security, so that it is not as great as it ought to be. Although I have an incipient faith, yet it is hindered by natural doubt, so that it is not firm enough. Although I have an incipient love, yet it is hindered by concupiscence, so that it does not sufficiently burn and blaze. He speaks, however, not of light affections and temptations, but of most bitter motions. And therefore he used illustrious words. He names warfare and captivity, so that he might signify that the motions are vehement, just as we experience in calamities, in death, how difficult it is to obey. The whole of nature roars, is indignant, and resists; item, natural doubt and the sight of sin so terrify that even the pious are almost overwhelmed and despairing, just as David often complains.

This captivity is clearly seen in impatience and fears. But the secure and the impious do not discern these interior sins; therefore, they diminish original sin and concupiscence. Wherefore let us hold this passage, and oppose it to false opinions concerning the Law and sin. From this we learn that the fulfillment of the Law is not merely external discipline, that original sin is in reality a certain corruption in the nature of man, which is condemned by the Law of God, that concupiscence even in the saints is sin by its own nature, but is pardoned to the pious who believe. Likewise, that not even the saints satisfy the law of God; likewise, that the saints always have need of the remission of sins; that our fulfillment of the Law, or love, or works, are not worthy on account of which we may be righteous, that is, accepted, nor are they worthy of eternal life, but by faith on account of the mediator Christ we receive the remission of sins, and by the imputation of righteousness, eternal life. Therefore, this chapter contains a manifold doctrine concerning sin, concerning the law, and concerning the remnants of sin in the saints. Wherefore let us diligently remember where this chapter is to be used, because it refutes many false and carnal opinions concerning sin and the Law. Furthermore, here must be reproved the false imagination of those who imagine that Paul is assuming the person of an ungodly man in this place, and deny that this struggle, which is described here, pertains to the person of one who is converted and sanctified, as if in the sanctified there were no remnants of sin, or nature were entirely renewed, and there were no vicious motions. That imagination, however, can easily be refuted by the consensus of the scriptures. For also in Galatians this struggle in the saints is similarly described, when he says: The spirit lusts against the flesh, the flesh against the spirit. And often in the psalms David, converted and holy, deplores present sin, as in the psalm De profundis etc. Psal. xviii. Who understands his faults? Cleanse me from my secret ones, and psalmo cxxxxii. Enter not into judgment with thy servant, for in thy sight shall no man living be justified, and psalm xxxi. For this shall every holy one pray unto thee etc. These testimonies of the psalms entirely agree with this place of Paul, and teach the same thing that Paul argues here, namely that no one satisfies the Law, that remnants of sin remain in the saints, that the saints, that is, those accepted through mercy, believing that their sins are forgiven them on account of Christ. Just as therefore in the psalms by the example of David are described all converted and holy in the Church, so also here Paul speaks of himself as converted and sanctified, and by his own example describes all the holy in the Church, and the words themselves show this, when he says: I delight in the Law of God, also: with the mind I serve the Law of God, also: To will is present with me. For in the ungodly, even if there is some knowledge of the Law, yet there is not that willing or delighting in the Law of God, of which he speaks here. For these words are not to be understood coldly: I delight in the Law of God: to will is present with me, etc., but Paul testifies that he has an inchoate obedience, that he acknowledges God, that he trusts in God, that he is not left in doubt, but is raised up by faith, also that he willingly obeys God in afflictions. The word: I delight in the Law of God, signifies these things, which certainly are not in the ungodly. Again, the reader must also be warned here about the distinction between the inner and outer man, about the mind and the flesh: The inner man signifies the man, insofar as he is renewed by the Holy Spirit, that is, insofar as he has true fear and true trust. So also the mind does not signify here only the knowing part, but both parts, the knowing and the desiring, insofar as it is renewed by the Holy Spirit, as he says: But I with the mind serve the Law of God. On the contrary, the outer Man, or flesh, signifies the whole man, insofar as he is not renewed by the Holy Spirit, and they signify not only the appetites of the senses, or external members, but also the higher powers, reason and will, insofar as they are not renewed, as must be said again below. What he says: Wretched man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death? is the voice not of an impious and secure person, but of one converted, who is engaged in that struggle which is proper to repentance. Let us therefore propose this passage to ourselves among the examples of repentance, and let us learn that such is the perpetual repentance of the pious, namely, to acknowledge misery with immense grief, that is, to be terrified in some way seeing the disease of nature, that pious motions are not ardent in us, fear, faith, love grow cold, and meanwhile carnal cares and affections are more prominent, and a great part of life is directed toward carnal counsels, the glory of God is not sought with total impetus. Pious people, performing repentance, ought to see these vices, so that we may exclaim with Paul: Who shall deliver us from the body of this death? The form of speech is also to be observed, that he does not say, who shall deliver me from this death, but from the body. For he does not speak only of the punishment, but concerning sin, and the body itself testifies, that is, that this carnal nature is immersed in sin and death. For when he names the body of death, he understands the nature immersed in sin, and on account of sin subjected to death, that is, subjected to the wrath of God, to punishments, to terrors, to eternal death, etc. Just as it is said in Psalm 38: Because of iniquity you have chastened man.

Latin:

Lex Spiritualis est.

Diluit tacitam obiectionem, poterat enim obiici, quid videatur de illis qui legi obediunt, quales sunt non modo hipocritae, quorum est inculpata vita, sed etiam sancti, ut Esaias, Iohannes Baptista &c. De his quaeritur an non sint Lege iusti, an Lex non prosit eis ad vitam, hoc est, ad remissionem peccatorum & vivificationem. Hic Paulus respondet : Imo inquit Lex est spiritualis, ego autem carnalis, quasi dicat, neque ego nequè quisquàm Legi satisfacit, quia Lex est spiritualis, id est, requirens spiritualem & perfe ctam obedientiam, quam non praestat natura carnalis. Estque diligenter hoc loco observandum, quid vocet spirituale. Opponit enim politicae seu externae disciplinae, quae vocatur carnalis disciplina & iusticia, quasi dicat, Lex non est tantum doctrina politita, id est, cui externa disciplina satisfacere possit, sed requirit spiritualem obedientiam, id est, spirituales motus, illustrem agnitionem Dei, timorem, fiduciam, dilectionem Dei, & alios motus pios ardentes sine concupiscencia. Quia vero cor hominis non est tale, ideo Lex est ministerium damnans peccatum & vere perterrefaciens corda. Aliena est igitur ab hoc dicto Pauli interpretatio Originis, & similium qui spirituale putant significare, idem quòd allegoricum, & postea totam Legem tantum intelligunt esse doctrinam de externis moribus, & putant posse Legi satisfieri. Sed nos antithesin teneamus, quod spirituale opponat externae disciplinae, quae est carnalis iusticia, non spiritualis, quia spirituale significat motus agentes cum Deo. Haec igitur antithesis multum lucis addit cum interpretamur : lex est spiritualis, id est, non tantum politica, sed requirens piritualem & perfectam obedientiam, & ministerium non tantum externum, sed quo Deus iudicat & damnat peccata et perterrefacit corda. Porro &si ratio humana tantum intelligit Legem de politicis moribus tamen Evangelium in praedicatione paenitentiae, detrahit humanis cordibus velum Mosi, id est, falsam opinionem de Lege et arguit ipsam isticiam legis, id est iusticia non satisfieri Legi, & testatur quod Lex requirat perfectam obedientiam &c. Deinde Paulus declarat institutam propositionem: Lex est spiritualis, ego autem sum carnalis, cum commemorat se non satisfacere Legi, sed habere in carne impetus pugnantes cum Lege Dei. Addit etiam declarationem quid velit intelligi per haec verba: Ego sum carnalis, quia subiicit haec verba: venundatus sub peccatum. Quibus verbis significat naturam non habere spiritualem obedientiam, sed vitiosam esse, & servam seu captivam peccati, id est, corruptam. Hic totus locus declarat qualis sit corruptio naturae, & quod peccatum originale non sit tantum imputatio, sed reipsa quaedam corruptio in natura. Haec necesse est tradi in Ecclesia, ut agnoscamus peccatum, & è regione magnitudo beneficii Christi cognosci possit. Quare diligenter haec verba expendenda sunt : venundatus sub peccatum, ut magnitudo peccati & servitus intelligatur, quod videlicet natura vere corrupta & vitiosa sit. Haec eludunt aliqui & fingunt Paulum hic loqui non de sua persona, non de conversis & sanctis, sed de impiis. Haec cavillatio repudianda est, ut enim David de se & de omnibus sanctis loquitur, cum ait : Non iustificabitur in conspectu tuo omnis vinens, aut cum ait : Ecce in iniquitatibus conceptus sum &c. Ita Paulus de se loquitur & suo exemplo omnes sanctos complectitur. Cum igitur haec interpretatio Pauli habeat firma & illustria testimonia in psalmis, est certa, nec affingendae sunt alienae interpretationes. Significat autem carnalis natura, naturam hominis per sese non intelligentem, nec appetentem spiritualia, id est, dubitantem de Deo, vacuam timore Dei & saecuram, & aut contemnentem iudicium Dei, aut irascentem iudicio Dei, et èregione appetentem carnalia voluptates, opes, gloriam, confidentem non Dei auxilio, quod non cernit, sed praesentibus rebus, viribus sapientiae aut iusticiae. Talis est natura humana sine spiritu sancto, sed cum fide renovatur per spiritum sanctum, incipit spiritualis novitas luctari cum carnali corruptione, quae adhuc reliqua est, donec vivimus in hoc corpore mortali. Illud cettamen deinde describit Paulus: Quod operor, non agnosco, id est, non approbo, quasi dicat, sentio meam naturam repugnare Legi Dei, me non habere ardentes motus, timoris, fidei, dilectionis Dei: Item in afflictionibus repugnat natura voluntati Dei, cupit excutere afflictiones, & quaerit praesidia corparalia, incurrunt in animun saepe dubitationes de Deo. Tales interiores motus significat Paul. cum inquit: Quod operor non approbo, id est, cum illis vitiosis motibus luctatur in me spiritualis novitas, & improbat illa vitia. Hanc pugnam deinde pluribus verbis describit : Non quod volo bonum id facio, id est, etsi habeo inchoatum timorem, tamen ille impeditur naturali securitate, ne sit tantus, quantus esse debeat. Etsi habeo inchoatam fidem, tamen illa impeditur naturali dubitatione, ne sit satis firma. Etsi habeo inchoatam dilectionem, tamen illa impeditur concupiscentia, ne satis ardeat & flagret. Loquitur autem non de levibus affectibus & tentationibus, sed de acerrimis motibus. Ideoque usus est verbis illustribus. Nominat militiam & captivitatem, ut significet vehementes motus esse, sicut experimur in calamitatibus, in morte, quàm difficile sit obedire. Tota natura fremit, indignatur, & repugnat, item dubitatio naturalis et conspectus peccati ita terrent, ut etiam pii pene opprimantur desperabundi, sicut David saepe conquaeritur.

Haec captivitas in impatientia, & pavoribus perspicue conspicitur. Sed haec peccata interiora non cernunt securi & impii, ideo extenuant peccatum orignale & concupiscentiam. Quare hunc locum teneamus, & falsis opinionibus de Lege & peccato opponamus. Hinc discimus, quòd Legis impletio non sit tantum externadisciplina, quod peccatum originale sit reipsa corruptio quaedam in natura hominis, quae damnatur Lege Dei, quòd concupiscentia etiam in sanctis sit peccatum sua natura, sed piis credentibus condonatur. Item, quod nec sancti satisfaciant legi Dei, item, quod sancti semper habeant opus remissione peccatorum, quòd nostra impletio Legis seu dilectio seu opera non sint digna propter quae simus iusti, id est, accepti, nec sint digna vita aeterna, sed fide propter mediatorem Christum accipimus remissionem peccatorum, & imputatione iustitiae, vitam aeternam. Itaque multiplicem doctrinam continet hoc caput de peccato, de lege, de reliquiis peccati in sanctis. Quare diligenter meminerimus, ubi utendum sit hoc capite, quia multas falsas, & carnales opiniones refutat de peccato & Lege. Praeterea hic reprehendenda est salsa imaginatio illorum, qui fingunt Paulum assumere alienam personam impii in hoc loco, & negant hoc certamen, quod hic describitur, convenire in personam conversi & sanctificati, quasi in sanctificatis nullae sint reliquiae peccati, aut natura penitus sit renovata, & nulli sint vitiosi motus. Facile autem illa imaginatio revelli potest consensu scripturarum. Nam & in Galat. similiter describitur hoc certamen in sanctis, cum inquit : Spiritus concupiscit adversus carnem, caro adversus spiritum. Et saepe in psalmis David converfus & sanctus deplorat praesens peccatum, ut in psal. De profundis &c. Psal. xviii. Delicta quis intelligit? ab ocultis meis munda me, & psalmo cxxxxii. Non intres in iudicium cum servo tuo, quia non iustificabitur in conspectu tuo omnis vivens, & psalmo xxxi. Pro hoc orabit ad te omnis sanctus &c. Haec testimonia psalmorum prorsus consentiunt cum hoc loco Pauli, & idem docent, quod hic disputat Paulus, videlicet quòd nemo Legi satisfaciat, quod maneant in sanctis reliquiae peccati, quod sancti, id est, accepti per misericordiam, credentes sibi remitti peccata propter Christum. Sicut igitur in psalmis exemplo Davidis describuntur omnes conversi & sancti in Ecclesia, ita & hic Paulus de se converso & sanctificato loquitur, & suo exemplo describit omnes sanctos in Ecclesia, idquè ostendunt ipsa verba, cum inquit : Delector Lege Dei, item: mente servio Legi Dei, item: Velle adest mihi. Nam in impiis etiamsi est notitia aliqua Legis, tamen non est illud, velle aut delectari Lege Dei, de quo hic loquitur. Non enim frigide intelligenda sunt haec verba : delector Lege Dei : velle adest mihi &c. sed testatur Paulus se habere inchoatam obedientiam, agnoscere Deum, confidere Deo, non relinqui in dubitatione, sed erigi fide, item libenter obedire Deo in afflictionibus. Haec significat verbum: delector Lege Dei, quae certe non sunt in impiis. Rursus etiam hic monendus est lector de discrimine interioris & exterioris hominis, de mente & de carne: Interior homo significat hominem, quatenus renovatus est spiritu sancto, hoc est, quatenus habet verum timorem & veram fiduciam. Ita & mens non significat hic tantum partem cognoscentem, sed utramque partem, cognoscentem & appetentem, quatenus renovata est spiritu sancto, sicut inquit : Ego autem mente servio Legi Dei. E contra exterior homo, seu caro, significant totum hominem, quatenus non est renovatus spiritu sancto, & significant non tantum appetitiones sensuum, aut externa membra, sed etiam potentias superiores, rationem & voluntatem, quatenus non sunt renovati, sicut infra rursus dicendum est. Quod inquit : Miser ego, quis me liberavit à corpore huius mortis? vox est non impii & securi, sed conversi, qui versatur in eo certamine, quod est proprium paenitentiae. Hunc igitur locum nobis inter exempla paenitentiae proponamus, & discamus talem esse perpetuam paenitentiam piorum, videlicet agnoscere miseriam cum ingenti dolore, hoc est, expavescere aliquo modo videntes morbum naturae, quod non sunt ardentes pii motus in nobis, timor, fides, dilectio frigent, & interim carnales curae & affectus magis eminent, & magna pars vitae directa est ad carnalia consilia, non toto impetu quaeritur gloria Dei. Haec vitia videre debent pii, agentes paenitentiam, ut exclamemus cum Paulo. Quis nos liberabit à corpore mortis huius? Est & forma sermonis observanda, quòd non inquit, quis liberabit me ab hac morte, sed à corpore. Non enim de poena tantum loquitur, sed de peccato, & testatur corpus ipsum, hoc est, hanc naturam carnalem īersam esse peccato & morti. Cum enim nominat corpus mortis, intelligit naturam immersam peccato, & propter peccatum subiectam morti, hoc est, subiectam irae Dei, poenis, terroribus, morti aeternae &c. Sicut Psalmo xxxviii. dicitu : Propter iniquitatem corripuisti hominem.

## 7:7
What then shall we say? The Law.

With the digression finished, he returns to that comparison which he instituted above concerning the Law and grace, and here he preaches especially concerning the use of the Law, in order to correct these two opinions clinging not only in the Jews, but universally in the minds of all men: the justice of the Law, which a man can perform, to satisfy the Law, and to be justice before God; that is, men neither see sin and the corruption of nature, nor do they see that the discipline which they perform in any way through the Law does not satisfy the Law, and is not justice before God. Although the Jews most especially defended those opinions concerning the Law, nevertheless they are common to all men, but they are refuted by the Gospel, which teaches that the Law is not only a civil discipline, and that men are not just by the Law. Therefore it is necessary for the Apostles to preach concerning this matter, nor does Paul quarrel here only about ceremonies, but he speaks about the whole Law and especially about the decalogue, just as he cites an example from the decalogue, and argues that no one satisfies the Law, and therefore all are accused by the Law, and for that reason the Law is a ministry of wrath and death. It is necessary that these things be handed down in the Church, so that the benefit of Christ may become illustrious, and it may be understood what is the work of the Gospel, what is the work of grace, and another justice than the justice of the Law. For because we are not justified by the Law, therefore God gave his son for us and reveals the Gospel, that he wishes to forgive us freely on account of the son, to pronounce us just, and to renew us. I have prefaced these things to this place, so that students may more diligently consider with what purpose these things are disputed by Paul, to what they pertain, and how necessary they are. For they declare what kind of sin is inherent in nature, and the corruption of nature. Likewise that the Law does not only require external civil duties, but perfect obedience. Likewise how much the Law accomplishes and that there is need of another word and benefit of Christ. They are also useful so that the distinction between Law and Gospel may be rightly and truly understood. It is necessary, however, that the knowledge of these places exist in the Church. And this part of the Pauline epistle is to be considered the more diligently, because even the ancients labored greatly in explaining it, and few have treated it skillfully and rightly. For since they did not see that Paul was speaking about the struggle of the conscience, but thought it was said about the civil use of the Law, they attached many absurd interpretations, and which are irrelevant to the matter. It is, however, of great importance to the Church that the true meaning of this passage be retained, for if it is suppressed, it cannot be sufficiently understood what and how great original sin is, what the distinction between Law and Gospel is, and what grace and the righteousness of faith are. Now I approach the text, and in summary this is the meaning: We are not righteous by the Law, because the corruption of nature is such that no one can satisfy the Law. Therefore the Law always accuses, and when hearts feel this judgment and the wrath of God, they are terrified and driven to despair and eternal death. Thus the Law is a ministry of wrath and death, and it increases sin, namely not external sin, but it increases it within, that is, it arms sin so that it may terrify and kill us. As he says to the Corinthians: The sting of death is sin: and the power of sin is the Law. And Paul, as a diligent teacher, adds an example from his own experience. At the beginning, however, he prefixes the explanation that the Law is a ministry of death, which does not happen through a fault of the Law, but because of our sin, because corrupt nature cannot satisfy the Law. Therefore the Law accuses us, and he gives an example from the commandment: You shall not covet: so that he may warn that the Law does not only accuse external civil offenses, but also the corruption of nature. Therefore he used these words: Sin having taken occasion, that is, recognized through the Law, stirred up concupiscence, that is, terrified me, and in those terrors, it moves that doubt, distrust, and indignation against God, so that the heart flees from God and is angry at the judgment of God. Without the Law sin is dead, that is, if the Law did not accuse, those terrors and confusion of conscience would not exist: But I once lived without the Law, that is, when I was a Pharisee I was secure, I thought that I satisfied the Law, that I was righteous. For he calls that living without the Law, not to hear the Law showing sin and accusing, not to be affected by that accusation, not to feel pains. Therefore, establish three degrees of men. One is of the carnal who live secure, either as Epicureans or as Pharisees, and they do not have true terrors of conscience. Such a kind of life is to live without the Law, namely judging, accusing, etc. Because the Law in them does not have its principal effect, to show and accuse sin. For the Law is then truly law when it judges and accuses, not when it is written on walls. The second degree is of those who are oppressed by terrors and torments of conscience, like Judas or Saul. These, because they do not hear the voice of the Gospel, they succumb in these terrors, and feel themselves to be damned. Therefore he says here: when the Law came, sin revived, that is, it began to be effective and to terrify, and I died. For unless Paul heard the voice of the Gospel, he too would perish in such terrors. There is therefore a third degree of those who are raised up in terrors by the voice of the Gospel, as he says above: being justified we have peace etc. With these three degrees considered, the text of Paul can be more easily understood, for to the first degree belongs what he says: Without the Law sin is dead. But I once lived without the Law, because in secure and idle Epicureans or Pharisees there are no terrors, there is no recognition of sin. In such people sin is dead, that is, it does not terrify, it does not oppress them with terrors and a sense of damnation, because they do not feel themselves to be accused by the Law. To the second degree belong those who are in true terrors, such as are often described in the psalms Psalm. xxxvii. There is no soundness in my flesh because of your wrath. There is no peace in my bones, because of my sins. And Isaiah says: Like a lion he has crushed all my bones: in this sense he said: When the Law came, sin revived, that is it is, it was effective for striking terrors and a sense of damnation. To the third degree belong those who are raised up in terrors. For this struggle remains in the pious, so that faith may wrestle with dreads. Therefore Paul proposes his own example, so that he may teach the whole Church about this struggle. Some imagine that Paul is not speaking about himself, but about the person of some impious man. This imagination can be openly refuted by the examples of the psalms. For if we concede that David speaks about himself in this very way, why should we not concede the same about Paul? And the example of both is proposed, so that it may testify that these things are thus carried out and happen in other pious people. In the end Paul repeats the transition, saying that the Law itself is not evil, but our sin, which the Law offends and accuses, is the cause of terrors and damnation. However, this particle must be diligently observed, which he says, that sin might become exceedingly sinful. This is the meaning: the magnitude of sin is not discerned by the idle and the secure, just as for so long as David was of an idle mind, he did not see how horrible a thing sin was, because a secure mind does not establish that God is truly angry at sin, and since it does not yet feel the wrath of God, it does not see that which is chief in sin, namely guilt, that is, that God is truly angry at sin. But when hearts are terrified, there they truly conclude that God is angry, then they see that which is the proper and chief sin, namely guilt and the wrath of God. Therefore then sin is seen to be truly sin and becomes very harmful, or vicious, or guilty, and brings condemnation.

Latin:

Quid igitur dicemus? Lex.

Absoluta digressione redit ad illam collationem, quam supra instituit de Lege & de gratia, ac praecipue hic concionatur de usu Legis, ut has duas opiniones non tantum in Iudaeis, sed universaliter in omnium hominum animis haerentes, emendet, iusticiam Legis, quam praestare homo potest, satisfacere Legi, & esse iusticiam coram Deo, hoc est, homines nec vident peccatum & corruptionem naturae, nec vident disciplinam quam utcunque praestant per Legem, non satisfacere Legi, non esse iusticiam coram Deo. Quanquàm autem illas opiniones de Lege maxime defendebant Iudaei, tamen sunt communes omnium hominum, sed refutantur ab Evangelio, quod docet Legem non esse tantum civilem disciplinam, & Lege non esse iustos homines, Ideo necesse est Apostolos de hac re concionari, nec rixatur hic Paulus tantum de caeremoniis, sed de tota Lege loquitur ac praecipue de decalogo, sicut citat ex decalogo exemplum, & disputat neminem Legi satisfacere, ideoque omnes accusari à Lege, eamque ob causam Legem esse ministerium irae & mortis. Haec necesse est tradi in Ecclesia, ut beneficium Christi fiat illustre, & intelligi possit quod sit opus Evangelio, quod sit opus gratia, & alia iusticia, quàm iusticia Legis. Quia enim Lege non iustificamur, ideo Deus dedit pro nobis filium & revelat Evangelium, quod velit nobis propter filium gratis ignoscere, nos pronunciare iustos & renovare. Haec sum praefatus in hunc locum, ut studiosi diligentius considerent, quo consilio haec à Paulo disputantur, quo pertineant, quam necessaria sint. Declarant enim quale sit peccatum haerens in natura, & corruptio naturae. Item quod Lex non tantum requirat externa civilia officia, sed perfectam obedientiam. Item quantum efficiat Lex et quod sit opus alio verbo & beneficio Christi. Prosunt item ut discrimen Legis & Evangelii recte & vere intelligatur. Oporter autem horum locorum cognitionem in Ecclesia extare. Estque eo diligentius consideranda haec pars epistolae Paulinae, quia etiam veteres in ea explicanda admodum sudaverunt, & pauci dextre & recte tractarunt. Cum enim non viderent Paulum loqui de agone conscientiae, sed putarent dici de civili usu. Legis, affinxerunt multas absurdas interpretationes, & nihil ad rem pertinentes. Multum autem interest Ecclesiae, retineri veram huius loci sententiam, quo obruto non satis intelligi potest quid & quantum sit peccatum originale, quod sit discrimen Legis & Evangelii, quid sit gratia & iusticia fidei. Nunc accedo ad textum, estque in summa haec sententia : Non sumus iusti Lege, quia talis est corruptio naturae, ut Legi nemo satisfacere possit.
