Ideo Lex semper accusat, & cum corda sentiunt hoc iudicium & iram Dei, perterrefiunt & adiguntur ad desperationem & aeternam mortem. Ita Lex est ministerium irae & mortis, & auget peccatum, videlicet non externum, sed intus auget, id est armat peccatum, ut nos perterrefaciat & occidat. Sicutad Corinth. inquit : Aculeus mortis peccatum est : Virtus autem peccati Lex est. Et Paulus tanquàm diligens doctor addit exemplum de sua experientia. Initio autem praeponit translationem, quod Lex est ministerium mortis non fit Legis vitio, sed propter nostrum peccatum, quia corrupta natura non potest satisfacere Legi. Ideo Lex accusat nos, & dat exemplum de praecepto: Non concupisces : ut moneat, quod Lex non tantum accufet externa civilia delicta, sed etiam naturae corruptionem. Ideo usus est his verbis : Peccatum occasione accepta, id est, agnitum per Legem irritavit concupiscentiam, id est, perterrefecit me & in illis terroribus, movet illam dubitationem, diffidentiam, indignationem adversus Deum, ut fugiat cor Deum & irascatur iudicio Dei. Sine Lege peccatum est mortuum, id est, si Lex non accusaret, non existerent illi terrores & confusio conscientiae : Ego autem aliquando sine Lege vixi, id est, cum Pharisae us eram securus, arbitrabar me Legi satisfacere, me iustum esse. Id enim vocat vivere sine Lege, non audire Legem ostendentem peccatum & accusantem, non affici accusatione illa, non sentire dolores. Itaque tres hominum gradus constitue. Unus est carnalium qui vivunt securi, seu ut Epicuraei seu ut Pharisaei, nec habent veros pavores conscientiae. Tale vitae genus est vivere sine Lege, scilicet iudicante accusante &c. Quia Lex in illis non habet suum principalem effectum, ut ostendat et accuset peccatum. Lex enim tunc vere lex est cum iudicat et accusat, non cum scripta est in parietibus. Secundus gradus est eorum, qui opprimuntur terroribus & cruciatibus conscientiae, sicut Iudas aut Saul. Hi quia non audiunt vocem Evangelii, succumbunt in his terroribus, & sentiunt se damnari. Ideo hic ait: veniente Lege peccatum revixit, id est, caepit esse efficax & terrere, & ego mortuus sum. Nisi enim Paulus audiret vocem Evangelii, ipse quoque periret in talibus terroribus. Est igitur tertius gradus illorum, qui eriguntur in terroribus voce Evangelii, sicut supra inquit: iustificati pacem habemus &c. His tribus gradibus consideratis textus Pauli facilius intelligi potest, nam ad primum gradum pertinet quod ait : Sine Lege peccatum est mortuum. Ego autem aliquando sine Legevixi, quia in securis & ociosis Epicureis aut Phariseis nulli sunt terrores, non est agnitio peccati, In talibus peccatum est mortuum, id est, non perterrefacit, non opprimit eos terroribus et sensu damnationis, quia non sentiunt se accusari à Lege. Ad secundum gradum pertinent ii, qui sunt in veris terroribus, quales describuntur saepe in psalmis Psalm. xxxvii. Non est sanitas in carne mea à facie irae tuae. Non est pax ossibus meis, a facie peccatorum meorum. Et Esaias inquit : Sicut leo contrivit omnia ossa mea: in hanc sententiam dixit: Veniente Lege peccatum revixit, id est, fuit efficax ad incutiendos terrores & sensum damnationis. Ad tertium gradum pertinent, qui in terroribus eriguntur. Manet enim hoc certamen in piis, ut fides luctetur cum pavoribus, Ideo Paulus suum exemplum proponit, ut universam Ecclesiam de hoc agone doceat. Quidam fingunt Paulum non loqui de seipso, sed de persona alicuius impii. Haec imaginatio aperte resutari potest per exempla psalmorum. Si enim concedimus Davidem hoc ipso modo de sese loqui, cur idem non concedamus de Paulo? Et utriusque exemplum propositum est, ut testetur, ista sic geri & fieri in caeteris piis. In fine repetit Paulus translationem, inquiens, Legem ipsam non esse malam, sed nostrum peccatum, quod Lex offendit & accusat, est causa terrorum & damnationis. Diligenter autem haec particula observanda est, quod ait, ut peccatum fiat excellenter peccatum. Est autem haec sententia : peccati magnitudo non cernitur ab ociosis & securis, ut tantisper dum David erat ocioso animo, non videbat quàm horribilis res esset peccatum, quia securus animus non statuit Deum vere irasci peccato, cumque nondum sentiat iram Dei, non videt id quod praecipuum est in peccato, scilicet reatum, hoc est, quod Deus vere irascatur peccato. Sed quando expavescunt corda, ibi vere statuunt, Deum irasci, tunc vident id quod est proprium & praecipuum peccatum, videlicet reatum & iram Dei. Ergo tunc peccatum conspicitur esse vere peccatum & fit valde nocens, seu vitiosum. seu reum, & affert damnationem.

## 8:1 Argument
CHAPTER VIII.

Thus far he has spoken concerning sin and concerning the Law, now he returns to the description of grace, for it can be asked: If sin is still in the reborn, how therefore are they righteous, how are they made saved? Here he answers and declares the amplitude of grace. It was said, however, above, that grace signifies gratuitous acceptance, which he here describes negatively. There is now no condemnation to those who walk in Christ Jesus, that is, those justified by faith are pleasing to God on account of Christ, even if sin still clings in them, namely concupiscence and vicious affections. For he says, not that there is no sin in the pious, but no condemnation, and this is the principal proposition In this place concerning grace, and it is a doctrine simply necessary in the Church, that is to say, that the reborn are righteous, that is, accepted, not on account of the fulfillment of the Law, or their own dignity, but on account of Christ through faith, although sin, that is, concupiscence, still clings to them. But in the proposition it is added: to those walking according to the spirit. This addition is made for two reasons; the former is, that it may show that faith is not a human thought, but a motion of the Holy Spirit. The other reason is, that we may know that this faith is not in those who walk according to the flesh, that is, who are without repentance, and rush into sins against conscience. For in these, because they delight in sin, there is neither contrition, nor remission of sin. Therefore Paul teaches how the justified are pleasing, namely, not because they satisfy the Law, but because they believe in Christ, and that such faith is a motion of the Holy Spirit, and is not in those who walk according to the flesh, that is, who are without repentance, and indulge in carnal affections against conscience.

Then he adds the reason or declaration of the proposition: because the Law of the spirit of life &c. that is, I am thus justified, because by faith by which I apprehended Christ I have been freed from the terrors of sin and death, and this very liberation is vivification, that is, the beginning of a new and eternal life. Diligently , however, the terms in this place must be considered. For the Law in these words: The law of the spirit of life &c. does not signify the doctrine of the Law, for he says the Law of the spirit, that is, the spirit governing, or moving, or vivifying. And it is a metalepsis, the Law of the spirit, that is, the governance or motion of the spirit, and so that faith, which apprehends Christ, may be clearly understood, and no work of the Law may be understood, Paul himself adds: The law of the spirit of life in Christ Jesus, that is, that spiritual governance which vivifies by apprehending Christ Jesus. He wishes, therefore, for us to be vivified and liberated from sin and from death by faith and the acknowledgment of Christ, as if he were saying, not on account of the fulfillment of the Law, but because you have apprehended Christ. He makes, therefore, an antithesis, he opposes faith and the acknowledgment of Christ to that which is properly called law, as if he were saying, faith and the acknowledgment of Christ takes away the Law accusing and condemning, just as Afterwards, he says: he has freed me from the Law of sin and death. And the sum of the sentence is, for those who are justified there is no condemnation, not because they have the fulfillment of the Law, but because they are vivified by faith in Christ, and are freed from the curse of the Law, or from condemnation. There follows the reason in which the antithesis of the Law and the benefit of Christ is again proposed. But first let the grammatical syntax be considered, and let the period be constructed in this way. Because since it is impossible for the Law, namely to take away sin, for the reason that through the flesh the Law could not be done, God sent his son in the likeness of the flesh, of sin, and through sin condemned sin, in the flesh, so that the justification of the Law might be fulfilled. This whole sentence is διδασκαλικὴ and contains the principal testimonies, concerning the Law, concerning works, and concerning justification or concerning the merit of Christ, and first it clearly says, that the Law is not done nor fulfilled through this corrupt nature. It teaches also, that our works do not take away sin, or do not free us from sin and from death; therefore the imagination of the adversaries is false, who pretend that men merit the remission of sins through their own works. Also, that men are just on account of their own fulfillment of the Law. These things are handed down in the first part of the period: Since it was impossible for the Law to take away sin, likewise when he says afterwards: because it was weak through the flesh, that is, it could not be done through this corrupt nature.

With his own son sent under the likeness of flesh.

There is great emphasis in these words: He sent his son in the likeness of sinful flesh: Likewise, by sin he condemned sin. For he understands that Christ was sent in such a way that he was subjected to the punishments of sin, to sorrows, to terrors, and to death, just as he says to the Philippians ii: Being made in the likeness of men and found in fashion as a man etc. And afterwards he calls Christ sin, when he says by sin, namely he condemned Christ, that is, he took away, or made void sin, and condemnation in men, that is, after Christ himself was made a sacrifice satisfying for us, we were then freed from sin and from punishment etc. Moreover, the phrase is first to be observed, that he says Christ was made sin, or a sacrifice for sin. For in this place: by sin, the word sin signifies in the Hebrew manner a sacrifice for sin, that is, a penalty, or satisfaction for sin, just as the Latins said piaculum, the Greeks καθάρμα, and the meaning is similar, as in the words maledictum and anathema, which signify things destined for punishment, to appease the wrath of God. Thus Isaiah says of Christ: Because he will lay down his soul as sin, that is, a sacrifice for sin. Therefore also Paul so often inculcates ii. Corinth. v. Him who knew no sin, he made sin for us, that is, a sacrifice, which would sustain the punishment of sin and satisfy for our sins, and to the Galatians similarly he says that Christ was made a curse, that is, a piaculum sustaining the curse, and the wrath of God against sin. It is therefore to be considered secondly, how great is the humiliation of Christ. For since he suffered for the sins of all, he sustained the wrath of God and true terrors against sins, in our stead, as the lowest and most abject of all sinners, as Isaiah says: The Lord has laid on him the iniquities of us all. These things must be pondered, so that they may arouse fear and faith, nor should we think that these things were done in vain, but we should consider the magnitude of the wrath of God against sin, and again raise up faith, when we shall ponder what kind of sacrifice this is it may be, how it has been humbled, how horribly God is angered by sin, since He willed His Son to become such a victim, and again how great a pledge of mercy we have in that that victim transferred the wrath onto Himself, etc. All these things are proposed also in those words: Behold the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world. For He is called a lamb because He is a victim, and sacrifices from that time even from the beginning of the world signified such a host was to come, which was to die for the sins of the human race. In the text there is περὶ ἀμαρτίας, which can be explained on account of sin, that is, on account of the host, or for that host, and it is a figure of speech taken from Leviticus, where the Greeks translated a host for sin with this formula περὶ ἁμαρτίας; you will therefore be able to interpret, He condemned sin in the flesh, that is, the sins of men. On account of sin, that is, on account of the host exhibited, or for sin, that is, for the host exhibited. The histories and ancient rites will also contribute somewhat to understanding the force of the words. For καθάρματα were called those polluted by the most atrocious crimes, whom God and men would execrate, and on account of whom the nature of things seemed to be polluted, and God to punish the remaining men, just as Atreus, who concerning He gave children to be devoured by a brother, Nero and similar monsters. Such are blasphemers, idolaters, heretics, tyrants, the incestuous, and parricides, just as he says in the tragedy: Learn from me, lest the shadow harm the good.

He took away sin.

It is a Hebrew phrase, He condemned sin for He punished, that is, He abolished and extinguished it, so that it was now void, or there was absolutely nothing remaining. It is a dissimilar phrase if you say that sin had been condemned by the Law, for then to condemn signifies not to take away sin, but to convict the guilty party while sin remains and while guilt and wrath remain. But in this place, when Paul says that sin was condemned on account of the sacrifice of Christ, to condemn signifies to take away, or to extinguish sin, and to take away guilt and wrath. This dissimilarity in the phrase must be observed. Therefore, this is the meaning: On account of Christ, sin in the flesh, that is, the nature of men, is abolished. And this ought to be understood in two ways: first, by imputation, because since it is forgiven, and sin, still clinging to our nature, is not imputed to us who believe, therefore it is abolished, that is, it is void, so that it may not accuse, so that it may not condemn not believing. Secondly, it is abolished in such a way that it has already begun to be extinguished in reality, and a spiritual newness is begun, which will be consummated when in the resurrection we shall be clothed with a new nature, and righteousness without sin. To the same point pertains what follows afterwards: That the right of the Law may be fulfilled in us, that is, that we may have consummately that which the Law requires, that is, that we may be reckoned righteous. Therefore, let the first be understood concerning imputation, that by faith on account of Christ the Law is fulfilled in us, namely imputatively, that is, that by faith on account of Christ we are reckoned righteous, just as if we were satisfying the Law, when nevertheless sin still clings to us, and we are far from the fulfillment of the Law. Secondly, let it be understood concerning the effect, namely, that a newness is begun in us by the gift of the Holy Spirit, and that newness will be perfect and consummated righteousness, and obedience, and fulfillment of the Law, then when, with this infirmity of the flesh having been utterly deleted, we shall be clothed with total spiritual newness, which is integral righteousness and obedience without sin. Let the reader know, however, that this reasoning is to be accommodated to the established proposition, namely: There is now no condemnation to those who are in Christ, etc. For in order to confirm this proposition, he adds the following, And this is the summary. Believers are righteous, that is, accepted by God on account of Christ, even if they do not satisfy the Law. The reason is, because Christ was made a victim for us, and took away sin. Therefore, the Law no longer accuses believers, but we are righteous on account of Christ by faith, just as if we were satisfying the Law. Just as he also says in Galatians: Christ freed us from the curse of the Law, having been made a curse for us. This is the summary of the application, but the use must also be considered, for it contains a double doctrine, as I warned above. It consoles the pious, so that they may understand how they please God. Again, it also humbles the proud, so that we may remember that we have sin and do not satisfy the Law. Wherefore the opinions of the adversaries concerning the merit of condignity, concerning perfection, etc., are to be rejected. It is necessary to warn of these things concerning application and use. For without use, the magnitude of this benefit cannot be understood. Furthermore, in the text it is added: To those who do not walk according to the flesh, but according to the spirit. Here, as I said above, he testifies that the Holy Spirit is given. Likewise, that those who are without repentance and do not resist carnal desires do not retain the righteousness that has been given.

Latin:

CAPUT VIII.

Hactenus dixit de peccato & de Lege, nunc redit ad descriptionem gratiae, potest enim quaeri : Si adhuc est peccatum in renatis, quomodo igitur sunt iusti, quomodo fiunt salvi? Hic respondet & declarat amplitudinem gratiae. Dictum est autem supra, quòd gratia significet acceptationem gratuitam, quam hic describit negativè. Nulla nunc condemnatio est his, qui in Christo Iesu ambulant, id est, iustificati fide placent Deo propter Christum, etiamsi adhuc in eis haeret peccatum, videlicet concupiscentia & vitiosi affectus. Non enim, inquit, nullum esse peccatum in piis, sed nullam condemnationem, & haec est principalis propositio in hoc loco de gratia, estque doctrina simpliciter necessaria in Ecclesia, quòd videlicet renati non propter impletionem Legis, aut propriam dignitatem, sed propter Christum fide sint iusti, id est, accepti, quanquàm adhuc in eis haeret peccatum, id est coucupiscentia. Sed in propositione additu : ambulantibus secundum spiritum. Hoc adiectum est propter duas causas, prior est, ut ostendat fidem non esse cogitationem hamanam, sed motum spiritus sancti. Altera causa est, ut sciamus hanc fidem non esse in his, qui ambulant secundum carnem, hoc est, qui sunt sine paenitentia, & ruunt in peccata contra conscientiam. Nam his, quia delectantur peccato, neque contritio est, neque remissio peccati. Docet igitur Paulus, quomodo iustificati placeant, scilicet, non quia Legi satisfaciunt, sed quia credunt in Christum, & quod talis fides sit motus spiritus sancti, & non sit in his, qui ambulant secundum carnem, hoc est, qui sunt sine paenitentia, & indulgent affectibus carnalibus contra conscientiam.

Deinde addit rationem seu declarationem propositionis: quia Lex spiritus vitae &c. id est, ita iustificatus sum, quia fide qua apprehendi Christum liberatus sum à terroribus peccati et mortis, et haec ipsa liberatio est vivificatio, id est, inchoatio novae & aeternae vitae. Diligenter autem hoc loco vocabula consideranda sunt. Nam Lex in his verbis: Lex spiritus vitae &c. non significat doctrinam Legis, inquit enim Lex spiritus, hoc est, spiritus gubernans, seu movens, seu vivificans. Estque metalepsis, Lex spiritus, id est, gubernatio seu motus spiritus, & ut diserte intelligatur fides, quae apprehendit Christum, nec intelligatur aliquod opus Legis, ipse Paulus subiicit: Lex spiritus vitae in Christo Iesu, id est, illa gubernatio spiritualis, quae vivificat apprehendens Christum Iesum. Vult igitur nos fide & agnitione Christi vivificari & liberari à peccato, & à morte, quasi dicat, non propter Legis impletionem, sed quia apprehendistis Christum. Facit igitur antithesin, opponit fidem & agnitionem Christi, ei quod proprie lex dicitur, quasi dicat, fides & agnitio Christi tollit Legem accusantem & damnantem, sicut postea, inquit: liberavit me à Lege peccati & mortis. Estque summa sententiae, Iustificatis non est condemnatio, non quia habent Legis impletionem, sed quia fide in Christum vivificantur, & liberantur à maledictione Legis, seu à damnatione. Sequitur ratio in qua iterum proponitur antithesis Legis & beneficii Christi. Primum autem grammatica syntaxis consideretur, & construatur periodus hoc modo. Quia cum impossibile est Legi, scilicet tollere peccatum, eo quod per carnem Lex non poterat fieri, Deus misit filium suum in similitudine carnis, peccati, & per peccatum damnavit peccatum, in carne, ut iustificatio Legis impleretur. Haec sentia tota est διδασκαλικὴ & continet praecipua testimonia, de Lege, de operibus & de iustificatione seu de merito Christi, & primum clare dicit, quod Lex non fiat nec impleatur per hanc corruptam naturam. Docetitem, quod opera nostra non tollant peccatum, seu non liberant nos à peccato & à morte ergo falsa est imaginatio adversariorum, qui fingunt homines mereri remissionem peccatorum per propria opera. Item, homines esse iustos propter propriam Legis impletionem. Haec traduntur in prima parte periodi: Cum Legi impossibile esset tollere peccatum, item cum postea ait : quia infirmabatur per carnem, id est, non poterat fieri per hanc corruptam naturam.

Proprio filio misso sub specie carnis.

Magna est emphasis in his verbis : Misit filium in similitudine carnis peccati : Item, per peccatum damnavit peccatum. Intelligit enim Christum ita missum esse, ut subiiceretur poenis peccati, doloribus, pavoribus & morti, sicut ad Philippenses ii. inquit: In similitudine hominum factus & habitu inventus, ut homo &c. Et postea vocat Christum peccatum, cum ait per peccatum, scilicet Christum damnavit, id est, sustulit, seu irritum fecit peccatum, & damnationem in hominibus, id est, postquàm ipse Christus factus est hostia pro nobis satisfaciens, nos deinde sumus liberati à peccato & à poena &c. Est autem primum observanda phrasis, quod ait Christum factum esse peccatum, seu hostiam pro peccato. Nam in hoc loco: per peccatum, vox peccati significat Hebraico more hostiam pro peccato, id est, mulctam, seu satisfactionem pro peccato, sicut Latini piaculum dixerunt, Graeci καθάρμα, estque similis significatio, ut in vocabulis maledictum & anathema, quae significant res destinatas ad poenam, ad placandam iram Dei. Ita Esaias de Christo inquit: Quia ponet animam suam peccatum, id est, hostiam pro peccato. Ideo & Paulus toties inculcat ii. Corinth. v. Eum qui non noverat peccatum, pro nobis fecit peccatum, id est, hostiam, quae sustineret poenam peccati & satisfaceret pro peccatis nostris, & ad Galat. similiter Christum, ait, factum esse maledictum, id est, piaculum sustinens maledictionem, & iram Dei adversus peccatum. Est itaque secundo considerandum, quanta sit humiliatio Christi. Cum enim pro omnium peccatis passus sit, sustinuit iram Dei & veros terrores adversus peccata, nostra vice, velut infimus & abiectissimus omnium peccatorum, sicut inquit Esaias: Dominus posuit in eo iniquitates omnium nostrum. Haec cogitanda sunt, ut timorem & fidem exuscitent, nec existimemus frustra haec facta esse, sed magnitudinem irae Dei adversus peccatum consideremus, & rursus erigamus fidem, cum cogitabimus qualis haec hostia fuerit, quomodo sit humiliata, quàm horribiliter Deus irascatur peccato, cum voluerit filium fieri talem victimam, & rursus quantum habeamus pignus misericordiae quòd illa victima iram in se transtulit &c. Haec omnia proponuntur etiam in illis verbis : Ecce agnus Dei qui tollit peccata mundi. Dicitur enim agnus, quia est victima, & sacrificia inde usque ab initio mundi significarunt venturam talem hostiam, quae moritura esset pro peccatis humani generis. In textu est περὶ ἀμαρτίας, quod potest exponi propter peccatum, id est, propter hostiam, vel pro illa hostia, estque figura orationis ex Levitico sumpta, ubi hostiam pro peccato Graeci verterunt hac formula περὶ ἁμαρτίας, poteris igitur interpretari, condemnavit peccatum in carne, id est, hominum peccata. Propter peccatum, id est, propter hostiam exhibitam, vel pro peccato, id est pro hostia exhibita. Nonnihil etiam ad vocabulorum vim intelligendam conducent historiae & veteres ritus. Nam καθάρματα vocabantur atrocissimis delictis polluti, quos Deus & homines execrarentur, & propter quos videretur polui natura rerum, & Deus plectere reliquos homines sicut Atreus, qui de dit fratri liberos edendos, Nero & similia portenta. Tales sunt blasphemi, Idolatrae, Haeretici, Tyranni, incoesti, parricidae, sicut ille in tragedia inquit: Discite à me, ne umbra noceat bonis.

Sustulit peccatum.

Phrasis est Hebraica, Condemnavit peccatum pro punivit, hoc est, abolevit & extinxit, ut iam irritum esset, vel prorsus non esset reliquum. Dissimilis phrasis est, si dicas Lege autem fuisse condemnatum peccatum, tunc enim damnare significat, non tollere peccatum, sed reum arguere manens peccatum & manente reatu & ira. Sed in hoc loco, cum Paulus inquit, peccatum condemnatum esse propter hostiam Christum, damnare significat tollere, seu extinguere peccatum, & tollere reatum & iram. Haec dissi militudo in phrasi observanda est. Itaque haec est sententia, Propter Christum peccatum in carne, id est, natura hominum, est abolitum. Idque dupliciter intelligi debet, primum imputatione, quia enim remissum est, & non imputatur nobis credentibus peccatum, ad huc haerens in natura nostra, ideo est abolitum, hoc est irritum, ne accuset, ne condem net credentes. Secundo, sic abolitum est, ut iam coeperit re ipsa extingui, & inchoetur novitas spiritualis, quae erit consummata, cum in resurrectione vestiemur nova natura, & iusticia sine peccato. Eodem pertinet quòd postea sequitur: Ut ius Legis in nobis impleatur, id est, ut consummate habeamus id quod Lex requirit, id est, ut iusti reputemur. Primum ergo de imputatione intelligatur, quòd fide propter Christum Lex in nobis impleatur, scilicet imputativè, hoc est, quod fide propter Christum reputemur iusti, perinde ac si Legi satisfaceremus, cum tamen adhuc haereat in nobis peccatum, & procul absimus ab impletione Legis. Secundo intelligatur de essectu, videlicet, ut inchoetur in nobis novitas donato spiritu sancto, eaque novitas erit perfecta & consūata iusticia, & obedientia, & impletio Legis, tunc cum prorsus deleta hac infirmitate carnis, vestiemur tota novitate spirituali, quae est integra iusticia & obedientia sine peccato. Sciat autem lector hanc rationem accommodandam esse ad institutam propositionem, vi delicet : Nulla nunc condemnatio est his, qui sunt in Christo &c. Nam ut hanc propositionem confirmaret adiicit sequentia, estque haec summa. Credentes sunt iusti, id est, accepti Deo propter Christum, etiamsi Legi non satisfaciunt. Ratio est, quia enim Christus pro nobis factus est victima, & sustulit peccatum. Ideo iam non accusat Lex credentes, sed sumus iusti propter Christum fide, perinde ac si Legi satisfaceremus. Sicut et in Galat. inquit: Christus liberavit nos à maledictione Legis, factus pro nobis maledictum. Haec est summa accommodationis, sed usus etiam cogitandus est, continet enim duplicem doctrinam, ut supra monui. Consolatur pios, ut intelligant quomodo placeant Deo. Rursus etiam humimiliat superbos, ut meminerimus nos habere peccatum & non satisfacere Legi. Quare repudiandae sunt opiniones adversariorum, de merito condigni, de perfectione &c. Haec de accommodatione & usu monere necesse est. Nam sine usu non potest intellgi amplitudo huius beneficii. Caeterum in textu additum est : Non secundum carnem ambulantibus, sed secundum spiritum. Hic, ut supra dixi, testatur, quod donetur spiritus sanctus. Item quod non retineant iusticiam donatam illi, qui sunt sine paenitentia & non repugnant carnalibus cupiditatibus.

## 8:1
For those who are carnal.

An antithesis is established, so that human justice may be distinguished from this spiritual and eternal one, about which the Gospel preaches. And here is the principal dispute, what the term flesh signifies. For some have imagined that by flesh are signified only the appetites of the senses. Then they feign that reason and the will, even without the Holy Spirit, can obey the Law of God and effect the love of God, faith, and similar motions. And they understand spirit as the thoughts and endeavors of reason and the will without the Holy Spirit. And thus they transform the Gospel into philosophy. This depravation of the Pauline sentence is to be repudiated from afar, and on the contrary it must be established that flesh truly

λόγον , when they divide man into λόγον & ὁρμην , they understand the will obeying the dictate of reason and the intellect. ὅρμας affections insofar as they are not ruled by λόγῷ , the organ ὁρμῶν is the heart. The heart is the organ serving the whole sensitive appetitive power. The vegetative appetite does not pertain to this.

& properly signifies the whole nature of man, the appetites of the senses and reason and the will without the Holy Spirit, and conversely spirit signifies the Holy Spirit, or motions arisen from the Holy Spirit in us. Therefore to be according to the flesh signifies to be without the Holy Spirit. And to mind according to the flesh signifies to have a thought, or rational judgment, and affections of sense and will, such as they are without the Holy Spirit, as to understand and desire pleasures, riches, tranquility, glory, and this is the highest degree, to understand civil justice, and to value and desire this highly, when meanwhile the heart is without the fear of God, full of doubt and ignorance of God. Conversely to mind according to the spirit is to judge spiritually, and to have spiritual motions, that is, the light by which God is acknowledged, and true terrors, and true confidence struggling with doubt.

Latin:

Nam qui carnales sunt.

Instituitur antithesis, ut discernatur iustitia humana ab hac spirituali & aeterna, de qua concionatur Evangelium. Estque hic praecipua disputatio, quid vocabulum caro significet. Aliqui enim imaginati sunt, carne significari tantum appetitiones sensuum. Deinde affingunt rationem & voluntatem Legi Dei, etiam sine sp iritu sancto, posse obedire & efficere dilectionem Dei, fidem & similes motus. Et spiritum intelligunt cogitationes & conatus rationis, & voluntatis sine spiritu sancto. Atque ita transformant Evangelium in philosophiam. Haec depravatio Paulinae sententiae procul repudianda est, & econtrà statuendum, quod caro verè

λόγον, quando dividunt hominem inλόγον & ὁρμην, intelligunt voluntatem obtemperantem dictamini rationis & intellectum.ὅρμαςaffectus quatenus non reguntur aλόγῷ, Organumὁρμῶνest cor. Cor est organum serviens toti virtuti appetitivae sensitivae. Huc non pertinet appetitus vegetativus.

& propriè significet totam naturam hominis, appetitiones sensuum & rationem & voluntatem sine spiritu sancto, & ècontra spiritus significet spiritum sanctum, aut motus ortos à spiritu sancto in nobis. Itaque secundum carnem esse, significat sine spiritu sancto esse. Et sapere secundum carnem, significat habere cogitationem, seu iudicium rationale, & affectus sensus & voluntatis, quales sunt sine spiritu sancto, ut intelligere & appertere voluptates, opes, tranquillitatem, gloriam, & hic summus gradus est, intelligere civilem iusticiam, & hanc plurimi facere & appetere, cum interim cor sit sineti more Dei, plenum dubitatione & ignoratione Dei. Econtrà sapere secundum spiritum est spiritualiter iudicare, & habere motus spirituales, id est, lucem qua agnoscitur Deus, & veros pavores, ac veram fiduciam luctantem cum dubitatione.

## 8:5
The affections of the spirit indeed.

That is, true consolation, which is brought about by faith through the Holy Spirit, is a motion by which God is truly acknowledged, apprehended, and invoked, and new light, knowledge, life, and joy of conscience are conceived. As he says below: You have received the spirit of adoption of sons, by which we cry Abba Father, that is, by which we truly acknowledge God, and these motions are a liberation from eternal death, and a beginning of eternal life, as Christ says: This is eternal life, etc. Such motions do not exist in men without faith and without the Holy Spirit. Therefore Paul institutes this comparison, that he may distinguish between spiritual and carnal righteousness, and the reason follows, which declares what kind of motions are in the nature of man, without faith and without the Holy Spirit.

Latin:

Affectus vero spiritus.

Id est, vera consolatio, quae fit fide per spiritum sanctum, est motus quo vere agnoscitur, apprehenditur, & invocatur Deus, & concipiuntur nova lux, notitia, vita, & gaudium conscientiae. Sicut infra inquit: Accepistis spiritum adoptionis filiorum, quo clamamus abba pater, id est, quo vere agnoscimus Deum, & hi motus sunt liberatio à morte aeterna, & inchoatio vitae aeternae, sicut Christus inquit: Haec est vita aeterna &c. Tales motus existunt in hominibus sine fide & sine spiritu sancto. Ideo hanc collationem instituit Paulus, ut discernat spiritualem & carnalem iusticiam, & sequitur raito, quae declarat, quales sint motus in natura hominis, sine fide & sine spiritu sancto.

## 8:6
The affection of the flesh is death.

Here sense signifies the thought, and appetitions of the senses and of the will. For Paul embraces λόγον and ὅρμας and Paul speaks concerning thought and appetition toward God. And the sentence is that human justice, philosophy, the laws of cities, indeed the very law of God, just as reason without faith and without the spirit thinks and strives for what is holy, are death, that is, things not vivifying before God. Indeed, the motions of reason, acting with God without faith, are even sins, wherefore they are truly death, that is, a condemned thing. Nor does it follow from this that philosophy or the Laws are evil. But philosophy and the Laws serve the bodily life, and although they are good things, when we use them in their place, nevertheless they do not vivify in the judgment of God; indeed, not even the Law of God vivifies, and it is not even sufficiently understood without the Holy Spirit.

Latin:

Affectus carnis mors est.

Hic sensus significat cogitationem, et appetitiones sensuum et voluntatis. Nam Paulus complectitur λόγον et ὅρμας & loquitur Paulus de cogitatione & appetitione erga Deum. Estque sententia quòd iusticia humana, philosophia, Leges civitatum, imo ipsa lex Dei, sicut eam ratio sine fide & sine spiritu sancto cogitat & conatur, sint mors, id est, res non vivificantes coram Deo. Imo motus rationis, agentes cum Deo sine fide, sunt etiam peccata, quare vere sunt mors, id est, res damnata. Nequè sequitur inde philosophiam, aut Leges malas esse. Sed philosophia & Leges serviunt corporali vitae, & quanquàm sunt res bonae, cum suo loco utimur, tamen non vivificant in iudicio Dei, Imo nec Lex Dei vivificat, ac ne quidem satis intelligitur sine spiritu sancto.

## 8:7
The affection of the flesh is enmity.

This passage most greatly refutes the Pelagians, and all who imagine that men without the Holy Spirit obey the Law of God, nay, even satisfy the Law of God. But this error arises from the fact that they think that only external discipline is required by the Law of God. This imagination leads them away from the right path. It must be known, therefore, that interior obedience is required by the Law of God, and indeed perfect and whole. Paul speaks, therefore, here of interior vices, of the disease of origin, of the ignorance of God, of perpetual doubt, of concupiscence: A secure mind without the Holy Spirit does not see the wrath and judgment of God. This doubt and security is contempt of God. Again, a terrified mind, as in Saul and Judas, where there are terrors without faith and the consolation of the Holy Spirit, flees the wrath and judgment of God, and conceives a horrible raging and indignation against God. And so Paul accuses here not only the inordinate appetites of the senses: such as lusts, or other known vices, hatreds, rapacity and the like, but much more the fountains of these of evils, namely ignorance of God, doubt, contempt, indignation against God. Finally, he embraces all impulses fighting against the Law of God, when he says: The mind of the flesh is enmity against God. Paul used a harsh term, so that the reader might consider the infirmity of human nature to be much greater than human reason can sufficiently see and judge.

Latin:

Affectus carnis inimicitia est.

Hic locus maximè refutat Pelagianos, & omnes qui imaginantur, homines sine spiritu sancto Legi Dei obedire, imo etiam Legi Dei satisfacere. Sed hic error inde oritur, quòd putant Lege Dei tantum externam disciplinam requiri. Haec imaginatio abducit eos à recta via. Sciendum est igitur Lege Dei requiri interiorem obedientiam, & quidem perfectam ac integram. Loquitur ergo Paulus hic de interioribus vitiis, de morbo originis, de ignoratione Dei, de perpetua dubitatione, de concupiscentia: Animus securus sine spiritu sancto non videt iram & iudicium Dei. Haec dubitatio & securitas est contemptus Dei. Rursus animus perterrefactus, ut in Saul & Iuda, ubi sunt terrores sine fide, & consolatione spiritus sancti, fugit iram & iudicium Dei, & concipit horribilem fremitum, & indignationem adversus Deum. Itaque Paulus non tantum appetitiones inordinatas sensuum: ut libidines, vel alia nota, vitia, odia, rapacitatem & similia hic accusat, sed multo magis fontes horum malorum, scilicet ignorationem Dei, dubitationem, contemptum, indignationem adversus Deum. Denique omnes impetus pugnantes cum Lege Dei complectitur, cum ait: Sensus carnis inimicitia est adversus Deum. Usus est Paulus atroci vocabulo, ut cogitet lector multo maiorem esse infirmitatem naturae humanae, quàm ut ratio humana possit eam satis videre & iudicare.

## 8:8
But those who are in the flesh cannot please God, etc.

This antithesis must be diligently observed, because it clearly shows what Paul calls flesh and spirit. For because he says: the spirit of God, likewise the spirit of Christ, it is sufficiently evident that he is speaking of the Holy Spirit, God. Therefore, on the contrary, flesh must be understood as whatever is in man without the Holy Spirit, namely not only the sensitive appetite, but also reason and will without the Holy Spirit. This passage is therefore to be observed, so that we may have a testimony concerning the meaning of these words. Likewise, the Pelagians and their like are manifestly refuted, who imagine that men without the Holy Spirit are righteous. Likewise, as the Scholastics said, to merit the remission of sins, and grace, without the Holy Spirit. Here, however, let consciences be instructed, that they may learn that the motions of the Holy Spirit are brought about through the Word. Spiritual motions are therefore brought about when, in true terrors, we again console ourselves with the word of the Gospel, just as the text says: faith is from hearing. Likewise to the Galatians, that the promise of the Spirit might be given through faith, etc.

Latin:

Qui vero in carne sunt, Deo placere &c.

Haec antithesis ideo diligenter observanda est, quia clare ostendit, quid Paulus vocet carnem et spiritum. Quia enim inquit: spiritus Dei, item spiritus Christi, satis constat cum loqui de spiritu sancto, Deo. Ergo è contra caro intellgi debet, quicquid est in homine sine spiritu sancto, videlicet non tantum appetitus sensitivus, sed etiam ratio et voluntas sine spiritu sancto. Est igitur hic locus observandus, ut habeamus testimonium de significatione harum vocum. Item, manifestè refutantur Pelagiani & similes, qui singunt homines sine spiritu sancto esse iustos. Item, ut Scholastici dixerunt, mereri remissionem peccatorum, & gratiam, sine spiritu sancto. Hic autem erudiantur conscientiae, ut discant effici motus spiritus sancti per verbum. Fiunt igitur motus spirituales, cum in veris pavoribus, iterum consolamur nos verbo Evangelii, sicut textus inquit: fides ex auditu est. Item ad Galat. ut promissio spiritus detur per fidem &c.

## 8:9
If Christ is in you.

That which he says: If Christ is in you, is to be understood through the Spirit, just as he says afterwards: The body indeed is dead because of sin, etc. This sentence teaches why there are remaining afflictions and death in the saints. For it could be objected: If believers are righteous and sons of God, and heirs of eternal life, why are they still burdened with death and other miseries? Indeed, no class of men is more calamitous than the pious, because the devil and the world exercise horrible cruelty against them. For what reason? Paul answers, because there is still remaining sin in the flesh. Although, therefore, in the ungodly, calamities and death are simply punishments for sin, nevertheless in the saints they are exercises, in which ought to grow. Spiritual newness and death is the way by which, having been completely stripped of sin, we may be clothed with a new nature. This distinction must be diligently observed, that in the ungodly afflictions are simply punishments, but in the saints they are exercises and the way by which the vicious and iniquitous flesh is abolished. Thus, therefore, let this passage be understood: the body is dead, that is, it is being mortified on account of sin, namely the present sin, which still clings to the flesh of the saints, and must be abolished by this death, so that we may be clothed with renewed flesh. Here are added disputes concerning satisfactions, whether after the remission of guilt, God or the keys impose any punishments which are a satisfaction for eternal death. I answer briefly, the Power of the keys does not have a mandate to impose punishments. Secondly, even if

God imposed calamities upon Adam after the remission of guilt. Item, He imposed punishments upon David after adultery: Therefore God imposes punishments. R. He imposes them, and often, but not universally. For example's sake, He often imposes punishments and they are punishments, but to the believer they become exercises. Secondly, even if they are punishments, nevertheless they are not a compensation for eternal death. But the Power of the keys can neither impose punishments, nor take them away.

God sometimes imposes punishments, as to David after adultery, yet from that a universal rule is not made, and it must by no means be thought that no sin is forgiven without punishment, because the promises so often inculcate upon us even the remission of punishments. Item, Even if God imposes bodily punishments upon some, yet they cannot be remitted by the power of the keys, such as diseases, wars, and similar calamities. Furthermore, peculiar afflictions are sometimes imposed upon the saints, as Isaiah was sawn asunder, Jeremiah stoned, John the Baptist beheaded, etc. These afflictions are not punishments for certain sins, but singular works in which God wishes to show His glory. Just as the prophet also says: Even the innocent shall drink the cup, etc. And to this pertains the disputation of Job, who denies that he is afflicted on account of sins. For he teaches the pious both things, that they are not righteous because of afflictions: Item, that afflictions are imposed also for another counsel of God, and are not always punishments of certain sins. Hence it is clear that a rule is not to be made that afflictions are satisfactions, or punishments for certain sins. Therefore, just as afflictions are not always punishments, so sins are often remitted without certain punishments, just as God promises in the scriptures to those doing penance that He will mitigate calamities, And Paul says: If we judged ourselves, we would not be judged by the Lord. Finally, this must be known, that even if punishments or exercises are imposed, they are nevertheless not compensations for eternal death, because only the death of Christ is the satisfaction and compensation for eternal death, as it is written: Because he shall lay down his soul for sin, etc. Therefore, the opinion of the adversaries concerning satisfactions is to be rejected. Furthermore, it is profitable that both things be inculcated in the Churches: both that God punishes sins, even with bodily punishments, and that He mitigates or changes punishments on account of repentance. The pious are also to be taught in afflictions, so that they may know that afflictions are not signs of wrath, even if they were punishments, and yet that they are not always punishments, but exercises or singular works, in which God wishes us to acknowledge our infirmity, and again to be raised up by faith and invocation, so that spiritual newness may grow. Thus the Church is subject to afflictions, as will be said again below: We must be made like the image of the Son of God. And here, he says, the Church is subject to death, on account of present sin, so that the vicious flesh may be abolished, and yet he adds that believers are freed from death, namely because they live in the spirit, and God is again going to vivify their bodies.

Epilogue.

Therefore in this collation he handed down these things: That human nature cannot satisfy the Law of God. Wherefore carnal justice is not justice before God, nor does it give life. But even though in the saints there is remaining flesh, nevertheless they are pleasing to God on account of Christ, and are freed from death, so that they may live by the spirit, because Christ is efficacious in them, and has begun to give them life by the Holy Spirit. But the flesh, on account of sin, is destined for death, so that with the oldness abolished we may again be clothed with flesh, in which there is no vice. Hence this passage contains manifold doctrine, First that human nature cannot satisfy the Law of God. Second, that carnal justice neither justifies nor gives life before God. Third, how the saints are pleasing and are freed from death, even though sin still clings to them. Fourth, for what cause the Church is subject to afflictions and death. Fifth, what the terms flesh and spirit truly signify.

Latin:

Si Christus in vobis est.

Quod inquit: Si Christus in vobis est, intelligendum est per spiritum, sicut postea dicit: Corpus quidem mortuum est propter peccatum &c. Haec sententia docet, quare in sanctis sint reliquae afflictiones, & mors Poterat enim obiici: Si credentes sunt iusti & silii Dei, & haeredes vitae aeternae, cur adhuc sunt onerati morte & aliis miseriis? Immo nullum genus hominum est calamitosius, quàm pii, quia diabolus & mundus exercent adversus eos horribilem saevitiam. Quam ob causam? Paulus respondet, quia adhuc in carne reliquum est peccatum. Quanquàm igitur in impiis calamitates, & mors sunt simpliciter poenae pecati, tamen in sanctis sunt exercitia, in quibus debet crescere novitas spiritualis & mors, est via, qua prorsus exuti peccato, vestiamur nova nanatura. Hoc discrimen diligenter observandum est, quod in impiis afflictiones simpliciter sint poenae, in sanctis vero exercitia & via, qua aboleatur vitiosa & iniquinata caro. Sic ergo intelligatur hic locus: corpus est mortuum, id est, mortificatur propter peccatum, scilicet praesens, quod adhuc haeret in carne sanctorum, & abolendum est ista morte, ut possimus renovata carne vestiri. Hic adduntur disputationes de satisfactionibus, an post remissionem culpae, imponat Deus aut claves poenas aliquas, quae sint satisfactio pro morte aeterna. Breviter respondeo, Potestas clavium non habet mandatum imponendi poenas. Secundo, Etiamsi

Adae post remissionem culpae, imposuit Deus calamitates. Item Davidi post adulterium imposuit poenas: Ergo imponit Deus poenas. R. Imponit & saepe sed non univer saliter. Exempli caussa saepe imponit poenas & sunt poenae, sed credenti fiunt exercitia. Secundo, Etiamsi sunt poenae, tamen non sunt compensatio pro morte aeterna. Sed Potestas clavium neque potest imponere poenas, neque tollere.

Deus aliquando imponit poenas, ut Davidi post adulterium, tamen inde non fit regula universalis, & nequaquàm sentiendum est nullum peccatum remitti sine poena, quia promissiones toties inculcant nobis etiam poenarum remissionem. Item, Etiamsi Deus poenas corporales aliquibus imponit, tamen non possunt remitti potestate clavium, ut morbi, bella, & similes calamitates. Praeterea peculiares afflictiones interdum sanctis imponuntur, ut Esaias est dissectus, Ieremias lapidatus, lañes Baptista decollatus &c. Hae afflictiones non sunt poenae pro certis peccatis, sed singularia opera in quibus Deus vult ostendere suam gloriam. Sicut et propheta inquit: Etiam innocentes bibent calicem &c. Et huc pertinet disputatio Iob, qui negat se propter peccata affligi. Docet enim pios utrumque, quod propter afflictiones non sint recti: Item, quod afflictiones imponantur etiam alio consilio Dei, nec semper sint poenae caertorum peccatorum. Hinc perspicuum est non esse regulam faciendam, quòd afflictiones sint satisfactiones, aut poenae pro certis peccatis. Ut igitur afflictiones non sunt semper poenae, ita sine certis poenis saepe remittuntur peccata, sicut promittit Deus in scripturis agentibus paenitentiam, mitigaturum se esse calamitates, & Paul. inquit: Si nos ipsi iudicaremus, non iudicaremur à domino. Postremo illud sciendum est, & si imponuntur poenae, vel exercitia, tamen non sunt compensationes pro morte aeterna, quia tantum mors Christi est satisfactio & compensatio pro morte aeterna, sicut scriptum est: Quia ponet animam suam pro peccato &c. Quare opinio adversariorum de satisfactionibus reiicienda est. Caeterum prodest utrumque inculcari Ecclesiis, & quod puniat Deus peccata, etiam corporalibus poenis, & quod mitiget poenas, aut mutet propter paenitentiam. Sunt & docendi pii in afflictionibus, ut sciant affli ctiones non esse signa irae, etiamsi essent poenae, & tamen ne quidem semper poenas esse, sed exercitia aut singularia opera, in quibus Deus vult nos agnoscere infirmitatem nostram, & rursus fide & invocatione erigi, ut crescat novitas spiritualis. Ita Ecclesia est fubiecta afflictionibus, sicut infra rursus dicetur: Oportet nos fieri similes imaginis filii Dei. Et hic, ait, Ecclesiam subiectam esse morti, propter praesens peccatum, ut aboleatur vitiosa caro, & tamen addit esse liberatos à morte credentes, scilicet quia vivant spiritu, & Deus rursus sit vivificaturus corpora.

Epilogus.

Itaquein hac collatione haec tradidit: Humanam naturam non posse satisfacere Legi Dei. Quare iusticia carnalis non est iusticia coram Deo, nec vivificat. Etiamsi autem in sanctis est reliqua caro, tamen placent Deo propter Christum, & sunt liberati à morte, ita ut spiritu vivant, quia Christus in eis est efficax, & incoepit eos vivificare spiritu sancto. Caro autem propter peccatum morti destinata est, ut abolita vetustate rursus vestiamur carne, in qua nihil sit vitii. Proinde continet hic locus multiplicem doctrinam, Primo quod humana natura non possit satisfacere Legi Dei. Secundo, quod iusticia carnalis nec iustificet nec vivificet coram Deo. Tertio, quomodo plceant sancti & liberentur à morte, etiamsi adhuc haeret in eiis peccatum. Quarto, propter quam causam Ecclesia sit subiecta afflictionibus & morti. Quinto, quid vere significent vocabula carnis & spiritus.

## 8:12
Therefore brothers we are debtors &c.

Thus far he has completed the doctrine concerning justification. Now therefore it is necessary that the doctrine be added. concerning new obedience. For this part also must exist in the Church, so that it may be understood what kind of obedience is in the saints, and what kind of sin it is, on account of which they fall from grace, and lose faith and the Holy Spirit. Therefore Paul establishes the proposition: We are debtors, not to live according to the flesh. For when we are reborn by faith, spiritual newness is begun, which is begun obedience toward God, or the beginning of the Law in hearts, as it is written. I will give my Law into their hearts. Therefore, let that newness now have its affections, let it acknowledge God and obey Him, and let it resist the motions of the flesh, which drag one against the will of God. He says, however, expressly: we are debtors. He opposes this word to those who wrongly understand Evangelical liberty, which frees us so that we are not accused by the Law, but does not free us so that we do not obey. For the eternal and immutable ordinance remains, that we should obey God, and the Gospel not only begins obedience, but also subjects us to obedience toward God.

Latin:

Proinde fratres debitores su-mus &c.

Hactenus absolvit doctrinam de iustificatione. Nunc igitur necesse est addi doctrinam de nova obedientia. Nam & haec pars in Ecclesia extare debet, ut intelligatur, qualis sit obedientia in sanctis, & quale sit peccatum, propter quod excidunt à gratia, & amittunt fidem & spiritum sanctum. Instituit ergo Paulus propositionem: Debito res sumus, ne obediamus carni. Nam cum fide renascimur, inchoatur novitas spiritualis, quae est inchoata obedientia erga Deum, seu Legis inchoatio in cordibus, ut scriptum est. Dabo Legem meam in corda eorum. Ergo iam illa novitas habeat suos affectus, agnoscat Deum & ei obediat, & repugnet motibus carnis, qui rapiunt contra voluntatem Dei. Dicit autem diserte: debitores sumus. Hanc vocem opponit male intelligentibus libertatem Evangelicam, quae liberat, ne accusemur à Lege, non liberat, ne obediamus. Manet enim aeterna & immutabilis ordinatio, ut obediamus Deo, & Evangelium, non modo inchoat obedientiam, sed etiam subiicit nos obedientiae erga Deum.

## 8:13
For if you live according to the flesh &c.

He adds two reasons to the proposition. The first is taken from the punishments. And this passage is to be observed for this reason is, let us hold the distinction of mortal sin, and venial ones, that is, such as exist in the saints. For because he says: If you mortify the actions of the flesh by the Spirit, you shall live, he testifies that there are in the saints some vicious actions, namely concupiscence and manifold vicious affections, doubt concerning God, not burning with the fear of God, with faith, with love, sluggishness in invocation (which they called ἀκηδίαν), impatience, flames of lusts, not obeying superiors, being inflamed with the desire of vengeance, hatred, avarice, etc. Such diseases in the saints, although they are by their own nature mortal sins, that is, worthy of eternal death, nevertheless are pardoned to those believing in Christ, who both resist these diseases, and by faith apprehend the mediator Christ, thus they become venial, that is, pardoned. On the contrary, however, they become mortal when those who had been sanctified indulge and obey such affections, and do not resist, and are without repentance. For such lose faith and the Holy Spirit, and are condemned by eternal death, unless they return to repentance. Just as David, having become an adulterer, was without faith and without the Holy Spirit, and would have perished had he not afterwards been restored through repentance. To this pertains the saying in this place:

If you live according to the flesh, that is, if you obey vicious affections, you shall die, and the same sentence is often repeated in the scriptures Matthaei v. Unless your righteousness shall exceed the righteousness of the Pharisees &c. First Iohan. iii. Everyone who does not do righteousness is not of God. 1. Corinth. vi. Do not err, fornicators, idolaters &c. shall not possess the kingdom of God. Galat. v. Those doing such things shall not possess the kingdom of God, Coloss. iii. On account of which the wrath of God comes upon the disobedient &c. But here it is asked concerning the degree, when those lapses become mortal sins. The first degree here is undoubtedly a mortal sin, when men rush against conscience, against the commandments of God, and therefore Paul, describing what the life of the saints is, establishes this degree, that they should not act against conscience. 1. Timoth. 1. The sum of the commandment is love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and faith not feigned. Therefore, when deeds are committed against the commandments of God against conscience, or when one does not resist a vicious affection, they become mortal sins. This degree is manifest. But short of this degree there also occur more obscure lapses, many of which become mortal sins, which reason one can sufficiently judge what David's error was when he ordered the people to be numbered. Truly, even these lapses are forgiven to those returning to faith, but as long as the purpose of acting against conscience remains, faith cannot be present, because it is impossible for faith to exist with a bad conscience. For faith is a trust which establishes that we are pleasing to God on account of Christ. A bad conscience, which the purpose of acting against the commandments of God produces, resists this trust. Paul handed down these things here concerning the distinction of sins. Wherefore let us diligently remember this passage, and let us beware lest, having lost the benefit of Christ, we rush into destruction, just as Peter also says: Strive to make your calling and election firm, that is, persevere in this newness which you have attained, lest the calling and election by which you have been separated from the world be made void again by the impious.

Latin:

Nam si secundum carnem vi-xeritis &c.

Propositioni addit duas rationes. Prima est sumpta à poenis. Et hiclocus eo observandus est, teneamus discrimen peccati mortalis, & venialium, hoc est, talium, quae existunt in sanctis. Quia enim inquit: Si actiones carnis spiritu mortificabitis, vivetis, testatur esse in sanctis aliquas actiones vitiosas, videlicet concupiscentiam & vitiosos affectus multiplices, dubitationem de Deo, non ardere timore Dei, fide, dilectione, segnitiem in invocatione (quod illi vocarunt ἀκηδίαν) impatientiam, flammas libidinum, non obtemperare superioribus, incendi cupiditate vindicatae, odio, avaricia &c. Tales morbi in sanctis, etsi sunt sua natura peccata mortalia, id est, digna morte aeterna, tamen credentibus in Christum condonantur, qui & repugnant his morbis, & fide apprehendunt mediatorem Christum, sic fiunt venialia, id est, condonata. E contra vero mortalia fiunt, cum ii qui fuerant sanctificati, indulgent & obtemperant talibus affectibus, nec repugnant, & sunt sine paenitentia. Tales enim amittunt fidem & spiritum sanctum, & damnantur aeterna morte, nisi redeant ad paenitentiam. Sicut David factus adulter, erat sine fide & sine spiritu sancto, & periisset nisi postea per paenitentiam restitutus esset. Huc pertinet dictum hoc loco:

Si secundum carnem vixeritis, id est, si obtemperabitis vitiosis affectibus, moriemini, & eadem sententia saepe repetitur in scripturis Matthaei v. Nisi abundaverit iusticia vestra super iusticiam Pharisaeorum &c. Primo Iohan. iii. Omnis qui non facit iusticiam, non est ex Deo. 1. Corinth. vi. Neerretis, Scortatores, Idolatrae &c. regnum Dei non possidebunt. Galat. v. Talia facientes, regnum Dei non possidebunt, Coloss. iii. Propter quae venit ira Dei super inobedientes &c. Sed hic quaeritur de gradu, quando lapsus illi fiunt mortalia peccata. Primum hic gradus haud dubie est peccatum mortale, cum ruunt homines contra conscientiam, adversus mandata Dei, ideoque Paulus describens qualis sit vita sanctorum, constituithunc gradum, ne agant contra conscientiam. 1. Timoth. 1. Summa mandati est dilectio ex corde puro, conscientia bona, & fide non ficta. Ergo cum adversus mandata Dei committuntur facta contra conscientiam, aut cum non repugnatur vitioso affectui, fiunt peccata mortalia. Hic gradus manifestus est. Sed citra hunc gradum etiam incidunt lapsus obscuriores, quorum multi fiunt peccata mortalia, quos ratio non satis iudicare potest, quale fuit Davidis erratum, quando iussit numerari populum. Verum & hi lapsus condonantur redeuntibus ad fidem, sed donec manet propositum agendi contra conscientiam, non potest adesse fides, quia impossibile est fidem existere cum mala conscientia. Fides enim est fiducia, quae statuit quod Deo placeamus propter Christum. Huic fiduciae repugnat mala conscientia, quam parit propositum agendi contra mandata Dei. Haec de discrimine peccatorum Paulus hic tradidit. Quare hunc locum diligenter meminerimus, & caveamus ne amisso beneficio Christi, ruamus in exitium, sicut & Petrus inquit: Studete firmam facere vocationem & electionem vestram, id est, perseverate in hac novitate, quam consecuti estis, ne vocatio et electio, qua ex mundo segregati estis, ab impiis rursus fiat irrita.

## 8:14
Whoever are led by the Spirit of God.

The other argument is taken from the efficient cause: The Holy Spirit is effective in those to whom He is given: You have received the Holy Spirit: Therefore He is effective in you. Paul recites the major premise with these words. Whoever are led by the Spirit of God, these are the sons of God. And there is the use of to be led by the word, so that we may understand that the Holy Spirit is efficacious, not idle. Wherefore one must not resist the Holy Spirit who moves. Afterwards he declares what kind of motions the Holy Spirit has, and distinguishes this new word, namely the Gospel, from the Law. For those made terrified by the Law, if consolation does not approach, rush into desperation, flee from God, and do not call upon Him. These terrors, doubt, and flight he calls the spirit of bondage unto fear. On the contrary, however, when by the Gospel and faith minds are raised up, they conceive the life-giving Holy Spirit, and they recognize now that the Holy Spirit is appeased, and wishes to hear them. That consolation, indeed, in true terrors, is the motion and testimony of the Holy Spirit. Paul therefore feels that another word has now been revealed, by which we are made sons, with the remission of sins granted, and the Holy Spirit granted. But because he names them adopted sons, he distinguishes the rest of the saints from Christ, and that distinction must be held, so that we may know that Christ is by nature the Son of God, and equal to the Father, and consubstantial, just as it is written: We saw His glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, etc. But the saints are sons by adoption, because they are received on account of Christ, and are endowed with the gifts of Christ, namely the Holy Spirit, and new eternal life, wisdom, and righteousness, etc.

Latin:

Quicunque spiritu Dei ducuntur.

Alterum argumentum à causa efficiente sumptum est: Spiritus sanctus est efficax in iis, quibus donatur: Vos accepistis spiritum sanctum: Ergo sit in vobis efficax. Maiorem Paulus his verbis recitat. Quicunque ducuntur spiritu Dei, hi sunt filii Dei. Estque usus verbo duci, ut intelligamus efficacem esse spiritum sanctum, non ociosum. Quare non est repugnandum moventi spiritu sancto. Postea declarat quales sint motus spiritus sancti, & discernit hoc novum verbum, scilicet Evangelium à Lege. Nam Lege perterre facti, si non accedat consolatio, ruunt in desperationem, fugiunt Deum, non invocant. Hos terrores, dubitationem & fugam vocat spiritum servitutis in timorem. Econtra vero cum Evangelio & fide eriguntur animi, concipiunt spiritum sanctum vivificantem, & agnoscunt iam spiritum sanctum placatum esse, & velle exaudire. Illa vero consolatio in veris pavoribus, est motus & testimonium spiritus sancti. Sentit ergo Paulus aliud verbum iam revelatum esse, quo efficimur filii, donata remissione peccatorum, et donato spiritu sancto. Quod autem nominat filios adoptatos, discernit à Christo reliquos sanctos, idque discrimen tenendum est, ut sciamus Christum natura filium Dei esse, et aequalem patri, & consubstantialem, sicut scriptum est: Vidimus gloriam eius tanquam unigeniti à patre &c. Sed sancti sunt adoptione filii, quia propter Christum recepti sunt, & donatur Christi donis, scilicet spiritu sancto, & nova aeterna vita, sapientia & iusticia &c.

## 8:15
You have received the spirit of adoption, etc.

As long as the conscience is without faith, it is desperate in terrors, it flees from God, it doubts whether He hears, whether He regards, etc. It does not call upon God. Therefore Paul joins consolation and invocation, and attributes them only to those who are already raised up by faith through the Gospel. For when he says: we cry Abba Father, he signifies this, that we already acknowledge God to be Father, and that He truly hears us, and by this faith we conceive consolation and call upon God. This faith and acknowledgment of the mercy of God makes the distinction properly between Christians and the impious, because in the impious there remain doubt and indignation against God. But in believers, faith is a new acknowledgment of the mercy of God, and it resists doubt, and establishes that we are truly heard on account of Christ. This very faith is consolation and vivification, and the testimony of the Holy Spirit in our hearts, of which he speaks here: The Spirit gives testimony to our spirit, that is, the Holy Spirit through the word of the Gospel effects consolation in true terrors.

David's sins were forgiven: Therefore he had no mortal sin. Item, David was ordained and predestined from eternity: Therefore all his sins were venial, and he had no mortal sin. R. One must not judge according to election or predestination, but according to the word. The present word teaches David that adultery is a mortal sin, and unless he does penance it is not forgiven him. Concerning sin and justice one must judge according to the present word, not according to election and the unrevealed will. Those thoughts about predestination are to be removed; they do not agree with the opinion of Paul, who declares that one must judge according to this doctrine, etc.

Latin:

Accepistis spiritum adopti-onis &c.

Donec conscientia sine fide est, in pavoribus desperabunda, fugit Deum, dubitat an exaudiat, an respiciat, &c. Non invocat Deum. Ideo Paulus consolationem & invocationem coniungit, & tantum his tribuit, qui iam per Evangelium fide eriguntur. Nam cum, ait: clamamus abba pater, hoc significat, iam agnoscimus Deum esse patrem, & vere nos exaudire, & hac fide concipimus consolationem & invocamus Deum. Haec fides & agnitio misericordiae Dei, facit propriè discrimen inter Christianos et impios, quia in impiis manent dubitatio & indignatio adversus Deum. Sed in credentibus fides est nova agnitio misericordiae Dei, & repugnat dubitationi, & statuit nos vere propter Christum exaudiri. Haec ipsa fides est consolatio & vivificatio, & testimonium spiritus sancti in cordibus, de quo hic loquitur: Spiritus dat testimonium spiritui nostro, id est, spiritus sanctus per verbum Evangelii efficit consolationem in veris pavoribus.

Davidi peccata fuerunt remissa: Ergo nullum babuit mortale peccatum. Item, David ab aeterno fuit ordinatus, praedestinatus: Ergo omnia peccata fuerunt ei venialia, & nullum habuit mortale. R. Non est iudicandum secundum electionem, vel praedestinationem, sed secundum verbum. Praesens verbum docet Davidem, quòd adulterium sit peccatum mortale, & nisi agat paenit entiam non remittitur ei. De peccato & iusticia est iudicandum secundum praesens verbum, non secundum electionem & voluntatem non revelatam. Illae cogitationes de praedestinatione sunt removendae, non congruunt ad sententiam Pauli, qui pronunciat esse secundum istam doctrinam iudicandum &c.

## 8:17
If children, then also heirs, etc.

After he delivered the doctrine that there must exist a new obedience, he directed the gradation concerning glorification, which follows justification. And to this passage he mixes in a proposition concerning afflictions, that this new obedience is occupied among afflictions, because it is repugnant to the flesh, the devil, and the world, that is, to the whole kingdom of sin. But what he says, co-heirs of Christ, if indeed we suffer together.

This proposition describes necessity, as if it were saying, it is necessary to suffer since Christ also suffered, and with that word it embraces the whole new obedience occupied among afflictions. Nor does it follow, if we suffer, we shall be glorified: Therefore our afflictions are the price or merit of eternal life. For thus the promise would become uncertain, because no one is sufficiently patient, no one satisfies the Law. Likewise Paul clearly says: You have been saved freely, and Christ: Say we are unprofitable servants, and here: The afflictions are not worthy of the future glory &c. And Augustine says: Eternal life is rendered to no human merits, but is given by the grace of God bestowing it. This sentence must therefore be retained, that our obedience and afflictions are not the merit, or price of eternal life. But that by faith freely on account of Christ we are made sons and heirs of eternal life, thus the certainty remains. What therefore does the condition posit, if we suffer together: I answer, Not a price or merit, but a necessity, because that obedience is that very newness, by which eternal life is begun in believers, according to that: If we shall not be found naked. Or it is necessary, as an effect necessarily following justification. He institutes moreover a most ample and most ornate consolation, which you will be able to distinguish into six arguments.

The first is taken from the outcome of afflictions, and it is similar to the Topic from rewards: A huge glory will be rendered to us for these afflictions: Therefore let us patiently await the outcome and liberation.

The second argument is from the example of creatures. The whole nature of things is subject to corruption, and to the abuse of the impious, meanwhile until it will be liberated: Therefore let us also await liberation. And there is here some sublime movement in Paul, by which, looking upon the horrible confusion of human life, and the corruption of all things, slaughters, wars, devastations, and other evils of the world, he sees how great is the power of sin, how great the Tyranny of the devil, and how unworthy it is that the nature of things should be subject to the devil, and to death on account of the sin of man. Here first must be considered the affection of the pious, in every affliction. Delay tortures souls, and the fact that we do not foresee the manner of liberation. Item, Miseries grow constantly. Thus also the souls of the pious are tortured by public care, when they avoid the huge dangers of the Church, and see liberation being deferred, and evils growing.

Whether, therefore, these are private afflictions, or we grieve for a public cause, he proposes consolation from the example of heaven and earth, and of the whole of nature, which is subjected to the abuse of the impious. The tyrant holds empires, the impious enjoy the riches of the world, but the Church, for whose sake all things were created, is slaughtered, and the use of life, light, or other creatures is not granted to her. Yet created things were made so that they might serve the pious for the glory of God. Wherefore, since they are in horrible abuse, and on account of the sin of Adam are subjected to corruption, the creatures themselves also await liberation. This, therefore, is the consolation: Heaven and earth sustain a huge burden, namely the abuse of the impious, and yet they await liberation. Therefore, let us together endure these common miseries, and let us tolerate the delay. For even if liberation is deferred, yet it will eventually happen to us. Paul has used very significant words, and has made a personification: The creature groans and travails in pain together. By these words he signifies that the creatures sustain injury, but the pain of that injury reaches the Church, against whom the impious rage at the same time as they rage against the creatures, as when tyrants and the impious seize creatures, and persecute the Church.

The third from the example of the Apostles. We We who have more excellent gifts are afflicted and struggle with the consciousness of our sins, of scandals, with the terrors of the devil, with our own infirmity, with external dangers and persecutions, and we await liberation. Therefore you also should await it. (He calls the more excellent gifts the firstfruits.)

The fourth argument is from the definition of hope. Hope is of those things which are not yet present. By hope we have been saved, that is, by hope we have been liberated from death and all evils. Therefore that liberation from death and other evils is not yet at hand. But here it must be asked, whether or not

Believers are righteous in the present: Therefore they are liberated in the present: Therefore not by hope. R. To the antecedent, we are righteous imputatively, but we hope for liberation and new obedience.

we are liberated from sin in the present. I answer, imputatively we are righteous and liberated from sin in the present. But the disease still remains in our nature, from which we are liberated in hope, that is, we hope for complete newness. Therefore in reality we still labor under infirmity, and are exercised by the terrors of sin, and other afflictions. But among these miseries we ought to raise ourselves up and establish that in the present we have the remission of sins, and by imputation we are righteous and please God on account of Christ. As he says above: Being justified by faith we have peace. And here a notable difference between faith and hope is discerned. Faith in the present receives the remission of sins and the imputation of righteousness. Hope, however, has another object, namely, it expects complete liberation. And concerning hope two things must be held. First, that it is a commandment to hope for eternal life. For he who does not expect the promises, he denies that God is truthful. Therefore, so that the glory of truth may be attributed to God, it is necessary to hope for the promises. It must be known, however, that hope is not doubting, but that it opposes doubting, and overcomes it. But someone might object, I acknowledge the commandment, but the condition of merits, or of our worthiness, is required, or ought even the unworthy to hope for salvation? This question especially exercises minds, and shakes hope: This voice is the voice of the Law, and a handwriting in our minds, which condemns us, and forbids us to hope, because we are unworthy. This second doctrine is therefore most necessary, namely, it must be known that the cause of hope is not our merits, nor our worthiness, but the gratuitous promise of Christ. It is commanded that we hope salvation, and it is commanded that we should hope not on account of our own dignity, but freely on account of Christ, because eternal life is given on account of Christ to the believer, not on account of our dignity: Therefore, even if we are unworthy, nevertheless free hope must be held, and unworthiness must be acknowledged, and in this way the sentences concerning hope must be received. God commands us to hope for this reason, because unworthiness deters us. Therefore hope is not to be cast away on account of unworthiness, rather it is to be opposed to unworthiness on account of the promise. Thus in Psalm 41. He acknowledges and confesses his unworthiness, then he opposes hope to it. Why are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me? Hope in God, because I shall yet confess to him. Thus Psalm 129. In the beginning he confesses sin: If you should observe iniquities, O Lord, who shall endure? Then he sustains himself with hope: My soul has endured in his word, my soul has hoped in the Lord. Because with the Lord there is mercy, etc. In such sayings let it always be understood that hope depends upon the free promise, not upon the condition of our merits and dignity, or upon the condition of the law. Thus those sentences will grow sweet, and will produce true and efficacious consolation. And this hope must be exercised in invocation, just as it is said in Psalm 27 In him my heart has hoped, and I have been helped. And psal. xxxiii. Blessed is the man who hopes in him &c. And psalmo xxiiii. All who wait for you shall not be confounded. Psalmo iiii. Sacrifice a sacrifice of justice, and hope in the Lord.

Thus far it has been spoken concerning the fourth argument, namely that we are liberated in the present, as far as imputation pertains. Then that we are liberated by hope, as far as it pertains to complete newness. It has also been said, which is most necessary to be warned concerning hope, namely, that it is a commandment that we hope for the promised things, and that the condition of our dignity, or of merits, is not to be stitched on. Thus, therefore, hope is to be defined. Hope is the certain expectation of promised salvation for those believing on account of Christ, not on account of our dignity.

We wait through patience.

He says clearly: we wait through patience, so that he may signify not only that liberation is deferred, but that it is so deferred, that in the meantime great and huge struggles must be sustained. The saints are vexed by the terrors of sin, the snares of the devil, scandals, persecution, and various occurrences by which faith is shaken, and in some is extinguished. In order, therefore, that we may foresee these dangers And let us understand, and so that minds may be prepared for these struggles, he orders patience of hope to be added. Here it must be considered what patience properly signifies, which can be understood better from a comparison. Therefore, I will first say what patience signifies to the philosophers. For patience, according to the judgment of reason, is a certain obedience toward reason, which moderates sorrows and prevents us, overcome by sorrow, anger, or some desire, from acting against justice, just as the impulse of Saul, from the sorrow of the received defeat, brought death upon himself. Catiline, having conceived indignation on account of a rejection, stirred up civil war. In such examples, it can be seen what impatience is. From the opposite region, therefore, philosophers call patience a certain obedience moderating sorrow and preventing us from rushing against justice, but there are far more circumstances in Christian patience; first, the causes differ. For here three other causes exist; the first is the command of God. For it is necessary for all to know that it is the command of God that we obey in afflictions, and that indignation or impatience in afflictions is a sin; therefore Christ commands: In your patience possess your souls. And the psalm says, Be angry.

And do not sin, that is, when you are angry, when nature rages in afflictions, do not succumb, but overcome indignation, and Paul says: Let the peace of God rule your hearts. The second cause is the Gospel, which interprets afflictions as not being signs of wrath. This cause is unknown to reason and the Law, it is only revealed in the Gospel. Then, therefore, obedience can be rendered, when the mind not only looks upon the commandment of God, but also sees another object, namely that the things themselves are not signs of wrath, but of the good will of God. Here, concerning afflictions, those things must be gathered which were said above, that they do not happen by chance, that they are not signs of the wrath of God, etc. The third cause is the promise of help, which diminishes and lightens the appearance of evil in afflictions. For David obeys for this reason, because he both sees that they are not signs of wrath, and expects deliverance. But philosophical patience is without hope of help, with human supports lost. Christian patience is therefore a certain obedience in afflictions, but on account of the commandment of God, to which is added faith, which according to the Gospel perceives that afflictions are not signs of wrath and expects and seeks help, according to that: Call upon me in the day of tribulation and I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me &c. Paul describes such patience in this place. For he demands not only that we obey in afflictions, but also that we determine that we are not cast away, likewise that we call upon, likewise that we expect help.
