Therefore he himself immediately attaches a fifth argument, concerning the help of the Holy Spirit, and concerning invocation, as if he were saying: I require such patience, in which you may at the same time call upon and hope for help, which indeed is promised to you. Just as Christ says: I will not leave you orphans &c.

Latin:

Si filii, igitur et haeredes &c.

Postquàm tradidit doctrinam, quòd oporteat existere novam obedientiam, at rexit gradationem de glorificatione, quae sequitur iustificationem. Et huic loco admiscet propositionem de afflictionibus, quod illa nova obedientia versetur inter afflictiones, quia repugnat carni, diabolo & mundo, hoc est, toti regno peccati. Quod autem dicit cohaeredes Christi, siquidem simul affligimur.

Haec propositio describit necessitatem, quasi dicat, necesse est pati cum & Christus passus sit, & illo verbo complectitur totam novam obedientiam versantem inter afflictiones. Nec sequitur, si patimur, glorificabimur: Ergo nostrae afflictiones sunt precium vel meritum vitae aeternae. Sic enim fieret incerta promissio, quia nemo est satis patiens, nemo satisfacit Legi. Item Paulus clarè inquit: Gratis salvati estis, & Christus: Dicite servi inutiles sumus, & hic: Non sunt dignae afflictiones ad futuram gloriam &c. Et Augustinus inquit: Vita aeterna nullis humanis meritis redditur, sed Dei donantis gratia largiente donatur. Retinenda est igitur haec sententia, quod nostra obedientia & afflictiones non sint meritum, vel precium vitae aeternae. Sed quod fide gratis propter Christum efficiamur filii & haeredes vitae aeternae, ita manet certitudo. Quid igitur ponit conditio, si compatimur: Respondeo, Non praetium aut meritum, sed necessitatem, quia illa obedientia est illa ipsa novitas, qua inchoatur in credentibus vita aeterna, iuxta illud: Si non nudi inveviemur. Vel est necessaria, tanquàm effectus necessario sequens iustificationem. Instituit autem amplissimam & ornatissimam consolationem, quam poteris distinguere in sex argumenta.

Primum sumptum est ab exitu afflictionum, estque simile Loco à praemiis: Ingens gloria nobis reddetur pro his afflictionibus: Ergo patienter expectemus exitum & liberationem.

Secundum argumentum ab exemplo creaturarum. Tota rerum natura subiecta est corruptioni, & abusui impiorum, interea donec liberabitur: Ergo & nos expectemus liberationem. Estque hic sublimis aliquis in Paulo motus, quo intuens horribilem confusionem vitae humanae, & omnium rerum corruptionem, caedes, bella, vastitates, & caetera mala mundi, videt quanta sit potentia peccati, quanta Tyrannis diaboli, & quam indignum sit naturam rerum subiectam esse diabolo, & morti propter peccatum hominis. Hic primum considerandus est affectus piorum, in omni afflictione. Mora cruciat animos, & quod non providemus modum liberationis. Item, Aerumnae crescunt assiduem. Sic etiam cruciantur animi piorum publica cura, cum vitent igentia pericula Ecclesiae, & vident differri liberationem, et crescere mala.

Sive igitur privatae afflictiones sunt, sive publica causa dolemus, proponit consolationem ab exemplo caeli & terrae, & totius naturae, quae est subiecta abusui impiorum. Tyranni tenet imperia, impii fruuntur opibus mundi, Ecclesia vero, cuius causa omnia condita sunt, trucidatur, non conceditur ei, vitae, lucis, aut aliarum creaturarum usus. Sunt autem conditae res, ut serviant piis ad gloriam Dei. Quare cum sint in horribili abusu, & propter peccatum Adae sint subiectae corruptioni, expectant & ipsae creaturae liberationem. Est igitur haec consolatio: Caelum & terra sustinent ingens onus, scilicet abusum impiorum, & tamen expectant liberationem. Ergo nos una perferamus has communes aerumnas, & tolleremus moram. Etsi enim differtur liberatio, tamen aliquando continget nobis. Paulus est usus admodum significantibus verbis, & fecit prosopopaeiam: Creatura una gemit & parturit. His verbis significat creaturas sustinere iniuriam, sed dolor istius iniuriae pervenit ad Ecclesiam, in quam simul seviunt impii saevientes in creaturas, ut cum Tyranni & impii rapiunt creaturas, et persequuntur Ecclesiam.

Tertium ab exemplo Apostolorum. Nos qui excellentiora dona habemus, affligimurus luctamur cum conscientia peccatorum nostrorum, scandalorum, cum terroribus diaboli, cum infirmitate nostra, cum externis periculis & persecutionibus, & expectamus liberationem. Quare vos quoque expectetis. (Primitias vocat excellentiora dona.)

Quartum argumentum à definitione spei. Spes est earum rerum, quae nondum sunt praesentes. Spe salvi facti sumus, id est, spe liberati sumus à morte & omnibus malis. Ergo nondum praesto est illa liberatio à morte & caeteris malis. Sed hic quaerendum est, an non

Credentes sunt in praesentia iusti: Ergo sunt in praesentia liberati: Ergo non spe. R. Ad antecedens, imputative iusti sumus, sed speramus liberationem & novam obedientiam.

in praesentia simus liberati à peccato. Respondeo, imputativè in praesentia iusti & liberati à peccato. Sed manet adhuc in natura morbus, à quo sumus liberati in spe, id est, speramus integram novitatem. Ideo reipsa adhuc laboramus infirmitate, et exercemur terroribus peccati, & aliis afflictionibus. Sed inter has aerumnas erigere nos debemus & statuere, quòd in praesentia habeamus remissionem peccatorum, & imputatione simus iusti & placeamus Deo propter Christum. Sicut supra inquit: Iustificati fide pacem habemus. Et hic discernitur insignis differentia fidei & spei. Fides in praesentia accipit remissionem peccatorum & imputationem iusticiae. Spes autem aliud obiectum habet, videlicet expectat integram liberationem. Ac de spe duo tenenda sunt. Primum, quod sit praeceptum, sperare vitam aeternam. Nam qui non expectat promissa, is negat Deum veracem esse. Ideo ut tribuatur Deo gloria veritatis, necesse est sperare promissa. Sciendum est autem, spem non esse dubitationem, sed repugnare dubitationi, eamque vincere. Sed obiiciat aliquis, agnosco praeceptum, sed requiritur conditio meritorum, seu dignitatis nostrae, an etiam indigni sperare salutem debent? Haec quaestio praecipue exercet animos, & excutit spem: Haec vox est vox Legis, & chirographum in mentibus nostris, quod damnat nos, ac prohibet sperare, quia sumus indigni. Est igitur haec secunda doctrina maximè necessaria, videlicet sciendum est spei causam esse non merita nostra, nec dignitatem nostram sed gratuitam promissionem Christi. Mandatum est, ut speremus salutem, & mandatum est, ut non propter nostram dignitatem, sed gratis speremus propter Christum, quia vita aeterna datur propter Christum credenti, non propter dignitatem nostram: Ergo etiamsi sumus indigni, tamen spes gratuita tenenda est, et agnoscenda indignitas, atque ita accipiendae sunt sententiae de spe. Ideo iubet Deus sperare, quia indignitas nos deterret. Ergo non est abiicienda spes propter indignitatem, imo opponenda est indignitati propter promissionem. Sic psal mo xli. Agnoscit & fatetur indignitatem, deinde opponit spem. Quare tristis es anima mea, & quare conturbas me? Spera in Deo, quia adhuc confitebor illi. Sic psal. cxxix. Initio confitetur peccatum: Si iniquitates observaris domine, quis sustinebit? Deinde sustentat sespe: Sustinuit anima mea in verbo eius, speravit anima mea in domino. Quia apud dominum misericordia &c. In talib. dictis sempet intelligatur, spes ex gratuita promissione pendere, non ex conditione meritorum & dignitatis nostrae, seu ex conditione legis. Ita dulcescent illae sententiae, & parient veram et efficacem consolationem. Et haec spes in invocatione exercenda est, sicut psal. xxvii. dicitur In ipso speravit cor meum, & adiutus sum. Et psal. xxxiii. Beatus vir qui sperat in eo &c. Et psalmo xxiiii. Universi qui te expectant, non confundentur. Psalmo iiii. Sacrificate sacrificium iusticiae, & sperate in domino.

Hactenus de quarto argumento dictum est, videlicet quod in praesentia simus liberati, quod ad imputationem attinet. Deinde quod simus spe liberati, quod attinet ad integram novitatem. Dictum est etiam id, quod de spe maxime moneri necesse est, scilicet, quod praeceptum sit, ut speremus promissa, & quod non assuenda sit conditio dignitatis nostrae, seu meritorum. Sic igitur definienda est spes. Spes est certa expectatio promissae salutis propter Christum credentibus, non propter dignitatem nostram.

Per patientiam expectamus.

Diserte inquit: per patientiam expectamus, ut significet non tantum differri liberationem, sed ita differri, ut interea magna & ingentia certamina sustinenda sint. Sancti vexantur terroribus peccati, insidiis diaboli, scandalis, persecutione et variis casibus quibus fides concutitur, & in aliquibus extinguitur. Ut igitur haec pericula prospiciamus & intelligamus, & ut praeparentur animi ad haec certamina, addi iubet spei patientiam. Hic considerandum est, quid proprie significet patientia, quod ex collatione magis intelligi potest. Primum igitur dicam quid philosophis significet patientia. Est enim patientia iuxta iudicium rationis, quaedam obedientia erga rationem, quae moderatur dolores, & prohibet ne dolore, ira, aut cupiditate aliqua victi faciamus contra iusticiam, sicut impulsus Saul dolore acceptae cladis sibi conscivit mortem. Catilina indignatione concepta propter repulsam, movit bellum civile. In talibus exemplis conspici potest, quid sit impatientia. Eregione igitur, philosophi vocant patientiam obedientiam quandam moderantem dolorem, & prohibentem, ne ruamus contra iusticiam, sed longe plures circumstantiae sunt in Christiana patientia, primum causae differunt. Hic enim tres causae aliae sunt, prima est mandatur Dei. Oportet enim scire omnes, quod mandatum Dei sit, ut obediamus in afflictionibus, & quod indignatio, seu impatientia in afflictionibus sit peccatum, ideo praecipit Christus: In patientia possidete anima vestras. Et psalmus inquit, Irascemini.

& nolite peccare, id est, cum irascimini, cum in afflictionibus fremit natura, nolite succumbere, sed vincite indignationem, & Paulus inquit: Pax Dei gubernet corda vestra. Secunda causa est Evangelium, quod interpretatur asflictiones, non esse signa irae. Haec causa est ignota rationi & Legi, tantum revelatur in Evangelio. Tuncigitur potest obedientia praestari, cum mens non tantum intuetur mandatum Dei, sed etiam alterum obiectum videt, scilicet res ipsas non esse signa irae, sed bonae voluntatis Dei. Hic de afflictionibus colligenda sunt illa, quae supra dicta sunt, quod non eveniant casu, quod non sunt signa irae Dei &c. Tertia caussa est promissio auxilii, quae minuit, & levat speciem mali in afflictionibus. Ideo enim David obtemperat, quia & videt non esse signa irae, & expectat liberationem. At philosophica patientia sine spe auxilii est, amissis humanis praesidiis. Est igitur Christiana patientia quaedam obedientia in afflictionibus, sed propter mandatum Dei, ad quam accedit fides, quae iuxta Evangelium sentit afflictiones non esse signa irae & expectat & petit auxilium, iuxta illud: Invoca me in die tribulationis & eripiam te, & glorificabis me &c. Talem patientiam hoc loco describit Paulus. Postulat enim non solum ut obediamus in afflictionibus, sed etiam ut statuamus nos non esse abiectos, item ut invocemus, item ut expectemus auxilium. Ideo ipse statim attexit quintum argumentum, deauxilio spiritus sancti, & de invocatione, quasi dicat: Talem patientiam requiro, in qua simul invocetis, & speretis auxilium, quod quidem promissum est vobis. Sicut Christus inquit: Non relinquam vos orphanos &c.

## 8:26
Likewise also the Spirit helps &c.

Because he spoke above concerning patience, and concerning hope, he adds a fifth argument, taken from help. For in order that patience might be retained, so that invocation and hope might not be shaken off in such a magnitude of afflictions, in such infirmity of the human heart, which is full of doubt, it is necessary also that help be shown. And so he argues thus. God is truly present and helps us in afflictions. Therefore let us not succumb, let us not cast away faith and confession overcome by despair. Here it is profitable to have collected and in sight similar promises, such as: Ask and you shall receive: How much more will your father give the holy spirit to those who ask: Come to me all who labor: I will not leave you orphans. I will ask the father, and he will give you another paraclete, that he may remain with you forever.

But how is the holy spirit given, and how is it effective? I answer, when we sustain ourselves with the word in the very struggles, and we call upon God. Paul joins these two here, just as it is said very often in the psalms: My soul has sustained itself in his word. Likewise concerning invocation psal. iiii. When I called, the God of my righteousness heard me, and Christ says concerning invocation: He will give the holy spirit to those who ask. But Paul describes here in brief words a huge struggle, which our infirmity sustains. For in dangers, persecution, death, and whatever afflictions and miseries, bodily or spiritual, nature reluctantly obeys, and immediately desires to shake them off. Therefore Paul says: We do not know what we should pray for, namely when with natural weakness we ask to be immediately freed, and we bear the cross impatiently. Meanwhile Yet the Holy Spirit brings it about that we obey and call upon Him in some measure. Paul calls this obedience and invocation inexpressible groanings. For in the Spirit we submit ourselves to God, and we seek liberation according to the will of God, not according to carnal desire. Paul, however, speaks of a true and great struggle, not of cold and idle thoughts. Therefore, these things cannot be understood by the secure, but individuals, according to their own manner in their own temptations, ought to experience in some part the power of this consolation in invocation. For nothing greater can be promised than the presence and efficacy of God. For this is promised when the Holy Spirit is promised.

Furthermore, this passage also provides us with testimony against the Pelagians, who imagine that without the Holy Spirit, men are made righteous and saved. Here, on the contrary, Paul openly testifies that the Holy Spirit is given, and that these movements, faith and invocation, are excited by the Holy Spirit agitating and moving.

Latin:

Similiter autem & spiritus au-xiliatur &c.

Quia supra dixit de patientia, & de spe, addit quintum argumentum, sumptum ab auxilio. Ut enim patientia retineri posset, ut invocatio & spes non excutiantur in tanta magnitudine afflictionum, in tanta infirmitate humani cordis, quod est plenum dubitatione, necesse est etiam ostendi auxilium. Itaque sic argumentatur. Deus vere adest & adiuvat nos in afflictionibus Ergo non succumbamus, non abiiciamus fidem & confessionem victi desperatione. Hic prodest habere collectas & in conspectu similes promissiones, ut: Petite & accipietis: Quanto magis pater vester daturus est spiritum sanctum petentibus: Venite ad me omnes qui laboratis: Non relinquam vos orphanos. Rogabo patrem, & alium paracletum dabit vobis, ut maneat vobiscum in aeternum.

Quomodo autem datur spiritus sanctus, & quomodo est efficax? Respondeo, Cum sustentamus nos verbo in ipsis certaminibus, & invocamus Deum. Haec duo Paulus hic coniungit, sicut in psalmis sae pissime dicitur: Sustinuit anima mea in verbo eius. Item de invocatione psal. iiii. Cum invocarem, exaudivit me Deus iusticiae meae, & Christus inquit de invocatione: Dabit spiritum sanctum petentibus. Describit autem Paulus hic brevibus verbis ingens certamen, quod sustinet infirmitas nostra. Nam in periculis, persecutione, morte, & quibuscunque afflictionibus ac aerumnis corporalibus aut spiritualibus, natura aegrè obtemperat, ac statim eas excutere cupit. Ideo Paulus, inquit: Nescimus quid oremus, scilicet cum naturali imbecillitate petimus, nos statim liberari, & impatienter ferimus crucem. Interea tamen spiritus sanctus efficit, ut aliqua a parte obediamus & invocemus. Hanc ob-edientiam & invocationem vocat Paulus gemitus inenarrabiles. Spiritu enim subiicimus nos Deo, & iuxta voluntatem Dei petimus liberationem, non iuxta carnale desiderium. Loquitur autem Paulus de vera & in genti lucta, non de frigidis & ociosis cogitationibus. Ideo haec à securis non possunt intelligi, sed singuli pro suo modo in suis tentationibus, aliqua ex parte experiri debebant in invocatione vim huius consolationis. Nihil enim, promitti maius potest, quàm praesentia & efficatia Dei. Haec enim promittitur, cum promittitur spiritus sanctus.

Porro suppeditat nobis & hic locus testimonium contra Pelagianos, qui imaginantur sine spiritu sancto, homines fieri iustos et salvos. Hic contra Paulus aperte testatur, dari spiritum sanctum, & hos motus fidem & invocationem excitari, agitante, & movente spiritu sancto.

## 8:28
We know, however, that to those who love God, etc.

The sixth argument taken from the outcome God does not glorify otherwise than through afflictions: Therefore endure them, since they are the way to glorification.

The antecedent proves the proposed image of Christ. It is necessary for us to be made similar to the image of the Son of God, the Son of God is glorified through passion: Therefore it is necessary for us also to be afflicted. And this is the chief consolation of the pious, to gaze upon this image of the Son of God. No philosophy and no human wisdom can see why this weak human nature is burdened with these huge calamities. Reason argues whether they happen by chance. The Law of God cries out that they are punishments for sin, and signs of the wrath of God, which testify that we are cast away. But the Gospel rebukes both errors, and proposes to us the Son of God, hence it testifies that we are subjected to afflictions not by chance, but by the certain counsel of God, not that we may perish, but by the good will of God that we may be exercised, so that when God consoles us, faith and the knowledge of God may grow in us. This wisdom concerning the cause and end of human calamities is entirely above and outside the grasp of reason, and is revealed only in the Gospel, and is especially seen in this image of the Son of God.

Latin:

Scimus autem quòd diligenti-bus Deum &c.

Sextum argumentum ab exitu sumptum est. Deus non aliter glorificat nisi per afflictiones: Ergo tollerate eas, cum sint via ad glorificationem.

Antecedens probat proposita imagine Christi. Oportet nos similes sieri imaginis filii Dei, filius Dei est glorificatus per passionem: Ergo & nos oportet affligi. Et haec est praecipua consolatio piorum, intueri hanc imaginem filii Dei. Nulla philosophia & nulla humana sapientia videre potest, quare haec infirma natura humana istis ingentibus calamitatibus onerata sit. Ratio disputat utrum casu accidant. Lex Dei clamitat esse poenas peccati, & signa irae Dei, quae testentur nos obiectos esse. Sed Evangelium utrumque errorem reprehendit, & proponit nobis filium Dei, hinc testatur non causu, sed certo consilio Dei nos subiectos esse afflictionibus, non ut pereamus, sed bona voluntate Dei ut exerceamur, ut cum Deus nos consolatur, crescant in nobis fides & agnitio Dei. Haec sapientia de causa & fine humanarum calamitatum, prorsus est supra & extra captum rationis, & tantum in Evangelio revelatur, & praecipue in hac imagine filii Dei conspicitur.

## 8:30
Whom He predestined, them He also called, etc.

But why does He begin from election? Whom He chooses, them He also calls, then justifies and glorifies, etc. I answer, He wished to embrace the whole order by which the Church is founded by God. And first He warns that election is the cause of calling, not human merits or the righteousness of the Law. It is profitable to know this for this reason, that we may hold fast to consolation against the opinion of merit, and also against that people which falsely arrogates to itself the title of Church on account of the righteousness of the Law, etc. It is necessary for us to establish that the Church is elect, not on account of dignity and human merits, not on account of the righteousness of the Law, not on account of human authority, not on account of the prerogative of succession. Also it must be known that that Church which has the title persecutes the true Church. Wherefore at the beginning it remains that there is some elect Church, so that we may look upon and recognize the true Church. But immediately He adds concerning calling, so that He may lead us to the word, and here He warns that the calling is not void. But God is truly present to this His calling, He justifies and

he will glorify those who are called. He wishes, therefore, for us to look upon our calling, and to remember that it was done divinely, so that we may persevere in it, because God is going to be present to this calling of his, and to his word.

The seventh argument meets the question especially, for it is taken from the object and the cause of fear. For the cause of fear is that, even among afflictions, the sight of our sins terrifies us, and we judge that God is angry with us. Paul heals this question here, and shows that another object must be apprehended, and he argues thus: God testifies that he is propitious to us by having given his son, etc., and indeed he intercedes for us assiduously. Therefore, let us not cast away faith and the hope of deliverance. What shall we say to these things? That is, what more, or what greater thing can be proposed for consolation than that we have God favoring us? He amplifies that by adding the pledge of grace, namely, that he gave his son for us, and he clearly adds: let not sins terrify us. Who shall accuse? As if he were saying, even if we feel that we are unworthy, and still have sins, and immense infirmity and uncleanness, nevertheless no one shall accuse, or condemn us, after that on account of the high priest We are righteous, that is, accepted, through Christ. Therefore he says: It is God who justifies, that is, pronounces righteous. Likewise, Christ intercedes for us, God justifies us, and justifies on account of the interceding Christ. Thus he amplifies this sentence, with mention of the mediator Christ, and makes mention first of his death, then of his resurrection, thirdly of his kingdom, fourthly of his priesthood. He commemorates these briefly, which nevertheless are not to be looked at only in passing. First, concerning his death and sacrifice, it is an insult, and to make sin of more value than this sacrifice. Secondly, Christ by his resurrection conquered the entire power of the Devil. Let us know this victory to be efficacious, and also profitable to us. Thirdly, the Kingdom is not idle: He sits at the right hand of the Father, and by divine power preserves, sustains, and vivifies believers, provided that we do not fall away from him. Fourthly, he adds the priesthood and intercession of Christ. Nor indeed is there any sweeter consolation than to acknowledge Christ as priest and intercessor for us. Moreover, it would be an insult against the priesthood of Christ if we were to think his intercession to be void. Likewise if we were not to join our invocation to his intercession.

Latin:

Quos praedefinierat, eosdem vocavit &c.

Quare autem orditur ab electione? Quos degit eosdem & vocat, deinde iustificat ac glorificat &c. Respondeo, Totum ordinem complecti voluit, quo Ecclesia condita est à Deo. Ac primum monet electionem esse causam vocationis, non humana merita, aut iusticiam Legis. Hoc ideo prodest scire, ut teneamus consolationem contra opinionem meriti, item contra illum populum, qui sibi falso arrogat titulum Ecclesiae propter iusticiam Legis &c. Necesse est ē nos statuere quòd sit Ecclefia electa, non propter dignitatem & merita humana, non propter iusticiam Legis, non propter autoritatem humanam, non propter praerogativam successionis. Item sciendum est, quòd illa Ecclesia, quae titulum habet, persequitur veram Ecclesiam. Quare initio manet esse aliquam electam Ecclesiam, ut intueamur & agnoscamus veram Ecclesiam. Statim autem attexit de vocatione, ut deducat nos ad verbum, & hic monet vocationem non esse irritam. Sed Deus huic suae vocationi vere adest, iustificat &

glorificabit vocatos. Vult igitur nos intueri vocationem, ac meminisse quod sit divinitus facta, ut in ea perseveremus, quia Deus huic suae vocationi, & suo verbo affuturus est.

Septimum argumentum, occurit praecipue quaestioni, sumptum est enim ab obiecto & causa pavoris. Nam causa pavoris est, quod inter afflictiones etiam terret nos conspectus nostrorum peccatorum, & iudicamus Deum nobis irasci. Huic quaestioni hic medetur Panlus, et ostendit aliud obiectum apprehendendum esse, & sic argumentatur: Deus testatur se nobis esse propitium dato filio &c. & quidem ille assiduè pro nobis interpellat. Ergo non abiiciamus fidem & spem deliberationis. Quid dicemus ad haec? id est, quid amplius, aut maius ad consolationem proponi potest, quàm quod habemus Deum faventem? Id amplificat addito pignore gratiae, scilicet, quod dederit pro nobis filium, & clare addit: ne peccata deterreant nos. Quis accusabit? quasi dicat, etiamsi sentimus nos indignos esse, & adhuc habere peccata, & ingentem infirmitatem ac immundiciem, tamen nemo accusabit, aut condemnabit nos, postquàm propter pontifitem Christum iusti, id est, accepti sumus. Ideo inquit: Deus est qui iustificat, id est, iustos pronunciat. Item, Christus interpellat pro nobis, Deus iustificat nos, & iustificat propter interpellantem Christum. Ita amplificat hanc sententiam, mentione mediatoris Christi, ac facit mentionem primum mortis, deinde resurrectionis, tertio regni, quarto pontificatus. Haec breviter commemorat, quae tamen non sunt obiter tantum aspicienda. Primum de morte & sacrificio contumeliam esse, & illum peccatum pluris facere, quam hoc sacrificium. Secundo, Christus resurrectione sua vicit universam Diaboli potentiam. Hanc victoriam sciamus efficacem esse, & nobis quoque profuturam. Tertio, Regnum non est ociosum: Sedet ad dexteram patris, & potentia divina credentes servat, sustentat & vivificat, modo ne deficiamus ab eo. Quarto addit pontificatum & intercessionem Christi. Nec vero ulla est dulcior consolatio, quàm agnoscere Christum pontificem, & interpellatorem esse pro nobis. Esset autem adversus pontificatum Christi contumelia, si existimaremus eius intercessionem irritam esse. Item si nostram invocationem non adiungeremus ad eius intercessionem.

## 8:35
Who shall separate us:

The conclusion is of the nearest argument: Since God loves us so greatly, He will by no means cast us away, even if we are weak, and are exercised by every kind of affliction: For he calls it the love of God, with which God loves us, just as Paul himself interprets it afterwards: because of Him who loves us. For Paul repeats at the end of the consolation this proper and principal voice of the Gospel, that God loves us, because it is the most efficacious consolation in all afflictions, indeed in every invocation, but placed far above the sense of the human heart, which is full of doubt and dread, and does not dare to establish that we are loved by God. Therefore Paul exaggerates this consolation with many words, as if he were saying: Let not the magnitude of afflictions break you, but in all terrors look upon this consolation, that God certainly loves you. Nor is there need of a prolix interpretation in this particle, but in life and in invocation let us learn what God requires, that we should establish that we are loved, and let us rouse ourselves, and by this faith truly invoke Him. Readers are to be admonished here,

That is the proper preaching of the Gospel, that God loves we who believe freely on account of Christ, who truly believe in Christ, that is, who doing penance, raise ourselves up and establish for ourselves that God is propitious. This is the voice of the Gospel, immutable and certain to those who believe.

concerning the inept questions agitated in this place. For the Scholastics have disputed whether a just man can lose his virtues, since Paul says: Who shall separate us from the love, as if he means this: How shall we be able to lose our love. For they thought that love was to be interpreted concerning our virtues, that is, concerning the love with which we love God, but this untimely interpretation is to be rejected, and it is certain that the saints can fall, and lose the holy spirit, and faith, and love: Just as the prophet condemns David on account of adultery. Why therefore does he say that the love of God is perpetual? I answer, As the Evangelical promise is perpetual and ratified, but in such a way that it requires faith, so here Paul speaks to believers, as if he were saying, So long as you believe, so long as you sustain yourself by faith, it is most certain that the love of God toward you is ratified. The meaning is therefore, Without doubt the love with which God loves us is always valid, firm, and certain to the believer. This is the proper proclamation of the Gospel, as has been said above. Therefore, Paul here at the end of the consolation amplifies it. Others twist it toward predestination, but there is no need to resort to that in this place. For he speaks of our victory, and we conquer by the revealed mercy and love in the Word, when we oppose this consolation to the terrors of sin and death. Wherefore the meaning will be simple and plain, if it is understood concerning believers. These must establish that they are truly and certainly loved by God on account of Christ.

Latin:

Quis nos separabit:

Conclusio est proximi argumenti: Cum Deus tantopere diligat nos, nequaqam abiiciet nos, etiamsi sumus infirmi, & exercemur omni genere afflictionum: Nam dilectionem Dei vocat, qua Deus nos diligit, sicut postea interpretatur ipse Paulus: propter eum qui diligit nos. Repetit enim Paulus in fine consolationis, hanc propriam & principalem Evangelii vocem, quòd Deus diligat nos, quia est efficacissima consolatio in omnibus afflictionibus, immo in omni invocatione, sed procul posita supra cordis humani sensum, quod est plenum dubitatione & pavore, & non audet statuere nos diligi à Deo. Exaggerat igitur Paulus hanc consolationem multis verbis, quasi dicat: Non frangat vos magnitudo afflictionum, sed hanc consolationem in omnibus terroribus intuemini, quòd Deus certo vos diligat. Nec est opus prolixa interpretatione in hac particula, sed in vita & in invocatione discamus, quod requirat Deus, ut statuamus nos diligi, & exuscitemus nos, & hac fide vere invocemus eum. Admonendi sunt hic lectores,

Illa est propria Evangelii concio, quòd Deus diligit nos gratis propter Christum credentes, qui verè credunt in Christum, id est, qui agentes paenitentiam, erigunt se & statuunt sibi Deum esse propitium. Haec est vox Evangelii immutabilis & certae credentibus.

de ineptis quaestionibus hoc loco agitatis. Disputaverunt enim Scholastici, an iustus possit amittere suas virtutes, cum Paulus dicat: Quis seperabit nos à diectione, quasi hoc velit: Quomodo poterimus amittere nostram dilectionem. Putabant enim dilectionem interpraetandam esse de nostris virtutibus, hoc est, de dilectione, qua nos diligimus Deum, sed haec intempestiva interpraetatio reiicienda est, & constat sanctos posse labi, & amittere spiritum sanctum, & fidem, ac dilectionem: Sicut Davidem propheta condemnat propter adulterium. Quare igitur dicit dilectionem Dei perpetuam esse? Respondeo, Ut promissio Evangelica est perpetua & rata, sed ita, ut requirat fidem, ita hic Paulus credentibus loquitur, quasi dicat, Tantisper dum credis, dum te fide sustentes, certissimum est ratam esse dilectionem Dei erga te. Est igitur sententia, Haud dubiè dilectio, qua Deus nos diligit, semper rata, firma, certa est credenti. Haec est propria Evangelii concio, ut supra dictum est. Ideo Paulus hic in fine consolationis amplificat eam. Alii detor servunt ad prae destinationem, sed eo decurrere in hoc loco non est opus. Loquitur enim de nostra victoria, & vincimus revelata misericordia, & dilectione in verbo, cum hanc consolationem opponimus terroribus peccati & mortis. Quare simplex & plana sententia erit, si de credentibus intelligatur. Hi statuere debent vere & certè à Deo diligi propter Christum.

## 9:1 Argument
CHAPTER IX.

A completely new discussion is instituted, in which, although he repeats and interweaves the doctrine of justification in some places, he nevertheless treats two other matters principally, namely, who is truly the people of God, or what is the true Church, and concerning the calling of the Gentiles. For the Jews objected that the promises had not yet been exhibited, wherefore they contended that Christ had not yet appeared. Thus they argued. It behooves the people to obtain the promises when Christ has come, the people have obtained nothing: Therefore the promises have not yet been exhibited, nor has Christ appeared. They proved the minor premise, because the people signifies not some few as if inciting a sedition, but it signifies the princes, the priests, the learned, the good, and the most flourishing part of the people in any Republic whatsoever: But in the Jewish Republic, the princes, the priests, and the principal part of the people did not feel that they were better off, nay rather the whole Republic was rushing more and more to ruin: Therefore they by no means judged themselves to have been helped by Christ. The weak were greatly moved by this argument, for the Apostles were contending that the promises had been exhibited, that the people had been saved. They on the contrary objected that the Apostles were some few seditious men, who are not the people. In order, therefore, that he may dissolve this argument, it is necessary for Paul to dispute concerning this scandal of paucity, and to distinguish the true people of God from that which holds the title, and this doctrine is useful. In all ages there are two bodies of the Church: The one of the true Church, the other of that bearing the title, which nevertheless persecutes the true Church. And great is the authority, great is the power of that one bearing the title. Therefore, lest the weak be deceived, it is necessary that the pious be fortified against this external appearance, as that they may understand what is the true Church, the true people of God. Thus they argue even now: The Church cannot err: The congregation of bishops, and priests, and followers is the Church: Therefore this congregation cannot err. They prove the minor premise, because these alone have been in the ministry of the word for so many centuries, they have the examples of the fathers, etc. Therefore they are the Church.

Here it is necessary to show that even if they are in the place of the ministry, yet if they teach impious things, they do not have the ministry of the Gospel, nor are they the Church. It is not, however, a light scandal that this honor, namely the title of Church, is taken away from pontiffs, princes, and the whole most beautifully ordered state, and this august title is conferred upon a few abject and miserable men, and indeed who seem to stir up sedition against the ordinary form of the Church. By this scandal many are deterred from the Gospel, and from the true Church; therefore men must be taught concerning election, that the true Church is not just any multitude, but the elect and called to the Gospel, retaining the word of God, and fighting against the wisdom and power of the world. This is the occasion of the Pauline disputation in this place. For the Jews were agitating these two arguments: That they were the people of God: Therefore unless it were so, that is, it would be better for the whole Jewish polity that the promises had not yet been exhibited. Item, because they themselves are the seed of Abraham, the promise does not pertain to the nations. Here Paul opposes a contrary opinion, namely that the people of God is a certain multitude elected through mercy, and called through the Gospel, and sanctified through the Holy Spirit, nor does it become the people of God through carnal propagation and the worship of the Law. This is the sum of the opinion and the principal proposition: he speaks therefore of the effect of election, that it is the true Church elected through mercy, and he removes two causes: carnal propagation and the Law. Here it is disputed concerning predestination: Item, concerning the freedom of the human will and concerning certain other matters, namely concerning the general and special action of God: Item concerning contingency. Nor is it useless to consider those things which are said concerning such great matters, but piously and with the fear of God, those things are to be chosen which have been handed down in the scriptures, and have the testimonies of received and approved writers, and are profitable to consciences. Wherefore we shall briefly collect a few things.

First concerning the reprobation of the impious, the writers do not dissent, but all confess that the cause of reprobation in those who are damned is their impious will and their sins. On the contrary they speak differently concerning the cause of predestination, or the election of those to be saved. More recent scholastics have said only by human judgment that the cause of election is merits, or the good works of the human free will. And this imagination arose from ignorance of the Gospel, because indeed they thought man to be justified on account of his own dignity, or merits, or the fulfillment of the Law: Likewise they thought the Law to be fulfilled, they asserted this imagination, that on account of the fulfillment of the Law those to be saved would be elected. But the Gospel affirms that no one satisfies the Law, and therefore it removes merit, which pertains to justification and salvation, and teaches that men are reckoned righteous through mercy on account of Christ, not on account of their own dignity: Therefore, own dignity, or merits, or the fulfillment of the Law, are not the cause of election.

The other opinion is that the mercy of God is made the cause of election, just as Paul clearly teaches, in this place and elsewhere: If it were of works, it would no longer be grace. For the Church does not depend on human counsel, or human powers, but God in Christ has loved and elected those to be saved.

However, two questions concerning election torment the mind here: The former is concerning the dignity by merit. For the mind disputes, if I were worthy, sufficiently pure, or well-deserving, I would determine that I too would obtain mercy, and the other promised benefits. This temptation arises from the judgment of the Law, which requires worthiness and merits. Here, therefore, it is very useful to hold the doctrine of the Gospel concerning gratuitous mercy. For the Gospel is preached concerning gratuitous mercy, not that it may drive minds to despair, but that it may heal our diffidence and despair. And mercy is shown, not that we should do nothing, or not receive the word, but that our worthiness may be taken away, and the benefit of God may be certain.

The second scruple is concerning particularity. For because we hear that mercy is the cause of election, and yet that few are elected, we are even more distressed, we dispute whether there is with God προσωποληψία : Item why He does not have mercy on all. To this temptation also the universal promises of the Gospel ought to be opposed, which teach that God, on account of Christ, promises salvation both freely and to all, according to that: The righteousness of God through faith of Jesus Christ unto all and upon all. And elsewhere: The same Lord of all, rich unto all.

Likewise, all who shall have called upon the name, etc. These universal sentences must be opposed to the temptation concerning particularity. Then it must be established thus, that one must not judge concerning the will of God from reason without the word of God. Likewise, just as concerning justification, so also concerning election, one must not judge from reason or the Law, but from the Gospel. When, therefore, we dispute: If merits do not make a distinction, why does He not have mercy on all? I answer, We, as far as the word and promises pertain, ought to retain the universal. But not all obtain the benefits, because most resist the word. And it is manifest that to resist is of the human will, because God is not the cause of sin. Then, if we shall speak concerning election for the utility of the conscience, let us say, just as we say concerning justification: That those are righteous who believe, so those are elect who do not resist the calling, but believe the Gospel, and in the end do not cast it away. And yet meanwhile it must be held that to believe and not to resist are motions which occur with the Holy Spirit impelling. I speak, however, concerning our judgment, which does not scrutinize the secret majesty without the word, but looks upon God calling through the promise, and apprehends His will in the word, which is universal. Thus Paul says: It is not of him who wills nor of him that runneth, but of God that showeth mercy, that is, mercy is indeed the cause of election, not our willing or running, and yet these things are done in the one willing and running, not in one resisting.

Now I come to the text, in which we may establish this scope, that it teaches that the true and elect Church must be discerned from that which has the title or carnal prerogatives. This is a necessary doctrine against that magnificent appearance which the false Church boasts, namely antiquity, the examples of the fathers, the consensus of the multitude. When these strike the eyes, let us discern the Churches, as Paul here discerns the peoples of God: The true people is elected through mercy, which has the Gospel. But the Jews contended that they were the people of God, because they were propagated from Abraham, had the Law, the fathers, the examples, the miracles. Thence they reasoned in this way: That Christ has not yet been exhibited, because Christ coming will save the people: The people is not saved, but some few, as if seditious they boast themselves to be saved: Therefore Christ has not yet come. Here Paul responds to the minor premise, and teaches that the people are those elected through mercy, not on account of carnal prerogatives or on account of the Law. But if the disputation of Paul is referred to this sum, it will be more expeditious, and it will be able to be transferred to our use, so that we may learn what the Church truly is. Paul begins, however, from a most grave complaint, in which he testifies that he grieves for the destruction of his own nation, just as all holy men are affected with immense grief when they think that such a great multitude of men is being damned, and they marvel at that secret counsel, that the Church is a small, weak, and abject multitude. But among those first-born in that people it was miserable that this nation, in which there were fathers and prophets, was rejected. And here let us consider the argument of Paul, so that we may learn to fear God. If He did not spare those who were the descendants of the fathers and prophets, of whom the promises spoke openly, how much less will He spare the nations.

But I do not say this, because the word of God has failed.

Correction, Even though I deplore the destruction of the nation, nevertheless I do not command anyone to despair. For I do not feel this, that none of the Jews can be saved; rather, the promise still pertains to us, nor is it void. Would that the promise you may believe, that whoever shall do so shall be saved.

Latin:

CAPUT IX.

Prorsus nova disputatio instituitur, in qua tametsi doctrinam de iustificatione alicubi repetit & intertexit, tamen duas alias materias principaliter tractat, videlicet quis sit vere populus Dei, seu quae sit vera Ecclesia, & de vocatione gentium. Nam Iudaei obiiciebant nondum esse exhibitas promissiones, quare contendebant nondum apparuisse Christum. Sic ē argumentabantur. Populum oportet consequi promissiones, cum venerit Christus, populus nihil est consecutus: Ergo promissiones nondum sunt exhibitae, nec apparuit Christus. Minorem probabant, quia populus significat non paucos quosdam tanquàm seditionem concitantes, sed significat principes, sacerdotes, doctos, bonos, & florentissimam partem populi in qualibet Republica: At in Repub. Iudaica, principes, sacerdotes, & praecipua pars populi non sentiebat se melius habere, imo magis magisque ruebat tota Respub: Ergo nequaquam iudicabant se à Christo adiutos esse. Hoc argumento valdè movebantur infirmi, nam quod Apostoli contendebant exhibitas esse promissiones, salvatum esse populum. Illi ècontra obiiciebant, Apostolos, paucos quosdam seditiosos homines esse, qui non sint populus. Ut igitur diluat hoc argumentum, necesse est Paulo disputare de hoc scandalo paucitatis, & discernere verum populum Dei, ab eo qui titulum tenet, estque utilis haec doctrina. Omnibus aetatibus duo sunt Ecclesiae copora: Alterum verae Ecclesiae, alterum gerentis titulum, quae tamen persequitur veram Ecclesiam. Et magna est autoritas, magna potentia illius gerentis titulum. Ideo ne decipiantur infirmi, necesse est muniri pios contra hanc externam speciem, ut quae sit vera Ecclesia, verus populus Dei, intelligant. Ita nunc quoque argumentantur: Ecclesia non potest errare: Congregatio Episcoporum, & sacerdotum, & sequacium est Ecclesia: Ergo haec congregatio non potest errare. Minorem probant, quia hi soli tot seculis fuerunt in ministerio verbi, habent patrum exempla &c. Ergo sunt Ecclesia.

Hic necesse est ostendere, quod etiamsi sint in loco ministerii, tamen si doceant impia, non habeant ministerium Evangelii, nec sint Ecclesia. Non est autem leve scandalum, detrahi hunc sū honorem, videlicet titulum Ecclesiae, pontificibus, principibus, et universo statui pulcherrime ordinato, & conferri hunc Augustum titulum in paucos abiectos & calami tosos, & quidem qui videantur seditiose tumultuari adversus ordinariam formam Ecclesiae. Hoc scandalo multi deterrentur ab Evangelio, & à vera Ecclesia, ideo docendi sunt homines de electione, quod vera Ecclesia sit non quaelibet multitudo, sed electi & vocati ad Evangelium, retinentes verbum Dei, & propugnantes adversus sapientiam, & potentiam mundi. Haec est occasio Paulinae disputationis hoc loco. Nam Iudaei haec duo argumenta agitabant: Se esse populum Dei: Ergo nisi sis, hoc est, toti Iudaicae politiae melius esset, nondum exhibitas esse promissiones. Item, quia ipsi semen Abrahae, non pertineat promissio ad gentes. Hic Paulus opponit contrariam sententiam, videlicet quod populus Dei sit quaedam multitudo electa, per misericordiam, et vocata per Evangeliu, et sancti ficata per spiritum sanctum, nec fiat populus Dei per propagationem carnalem, & cultus Legis. Haec est summa sententiae & principalis propositio: Loquitur igitur de electionis effectu, quod sit vera Ecclesia electa per misericordiam, & tollit causas duas propagationem carnalem, & Legem. Hic disputatur de praedestinatione: Item, de libertate voluntatis humanae & de aliis quibusdam materiis, videlicet de generali & speciali actione Dei: Item de contingentia. Nec est inutile considerare ea, quae derebus tantis dicuntur, sed pie et cum timore Dei, eligenda sunt ea, quae tradita sunt in scripturis, et habent testimonia receptorum & probatorum scriptorum, & prosunt conscientiis. Quare pauca quaedam breviter colligemus.

Primum de reprobatione impiorum, non dissentiunt scriptores, sed fatentur omnes causam reprobationis in damnandis esse impiam voluntatem & peccata eorum. Eregione vero de causa praedestinationis, seu electioonis salvandorum dissimiliter loquuntur. Recentiores scholastici tantum humano iudicio dixerunt causam electionis esse merita, seu bona opera liberae voluntatis humanae. Et haec imaginatio orta est ex ignoratione Evangelii, quia enim putabant hominem iustificari propter propriam dignitatem, seu merita, seu impletionem Legis: Item putabant Legem impleri, assuerunt hanc imaginationem, quod propter impletionem Legis salvandi essent electi. Sed Evangelium affirmat neminem Legi satisfacere, ideoque tollit meritum, quod ad iustificationem & salvationem attinet, ac docet homines reputari iustos per misericordiam propter Christum, non propter propriam dignitatem: Ergo propria dignitas, seu merita, seu impletio Legis, non sunt causa electionis.

Altera sententia est, quod misericordia Dei fit causa electionis, sicut Paulus clarè docet, hoc loco & alibi: Si ex operibus, iam non esset gratia. Non enim pendet Ecclesia, ab humano consilio, aut humanis viribus, sed Deus in Christo dilexit & elegit salvandos.

Discruciant autem hic animum duae quaestiones de electione: Prior est de dignitate saeu merito. Disputat enim animus, si essem dignus, satis purus, aut bene meritus, statuerem me quoque consecuturum esse misericordiam, & caetera beneficia promissa. Haec tentatio à iudicio Legis oritur, quae requirit dignitatem & merita. Hic igitur valde prodest, tenere doctrinam Evangelii de gratuita misericordia. Ideo enim Evangelium concionatur de gratuita misericordia, non ut adigat mentes ad desperationem, sed ut medeatur nostrae diffidentiae & desperationi. Et misericordia ostenditur, non ut nos nihil agamus, seu non accipiamus verbum, sed ut tollatur nostra dignitas, & beneficium Dei sit certum.

Alter scrupulus est de particularitate. Quia enim audimus misericordiam esse causam electionis, & tamen paucos elegi, magis etiam angimur, disputamus an sit apud Deum προσωποληψία: Item cur non omnium miseriatur. Huic tentationi etiam debent opponi promissiones Evangelii universales, quae docent Deum propter Christum, & gratis & omnibus salutem promittere, iuxta illud: Iusticia Dei per fidem Iesu Christi in omnes & super omnes. Et alibi: Idem dominus omnium, dives in omnia.

Item omnes, qui invocaverint nomen &c. Hae universales sententiae opponendae sunt tentationi de particularitate. Deinde ita statuendum, quod de voluntate Dei non sit iudicandum ex ratione sine verbo Dei. Item sicut de iustificatione, ita & de electione non est iudicandum ex ratione, aut Lege, sed ex Evangelio. Cum igitur disputamus: Si merita non faciunt discrimen, cur non omnium miseretur? Respondeo, Nos quod ad verbum & promissiones attinet, debemus retinere universalem. Sed non omnes consequ untur beneficia, quia plaerique repugnant verbo. Et manifestum est, quod repugnare sit voluntatis humanae, quia Deus non est causa peccati. Deinde si de electione pro utilitate conscientiae loquemur, dicamus, sicut de iustificatione dicimus: Iustos esse, qui credunt, ita electos esse, qui non repugnant vocationi, sed credunt Evangelio, et in fine non abiiciunt. Et tamen interea tenendum est, quod credere & non repugnare sint motus, qui fiunt impellente spiritu sancto. Loquor autem de nostro iudicio, quod non scrutatur arcanam maiestatem sine verbo, sed intuetur Deum vocantem per promissionem, & voluntatem eius apprehendit in verbo, quod est universale. Ita Paulus inquit: Non est volentis nequè currentis, sed Dei miserentis, id est, misericordia est quidem causa electionis, non nostrum velle aut cursus, & tamen haec siunt in voluntare, & currente, non in repugnante.

Nunc ad textum venio, in quo constituamus hunc scopum, quod docet discernendam esse veram & electam Ecclesiam ab illa, quae titulum habet, aut praerogativas carnales. Haec est necessaria doctrina adversus illam magnificam speciem, quam iactat falsa Ecclesia, videlicet antiquitatem, exempla patrum, consensum multitudinis. Haec cum incurrunt in oculos, discernamus Ecclesias, ut hic discernit Paulus populos Dei: Verus populus est elect us per misericordiam, qui habet Evangelium. Sed Iudaei contendebant se esse populum Dei, quia essent propagati ab Abraham, haberent Legem, patres, exempla, miracula. Inde ratiocinabantur hoc modo: Nondum exhibitum esse Christum, quia Christus veniens salvabit populum: Populus non est salvatus, sed pauci quidam, tanquam seditiosi gloriantur se esse salvatos: Ergo nondum venit Christus. Hic respondet Paulus ad minorem, & docet populum esse electos per misericordiam, non propter carnales praerogativas aut propter Legem. Quod si ad hanc summam referetur disputatio Pauli, erit expeditior, & poterit transferri ad usum nostrum, ut discamus, quae sit verè Ecclesia. Incipit autem Paulus à gravissima quaerela, in qua testatur se dolere interitum suae gentis, sicut omnes sancti viri ingenti dolore afficiuntur, cum cogitant tantam multitudinem hominum damnari, & admirantur illud arcanum consilium, quòd Ecclesia est exigua multitudo, infirma, abiecta. In primis autem natis in illo populo fuit miserabile, hanc gentem reiici, in qua fuerunt patres & prophetae. Et hic cogitemus Pauli argumentum, ut discamus timere Deum. Si illis non pepercit, qui fuerunt posteri patrum, & prophetarum, de quibus promissiones loquebantur apertè, quanto minus parcet gentibus.

Non autem haec loquor, quòd exciderit sermo Dei.

Correctio, Etiamsi deploro gentis interitum, tamen non iubeo quenquàm desperare. Non enim hoc sentio, nullos ex Iudaeis servari posse, immo promissio adhuc pertinet ad nos, nec est irrita. Utinam promissioni credatis, quod quicunquè facient erunt salvi.

## 9:4
For not all who are of Israel &c.

This is the principal proposition, in which he responds to the objection concerning the people, who is truly the people of God. The Jews contended that they were the people of God, that they were the Church, and that the promise belonged to them alone. Paul responds that the elect are the people of God, and he distinguishes the true people from those who have the title. Thus the true Church must be distinguished from that kingdom which has the title, and yet wars against the true Church, and Paul clearly explains the proposition: Children of God are made not by carnal propagation, nor by natural gifts, or merits, but by the election of God. In order to declare this sentiment, he leads us to scripture, so that we may contemplate how God has always segregated some by his election, so that he might prepare the Church, and show that the Church is not made by human counsel. If they were made children by nature or merits, there would have been no need for God to segregate the child of his promise from the rest. The Chaldeans, the Egyptians were not inferior in gifts, or natural merits, than Isaac. Alexander the Macedonian, Fabius, Scipio, were more instructed with natural gifts than we, and yet they did not have the Gospel: Therefore the Church is made by election, not by natural gifts or merits. He adapts this passage concerning Isaac to this opinion. And this is the first proof of the proposition.

He is the son whom God by His promise chose for Himself, and separated from the remaining sons of Abraham: Therefore the sons of God are made by election. These things, on account of brevity, are not sufficiently perceived, although they contain most grave doctrine, namely that the Church is not made by human counsel, gifts, or natural merits, but by divine election and promise.

Second proof. Jacob is a son, not on account of works, but on account of Him who calls: Therefore the sons of God are made by election, not by gifts, or natural merits, or the Law.

Latin:

Non enim omnes qui sunt ex Israhel &c.

Haec est principalis propositio, in quarespondet ad obiectionem de populo, quis sit vere populus Dei. Iudaei contendebant se esse populum Dei, se esse Ecclesiam, ad se solos pertinere promissionem. Paulus respondet electos esse populum Dei, & discernit verè populum, ab his qui titulum habent. Ita discernenda est vera Ecclesia ab illo regno, quod titulum habet, & tamen belligeratur cum vera Ecclesia, & Paulua propositionem clare exponit: Filii Dei fiunt non propagatione carnali, nò naturalibus donis, aut meritis, sed electione Dei. Hanc sententiam ut declaret, deducit nos ad scripturam, ut intueamur quomodo Deus semper sua electione segregaverit aliquos, ut còpararet Ecclesiam, & ostenderet non fieri Ecclesiam humano consilio. Si natura aut meritis fierent silii, nihil opus fuisset Deo, segregare silium suae promissionis à reliquis. Chaldaei, Aegiptii nò erant inferiores donis, aut meritis naturalibus, quàm Isaac. Alexander Macedo, Fabius, Scipio, magis fuerunt instructi donis naturalibus, quàm nos, & tamen non habuerunt Evangelium: Ergo Ecclesia fit electione, non donis naturalibus aut meritis. In hanc sententiam accommodat hunc locum de Isaac. Estque haec prima probatio propositionis.

Ille est filius, quem Deus sua promissione sibi delegit, & segregavit à reliquis filiis Abrahae: Ergo silii Dei fiunt electione. Haec propter brevitatem non satis conspiciuntur, cum tamen gravissimam doctrinam contineant, videlicet quod Ecclesia non fiat humano consilio, donis, aut meritis naturalibus, sed electione divina & promissione.

Secunda probatio. Iacob sit filius, non propter opera, sed propter vocantem: Igitur filii Dei fiunt electione, non donis, aut meritis naturalibus, aut Lege.

## 9:14
Is there injustice with God?

But Paul sees that these things are placed far above the sight of human reason, wherefore he interrupts himself, and the common argument, which comes into the mind of all sane men as necessary, he proposes and resolves. If Esau and Jacob are equals, God ought to have chosen or rejected both, because a just judge renders equal things to equals. Paul resolves this in this way: equal things are to be rendered to equals when a debt is paid; in a donation, or when it is acted through mercy, there is no need to render equal things to equals. Just as Christ also shows in the parable of those hired into the vineyard, that through mercy equal things are given to unequals. To this opinion this saying is cited: I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, that is, on whom it has seemed good to me to have mercy, as if he were to say: Salvation happens through mercy, not through debt, and he attaches the consequence: It is not of him who wills nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy. This sentence testifies that men are chosen through mercy, and called so that they may will and run.

Previously he cited sayings about mercy, and showed mercy to be the cause of election, and that the people of God are truly that Church of the elect. Now, from the opposite side, he adds testimonies and a discussion about the reprobate, that there is some multitude of the reprobate, which God allows to exist, so that in persecution the glory of the Gospel may be more visible. And that is said for this reason, that we may be fortified against the scandal of the multitude, nor let us think that the example of the multitude is to be followed. Gamaliel sees that a still greater and more excellent part of the people is opposed to the Gospel. Therefore he thinks that he too must remain in this assembly. Thus do countless men now judge concerning the Church, which arrogates the title to itself. Therefore Paul draws us away from these judgments, and warns that the few elect are the Church, and that on the contrary a huge multitude of the reprobate is waging war with the Gospel. He therefore alleges the history of Pharaoh, which contains two things, namely that he is reprobate, and yet was raised up for this, that the glory of God might be made more conspicuous in persecution. Paul adds the conclusion: Therefore he has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens. Let this conclusion not be understood concerning the causes equally, but concerning the effect of election, that some are elect, others are hardened, who oppose the Gospel. But first concerning the phrase you should learn, that among the Hebrews transitive verbs most commonly have the meaning of one permitting. Such as is: Do not lead us into temptation, that is, do not allow us to be led: You have made us to err, that is, you have suffered us to fall into error. Thus to harden signifies not to free some, or to allow them to continue to resist God. It is therefore Opinion: He hardens whom he wills, that is, he does not free, he does not convert, because they continue to resist God who is calling. Secondly, Paul does not say in this place that there is no cause of hardening or reprobation in the impious themselves: Therefore prudence must be applied here, and it must be held that in the impious themselves there is a cause of hardening or reprobation, namely because they do not cease to resist God who is calling. And yet meanwhile these things which Paul says stand, that there is an ungrateful or rejected multitude, warring with the word of God. If anyone however obeys the word of God, this one is not from that number. And let us learn in this place what kind of judgment there is concerning those who resist the word of God. For because they resist, they are hardened, and they show themselves to be from the number of the reprobate. When however he has said, he hardens whom he wills, he immediately adds an objection: If hardening happens by the will of God: Therefore that multitude cannot be converted: If it cannot be converted, why is it accused? He answers by conceding that it cannot be converted, namely by necessity of consequence, as if he were to say: It is true that the multitude is rejected, and cannot be converted, because it is rejected, but it is rejected on account of its own impiety: If anyone however obeys God who is calling, he is not from that number. Thus He responds by concession, and adds the final cause why God ordained these things in this way, namely so that both might be more clearly seen, namely wrath and mercy, thus I accommodate Paul's response. Why do you contend with God? that is, when you see this wonderful counsel of God, by which He chooses a few and rejects many, obey God, and fear His judgment, lest you be offended by the example of the multitude, but know that God declares mercy in saving us, and wrath in punishing those who do not comply. This is a not at all intricate exposition. For it is not to be thought that there is no cause of hardening or reprobation in the impious themselves, nor does Paul say this, and the similitude of the clay and the potter does not mean this, that the impious do nothing, but it agrees to this extent, that out of one mass of the human race, God by His judgment saves some, and damns others. The causes in the similitude cannot be entirely accommodated. For the opinion must be held that God is not the cause of sin. This also must be retained, that the promise is universal. Just as Paul himself later adds the reason why Israel perishes, because it does not want to accept the Gospel by pursuing, it does not attain righteousness, because it is not from faith etc.

Here he expressly sets forth the cause of reprobation, namely because they are repugnant to the Gospel.

Not only from the Jews.

After he established the thesis, that the people of God is the Church of the elect, he now comes to the hypothesis, that the elect are from the Jews and the Gentiles, and he proves this with testimonies of scripture, so that he may show the Gospel to pertain to the Gentiles. And first he cites a passage from Hosea. It is, however, a sufficiently clear testimony. The reader is to be admonished of this in passing, as often as it is spoken of the calling of the Gentiles, it is to be known that grace is commended, because we are pleasing not on account of the Law, but freely on account of Christ etc. The other testimony is of Isaiah, which prophesies concerning the defection of the people. First he says, Even if there shall be a huge multitude of people, nevertheless only a few shall be saved. This is what the phrase means when it says Remnant, for remnant signifies a few, who are left behind when the rest have been consumed. Then follows a repetition of the same sentiment: A consummation abbreviated shall overflow with justice. For the Lord shall make a consummation and an abbreviation. Consummation signifies the end, or the destruction of the people. That is to say

A great slaughter of the people, or destruction, is about to come, and yet then justice will overflow, that is, then the promised justice and benefit will be revealed and given, when toward the end of the people a great multitude is about to perish, and some will be saved, who will believe in the Gospel, and will receive that promised justice. The consummation is abbreviated, that is, certainly predetermined or established. Paul cites the Greek version, which is less clear, but only contains the same meaning, if you understand the word for the thing, as the Hebrews speak. God will make an abbreviated word, that is, an abbreviated thing, or an abbreviation, or an end. And in this consummation he will cause justice to overflow. Others have invented various interpretations. They interpret the abbreviated word as the Gospel, because the Law is a long doctrine, yet not justifying. This interpretation is untimely. Someone else has interpreted it as, A perfect sentence will overflow with justice, that is, a wise judge will pass a just sentence. This one runs completely off the path. Let us retain the one and simple meaning consistent with the continuous narrative in the text, namely that the people are about to perish, but that Christ is about to come a little before, and

that some from the people would obtain those most ample promises, made to the fathers, with the rest of the multitude rejected. There is also an emphasis to be observed in the particle will overflow, which signifies the amplitude of grace.

Latin:

Num iniusticia est apud Deum:

Sed videt Paulus haec longè posita esse supra conspectum rationis humanae, Quare interpellat ipse sese, & argumentum commune, quod omnibus sanis in mentem venire necesse est, proponit & diluit. Si Esau & Iacob sunt pares, Deus utrunque eligere, aut reiicere debuit, quia iustus iudex reddit paria paribus. Paulus diluit hoc modo, paria paribus reddenda sunt cum solvitur debitum, in donatione vel cum agitur per misericordiam, nihil opus est paria reddere paribus. Sicut & Christus in parabola de conductis in vineam ostendit, per misericordiam dari paria disparibus. In hanc sententiam citatur hoc dictum: Miseror cuius miseror, id est, cuius mihi visum est misereri, quasi dicat: Salvatio contingit per misericordiam, non per debitum, & attexit consequens: Non est volentis nequè currentis, sed Dei miserentis. Haec sententia testatur, homines eligi per misericordiam, & vocari ut velint & currant.

Antea citavit dicta de misericordia, & ostendit misericordiam esse causam electionis, & populum Dei vere esse illam electorum Ecclesiam. Nunc è regione addit testimonia & disputationem de reprobatis, quod sit aliqua multitudo reprobatorum, quam Deus sinit existere, ut in persecutionesit conspectior gloria Evangelii. Idque eo dicitur, ut simus muniti contra scandalum multitudinis, nec cogitemus sequendum esse exemplum multitudinis. Gamaliel videt adhuc maiorem & praestantiorem partem populi adversari Evangelio. Ergo ita cogitat sibi quoque manendum esse in hoc coetu. Ita nunc iudicant innumerabiles homines, de Ecclesia, quae sibi titulum arrogat. Ideo Paulus ab his iudiciis nos abstrahit, & monet paucos electos esse Ecclesiam, & è regione ingentem multitudinem reproborum belli gerantem cum Evangelio. Allegat igitur historiam Pharaonis, quae duo continet, quòd videlicet sit reprobatus, & tamen eò tolleretur, ut fiat in persecutione conspectior gloria Dei. Addit Paulus conclusionem: Ergo cuius vult miseretur, quem vult indurat. Haec conclusio non de causis pariter intelligatur, sed de effectu electionis, quòd sint alii electi, alii sint indurati, qui adversantur Evangelio. Primum autem de phrasi discas, Hebraeis verba transitiva communissime habent significationem permittentis. Quale est: Ne nos inducas in tentationem, id est, ne sinas nos induci: Tu errare nos fecisti, id est, passus es, ut incideremus in errorem. Ita indurare significat non liberare aliquos, aut sinere, ut pergant repugnare Deo. Est ergo sententia: Quod vult indurat, id est, non liberat, non convertit, quia pergunt repugnare vocanti Deo. Secundo, Non dicit Paulus hoc loco, non esse causam indurationis, aut reprobationis in ipsis impiis: Ideo prudentia hic adhibenda est, & sentiendum, quod in ipsis impiis sit causa indurationis, seu reprobationis, scilicet quia non desinunt repugnare. Deo vocanti. Et tamen interim constant haec, quae dicit Paulus, quòd sit multitudo ingrata seu reiecta, belligerans cum verbo Dei. Si quis autem obtemperat verbo Dei, hic non est ex illo numero. Et discamus hocloco, quale sit iudicium de istis, qui repugnant verbo Dei. Quia enim repugnant, indurantur, & ostendunt se esse ex numero reprobatorum. Cum autem dixerit, quem vult indurat, statim addit obiectionem: Si voluntate Dei fit iuduratio: Ergo non potest multitudo illa converti: Si non potest converti, quare accusatur? Respondet concedens non posse converti, scilicet necessitate consequentiae, quasi dicat: Verum est esse reie ctam multitudinem, nec posse converti, quia reiecta est, sed est reiecta propter propriam impietatem: Si quis autem obtempetat Deo vocanti, non est ex illo numero. Ita respondet per concessionem, & addit causam finalem, quare Deus haec ita ordinaverit, videlicet ut magis possit utraque conspici, videlicet ira & misericordia, sic accommodo Pauli responsionem. Quare litigas cum Deo? id est, cum vides hoc mirabile consilium Dei, quo paucos eligit & multos reiicit, obedias Deo, & timeas eius iudicium, ne offendaris exemplo multitudinis, sed scito Deum declarare misericordiam in nobis servandis, & iram in puniendis illis, qui non obtemperant. Haec est minimè intricata enarratio. Neque enim sentiendum est, non esse causam indurationis seu reprobationis in ipsis impiis, neque id dicit Paulus, & similitudo deIudo & figulo non hoc vult, nihil agere impios, sed eatenus convenit, quod exuna massageneris humani, Deus alios suo iudicio salvat, alios damnat. Causae in similitudine non omnino accommodari possunt. Tenenda est enim sententia, quòd Deus non sit causa peccati. Retinendum & hoc est, quod promissio sit universalis. Sicut & postea ipse Paulus addit rationem, quare pereat Itrahel, quia nolit accipere Evangelium sectando, iusticiam non assequitur, quia non ex fide &c.

Hic expresse ponit causam reprobationis, scilicet quia repugnent Evangelio.

Non solum ex Iudaeis.

Postquàm constituit thesin, quòd populus Dei sit Ecclesia electorum, iam venit ad hypothesin, electos esse ex Iudaeis & gentibus, idque probat testimoniis scripturae, ut ostendet Evangelium pertinere ad gentes. Ac primum citat locum ex Osea. Est autem satis perspicuum testimonium. Illud obiter admonendus est lector, quoties de vocatione gentium dicitur, sciendum est commendari gratiam, quod non propter Legem, sed gratis propter Christum placeamus &c. Alterum testimonium est Esaiae, quod vaticinatur de defectione populi. Primum ait, Etiamsi fuerit ingens multitudo populi, tamen pauci tantum salvabuntur. Hoc vult phrasis, cum ait Reliquiae, nam reliquiae significat paucos, qui reliqui sunt reliquis absumptis. Deinde sequitur repetitio eiusdem sent7emacr;tiae: Consūo abbreviata exundabit iusticiam. Consūonem enim & abbrevitionem faciet dominus. Consummatio significat finem, seu cladem populi. q. d.

Ventura est magna clades populi, seu interitus, & tamen tunc exundabit iustitia, id est, tunc revelabitur & donabitur promissa iusticia & beneficium, cum circa finem populi magna multitudo peritura est, & aliqui erunt salvi, qui credent Evangelio, & accipient illam promissam iusticiam. Consummatio abbreviata, id est, certo praefinita seu constituta. Paulus allegat versionem Graecam, quae minus perspicua est, sed tantum eandem sententiam continet, si verbum intelligas pro re, ut loquuntur Hebraei. Deus faciet verbum abbreviatum, id est, rem abbreviatam, seu abbreviationem, seu finem. Et in hac consummatione exundabit iusticiam. Alii varias interpretationes confinxerunt. Interpretantur verbum abbreviatum de Evangelio, quia Lex sit longa doctrina, nec tamen iustificans. Haec interpretatio est intempestiva. Alius quispiam est interpretatus, Perfecta sententia exundabit iusticiam, id est, sapiens iudex feret iustam sententiam. Hic prorsus extra viam currit. Nos unam & simplicem sententiam convenientem perpetuae narrationi in textu retineamus, videlicet quod populus periturus sit, sed paulo ante venturum esse Christum, &

aliquos ex populo consecuturos esse illas amplissimas promissiones, factas patribus, reiecta reliqua multitudine. Est & emphasis observanda particulae exundabit, quae significat amplitudinem gratiae.

## 9:14
What then shall we say:

Here he expressly posits the cause of reprobation, namely because they are unwilling to believe the Gospel. Therefore I said above that the similitude of the potter is not to be so accepted, as if there were not in the human will itself a cause of reprobation. For here Paul expressly posits the cause, and adds the reason which deters the impious from believing, because the Gospel argues against human justice and worships, and proposes another justice. Here, when wise men judge it to be most absurd that praise is detracted from external justice and obedience, and likewise from worships: likewise they see that with worships changed, Republics are changed and dissipated, they become indignant, and begin to hate and persecute this kind of doctrine, as blasphemous, because it harms the glory of God by abolished worships, with the bridle of licentiousness loosened: likewise, as seditious, because it dissipates Republics. This has always been the principal cause of persecution, and it most greatly inflames the Jews who had the Law given by God, and worships ordained by God. Thus now our adversaries pursue us furiously and cruelly, because we say that the Law cannot be satisfied, that men are not justified before God on account of good works, but by faith on account of Christ. Then they rage even more when worships are criticized, such as masses, monasticism, and the like. For with these ordinances changed, it seems that the Republic is undermined, shaken, and dissipated; likewise, that the glory of God is harmed. From this, hatreds are kindled, and huge struggles arise, for those scandals greatly move human reason, by which both the glory of God seems to be harmed and common society to be dissipated. And it is difficult for the saints to confirm themselves in such a way that those scandals do not shake their faith. Therefore Paul says later, I confess that the Jews have a zeal, and in Corinthians he says that the Jews do not believe the Gospel because they look at the veiled Law, that is, because they feel that the righteousness of the Law is righteousness before God. Because this is disapproved by the Gospel, they are incited to persecution. Thus Christ becomes a stone of stumbling for this reason, because reason thinks it is blasphemous and seditious doctrine to disapprove of external righteousness and worships.

Everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame, etc.

He will not be confounded, that is, he will not be frustrated, but he will attain this very thing which he expects. For it is a customary phrase among the Hebrews for 'to be confounded' to mean 'to be frustrated,' as if I should say, 'A messenger sent to seek money is confounded,' that is, he is frustrated. Thus it was said above, 'hope does not confound,' that is, it is not void, it is not frustrated. Furthermore, in these sentences concerning faith, it is always necessary to understand the particle 'freely,' lest we think thus: 'If I shall be sufficiently worthy, then he will be to be believed,' for this is not to trust in Christ, but to trust in one's own worthiness. Therefore he says: 'He who believes in him,' that is, he who trusts that on account of Christ himself, not on account of our worthiness, God is propitious to us, he will be saved.

Latin:

Quid igitur dicemus:

Hic expresse ponit causam reprobationis, quia scilicet nolint credere Evagelio. Ideo supra dixi, similitudinem doluto non ita accipiendam esse, quasi non sit in ipsa voluntate humana causa reprobationis. Hic enim Paulus expresse ponit causam, & addit rationem, quae impios remoratur ne credant, quia Evangelium arguit humanam iustitiam & cultus, & proponit aliam iustitiam. Hic cum homines sapientes iudicent, absurdissimum esse, detrahi laudem iustitiae externae obedientiae, item cultibus: Item videant mutatis cultibus mutari ac dissipari Respublicas, indignantur, & incipiunt hoc doctrinae genus odisse ac persequi, tanquam blasphemum, quod laedat gloriam Dei abolitis cultibus, laxato freno vulgilicentiae: Item, tanquàm seditiosum, quòd dissipet Respub. Haec semper fuit principalis causa persecutionis, ac Iudaeos maximè accendit, qui habebant Legem divinitus datam, & cultus divinitus ordinatos. Ita nunc furenter & crudeliter nos insectantur adversarii, quod dicimus Legi non posse satisfieri, non iustificari homines coram Deo propter bona opera, sed fide propter Christum. Deinde magis etiam fremunt, quando cultus reprehenduntur, ut missae, monachatus & similia. Nam his ordinationibus mutatis, videtur labefactari, concuti, et dissipari Respub. item, laedi gloria Dei. Inde incenduntur odia, & existunt ingentia certamina, valde enim movent rationem humanam scandala illa, quibus & laedi gloria Dei videtur, & dissipari communis societas. Ac sanctis difficile est ita se confirmare, ne illa scandala excutiant eis fidem. Ideo Paulus postea inquit, Fateor Iudaeos habere Zelum, & in Corinth. ait, ideo Iudaeos non credere Evangelio, quia aspiciant Legem velatam, hoc est, quia sentiant iusticiam Legis esse iusticiam coram Deo. Hoc quia improbatur ab Evangelio incitantur ad persecutionem. Ita Christus fit lapis offensionis propterea, quia ratio putat esse blasphemam, & seditiosam doctrinam, improbare externam iusticiam & cultus.

Omnis qui credit in eum, non pudefiet &c.

Non confundetur, id est, non frustrabitur, sed hoc ipsum assequetur quod expectat. Est enim usitata phrasis Hebr aeis confundi pro frustrari, ut si dicam, Nuncius missus ad petendam pecuniam confunditur, id est, frustratur. Ita supra dictum est, spes non confundit, id est, non est irrita, non frustratur. Caeterum in his sententiis de fide, semper intelligi oportet particulam gratis, ne sic cogitemus: Si fuero satis dignus, tum erit credendus, hoc est enim non confidere Christo, sed confidere propriae dignitati. Ideo dicit: Qui credit in ipsum, id est, qui confidit quod propter ipsum Christum, non propter nostram dignitatem Deus sit nobis propitius, is erit salvus.

## 10:1 Argument
CHAPTER X.

That they have a zeal for God.

Concerning the cause of the persecution of the Gospel, Therefore, he says, they wage war with the Gospel, because they do not want the righteousness of the Law, nor do they understand that there is a need for another righteousness before God, wherefore they tenaciously retain the righteousness of the Law and of worship. Moreover, he adds a complaint about the destruction of the nation, as above, and attributes to all a zeal, that is, a pursuit of piety, but he joins it with error, and the error is in the chief articles of faith, namely, what is the office and kingdom of Christ, whence is the remission of sins, what is true righteousness, what is sin. Furthermore, a grave threat is added to those defending impious opinions about the righteousness of the Law, when he says: Their own righteousness does not suffice for them. Therefore, he clearly condemns all who oppose the righteousness of faith.

Latin:

CAPUT X.

Quòd studium Dei habent.

De causa persecutionis Evangelii, Ideo, inquit, belligerantur cum Evangelio, quia nolunt iusticiam Legis, nec intelligunt esse opus alia iusticia coram Deo, quare mordicus retinent iusticiam Legis & cultus.
