Addit autem quaerelam de gentis interitu, ut supra, et tribuit omnibus Zelum, id est, studium pietatis, sed cum errore coniungit, & error est in articu is fidei praecipuus, scilicet quod sit Christi officium & regnum, unde sit remissio peccatorum, quae sit vera iusticia, quid sit peccatum. Est autem gravis comminatio addita defendentibus opiniones impias de iusticia Legis, cum inquit: Non sufficit illis iusticia sua. Damnat igitur clare omnes adversantes iusticiae fidei.

## 10:4
For Christ is the perfection of the Law, etc.

Here he institutes a comparison of the righteousness of the Law and the righteousness of the Gospel, and defines both, and proposes a sentiment opposed to the Jewish imaginations about the Law, as if he were to say: The Jews seek righteousness from the Law, and do not understand that Christ is the end of the Law, that is, the one promised by the Law, so that he himself might take away sin and death, which the Law only reveals. Therefore, the sentiment is: Christ is the end of the Law, that is, the fulfillment or consummation, grants that which the Law requires, that is, he who believes in Christ has that which the Law demands, that is, he is righteous by imputation, and is freed from death. But this liberation is only begun in this life, even if meanwhile the believer is truly righteous by imputation.

For Moses writes etc.

In this antithesis some have imagined that the state of the comparison is in these words: He shall live in them, that is, that double works are conferred in relation to rewards: That the works of reason have temporal rewards: But good works born from the Holy Spirit have eternal rewards. This interpretation is foreign to the disputation of Paul, for there is no comparison of rewards being made, nor is it being disputed concerning final causes, but formal ones: what the righteousness of the Law is in reality, and on the contrary what the righteousness of the Gospel is. Therefore the state of the comparison is in these two words, to do and to believe: The righteousness of the Law is to do the Law, that is, to provide perfect obedience according to the Law. Thus he says that righteousness is described by Moses, when he says: doing them, as if he were to say, the righteousness of the Law is this very obedience, by which those things which the Law commands are truly and integrally done, such as, to burn with the love of God with one's whole heart, to glorify God, to love the neighbor, without concupiscence, without any vicious affection, without sin. This is the justice which the Law requires, which human nature so far from performing, that it does not understand what that love of God is. On the contrary, the justice of faith is not to be just on account of the fulfillment of the Law, or our virtues, but it is to believe that on account of Christ we are just, that is, accepted by God. Hence can be seen the distinction of faith and love, and why it must be said, by faith we are just: Item, how this ought to be understood. For it is not to be imagined, by faith we are just, that is, on account of new qualities, or our virtues we are just, but correlatively, that is, on account of Christ we are just, who nevertheless cannot be apprehended otherwise than by faith. But to say by love we are just, is the same as to say, that on account of our virtues, or the fulfillment of the Law we are just. But it is evident that the Law is not satisfied. Therefore it is necessary that this saying be purely retained, by faith we are reputed just, so that it may be understood, that not on account of our virtues, but on account of the mediator Christ, through mercy we are freely by imputation just, that is, accepted. These things which Paul has so wonderfully amplified by this definition of his with certain cited. with words from Deuteronomy.

Latin:

Nam perfectio Legis Chri-stus &c.

Hic instituit collationem iusticiae Legis & iusticiae Evangelii, & utramque definit, ac proponit sententiam oppositam Iudaicis imaginationibus de Lege, quasi dicat: Iudaei quaerunt iusticiam ex Lege, nec intelligunt Christum esse finem Legis, hoc est, promissum Lege, ut ipse tolleret peccatum & mortem, quae Lex tantum revelat. Est ergo sententia: Christus est finis Legis, id est, impletio seu consummatio, donat id quod Lex requirit, hoc est, qui credit in Christum, habet id quod Lex postulat, id est, est iustus imputatione, & liberatur à morte. Sed haec liberatio in hac vita tantum inchoatur, &si interea credens vere est iustus imputatione.

Moses enim scribit &c.

In hac antithesi quidam imaginati sunt, statum collocationis esse in his verbis: Vivet in eis, hoc est, penes praemia conferri duplicia opera: Opera rationis habere praemia temporalia: Sed bona opera orta à spiritu sancto habere praemia aeterna. Haec interpraetatio aliena est à disputatione Pauli, non enim fit collatio praemiorum, neque de causis finalibus, sed formali disputatur: quid re ipsa sit iusticia Legis, & è contra quid sit iusticia Evangelii. Est igitur status collationis in his duobus verbis, facere & credere: Iusticia Legis est facere Legem, hoc est praestare perfectam obedientiam iuxta Legem. Sic ait describi à Moise iusticiam, cum inquit: faciens ea, quasi dicat, iusticia Legis est haec ipsa obedientia, qua vere & integre fiunt ea, quae Lex praecipit, ut, toto pectore ardere dilectione Dei, glorificare Deum, diligere proximum, sine concupiscentia, sine ullo vitioso affectu, sine peccato esse. Haec est iusticia, quam Lex requirit, quam adeo non praestat humana natura, ut non intelligat quid sit illa dilectio Dei. Econtra iusticia fidei, non est propter impletionem Legis, aut nostras virtutes esse iustum, sed est credere, quod propter Christum simus iusti, id est accepti Deo. Hinc potest conspici discrimen fidei & dilectionis, & quare dicendum sit, fide sumus iusti: Item, quomodo hoc intelligi debeat. Non est enim imaginandum, fide sumus iusti, hoc est propter novas qualitates, aut nostras virtutes sumus iusti, sed correlativè, id est, propter Christum sumus iusti, qui tamen non aliter apprehendi potest, quam fide. Dicere autem dilectione iusti sumus, est idem dicere, quod propter nostras virtutes, seu impletionem Legis sumus iusti. Constat autem Legi non satis fieri. Ideo necesse est hoc dictum pure retineri, fide reputamur iusti, ut intelligatur, quod non propter nostras virtutes, sed propter mediatorem Christum, per misericordiam gratis sumus imputatione iusti, id est, accepti. Hae cut Paulus hac sua definitione quàm mirifice amplificavit citatis quibusdam verbis ex Deuteronomio.

## 10:6
Do not say in your heart.

Paul borrows the description of faith from the saying of Moses, nor does he twist it to a different or unsuitable meaning. For Moses also truly describes and requires faith in that same place. But it is a general saying about the word and about faith, which Paul applies to this word concerning Christ, and to faith in Christ. Let us therefore first examine the saying of Moses, who depicts the impiety of the human heart with illustrious figures, which, even if it thinks that God exists, nevertheless doubts whether God cares for us, denies that the will of God toward us can be known, denies that we are heard, or saved. That these doubts cling to the souls of men is sufficiently apparent. Therefore the Law of God refutes them, and requires faith. Do not say in your heart: Who shall ascend into heaven, that is, do not be an Epicurean, do not think that there is no God, or that it is unknown whether God exists, or whether He cares for human affairs, do not think that God is so hidden that His will does not exist in some word, do not think that His will is unknown because He Himself is not discerned by bodily eyes, do not think that He does not hear, does not have mercy, does not require this worship, which He has delivered in His word, etc. How therefore can God be found and apprehended? The word is near, he says, etc., that is, I lead you here to the word, hear this, thus you may believe God is apprehended, and His will is perceived, when you hear the word, and believe this to be His will, that He wills to be worshipped thus, that He wills to hear as He has promised. That this is the meaning of the saying in Moses is sufficiently clear, nor is there any doubt but that this Moses is preaching about faith, and requires faith, which believes not only that God exists, but also that God wills to be acknowledged in His word, and thus to be invoked, wills to hear and to show mercy according to the promise, and requires these acts of worship. These things said generally, even if they contain the doctrine of faith, are nevertheless still obscure, and are voices of the Law: Therefore Paul proposes another word, and names the mediator, so that he may propose the gratuitous mercy promised on account of Christ. When we acknowledge this, faith becomes certain, namely that freely on account of Christ, not on account of the Law, we are heard, we are saved, etc.

He therefore adapts this passage: Do not say in your heart, who shall ascend into heaven, for this is to bring Christ down, that is, first do not be an Epicurean, then do not doubt but that this is the will of God, that Christ is the mediator, that God wills to save us on account of Christ. If you do not believe Christ to be the mediator, that he may save us, you drag him down from heaven, you deny that he reigns, and you accuse God of a lie, as if his promise were void: Do not say who shall ascend into the Abyss, do not think in the manner of Epicurus, that after death there remains no other life, do not think that men cannot be freed from death and from sin: If you shall doubt, you will deny that Christ has risen, you will imagine that Christ still lies extinguished, that he is still to be resurrected, and that he is not the victor of death and sin. And the sum of the sentence is: Do not doubt that Christ is the mediator and ruler: Do not doubt that on account of him God truly has mercy on us, forgives sins, hears, and saves us. Thus Paul adds to the saying of Moses the Gospel concerning the mediator, and includes the exclusive, so that faith may be certain. Let us therefore oppose to our weakness and doubt this most weighty sermon of Paul, and in it let us contemplate how great an impiety it is to doubt whether God wills to forgive sins, whether he wills to hear, to help, to save, and finally to provide those things which he promised through Christ. In every invocation let us think on these words: Do not say, who has ascended into heaven. For that would be to pull Christ down, but you should maintain that Christ truly sits at the right hand of the Father, and is an intercessor, so that we may be heard. In this use we learn to understand the force and meaning of this saying. For those who do not call upon him, deny that Christ sits at the right hand of the Father, and is an intercessor.

Latin:

Ne dixeris in corde tuo.

Paulus mutuatur descriptionem fidei ex dicto Mosi, nec detorquet illud ad diversam aut non convenientem sententiam. Nam & Moises ibidem vere describit, & requirit fidem. Sed generale dictum est de verbo & de fide, quod Paulus applicat ad hoc verbum de Christo, & ad fidem in Christum. Primum igitur dictum Moisi inspiciamus, qui illustribus figuris impietatem humani cordis depingit, quod etiamsi cogitat esse Deum, tamen dubitat an Deus curet nos, negat voluntatem Dei erga nos cognosci posse, negat exaudiri nos, aut salvari. Has dubitationes haerere in hominum animis satis apparet. Ideo Lex Dei eas arguit, & requirit fidem. Ne dixeris in corde tuo: Quis ascendit in caelum, id est, ne sis Epicureus, ne cogites nihil esse Deum, aut nesciri an sit Deus, an curet humana, ne cogites Deum ita latere, ut non extet eius voluntas in aliquo verbo, ne cogites eius voluntatem ignotam esse, quia ipse non cernitur oculis corporalibus, ne cogites eum non exaudire, non misereri, non requirere hunc cultum, quem in verbo suo tradidit &c. Quomodo igitur inveniri & apprehendi Deus potest? Prope est inquit verbum &c. id est, huc te deduco ad verbum, hoc audi, sic credas apprehendi Deum, & voluntatem eius conspici, cum verbum audis, & credis hanc esse voluntatem eius, velle eum sic coli, velle exaudire sicut promisit. Hanc esse sententiam dicti in Moise satis liquet, nec dubium est, quin de fide concionetur hic Moises, & requirat fidem, quae credat non solum esse Deum, sed etiam Deum velle agnosci in verbo suo, & sic invocari, velle exaudire & misereri iuxta promissionem, requirere hos cultus. Haec generaliter dicta, & si continent doctrinam de fide, tamen sunt adhuc obscura, & sunt voces Legis: Ideo Paulus proponit aliud verbum, & nominat mediatorem, ut proponat gratuitam misericordiam propter Christum promissam. Hanc cum agnoscimus, fides fit certa, scilicet quod gratis propter Cheistum, non propter Legem, exaudiamur, salvemur &c.

Accommodat igitur hocloco: Ne dicas in corde tuo, quis ascendet in caelum, hoc est enim Christum deducere, id est, primum ne sis Epicureus, deinde ne dubites, quin haec sit voluntas Dei, ut Christus sit mediator, quod velit nos Deus salvare propter Christum. Si non credis Christum esse mediatorem, ut salvet nos, detrahis eum de caelo, negas eum regnare, & arguis Deum mendacii, quasi promissio eius sit irrita: Ne dicas quis ascendet in Abyssum, ne cogites Epicuri more, post mortem non restare aliam vitam, ne cogites homines non posse liberari à morte & à peccato: Si dubitabis, negabis Christum resurrexisse, finges Christum adhuc iacere exctintum, adhuc resuscitandum esse, nec esse victorem mortis & peccati. Estque summa sententiae: Ne dubita, quin Christus sit mediator & regent: Ne dubita, quin propter ipsum vere misereatur nostri Deus remittat peccata, exaudiat et salvet nos. Ita addit Paulus dicto Moisi Evangelium de mediatore, & complectitur exclusivam, ut fides sit certa. Opponamus igitur infirmitati, & dubitationi nostrae hanc gravissimam Pauli concionem, & in ea contemplemur, quanta sit impietas dubitare an Deus velit remitterepeccata, an velit exaudire, iuvare, salvare, deniquè praestare illa quae per Christum promisit. In omni invocatione cogitemus haec verba: Ne dixeris, quis ascendit in caelum. Id enim fuerit detrahere Christum, sed statuas Christum verè ad dextram patris sedere, esse intercessorem, ut exaudiamur. In hoc usu discimus intelligere huius dicti vim & sententiam. Nam qui non invocant, negant Christum sedere ad dextram patris, & esse intercessorem.

## 10:8
The word is near you in your mouth etc.

Before he reproved doubt, now he adds an affirmative description of faith: The word is near in your mouth. And thus he defines the righteousness of faith, that it is not to doubt, but to believe this word concerning Christ, and to maintain that Jesus is Lord, namely he through whom the blessing is promised, who delivers from death and sin. There is therefore a clear antithesis, the righteousness of the Law is to do the Law, that is, it is our obedience according to the Law, whether complete or political. But the righteousness of faith is to believe that on account of Christ we are accepted, not on account of our dignity, qualities, or virtues: He therefore opposes the former definition, in which he says to do: Now in the other definition the word, in the mouth and heart, namely because by the word we apprehend Christ, on account of whom we are righteous and accepted, not on account of our own dignity. That also is worthy of observation here concerning the necessity of the ministry, and of the vocal word, and concerning the manner in which God acts with us. It is not to be imagined that God sends the Holy Spirit without His word. But Paul leads us to the ministry, and to the vocal word; God is not found elsewhere outside of His word, or without His word; in this He wills to be acknowledged. By this instrument He wills to be effective. Therefore, in every temptation let us seek God through the word and in the word let us resist, and let us establish that this is certainly the will of God, which is proposed in His word. Therefore, here concerning such a great matter, concerning salvation, he says: The word is near in your mouth: Item, The word of faith which we preach, and afterwards he repeats this manner, faith is from hearing, hearing is through the word of God. But that which he says, If you shall have confessed the Lord Jesus, it is to be resolved thus: If you shall have confessed Jesus to be Lord, that is, not idle, but that Lord, concerning whom the promises were made, who frees the human race from sin and from death, who was made a victim for us, who sits at the right hand of the Father, that He may save. For what this honor of the Lord is, and what benefits it embraces, is from all the promises it ought to be gathered, just as in the psalm: The Lord said to my Lord, and others.

Latin:

Prope te verbum est in ore tuo &c.

Antea reprehendit dubitationem, nunc addit affirmativam descriptionem fidei: Verbum est prope in ore tuo. Et sic definit iusticiam fidei, quod sit non dubitare, sed credere huic verbo de Christo, & statuere quod Iesus sit dominus, videlicet ille per quem est promissa benedictio, qui liberat à morte & peccato. Est igitur perspicua anthithefis, iusticia Legis est facere Legem, id est, est nostra obedientia iuxta Legem, seu integra seu politica. Sed iusticia fidei est credere quod propter Christum accepti simus, non propter nostram dignitatem, qualitates, aut virtutes: Opponit igitur superiori definitioni, in qua inquit facere: Iam in altera definitione verbum, in ore & corde, videlicet quia verbo apprehendimus Christum, propter quem iusti et accepti sumus, non propter dignitatem nostram. Est & illud hic observatu dignum de necessitate ministerii, & verbi vocalis, & de modo quo agit Deus nobiscum. Non ēaginandum est, quod Deus mittat spiritum sanctum sine verbo suo. Sed Paulus deducit nos ad ministerium, & ad verbum vocale, non invenitur alibi Deus extra suum verbum, aut sine verbo suo in hoc vult agnosci. Hoc instrumento vult esse efficax. Ideo in omni tentatione quaeramus Deum per verbum & in verbo resistamus, & hanc esse certo voluntatem Dei statuamus, quae in verbo ipsius proponitur. Ideo hic de re tanta, de salvatio nedicit: Prope est verbum in ore tuo: Item, Verbum fidei quod praedicamus, & postea repetit hunc modum, fides ex auditu est, auditus per verbum Dei est. Quod autem, inquit, Si confessus fueris dominum Iesum, ita resolvendum est, Si confessus fueris Iesum esse dominum, id est, non ociosum, sed illum dominum, de quo factae sunt promissiones, qui liberat genus humanum à peccato & à morte, qui est pro nobis factus victima, qui sedet ad dextram patris, ut salvet. Nam hic honos domini qualis sit et quae beneficia complectatur, ex omnibus promissionibus colligi debet, sicut in psalmo: Dixit dominus domino meo, & aliis.

## 10:9
For with the heart it is believed etc.

It is a manifest testimony that we are justified by faith, for to the adversaries these words are plainly idle and signifying nothing, afterwards they attach many sophistical interpretations. But let us not corrupt the saying of Paul, but let us truly attribute to faith that which Paul attributes, nor is it obscure what he calls faith, namely that which the word sounds, to trust in Christ, just as he himself here interprets faith, which believes Jesus to be Lord, and above which receives the promise, and here: Everyone who believes in him, which certainly signifies who trusts in him, that is, who trusts that on account of him God is propitious to us. This is the imagination of many, even if good works do not merit the remission of sins, nevertheless afterwards to merit eternal life, just as many men have said, even if they do not merit the first grace, nevertheless afterwards to merit eternal life. To this they cite many sayings: With the mouth confession is made unto salvation: Item, I was hungry and you gave me food: Item, If I should have all faith, but if I do not have love, I am nothing. To all these sayings I respond in one way. I concede that begun obedience is necessary, but it does not merit eternal life, it is not a thing worthy of eternal life, or the price of eternal life, nor does it please except because we believe in Christ. For because obedience pleases on account of faith, it is a contradiction to imagine that works either justify or merit eternal life. For by faith we establish that the remission of sins and eternal life are given to us freely on account of Christ, and yet an effect necessarily follows faith, namely begun newness, since hearts are vivified by faith. This response has nothing of perplexity; it concedes that obedience is necessary, and it removes the opinion of merit, and it teaches how it pleases, so that its honor may be attributed to Christ, and faith may remain certain. For it would become uncertain if it were to be thought thus, that we then please God when we have enough merits. It is useful for this to be known in general concerning all sayings of this kind. Now let us return to the text. It is certain that Paul does not approve of confession unless faith is present: Therefore he does not attribute to confession that it is the price or merit of eternal life. For it would be a contradiction, as has been said, and yet He requires confession, because obedience, as has been said, is necessary, and Paul wished to show that he is speaking, not of the hypocrisy of faith, that is, of an idle thought, but of the true movement of the heart, which apprehends the mercy promised on account of Christ, and therefore shines in confession, patience, and good examples of every kind. Furthermore, he distinguishes justice and salvation on account of perseverance. For although whoever is just is an heir of eternal life, yet it can happen that a just person may again lose justice. Therefore he says: If you will confess, namely on account of faith, as if he were to say: If faith shall have been firm and persevering. For he does not approve of confession except on account of faith.

For whoever shall have called upon.

First, it is to be observed that he inculcates the universal particle, so that we may remember that the promises are universal. Second, it is to be considered what this new sentence means, and whether it agrees with the Gospel, everyone who shall have called upon etc. I answer, This is a new prophecy, distinguishing the Gospel from the Law, because the Law also teaches invocation, with the condition of perfect obedience. But this prophecy promises salvation to those calling upon Him to whom the Law could not previously bring aid, and who are now such that they do not provide the obedience which the Law requires. To such as these He now promises salvation, who call upon the name of the Lord, that is, who call upon that Lord who reveals Himself in that word which He gave to the fathers, which He will exhibit in the coming of the Son. Wherefore it is necessary here to understand the invocation with the particle freely, for it requires that we believe we are heard and saved freely on account of that promised Lord. For this promise must be set against the Law. As if to say: because the Law could not bring aid, because you are under sin and death, salvation is promised in another way. God will give a teacher, He will pour out of His Spirit, and you by the invocation of the Lord will be saved from those very evils, from sin and from death, from which the Law did not deliver. This is the simple and true meaning of this proposition. Therefore it fits aptly to the Gospel, and adds some light to the definition of the righteousness of faith, which he handed down above: The righteousness of the law is to do the Law. But the righteousness of faith is to call upon the Lord, and to establish that on account of the Son of God we are delivered from sin and from death, and from the wrath of God, from which the Law could not deliver. The promise will therefore grow sweet, when the particle freely is understood in it, and thus is to be exercised. it is invocation, so that our unworthiness may not deter us, but let us know that it is the command of God that we should invoke, and likewise that it is a command that we should believe that we are heard on account of Christ, not on account of our own worthiness. Wherefore let us obey God, and let us perform this worship, and when we invoke, let us remember that we bring unworthiness and sins, and let us ask on account of Christ that we may be delivered and heard, which when we do, we at the same time perform repentance. Now it is easy to reconcile the dissimilar opinions: God does not hear sinners, that is to say, those who invoke without repentance and without faith.

Latin:

Corde enim creditur &c.

Manifestum testimonium est, quod fide iustificemur, nam adversariis haec verba plane sunt ociosa & nihil significantia, postea affingunt multas sophisticas interpretationes. Nos vero non corrumpamus dictum Pauli, sed vere tribuamus fidei, id quod tribuit Paulus, nec obscurum est quid fidem vocet, scilicet id quod vocabulum sonat confidere in Christum, sicut ipse hic interpretatur fidem, quae credit Iesum esse dominum, & supra quae accipit promissionem, & hic: Omnis qui credit in eum, quod certè significat qui confidit in eum, id est, qui confidit quod propter ipsum Deus sit nobis propitius. Multorum haec imaginatio est, etiamsi bona opera non merentur remissionem peccatorum, tamen postea mereri vitam aeternam, sicut multi dixerunt homines, etiamsi non mereantur primam gratiam, tamen deinde merei vitam aeternam. Ad hoc citant multa dicta: Ore fit confessio ad salutem: Item, Esurivi & dedistis mihi cibum: Item, Si habeam omnem fidem, dilectionem autem non habeam, nihil sum. Ad haec dicta omnia uno modo respondeo. Concedo necessariam esse inchoatam obedientiam, sed non meretur vitam aeternam, non est res digna vita aeterna, seu praecium vitae aeternae, nec placet nisi quia credimus in Christum. Quia enim placet obedientia propter fidem, contradictio est imaginari, quòd opera vel iustificent, vel mereantur vitam aecernam. Fide enim statuimus nobis propter Christum gratis donari remissionem peccatorum, & vitam aeternam, & tamen fidem necessario sequitur effectus, scilicet inchoata novitas, cum fide corda vivificentur. Haec responsio nihil habet perplexitatis, concedit necessariam esse obedientiam, & detrahit opinionem meriti, & docet quomodo placeat, ut Christo tribuatur suus honos, & fides certa maneat. Fieret enim incertum, si sic sentiendum esset, tunc nos placere Deo, cum satis meritorum habemus. Haec in genere de omnibus huiusmodi dictis sciri prodest. Nunc ad textum redeamus. Certum est Paulum non probare confessionem, nisi adsit fides: Ergo non tribuit confessioni, quod sit precium aut meritum vitae aeternae. Esset enim contradictio, ur dictum est, & tamen requirit confessionem, quia obedientia, ut dictum est, est necessaria, & ostendere voluit Paulus se loqui, non de hipocrisi fidei, id est, de ociosa cogitatione, sed de vero motu cordis, qui apprehendit misericordiam promissam propter Christum, & propterea lucet in confessione, patientia, & bonis exemplis omnis generis. Praeterea discernit iusticiam & salutem propter perseverantiam. Etsi enim quisquis est iustus, est haeres vitae aeternae, tamen fieri potest, ut iustus iterum amittat iusticiam. Ideo inquit: Si confiteberis, videlicet propter fidem, quasi dicat: Si fides fuerit firma, & perseverans. Non enim probat confessionem nisi propter fidem.

Quisquis enim invocaverit.

Primum observandum est, quod inculcat particulam universalem, ut meminerimus promissiones esse universales. Secundo considerandum est, quid sibi velit haec nova sententia, & an ad Evangelium conveniat omnis qui invocaverit &c. Respondeo, Haec est nova prophetia, discernens Evangelium à Lege, quia Lex etiam docet invocationem, cum conditione perfectae obedientiae. Sed haec prophetia promittit salutem invocantibus, scilicet quibus antea Lex non poterat opitulari, & qui sunt iam tales, ut non praestent obedientiam, quam Lex requirit. Talibus iam promittit salutem, qui invocent nomen domini, id est, qui invocent illum dominum, qui se revelat in illo verbo, quod dedit patribus, quod exhibebit in adventu filii. Quare hic necesse est intelligi invocationem cum particula gratis, requirit enim, ut credamus gratis propter illum promissum dominum nos exaudiri & salvari. Nam haec promissio opponenda est Legi. q. d. quia Lex non potuit opitulari, quia estis sub peccato & morte, alio modo promittitur salvatio. Deus dabit doctorem, effundet de spiritu suo, & vos invocatione domini salvi eritis ab illis ipsis malis, à peccato & à morte, à quibus non liberabat lex. Haec est simplex & vera sententia huius propositionis. Ideo aptè quadrat ad Evangelium, & addit aliquid lucis definitioni iusticiae fidei, quam supra tradidit: Iusticia legis est facere Legem. Sed iusticia fidei est invocare dominum, & statuere, quod propter filium Dei liberemur à peccato & à morte, & ab ira Dei, à quibus Lex non poterat liberare. Dulcescet igitur promissio, cum particula gratis in ea intelligitur, et sic exercenda est invocatio, ne deterreat nos indignitas nostra, sed sciamus mandatum Dei esse, ut invocemus, item mandatum esse, ut credamus nos exaudiri propter Christum, non propter dignitatem nostram. Quare obediamus Deo, & hunc cultum praestemus, cumque invocamus, meminerimus nos afferre indignitatem & peccata, & petamus propter Christum, ut liberemur & exaudiamur, quod cum facimus, simul agimus paenitentiam. Iam facile est dissimiles sententias conciliare: Peccatores Deus non exaudit, scilicet, qui sine paenitentia & sine fide invocant.

## 10:14
How then shall they call on him? in whom they have not believed.

Paul adds the manner by which the benefits of the Gospel come to us, namely through the ministry of the word of God. And this is a principal passage concerning the necessity and dignity of the ministry to be most diligently observed, so that we may know how God is efficacious in us, and that we may not seek other illuminations outside the word, nor admit imaginations and opinions about God, without the certain word of God. This precept concerning the vocal word extends most widely, for it is It is difficult for man to resist in the word of God, and to determine with certainty that this is the will of God which He proposes in the word; therefore, he easily slips into other imaginations, just as Eve, thinking lightly of the word, adds an imagination: perhaps God did not feel so harshly. Thus it happens in many articles; the word says clearly: We are righteous by faith on account of Christ. Holding this word more languidly, and following their own imagination, evil teachers thought it more convenient to say that men are righteous on account of their own virtues and merits. Then they added that one must doubt, and they completely overwhelmed the true doctrine of faith, just as even now the Anabaptists despise the doctrine of faith, and shout that men are righteous by the magnitude of their afflictions, and by certain illuminations of their own, and thus they cast away the word and the doctrine of faith. Such were the ravings of the Manichaeans and the Enthusiasts of old. Nor is such an error of one time only, for men easily slip into such imaginations when they think lightly of the word of God. These Enthusiasts are to be shunned and execrated, and it must be known that God does not wish His will concerning sin and grace to be acknowledged and apprehended in any other way than in the word, and

that the Holy Spirit is effective through the word. Let us hold this rule, and because of this great cause let us treat the public ministry of the word with every honor, and defend it. And let us always have these sentences in sight: Faith is from hearing, hearing through the word of God. Likewise, How shall they hear without a preacher? Likewise, How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the Gospel. Secondly, this passage teaches that faith is required in invocation, that is, this very confidence by which we believe that our sins are forgiven us, and that we are heard on account of Christ, just as Christ says: Whatever you ask the Father in my name, that is, not bringing your own dignity, but believing that you are received and heard on account of Christ. So also here he teaches: How shall they call upon him in whom they have not believed? that is, if they do not believe that God is favorable to them, and hears and receives their prayers, they cannot call upon him. It is certain, therefore, that faith is required in invocation. And this makes a distinction between the invocation of the pious, and that which is ethnic or hypocritical. The heathens also invoke, but with this doubt. They do not believe that God is appeased toward them, and that their prayers are regarded, or heard. Thus also invoke all who do not understand the doctrine of the Gospel concerning justification and faith. Such, however, is the invocation that is mutilated and condemned. From this it can be understood how great the darkness is of those who boast that they are teachers of good works, and yet turn away from the doctrine concerning faith. For they abolish the chief and proper works of the pious, namely invocation: Therefore, not only those ceremonies and public prayers of the enemies of the Gospel, but all their private prayers are also condemned, and are similar to the invocations of the Heathens, such as exist everywhere in poems. This must be diligently considered, so that we may learn what kind of invocation or prayer ought to be. Likewise, what the difference is between the prayer of the pious and the impious. Likewise, what kind of faith the pious ought to bring to invocation: For wherever the doctrine concerning this faith, of which we speak here, is ignored, there it is impossible for true invocation to exist. For doubt and incredulity are confirmed, that God does not hear, does not care, nay, has cast off the one invoking. But let us Christians learn that this incredulity is a sin, and let us resist this sin, and let us raise ourselves up with the true doctrine concerning faith, let us know that it must be brought to invocation, namely that we believe God is truly propitious to us, and receives our prayers on account of the high priest Christ. Thirdly, this passage teaches that God is not pleased by worship instituted without the word of God, because without the word of God faith cannot exist. Therefore it is said here: How shall they believe if they have not heard. This passage therefore contains manifold doctrine, namely that the benefits of Christ are obtained through the ministry of the word. Also how great is the necessity and dignity of the ministry. Also what is true invocation, what worship pleases God. He adds moreover a most sweet sentence from Isaiah, where he describes the kingdom of Christ, and admonishes that the kingdom is to be administered through the word, and indeed by the preaching of the new word, namely the Gospel, in which peace will be announced, that is, salvation or deliverance divinely bestowed. And it is an antithesis opposed to the Law, and to sin, and to human miseries. As if to say: Then sin will be taken away, and other evils will be taken away, which the Law could not take away, and truly consolation will be brought, and the gift of righteousness and eternal life.

Latin:

Quomodo igitur invocabunt eum? in quem non crediderunt.

Addit Paulus modum, quo beneficia Evangelii nobis contingant, scilicet per ministerium verbi Dei. Estque hic locus praecipuus de necessitate & dignitate ministerii diligentissimè observandus, ut sciamus, quomodo Deus sit efficax in nobis, nec quaeramus alias illuminationes extra verbum, nec admittamus imaginationes & opiniones de Deo, sine certo verbo Dei. Latissime patet hoc praeceptum de verbo vocali, est enim difficile homini resistere in verbo Dei, & statuere certo, hanc esse voluntatem Dei, quam in verbo proponit, ideo facile delabitur in alias imaginationes, sicut Eva leviter sentiens de verbo addit imaginationem, fortasse non tam duriter sensit Deus. Sic in multis articulis accidit, verbum dicit clare: Fide sumus iusti propter Christum. Hoc verbum mali doctores tenentes languidius, & sequentes suam imaginationem, cogitarunt commodius dici homines esse iustos, propter suas virtutes & merita. Deinde addiderunt dubitandum esse, & omnino obruerunt veram doctrinam de fide, sicut & nunc Anabaptistae contemnunt doctrinam de fide, et vociferantur homines iustos esse magnitudine afflictionum, & suis quibusdam illuminationibus, atque ita abiiciunt verbum et doctrinam de fide. Prorsus talia fuerunt olim deliramenta Manicheorum, & Enthusiastarum. Nec est unius temporis talis error, facile enim delabuntur homines in tales imaginationes, cum leviter sentiunt de verbo Dei. Hi Enthusiastae sugiendi & execrandi sunt, & sciendum, quod Deus non velit aliter agnosci, & apprehendi suam voluntatem de peccato & de gratia, nisi in verbo, &

quòd spiritus sanctus per verbum sit efficax. Hanc regulam teneamus, & propter hanc tantam causam omni honore afficiamus, & defendamus ministerium verbi publicum. Et has sententias semper habeamus in conspectu: Fides ex auditu est, Auditus per verbum Dei. Item Quomodo audient sine praedictane? Item, Quàm speciosi pedes Evangelizantium. Secundo docet hic locus, quod in invocationerequiratur fides, id est, haec ipsa fiducia, qua credimus nobis remitti peccata, & nos exaudiri propter Christum, sicut inquit Christus: Quicquid petieritis patrem in nomine meo, id est, non afferentes vestram dignitatem, sed credentes recipi vos, & exaudiri propter Christum. Ita & hic docet: Quomodo invocabunt, in quem non crediderunt? id est, si non credant Deum esse proptium ipsis, et exaudire ac recipere preces ipsorum, non possunt eum invocare. Constat igitur requiri in invocatione fidem. Et haec discrimen facit inter invocationem piorum, & ethnicam seu hypocriticam. Ethnici etiam invocant, sed cum hac dubitatione. Non credunt sibi Deum esse placatum, & preces suas respici, aut exaudiri. Sic etiam invocant omnes, qui non intelligunt doctrinam Evangelii de iustificatione & fide. Talis autem invocatio est mutilis & damnata. Hinc intelligi potest, quantae tenebrae sint illorum, qui iactitant se esse doctores bonorum operum, & tamen aversantur doctrinam de fide. Abolent enim praecipua opera & propria piorum, scilicet invocationem: Ergo non solum illae caere moniae & orationes publicae hostium Evangelii, sed omnes eorum privatae preces etiam damnatae sunt, & sunt similes Ethnicis invocationibus, quales passim extant in poematis. Hoc diligenter considerandum est, ut discamus, qualis esse debeat invocatio seu oratio. Item, quid intersit inter pii & impii orationem. Item qualem fidem afferre pios ad invocandum oporteat: Nam ubicunque ignoratur doctrina hac fide, de qua hic loquimur, ibi impossibile est existere veram invocationem. Confirmatur enim dubitatio et incredulitas, quod Deus non exaudiat, non curet, imo abiecerit invocantem. Nos autem Christiani discamus hanc incre dulitatem peccatum esse, & repugnemus huic peccato, & erigamus nos vera doctrina de fide, eam sciamus ad invocationem afferendam esse, videlicet ut credamus Deum vere nobis propitium esse, & recipere nostras preces propter pontificem Christum. Tertio docet hic locus non placere Do cultus institutos sine verbo Dei, quia sine verbo Dei non potest existere fides. Ideo hi dicitur: Quomodo credent si non audierint. Continet igitur hic locus multiplicem doctrinam, videlicet quod contingant beneficia Christi per ministerium verbi. Item quanta sit necessitas & dignitas ministerii. Item quae sit vera invocatio, qui cultus Deo placeant. Addit autem dulcissimam sententiam ex Esai, aquae describit regnum Christi, & admonet regnum iladministrandum esse per verbum, & quidem praedicatione novi verbi, scilicet Evangelii, in quo annunciabitur pax, id est, salus seu salvatio divinitus donata. Estque antithesis opposita Legi, & peccato, & miseriis humanis. q. d. Tunc tolletur peccatum, & tollentur caetera mala, quae non potuit Lex auferre, & afferetur vere consolatio, & donatio iusticiae & vitae aeternae.

## 10:15
How beautiful are the feet of those who announce peace.

That he says the feet are lovely, is a metaphor concerning messengers, and concerning the word. As if to say: The ministry or word, which will be preached in that new kingdom, will be lovely in a wonderful way, because it brings the best things, the acknowledgment of mercy of God, justice, and eternal life. But the Prophet opposes this praise of his to the judgments of the world. For there is the highest bitterness of hatred against the Gospel, and the ministers of the Gospel, just as Paul signifies that the Apostles are held as caturmatis. Wherefore the world by no means judges these feet, that is, messengers, to be salutary and lovable. Against such judgments of the world the Prophet consoles and teaches us, so that we may love the ministry even if it is despised and invisible to the world, and know it to be efficacious, and to bring salvation to those who believe. Just as Paul also says: I am not ashamed of the Gospel. Thus let us confirm ourselves against the impious judgments of the world, and let us consider what a great crime it is to exercise cruelty against the pious ministers of the Gospel.

Latin:

Quam speciosi pedes annunci-antium pacem.

Quod ait pedes esse amabiles, metaphora est de nunciis, & de verbo. q. d. Ministerium seu verbum, quod in illo novo regno praedicabitur, mirum in modum amabile erit, quia affert res optimas, agnitionem misericordiae Dei, iusticiam & vitam aeternam. Opponit autem Propheta hanc suam laudationem iudiciis mundi. Est enim summa acerbitas odii adversus Evangelium, et Evangelii ministros, sicut Paulus significat Apostolos haberi pro caturmatis. Quare mundus nequaquàm hos pedes, id est, nuncios iudicat esse salutares & amabiles. Adversus talia mundi iudicia consolatur & docet nos Propheta, ut ministerium etiamsi spretum & invisum mundo, tamen amemus, & sciamus efficax esse, & afferre salutem credentibus. Sicut & Paulus inquit: Non pudet me Evangelii. Ita confirmemus nos contra impia iudicia mundi, & consideremus quantum scaelus sit, exercere crudelitatem contra pios ministros Evangelii.

## 11:1 Argument
CHAPTER XI.

He mitigates the previous complaint about the defection, and testifies that the promise still pertains to the people, and that many will attain it, namely those who believe. And first he argues from his own example: I am an Israelite, and I have attained the promise: Therefore Israelites can attain it. The second reason is taken from the example of the times of Elijah.

Thus he always warns that the Church is small, and that the number and power of the wicked is much greater, and he adds the doctrine that the Church is not chosen because of the Law, because of the polity, but that those are chosen as the people of God who apprehend the Gospel by faith. Therefore he added that mercy is the cause of election, not the Law, not the polity, just as was said above concerning the distinction of the two peoples. The Synagogue has the title of the people of God, and it wages war with the true people, and with the true Church. Against this scandal we must be instructed and forewarned, so that we may understand that the Church is not that assembly which persecutes the Gospel, even if they have rites or a polity.

Latin:

CAPUT. XI.

Mitigat superiorem querelam de defectione, & testatur promissionem adhuc pertinere ad populum, & multos eam consecuturos esse, videlicet qui credunt. Ac primum àsuo exemplo argumentatur: Ego sum Israhelita, & adeptus sum promissionem: Ergo Israhelitae possunt eam consequi. Altera ratio sumpta est ab exemplo temporum Heliae.

Ita monet semper Ecclesiam exiguam esse, & multo maiorem numerum ac potentiam impiorum, & addit doctrinam, quod Ecclesia non sit electa propter Legem, propter politiam, sed populum Dei esse electos, qui Evangelium fide apprehendunt. Ideo a ddidit misericordiam esse causam electionis, non Legem, non politiam, sicut supra de discrimine duorum populorum dictum est. Synagoga habet titulum populi Dei, & belligeratur cum vero populo, & cum vera Ecclesia. Adversus hoc scandalum oportet nos esse instructos & praemunitos, ut intelligamus non esse Ecclesiam illum coetum, qui persequitur Evangelium, etiamsi habent cultus aut politiam.

## 11:8
The spirit of compunction, etc.

That is, a mind angered and embittered by hatred of God and of the Gospel. For there is a certain horrible bitterness of hatred in the enemies of the Gospel, such as is described in Cain, Pharaoh, and the like. First, because the devil inflames those wicked men. Second, because human reason itself is vehemently offended by the dissipation of rites and of the Republic. He imagines that the doctrine is blasphemous and seditious. For they think that glory is harmed by the change of rites, as when the Apostles abrogated the Levitical ceremonies. And now when human rites are reproved, the abuse of the mass, then the change of rites, it also changes polities, as now it certainly distracts the Church. But both beget huge hatred, namely that both the glory of God is thought to be harmed, and others grieve that authority is being undermined, the order of the Church is being dissipated, etc.

Let their table be turned, etc.

He heaps up many sentences, which describe the punishments of impiety, the contempt of the Gospel, blindness and induration accompany it, which so occupy minds that they cannot repent. Then that very blindness both accumulates errors, summons fury, scandals, and horrible bodily and eternal evils. Thus he says concerning blindness: They are blinded, etc. Concerning other punishments: let their table become a snare, a scandal, etc. For the table signifies this very thing, in which men chiefly acquiesce, which seems to bring consolation, help, recreation, rest, just as the table of Pompey was an Egyptian king, that very one to whom he fled, by whose protection he hoped he would be safe, was his destruction. Thus for the Jews the law and the present polity, and that most glorious title of the people of God was a table. They knew these things were divinely entrusted, and had been defended for so long, and they thought they could not be changed. Wherefore they condemned the doctrine which seemed to be opposed, and they hoped they would be victors, just as their fathers had triumphed before. These things were a snare, that is, they held their minds ensnared by a bad persuasion, and afterwards destroyed them etc. Thus now the title of the Church is a table for the adversaries of the Church, and it ensnares minds with a false persuasion, and it will be their destruction.

Latin:

Spiritum compunctionis &c.

Id est, animus iratus, atque acerbatus odio Dei, & Evangelii. Est enim horribilis quaedam odii acerbitas in hostibus Evangelii, qualis describitur in Cain, Pharaone, & similibus. Primum quia diabolus inflammat illos impios. Secundo, quia ipsa humana ratio vehementer offenditur, dissipatione cultuum & Reipubl. Imaginatur doctrinam esse blasphemiam & seditiosam Putant enim laedi gloriam mutatione cultuum, ut cum Apostoli abrogarent caeremonias Leviticas. Et nunc cum reprehenduntur cultus humani, abusus missae, deinde mutatio cultuum, mutat etiam politias, ut nunc certe distrahit Ecclesiam. Utrumquè autem parit igens odium, videlicet quod & gloria Dei laedi putatur, & alii dolent labefactari autoritatem, dissipari ordinem Ecclesiae &c.

Vertatur mensa illorum &c.

Coacervat multas sententias, quae describunt poenas impietatis, contemptum Evangelii, comitatur coecitas et induratio, quae ita occupant animos, ut non possint resipiscere. Deinde illa ipsa coecitas & cumulat errores, accersit furorem, scandala, & horribilia mala corporalia & aeterna. Sic de coecitate iuquit: Excoecati sunt &c. De aliis pce nis: mensa fiat in eis laqueum, scandalum &c. Significat enim mensa hoc ipsum, in quo praecipuè acquiescunt homines, quod videtur afferre consolationem, auxilium, recreationem, quietem, sicut mensa Pompei fuit rex Aegyptius, ille ipse ad quem confugit, cuius praesidio sperabat se fore tutum, fuit ei exitio. Ita Iudaeis lex & praesens politia, & ille gloriosissimus titulus populi Dei erat mensa. Has res sciebant divinitus creditas, & tamdiu defensas esse, & existimabant non posse mutari. Quare damnabant doctrinam, quae videbatur adversari, & sperabant se fore victores, sicut antea patres triumphaverant. Hae res fuerunt laqueus, id est, mala persuasione tenuerunt irretitos animos, & postea perdiderunt &c. Ita nunc titulus Ecclesiae, est mensa adversariorum Ecclesiae, & illaqueat animos falsa persuasione, & erit eis exitium.

## 11:10
And bow down their back always etc.

That is, burden them more and more with errors, scandals, sins, calamities, and finally oppress them with eternal servitude, so that they may not flourish again, so that they may not recover authority and kingdom. The Anabaptists provide an illustrious example; They were continually bringing forth new errors, so that their madness might now become manifest, most foul scandals, seditions, lusts, blasphemies were added, until at last they were completely destroyed. Similar things happened to the Jews after the persecution of the Gospel. The threat of these horrible punishments warns us not to despise the Gospel, lest we bring such punishments upon ourselves.

Did they stumble so that they might fall, etc.?

The proposition established above is repeated. The Jews did not stumble in such a way that the whole nation perished. The reasoning is cleverly thought out, and has an easy meaning. For it is an argument taken from the final cause of the reception of the Gentiles, in this way: The Gentiles were received so that the Jews might be provoked to believe, when they saw the Gospel to be effective among the Gentiles; therefore it is necessary that there be some remaining among the Jews who are going to believe. For to what end would there be a need to provoke them, when none were going to believe? Paul attaches the consequent thus. If the ruin was profitable, and it was profitable for provoking: Therefore there is some remaining safety, that is, therefore it is necessary that some part remain curable. Or it is an amplification from the lesser: If the ruin was profitable, so that the Gentiles might be received, how much more profitable will their safety be then when they, having been provoked, shall obey, because God provokes them for this reason, that He may heal them again, and render them safe.

Latin:

Et tergum illorum semper in-curva &c.

Id est, magis magisque onera eos erroribus, scandalis, peccatis, calamitatibus, deniquè opprime aeterna servitute, ne reflorescant, ne recuperent autoritatem & regnum. Illustre exemplum praebent Anabaptistae, subinde novos errores pariebant, ut iam manifestus fieret furor, accedebant foedissima scandala, seditiones, libidines, blasphemiae, donec tandem prorsus deleti sunt. Similia acciderunt Iudaeis post persecutionem Evangelii. Harum horribilium poenarum comminatio nos admonet, ne contemnamus Evangelium, ne tales poenas nobis accersamus.

Num ideo impegerunt, ut con-ciderent &c?

Propositio supra instituta repetitur. Non ita impegerunt Iudaei, ut tota gens perierit. Ratio est argutê cogitata, & habet facilem sententiam. Est enim argumentum sumptum ex causa finali receptionis gentium, hoc modo: Gentes receptae sunt, ut Iudaei provocentur ad credendum, cum viderint Evangelium in gentibus esse efficax, igitur necesse est aliquos esse reliquos inter Iudaeos, qui credituri sunt. Quorsum enim opus esset provocare eos, cum nulli credituri essent. Consequens sic attexit Paulus. Si ruina profuit, & profuit ad provocandum: Ergo est reliqua incolumitas aliqua, id est, ergo necesse est aliquam partem restare sanabilem. Vel est amplificatio ex minore: Si profuit ruina, ut gentes reciperentur, quanto magis profutura est incolumitas tunc cum provocati obtemperabunt, quia Deus ideo provocat eos, ut rursus sanet, & reddat incolumes.

## 11:13
For I say to you, Gentiles.

To the reason taken from the final cause, he adds his own example. I, he says, study with the greater diligence to propagate the Gospel among the Gentiles, so that the Jews may be provoked to believe, when they shall have seen the Gospel to be effective among the Gentiles. This is what he says, I glorify my ministry, that is, I teach the Gospel with great faith and diligence, by which the glory of God is adorned and illustrated, so that I may provoke my flesh, that is, the Jews. And he adds an amplification from the lesser: If the rejection was profitable, how much more glorious will the restoration be, which is to be as it were a resurrection from the dead. This is a simple and in no way intricate interpretation.

But if the firstfruits are holy.

The third argument, that the nation of the Jews is not rejected, taken from the promise, which is immutable, and pertains equally to the stock, and to the descendants. The root is holy, namely on account of the promise, when the fathers believed: Therefore also the branches are holy, because to these also the promise pertains, but there is need for the promise to be received by faith.

Latin:

Vobis enim dico gentibus.

Rationi sumptae ex caussa finali addit exemplum suum. Ego inquit eo maiori saedulitate studeo propagare Evangelium inter gentes, ut provocentur Iudaei ad credendum, cum viderint Evangelium esse efficax inter gentes. Hoc est quod ait, glorifico ministerium, id est, magna fide & sedulitate doceo Evangelium, quo ornatur & illustratur gloria Dei, ut provocacem carnem, id est, Iudaeos. Et addit amplificationem ex minore: Si reiectio profuit, quanto gloriosior futura est restitutio, quae est futura quasi resurrectio ex mortuis. Haec est simplex & minimè intricata interpretatio.

Quod si primitiae sanctae.

Tertium argumentum, quod gens Iudaeorum non sit reiecta, sumptum ex promissione, quae est immutabilis, & pertinet pariter ad stirpem, & ad posteros. Radix est sancta, scilicet propter promissionem, cum patres crediderunt: Ergo & rami sunt sancti, quia ad hos quoque pertinet promissio, sed opus est fide accipi promissionem.

## 11:18
Do not boast against the branches.

This is an apostrophe to the Gentiles, whom he exhorts not to despise the Jews with carnal confidence, nor to rush securely against God, trusting in this title, that they are the people of God, or the Church, just as now by carnal security the pontiffs promise themselves that they are the Church, and by this opinion they establish and do many things against the word of God. God will undoubtedly punish this impiety, according to the second commandment. And what Paul here prophesies concerning the ruin of the Church of the Gentiles, the outcome shows it; the Church in Asia and Africa has been almost utterly destroyed by the fury of Mahomet. In Europe it has been oppressed by horrible idolatry and impiety, such as the profanation of masses, the invocation of saints, superstitious opinions of human worships, and ignorance of the doctrine of faith, but yet among these scandals we ought to console ourselves, because the promises of the Gospel are always valid for those who truly believe and because there is always some true church, namely those very ones who, doing penance, truly believe, because Christ promises that the Church will always remain, and that the promises are immutable.

For I do not want you to be ignorant.

He adds a prophecy concerning the conversion of the Jews, which perhaps is to be understood in this way, that it will come to pass that from time to time until the end of the world some from among the Jews will be converted. For I do not know whether he means this, that there still remains some conversion of a great multitude around the end of the world. Since that is a mystery, let us entrust it to God. The prophecy of Isaiah preaches about the liberation of the people, namely that of which the Gospel speaks properly, that is, about the remission of sins, and it is a sweet sentiment, because it clearly teaches that the remission of sins is to be preached in the New Testament. This liberation of the people is to be understood from then, all the way from the beginning of the preaching of the Gospel to the end.

For God has shut up all.

It is an epiphonema, in which there is an equalization of the Gentiles and the Jews, and the confidence of merits is taken away from both. He exhorts all to repentance, then he equally proposes consolation to all. And it is a most serious doctrine in both members, for to be shut up under sin is not to be understood idly, but it embraces guilt, terrors, or judgment, and the punishments of sin, as if he were saying, all are guilty, all will be subject to the judgment of God, to death and afflictions, just as David was concluded under sin, when he was driven into exile, when he was exercised with horrible pains. In these afflictions, this consolation, which is delivered here, must be held especially. For he teaches concerning the cause of afflictions, and of judgment, and of the outcome. He confesses that we are subject to these evils on account of sin, but yet not so that we may perish. Therefore he adds the manner of liberation, gratuitous mercy is promised, so that there may be certain consolation, he commands us to believe that we are justified and saved through mercy, not on account of our dignity or merits. Indeed, he commands us, concluded under sin, that is, truly guilty, to flee to mercy, and not to spurn the offered mercy, but to determine that we obtain the remission of sins freely on account of Christ. Thus this sentence will become clear and sweet, when we transfer it to use, when we feel in true terrors and afflictions that it pertains to us, and we sustain ourselves with this promise of mercy. It is therefore a useful sentence, and to be used in all afflictions, because it warns of the final cause of afflictions. Also concerning gratuitous mercy. And the universal particle is to be observed, so that we may know that the promise is universal, and that we may each truly include ourselves in that universal.

O the depth of the riches.

An exclamation is added, so that it may restrain human arrogance and human thoughts concerning the counsel of God, by which He wonderfully constitutes and governs His Church. For many things offend reason, namely that only a few and abject men become the people of God, and that such a great multitude, which excels in number, virtue, and the glory of deeds performed, is condemned. The Jews indeed were wonderfully offended when they heard that the synagogue was rejected, which had the most honorable title of the people of God. Thus also now the minds of many are offended, and they rage, when they hear that those who hold the title of the Church are not the Church. Against these scandals Paul opposes this exclamation, in which he teaches that we should submit ourselves to the wisdom and word of God, and not depart from the word, even if we do not understand why God governs the Church by such a wonderful counsel, and that we should perform both, let us acknowledge the magnitude of the wrath in the rejection of so many nations, of so many ages and of such great men. Let this wrath exhort us to fear, lest we despise the word of God. Again, let us also acknowledge the mercy that God has repeatedly renewed his word, and at length scattered it into the whole world. By this testimony of mercy let us be confirmed, and let us determine that God truly receives us, truly makes us a people for himself, truly wishes to save those who call upon him. This is the sum of the Pauline exclamation, by which he meets scandals, and prohibits human judgments concerning that secret counsel of God. Likewise he prohibits arrogance, lest on account of carnal prerogatives or merits we trust that we are made the people of God, just as Bishops on account of succession contend that they are the Church etc.

The general action of God is the preservation and creation of nature. But it is spiritual, when through the Holy Spirit he renews hearts. In both ways sin is excluded, because God is not the author of sin.

Latin:

Ne glorieris adversus ramos.

Apostrophe est ad gentes, quas hortatur ne carnali fiducia despiciant Iudaeos, neve securi ruant contra Deum, confisi hoc titulo, quod sint populus Dei, seu Ecclesia, sicut nunc carnali securitate promittunt sibi pontifices, quod sint Ecclesia, & hac opinione multa contra verbum Dei constituunt & agunt. Hanc impietatem Deus haud dubiè puniet, iuxta secundum praeceptum. Et quod Paulus hic vaticinatur de ruina Ecclesiae gentium, id eventus ostendit, Ecclesia in Asia & Aphrica penè funditus deleta est Machometi furore. In Europa oppressa est horribili Idolatria & impietate, ut prophanatione missarum, invocatione sanctorum, superstitiosis opinionibus cultuum humanorum, inscitia doctrinae de fide, sed tamen inter haec scandala consolari nos debemus, quod promissiones Evangelii semper sint ratae vere credentibus quodque semper sit aliqua vera ecclesia, sclicet illi ipsi, qui agentes paenitentiam vere credunt, quia Christus pollicetur Ecclesiam semper mansuram esse, & promissiones immutabiles esse.

Non enim volo vos ignorare.

Addit vaticinium de conversione Iudaeorum, quod fortasse ita intelligendum est, futurum, ut subinde usque ad finem mundi aliqui ex Iudaeis convertantur. Nescio enim an hoc velit, restare adhuc aliquam conversionem magnae multitudinis circa finem mundi. Id cum sit mysterium, Deo committamus. Esaiae vaticinium concionatur de liberatione populi, videlicet illa, de qua proprie loquitur Evangelium, hoc est, de remissione peccatorum, & est dulcis sententia, quia clare docet in novo testamento praedicandam esse remissionem peccatorum. Haec liberatio populi intelligenda est, inde usquè à principio praedicationis Evangelii ad finem.

Conclusit enim Deus omnes.

Epiphonema est, in quo est exae quatio gentium & Iudaeorum, & detrahitur fiducia meritorum utrisque. Hortatur omnes ad paenitentiam, deinde aequaliter proponit omnibus consolationem. Estque gravissima doctrina in utroque membro, nam concludi sub peccato, non est ociose intelligendum, sed complectitur reatum, pavores, seu iudicium, & poenas peccati, quasi dicat, omnes rei sunt, omnes erunt subiiciendi iudicio Dei, morti & afflictionibus, ut David erat conclusus sub peccatum, cum pelleretur in exilium, cum horribilibus doloribus exerceretur. In his afflictionibus praecipuè tenenda est haec consolatio, quae hic traditur. Docet enim de causa afflictionum, & iudicii, & de exitu. Fatetur nos propter peccatè subiectos esse his malis, sed tamen non ut pereamus. Ideo addit modum liberationis, promittitur gratuita misericordia, ut sit certa consolatio, iubet credere quòd per misericordiam non propter nostram dignitatem aut merita iustificemur & salvemur. Imo iubet nos conclusos sub peccatum, id est, vere reos confugere ad misericordiam, nec aspernari oblatam misericordiam, sed statuere, quod gratis propter Christum, consequamur remissionem peccatorum. Ita fiet perspicua & dulcis haec sententia, cum ad usum transferemus, cum in veris pavoribus et afflictionibus eam ad nos pertinere sentiemus, nosque hac promissione misericordiae sustentabimus. Est igitur utilis sententia, & in omnibus afflictionibus usurpanda, quia monet de causa finali afflictionum. Item de gratuita misericordia. Est & universalis particula observanda, ut sciamus promissionem esse universalem, & ut singuli nos vere in illam universalem includamus.

O profunditatem divitiarum.

Exclamatio addita est, ut compescat humanam arrogantiam, & humanas cogitationes de consilio Dei, quo mirabiliter Ecclesiam suam constituit et gubernat. Multa enim offendunt rationem, videlicet quod pauci tantum & abiecti homines fiunt populus Dei, quod tanta multitudo, quae praestat numero, virtute, gloria rerum gestarum, damnatur. Iudaei vero mirifice offendebantur, cum audirent synagogam reiici, quae habebat honorificentissimum titulum populi Dei. Ita & nunc offenduntur plurimorum animi, et fremunt, cum audiunt illos, qui tenent titulum Ecclesiae, non esse Ecclesiam. Adversus haec scandala opponit Paulus hanc exclamationem, in qua docet, ut nos subiiciamus sapientiae & verbo Dei, nec dificiamus à verbo, etiamsi non intelligimus, quare tam mirabili consilio Deus gubernet Ecclesiam, & utrumque praestemus, agnoscamus magnitudinem irae in reiectione tot gentium, tot seculorum tantorum hominum. Haec ira nos ad timorem hortetur, ne contemnamus verbum Dei. Rursus etiam agnoscamus misericordiam quod subinde renovavit Deus suum verbum, & tandem sparsit in totum orbem. Hoc testimonio misericordiae confirmemur, & statuamus Deum vere nos recipere, vere sibi populum facere, vere velle salvare invocantes. Haec est summa exclamationis Paulinae, qua occurrit scandalis, & prohibet humana iudicia de illo arcano consilio Dei. Item prohibet arrogantiam, ne propter carnales praerogativas aut merita confidamus nos fieri populum Dei, sicut Episcopi propter successionem contendunt se esse Ecclesiam &c.

Actio generalis Dei est conservatio et conditio naturae. Sedspiritualis est, quando per spiritum sanctum renovat corda. Utroque modo excluditur peccatum, quod Deus non sit autor peccati.

## 12:1 Argument
CHAPTER XII.

He institutes a new part, namely precepts concerning good works. For above he delivered the proper place of the Gospel, namely the doctrine concerning justification and concerning faith. This is not the doctrine of the Law, and it is far distant from the Law, as has been said in its own place. For first, it is necessary that the remission of sins, justification, and the gift of the Holy Spirit be received freely by faith on account of Christ. Afterwards, it is necessary that new obedience follow, which is a certain beginning, the fulfillment of the Law. And therefore the precepts are delivered after the doctrine concerning faith. But why is it necessary that the precepts be delivered, when the spirit obeys God of its own accord? I answer, first, the word is necessary, so that the carnal part may be restrained. Then, it is necessary that the doctrine of repentance always be delivered, and that the remnants of sin be mortified in us, and that repentance grow. Thirdly, the word is necessary for the righteous, through which they may be taught what works please God, and through which spiritual motions are excited. Therefore, the doctrine of the Gospel concerning faith having been proposed, the precepts or the Law are also delivered. Now here the doctrine concerning good works must be known, what kind of works are required, and how they please.

First, what kind, for good works divinely commanded are required, interior and exterior, namely the fear of God, faith, love, repentance, patience, invocation. These interior motions are not in the ungodly, even if external civil discipline is present. Therefore, it must be diligently considered what kind of works ought to exist in believers. But how do they please? This doctrine is necessary for the Churches, and is handed down above cap. viii. It is necessary to hold both. First, that we are not righteous on account of our virtues or works, and that sin still clings to us, by which even good works are contaminated. Therefore, the recognition of our infirmity and repentance ought to grow in us. Then, although we are not righteous on account of our virtues, yet after we are reconciled and righteous by faith, even begun obedience pleases, not because it satisfies the Law, or because it is without vice, but on account of Christ the high priest interceding for us, etc. This doctrine is a great consolation to the pious, and the greatness of mercy exhorts to working well. For when the pious mind hears that this obedience, however small and contaminated, certainly pleases, when it hears that it is the worship of God and a sacrifice, it is undoubtedly kindled to perform it with greater zeal. This whole topic was handed down above in the eighth chapter, where it was also said what kind of sins are in the saints. Likewise concerning the distinction between venial and mortal sin. These topics pertaining to the doctrine of works have been considered here at the beginning.

Now I return to the text. The twelfth chapter is ἤθικον, that is, it delivers precepts concerning private virtues, the thirteenth is political concerning the magistrate and obedience, the fourteenth is ceremonial concerning the use of ceremonies.

Latin:

CAPUT XII.

Instituit novam partem, scilicet praecepta de bonis operibus. Nam supra tradidit locum Evangelii proprium, scilicet doctrinam de iustificatione & de fide. Haec non est doctrina Legis, aclonge distat à Lege, ut suo loco dictum est. Primum enim fide propter Christum gratis accipi oportet remissionem peccatorum, iustificationem, & donationem spiritus sancti. Postea necesse est sequi novam obedientiam, quae est quaedam inchoatio, Legis impletio. Ideoque traduntur praecepta post doctrinam de fide. Quare autem opus est tradi praecepta, cum spiritus ultro obtemperet Deo? Respondeo, Primum opus est verbo, ut coherceatur pars carnalis. Deinde necesse est semper tradi doctrinam paenitentiae, & mortificari reliquias peccati in nobis, & crescere paenitentiam. Tertio opus est iustis verbo, per quod doceantur, quae opera placeant Deo, & per quod spirituales motus excitantur. Ideo proposita doctrina Evangelii de fide traduntur etiam praecepta seu Lex. Iam hic scienda est doctrina de bonis operibus, qualia opera requirantur, & quomodo placeant.

Primum qualia, Requiruntur enim bona opera divinitus praecepta, interiora et exteriora, videlicet timor Dei, fides, dilectio, paenitentia, patientia, invocatio. Hi interiores motus non sunt in impiis, etiamsi adest externa civilis disciplina. Ideo diligenter considerandum est, qualia opera existere in credentibus debeant. Sed quomodo placent? Haec doctrina necessaria est Ecclesiis, & supra traditur cap. viii. Utrumque tenere necesse est. Primum quòd non sumus iusti propter nostras virtutes aut opera, & quòd adhuc haereat in nobis peccatum, quo contaminantur etiam bona opera. Ideo crescere in nobis agnitio nostrae infirmitatis & paenitentia debet. Deinde etsi non sumus iusti propter nostras virtutes, tamen postquàm fide reconciliati & iusti sumus, placet etiam inchoata obedientia, non quia satisfaciat Legi, aut quia sit sine vitio, sed propter Christum pontificem interpellantem pro nobis &c. Haec doctrina magna consolatio est piis, & magnitudo misericordiae hortatur ad bene operandum. Cum enim audit pia mens certo placere hanc quantulamcunque obedientiam & contaminatam, cum audit cultum Dei, & sacrificium esse, haud dubiè accenditur, ut eam maiore studio praestet. Hic totus locus supra in octavo capite traditus est, ubi etiam dictum est qualia peccata sint in sanctis. Item de discrimine peccati venialis & mortalis. Hi loci pertinentes ad doctrinam operum hic initio considerati sunt.

Nunc redeo ad textum. Duodecimum caput est ἤθικον, id est, tradit praecepta de privatis virtutibus, xiii. est politicum de magistratu & de obedientia, xiiii. est caerimoniale de usu caeremoniarum.

## 12:1
I beseech you therefore, brethren.

In the beginning he proposes a general precept, namely that we should exhibit some worship to God, and indeed a rational one, that is, such a one in which God is acknowledged and apprehended, or in which these divine motions exist, namely the fear of God and trust. Then he names this worship, namely that we should offer our bodies as sacrifices, that is, that our bodies should be mortified, and thus become victims, namely with carnal affections mortified, and by sustaining afflictions. It is therefore a general precept, in which this is notable, that he wishes this obedience to be a rational worship, and that we should become victims. For because it is necessary for the people of God to have some worship, priesthood, and sacrifices. We also have a priesthood and sacrifices, and here first the whole doctrine concerning the priesthood and the difference of sacrifices must be repeated. Secondly, it must be diligently observed that he requires faith in that obedience, and in all good works. Thirdly, what kind of emphasis there is, that He calls us victims. The priest has properly three offices: to hold and confess the Gospel divinely handed down, to have the command and promise concerning invocation, and sacrifice. These primarily belong to Christ, through whom the Gospel has been revealed, who alone has the right of interceding for others, and of offering his own sacrifice for others. Then Christ so imparts the honor of the priesthood to believers, because he gives them his word, and adds the promise that God will hear those who call upon him, and grants them the fruit of his sacrifice. Then he also requires sacrifices from them themselves, namely confession, and obedience in good works and afflictions. Since, therefore, believers are priests, Paul also preaches here concerning sacrifices, just as Peter says: You are a holy priesthood, that you may offer spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God through Jesus Christ. Where it is expressly said that our acts of worship are acceptable not because of our dignity, but because of the high priest Christ. Here, however, the customary distinction of sacrifice must also be held. One is a propitiatory sacrifice for others, i.e., that which merits for others the remission of sins, namely the death of Christ. Believers therefore have that first, foreign sacrifice, which nevertheless has been given to us, so that by faith we may establish that the fruit is truly given to us, or the merit of this sacrifice. Next, believers also render their own sacrifices, but these do not merit the remission of sins for the one doing them or for others, but they are pleasing in those who are reconciled on account of the high priest Christ. We call these sacrifices εὐχαριστικὰ. Moreover, it is of the nature of this sacrifice to perform a work commanded by God, with this end, that we may give thanks to God, and glorify him, that is, that by this very obedience we may testify that this is truly the God whom we invoke, and that those things which we preach about him are true, and thus invite others by our example. This is the principal end of sacrifice, that the glory of God may be made more illustrious, and God may become known. Sacrifices are, however, either ceremonial or spiritual. In the Old Testament, the slaughtering of cattle and other ceremonies were performed, which then had the command of God, so that they might be shadows of the benefits of the Gospel. These shadows ceased after the Gospel was revealed, and since the New Testament brings righteousness and eternal life into hearts, now worship and sacrifices must be true and perpetual motions of the heart, a perpetual glorification of God, just as Christ says: True worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and truth, that is, with true and spiritual of the motions of the heart, Paul means this very thing when in this place he requires a rational service, that is, a service of the mind, in which God is acknowledged and apprehended, that is, in which true motions toward God exist: fear, faith, invocation, confession. Therefore, Paul excludes not only animal sacrifices, but also the works of men, and not only the traditions of monks, but also moral works, whenever they are done without the fear of God and without faith. Furthermore, Paul's statement universally fights against the opinion concerning the work performed, and it is an abominable error of the adversaries, who imagine that the mass is valid by the work performed without a good motion of the one using it. For here Paul, when he requires a rational service, demands a good motion of the one using it, namely, true motions of fear and of faith toward God. Therefore, this is Paul's proposition: I beseech you, that you may offer to God true spiritual services, or motions of the heart, so that your bodies may obey, and you may become sacrifices, or that you may obey, and you may become sacrifices. But what is the emphasis in the word sacrifices? First, the offering is a confession, or a testifying, that we acknowledge God. And the slaughter signifies that some death in sin had been destined. Likewise, that this vicious nature it is necessary that it be abolished, and that in that death obedience must be rendered to God. Therefore, he includes these three things when he names a sacrifice, namely, the acknowledgment or glorification of God, the mortification of ourselves, or the obedience to be rendered in mortification, and indeed, by which we believe that on account of the sacrifice Christ these sacrifices are pleasing to God, whom all sacrifices have always signified, and on account of whom they were accepted. The meaning, therefore, is: Be sacrifices, that is, acknowledge, proclaim, or glorify God, and endure mortification, and believe that these acts of worship of yours are pleasing to God on account of Christ, on account of whom you also are sacrifices. This is the simplest meaning. Now if we shall think that we are sacrifices, we shall understand that we are called, not to the pleasures, riches, and power of this world, but to slaughter, horrible hatred, and afflictions of every kind, by which we are attacked by the devil and impious men, and just as a sacrifice stands at the altar waiting assiduously until it is struck, so let us stand at the altar, that is, in the confession and glorification of God, and let us render obedience to God in the persecutions and calamities by which we are overwhelmed, and in these let us call upon God, and let us believe that these acts of worship are pleasing on account of Christ, on account of from which we shall also one day be delivered. He adds living, because the new testament brings perpetual righteousness and life. Therefore, perpetual sacrifices, perpetual praises, and acts of thanksgiving are now required; cattle are no longer to be slaughtered, but such sacrifices as, although they are mortified, yet at the same time conceive a new life, so that they may perpetually glorify God, holy, that is, destined for divine uses, for the invocation of God, for preaching, glorification, and other good works, but in such a way that they are directed to this end, that the glory of God may be adorned. Pleasing to God) But in order that a work may please God, two things are required, namely that it be commanded by God, and that it be done in faith or trust in Christ, as it is written: The just shall live by faith. Therefore, this faith is required also in this place in all good works, that we may believe that this our obedience is pleasing, not on account of our own dignity or our own purity, but on account of the high priest Christ, just as Peter also says: Offering up spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God by Jesus Christ, and Hebrews last: By him let us offer the sacrifice of praise. The sum therefore is of this proposition, he commands that we obey God, and that this obedience be performed in true fear of God, in true faith, and to this end, that it may illustrate the glory of God, and invite others to piety, and because he transferred the doctrine concerning good works to the common place concerning sacrifices, he has embraced very many things, namely that it is necessary to offer worship to God, that it is fitting for us to be subject to afflictions. Item, that it is fitting that all good works be done in faith, and be referred to as an example for exciting others, so that God may become known. Item, since they are sacrifices, they please God on account of the high priest Christ, when faith is added.
