And do not accommodate yourselves to the figure of this world.

In this saying the previous sentiment is repeated by antithesis, that we should not have affections similar to those of worldly people, but new affections obedient to God. For when he forbids imitating the world, he does not disparage things, the use of which God has ordained, he does not forbid the use of foods, marriage, governments, judgments, contracts, and other ordinances of God, but he prohibits vicious affections. Therefore he says gestures, that is, the habits of the mind should not be similar to worldly ones, as the wicked seek pleasure against the ordinance of God, seek wealth and power by unjust means, and flee the light. He condemns such desires, which have occupied the greatest part of the world, just as we see everywhere the minds of men burning with various desires, avarice, ambition, and lusts, and on account of these mixing the world with tumults, slaughters, and wars, as daily life testifies, and the histories of all times. On the contrary, however, He commands the mind to be renewed, that is, He commands us to think otherwise, to conceive other notions about God, and other affections, namely, the true fear of God, and true faith, so that we may prefer the will of God to our own desires. Therefore He adds, that you may recognize what is the good will of God, etc. For I understand that simply, concerning the will of God proposed in the commandments and promises. For He commands us to be renewed in such a way that we conceive a new notion about God, and put on new affections, namely, the true fear of God, and true faith, and these affections exert themselves in every kind of good works, and in afflictions, namely, that in afflictions we may understand that obedience pleases God, and therefore we may endure adversities, and not flee the cross.

Among the virtues which pertain to ministry, or government, or administration, there are two that are principal: Obedience in Invocation, in seinem beuelch pleiben,, and in judging or instituting, not to depart from the prescribed rule or mandate. Wherefore he preaches about these two virtues at the beginning, and says thus: Let no one think arrogantly of himself, that is, let no one break forth outside his own calling, and arrogantly undertake something other than what the reason of his office demands. Item: Let no one arrogantly dare to judge concerning dogmas, against the handed-down rule, or to sow new opinions, or to institute new cults, infatuated by a persuasion of great wisdom, or of holiness beyond the measure of his gift. Both precepts are necessary, especially in the Church, for just as in cities πολυπραγμοσύνη it does the greatest harm when private men thrust themselves into business and impede ordinary actions, just as Marius Brutus and others disturbed the Republic, so in the Church there exists a huge danger when some, incited either by foolish Zeal or by other desires, break forth outside their calling and attempt to reform many things in doctrine or rites, or on the contrary, when teachers outside their office they recall civil affairs to their own power, and have one foot in the court, the other in the Church, just as Aristophanes said of Cleon, that he had one foot in the camp, the other in the assembly. First, therefore, let us remember that it is commanded here, that we do not disturb vocations, but that individuals diligently perform the duties of their own vocation. The second precept forbids judging against the prescribed rule, that is, against the word of God, and sounder judgments, just as some, swelling with the empty persuasion of singular wisdom, serve new opinions, institute new cults, and cast a fog over true and necessary articles. Let us remember that this audacity is primarily prohibited here, when he commands that each one should acknowledge the measure of his gift, that is, both obey his own vocation, and not take upon himself judgment beyond the measure of his gift, and not affirm uncertain things. Paul calls the measure of faith the measure of the gift, which ought to be exercised in faith, and was given through faith, just as in an army one is a leader, another a tribune, another a quaestor. So in the Churches some teachers have greater gifts than others. Therefore, Paul later adds an enumeration, so that individuals may remember their own vocation and their own measure.

Latin:

Obsecro igitur vos fratres.

Initio proponit generale praeceptum, videlicet ut exhibeamus aliquem cultum Deo, et quideem rationalem, hoc est, talem, in quo agnoscitur & apprehenditur Deus, seu in quo existunt hi motus divini, videlicet timor Dei et fiducia. Deinde nominat hunc cultum, videlicet ut offeramus hostias corpora nostra, id est, ut mortificentur corpora nostra, & sic fiant victimae, scilicet mortificatis affectibus carnalibus, & sustinendis afflictionibus Est igitur generale praeceptum, in quo illud est insigne, quod hanc obedientiam vult esse cultum rationalem, & nos fieri victimas. Quia enim populum Dei necesse est habere aliquem cultum, sacerdotium & sacrificia. Habemus & nos sacerdotium & sacrificia, & hic primum tota doctrina de sacerdotio, & sacrificiorum differentia repetenda est. Secundo diligenter observandum, quod requirat fidem in illa obedientia, & in omnibus bonis operibus. Tertio qualis sit emphasis, quod vocat nos victimas. Sacerdotis propriè tria sunt officia, tenere et confiteri Evangelium divinitus traditum, habere mandatum & promissionem de invocatione, & sacrificio. Haec primum competunt Christo, per quem revelatum est Evangelium, qui solus habet ius intercedendi pro aliis, & offerendi sacrificii sui pro aliis. Deinde Christus ita impertit honerem sacerdotii credentibus, quia dat eis verbum suum, & addit promissionem, quod exauditurus sit Deus invocantes, & donat eis sui sacrificii fructum. Deinde ab ipsis etiam requirit sacrificia, scilicet confessionem, & obedientiam in bonis operibus & afflictionibus Cum igitur credentes sint sacerdotes, concionatur et Paulus hic de sacrificiis, sicut Petrus inquit: Vos estis sacerdotium sanctum, ut offeratis spirituales hostias, acceptas Deo per lesum Christum. Ubi diserte dicitur nostros cultus acceptos esse non propter nostram dignitatem, sed propter pontificem Christam. Hic autem tenenda est etiam distinctio sacrificii usitata. Unum est sacrificium propitiatorium pro aliis. i. quod aliis meretur remissionem peccatorum, scilicet mors Christi. Habent ergo credentes primum illud alienum sacrificium, quod tamen nobis donatum est, ita ut fide statuamus vere nobis donari fructum, seu meritum huius sacrificii. Deinde reddunt credentes etiam propria sacrificia, sed haec non merentur remissionem peccatorum facienti aut aliis, sed placent in reconciliatis propter pontificem Christum. Haec sacrificia vocamus εὐχαριστικὰ. Est autem de natura huius sacrificii, facere opus à Deo mandatum, hoc fine, ut gratias agamus Deo, & glorificemus eum, hoc est, ut hac ipsa obedientia testemur, hunc vere Deum esse, quem invocamus, & vera esse, quae de eo praedicamus, atque ita invitemus nostro exemplo alios. Hic est principalis finis sacrificii, ut gloria Dei fiat illustrior, & Deus innotescat. Sunt autem sacrificia vel caeremonialia vel spiritualia. In veteri testamento fiebant mactationes pecudum & aliae caeremoniae, quae tunc habebant mandatum Dei, ut essent umbrae beneficiorum Evangelii. Hae umbrae cessaverunt postquàm Evangelium revelatum est, cumque novum testamentum afferat in cordibus iusticiam & vitam aeternam, iam cultus & sacrificia esse debent veri & perpetui motus cordis, prepetua glorificatio Dei, sicut inquit Christus: Veri adoratores adorabunt patrem in spiritu & veritate, id est, veris & spiritualibus motibus cordis, hoc ipsum vult Paulus, cum hoc loco requirit rationalem cultum, id est, cultum mentis, in quo agnoscitur & apprehen ditur Deus, id est, in quo existunt veri motus erga Deum timor, fides, invocatio, confessio. Excludit ergo Paulus non modo pecvinas hostias, sed etiam hominum opera, ac non solum monachorum traditiones, sed etiam moralia opera, quandocunque sine timore Dei, & sine fide fiunt. Pugnat etiam Pauli dictum universaliter cum opinione de opere operato, estque abominandus error adversariorum, qui fingunt missam ex opere operato valere sine bono motu utenis. Hic enim Paulus, cum requirit rationalem cultum, postulat bonum motum utentis, scilicet veros motus timoris, & fidei erga Deum. Est igitur haec Pauli propositio: Obtestor vos, ut praestetis Deo veros cultus spirituales, seu motus cordis, ita ut obtemperent corpora vestra, & fiatis hostiae, seu ut vos obtemperetis, & fiatis hostiae. Quae est autem emphasis in vocabulo hostiae? Primum oblatio est confessio, seu testificatio, quod agnoscamus Deum. Et mactatio significat fuisse destinatam aliquam mortem in peccato. Item, quod hanc naturam vitiosam aboleri oporteat, & quod in ea morte obedientia Deo praestanda sit. Itaque haec tria comprehendit cum nominat hostiam, videlicet agnitionem seu glorificationem Dei, mortificationem nostri, seu obedientiam in mortificationem praestandam, & quidem, qua credimus, quod propter hostiam Christum hae hostiae placeant Deo, quem omnes hostiae semper significaverunt, & propter quem fuerunt acceptae. Est ergo sententia, Fiatis hostiae, idest, agnoscite, praedicate seu glorificate Deum, & sustinete mortificationem, & credite quod hi vestri cultus placeant Deo propter Christum, propter quem & vos estis hostiae. Haec est simplicissima sententia. Iam si cogitabimus nos esse hostias, intelligemus nos vocatos esse, non ad huius mundi voluptates, opes, potentiam, sed ad necem, horribile odium, afflictiones omnis generis, quibus oppugnamur à diabolo, & impiis hominibus, & sicut hostia stat ad aram expectans assidue donec feriatur, Ita nos stemus ad aram, id est, in confessione et glorficatione Dei, & praestemus Deo obedientiam in persecutionibus & calamitatibus, quibus obruimur, & in his invocemus Deum, & credamus placere hos cultus propter Christum, propter quem etiam aliquando liberabimur. Addit vivam, quia novum testamentum affert perpetuam iusticiam & vitam. Ideo requiruntur iam perpetuae hostiae, perpetuae laudes, & gratiarum actiones, non iam pecudes mactandae sunt, sed tales hostiae, quae quanquàm mortificantur, tamen simul concipiunt novam vitam, ut perpetuo Deum glorificent, Sanctam id est, ad usus divinos destinatam, ad invocationem Dei, ad praedicationem, glorificationem, & alia bona opera, sed ita ut ad hunc finem directa sint, ut gloria Dei ornetur. Deo placentem) Ut autem opus Deo placeat, duo requiruntur, videlicet quod sit mandatum à Deo, & quod fiat in fide seu fiducia Christi, sicut scriptum est: Iustus ex fide vivet. Requiritur igitur & hoc loco haec fides in omnibus bonis operibus, ut credamus placere hanc nostram obedientiam, non propter nostram dignitatem, aut propriam puritatem, sed propter pontificem Christum, sicut & Petrus inquit: Offerentes hostias spirituales, acceptas Deo per Iesum Christum, & Hebraeor. ultimo: Per ipsum offeramus hostiam laudis. Est ergo summa huius propositionis, praecipit ut Deo obediamus, & ut haec obedientia praestetur in vero timore Dei, vera fide, & hoc fine, ut illustret gloriam Dei, & invitet alios ad pietatem, & quia transtulit doctrinam de bonis operibus ad locum communem de hostiis, valde multa complexus est, videlicet quod sit necesse Deo praestare cultum, quod oporteat nos subiectos esse afflictionibus. Item, quod oporteat omnia bona opera fieri in fide, & referri ad exemplum ad excitandos alios, ut innotescat Deus. Item cum sint sacrificia, placeant Deo propter pontifiem Christum, cum accedit fides.

Et ne accommodetis vos ad fi-guram huius seculi.

In hoc dicto repetitur superior sententia per antithesin, ne habeamus affectus similes mundanorum, sed novos affectus Deo obedientes. Nam cum vetat imitari mundum, non vituperat res, quarum usum Deus ordinavit, non vetat usum ciborum, coniugii, imperiorum, iudiciorum, contractuum, & aliarum Dei ordinationem, sed prohibet vitiosos affectus. Ideo inquit gestus, id est, mores animi non sint similes mundanis, ut contra ordinationem Dei appetunt impii voluptatem, quaerunt opes & potentiam iniustis modis, fugiunt lucem. Tales cupiditates damnat, quae occuparunt maximam mundi partem, sicut videmus ubique animos hominum ardere alios aliis cupiditatibus, avaritia, ambitione, libidinibus, & propter has miscere orbem terrarum tumultibus, caedibus, bellis, sicut quotidiana vita testatur, & historiae omnium temporum. Econtra autem iubet renovari mentem, id est, iubet nos aliter sentire, alias notitias de Deo, & alios affectus concipere, videlicet verum timorem Dei, & veram fidem, ut anteferamus voluntatem Dei nostris cupiditatibus. Ideo addit, ut agnoscatis quae sit voluntas Dei bona &c. Id enim simpliciter intelligo, de voluntate Dei proposita in praeceptis & promissionibus. Iubet enim ita renovari, ut novam notitiam de Deo concipiamus, & induamus novos affectus, videlicet verum timorem Dei, & veram fidem, & hi affectus exerant se in omni genere bonorum operum, & in afflictionibus, videlicet ita in afflictionibus intelligamus Deo placere obedientiam, & propterea sustineamus adversa, nec fugiamus crucem.

Inter virtutes, quae ad ministerium, seu gubernationem, seu administrationem, pertinent, duae sunt praecipuae,Obedientia in Invocatione, in seinem beuelch pleiben, & in iudicando seu instituendo, nond iscedere à praescripta regula seu mandato. Quare de his duabus virtutibus initio concionatur, & ita inquit: Nemo arroganter de se sentiat, id est, nemo erumpat extra suam vocationem, & arroganter aliud suscipiat, quam postulat sui officii ratio. Item: Nemo arroganter ausit iudicare de dogmatibus, contra traditam regulam, aut serere novas opiniones, aut instituere novos cultus, infatuatus persuasione magnae sapientiae, aut sanctitatis supra modum sui doni. Utrumque autem praeceptum necessarium est, maximèin Ecclesia, ut enim in civitatibus πολυπραγμοσύνη plurimum nocet, cum ingerunt se privati homines negociis, & impediunt ordinarias actiones, sicut Marius Brutus, & alii turbabant Rempub. ita in Ecclesia ingens periculum existit, cum aliqui vel stulto Zelo, vel aliis cupiditatibus incitati extra vocationem suam erumpunt, & multa reformare in doctrina vel ritibus conantur, aut èregione, cum doctores extra suum officium civilia negocia ad suam potestatem revocant, & habent alterum pedem in curia, alterum in Ecclesia, sicut Aristophanes dicebat de Cleone, habere eum alterum pedem in castris, alterum in concione. Primum igitur meminerimus hic praecipi, ne conturbemus vocationes, sed ut singuli suae vocationis officia diligenter faciant. Alterum praeceptum vetat iudicare contra praescriptam regulam, hoc est contra verbum Dei, & saniora iudicia, sicut aliqui tumentes inani persuasione singularis sapientiae, servunt novas opiniones, instituunt novos cultus, offundunt caliginem veris & necessariis articulis. Hanc audaciam in primis meminerimus hic prohiberi, cum iubet ut unusquisque agnoscat mensuram sui doni, id est, & vocationi suae obtemperet, & non sumat sibi iudicium supra modum sui doni, non incerta affirmet. Paulus vocat mensuram fidei mensuram doni, quod in fide exerceri debet, & per fidem dabatur, ut in exercitu alius est dux, alius tribunus, alius quaestor. Ita in Ecclesiis alii doctores habent maiora donaaliis. Ideo postea addit Paulus enumerationem, ut singuli meminerint suae vocationis & sui modi.

## 12:6
Or prophecy according to the proportion of faith, etc.

In the enumeration he prescribes rules for certain ones, as concerning prophets. Now prophecy signifies revelations, that is, either predictions about future things, or the interpretation of Scripture, because for this also some revelation is necessary. For what true faith is, and true consolation of conscience, and true acknowledgment of sin, no one understands without divine motion, and some have more illustrious motions than others. He commands, therefore, that the interpretation of the word of God be analogous, that is, consenting to the faith, that is, that it may not depart from the articles of faith, that it may not extinguish the true knowledge of Christ, and faith in Christ. Just as in the beginning Ebion, Samosatenus, and others departed from the articles of faith, who contended that in Christ there was only a human nature. Then the Arians, who denied that the Son of God was God by nature, the Manichaeans, who feigned two Gods, and condemned marriage, judgments, and the eating of meat. Thus they feigned that men are righteous not by faith, but by such observances. The Pelagians departed from the analogy of faith, because they denied that there was any original sin, and feigned that the Law of God is satisfied by these rational works, which men can perform in any way. And so they thought that man merits the remission of sins by these works, and is righteous on account of rational discipline, and they taught nothing at all about justifying faith. Likewise, they taught that men are righteous and are saved without the Holy Spirit. These Pharisaical opinions utterly destroy the Gospel concerning Christ. For Christ was given to us for this reason, because we do not satisfy the Law, and because we are not righteous on account of the Law. Another righteousness has been proposed, namely, that we are reputed righteous by faith on account of Christ. Wherefore Pelagian opinions, since they take away the benefits of Christ, are by no means analogous to faith. Such also are the opinions of our adversaries, who imagine that men can satisfy the Law of God, and merit the remission of sins by works, and be righteous on account of works, but they have said nothing about justifying faith. Therefore their doctrine is not analogous to faith. The opinion concerning the mass also fights against faith, that it is a work to be applied to others, because the mass is of no benefit, except to one remembering the death of Christ, just as the text itself testifies. Wherefore one should not have believed the apparitions of spirits requesting masses. Likewise, the opinions of the monks dissent from faith, that those works of traditions are worship of God, are perfection. Nor is the invocation of saints analogous to faith. Therefore, one should not have believed in the apparitions or miracles which confirmed those cults, because against the manifest word of God one must by no means believe in miracles or apparitions, as is clearly commanded in Deuteron. xiii.. To which passage Paul alludes here, when he opposes the rule concerning the analogy of faith to the authority of those who seem to be prophets.

Μηδὲ τὰ τῶν ἑτέρων τοῖς ἑτέροισι δίδου Theog. P reverence is a virtue preceding others in honor ) virtue is reverence. Envy, spite, detraction, and emulation fight against this. These are most harmful vices: Therefore, it is necessary that reverence toward others be a distinguished virtue.to attribute honor to others is to acknowledge the gifts and endowments of others, to esteem them highly, to help them, not to suppress them, to attribute to them their due place, and also testimony in its place. Humility also pertains to this, because reverence arises from a true recognition of oneself and others from a true judgment about us and others.

Latin:

Sive prophetiam iuxta portio-nem fidei &c.

In enumeratione praescribit quibusdam regulas, ut de prophetis. Significat autem prophetia revelationes, hoc est, seu praedictiones de futuris, seu interpretationem scripturae, quia ad hanc etiam opus est aliqua revelatione. Nam quid vera sit fides, & vera consolatio conscientiae, & vera agnitio peccati nemo intelligit sine divino motu, & habent alii motus illustriores aliis. Praecipit igitur ut interpretatio verbi Dei sit analoga, id est, consentiens fidei, hoc est, ne discedat ab articulis fidei, ne extinguat notitiam veram Christi, & fidem in Christum. Sicut initio ab articulis fidei discesserunt Ebion, Samosatenus & alii, qui contenderunt in Christo tantum esse naturam humanam. Deinde Ariani, qui negaverunt filium Dei natura Deum esse, Manichei, qui finxerunt duos Deos, et damnaverunt coniugium, iudicia, esum carnium. Ita finxerunt homines non fide, sed talibus observationibus iustos esse. Pelagiani discesserunt ab analogia fidei, quia negarunt esse aliquod peccatum originale, & finxerunt Legi Dei satisfieri per haec rationalia opera, quae homines utcunque efficere possunt. Itaque senserunt hominem his operibus mereri remissionem peccatorum, & esse iustum propter rationalem disciplinam, de fide iustificante nihil prorsus docuerunt. Item docuerunt homines sine spiritu sancto iustos esse & salvari. Hae Pharisaicae opiniones prorsus delent Evangelium de Christo. Ideo enim Christus nobis donatus est, quia nos non satisfacimus Legi, & quia propter Legem non sumus iusti. Proposita est alia iusticia, ut scilicet fide propter Christum iusti reputemur. Quare Pelagianae opiniones, cum tollant beneficia Christi, nequaquàm sunt analogae fidei. Tales sunt etiam opiniones adversariorum nostrorum, qui fingunt homines posse Legi Dei satisfacere, & operibus mereri remissionem peccatorum, & propter opera iustos esse, de fide iustificante vero nihil dixerunt. Ideo eorum doctrina non est analoga fidei. Pugnat cum fide etiam opinio de missa, quod sit opus applicandum aliis, quia missa non prodest, nisi recordanti mortem Christi, sicut textus ipse testatur. Quare non fuit credendum apparitionibus spirituum petentium missas. Item, dissentiunt à fide monachorum opiniones, quod illa opera traditionum sint cultus Dei, sint perfectio. Nec est analoga fidei invocatio sanctorum. Ideo non fuit credendum apparitionibus aut miraculis, quae illos cultus confirmaverunt, quia contra manifestum verbum Dei nequaquàm credendum est miraculis aut apparitionibus, ut Deuteron. xiii. manifestà praecipitur. Ad quem locum hic alludit Paulus, cum autoritati illorum, qui videntur esse prophetae, opponit regulam de analogia fidei.

Μηδὲ τὰ τῶν ἑτέρων τοῖς ἑτέροισι δίδουTheog. P raevenientes alios honore ) virtus est reverentia. Cum hac pugnant invidia, livor, obtrectatio, aemulatio. Haec sunt vitia nocentissima: Ergo necesse est praeclaram esse virtutem reverentiam erga alios.tribuere aliis honorem, est agnoscere aliorum dona, dotes, eos magnifacere, iuvare, non premere, tribuere eis debitum locum, & testimonium quoque in loco. Huc etiam pertinet humilitas, quia reverentia oritur ex vera agnitione sui & aliorum ex vero iudicio de nobis & aliis.

## 13:1 Argument
CHAPTER . XIII.

Above he proposed precepts concerning private morals, and delivered them as if they were ethics. Now He adds precepts concerning political life. Although it does not pertain to the Gospel, but to the judgment of reason and the counsel of the magistrate, to enact laws concerning contracts, successions, actions, punishments, war, and similar civil or forensic matters, just as architecture or the art of medicine pertains to reason, nevertheless in general it is necessary that the word of God exist concerning the use of these arts for two reasons: that the works of God may be acknowledged, and then that we may know that their use is granted to the pious, because our works must have testimony from the word of God. Therefore, let readers first observe here to what extent the Gospel preaches about political matters, namely in general. Then let them remember that the Gospel does not establish another worldly polity, but approves the polities of all nations and the laws concerning civil matters that are congruent with reason, just as it approves medicine or architecture. Meanwhile, however, the Gospel properly teaches the pious concerning spiritual and eternal life, so that eternal life may be begun in their hearts, and yet it wills that our bodies outwardly move in this civil society and use the common bonds of that society, the distinction of dominions, contracts, laws, judgments, magistrates, and the rest. These external things do not hinder, so that the knowledge of God, fear, faith, invocation, and other virtues might not be absent from hearts; nay, God proposed those external things so that they might be occasions in which faith, invocation, the fear of God, patience, and love are exercised, and it is a certain wisdom worthy of a Christian to understand why God has cast the Church into these middle occupations, namely because He wishes to be made known in common society among men. Therefore, He willed all the duties of society to be exercises of confession, and at the same time to be exercises of our faith and love. Furthermore, minds must be accustomed to think reverently about all parts of civil society, because those fanatical opinions, which imagine that empires, laws, judgments, and contracts are things devised by human cunning, and are only instruments of human desires—such as that empires are instruments of exercising unjust power against the weaker, and that judgments serve the desire for vengeance or avarice—harm souls to a great extent. Thus, monks look upon these things, and therefore they disapprove of them, or at least obscure their dignity. We, on the contrary, should think honorably of them as gifts and ordinances of God delivered, first for this end, that this society might be preserved for teaching cause. Secondly, that these very duties of society may be exercises of confession. Thirdly, that in these works we may exercise the fear of God, faith, invocation, love, etc. Wherefore let us know that it is impious to spurn or hold in low esteem these divine things.

Latin:

CAPUT . XIII.

Supra proposuit praecepta de privatis moribus, ac velut ethnicen tradidit. Nunc addit praecepta de vita politica. Quanquam e nim non pertinet ad Evangelium, sed ad iudicium rationis & consilium magistratus, leges ferre de contractibus, succesionibus de actionibus, poenis, bello, & similibus rebus civilibus aut forensibus sicut Architectonica, aut ars medicorum ad rationem pertinet, tamen in genere de usu harum artium nacesse est extare verbum Dei propter duas causas, ut agnoscantur opera Dei, deinde ut sciamus usum concessum esse piis, quia oportet opera nostra habere testimonium ex verbo Dei. Primum igitur hic observent lectores, quatenus Evangelium concionetur de rebus politicis scilicet in genere. Deinde meminerint Evangelium non constituere aliam politiam mundanam, sed approbare omnium gentium politias, ac leges de rebus civilibus rationi congruentes, sicut approbat medicinam aut architectonicam. Interea vero Evangelium proprie de spirituali & aeterna vita docet pios, ut in cordibus inchoetur vita aeterna, & tamen foris vult corpora nostra versari in hac civili societate, & uti communibus vinculis illius societatis, distinctione dominiorum, contractibus, legibus, iudiciis, magistratibus & reliquis. Hae res externae non impediunt, quo minus existant in cordibus agnitio Dei, timor, fides, invocatio, & caeterae virtutes, imo Deus proposuit illas externas res, ut essent occasiones in quibus exerceantur fides, invocatio, timor Dei, patientia, dilectio, & est quaedam sapientia digna Christiano, intelligere quare Deus Ecclesiam coniecerit in has medias occupationes, scilicet quia vult in societate communi inter homines innotescere. Ideo voluit omnia officia societatis esse exercitia confessionis, & simul exercitia esse nostrae fidei & dilectionis. Deinde assuefaciendae sunt mentes, ut reverenter sentiant de omnibus partibus societatis civilis, quia ad modum nocent animis illae fanaticae opiniones, quae imaginantur imperia, leges, iudicia, contractus, esse res cogita tas humana astutia, & esse tantum instrumenta humanarum cupiditatum, ut imperia esse instrumenta exercendae iniustae potentiae contra imbecilliores, iudicia servire cupiditati vindictae aut avariciae. Sic monachi has res intuentur, ideoque improbant eas, aut certe obscurant earum dignitatem. Nos è contra honorifice de eis cogitemus esse dona, & ordinationes Dei traditas, primum propter hunc finem, ut haec societas conservetur docendi causa. Secundo, ut haec ipsa officia societatis sint exercitia confessionis. Tertio, ut in his operibus exerceamus timorem Dei, fidem, invocationem, dilectionem &c. Quare sciamus esse impium, has res divinas aspernari aut vilore.

## 13:1
Let every soul be subject to the higher powers, etc.

In the beginning he delivers the precept simply and clearly, that everyone should obey his own magistrate. For the particle, which are over you, is not added in vain, but excludes foreign magistrates. For there is no need for a citizen of Cologne to obey the magistrate of Paris. But Paul teaches this, that we should obey that magistrate who is over us, or that everyone should obey his own magistrate. Then he adds the reason for the precept: For there is no power but from God, which, because it teaches what a magistrate is, and from where it is, shows that one must obey in a different way than how one tolerates the unjust violence of a robber or a thief. But in such a way that we may remember both that the polity itself or the magistrate is a good thing divinely ordained, and that we may determine that this obedience is required by God, as if to his own ordinance, and there was a need in the Church for this forewarning, so that the pious might know what should be thought concerning political matters, lest they condemn empires, judgments, and other political offices, especially since many abuse these things. And a man not rightly instructed, looking at these vices, does not distinguish between empires and robberies. Thus the Pharisees condemned polities in their entirety. Monks also obscured the true doctrine concerning the magistrate, when they feigned that it is perfection to abstain from civil offices. But the contrary ought rather to have been taught, if there were any perfection. Because these works are things proposed by God, so that God may become known in society, and so that we may have exercises of confession, patience, faith, and love. To flee these exercises is infirmity rather than perfection, as it is accustomed to be said: The magistracy shows the man. Finally, in all times there are inconvenient opinions scattered in the Church concerning civil matters. Therefore it is very profitable to hold the true doctrine concerning this business. There is therefore first this proposition of Paul, that the magistrate, that is, the ordering of empires, or polity, is a good thing, which God both instituted and preserves by his own work, just as the ordering of celestial motions is both instituted by God and preserved by him. Wherefore when Paul says that empires are from God, let us understand them not only to be permitted by God, as Sins are said to be permitted (to be permissive from God, just as God is not the efficient cause of sin) but rather that they are instituted and preserved by the work of God, and confirmed by the word. Therefore Paul expressly calls the polity the ordinance of God, that is, a thing which is instituted by the counsel of God, so that it may agree with his will, or so that it may be approved by him. Wherefore sins are not the ordinance of God, nay, they are truly the dissipation of the ordinance. These things are said briefly by Paul, but they have very much importance. For first, it is necessary that this doctrine exist in the Church, so that the work of God may not be attributed to the devil, but that the works of God and the works of the devil may be discerned. Secondly, that we may understand that those very offices are proposed by God, so that they may be examples of confession, invocation, and other virtues, and may become true worships of God. Thirdly, that obedience may be confirmed, so that we may not violate the divine ordinance, but may remember that God is the avenger and preserver of his own ordinance. Fourthly, that the magistrate and all of us in civil life may have consolation, because God governs these dangers of civil life, and preserves kingdoms, civil justice, and peace in the world, and punishes tyrannies and robberies. This is a huge consolation to all the pious in such great dangers of empires, and of these The pious ought to consider the magnitude, namely that republics are shaken not only by human audacity, but much more by the fury of the devil, who is the enemy of discipline and honesty. Therefore Christ calls him a murderer, and it is written in Daniel that a good angel defended the Persian kingdom against an evil angel. The devil therefore incites his members to dissipate public harmony, and not only are the authors of the danger to be considered, but also, having been warned by this consolation of scripture, that God wishes to preserve polities, we ought to add invocation, just as scripture commands in many places. I have briefly reviewed these things, so that we may think about what this doctrine is useful for, and so that we may transfer it into use in life, and in political offices exercise confession and invocation, which are the principal ends of civil society. Then let a comparison be made. No philosophy could speak so honorably about empires. For although reason is moved by certain signs to think that empires are from God, nevertheless it doubts on account of various scandals, since it is not confirmed by the word of God. It certainly does not see that God wishes to govern our dangers in civil administration, wishes to be invoked, and the administration of these affairs to become the worship of God. Let students therefore collect from other places testimonies of Scripture, which confirm the opinion which Paul has delivered here. Let them also observe how those things are to be refuted which are objected concerning the prohibition of vengeance and others.

However, this proposition having been established, that polities are good things, which God both instituted and approves, there follows now the conclusion of Paul that the magistrate must be obeyed, because God wills that his ordinance not be violated, and a reason is added concerning punishment, which ought to be understood not only of those punishments which the magistrate inflicts, but in general of all punishments into which the seditious and contumacious fall, because they are divinely drawn to punishments, even if no danger threatens from the magistrate, as Solomon says: There is no escape for the wicked in war.

Thus far he has delivered two rules, namely that the magistrate or polity is a good thing and approved by God. Also that it must be obeyed, where he added the doctrine concerning punishment, which he will repeat later. Meanwhile he inserts a description of the magistrate, what he is, in this way: The magistrate is a minister of God to us for good, an avenger to defend rightly done deeds and to punish crimes by the sword, that is, by corporal punishments. This definition is complete, even better than the Aristotelian one, which sounds thus: The magistrate is the guardian of the Laws. For Paul added the efficient cause, namely that he is instituted by God, and in the final cause he adds an illustrious particle: for your good, where he distinguishes the Tyrant from the true magistrate. For magistrates ought to feel that they have been placed by God in this office in such a way that they consult for the utility of others, just as Aristotle advises Alexander, that he should think that the empire has happened to him for the sake of doing good to the whole human race, not so that he may be petulant and contumelious toward others ( πρὸς ἐνεργεσίαν οὐ πρὸς ὕβριν ) and Daniel says to the King: Free yourself from sin through justice, and good deeds toward the miserable. And that saying of Xenophon is praised: A good prince differs in nothing from a good father. Thus the magistrate will feel that empire and wealth have happened to him, not so that he may abuse them to satisfy his own desires, but so that he may be able to consult for the common utility, and to protect things rightly done, that is, the true worships of God, discipline, judgments, peace. But in this definition it is asked, whence do we know what things are rightly done? I answer, Paul here omits a longer description, and therefore he speaks generally, that he approves the laws of all nations concerning civil affairs, provided, however, that they agree with the Law of nature. For from this he wishes right actions in civil affairs to be judged. He therefore hands down here a third rule, namely that a Christian is not bound to the Mosaic polity, but it is permitted for him to use the laws of all nations which agree with reason. Indeed, just as a Christian owes obedience to the present magistrate, as was said above in the section: to the magistrate who presides, so he owes obedience to the present laws that are congruent with reason. Wherefore it is permitted to hang thieves, it is permitted to divide inheritances by our Laws, because the Gospel does not establish a new worldly polity, but preaches about eternal and spiritual life, and meanwhile allows us to use different polities, just as different spaces.

Whatever is against the word of God is sin: To hang a thief is against the word of God: Therefore it is sin. I respond to the major, Whatever is against the word of God, namely binding us. I deny the minor, because it is against the Mosaic judicial Law, which does not bind us of days. For because obedience is commanded toward present magistrates, it is also commanded that we use present Laws, and Luke 3 the Roman military service is approved, & Acts 15. The Apostles forbid the Gentiles from being burdened by the polity of Moses, & Paul says that in Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek.

He adds to the precept concerning obedience a necessary declaration, so that the Church may know what kind of necessity there is to obey, & what kind of sin it is not to comply, because it is often disputed whether it is a mortal sin not to obey the magistrate. And the argument is agitated that since the magistrate cannot understand eternal punishment, it seems that the edicts of magistrates do not bind under eternal punishment, but in this reasoning those who follow it do not see that they are deceived in this, that eternal punishment is inflicted on account of the violation of the divine command which prescribes obedience. For God subjected us to the magistrate, & added a command that we should obey their laws, & added concerning the punishment that He Himself would punish those who do not obey. It must therefore be established that not to obey the political magistrate or the one bearing the sword, of whom he speaks here, is a mortal sin, because Paul says expressly: It is necessary to obey, & he adds, for the sake of conscience. Therefore he feels that consciences are made guilty in those who refuse authority. Now these are mortal sins, which make the conscience guilty, & cast out faith. Thus, therefore, he declares the necessity, so that it may be understood concerning the obligation of conscience, and concerning eternal punishments. But who does not see what kind of bridle is here cast upon all men for preserving obedience toward authority.

Christians are free from the Law: Therefore from that obligation which is owed to political magistrates. I respond to the antecedent, That as far as justification in the spirit pertains, another thing is proposed on account of which we are just. This does not take away obedience in bodily life Elsewhere it is said that believers are free from the Law. Here, however, they are subjected to the laws of magistrates, and they are so subjected that Paul says they are condemned if they do not obey, but it must be known that spiritual liberty does not exclude this obligation, which remains on account of bodily life. We are free from the Law, as far as it pertains to justification in the spirit, that is, it must be felt by us that we are forgiven and we are reckoned just not on account of the Law, but on account of Christ, and yet meanwhile obedience in bodily life is necessary. For bodily life is subject to ordinances which pertain to the body, namely medical laws, marital laws. So also to civil laws. Then this obligation is to be amplified.

For if the conscience becomes guilty, there follows the curse and wrath of God, which brings present and eternal punishments, just as we manifestly see the guilty who have escaped, yet are divinely drawn back to punishments. Likewise the contumacious, even if they cannot be restrained in the present, yet afterwards fall into certain snares, so that they pay the penalty, as happened to Clodius, Catiline, Antony, and others, who had repeatedly stirred up new tumults. And God curses the counsels and businesses of such men, so that at length they fall into civil and eternal punishments. Paul embraces all these things when he says: on account of conscience. Nor indeed do these things pertain only to subjects, but also to the magistrate, who when they become tyrants, no less dissipate the ordinance of God than the seditious. Therefore their conscience also becomes guilty, because they do not obey the ordinance of God, that is, the laws which they ought to obey. Therefore the threats placed here also pertain to them, just as elsewhere the scripture says: You do not exercise the judgment of man, but of the Lord: Whatever you shall have judged, it will redound upon you. For that sentence must always be kept in view, that the polity is an ordinance of God. Therefore whoever violates whether inferior or superior, he sins, and will give account to God, as if he were to trample upon the sacraments in the temple. Therefore, let the truth of this commandment move all, lest they think the violation of the political state to be a light sin, and on the contrary let us learn that the works of public and domestic life, in those who believe in Christ, are good works and worship of God, and are not merely profane things, because society is to be preserved for this reason, that God may be made known in it. This end is not a profane thing, wherefore since all actions of political life are distinguished toward this end, God willed them to be exercises of confession, and for the sake of this end He proposed them to us. Therefore the Prophets require these works, and indeed before ceremonies, as Isaiah 1: Judge for the orphan. But here it is asked: If the violation of civil Laws is a mortal sin, what is to be thought concerning the violation of Ecclesiastical traditions, which have been established by Bishops? I answer, First, traditions which conflict with the commandment of God are not to be obeyed, whether they have arisen from Magistrates bearing the sword, or from Bishops, because God must be obeyed rather than men. Such however, there are traditions concerning celibacy, the abuse of the Mass, and the invocation of the saints. And although the eating of meats and certain other similar things are in themselves ἀδιαφορὰ, yet because they are commanded with an impious opinion and for the sake of establishing impious worship, therefore those who do not obey act rightly, just as the brothers in the history of the Maccabees acted rightly, who refused to eat swine's flesh. For there ought to exist examples of confession where doctrine has been handed down, just as Paul also refused to have Titus circumcised. Secondly, if there are traditions concerning indifferent matters and made for the sake of a political end, such as the observance of a certain day or the reading of a certain history for the sake of learning. The violation of these traditions, outside the case of scandal, is not a mortal sin, because Paul says: Let no one judge you in part of a feast day, etc. But here the example of civil laws is proposed: Why do these bind more than ecclesiastical ones? I answer most simply, Scripture hands down this diversity. It clearly says that consciences are defiled if anyone does not obey the magistrate bearing the sword. And again it clearly says that consciences are not defiled by the violation of traditions which Bishops establish, as the sayings to the Galatians and Colossians testify. Let this reason suffice for the pious. But may object. Someone asks, is greater reverence owed to civil authority? Nay, the greatest is owed to the Church and to the ministers of the Gospel, and without any doubt all who do not obey the word, which is entrusted to ecclesiastical authority, sin mortally. Secondly, those also sin mortally who in a case of scandal violate the traditions of pastors, as if someone by his own example in a rightly instituted Church invites others to contempt of the doctrine or of the ministers, but one violating without contumacy and without bad example does not sin mortally. Christ wills this liberty to exist and to be understood in the Church. Reasons can also be gathered from the difference of the powers. God has committed to magistrates that they themselves should establish just laws, therefore He also wills us to be subject to those laws: But to pastors He has delivered a certain word, nor does He will us to be legislators besides, or to add other laws: Therefore He requires that we be subject to that delivered word, not to new laws which they themselves are to add besides. Thus the difference of the powers adds some light to this question, but nevertheless it is safer to rely on the other reason, namely that apostolic doctrine demands that we hold the violation of civil laws to be a mortal sin. But on the contrary the violation of ecclesiastical of traditions, outside the case of scandal and contumacy, is not a mortal sin.

Previously he spoke in general about obedience, now he names certain duties in particular, and first tributes, by which name he includes all things which are owed to magistrates for the defense of discipline and peace, namely services, military duty, and taxes. And the praise of the office is repeated again, because he calls them ministers of God. He testifies therefore that the function of the magistrate is a good work, because the devil is an enemy of God, he is not a minister, and sins are not a function by which one ministers to God, but they offend God and dissipate the functions by which one ministers to God. And this argument becomes more illustrious when the circumstance placed above is added, namely that it is a ministry ordained by God. For it is manifest that sin is not a thing ordained by God, but rather a dissipation of the ordinance of God.

There is also added here a notable particle concerning the diligence which is required in magistrates. For Paul says: For this they are assiduous, that is, to the ministry of God, that is, to the propagation of true worship and to the defense of discipline and peace, which are divine benefits. And assiduity is a great intention of the mind, not remitting care, vigilance, and labor, just as it is most true that empires are a burden to which no human wisdom can be equal. And yet the diligence of magistrates is required, which he here calls assiduity, which with God helping is fortunate. Then he adds a general precept concerning all civil duties: Render to all their dues. By this word he embraces all duties necessary in society, namely, he commands that due obedience be rendered to superiors, he commands that due money be rendered in contracts to anyone, he commands that due duties be rendered to the family, to citizens, to parents, to a spouse, to children, to servants. But what duties are owed to individuals, the decalogue indicates, which he here repeats, so that we may hold to a certain doctrine as to which works are necessary. For it is necessary for consciences to have a certain word, even concerning works by which they may be governed, lest they invent forms of worship without the command of God, concerning which Christ says: In vain do they worship me with the commandments of men.

Some distort this sentence against the doctrine of faith, because here Paul says that the law is fulfilled by love, from which they argue thus: The fulfillment of the law justifies: Love is the fulfillment of the law: Therefore love justifies. I respond most briefly to the minor premise, the minor premise is true concerning perfect love, but not of such a kind as any men provide. Paul speaks rightly and properly concerning the Idea or the species, that love fulfills the law, that is, it is this very thing which the law requires. But from this it does not follow that the law is fulfilled by our love, because our love is unclean, and is far from perfection. Since therefore no one can provide perfect love, or fulfillment, we have need of another righteousness, namely faith apprehending the mercy promised on account of Christ. This faith is the fulfillment of the Law, namely imputatively, that is, believers are reckoned righteous, just as if they had fulfilled the Law. Then let this also be added, that faith begins the fulfillment of the Law in us, and this beginning is pleasing for this reason, because we are in Christ.

Latin:

Omnis anima potestatibus &c.

Initio simpliciter & perspicue tradit praeceptum, ut suo quisque magistratui obediat. Nam particula, quae praesunt, non est ocio se addita, sed excludit alienos magistratus. Non enim opus est civem Coloniensem obedire magistratui Parisiensi. Sed hoc docet Paulus, ut illi magistratui obediamus, qui nobis praeest, vel ut suo quisque magistratui obediat. Deinde addit rationem praecepti: Non est enim potestas nisi à Deo, quae quia docet quid sit magistratus, & unde sit ostendit aliter obediendum esse, quam quemadmodum tolerat aliquis iniustam violentiam praedonis aut latronis. Sed ita ut meminerimus & politiam ipsam seu magistratum esse rem bonam divinitus ordinatam, & statuamus hanc obedientiam à Deo requiri, tanquàm ipsius ordinationi, & fuit opus in Ecclesia hac praemunitione, ut pii scirent quid sit sentiendum de rebus politicis, ne damnarent imperia, iudicia, & alia politica officia, praesertim cum multi abutantur his. rebus. Et haec vitia intuens homo non recte institutus, non discernit imperia & latrocinia. Ita Pharisaei in totum damnabant politias. Monachi etiam obscuraverunt veram doctrinam de magistratu, cum finxerunt esse perfectionem, abstinere à civilibus officiis. At contrarium potius docendum erat, si qua esset perfectio. Quia haec opera sunt res à Deo propositae, ut iñotescat Deus in societate, & ut nos habeamus exercitia confesionis, patientiae, fidei, dilectionis. Haec exercitia fugere est potius infirmitas, quàm perfectio, sicut dici solet: Magistratus ostendit virum. Deniquè omnibus temporibus sunt in Ecclesia sparsae opiniones incommodae de rebus civilibus. Ideo valde prodest tenere veram doctrinam de hoc negocio. Est ergo primum haec propositio Pauli, quod magistratus, id est, ordinatio imperiorum, seu politia sit res bona, quam Deus suo opere & instituit et conservat, sicut ordinatio motuum caelestium et instituta est à Deo, et conservatur ab ipso. Quare cum inquit Paulus imperia à Deo esse, intelligamus ea nOn tantum permitti à Deo, sicut peccata dicuntur permitti (permissive esse àdeo, sicut Deus nOn est efficax causa peccati) sed potius opere Dei instituta esse & conservari, & per verbum confirmata esse. Ideo Paul. diserte vocat politiam ordinationem Dei, id est, rem quae instituitur cOnsilio Dei, ut congruat cum eius voluntate, seu ut approbetur ab ipso. Quare peccata nOn sunt ordinatio Dei, imo verè sunt ordinationis dissipatio. Haec breviter dicuntur à Paulo, sed plurimum habent momenti. Primum enim necesse est extare hanc doctrinam in Ecclesia, ne opus Dei tribuatur diabolo, sed ut discernantur opera Dei & opera diaboli. Secundo, Ut intelligamus illa ipsa officia à Deo proposita esse, ut sint exempla confessionis, invocationis, & caeterarum virtutum, & fiant veri cultus Dei. Tertio, Ut obedientia confirmetur, ne violemus divinam ordinationem, sed meminerimus Deum esse vindicem, & conservatorem suae ordinationis. Quarto, Ut magistr atus & nos omnes in civili vita habeamus consolationem, quòd Deus haec pericula civilis vitae gubernet, & conservet regna, iusticiam civilem, ac pacem in mundo, & puniat Tyrannides ac latrocinia. Haec est ingens cOnsolatio omnibus piis in tantis imperiorum periculis, & horum magnitudinem pii cOnsiderare debent, quod videlicet concutiantur Respubl. non tantum humana audacia, sed multo magis furore diaboli, qui est hostis disciplinae & honestatis. Ideo Christus eam vocat homicidam, & in Daniele scribitur bonus angelus defendisse regnum Persicum contra malum angelum. Incitat igitur diabolus sua membra ad dissipandam harmoniam publicam, neque tantum autores periculi considerandi sunt, sed etiam moniti hac consolatione scripturae, quod Deus velit conservare politias, addere debemus invocationem, sicut praecipit scriptura in multis locis. Haec breviter recensui, ut cogitemus, ad quid prosit haec doctrina, & ut transferamus in vita ad usum, & in politicis officiis exerceamus confessionem, & invocationem, qui sunt principales fines societatis civilis. Deinde fiat collatio. Nulla philosophia tam honorifice de imperiis loqui potuit. Etsi enim ratio movetur quibusdam signis, ut cogitet esse à Deo imperia, tamen dubitat propter varia scandala, cum non est confirmata verbo Dei. Illud certe non videt, Deum velle gubernarepericula nostra in administratione civili, velle invocari, & horum negociorum administrationem fieri cultus Dei. Colligant igitur studiosi ex aliis locis scripturae testimonia, quae confirmant sententiam, quam Paulus hic tradidit. Observent item, quomodo diluenda sint ea, quae obiiciuntur de prohibitione vindictae & alia.

Constituta autem hac propositione, quod politiae sint res bonae, quas Deus & instituit & approbat, sequitur iam conclusio Pauli quod sit obediendum magistratui, quia Deus velit suam ordinationem non violari, & addita est ratio de poena, quae debet intelligi non tantum de iis poenis, quas irrogat magistratus, sed in genere de omnibus poenis, in quas incidunt seditiosi & contumaces, quia divinitus retrahuntur ad poenas, etiamsi nihil periculi impender à magistrastu, sicut inquit Salomon: Non est evasio impio in bello.

Hactenus tradidit duas regulas, videlicet quod magistratus seu politia sit res bona & approbata à Deo. Item quod sit obediendum, ubi adiecit doctrinam de poena, quam postea repetet. Interea inserit descriptionem magistratus, quid sit, hoc modo: Magistratus est minister Dei nobis ad bonum, vindex ad defendenda recte facta & punienda delicta gladio, id est, poenis corporalibus. Haec definitio est integra, melior etiam quàm Aristotelica, quae sic sonat: Magistratus est custos Legum. Paulus enim addidit efficientem causam, scilicet quod sit institutus à Deo, & in cusa finali addit illustrem parti culam : tibi ad bonum, ubi discernit Tyrannum à vero magistratu. Debent enim magistratus sic sentire se divinitus in hoc officio collocatos esse, ut alienae utilitati consulant, sicut Aristoteles monet Alexandrum, ut cogitet imperium sibi contigisse ad benefaciendum toti generi humano, non ut in alios petulans & contumeliosus sit ( πρὸς ἐνεργεσίαν οὐ πρὸς ὕβριν) & Daniel inquit ad Regem: Libera te à peccato per iusticiam, & benefacta erga miseros. Et laudatur illud Xenophontis: Bonus princeps nihil à bono patre differt. Ita sentiet magistratus sibi contigisse imperium & opes, non ut eis abutatur ad explendas cupiditates suas, sed ut possit communi utilitati consulere, ac tueri recte sacta, id est, veros cultus Dei, disciplinam, iudicia, pacem. Sed in hac definitione quaeritur, unde scimus quae sint recte facta? Respondeo, Paulus hic omittit longiorem descriptionem, & ideo generaliter loquitur, ut leges omnium gentium approbet de civilibus negociis, si tamen consentiant cum Lege naturae. Nam hinc iudicari vult recte facta in civilibus negociis. Tradit ergo hic tertiam regulam, videlicet quod Christianus nOn sit alligatus ad politiam Mosaicam, sed liceat ei uti legibus omnium gentium, quae cOnsentiunt cum ratione. Imo sicut debet Christianus obedientiam praesenti magistratui, ut supra dictum est in particula: magistratui qui praeest, ita debet obedientiam presentibus legibus cum ratione congruentibus Quare licet fures suspendere, licet haereditates dividere nostris Legibus quia Evangelium non constituit novam politiam mundanam, sed cOncionatur de vita aeterna & spirituali, & interea sinit nos uti diversis politiis, sicut diversis spaciis

Quicquid est contra verbum Dei, peccatum est: Suspendere furem est contra verbum Dei: Ergo est peccatum. Respondeo ad maiorem, Quicquid est contra verbum Dei scilicet nos obligans. Minorem nego, quia est contra Legem Mosaicam iudicialem, quae nos non obligat dierum. Quia enim praecipitur obedientia erga praesentes magistratus, praecipitur etiam, ut praesentibus Legibus utamur, & Lucae tertio approbatur Romana militia, & Actuum. 15. Apostoli prohibent gentes onerari politia Moisi, & Paulus dicit in Christo, neque est Iudaeus neque Graecus.

Addit praecepto de obedientia necessariam declarationem, ut sciat Ecclesia, qualis necessitas sit obedire, & quale peccatum sit non obtemperare, quia saepe disputatur, utrum sit peccatum mortale, non obedire magistratui. Et ratio agitatur cum magistratus non possit intelligere poenam aeternam, videntur nec edicta magistratuum obligare sub poena aeterna, sed in hac ratione non vident illi, qui eam sequuntur, se falli in hoc quod poena aeterna irrogatur, propter violationem divini mandati, quod praecipit obedientiam. Deus enim subiecit nos magistratui, & addidit mandatum, ut obediamus illorum legibus, & adiecit de poena, se puniturum esse eos, qui non obediunt. Constituendum est igitur, quòd non obedire magistratui politico seu gerenti gladium, de quo hic loquitur, sit peccatum mortale, quia diserte inquit Paulus: Necesse est obedire, & addit, propter conscientiam. Ergo sentit conscientias fieri reas in his, qui detrectant imperium. Haec autem sunt peccata mortalia, quae conscientiam ream faciunt, & excutiunt fidem. Sic igitur declarat necessitatem, ut intelligatur de obligatione conscientiae, & de aeternis poenis. Quis autem nOn videt quale frenum hic iniiciatur omnibus hominibus ad conservandam obedientiam erga potestatem.

Christiani sunt liberi a Lege: Ergo ab illa obligatione, quae debetur magistratibus politicis. Respondeo ad antecedens, Quod ad iustificationem attinet in spiritu, alia res est proposita propter quam sumus iusti. Hoc non tollit obedientiam in vita corporali Alibi dicitur credentes esse liberosà Lege. Hic vero subiiciuntur Legibus magistratuum, & ita subiiciuntur, ut dicat Paulus eos condemnari, si non obtemperant, sed sciendum est, quod libertas spiritualis non excludit hanc obligationem, quae manet propter vitam corporalem. Liberi sumus à Lege, quod attinet ad iustisicationem in spiritu, id est, sentiendum est nobis ignosci & nos reputari iustos non propter Legem, sed propter Christum, & tamen interea obedientia in vita corporali necessaria est. Est enim corporalis vita subiecta ordinationibus quae ad corpus pertinent, videlicet Legibus medicis, coniugalibus. Ita etiam Legibus civilibus. Deinde amplisicanda est haec obligatio.

Etenim si rea fit conscientia, sequitur maledictio & ira Dei, quae affert praesentes poenas & aeternas, sicut manifestè videmus sontes elapsos, tamen divinitus ad poenas retrahi. Item contumaces, etiamsi non possunt in praesentia coherceri, tamen postea incidere in aliquos laqueos, ut dent poenas, sicut Clodio, Catilinae, Antonio, & aliis accidit, qui subinde novos tumultus excitaverant. Et Deus talium consiliis & negociis maledicit, ut tandem ruant in civiles & aeternas poenas. Haec omnia complectitur Paulus cum inquit: propter conscientiam. Nequè vero haec tantum pertinent ad subditos, sed etiam ad magistratum, qui cum fiunt Tyranni, non minus dissipant ordinationem Dei, quàm seditiosi. Ideo & ipsorum conscientia fit rea, quia non obediunt ordinationi Dei, id est, Legibus quibus debent parere. Ideo comminationes hic positae etiam ad ipsos pertinent, sicut alibi inquit scriptura: Non hominis exercetis iudicium, sed Domini: Quidquid iudicaveritis, in vos redundabit. Semper enim illa sententia intuenda est, quod politia sit ordinatio Dei. Ergo quisquis violat sive inferior, sive superior, peccat, & dabit Deo poenas, ut si in templo conculcaret sacramenta. Itaquè huius mandati se veritas moveat omnes, ne violationem politici status putent esse. leve peccatum, & è contra discamus opera vitae publicae, & oeconomicae in his, qui credunt in Christum, esse bona opera & cultus Dei, nec tantum esse res prophanas, quia ideo conservanda est societas, ut Deus in ea innotescat. Hic finis non est res prophana, quare cum omnes actiones vitae politicae sint distinctae ad hunc finem, Deus voluit eas esse exercitia confessionis, & propter hunc finem nobis proposuit ea. Ideo Prophetae requirunt haec opera, & quidem prae caeremoniis, ut Esaiae primo: Iudicate pupillo. Sed hic quaeritur: Si violatio Legum civilium est mortale peccatum, quid sentiendum est de violatione Ecclesiasticarum traditionum, quae sunt conditae ab Episcopis? Respondeo, Primum traditionibus, quae pugnant cum mandato Dei, non est obediendum, sive sint ortae à Magistratibus gerentibus gladium, sive ab Episcopis, quia Deo magis est obediendum quàm hominibus. Tales autem sunt traditiones de caelibatu, de abusu missarum, de invocatione sanctorum. Et quanquàm esus carnium, & alia quaedam similia per se sunt ἀδιαφορὰ, tamen quia praecipiuntur cum impia opinione, & ad stabiliendos impios cultus, ideo recte faciunt qui non obediunt, sicut recte faciebant fratres in historia Machabeorum, qui nolebant carnes suillas edere. Debent enim extare exempla confessionis, ubi tradita est doctrina, sicut & Paulus noluit Titium circumcidi. Secundo, si sunt traditiones de mediis rebus, & factae propter politicum finem, ut observatio certi diei, aut certae historiae lectio discendi causa. Harum traditionum violatio extra casum scandali non est peccatum mortale, quia Paulus dicit: Nemo vos arguat in parte diei festi &c. Sed hic proponitur exemplum civilium legum: Cur hae magis obligant quàm Ecclesiasticae? Respondeo fimplicissime, Scriptura tradit hanc diversitatem. Clare dicit pollui conscientias, si quis non obediat magistratui gerenti gladium. Et rursus clare dicit non pollui conscientias violatione traditionum, quas condunt Episcopi, ut testantur dicta ad Galat. & Coloss. Haec ratio sufficiat piis. Sed opponat aliquis, an maior reverentia debetur potestati civili? Imo maxima Ecclesiae & ministris Evangelii debetur, & sine ulla dubitatione peccant mortaliter omnes, qui non obediunt verbo, quod est commendatum potestati Ecclesiasticae. Secundo peccant mortaliter etiam qui in casu scandali violant pastorum traditiones, ut si quis exemplo suo in Ecclesia recte instituta, invitet alios ad contemptum doctrinae aut ministrorum, sed violans sine contumacia, & sine malo exemplo non peccat mortaliter. Hanc libertatem Christus in Ecclesia existere & intelligi vult. Possunt etiam rationes colligi ex differentia potestatum. Deus commisit magistratibus, ut ipsi iustas leges condant, Ergo vult etiam nos illis legibus subiectos esse: Sed pastoribus tradidit certum verbum, nec vult nos insuper esse legislatores, aut alias leges addere: Ergo requirit ut illi verbo tradito simus subiecti, non novis legibus, quas ipsi insuper addituri sunt. Ita differentia potestatum aliquid lucis addit huic quaestioni, sed tamen tutius est niti altera ratione, videlicet quod doctrina apostolica postulet, ut sentiamus violationem Legum civili um esse mortale peccatum. Econtra vero violationem Ecclesiasticarum traditionum, extra casum scandali, & contumaciae non esse peccatum mortale.

Antea dixit in genere de obedientia, nunc nominat in specie quaedam officia, ac primum tributa, quo nomine complectitur omnia, quae debentur magistratibus ad defensionem disciplinae & pacis, scilicet operas, militiam, stipendia. Estque iterum repetita laus officii, quia vocat ministros Dei. Testatur igitur functionem magistratus esse bonum opus, quia diabolus est hostis Dei, non est minister, & peccata non sunt functio, qua Deo ministratur, sed offendunt Deum, & dissipant functiones, quibus Deo ministratur. Fitque hoc argumentum illustrius, cum additur circumstantia supra posita, videlicet quod sit ministerium divinitus ordinatum. Manifestum est enim, peccatum non esse rem ordinatam divinitus, sed potius dissipationem ordinationis Dei.

Addita est etiam hic particula insignis de diligentia, quae requiritur in magistratibus. Ait enim Paulus: Ad hoc sunt assidui, id est, ad ministerium Dei, hoc est, ad propagationem veri cultus, & ad defensionem disciplinae & pacis, quae sunt beneficia divina. Et assiduitas est magna intentio animi, non remitttentis curam, vigilantiam, & laborem, sicut verissimum est imperia esse onus, cui nulla humana sapientia par esse potest. Et tamen requiritur magistratuum diligentia, quam hic vocat assiduitatem, quae Deo iuvante est fortunata. Deinde addit generale praeceptum de omnibus civilibus officiis: Reddite omnibus debita. Hac voce complectitur omnia officia in societate necessaria, videlicet iubet reddi debitam obedientiam superioribus, iubet reddi debitam pecuniam in contractibus cuicunque, iubet reddi debita officia familiae, civibus parentibus, coniugi, liberis, servis. Quae autem sint officia singulis debita, decalogus indicat, quem hic repetit, ut teneamus certam doctrinam, quae opera sint necessaria. Necesse est enim conscientias habere verbum certam, etiam de operibus quo regantur, ne fingant cultus sine mandato Dei, de quibus inquit Christus: Frustra colunt me mandatis hominum.

Hanc sententiam detorquent nonnulli contra doctrinam de fide, quia hic Paulus inquit dilectione legem impleri, unde sic argumentantur: Impletio legis iustificat: Dilectio est impletio legis: Ergo dilectio iustificat. Respondeo brevissime ad minorem, Minor est vera de perfecta dilectione, sed non de tali, qualem ulli homines praestant. Paulus recte & proprie loquitur de Idea seu de specie, quod dilectio impleat legem, id est, sit hoc ipsum, quod lex requirit. Sed hinc non sequitur nostra dilectione legem impleri, quia nostra dilecto est immunda, & procul abest à perfectione. Cum igitur nemo possit praestare perfectam dilectionem, aut impletionem, opus est nobis alia iusticia, videlicet fide apprehendente misericordiam promissam propter Christum. Haec fides est impletio Legis, scilicet imputative, hoc est, credentes reputantur iusti, perinde ac si Legem implessent. Deinde addatur etiam hoc, quod fides inchoet impletionem Legis in nobis, & haec inchoatio placet propterea, quia sumus in Christo.

## 13:11
That it is timely, that we now from sleep &c.

He adds an exhortation taken from the circumstance of time, namely from the occasion: Now salvation has been exhibited: the Gospel has been revealed. Wherefore let us not despise so great a gift, but let us greedily embrace and obey. Thus he often argues elsewhere from time ii. Corinth. vi.Ebr. iii. Such a time is, whenever God gives the true light of the Gospel, which, after Christ was exhibited, was widely scattered among the nations, whereas before they had been ignorant of the promises and the Gospel. He understands sleep as ignorance of true doctrine, but the vigils must be the new knowledge of the Gospel, and new actions. And because He commands us to wake up, He signifies that we are called to immense struggles, dangers, and vigilance. But on the contrary, the world, having heard the Gospel, becomes more sluggish and is lulled into a new sleep. For security begets negligence, by which various vices creep in little by little. He censures this negligence when He commands us to wake up; therefore, He afterwards commands us to be clothed with the armor of light. For He signifies that there is need of a great struggle, lest we fall away. Moreover, the armor of light is the very knowledge of the word of God, the recognition of God, faith, and the other virtues, which, using the word of God, fight against the devil. On the contrary, the works of darkness are ignorance of God, and the vices which ignorance begets. For there the devil rules.

Salvation is nearer to us now than then.

Let salvation be understood concerning Christ Himself, and concerning the ministry of the Gospel, not concerning the effect, that is, Christ Himself is now exhibited, and the remission of sins is openly promulgated and given and in the instituted ministry of the Gospel. But the Fathers were expecting, and believed that Christ was to come. Thus salvation is nearer to us, because Christ has been exhibited, and the remission of sins has been promulgated, and the ministry of the Gospel has been instituted. For the Fathers knew that Christ was to come, and they acknowledged the remission of sins wrapped up in the promises, but they did not yet have an instituted ministry by which it was expressly commanded that sins be remitted. Furthermore, concerning the effect, it must be known that the Fathers were saved by faith in the promised Christ, just as the Church is saved after Christ has been exhibited. Nor is there another salvation for the Fathers and the Church after Christ has been exhibited, but this is the only dissimilarity, that they believed in the Christ who was to come, we in the one who has been exhibited.

Latin:

Quod tempestivum sit, nos iam a somno &c.

Addit exhortationem à circumstantia temporis sumptam, videlicet ab occasione: Nunc exhibita est salus: Evangelium revelatum est. Quare non aspernemur tantum munus, sed avide amplectamur atque obediamus. Ita saepe ali âs à tempore argumentatur ii. Corinth. vi.Ebr. iii. Tale tempus est, quandocunque Deus donat veram lucem Evangelii, quae postquàm exhibitus est Christus, late sparsa est inter gentes, cum antea ignorassent promissiones & Evangelium. Somnum intelligit ignorantiam verae doctrinae, Vigiliae vero debent esse nova notitia Evangelii, & novae actiones. Et quia iubet nos expergisci, significat vocari nos ad ingentia certamina, pericula, vigilantiam. At ècontra mundus audito Evangelio fit segnior, & novo somno sopitur. Securitas enim parit negligentiam, qua paulatim obrepunt varia vitia. Hanc negligentiam taxat cum iubet nos expergisci, Ideo postea iubet indui arma lucis. Significat enim opus esse magno certamine, ne excidamus. Sunt autem arma lucis ipsa notitia verbi Dei, agnitio Dei, fides & caeterae virtutes, quae utentes verbo Dei pugnant adversus diabolum. Econtra opera tenebrarum sunt ignorantia Dei, & vitia quae parit ignorantia. Ibi enim dominatur diabolus.

Propius adest nobis salus quam tum.

Salus de ipso Christo intelligatur, & de ministerio Evangelii, non de effectu, id est, ipse Christus nunc exhibitus est, & palam promulgata & donata remissio peccatorum & in stitutum ministerium Evangelii. Patres vero expectabant, & credebant venturum esse Christum. Ita propior est nobis salus, quia Christus est exhibitus, & promulgata remissio peccatorum, et institutum ministerium Evangelii. Patres enim sciebant venturum esse Christum, & remissionem peccatorum agnoscebant involutam in promissionibus, sed nondum habebant ministerium institutum, quo expresse mandatum esset remitti peccata. Caeterum de effectu sciendum est, Patres fide in Christum promissum salvatos esse, sicut Ecclesia salvatur post exhibitum Christum. Nec est alia salvatio Patrum & Ecclesiae post exhibitum Christum, sed tantum haec est dissimilitudo, quod illi credebant in venturum Christum, nos in exhibitum.

## 13:14
But put on the Lord Jesus &c.

To put on Christ does not signify only imitation, as if to say to put on the adornment of Christ, that is, to imitate his virtues, but it signifies more, namely to apprehend Christ, that on account of him the Father is propitious to us, Item that he is efficacious in those who call upon him. For Christ is not only an example, as are the other saints, but he is the cause and author of our salvation, the victim and savior. Wherefore, to put on should be referred to both, namely that we apprehend him by faith as savior, and acknowledge him to be the shade by which we are covered against the wrath of God. Then let imitation follow.

τῆς σὰρκος πρόνοιας μη ποιεῖσαι that is, take care of your bodies according to the ordinance of God. He prohibits immoderate abstinence, which was customary in those times.

εἰς ἐπιθυμίας , that is, not for luxuries or illicit pleasures to nourish concupiscence.

Latin:

Sed induamini Dominum Ie-sum &c.

Induere Christum non significat tantum imitationem, q. d. induere ornatum Christi, id est, virtutes imitari, sed plus significat, scilicet apprehendere Christum, quod propter ipsum sit nobis pater propitius, Item quòd sit efficax in iis, qui eum invocant. Nam Christus non tantum est exemplum, ut reliqui sancti, sed est causa & autor nostrae salutis, victima & salvator. Quare induere referatur ad utrumque, videlicet quod fide apprehendamus eum tanquàm salvatorem, & agnoscamus eum esse umbraculum, quo tegimur adversus iram Dei. Deinde accedat imitatio.

τῆς σὰρκος πρόνοιας μη ποιεῖσαιid est, curate corpora iuxta ordinationem Dei. Prohibet immoderatam abstinentiam, quae illis temporibus eerat usitata.

εἰς ἐπιθυμίας, id est, non ad luxus aut illicitas voluptates ad alendam concupiscentiam.

## 14:1 Argument
CHAPTER XIV.

It was said before that there are three kinds of works: private, political, and ceremonies, and since most useful precepts have been handed down above concerning the others, now the doctrine concerning ceremonies is handed down. For because this life cannot be without ceremonies, that is, some ordinances of times or of certain executions, it is necessary for the Church to be admonished concerning the use of them. For error concerning ceremonies produces many huge inconveniences.

First, the doctrine of the Gospel concerning faith and the benefit of Christ is obscured when the opinion creeps in that such observances merit the remission of sins, or that on account of them we are righteous, just as the Jews imagined concerning their rites. This opinion naturally occupies minds, unless they are rightly taught from the Gospel.

Second, the doctrine concerning the difference of works is extinguished, because ceremonies are preferred to political life; indeed, they are even preferred to interior spiritual exercises, to patience and invocation. Just as the monks called their observances perfections.

Third, the opinion of necessity creeps in, which is a dangerous torture of consciences.

Fourth, the opinion of necessity begets incurable discords, just as there were once discords concerning the Passover.

Fifth, authority to establish new forms of worship is falsely attributed to Bishops, when the true use of ceremonies is ignored. Thus the doctrine of the New Testament is obscured, and impiety is confirmed, and the tyranny of the Bishops is increased.

Therefore, since the error concerning ceremonies produces such and so many inconveniences, it is necessary that the use be rightly taught. Therefore Paul here in summary teaches this: That neither Mosaic ceremonies, nor similar ones instituted by men, are necessarily to be observed, because the righteousness, about which the Gospel preaches, is not the observation of Mosaic or similar rites, but is the acknowledgment of Christ, a new and spiritual life in the heart. Meanwhile, however, in the exterior life, just as one may use other spaces of days at other times, so one may use other rites at other times. Therefore, it does not wish for the opinion of righteousness or necessity to be attached to rites, nor does it wish for discords to be sown concerning rites, whether Mosaic or human. This is the sum of this chapter, which does not speak of the sacraments, which have a commandment, because they are signs added to the promises. Likewise, they are testimonies of confession, but here it is also useful for human traditions to be distinguished. There are, therefore, three kinds. The first kind is of traditions which command something that cannot be performed without sin. Such is the tradition concerning celibacy, when it is imposed upon those who are not suitable. Likewise, the propagation of masses, the worship of saints. Concerning this kind, the rule must be held: It is necessary to obey God rather than men. Wherefore such traditions are violated by divine authority. The second kind is of traditions which make regulations concerning such things as are by their nature ἀδιάφορα, such as concerning days, clothing, foods. In These ends are to be considered. If the end is political, traditions are lawful, as when holidays are observed, not because that work is worship, but for the sake of order, so that the people may know at what time they are to assemble to hear the Gospel, and for the Lord's Supper. For because man naturally understands order, and ought to distribute his actions by order. Therefore, ecclesiastical actions also ought to have their own order, nor can life be without such rites and ordinances, which conduce to εὐταξίαν. Therefore also Paul commands that all things be done in the churches decently and in good order.

The third kind of tradition is when to ἀδιάφορα there is added an opinion of worship, merit, or necessity. Such traditions obscure the doctrine of the Gospel, and the added opinion makes out of ἀδιαφόροις impious traditions. Therefore they are rightly violated and abolished, so that that false opinion may be corrected, because it is necessary that errors concerning worship, merits, and necessity be cast away. Moreover, worship is such a work, whose immediate end is not bodily utility, but that through that work God may be affected with honor, just as concerning the distinction of foods the people think this work is done for this reason, because it is an honor, which God requires or approves.

Of these Christ says: in vain do they worship me with the commandments of men. And frequently there is added an opinion of merit, which has a more manifest impiety, namely that such a work merits the remission of sins, or eternal life, that it is righteousness, that it is perfection, that it is satisfaction. These errors must necessarily be reproved. The opinion of necessity is when a violation is thought to be a mortal sin. The Gospel also condemns this opinion, according to that: Let no one judge you in food, drink, etc. It must therefore be held that the Gospel has ordained this liberty in those things which are granted by the word of God, and does not wish righteousness or sin to be established in such things.

It is useful to remember these kinds of traditions, so that it may be known how traditions are rejected, or the use of which ones can be retained. Here it is necessary also to speak about Christian liberty. I make, however, for the sake of teaching, four degrees of Christian liberty.

The first is that not on account of the Law or our virtues, but freely on account of Christ, is the remission of sins, and the imputation of righteousness, or eternal life granted, provided that we believe these things happen to us on account of Christ.

Christ preaches concerning this degree: If the Son shall make you free, you shall be free indeed.

The second degree is that in the remission of sins the Holy Spirit is given, who may help us so that we may begin to obey the Law of God, and may rule and defend us against the snares of the devil. This degree is joined with the former, but I distinguish it in the enumeration so that the benefits of Christ may be more clearly seen. To this pertains the saying of Paul: Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty. For He directs hearts, lest they be oppressed by the terrors of sin, or by other terrors, or by death. He also impels them to begin to obey God, as it is said elsewhere: The Holy Spirit helps our infirmity.
