This liberty will be complete after the resurrection, yet in the meantime it must be begun in this life, in the exercises of faith and invocation. And in these exercises it is understood and grows, when we sustain ourselves with the Word of God, so that we may overcome terrors and sorrows. These two degrees are principally Christian liberty, and they pertain to the spiritual and eternal life, which nevertheless must be begun in this life, and the knowledge of them brings great consolation to the pious.

The third degree is that the Gospel frees us from ceremonies and forensic, or judicial laws of Moses. This degree in some way pertains to the exterior life, but it has its cause in the things above. For the Gospel does not require Levitical ceremonies for this reason, because it teaches that we are pronounced righteous, not on account of those cults, or our other works, but by faith through mercy on account of Christ. And since the Gospel teaches concerning the spiritual and perpetual righteousness of the heart, it does not require the polity and forensic laws of Moses, but it grants in this bodily life the use of the laws of all polities in which we live, provided that they are agreeable to reason, just as it grants the use of the architecture or medicine of all nations. But here someone might ask: Since the Gospel abrogates the Law of Moses, why does it not also abrogate the Decalogue? Especially since that part of the law is the most difficult. I answer, first most crudely, the Decalogue is not retained because it is written in the Law of Moses, but the carnal must be restrained by the moral Law because it is the common Law of all men. The regenerate, however, begin to obey that law, not because it is a Mosaic πολίτευμα, but because the Gospel preaches repentance and brings the Holy Spirit, who initiates spiritual cults in us. The Decalogue is therefore retained, that is, That law is common to all men, because it both convicts sins and teaches spiritual worships. This is a very crude response, which although it is true, yet nothing has been said about this matter as of yet. It is necessary, therefore, to add the principal cause and the doctrine concerning the abrogation of the law, or concerning liberty, namely first, that as far as justification pertains, the Gospel truly frees us from the whole law, that is, it teaches us that we are pronounced righteous on account of another, namely on account of Christ, not on account of the law. Wherefore those believing in Christ have the remission of sins, and are righteous, even if there still clings in them an infirmity, which causes them not to satisfy the law. And the principal cause, on account of which the abrogation of the law must be handed down, is this very thing, that consciences must be rightly taught concerning justification. Therefore it is necessary to add this response to the former. Secondly, Although we are freed as far as justification pertains, yet the law is not taken away, as far as obedience pertains, because the Gospel preaches repentance, and subjects us to God, and begins in us spiritual obedience. Wherefore it is necessary that those worships be begun, which are contained in the law moral. And yet because we do not satisfy the law, meanwhile it teaches us to be righteous by another thing, namely on account of Christ through faith. Thus it frees consciences from that horrible burden, namely terrors, and condemnation, which the law would bring, since we would not satisfy it, unless we were freed and righteous on account of something else. Paul teaches this, when he says that we have been freed from the curse of the law. For he says expressly from the curse, so that he may signify that liberation from the law is liberation from the terrors, and from the condemnation which the law brings, unless by faith we apprehend the mercy promised on account of Christ. From these it can be understood in some way, that we have been freed from the whole law, as far as justification pertains, and yet it is necessary that obedience be begun.

The fourth degree of Christian liberty is, that the Gospel, although it concedes that some ordinances of times, or of exercises in the Church be done for εὐταξίαν, nevertheless wishes us to feel that those observations are not acts of worship, do not merit the remission of sins, are not righteousness or perfection, Item outside the case of scandal they can be omitted without sin. Concerning this degree Paul teaches in Colossians: Let no one judge you in food, drink, etc. Nor does he speak only of Mosaic rites, but in general of Mosaic and of all other ceremonies which are instituted by human authority in the Church. Therefore, he later expressly names human traditions, saying: according to the precepts and doctrines of men, and the knowledge of this degree is quite necessary for the Churches, to avoid many errors. For because men are naturally prone to false worships, and in dangers they flee to their own righteousness or merits, by error they devise and accumulate worships. Therefore it is necessary for the Churches to be forewarned, so that they may truly understand the doctrine concerning faith, and concerning true invocation, and the worship of faith, and may know that worships instituted without a divine command are displeasing to God. David says concerning the Levitical ones: For if you had desired, I would have given sacrifice, you will certainly not be delighted with burnt offerings. In this verse he signifies that human minds in terrors seek sacrifices, but he recalls them from works to faith, and the acknowledgment of mercy. Since this is said concerning Levitical sacrifices, how much more must the opinion of worship or merit be taken away from human traditions. If anyone were now to restore circumcision, or Levitical burnt offerings, we would all deservedly abhor him. Thus we ought to abhor the Monastic life, and the ceremonies of the impious, which are performed with the opinion of worship or merit. This comparison must be proposed to the pious, so that they may more firmly establish that those forms of worship are to be disapproved and avoided. But I have reviewed above several reasons for which there is need in the Church for the knowledge of liberty concerning this fourth degree. For even the opinion of necessity becomes a dangerous torment of consciences. Wherefore it is useful for this rule to exist, that outside the case of scandal, traditions made in the Church by human authority can be omitted without sin, even if they do not command any impious work, and yet in the meantime the pious are to be taught in rightly instituted Churches, that with a free mind they should observe useful rites for the sake of example and good order, because this bodily life cannot be without certain ordinances, as is evident.

Concerning Scandal.

Scandal signifies an offense, which deters minds, or invites to imitation. It is, however, twofold. The other kind is called Pharisaical scandal, that is, an offense which hypocrites conceive on account of true doctrine, or a deed which God requires or approves, by which offense hypocrites are incited to hatred of true doctrine and of the pious. That scandal cannot be avoided, nor do the pious sin on account of such fury of the impious. Indeed, it is necessary to obey the command of God, against the judgments and hatreds of the impious, because Paul says: If anyone preaches another Gospel, let him be anathema. And the pious must be diligently instructed, and fortified, so that hypocrites do not deter them from the profession, when they object the dangers, commotions, and dissipations which follow persecution. Against these terrors it is necessary for minds to be well fortified, lest, having become weakened, they cast away the truth. The other kind of scandal is impious doctrine, or an evil deed, or an indifferent one petulantly undertaken among the weak, by which they are deterred from the Gospel, or in any way their minds are wounded. These scandals must be avoided, but the most harmful of all is impious doctrine, because it injures the glory of God, and destroys the souls of the hearers. Furthermore, any manifest evil deed is a scandal, because evil examples invite others to imitation, and diminish the reverence of God, and often cause the Church itself and the doctrine he may be spoken ill of, and moderate men may be deterred from true doctrine, just as the doctrine would have been spoken ill of, if Joseph had committed adultery. On the contrary, however, his continence was in many ways glorious to pious doctrine, and brought huge benefits to the whole kingdom. Since this example is illustrious, it shows how much it matters to avoid scandals of this kind, and that we should remember that all our deeds pertain not only to us, but also to the glory of God, as it is written: Because of you the name of God is spoken ill of among the gentiles. Rom. 2. Finally, in the use of indifferent things, petulance must be avoided, lest indifferent customs be changed among those who either have not yet heard the doctrine concerning liberty, or are still weaker, so that there is a danger that, moved by the change of such customs, they may be deterred from the Gospel, and yet they do not persecute pious doctrine, but are teachable. But after the doctrine has been handed down, and hypocrites oppose themselves, it is right that examples of liberty be shown to them, and these examples are a part of confession, Galat. 1. Thus the Apostles violated Pharisaical traditions.

Furthermore, him who is weak.

About to speak concerning the use of ceremonies and concerning liberty, he places at the beginning an admonition concerning tolerating the weak. He delivers, moreover, a precept which is to be used not against impious persecutors, enemies of the Gospel, but toward our members, that is, toward those who allow themselves to be taught and hear the Gospel; these he forbids to be deterred by unusual examples, so that they might not embrace the Gospel. He calls him weak in faith, not yet sufficiently learned in the doctrine of liberty. Furthermore, when he says he must be supported, lest he fall into doubts, he warns of both: that he not be forced to do anything against conscience, or with a disapproving conscience. Also, that he may be gradually advanced, and instructed, and freed from doubt. For doubt in any article whatsoever, if it is not corrected but increases, is a horrible plague, and shakes off faith, and summons despair, hatred of the whole Gospel, and manifest impiety, just as happened to Julian and many others.

Latin:

CAPUT. XIIII.

Dictum est antea tria esse genera operum, privata, politica, caeremonias, cumque de caeteris supra utilissima praecepta tradita sint, nunc doctrina de caeremoniis traditur. Quia enim haec vita non potest carere caeremoniis, hoc est, ordinationibus aliquibus temporum, aut certarum executionum, necesse est Ecclesiam admoneri de usu earum. Nam error de caeremoniis parit multa ingentia incommoda.

Primum, obscuratur doctrina Evangelii de fide & beneficio Christi cum obrepit opinio, quod tales observationes mereantur remissionem peccatorum, aut quod propter eas simus iusti, sicut imaginabantur Iudaei de suis ritibus. Haec opinio naturaliter occupat animos, nisi ex Evangelio recte doceantur.

Secundum, Extinguitur doctrina de differentia operum, quia caeremoniae anteferuntur vitae politicae, Imo anteferuntur etiam interioribus exercitiis spiritualibus, patientiae & invocationi. Sicut monachi suas observationes vocarunt perfectiones.

Tertium, Obrepit opinio necessitatis, quae est periculosa carnificina conscientiarum.

Quartum, Opinio necessitatis gignit discordias insanabiles, sicut olim de paschate fuerunt discordiae.

Quintum, Falso tribuitur Episcopis autoritas condendi novos cultus, cum ignoratur verus usus caeremoniarum. Ita obscuratur novi testamenti doctrina, et confirmatur impietas, & augetur tyrannis Episcoporum.

Proinde cum error de caeremoniis pariat tanta & tam multa incommoda, necesse est recte tradi usum. Ideo Paulus hic in summa docet hoc: Nec Mosaicas caerimonias, nec similes ab hominibus institutas necessario observandas esse, quia iusticia, de qua concionatur Evangelium, non est observatio rituum Mosaicorum aut similium, sed est agnitio Christi, nova & spiritualis vita in corde. Interea vero in vita exteriore, sicut aliâs aliis spaciis dierum, ita aliis ritibus aliâs uti licet. Ideo non vult affingi ritibus opinionem iusticiae aut necessitatis, nec vult seri discordias de ritibus seu Mosaicis, seu humanis. Haec est summa huius capitis, quod non loquitur de sacramentis, quae babent praeceptum, quia sunt signa addita promissionibus. Item sunt testimonia confessionis, sed hic etiam prodest discerni traditiones humanas. Sunt igitur tria genera. Primum genus est traditionum, quae praecipiunt aliquid, quod non potest sine peccato praestari. Talis est traditio de caelibatu, cum iis imponitur, qui non sunt idonei. Item propagatio missarum, cultus sanctorum. De hoc genere tenenda est regula: Oportet Deo magis obedire, quàm hominibus. Quare tales traditiones antoritate divina violantur. Alterum genus est traditionum, quae constituunt de talibus, quae sua natura sunt ἀδιάφορα, ut deferiis, vestitu, cibis. In his considerandi sunt fines. Si finis est politicus, sunt licitae traditiones, ut cum feriae servantur, non quod opus illud sit cultus, sed ordinis caussa, ut populus sciat quo tempore conveniendum est ad audiendum Evangelium, & ad cenam domini. Quia enim homo naturaliter intelligit ordinem, & ordine debet actiones suas distribuere. Ideo etiam actiones Ecclesiasticae suum ordinem hahere debent, nec potest vita talibus ritibus carere & ordinationibus, quae conducunt ad εὐταξίαν. Ideo & Paulus praecipit ut omnia fiant in Ecclesiis decenter & bono ordine.

Tertium genus est traditionum, cum ad ἀδιάφορα accedit opinio, cultus, meriti, aut necessitatis. Tales traditiones obscurant doctrinam Evangelii, & opinio accedens facit ex ἀδιαφόροις impias traditiones. Ideo recte violantur & abolentur, ut illa opinio falsa corrigatur, quia necesse est errores de cultu, meritis, et necessitate abiici. Est autem cultus tale opus, cuius finis immediatus est non corporalis utilitas, sed ut per id opus Deus honore afficiatur, sicut de discrimine ciborum sentit populus hoc opus ideo fieri, quia sit honos, quem requirat aut approbet Deus.

De his inquit Christus: frustra colunt me mandatis hominum. Et plerunque accedit opinio meriti, quae habet manifestiorem impietatem, videlicet quòd tale opus mereatur remissionem peccatorum, aut vitam aeternam, quod sit iusticia, sit perfectio, sit satisfactio. Hi errores necessario reprehendendi sunt. Opinio necessitatis est, cum violatio putatur esse peccatum mortale. Hanc opinionem etiam damnat Evangelium, iuxta illud: Nemo vos arguat in cibo, potu &c. Sentiendum est igitur, quod Evangelium ordinaverit hanc libertatem in iis, quae sunt concessa à verbo Dei, nec velit in talibus iusticiam aut peccatum constitui.

Haec genera traditionum meminisse prodest, ut sciatur quomodo reiiciantur traditiones, aut quarum usus retineri possit. Hic necesse est etiam dici de libertate Christiana. Facio autem docendi causa quotuor gradus libertatis Christianae.

Primus est, quod non propter Legem aut nostras virtutes, sed gratis propter Christum donatur remissio peccatorum, & imputatio iusticiae, vel vita aeterna, modo ut credamus haec nobis contingere propter Christum.

De hoc gradu concionatur Christus: Si vos filius liberaverit, vere liberi eritis.

Secundus gradus est, quod in remissione peccatorum donatur spiritus sanctus, qui adiuvet nos, ut obedire Legi Dei incipiamus, regat & defendat nos adversus insidias diaboli. Hic gradus cum superiori coniunctus est, sed ideo in enumeratione discerno, ut magis conspici beneficia Christi possint. Huc pertinet dictum Pauli: Ubi spiritus domini, ibi libertas est. Is enim irigit corda, ne opprimantur terroribus peccati, aut aliis terroribus, aut morte. Impellit etiam ut incipiant obedire Deo, sicut alibi dicitur: Spiritus sanctus adiuvat infirmitatem nostram. Haeclibertas erit integra post resurrectionem, interea tamen in hac vita inchoari eam oportet, in exercitiis fidei & invocationis. Et in his exercitiis intelligitur & crescit, cum sustentamus nos verbo Dei, ut vincamus terrores ac dolores. Hi duo gradus principaliter sunt Christiana libertas, & pertinent ad vitam spiritualem & aeternam, quae tamen in hac vita inchoanda est, & eorum cognitio magnam consolationem piis adfert.

Tertius gradus est, quod Evangelium liberat nos à caeremoniis & forensibus, seu iudicialibus Legibus Moisi. Hic gradus aliquo modo pertinet ad exteriorem vitam, sed habet causam in superioribus Ideo enim Evangelium non requirit caeremonias Leviticas, quia docet nos iustos pronunciari, non propter illos cultus, aut alia nostra opera, sed fide per misericordiam propter Christum. Et cum Evangelium doceat de spirituali & perpetua iusticia cordis, non requirit politiam, & Leges forenses Moisi, sed concedit in hac vita corporali uti legibus omnium politiarum, in quibus vivimus, modo ut sint consentaneae rationi, sicut concedit omnium gentium architectonica, aut medicina uti. Sed hic quaerataliquis: Cum Evangelium abroget Legem Moisi, cur non etiam decalogum abrogat? praesertim cum illa pars legis sit difficillima. Respondeo, Primum crassissim̀, Non retinetur decalogus, quia in Lege Moisi scriptus est, sed carnales cohercendi sunt Lege morali quia est Lex communis omnium hominum. Renati vero incipiunt obedire illi legi, non quia est Mosaicum πολίτευμα, sed quia Evangelium praedicat paenitentiam, & affert spiritum sanctum, qui spirituales cultus in nobis inchoat. Retinetur ergo decalogus, hoc est, Lex illa communis omnium hominum, quia & arguit peccata, & docet spirituales cultus. Haec est crassissima responsio, quae &si vera est, tamen nondum de hac re dictum est. Necesse est igitur adiici principalem causam, & doctrinam de abrogatione legis, vel de libertate, videlicet primum, quod ad iustificationem attinet, Evangelium vere liberat nos à tota lege, id est, docet nos pronunciari iustos propter aliud, scilicet propter Christum, non propter legem. Quare credentes in Christum habent remissionem peccatorum, &, sunt iusti, etiamsi adhuc haeret in eis infirmitas, quae facit ne satisfaciant legi. Ac principalis caussa, propter quam tradenda est legis abrogatio, haec ipsa est, quod oportet conscientias de iustificatione recte doceri. Ideo hanc responsionem adiici necesse est ad priorem. Secundo, Etsi sumus liberati quod ad iustificationem attinet, tamen lex non est sublata, quod ad obedientiam attinet, quia Evangelium praedicat paenitentiam, & subiicit nos Deo, & inchoat in nobis spiritualem obedientiam. Quare necesse est inchoari illos cultus, qui continentur in lege morali. Et tamen quia non satisfacimus legi, interea docet nos iustos esse alia re, scilicet propter Christum fide. Ita liberat conscientias ab illo horribili onere, scilicet terroribus, & damnatione, quam lex afferret, cum ei non satisfaciamus, nisi liberati essemus ac iusti propter aliud. Hoc docet Paulus, cum inquit nos à maledictione legis liberatos esse. Dicit enim diserte à maledictione, ut significet liberationem à lege, esse liberationem à terroribus, & à damnatione quam lex affert, nisi fide apprehendamus misericordiam propter Christum promissam. Ex his utcunque intelligi potest, quod à tota lege liberati simus, quod ad iustificationem attinet, & tamen obedientiam inchoari necesse sir.

Quartus gradus Christianae libertatis est, quod Evangelium &si concedit aliquas ordinationes temporum, aut exercitiorum in Ecclesia propter εὐταξίαν fieri, tamen vult nos sentire observationes illas non esse cultus, non mereri remissionem peccatorum, non esse iusticiam aut perfectionem, Item extra casum scandali posse eas omitti sine peccato. De hoc gradu docet Paulus ad Colossenses: Nemo vos iudicet in cibo, potu &c. Nec loquitur tantum de Mosaicis ritibus, sed in genere de Mosaicis & de omnibus aliis caeremoniis, quae humana autoritate instituuntur in Ecclesia. Ideo postea expresse nominat humanas traditiones, inquiens: iuxta praecepta & doctrinas hominum, estque huius gradus cognitio admodum necessaria Ecclesiis, ad multos errores cavendos. Quia enim homines naturaliter proni sunt ad falsos cultus, & in periculis confugiunt ad suam iusticiam aut merita, errore excogitant & cumulant cultus. Ideo necesse est Ecclesias praemoneri, ut vere intelligant doctrinam de fide, & de vera invocatione, & cultum fidei, & sciant Deo displicere cultus institutos sine mandato divino. David de Leviticis dicit: Quoniam si voluisses, sacrificium dedissem, utique holocaustis non delectaberis. In hoc versu significat humanas mentes in terroribus quaerere sacrificia, sed revocat eas ab operibus ad fidem, & agnitionem misericordiae. Hoc cum de sacrificiis Leviticis dicatur, quanto magis detrahenda est humanis traditionibus opinio cultus aut meriti. Si quis nunc restitueret circumcisionem, aut Levitica holocausta, omnes eum merito abominaremur. Sic abominari debemus Monasticam, et caeremonias impiorum, quae fiunt cum opinione cultus aut meriti. Haec similitudo piis proponenda est, ut firmius statuant, illos cultus improbandos & fugiendos esse. Sed recensui supra plures causas, propter quas opus est Ecclesiae cognitione libertatis de hoc quarto gradu. Nam & opinio necessitatis fit periculosa carnificina conscientiarum. Quare prodest extare hanc regulam, quod extra casum scandali traditiones in Ecclesia factae humana autoritate sine peccato omitti possint, etiamsi non praecipiunt aliquod impium opus, & tamen interim pii docendi sunt in Ecclesiis recte institutis, ut libero animo propter exemplum & bonum ordinem servent utiles ritus, quia haec vita corporalis non potest carere certis ordinationibus, ut constat.

De Scandalo.

Scandalum significat offensionem, quae deterret animos, vel invitat ad imitationem. Est autem duplex. Alterum genus vocatur Pharisaicum scandalum, id est offensio, quam concipiunt hypocritae propter veram doctrinam, aut factum, quod Deus requirit vel approbat, qua offensione incitantur hypocritae ad odium verae doctrinae & piorum. Id scandalum non potest vitari, nec peccant pii propter talem furorem impiorum. Imo necesse est obedire mandato Dei, contra impiorum iudicia & odia, quia Paulus inquit: Si quis aliud Evangelium praedicaverit, anathema sit. Ac diligenter erudiendi sunt pii, & muniendi, ne hypocritae deterreant eos à professione, cum obiiciunt pericula, motus, dissipationes, quae sequuntur persecutionem. Adversus hos terrores oportet animos bene munitos esse, ne languefacti abiiciant veritatem. Alterum genus scandali est impia doctrina, aut factum malum, aut indifferens petulanter susceptum apud infirmos, quo deterrentur ab Evangelio, vel quocunquè modo sauciantur eorum animi. Haec scandala sunt cavenda, sed nocentissimum omnium est impia doctrina, quia laedit gloriam Dei, & perdit auditorum animos. Deinde quodlibet factum malum manifestum est scandalum, quia mala exempla invitant alios ad imitationem, & minuunt reverentiam Dei, & saepe faciunt, ut ipsa Ecclesia & doctrina male audiat, & deterreantur moderati homines à vera doctrina, sicut male audisset doctrina, si Ioseph commisissit adulterium. Econtra vero eius continentia multis modis fuit gloriosa piae doctrinae, & attulit ingentia commoda toti regno. Hoc exemplum cum sit illustre, ostendit quantum referat huius generis scandala cavere, ac meminerimus omnia facta nostra pertinere non tantum ad nos, sed etiam ad gloriam Dei, sicut scriptum est: Propter vos male audit nomen Dei inter gentes. Postremo in usu indifferentium petulantia cavenda est, ne mores indifferentes mutentur apud eos, qui aut nondum audierunt doctrinam de libertate, aut adhuc sunt infirmiores, ut periculum sit, ne moti mutatione talium morum deterreantur ab Evangelio, & tamen non persequuntur piam doctrinam, sed sunt dociles. Verum postquàm tradita est doctrina, & hypocritae se opponunt, rectum est ostendi illis exempla ibertatis, & haec exempla sunt pars confessionis, Galat. primo. Sic Apostoli violabant traditiones Pharisaicas.

Porro eum, qui infirmatur.

Dicturus de usu caeremoniarum, & de libertate initio praeponit admonitionem de tollerandis infirmis. Tradit autem praeceptum, quo utendum est non adversus persecutores impios, hostes Evangelii, sed erga membra nostra, hoc est, erga eos qui doceri se sinunt, & audiunt Evangelium, hos vetat deterreri exemplis inusitatis, quo minus amplectantur Evangelium. Vocat autem infirmum in fide, nondum satis eruditum in doctrina libertatis. Porro cum inquit sublevandum esse, ne incidat in dubitationes, utrumque monet, ne cogatur aliquid facere contra conscientiam, seu improbante conscientia. Item ut paulatim provehatur, & erudiatur & liberetur à dubitatione. Nam dubitatio in quocunque articulo, si non emendetur, sed augescat, est horribilis pestis, & excutit fidem, & accersit desperationem, odium totius Evangelii, & manifestam impietatem, sicut accidit Iuliano et multis similib.

## 14:3
For God has received him.

First, however, you will observe the precept concerning avoiding doubt. Then you will observe here an excellent consolation is proposed. For Paul testifies that the weak have been received by God, but he understands not enemies or persecutors, but those who hear the Gospel, who are teachable, and have the beginnings of the fear of God, and of faith in Christ, just as the Apostles before the resurrection were righteous, even though they had their own infirmities, as appears in the Evangelical history. Let us transfer this example to ourselves, and let us remember that we too have many infirmities, and yet we should not on that account cast away faith, because here Scripture testifies that the weak are received, but it warns at the same time that the weak must also be advanced little by little. Thirdly, a precept is handed down against doubting, that is, that we should do nothing while the conscience disapproves: Let each one be certain in his own mind. This sentence forbids acting against conscience. For he who acts against conscience openly despises the commandment of God. Moreover, it can easily be understood that this contempt is truly a sin: Therefore every action against conscience is truly a sin.

Latin:

Deus enim illum assumpsit.

Primum autem observabis praeceptum de cavenda dubitatione. Deinde observabis hic egregiam consolationem propositam esse. Testatur enim Paulus infirmos à Deo receptos esse, sed intelligit non hostes aut persecutores, sed eos qui audiunt Evangelium, qui sunt dociles, & habent initia timoris Dei, & fidei in Christum, sicut Apostoli ante resurrectionem erant iusti, etiamsi habebant suas infirmitates, ut apparet in historia Evangelica. Hoc exemplum transferamus ad nos, et meminerimus nos quoque habere multas infirmitates, neque tamen propterea fidem abiiciamus, quia hic scriptura testatur infirmos recipi, sed monet simul etiam paulatim provehendos esse infirmos. Tertio traditur praeceptum contra dubitationem id est, ne quid faciamus improbante conscientia: Unusquisque in sua mente certus sit. Haec sententia vetat facere contra conscientiam. Nam qui contra conscientiam facit, palam contemnit mandatum Dei. Facile autem intelligi potest, hunc contemptum vere esse peccatum: Ergo omnis actio contra conscientiam vere est peccatum.

## 14:4
Who are you, who judge another?

He has handed down a necessary rule in the Church, that we should do nothing against conscience.

Afterwards he prohibits mutual condemnations in the use of indifferent things, such as rites regarding foods, days, and others of this kind. And he adds an argument concerning judgment. The judgment is Christ's: Therefore we ought not to arrogate judgment to ourselves, namely concerning the conscience of another, not concerning an external act that is openly illicit. This rule extends widely, just as that one: Do not judge. For ministries are not prohibited, namely doctrine, or fraternal admonition, or the office of the magistrate. For these have the commands of God, and are judgments divinely instituted. But private ones are prohibited, that is, condemnations outside those three offices which I have recounted, namely those arisen from a sickness of the soul, malevolence, or vanity. Furthermore, the judgment which is made by a man ought to be made concerning an external illicit act. But it is most customary in the world to interpret calumniously the words or acts of others that are not illicit. Paul disapproves of these judgments in the use of indifferent things, and forbids condemnations to be made on account of dissimilar rites of indifferent things, just as once there were contentions concerning the day of Easter, concerning leavened bread, and other things of this kind.

Latin:

Tu quis es, qui iudicas alium?

Tradidit regulam necessariam in Ecclesia, ne quid faciamus contra conscientiam.

Postea prohibet mutuas condemnationes in usu indifferentium, ut rituum in cibis, diebus, et aliis huius generis. Et addit argumentum de iudicio. Iudicium est Christi: Ergo nos non debemus nobis arrogare iudicium, videlicet de conscientia alterius, non de externo facto palam illicito. Haec regula late patet, sicut & illa: Nolite iudicare. Non enim prohibentur ministeria, scilicet doctrina, aut admonitio sraterna, aut officium magistratus. Haec enim habent mandata Dei, & sunt iudicia divinitus instituta. Sed prohibentur privata, hoc est condemnationes extra illa tria officia, quae recensui, videlicet ortae ex morbo animi, malevolentia, aut vanitate. Deinde iudicium, quod fit per hominem, fieri debet de externo facto illicito. Sed est usitatissimum in mundo calumniose interpretari aliorum dicta, aut facta non illicita. Haec iudicia in usu indifferentium improbat Paulus, & vetat condemnationes propter dissimiles ritus indifferentium fieri, sicut olim fuerunt certamina de die Paschatos, de fermentato, & huiusmodi alia.

## 14:13
But judge that more.

He adds a precept concerning the avoiding of scandals.

It was said above concerning the diverse kinds of scandal; now he speaks only of this kind, namely when either the more free abuse their liberty, or on the contrary the more harsh, who nevertheless are not enemies of the Gospel, rebuke the use of liberty. Both are to be chided, and although the abuse of liberty is to be blamed, nevertheless there is more vice in the other part, which also, on account of the appearance of gravity, does more harm, when the more morose wound the consciences of the pious who use liberty, and deter many simple people from the Gospel, and grieve the Holy Spirit for many. Since, therefore, there is very much danger on both sides, there is need for Christians of great diligence, lest they sin, either by morose rebukes or by the abuse of liberty, but let them hold the head, that is, the doctrine, that this use is indifferent, as Paul says 1. Corinth. viii. Food does not commend us to God. To the precept concerning avoiding scandals he added four reasons full of Christian erudition. The first is taken from the kind of works, namely that the use of things divinely ordained and granted is not of itself unclean or prohibited. I know, he says, that nothing is common of itself. He calls it for common, profane, illicit, prohibited, not holy in the Mosaic manner. For since the Jews are called the people of God, and holy, that is, separated from the nations for the worship of God, they called holy all things whose use was granted to them. And indeed they were holy, because they were ordained by the word of God. Conversely, they name profane and prohibited things common, that is, not holy, not separated for the use of the holy people, but which the nations used. I have said these things only concerning the appellation; now let the rule itself also be considered, which is briefly handed down here, but is explained more copiously elsewhere, namely that the Gospel does not require certain observations of foods, days, garments, and the like.

Latin:

Verum illud iudicate magis.

Addit praeceptum de vitandis scandalis.

Dictum est supra de diversis generibus scandali, nunc tantum loquitur de hoc genere, videlicet cum aut liberiores abutuntur libertate, aut ècontra duriores, qui tamen non sunt hostes Evangelii, reprehendunt usum libertatis. Utrique obiurgandi sunt, & quanquàm abusus libertatis est vituperandus, tamen in altera parte plus est vitii, quae etiam propter gravitatis speciem plus nocet, quando morosiores sauciant conscientias piorum, qui libertate utuntur, & deterrent multos simplices ab Evangelio, & multis contristant spiritum sanctum. Cum igitur in utramque partem plurimum sit periculi, opus est Christianis magna diligentia, ne peccent, aut morosis reprehensionibus, aut abusu libertatis, sed teneant caput, id est, doctrinam, quod hic usus sit indifferens, ut Paulus inquit 1. Corinth. viii. Esca non commendat nos Deo. Praecepto de vitandis scandalis adiecit quatuor rationes plenas Christianae eruditionis. Prima sumpta est ex genere operum, quod videlicet usus rerum divinitus ordinatus, & concessus, per sese non sit immundus, seu prohibitus. Scio, inquit, nihil esse commune per sese.Apppellat enim commune, prophanum, illicitum, prohibitum, non sanctum more Mosaico. Iudaei enim cum vocentur populus Dei, & sanctus, id est, separatus à gentibus ad cultum Dei, vocabant sancta omnia, quorum usus ipsis concessus erat. Et quidem erant sancta, quia erant ordinata verbo Dei. Econtra prophana & prohibita nominant communia, id est, non sancta, non sep arata ad usum populi sancti, sed quibus gentes utebantur. Haec de appellatione tantum dixi, nunc ipsa etiam regula consideretur, quae breviter hic tradita est, alibi vero copiosius explicatur, scilicet quod Evangelium non requirat certas observationes ciborum, dierum, vestium, & similes.

## 14:14
Unless to him who exists &c.

He added an appendix to the rule: Clean, that is, lawful things become illicit to those whose conscience judges them to be illicit. Therefore this passage must be diligently considered, so that we may learn that it is truly a sin to act against conscience. For the meaning of this statement is: A kind of food is indeed lawful in itself, but he who eats while his conscience disapproves, he sins, because to do something with a doubting or disapproving conscience, is to act out of contempt for God, and without faith.

Latin:

Nisi ei qui existat &c.

Adiecit regulae appendicem: Munda, hoc est, licita fieri illicita iis, quorum conscientia iudicat esse illicita. Ideo hic locus diligenter considerandus est, ut discamus vere peccatum esse facere contra conscientiam. Est enim sententia huius dicti: Cibi genus per se quidem est licitum, sed qui improbante conscientia vescitur, is peccat, quia facere aliquid dubitante vel improbante conscientia, est agere ex contemptu Dei, & sine fide.

## 14:15
But if because of food your brother &c.

The second reason is taken from the duty of brotherly love, and it is magnificently exaggerated, It is against brotherly love to harm others. Therefore beware lest your examples harm others. The argument should be accommodated to both, to the instructed, who petulantly abuse liberty, and to the morose, who bitterly judge those using liberty. For often that bitterness of judgments deters the weak from the Gospel, and wounds minds even moderately confirmed: Indeed it saddens the holy spirit, namely so that some desperate ones fall away from the Gospel, and lose the holy spirit. These scandals must be avoided with great zeal, according to that: Woe to the man through whom the scandal comes.

Let not your good therefore be subject to the evil speaking of men.

The third reason is taken from the dignity of the Gospel: One must take care lest the Gospel be ill-spoken of.

For the glory of God is injured when His word is reviled, and the progress of men is hindered. For men do not embrace the doctrine which they despise, and unnecessary quarrels alienate the minds of the unskilled and the simple from the Gospel, who begin to hate the kind of doctrine, as if it were a seedbed of hatreds. Added to this are those scandals which alienate minds. Those abusing liberty increase the license of the common people. On the other hand, morose men deter the weak by the virulence of their judgments, etc. He commands that these offenses of minds be diligently avoided, for the sake of the glory of Christ, so that more people may love and embrace the doctrine.

Latin:

Verum si propter cibum fra-ter tuus &c.

Secunda ratio sumpta ex officio fraternae dilectionis, & est magnifice exaggerata, Contra fraternam dilectionem est nocere aliis. Ergo cave ne tua exempla noceant aliis. Argumentum accommodetur ad utrosque, ad institutos, qui petulanter abutuntur libertate, & ad morosos, qui acerbe iudicant de utentibus libertate. Saepe enim illa acerbitas iudiciorum deterret infirmos ab Evangelio, & sauciat mentes etiam mediocriter confirmatas: Imo contristat spiritum sanctum, videlicet ita ut aliqui desperabundi deficiant ab Evangelio, & amittant spiritum sanctum. Haec scandala magno studio cavenda sunt, iuxta illud: Vae homini, per quem accidit scandalum.

Ne vestrum igitur bonum ho-minum maledicentiae sit obnoxium.

Tertia ratio à dignitate Evangelii sumpta est: Cavendum est ne male audiat Evangelium.

Leditur enim gloria Dei, cum eius verbum vituperatur, & impeditur profectus hominum. Non enim amplectuntur homines doctrinam, quam contemnunt, ac rixae non necessariae alienant animos imperitorum, & simplicium ab Evangelio, qui incipiunt odisse genus doctrinae, tanquàm seminarum odiorum. Accedunt & illa scandala, quae alienant animos. Abutentes libertate augent licentiam vulgi. Econtra moro si deterrent imbecilles virulentia iudiciorum suorum &c. Hac offensiones animorum iubet diligenter caveri, propter gloriam Christi, ut doctrinam plures ament & amplectantur.

## 14:17
For the kingdom is not, etc.

The fourth reason is taken from the comparison of necessary and unnecessary things, and it is a useful statement concerning the distinction between true and false worship. Necessary things are not to be corrupted by unnecessary things: Rites ἀδιάφοροι are not necessary: Therefore, for their sake, necessary things, namely faith and the peace of the Church, the edification of the neighbor, should not be corrupted. Furthermore, Scripture often teaches others that the true worships of God are repentance, faith, love, chastity, and similar spiritual movements, just as embraces this very summary. Elsewhere Paul says: In Christ Jesus neither circumcision avails, nor uncircumcision, but faith, which is effective through love. Likewise: They shall worship the Father in spirit etc. But on the contrary, concerning human traditions he says: In vain they worship me with the commandments of men. This doctrine is greatly necessary in the Churches, that works devised without the commandment of God are not the worship of God. But let minds be recalled to works divinely commanded. And it is a great consolation to the pious to understand these true forms of worship, to know that he truly requires invocation and faith, that he wishes to hear, that these common domestic and political duties are pleasing to him, if they are done in faith, which indeed on account of common afflictions are exercises of faith. And therefore in the Prophets and the Psalms this doctrine is so often repeated, as Psal. xlix. Call upon me in the day of trouble, and I will deliver you. And Esaiae i. and lviii. Micheae vi. Zachariae vii. To this sentiment, also here Paul says, that the kingdom of God is righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit. For he signifies by righteousness to be righteous, that is, accepted by God, and now subjecting oneself to God, and to begin obedience. Peace and joy signify the same, namely peace, a conscience toward God, which is made by faith, when we have truly acknowledged the remission of sins, and the acknowledgment of mercy, invocation and obedience follow, patience, diligence in maintaining concord, in avoiding scandals, in helping the Church. Thus Paul embraces all spiritual worships, just as he often does elsewhere.

Moreover, a notable clause is added: He who in these serves Christ, pleases God, and is approved by men. This passage contains a clear testimony concerning good works, that they please God, but Paul explicitly says: He who serves Christ, so that he may testify that he is speaking about the works of those who are righteous by faith in Christ, and acknowledge that that worship pleases on account of the mediator and high priest Christ. Then a useful doctrine is added: that those serving Christ should afterwards also fear the judgments of men, and especially of the Church, but he speaks about those who serve Christ, so that we may know that the judgments of men are not to be preferred to the doctrine and command of God. But when we retain the command of God and the doctrine, afterwards effort must be given so that our morals may adorn the Gospel, and invite others to believe, and to glorify God, according to that: Let your light shine before men.

Furthermore, whatever is from faith etc.

Often in this chapter he has inculcated the rule, lest we do anything against conscience, he now adds at the end, that this work also may be done from faith. This addition must be diligently considered, for to those ignorant of the true doctrine of the Gospel, this addition is not sufficiently clear. Commonly, however, they interpret the saying of Paul thus: Whatever is not from faith is sin, that is, whatever is done against conscience is sin, but they do not sufficiently explain this, for they only accommodate it to the law, so that theft is against the law, therefore it is sin, and against conscience, in him who steals knowingly. This interpretation is true and necessary: For it is necessary in acting first to consult the law, so that we may know which works God prohibits or commands, and there is no doubt that works against the law of God are sins. But when Paul names faith, he does not only require the law, or historical knowledge, but true faith, and he teaches that works commanded or permitted by God must be done in faith, that is, with this confidence, that God is propitious to us on account of the mediator Christ, and that on account of that high priest our works are pleasing. Wherefore it is necessary that the saying of Paul be accommodated not only to the law, but also to the Gospel.

But someone might ask: How are we to establish that we or our works please God, especially when they are contaminated by the contagion of conscience. I respond, those who are secure without repentance do not understand this doctrine of faith, but in true afflictions it shines upon them, when they think that they are not heard by God, that they are cast away, and that there will be no end to their calamities, etc. In such sorrows, minds must be raised up by faith, so that we may determine that God truly forgives us for the sake of Christ, truly hears us, and cares for us. In such consolation, it can be understood what faith is, and then faith resists natural doubt and overcomes diffidence. By this faith, first the person pleases God for the sake of Christ, then he determines that his good works also please Him for the sake of the high priest Christ, even though they are imperfect and unclean. And it is necessary that men be taught what God requires, that we serve in faith, not in perpetual doubt. Let them not think thus, that even if I serve God and call upon Him, nevertheless I ought to doubt whether these things please Him. This doubt contains many sins, denies the Gospel, denies that God forgives sins, expects nothing from God, and silently is indignant and rages against God. These are the sins which properly exist through the law, as Paul calls them.

Wherefore it is necessary that this doubting be reproved in the Church, and that the doctrine of faith be opposed to it. The most common error, which has been spread into the Church, must also be reproved, namely that a Christian ought to doubt whether he is in a state of grace, and also that this doubting is not a sin, and for this they allege a saying from Ecclesiastes: Man knows not whether he is worthy of love or hatred. Then conjectures are sought from works, whether we are in a state of grace, and yet the adversaries assert that one must doubt, and that doubting is not a sin. This whole imagination fights against the doctrine of faith. Furthermore, we do not deny that a natural doubting and diffidence, which all experience, clings in the souls. But this must be known, that this very doubting and diffidence is a sin, and arises from natural blindness, which rejects the promise of the Gospel. Although therefore that doubting clings in the souls, yet these two things must be opposed to it, namely the promise of the Gospel, and the commandment, which commands that we believe that promise. One must therefore resist doubting, and overcome diffidence, and it must be established that God truly forgives those who believe, and truly receives, cares for, and hears them. And let us know that this faith is effected and nourished by the word. And not only The promise requires that we believe, but an immutable commandment is also added, which most severely mandates that we believe that those things which have been promised truly happen to us on account of the Son of God, as it is said in John 3: This is his commandment, that we should believe in the name of his Son. Likewise, He who does not believe God, makes him a liar, because he does not believe in the testimony which God has testified concerning his Son. And Hebrews 4: Let us approach with confidence to the throne of grace. The doctrine which commands one to doubt is repugnant to these commandments and promises.

Wherefore one must struggle with doubt, and faith must be raised up in every invocation, just as James also commands: Let him ask in faith, nothing wavering. Nor are acts of worship pleasing to God in those who do not resist doubt, but silently retain distrust within themselves, that they are not looked upon, that they are cast away. Let us learn to acknowledge these sins, so that we may resist them, and truly stir up the exercises of faith. Thus, therefore, let the saying of Paul be understood: Everything that is not of faith is sin. Let us remember that works commanded or granted by God are to be done, and are to be done in this faith, that God is propitious to us on account of the mediator Christ, and on account of him hears and cares for us, and forgives our infirmity and approves good works. Now let hypocritical forms of worship be compared to this opinion. Since they perform works not commanded by God, they cannot believe that such worship pleases Him, because they have no word concerning the will of God. Secondly, because they disapprove of the doctrine of faith, and command one to doubt, another impiety is added; they invoke Him like the Gentiles, silently thinking to themselves that they are not regarded, not cared for, not heard by God, and perhaps even that they are cast away. This perpetual doubting is impiety, even if the world does not judge it a sin. How, therefore, is the saying of Solomon to be understood? Man knows not whether he is worthy of love or hatred. I answer most simply, Solomon is not speaking of the judgment of the conscience toward God, concerning grace or rejection, but of the events in this life; these he says are uncertain, and that similar things happen to the good and the bad in this life. This certainty offends the Epicureans, and moves them to deny providence. Abel is pious, and yet he is slaughtered by his brother. John the Baptist is killed, meanwhile a tyrant enjoys all pleasures, and many impious men have not had tragic ends. These arguments Solomon collected, so that he might admonish us not to fall away from God on account of this scandal, nor let us not judge from outcomes concerning the will of God, but from the word. Likewise, lest the pious become secure, and cast off the fear of God, lest they undertake anything by trust in their own righteousness without a calling.

Latin:

Non enim est regnum &c.

Quarta ratio sumpta est ex collatione necessariorum, & non necessariorum, & est utile dictum de discrimine verorum, & falsorum cultuum. Necessaria non sunt corrumpenda non necessariis: Ritus ἀδιάφοροι non sunt necessarii : Ergo propter eos non corrumpantur necessaria, scilicet fides & pax Ecclesiae, aedificatio proximi. Porro saepe alios docet scriptura, veros cultus Dei esse paenitentiam, fidem, dilectionem, castitatem, et similes motus spirituales, sicut hanc ipsam summam complectitur alibi Paulus: In Christo Iesu neque circumcisio valet, neque praeputium, sed fides, quae est per dilectionem efficax. Item: Adorabunt patrem in spiritu &c. Econtra vero de traditionibus humanis dicit: Frustra colunt me mandatis hominum. Haec doctrina magnopere necessaria est in Ecclesiis, opera sine mandato Dei excogita non esse cultus Dei. Sed revocentur animi ad opera divinitus mandata. Estque magna consolatio piis, intelligere hos veros cultus, scire quod vere requirat invocationem & fidem, quod velit exaudire, quod placeant ei haec communia officia oeconomica & politica, si fiant in fide, quae quidem propter communes afflictiones sunt exercitia fidei. Ideoque in Prophetis & psal. toties repetitur haec doctrina, ut Psal. xlix. Invoca me in die tribulationis, & eripiam te. Et Esaiae i. & lviii.Micheae vi.Zachariae vii. In hanc sententiam, et hic ait Paulus, regnum Dei esse iusticiam, pacem, & gaudium in spiritu sancto. Significat enim iusticia esse iustum, id est, acceptum Deo, et iam subiicientem se Deo, & inchoare obedientiam. Pax & gaudium significant idem, scilicet pacem, conscientiam erga Deum, quae fit fide, cum vere agnovimus remissionem peccatorum, et agnitionem misericordiae, sequuntur invocatio, obedientia, patientia, diligentia in retinenda concordia, vitandis scandalis, iuvanda Ecclesia. Sic complectitur Paulus omnes spirituales cultus, sicut alibi saepe.

Est autem insignis particula adiecta: Qui in his servit Christo, placet Deo, & est probatus hominibus. Hic locus continet perspicuum testimonium de bonis operibus, quod placeant Deo, sed diserte inquit Paulus: Qui servit Christo, ut testetur se loqui de operibus illorum, qui fide in Christum sunt iusti, & agnoscunt illum cultum placere propter mediatorem & pontificem Christum. Deinde addita est utilis doctrina: ut servientes Christo, postea etiam iudicia hominum, & maxime Ecclesiae vereantur, sed loquitur de his, qui serviunt Christo,ut sciamus non anteponenda esse iudicia hominum doctrinae & mandato Dei. Sed cum mandatum Dei & doctrinam retineamus, postea danda est opera, ut mores nostri ornent Evangelium, & invitent alios ad credendum, & glorificandum Deum, iuxta illud: Luceat lux vestra coram hominibus.

Porro quicquid ex fide &c.

Saepe in hoc capite inculcavit regulam, ne quid faciamus contra conscientiam, nunc in fine addit, ut etiam hoc opus fiat ex fide. Haec additio diligenter est consideranda, nam ignorantibus veram doctrinam Evangelii, non satis perspicua est haec additio. Vulgo autem sic interpretantur dictum Pauli: Quicquid non est ex fide, peccatum est, id est, quicquid fit contra conscientiam, peccatum est, sed hoc non satis explicant, tantum enim accomodant ad legem, ut furtum sit contra legem, ideo peccatum est, & contra conscientiam, in eo, qui sciens furatur. Haec interpretatio vere & necessaria est : Necesse est enim in operando primum consulere legem, ut sciamus, quae opera Deus prohibeat aut praecipiat, & opera contra legem Dei esse peccata, non dubium est. Sed cum Paulus nominat fidem, non tantum requirit legem, aut notitiam historicam, sed veram sidem, ac docet opera mandata aut concessa à Deo, facienda esse in fide, id est, cum hac fiducia, quod Deus propter mediatorem Christum nobis sit propitius, & quod propter illum pontificem nostra opera placeant. Quare dictum Pauli non tantum ad legem, sed etiam ad Evangelium accommodari necesse est.

Sed quaerat aliquis: Quomodo statuamus Deo placere nos aut opera nostra, praesertim cum contaminentur contagio conscientiae. Respondeo, Securi qui sine paenitentia sunt, non intelligunt hanc doctrinam defide, sed in veris afflictionibus illucescit eis, cum cogitant se non exaudiri à Deo, se abiectos esse, & nullum fore finem calamitatum &c. In talibus doloribus erigendi sunt animi fide, ut statuamus Deum nobis vere ignoscere propter Christum, vere nos exaudire, & curare. In tali consolatione potest intelligi, quid sit fides, ac tunc fides repugnat naturali dubitationi, & vincit diffidentiam. Hac fide primum persona placet Deo propter Christum, deinde statuit etiam placere bona opera propter pontificem Christum, tametsi sunt imperfecta & immunda. Et necesse est doceri homines, quod requirat Deus, ut in fide serviamus, non in dubitatione perpetua. Non sic cogitent, &si servio Deo & invoco eum, tamen dubitare debeo, an haec ei placeant. Haec dubitatio continet multa peccata, negat Evangelium, negat Deum remittere peccata, nihil expectat à Deo, & tacite indignatur, & fremit adversus Deum. Haec sunt peccata, quae proprie per legem existunt, ut vocat Paulus.

Quare necesse est hanc dubitationem in Ecclesia reprehendi, & opponi doctrinam de fide. Reprehendendus est etiam vulgatissimus error, qui in Ecclesiam sparsus est, scilicet quod Christianus debeat dubitare, an sit in gratia, Item quod haec dubitatio non sit peccatum, & ad hoc allegant dictum ex Ecclesiaste : Nescit homo an amore vel odio dignus sit. Deinde quaeruntur coniecturae ab operibus, utrum simus in gratia, & tamen asserunt adversarii, quod sit dubitandum, & quod dubitatio non sit peccatum. Haec tota imaginatio pugnat cum doctrina de fide. Porro non negamus, haerere in animis naturalem dubitationem, & diffidentiam, quam omnes experiuntur. Sed illud sciendum est, hanc ipsam dubitationem & diffidentiam esse peccatum, & oriri ex naturali caecitate, quae repudiat promissionem Evangelii. Etsi igitur haeret in animis illa dubitatio, tamen opponi debent haec duo, scilicet promissio Evangelii, & mandatum, quod praecipit, ut credamus illi promissioni. Repugnandum est igitur dubitationi, & vincenda diffidentia, ac statuendum, quod Deus vere ignoscat credentibus, eosque vere recipiat, curet, & exaudiat. Et hanc fidem, verbo effici, & ali sciamus. Nec solum promissio requirit, ut credamus, sed etiam praeceptum additum est immutabile, quod severissime mandat, ut credamus, vere nobis contingere propter filium Dei, ea quae promissa sunt, sicut dicitur in Iohan. iii. Hoc est mandatum eius, ut credamus in nomine filii eius. Item, Qui non credit Deo, mendacem facit eum, quia non credit in testimonium quod testificatus est Deus de filio suo. Et Ebraeos. iiii. Adeamus cum fiducia ad thronum gratiae. His mandatis & promissionibus repugnat doctrina, quae iubet dubitare.

Quare luctandum est cum dubitatione, & erigenda fides in omni invocatione, sicut & Iacob praecipit: Postulet in fide nihil haesitans. Nec placent Deo cultus in illis, qui non repugnant dubitationi, sed taciti apud se retinent diffidentiam, quod non respiciantur, quod sint abiecti. Haec peccata agnoscere discamus, ut eis repugnemus, et vere ex ercitia fidei excitemus. Sic ergo intelligatur dictum Pauli : Omne quod non est ex fide peccatum est. Meminerimus facienda esse opera praecepta, vel concessa à Deo, & facienda in hac fide, quod Deus sit nobis propitius propter mediatorem Christum, et propter eum exaudiat & curet nos, & condonet infirmitatem et bona opera approbet. Iam ad hanc sententiam conferantur cultus hipocritici. Cum faciant opera non mandata à Deo, non possunt credere, talem cultum ei placere, quia nullum habent verbum de voluntate Dei. Secundo, quia doctrinam de fide improbant, & iubent dubitare, accedit alia impietas, invocant sicut gentes, tacite cogitantes apud se, se non respici, non curari, non exaudiri à Deo, fortassis etiam abiectos esse. Haec perpetua dubitatio est impietas, eriamsi mundus eam non iudicat peccatum. Quomodo igitur dictum Salomonis intelligendum est? Nescit homo, an amore vel odio dignus sit. Respondeo simplicissime, Salomon non loquitur de iudicio conscientiae erga Deum, de gratia vel abiectione, sed de eventibus in hac vita, hos dicit esse incertos, & bonis & malis similia accidere in hac vita. Haec certitudo offendit Epicureos, & movet, ut negent providentiam. Abel est pius, & tamen trucidatur à fratre. Ioannes Baptista interficitur, interim Tyrannus fruitur omnibus voluptatibus, & multi impii non habuerunt Tragicos exitus. Haec argumenta collegit Salomon, ur admoneat nos ne propter hoc scandalum deficiamus à Deo, neve ex euntibus iudicemus de voluntate Dei, sed ex verbo. Item ne pii fiant securi, & exuant timorem Dei, ne fiducia propriae iusticiae aliquid moveant sine vocatione.

## 14:17 Concerning the Church and Concerning the Authority of the Word of God
CONCERNING THE CHURCH AND CONCERNING THE AUTHORITY of the word of God.

It is often accustomed to be disputed how much should be attributed to the opinions of the Church, the decrees of Synods, and the sayings of writers. For although we hold the rule that we should embrace the word of God, yet since ambiguous passages seem to occur in the Apostolic writings, some dispute that the opinions of the Church should be followed rather than the writings of the Apostles.

Then they falsely claim that the authority of the Church should be preferred to the word of God, and that the Church can change what has been handed down in the word of God. They cite for these opinions the saying of Augustine: I would not believe the Gospel, unless the authority of the catholic Church moved me. And so, under the false pretext of the name of the Church, the pontiffs decree and command many things according to their own pleasure against the word of God, they confirm and establish the impious doctrine, and impious cults, and the name of the Church alone even now deters very many from the true doctrine of the Gospel, which we profess. Therefore it is necessary for men to be rightly admonished concerning the authority of the Church.

Again, also certain more petulant minds, when they invent new opinions from sayings of scripture badly twisted, so that they utterly despise the consensus of the true Church, and all synods without distinction, as when Servetus quarrels with the Church of all times, and depraves the sayings concerning the Word Ioannis primo, and seeks a more elegant, as he himself thinks, interpretation. In order, therefore, that such petulance may be restrained, there is need in some way of the enclosures, if I may so speak, of the Church, just as the ancient synods and writers allege the first testimonies accepted from the Apostles and certain authors.

Tertullian against Praxeas says that this rule must be held against heresies: That is right which is first, but that is adulterated which is later. And indeed he calls that first which the Apostles certainly handed down, for thus he interprets himself.

Irenaeus against Florinus alleges the authority of superiors, and specifically of Polycarp, who had been a hearer of John the Apostle. He says For he says that he would have execrated the dogmas of Florinus, if he had heard them, and would have avoided the place in which those things were said, as if it were polluted.

Basil cites his nurse, whose piety he says was then especially praised, and he adds that she received doctrine from Gregory of Neocaesarea, who at that time was famous for learning and miracles, and refuted the Samosatene, and left a brief confession of faith, which contains an illustrious testimony concerning the Trinity. It exists, moreover, in book vii of the Ecclesiastical History.

Origen cites the Apostles concerning the baptism of infants. For he says in chapter vi to the Romans that the Churches received a tradition from the Apostles, that infants should be baptized. These men rightly cite the authority of the Church. Wherefore I shall say in order what the Church is, and that it must be heard, and that approved testimonies must be used, and yet that doctrine must be judged from the word of God, so that the highest authority of the word of God may remain, according to that: If anyone shall have taught another Gospel, let him be anathema.

But first, when I name the Church, I do not understand the Pontiffs, Bishops, and the others who approve of their opinions. For these are enemies of the true Church, partly Epicureans, partly manifest idolaters. But I call the Church the assembly of those who truly believe, who have the Gospel and the sacraments, and are sanctified by the Holy Spirit, just as the Church is described in Ephes. v., and in Ioannis x. My sheep hear my voice.

Although it is necessary that this true Church always endure, because the kingdom of Christ is perpetual, and it is written: I will remain with you until the consummation of the age, yet it must be known that this true Church does not always flourish equally, but is often very small, and from time to time is restored divinely, with true teachers being sent, just as in the time of Noah the Church was narrow, and an assembly of few.

Thus after the flood Melchizedek, who was Shem, the son of Noah, retained the true doctrine, and when idolatry had grown among the Chaldeans, and the true doctrine had been almost everywhere extinguished, God renewed the Church by calling Abraham. Afterwards the family of Abraham, and his few listeners, are the Church, while in the meantime the Chaldeans and Egyptians boasted that they were the descendants of the fathers, that they retained the examples and worship of the fathers, and they proclaimed themselves to be the people of God, although they had not retained the word of God, even if they had retained the ceremonies, to which, however, they had attached perverse opinions, and they had added idolatry.

In the time of Ahaz, the Church was almost extinguished in Israel; afterwards, through Elijah and Elisha, it was increased again, then it collapsed once more.

When Christ was born, the Church in Judah was very small: Mary, Joseph, the family of Zechariah, Simeon, Anna, the shepherds, and a few others. Meanwhile, the ecclesiastical government was in the hands of the Pharisees and Sadducees, who were openly impious. The Sadducees were also Epicureans, and yet they arrogated to themselves especially the title of the people of God.

So also in the time of the Prophets, the true Church was small . Isaiah 1: Unless the Lord had left us a seed, we would have become like Sodom and Gomorrah. These words most gravely warn us not to think of the Church as a worldly polity, not to measure it by the succession of bishops, or by the rank and position of pontiffs, but to establish the Church among those who retain the true doctrine of the Gospel. It is necessary that there be some true believers in this assembly. For the promises pertain to this assembly. Therefore, Isaiah draws that august title away from his princes and pontiffs, and says that a small seed remained in that very people which was called the people of God.

And in the time of Jeremiah, when kings and priests were opposed to him, the Church was not the assembly of the priests, but those who believed the sermons of Jeremiah. Amos 3. Thus shall Israel be delivered, as if a shepherd should snatch two legs from the jaws of a lion. Finally, the Church was small compared to the multitude of the impious, when all nations except the people of Judah had utterly lost the knowledge of God.

Scripture also predicts future disasters for the Church after the Apostles, Matth. xxiii. Many false prophets shall arise, and shall deceive many. Item: When you shall see the abomination of desolation standing in the holy place. Here it signifies that in the Church, which is so called, idolatry will arise, by which true doctrine and true worship will be overwhelmed, and there will be a desolation of the Church, that is, a solitude or extinction. And so it happened. After the abuses of the masses and the worship of traditions arose, there followed darkness concerning true worship, concerning faith, concerning invocation in faith, concerning the duties of one's calling. Because a conscience looking into its own merits cannot understand the remission of sins, nor true invocation, and the expectation of divine aid etc.

They will perform signs and wonders, so that if it were possible, even the elect might be led astray. ii. Thessal. ii. The falling away will come, etc. Lucae xviii. Do you think that when the Son of Man comes, He will find faith? Psal. lxxxviii. Have You made all the sons of men in vain, etc.? For there is a complaint about the coming ruin of the Church. These sayings testify, even if it is necessary for the Church to be preserved, yet especially in the last time it is exceedingly small and a gathering of few, who are despised and cast aside in this life, just as Paul says: Not many wise, not many powerful, etc.

I have cited these testimonies so that, first, it may be considered what the Church is, and the mind may be led away from carnal opinions, which imagine the Church to be a polity of pontiffs, and allege it to the ordinary succession of Bishops, just as empires consist in the ordinary succession of princes, but the Church behaves otherwise. For it is a gathering not bound to ordinary succession, but to the word of God. There the Church is reborn, where God restores doctrine and gives the Holy Spirit. And that churches are ruled and preserved in this way, not by ordinary succession, Paul testifies Ephes. iiii. He gave gifts to men, Apostles the Prophets, etc. For it teaches that it is properly the Church in which Christ is effective, and to which He gives true teachers.

Therefore, when the name and authority of the Church is objected to us, let us first consider whether mention is made of the true Church, or indeed of a gathering of pontiffs, and of that succession, and of polity, nor let us allow ourselves to be deterred from the word of God by the false pretext of the name of the Church.

Secondly, after it has been said what the true Church is, now it must be added that this true Church, which is small, and only of the saints, retains the true doctrine of the Gospel, or the articles of faith, just as Paul calls it the seat of truth. But this very true Church has doctrine at one time more, at another time less pure and clear. It also has many weak members, just as the Apostles were the Church, and yet they did not understand before the resurrection of Christ what the kingdom of Christ was going to be. Peter also, after the Holy Spirit was given, still imagined that the worship of the law was necessary, but being admonished from heaven, he learned that the kingdom of Christ is not a Jewish polity, but spiritual and perpetual worship, Acts 10.

Afterwards, with the preaching of the Apostle having been begun rum, the pure and clear doctrine shone in them, and yet meanwhile there were many weak ones, who although they were true members of the Church, and held the articles of faith, yet added something of error, as those who observed the worship of the law, and did not sufficiently understand the abrogation of the law, and true worships. This error was not light, and cast some darkness upon the articles of faith. Thus Christ predicts concerning the Church of the last time, that there will be great darkness, which will even hinder the elect, so that they will not have pure doctrine.

There remains therefore some true Church, which retains the articles of faith, but sometimes less pure, and obscured by some inconvenient opinions, and having something of error. And I am still speaking of true members of the Church, and saints, not of others, who having lost the light of the word, lose the holy spirit, and follow the judgment of reason, and when they think they are delivering very pious things, they say foreign and impious things. Just as now also there are many outstanding in doctrine, good morals, and the appearance of piety, who seem to themselves to say most holy things, when they are far from the true light, that is, from the true understanding of the word of God. Of such I am not yet speaking, but as yet mention is only made of true members of the Church, which are for the most part weak.

Thus therefore Paul says: No one can lay another foundation, besides that which is laid. But one builds upon it gold, another wood, stubble, etc. He understands the foundation to be the articles of faith, that is, the sum of Christian doctrine, and the doctrine concerning the benefits of Christ, but to this, he says, others will add useful doctrine, and explanation, and true spiritual worship. These he calls gold. Others will add stubble, that is, inconvenient opinions, and those having some error, just as in the beginning ceremonies were immediately established, which drew with them false opinions.

As I consider Ambrose to be a true member of the Church, he nevertheless says concerning the Lenten fast: Other fasts are of the will, this one is of necessity. This opinion is stubble added to the doctrine of faith.

Thus Basil added monasticism as if it were stubble, and he praises this kind of life with immoderate and false commendations, although he was indeed rebuked by his Bishop. But that it is no light error to institute new forms of worship, Scripture often warns, and this one sentence sufficiently signifies: In vain do they worship with the commandments of men.

It is a grave sin against the first commandment to institute or approve of acts of worship not commanded by God. For the first commandment, when it forbids foreign gods, also forbids foreign acts of worship.

Cyprian urges canonical penalties, of which there was then use, and he confirms opinions as if they were necessary, and that because of them sins are remitted; sometimes he says that absolution without them is useless. Perhaps he felt more correctly than he spoke; nevertheless, those errors are not light, but are very dense stubble, obscuring the pure doctrine concerning the benefits of Christ and concerning faith.

Furthermore, writers have often felt more correctly than they speak, because most were quite negligent and improper in speaking, and they borrow many opinions and formulas from the common people, in which there is some element of error; as Augustine takes the name of satisfactions from the common people, even though he openly reproves the errors concerning satisfactions. He twists himself in interpreting this opinion: every sin is voluntary, where he disputes concerning original sin, when nevertheless the opinion is a civil maxim, handed down concerning external offenses.

Thus they call the Lord's Supper an oblation, in the manner of the people, since the offering was not instituted, but Christ himself was the priest, offering his own sacrifice. And indeed, in the ceremony of the supper, the offering of the body and blood was not even performed formerly, but before the consecration, loaves and other things were offered, and the priest would say that he was offering prayers, thanksgiving, and the entire worship which is accustomed to be performed there. Although, therefore, the offering was not understood in one way, yet afterwards the name was twisted to the offering of the body, from which huge abuses followed.

Dionysius, in that book which contains the ceremonies of the Church, although he describes the rite of the synaxis diligently, yet he makes absolutely no mention of the offering of the Lord's body. Nor does the Canon of Basil contain this offering. But I will say more about the Lord's supper later. I have added these things only to show that the ancients sometimes borrowed awkward expressions from the people, as is accustomed to happen in all ages.

Sometimes they are overcome by the judgments and examples of the multitude, which is not pious, so that they are drawn into superstitions by some human imagination, as in the Nicene Synod, if Paphnutius alone had not stood in the way, the opinion of those who wanted a decree to be made, that , would have been approved. priests should abstain from their wives. Thus custom overcame Cyprian and many others, so that they approved the prohibition of marriage.

Likewise the whole Nicene Synod, overcome by the consensus of the multitude or of the time, approved the Canons of penance, which afterwards brought forth intolerable errors. Great examples often deceive even the pious, just as the example of Anthony cast darkness over many. Thus far I have spoken about the pious, who even if they are holy, are nevertheless very many of them weak. I will now add about the fallen.

Sometimes the pious fall completely, and lose the Holy Spirit, just as Origen is judged to have fallen completely, especially if he affirmed those prodigious errors, that there were innumerable worlds, that the devils are finally to be saved. Tertullian also impiously condemns second marriages, but perhaps they repented. For many truly fallen in life and doctrine, nevertheless repent. And it happens very often that the holy truly fall, and do not judge according to the word, and spiritual light, but are deceived by the imagination of reason, who nevertheless afterwards repent. Just as Gideon fell completely, instituting worship by human counsel.

From all these things follows the conclusion: Although the true Church, which is small, retains the articles of faith, yet that very true Church can have errors obscuring the articles of faith. Furthermore, many fall in such a way that they approve of entirely impious errors against the articles of faith, even if perhaps some repent.

First, therefore, when the authority of the Church is alleged, it must be asked whether there was a consensus of the true Church, consistent with the word of God.

Next, it must be said that the writers who exist have often fallen, and perhaps some are not even members of the Church.

Thirdly, another distinction must be added. In that assembly which is called the Church, there is a huge multitude of impious people, most of whom precede the others in authority, in the appearance of religion, and in the opinion of doctrine, such as were among the people of Judah in the time of Jeremiah, the impious high priests and priests, who themselves also alleged against Jeremiah the authority of the seat and the law, and the promises. The law shall not perish from the priests, they denied that their assembly could err, when nevertheless they were entirely erring and dissenting from Jeremiah. Likewise, in the time of Christ, there were very few pious ones, namely Zechariah and Simeon.

Furthermore, when the impious multitude dominates in the Church, it establishes in the name of the Church many false and impious things. Such a multitude has embraced the application of masses for the living and the dead, the worship of vows and saints, and afterwards the example harmed the pious. Such a multitude also in a synod established that the marriages of priests must be torn apart. However, it often happens in the Church that the impious, excelling in intellects, take the impetus of establishing religion by human wisdom, who, since they are not moved by the word of God, but are led by the image of reason, and seek elegant opinions, beget impious dogmas, just as Samosatenus, Arius, Pelagius. Others seek merits, or seek a specious government, εὐταξίαν of the people, and by these causes they are moved to institute and accumulate acts of worship, as monks, and Gregory, and at this time pontiffs, princes, and many learned men desiring to establish the Church, are moved by human wisdom, and with the word of God omitted, they wish to establish the Church according to their own imaginations. Nor do they see it to be a horrible impiety to depart from the word of God, to seek God without the word, to institute acts of worship by human judgment, without the command of God, to change true dogmas, and to oppress the purity of the word of God.

When therefore the authority of the Church is objected, as concerning the application of masses: The Church does not err, the Church has applied masses for so many centuries, Therefore the custom is to be observed.

It must be answered to the major premise, the universal Church, which is the multitude of those ruling in the Church, can err, just as the pontiffs and priests of Jeremiah's time, or of Christ's time, erred. And although besides that multitude there are some pious ones, who retain the articles of faith, yet these also, moved by examples, assent to certain errors. Thus it happens that they retain the articles of faith less pure, just as Bernard seems to have thought more conveniently than the others, and if he assented to many errors, such as the abuse of masses, the pontifical power, vows, the worship of saints.

Therefore the authority of the multitude is not to be alleged against the word of God, but one must return to the rule: If anyone shall have taught another Gospel, let him be anathema. Let the authority of the word divinely delivered be first. Then that is to be considered the Church, which agrees with that word, as Christ says: My sheep hear my voice, and Augustine: The question is, where is the Church, what therefore are we to do? In our words we are to seek it, or in the words of the head of his own, our Lord Jesus Christ? I think that we ought to seek in the words of him who is the truth, and knows his body best.

But here it is objected, if the authority of the Church is repudiated, then too great a license of petulance of minds is granted, for with the sentences of the Church rejected, many will devise new and impious interpretations of scripture. Since this danger is not to be despised, and it is profitable to restrain that license, it must be seen again to what extent the authority of the Church is to be sought. For Servetus, when he renews the impious error of Samosatenus, and denies that the word is to be understood as a person in this saying: In the beginning was the word, magnificently proclaims the authority of scripture, commands that this be preferred to the decrees of the Church, then cunningly argues that the discourse is to be understood simply. But since the word in the common speech of men does not signify a person, he denies that a person is to be understood in John, as if Demosthenes were to read this saying: In the beginning was the word, he certainly would not think that any person was meant.

I ask therefore whether it is not profitable to oppose the authority of the Church against such men? Here I answer that, just as the Gospel commands the Church to be heard, so I always say that the assembly, in whose possession the word of God was, and which is called the Church, must be heard, just as we also command our pastors to be heard. Let us therefore hear the teaching and admonishing Church, but it is not on account of the Church's authority that one must believe. For the Church does not establish articles of faith, it only teaches and admonishes. But one must believe on account of the word of God, when, namely, having been admonished by the Church, we understand that this opinion has been handed down truly and without sophistry in the word of God.

Perhaps Demosthenes would not think about a person if he were to read: In the beginning was the word.
