But the hearer, admonished by the Church that the word signifies a person, namely the son of God, is now helped by the teaching and admonishing Church, and he believes the article not on account of the Church's authority, but because he sees that this opinion has firm testimonies in the scripture itself; he sees it said of a certain person, who, having assumed human nature, lived in the world with men. He sees this person called λόγον. He gathers suitable and firm testimonies concerning the two natures in Christ, for he knows that concerning the nature of God one must believe to the heavenly voice, and that it is the height of impiety to invent opinions about the nature of God without His own testimony. ii. Petri1. And Matth.xvii. Hear Him.

Likewise the first Church is valid as a witness of the Apostles. I speak, however, of dogmas, not of human traditions. For they wished dogmas to be firm & perpetual. They did not wish human rites to be perpetual or immutable. Nor did the Apostles err in doctrine. Therefore it is useful to hold where the most ancient writers allege the authority of the Apostles.

As concerning the Trinity, Origen, Tertullian, Irenaeus, Gregory Neocaesariensis, Alexander, Bishop of Alexandria, & many others cite them, who, since they testify that the doctrine concerning the Trinity was received from the Apostles, greatly confirm the pious. And so such testimonies are not to be spurned.

I said, however, that writers are to be heard, just as we also say now that preachers are to be heard, because some remain in the Church who retain the truth, sometimes more purely, sometimes less purely. But it must be added that those heard are to be judged by the word of God, which always remains the rule of doctrine.

Examples.

Augustine on original sin contends more sharply than the rest. He teaches therefore and admonishes, and since we see him truly and without sophistry reciting the opinion of Scripture, we believe the article not because of Augustine, but because of the word of God, and we see that those before him thought the same, even if they did not treat this article as copiously, or as clearly.

Another.

Peter of Alexandria, Bishop, contends against Meletius that the lapsed are to be received and alleges ancient authority. For Epiphanius recites these words, as the doctrine which has reached even to us hands down. The Bishop, that Alexandrian one, therefore teaches and admonishes that the lapsed are to be received. We believe this not because of this Bishop, but because we see this opinion has been handed down in the word of God, and the testimonies of the ancient Church are added.

I say the same concerning synods, that the synods of the Church are to be heard, which, when they dispute concerning the word of God, teach and admonish us, but let judgment be added, and when they hand down true things, let us believe because of the word of God, as the Nicene synod piously and usefully taught, and admonished all posterity concerning the Son of God, but we believe the article not because of the synod, but because we see it has been handed down thus in the word of God.

The rest of the things which are outside the scriptures are not to be embraced in such a way, as the Nicene synod established the Canons of penance, which are human traditions outside of scripture, and were the seed of many superstitious opinions.

Samson's guests could not interpret the riddle proposed at the banquet, unless his wife was questioned. Wherefore Samson says: If you had not plowed with my heifer, you would not have found out my riddle. Thus it must be looked around, where the assembly is that has the word of God, and it must be seen which assembly of the Fathers and Synods is purer, that is, having fewer opinions outside the word of God. This Church teaches, warns, and testifies. But it must be seen whether those things which it proposes have firm testimonies of the word of God.

And indeed it behooves the pious to confess that the Fathers have deserved well of posterity, who defended and retained pious dogmas with the sharpest contentions; that benefit is not to be considered light. To this pertains the saying of Augustine: I would not believe the Gospel, unless the authority of the Church moved me. Augustine does not mean that the authority of the Church is greater than that of the divine word, or that the Church can abolish articles delivered in the word of God, but he feels that the Church is a teacher and a witness. We would not believe the Gospel, unless the Church taught us and testified that this doctrine was delivered by the Apostles.

This saying also avails for refuting new dogmas, which never existed in the Church, just as the Manichaeans devised new ravings. For it is necessary that dogmas necessary for piety existed at the beginning in the preaching of the Apostles. Therefore, new and entirely unknown things to the Apostolic Church are to be rejected. But the saying of Augustine has been disputed more copiously elsewhere; certainly, he does not grant the Church the authority of establishing against the word of God, or of abolishing articles delivered in the word of God, or of founding new articles of faith.

Catalogue.

I shall collect some examples of synods and Fathers, so that it may appear that dissimilar matters are contained in them, lest all the sayings of all men, or all the rites of the ancients, be received as necessary without discrimination. Just as certain foolish people so admire antiquity that they wish all ancient human rites to be restored, just as if the Spartans now wished to restore all the ancient rites of their Republic, since rites devised by men are partly vicious, partly even if they are probable, yet they do not suit all times.

The Synod of Neo-Caesarea forbids priests from attending the banquets of second marriages, lest they seem to approve of them. Many such ridiculous constitutions are mixed in with good ones. Therefore, a selection must be made, and one must not rashly applaud all the sayings of the ancients.

In the year of the Lord 324, the Council of Nicaea was convened by Constantine, in which Eustathius, Bishop of Antioch, presided. In this council, the most serious controversies of dogmas were judged, and the errors of Samosatenus and Arius were rightly condemned, likewise those of the Cathari, who denied that the lapsed should be received, and denied that they obtain the remission of sins.

Afterwards, certain political matters were ordained concerning the government of the Churches, so that the Bishop of Alexandria might preside over the Church of the East, and the Roman [Bishop] over the Churches of the neighboring nations. Likewise, that bishops be ordained by neighboring bishops. Although these political matters are useful, yet they did not wish them to be held as articles of faith.

Thirdly, they added certain ceremonial matters, namely the Canons of penance, as they called them, which in the beginning were less harsh, and perhaps had fewer superstitions. But afterwards the burden itself grew, and superstition grew, and free forgiveness was obscured. Wherefore in this matter the Fathers were not sufficiently cautious. And since the outcome afterwards showed that superstitions grow from such examples, we should not so wonder at the Synod in this matter, that we would wish either to approve or to restore those canons. Nor do we therefore dissent from the ancient Church; we retain the articles of the Synod concerning dogmas, which properly pertain to the Church. The others, which are outside or against the word of God, do not pertain to the Church.

In the year of our Lord 383, the Constantinopolitan synod was convened by Theodosius , in which the Bishop of Constantinople presided, a grave controversy was judged concerning the Holy Spirit, that He is a person proceeding from the Father and the Son, and is God, and Eunomius and others who had thought the contrary were rightly condemned. There are also certain political matters ordained, that bishops should not administer anything in the dioceses of others.

In the year 433, the Ephesian synod was convened by Theodosius the younger, in which Cyril of Alexandria presided. This synod rightly condemned Nestorius, who denied that the Word was united to human nature in Christ by a substantial union, but that the Word was only present, & to inhabit in human nature, as a guest in a dwelling, so that it might be efficacious there.

This was a controversy of great importance. For in Christ two natures are truly & substantially united. Nor is it true that human nature alone is Christ, and that it is a dwelling of the assisting Word. Hence the pious urged these forms of speaking about the unity of the person, that God was born, suffered, etc. Although Nestorius denied that he felt the same as Samosatenus, nevertheless I suspect that he felt the same thing in reality, but proposed the old delusion in appearance otherwise, covered in wrappings.

In the year 452, the Council of Chalcedon was convened by the Emperor Marcian, in which Eutyches was rightly condemned, who denied even two natures in Christ, and contended that the very nature of the Word sent from God was brought forth through the virgin, and that there are not two united natures. It seems that he also renewed the delusion of Samosatenus, but proposed it in another wrapping. This judgment of the synod is to be praised.

Furthermore, human traditions had already grown in the Church. Therefore this synod added some vicious constitutions, not about dogmas but about ceremonies and worship outside of scripture, and yet these constitutions are still more modest than others born later. In this synod was first made the constitution, which prohibits marriages to monks and virgins, who have made vows, and excommunicates such persons contracting marriages, although it adds a mitigation, that this can also be granted by the judgment of the Bishop.

But many political matters were usefully constituted then, that Bishops themselves should not hold the administration of Ecclesiastical resources, but that Churches should have Stewards, that no one should hold multiple ministries. Item, that no one should be ordained without a ministry, Item that in individual provinces Bishops should convene annually, and have synods concerning the present controversies of the Church.

These useful decrees of the synods the adversaries dissimulate, and meanwhile bring forward other lighter ones, so that it may seem to us that they are opposing the authority of the ancient Church.

There were meanwhile also other synods, whether provincial or more frequent, in which the Bishops of neighboring provinces convened. Such was the Antiochene synod before the Nicene, convened against Samosatenus, which piously and rightly condemned the impiety of Samosatenus. Such likewise was the Gangrense synod in Galatia, old and pure, it has excellent decrees against superstitions concerning marriage, concerning foods, concerning monasticism. And it appears that this synod met on account of Montanus, Marcion, and the like, who greatly increased those superstitions.

Other later ones followed, such as the Ancyran, which has this memorable constitution: If deacons at their ordination have not promised that they will live celibate, they are to be retained in the ministries, even if they take wives afterwards, but if they have promised, and yet afterwards have taken wives, they are to be removed from the ministry. It also has other canons concerning years of penance that are dangerous and superstitious.

The Laodicean rightly condemns the Novatians, but it errs in censuring digamists, even laymen; it orders them to be punished before they are admitted to communion; it also prohibits baptism after the two weeks of Lent. The rest are political and honorable, as when it prohibits marriages with heretics. This synod followed the Nicene after no long interval.

Under the Emperor Honorius was the first Toletan synod, which contains many useful chapters concerning doctrine. For it piously recounts the articles concerning the divinity and the natures of Christ, and certain others. Afterwards it attaches certain political ones and ceremonies concerning chrism, and concerning vows. This synod prohibits deacons from being raised to the office of presbyter, if they do not abstain from their lawful wives. Likewise, it excommunicates parents who, out of parental affection, embrace daughters bound by vows if they marry. Likewise, it does not admit the married women themselves to communion, unless they depart from their husbands.

The fifth Council of Carthage, held in the year 438 , prohibits bishops, presbyters, and deacons from the custom of lawful wives; thus the prohibition was gradually accumulated. Previously, the custom with wives was granted to deacons, as the Synod of Ancyra testifies; afterwards, the prohibition followed. And these constitutions concerning celibacy are subsequently repeated in all synods, and harsher penalties are added, just as a certain Council of Toledo decreed that the property of the women should be sold if they return to their husbands.

Furthermore, this Council of Carthage contains another memorable constitution concerning chapels and altars of the saints where their bodies are not buried. It orders bishops to demolish these altars and chapels , or if they fear riots, it orders them to dissuade the people in sermons from approaching those places. It appears that some wished to prohibit the growing superstition in the worship of the saints.

The Council of Carthage of the year 457 dealt with the appeal of Bishops. The Roman Pontiff demanded that the right of appeal be granted, wherever anyone had appealed to the Roman, and to obtain that, he committed a forgery, he cited a fictitious decree, which he affirmed had been issued to that effect in the Nicene Council. Afterwards, with copies requested from Constantinople, the vanity was detected, and the petition of the Roman Pontiff was rejected. Augustine was present at this council. By such artifices the Roman Pontiffs built for themselves a path to the primacy. This example warns us not to admire antiquity so much that we free it from all vices.

The fourth Council of Carthage contains a decree concerning prayer and oblation for the dead, in these words: Penitents, who have diligently kept the Canons of penance, if by chance they die before communion, let their memory be commended by prayers and oblations. That age did not yet have private masses, but nevertheless superstition had gradually grown. This Canon does not receive the dead, unless the rites of penance have been diligently kept. Item, he adds the custom concerning offerings.

The Milevitan synod, at which Augustine was present, treated a most serious cause, and rightly defended the pious doctrine concerning original sin, concerning grace, and concerning justification. It also has certain political matters, in which these things are memorable: it forbids appeal to bishops across the sea. Not even the Roman pontiff would accept this decree now. It likewise forbids that judges be sought from the Emperor, not bishops. That was appropriate for those times, now it would be harsh; it also decreed concerning divorce, that an innocent person should not contract marriage again, and it adds that it must be requested that the Emperor pass a law to that effect. That also is too harsh. For at Rome, Fabiola contracted another marriage, as appears from Jerome.

That synod confirms also the superstition concerning vows, it grants that virgins be veiled before the twenty-fifth year against the ancient canons. Although therefore it pronounced tolerably concerning doctrine, nevertheless afterwards some stubble and superstitious constitutions are added. Wherefore not all decrees of synods are to be approved without selection, and yet it must be confessed that pious synods have been well-deserving, because they preserved some articles of Christian doctrine, and concerning these it is profitable to hold the testimony of synods and of antiquity.

Latin:

DE ECCLESIA ET DE AUTO-ritate verbi Dei.

Saepe disputari solet, quantum tribuendum sit Ecclesiae sententiis, decretis Synodorum, & scriptorum dictis. Etsi enim regulam tenemus, ut verbum Dei amplectamur, tamen cum videantur in Apostolicis scriptis occurrere loci ambigui, disputant aliqui potius esse sententias Ecclesiae sequendas, quàm scripta Apostolorum.

Deinde affingunt autoritatem Ecclesiae anteferendam esse verbo Dei, ac posse Ecclesiam mutare tradita in verbo Dei. Citant ad has opiniones dictum Augustini: Evangelio non crederem, nisi me Ecclesiae catholicae commoveret autoritas. Itaque falso praetextu nominis Ecclesiae pontifices decernunt, & praecipiunt multa pro libidine contra verbum Dei, confirmant & stabiliunt impiam doctrinam, et impios cultus, ac plurimos etiam nunc deterret à vera doctrina Evangelii, quam profitemur, solum nomen Ecclesiae. Ideo necesse est de autoritate Ecclesiae recte admoneri homines.

Rursus etiam quaedam petulantiora ingenia, cum fingunt ex dictis scripturae male detortis novas opiniones, ut prorsus aspernantur consensum verae Ecclesiae, & omnes synodos sine discrimine, ut cum Servetus rixatur cum Ecclesia omnium temporum, & depravat dicta de Verbo Ioannis primo, & quaerit concinniorem, ut ipse putat, interpretationem. Ut igitur talis petulantia coherceatur, aliquo modo septis, ut ita dicam, opus est Ecclesiae, sicut veteres synodi & scriptores allegant prima testimonia ab Apostolis & certis autoribus accepta.

Tertulianus contra Praxeam inquit, hanc regulam tenendam esse adversus haereses: Rectum esse quodcunque primum est, adulterinum vero, quodcunque posterius. Et quidem vocat primum, quod Apostoli certo tradiderunt, sic enim ipse sese interpretatur.

Iraeneus contra Florinum allegat autoritatem superiorum, ac nominatim Polycarpi, qui fuerat auditor Ioannis Apostoli. Inquit quit enim exercraturum fuisse dogmata Florini, si ea audisset, & vitaturum locum, in quo illa dicta essent, tanquam pollutum.

Basilius allegat nutricem suam, cuius pietatem ait tunc in primis fuisse laudatam, et addit eam accepisse doctrinam à Gregorio Neocaesariensi, qui illo tempore eruditione & miraculis claruit, & refutavit Samosatenum, ac reliquit brevem confessionem fidei, quae continet illustre testimonium de trinitate. Extat autem in libro vii. Ecclesiasticae historiae.

Origenes allegat Apostolos de baptismo infantum. Ait enim in cap. vi. ad Rom. Ecclesias accepisse traditionem ab Apostolis, ut baptizentur infantes. Hi recte allegant autoritatem Ecclesiae. Quare ordine dicam, quid sit Ecclesia, & quòd audienda sit, ac probatis testimoniis utendum, & tamen doctrina iudicanda sit ex verbo Dei, ut maneat summa autoritas verbi Dei, iuxta illud: Si quis aliud Evangelium docuerit, anathema sit.

Primum autem cum nomino Ecclesiam, non intelligo Pontifices, Episcopos, & caeteros, qui probant ipsorum opiniones. Nam hi sunt hostes verae Ecclesiae, partim Epicurei, partim Idolatrae manifesti. Sed voco Ecclesiam coetum vere credentium, qui habent Evangelium & sacramenta, & sanctificantur spiritu sancto, sicut Ephes . v. describitur Ecclesia, & Ioannis x. Oves meae vocem meam audiunt.

Etsi autem necesse est, hanc veram Ecclesiam semper durare, quia regnum Christi est perpetuum, & scriptum est: Manebo vobibiscum usque ad consummationem seculi, tamen sciendum est hanc veram Ecclesiam non semper pariter florere, sed saepe admodum exiguam esse, ac subinde restitui divinitus, missis veris doctoribus, ut Noe tempore fuit angusta Ecclesia, & paucorum coetus.

Ita post diluvium retinuit veram doctrinam Melchisedech, qui fuit Sem, filius Noe, & cum idolatria apud Chaldaeos crevisset, ac pene ubique extincta esset vera doctrina, Deus renovat Ecclesiam vocato Abraham. Postea familia Abrahae, & pauci eius auditores sunt Ecclesia, cum interim Chaldaei & Aegyptii gloriarentur, se esse posteros patrum, se retinere patrum exempla & cultum, & praedicarent se esse populum Dei, cum verbum Dei non retinuissent, etiamsi caeremonias retinuerant, quibus tamen affinxerant perversas opiniones, & addiderant idolatriam.

Tempore Achaz fuit in Israhel pene extincta Ecclesia, postea per Eliam & Eliseum rursus aucta est, deinde iterum collapsa est.

Cum nasceretur Christus, fuit in Iuda ad modum exigua Ecclesia, Maria, Ioseph, familia Zachariae, Simeon, Anna, pastores, & pauci alii. Interea regimen Ecclesiasticum fuit penes Pharisaeos & Saducaeos, qui erant palam impii. Saducaeietiam erant Epicuraei, & tamen arrogabant sibi praecipuè titulum populi Dei.

Sic & tempore Prophetarum exigua fuit vera Ecclesia. Esaiae primo: Nisi Dominus reliquisset semen, sicut Sodoma & Gomorra facti essemus. Haec verba gruissime monent nos ne de Ecclesia cogitemus, tanquàm de mundana politia, ne eam successione Episcoporum, aut gradu, & loco pontificum metiamur, sed apud eos statuamus Ecclesiam, qui retinent veram doctrinam Evangelii. In hoc coetu esse aliquos vere credentes necesse est. Nam ad hunc coetum pertinent promissiones. Ideo Esaias de trahit illum augustum titulum suis principibus & pontificibus, & inquit exiguum semen reliquum esse in illo ipso populo, qui vocobatur populus Dei.

Et Ieremiae tempore, cum ei reges & sacerdotes adversarentur, non erat Ecclesia coetus sacerdotum, sed illi, qui credebant concionibus Ieremiae. Amos. iii. Sic liberabitur Israhel, ut si pastor duo crura Leoni ex faucibus eripiat. Denique fuit exigua Ecclesia prae multitudine impiorum, cum omnes gentes praeter populum Iuda prorsus amisissent noticiam Dei.

Praedicit & scriptura futuras post Apostolos Ecclesiae clades, Matth. xxiii. Multi pseudoprophetae surgent, & decipient multos. Item: Cum videbitis abominationem desolationis stantem in loco sancto. Hic significat in Ecclesia, quae sic dicitur, orituram esse idololatriam, qua obruentur vera doctrina & veri cultus, & fiet Ecclesiae vastitas, id est, solitudo seu extinctio. Atque ita accidit. Postquàm abusus missarum & cultus traditionum orti sunt, secutae sunt tenebrae de veris cultibus, de fide, de invocatione in fide, de officiis vocationis. Quia conscientia intuens in propria merita, non potest remissionem peccatorum intelligere, nec veram invocationem, & expectationem auxilii divini &c.

Item facient signa & prodigia, ut si fieri posset, seducantur etiam electi. ii. Thessal. ii. Veniet defectio &c. Lucae xviii. Putas quod veniens filius hominis inveniet fidem ? Psal. lxxxviii. Nunquid vane constituisti omnes filios hominum &c? Est enim quaerela de ventura Ecclesiae ruina. Haec dicta testantur, etiamsi Ecclesiam conservari necesse est, tamen praesertim postremo tempore ad modum exiguam & paucorum coetum esse, qui sunt spreti & abiecti in hac vita, sicut inquit Paulus: Non multi sapientes, non multi potentes &c.

Haec testimonia eò citavi, ut primum cogitetur, quid sit Ecclesia, & abducatur animus à carnalibus opinionibus, quae fingunt Ecclesiam esse politiam pontificum, et allegant eam ad ordinariam successionem Episcoporum, sicut imperia consistunt in ordinaria successione principum, sed Ecclesia aliter se habet. Est enim coetus non alligatus ad ordinariam successionem, sed ad verbum Dei. Ibi renascitur Ecclesia, ubi Deus restituit doctrinam, & dat spiritum sanctum. Et hoc modo regi & conservari Ecclesias, non ordinaria successione, testatur Paulus Ephes. iiii. Dedit dona hominibus, Aposto los, Prophetas &c. Docet enim eam esse proprie Ecclesiam, in qua Christus est efficax, & cui dat veros doctores.

Ideo cum obiicitur nobis nomen & autoritas Ecclesiae, primum consideremus, an fiat mentio verae Ecclesiae, an vero coetus pontificum, & successionis illius, & politiae, nec nos sinamus à verbo Dei deterreri falso praetextu nominis Ecclesiae.

Secundo, Postquàm dictum est, quae sit vera Ecclesia, iam addendum est, hanc veram Ecclesiam, quae est exigua, ac tantum sanctorum, retinere veram doctrinam Evangelii, seu articulos fidei, sicut Paulus eam vocat sedem veritatis. Sed haec ipsa vera Ecclesia habet doctrinam aliâs magis, aliâs minus puram & perspicuam. Habet & multa infirma membra, ut Apostoli erant Ecclesia, nec tamen intelligebant ante Christi resurrectionem, quale esset futurum regnum Christi. Petrus etiam post datum spiritum sanctum adhuc imaginabatur cultus legis necessarios esse, sed de caelo admonitus, didicit regnum Christi non esse politiam Iudaicam, sed cultos spirituales, ac perpetuos, Actuum ix.

Postea inchoata praedicatione Apostolo rum, lucebat in ipsis doctrina pura & perspicua, & tamen interea erant multi infirmi, qui tametsi essent vera membra Ecclesiae, & tenerent articulos fidei, tamen aliquid addebant erroris, ut qui observabant cultus legis, nec satis intelligebant abrogationem legis, et veros cultus. Hic error non erat levis, & aliquam caliginem offundebat articulis fidei. Ita Christus praedicit de Ecclesia postremi temporis, futuras magnas tenebras, quae etiam electos impedient, quo minus puram doctrinam habituri sunt.

Manet igitur aliqua vera Ecclesia, quae retinet articulos fidei, sed interdum minus puros, & obscuratos aliquibus incommodis opinionibus, & habentibus aliquid erroris. Ac loquor adhuc de veris Ecclesiae membris, & sanctis, non de aliis, qui amissa luce verbi, amittunt spiritum sanctum, & sequuntur rationis iudicium, & cum putent se admodum pia tradere, dicunt aliena & impia. Sicut nunc quoque multi sunt praestantes doctrina, bonis moribus, specie pietatis, qui videntur sibi sanctissima dicere, cum procul absint à vera luce, hoc est, à vero intellectu verbi Dei. De talibus nondum loquor, verum adhuc tantum fit mentio de veris membris Ecclesiae, quae magna ex parte sunt infirma.

Sic igtur inquit Paulus: Fundamentum aliud nemo potest ponere, praeter id quod positum est. Sed alius superaedificat aurum, alius lignum, stipulas &c. Fundamentum intelligit articulos fidei, hoc est, summam doctrinae Christianae, & doctrinam de beneficiis Christi, sed ad hanc, inquit, addent alii utilem doctrinam, & explicationem, & veros cultus spirituales. Haec vocat aurum. Alii addent stipulas, id est, opiniones incommodas, & aliquid erroris habentes, sicut initio statim conditae sunt caeremoniae, quae secum traxerunt falsas opiniones.

Ut Ambrosium existimo esse verum membrum Ecclesiae, Is tamen inquit de ieiunio quadragesimae: Caetera ieiunia sunt voluntatis, hoc necessitatis est. Haec opinio est stipula addita doctrinae fidei.

Sic Basilius addidit monasticen tanquam stipulas, & laudat hoc genus vitae immodicis & falsis praeconiis, cum quidem ab Episcopo suo reprehenderetur. Quod autem non sit leve erratum, instituere novos cultus, saepe monet scriptura, & satis significat haec una sententia: Frustra colunt memandatis hominum.

Grave peccatum est contra primum praeceptum, cultus non mandatos à Deo instituere aut approbare. Nam primum praeceptum, cum prohibet alienos Deos, etiam prohibet alienos cultus.

Cyprianus urget poenas canonicas, quarum tunc erat usus, & confirmat opiniones, quasi sint necessariae, & propter eas remittantur peccata, interdum in quit absolutionem sine illis inutilem esse. Fortasse sentiebat commodius, quàm locutus est, tamen illi errores non sunt leves, sed admodum densae stipulae, obscurantes puram doctrinam de beneficiis Christi, & de fide.

Porro saepe scriptores commodius senserunt, quàm loquuntur, quia plaerique fuerunt admodum in dicendo negligentes & improprii, & multas sententias ac formulas à vulgo mutuantur, in quibus aliquid inest errorum, ut nomen satisfactionum sumit Augustinus à vulgo, etiamsi errores de satisfactionibus palàm reprehendit. Torquet se in hac sententia interpretanda: omne peccatum est volunatarium, ubi disputat de peccato originis, cum tamen sententia sit civile dictum, de externis delictis traditum.

Sic vocant cenam Domini, oblationem, populi more, cum non sit instituta oblatio, sed Christus ipse fuerit sacerdos, suum offerens sacrificium. Ac ne fiebat quidem olim in caeremonia cenae oblatio corporis & sanguinis, sed ante consecrationem offerebantur panes, & aliae res, & sacerdos dicebat se offerre preces, gratiarum actionem, & totum cultum, qui ibi fieri solet. Etsi igitur oblatio non uno modo intellecta fuit, tamen postea nomen detortum est ad oblationem corporis, unde secuti sunt ingentes abusus.

Dionisius in eo libro, qui continet caeremonias Ecclesiae, cum ritum synaxis diligenter describat, tamen prorsus nullam facit mentionem de oblatione corporis dominici. Nec Canon Basilii continet hanc oblationem. Sed postea dicam plura de cena Domini. Haec tantum addidi, ut ostenderem veteres interdum mutuatos esse sermones incommodos à populo, ut fieri solet omnibus aetatibus.

Interdum vincuntur iudiciis & exemplis multitudinis, quae non est pia, ut trahantur in superstitiones aliqua humana imaginatione, ut in Synodo Nicena, nisi unus Paphnutius obstitisset, fuisset approbata sententia illorum, qui volebant decretum fieri, ut sacerdotes abstinerent à suis uxoribus. Sic Cyprianum & multos alios vicit consuetudo, ut probarent prohibitionem coniugii.

Item tota Synodus Nicena consensu multitudinis, aut temporis victa, approbavit Canones paenitentiae, qui postea pepererunt non tollerandos errores. Magna exempla etiam pios saepe fallunt, sicut Antonii exemplum multis offudit caliginem. Hactenus dixi de piis, qui etiamsi sunt sancti, tamen plurimi sunt infirmi. Addam nunc de lapsis.

Interdum pii prorsus labuntur, & amittunt spiritum sanctum, sicut Origenem iudicio prorsus fuisse lapsum, praesertim si affirmavit illos prodigiosos errores, quòd fuerint innumerabiles mundi, quòd diaboli postremo sunt salvandi. Tertulianus etiam impie damnat secundas nuptias, fortassis autem resipuerunt. Multi enim vere lapsi in vita et doctrina, tamen resipiscunt. Et saepissime fit, ut sancti vere labantur, nec iudicent iuxta verbum, & spiritualem lucem, sed de cipiantur imaginatione rationis, qui tamen deinde resipiscunt. Sicut Gedeon prorsus lapsus est, humano consilio instituens cultum.

Ex his omnibus sequitur conclusio: Etsi vera Ecclesia, quae est exigua, retinet articulos fidei, tamen illa ipsa vera Ecclesia potest habere errata obscurantia articulos fidei. Praeterea multi ita labuntur, ut approbent prorsus impios errores contra articulos fidei, etiamsi fortassis aliqui resipiscunt.

Primum igitur, cum autoritas Ecclesiae allegatur, quaerendum est, an fuerit verae Ecclesiae consensus, congruens cum verbo Dei.

Deinde dicendum est, scriptores qui extant saepe lapsos esse, & fortassis aliquos nequidem membra Ecclesiae esse.

Tertio addendum est aliud discrimen. In illo coetu, qui vocatur Ecclesia, est ingens multitudo impiorum, quorum plaerique antecedunt caeteros autoritate, specie religionis, opinione doctrinae, quales fuerunt in populo Iuda, tempore Hieremiae pontifices, & sacerdotes impii, qui & ipsi contra Hieremiam allegabant autoritatem sedis ac legis, & promissiones. Non peribit lex à sacerdotibus, negabant suum coetum errare posse, cum tamen prorsus errarent, & dissentirent à Hieremia. Item tempore Christi erant paucissimi pii, videlicet Zacharias & Simeon.

Porro cum impia multitudo dominatur in Ecclesia, constituit nomine Ecclesiae multa falsa & impia. Talis multitudo amplexa est applicationem missarum pro vivis & mortuis, cultus votorum & sanctorum, postea exemplum nocuit piis. Talis multitudo etiam in synodo constituit, divellenda esse coniugia sacerdotum. Saepe autem accidit in Ecclesia, ut impii excellentes ingeniis sumant impetus constituendi religionem humana sapientia, qui cum non moveantur verbo Dei, sed ducantur rationis imagine, & quaerant concinnas opiniones, gignunt impia dogmata, sicut Samosatenus, Arius, Pelagius. Alii quaerunt merita, aut quaerunt speciosum regimen, εὐταξίαν populi, & his causis moventur ad instituendos & cumulandos cultus, ut monachi, et Gregorius, et hoc tempore pontifices, principes, & multi viri docti cupientes constituere Ecclesiam, moventur humana sapientia, & omisso verbo Dei, volunt Ecclesiam iuxta suas imaginationes constituere. Nec vident esse horribilem impietatem, discedere à verbo Dei, quaerere Deum sine verbo, cultus instituere humano arbitrio, sine mandato Dei, vera dogmata mutare, & opprimere puritatem verbi Dei.

Cum igitur obiicitur autoritas Ecclesiae, ut de missarum applicatione: Ecclesia non errat, Ecclesia tot seculis applicavit missas, Igitur mos est servandus.

Respondendum est ad maiorem, Ecclesia universa, quae est multitudo dominantium in Ecclesia, potest errare, sicut errabant pontifices & sacerdotes Ieremiae, aut Christi tempore. Et quanquàm praeter illam multitudinem sunt aliqui pii, qui retinent articulos fidei, tamen hi quoque moti exemplis assentiuntur quibusdam erroribus. Ita fit ut articulos fidei minus puros retineant, sicut videtur Bernhardus commodius sensisse quàm caeteri, & si multis erroribus assensit, ut abusui missarum, potestati pontificiae, votis, cultui sanctorum.

Non igitur multitudinis autoritas alleganda est contra verbum Dei, sed redeundum ad regulam: Si quis aliud Evangelium docuerit, anathema sit. Prima sit autoritas verbi divinitus traditi. Deinde illa est Ecclesia existimanda, quae cum verbo illo consentit, ut inquit Christus: Oves meae vocem meam audiunt, & Augustinus: Quaestio est, ubi sit Ecclesia, quid ergo facturi sumus? In verbis nostris eam quae situri sumus, an in verbis capitis sui Domini nostri Iesu Christi? Puto quod in illius verbis quaerere debemus, qui veritas est, & optime novit corpus suum.

Sed hic obiicitur, si repudiatur autoritas Ecclesiae, conceditur deinde nimis magna licentia petulantiae ingeniorum, nam reiectis Ecclesiae sententiis, multi excogitabunt novas & impias interpretationes scripturae. Hoc periculum cum non sit contemnendum, & prosit illam licentiam cohercere, rursus videndum est, quatenus re quirenda sit autoritas Ecclesiae. Servetus enim, cum renovat impium errorem Samosateni, & negat verbum intelligi personam in hoc dicto: In principio erat verbum, magnifice praedicat autoritatem scripturae, iubet hanc anteferri Ecclesiae decretis, deinde callide disputat, sermonem simpliciter intelligendum esse. Cum autem verbum in communi hominum sermone non significet personam, negat apud Ioannem intelligendam esse personam, ut si Demosthenes hoc dictum legeret: In principio erat verbum, certe non cogitaret intelligi personam aliquam.

Quaero igitur an adversus tales non prosit opponere autoritatem Ecclesiae? Hic respondeo, sicut Evangelium praecipit audiri Ecclesiam, ita semper dico, eum coetum, penes quem fuit verbum Dei, & qui dicitur Ecclesia, audiendum esse, sicut iubemus quoque audiri nostros pastores. Audiamus igitur docentem & admonentem Ecclesiam, sed non propter Ecclesiae autoritatem credendum est. Nam Ecclesia non condit articulos fidei, tantum docet ac admonet. Verum propter verbum Dei credendum est, cum videlicet admoniti ab Ecclesia intelligimus hanc sententiam vere & sine sophistica in verbo Dei traditam esse.

Fortassis Demosthenes non cogitaret de persona, si legeret: In principio erat verbum. Sed auditor admonitus ab Ecclesia, quod verbum significet personam scilicet filium Dei, adiuvatur iam ab Ecclesia docente et ad monente, & articulum credit non propter Ecclesiae autoritatem, sed quia videt hanc sententiam habere firma testimonia, in ipsa scriptura, videt de quadam persona dici, quae assumpta humana natura, in mundo conversata est cum hominibus. Hanc personam videt appellari λόγον. Colligit testimonia apta & firma de duabus naturis in christo, scit enim de natura Dei credendum esse voci caelesti, ac summam impietatem esse, comminisci opiniones de natura Dei sine ipsius testimonio. ii. Petri1. Et Matth.xvii. Hunc audite.

Item valet prima Ecclesia, ut testis Apostolorum. Loquor autem de dogmatibus, non de humanis traditionibus. Nam dogmata volebant esse firma & perpetua. Ritus humanos non volebant esse perpetuos aut immutabiles. Nec errabant Apostoli in doctrina. Ideo prodest tenere, ubi allegent vetustissimi scriptores autoritatem Apostolorum.

Ut de Trinitate citant eos, Origenes, Tertulianus, Irenaeus, Gregorius Neocaesariensis, Alexander, Episcopus Alexandrinus, & alii multi, qui cum testentur doctrinam de Trinitate ab Apostolis acceptam esse, valde confirmant pios. Itaque talia testimonia non sunt aspernanda.

Dixi autem audiendos esse scriptores, sicut nunc quoque dicimus, audiendos esse concionatores, quia aliqui manent in Ecclesia, quire tinent veritatem aliâs purius aliâs impurius. Sed addendum est, ut auditi iudicentur ex verbo Dei, quod semper manet regula doctrinae.

Exempla.

Augustinus de peccato originali acrius contendit, quam reliqui. Docet igitur et monet, cumque videamus eum vere & sine sophistica recitare sententiam scripturae, credimus articulum non propter Augustinum, sed propter verbum Dei, & videmus idem sentire superiores, etimsi hunc articulum non tam copiose, aut tam perspicue tractarunt.

Aliud.

Petrus Alexandrinus Episcopus, contra Meletium contendit lapsos recipiendos esse & allegat veterem autoritatem. Nam haec verba recitat Epiphanius, ut doctrina, quae ad nos usque pervenit, tradit. Docet igitur & monet Episcopus, ille Alexandrinus, recipiendos esse lapsos. Id credimus non propter hunc Episcopum, sed quia videmus hanc sententiam traditam esse in verbo Dei, & accedunt testimonia veteris Ecclesiae.

Idem de synodis dico, Audiendas esse Ecclesiae synodos, quae, cum de verbo Dei disputant, docent & monent nos, sed iudicium accedat, & cum vera tradunt, credamus propter verbum Dei, Ut Nicena synodus pie et utiliter docuit, & admonuit omnem posteritatem de filio Dei, sed articulum credimus non propter synodum, sed quia viademus sic traditum esse in verbo Dei.

Caetera quae sunt extra scripturas, non sic amplectenda sunt, ut synodus Nicena condidit Canones paenitentiae, qui sunt traditiones humanae extra scripturam, et fuerunt femina multarum superstitiosarum opinionum.

Samsonis convivae non poterant interpretari aenigma in convivio propositum, nisi interrogata eius coniuge. Quare Samson inquit: Nisi arassetis vitula mea, non invenissetis meam quaestionem. Sic circumspiciendum est, ubi sit coetus, qui habet verbum Dei, & videndum, qui coetus Patrum ac Synodorum sit purior, hoc est, minus habens opinionum extra verbum Dei. Haec Ecclesia docet, monet, testatur. Sed videndum est an ea quae proponit, habeant firma testimonia verbi Dei.

Ac profecto pios fateri decet, Patres bene meritos esse de posteritate, qui acerrimis contentionibus propugnaverunt, & retinuerunt pia dogmata, id beneficium non est leve ducendum. Huc pertinet Augustini dictum: Evangelio non crederem, nisi me Ecclesiae moveret autoritas. Non sentit Augustinus, maiorem Ecclesiae autoritatem, quàm verbi divini, aut Ecclesiam posse abolere articulos in verbo Dei traditos, sed sentit Ecclesiam esse doctricem, & testem. Non crederemus Evangelio, nisi Ecclesia doceret nos & testaretur, hanc doctrinam ab Apostolis traditam esse.

Valet etiam hoc dictum ad refutanda nova dogmata, quae nunquam in Ecclesia extiterunt, sicut Manichaei nova deliramenta excogitaverunt. Nam dogmata necessaria pietati, necesse est initio extitisse in praedicatione Apostolorum, Ergo nova & prorsus ignota Ecclesiae Apostolicae sunt reiicienda. Sed de dicto Augustini alâs disputatum est copiosius, certe non concedit Ecclesiae autoritatem statuendi contra verbum Dei, aut abolendi articulos in verbo Dei traditos, aut condendi novos articulos fidei.

Cathalogus.

Aliquot synodorum, & Patrum exempla colligam, ut appareat in illis contineri dissimiles materias, ne sine discrimine omnia omnium dicta, aut omnes Veterum ritus pro necessariis recipiantur. Sicut inepti quidam ita admirantur antiquitatem, ut omnes veteres ritus humanos velint restitui, Perinde ac si nunc velint spartani omnes veteres ritus suae Reipubl. ristituere, cum ritus ab hominibus cxcogitati partim sint vitiosi, partim etiam si sunt probabiles, tamen non omnibus temporibus congruant.

Synodus Neocaesariensis vetat, ne sacerdotes accedant ad convivia secundarum nuptiarum, ne eas videantur approbare. Tales ridiculae constitutiones multae bonis admixtae sunt. Quare delectus habendus est, nec temere omnibus dictis veterum applaudendum.

Anno domini cccxxiiii. Nicena synodus à Constantino convocata est, in qua praefuit Antiochenus Episcopus Eustathius. In hac synodo gravissimae controversiae dogmatum diiudicatae sunt, et recte damnati sunt errores Samosateni et Arii, Item Catharorum, qui lapsos negabant recipiendos esse, ac negabant eos consequi remissionem peccatorum.

Postea politica quedam ordinata sunt, de gubernatione Ecclesiarum, ut Alexandrinus Episcopus prae esset Ecclesiae orientis, et Romanus Ecclesiis nationum vicinarum. Item ut Episcopi ordinentur à vicinis Episcopis. Haec politica etsi sunt utilia, tamen non volebant haberi pro articulis fidei.

Tertio, addiderunt quaedam caeremonialia, videlicet Canones paenitentiae, ut vocabant, qui initio minus duri erant, & fortasse minus habuerunt superstitionum. Sed post ea crevit onus ipsum, & crevit superstitio, & est obscurata gratuita condonatio. Quare in hac re Patres non satis cauti fuerunt. Cumque eventus postea ostendit talibus exemplis superstitiones crescere, non ita miremur in hac re Synodum, ut velimus illos canones aut approbare aut restituere. Nec propterea dissentimus à veteri Ecclesia, retinemus articulos Synodi de dogmatibus, quae propriè ad Ecclesiam pertinent. Caeterae, quae sunt extra vel contra verbum Dei, non pertinent ad Ecclesiam.

Anno domini ccclxxxiii. Constantinopolitana synodus à Theodosio convocata est, in qua praefuit Episcopus Constantinopolitanus, controversia gravis diiudicata est, de spiritu sancto, quod sit persona procedens à patre & filio, & sit Deus, & recte damnati sunt Eunomius & alii, qui contrarium senserant. Sunt & politica quaedam ordinata, ne Episcopi in alienis Diocesibus aliquid administrent.

Anno ccccxxxiii. Ephesina synodus convocata est à iuniore Theodosio in qua praefuit Cyrillus Alexandrinus. Haec synodus recte damnavit Nestorium, qui negabat in Christo unitum esse verbum humanae naturae substantiali unione, sed tantum adesse verbum, & inhabitare in humana natura, velut hospitem in domicilio, ut ibi esset efficax.

Haec fuit magni momenti cotroversia. Nam in Christo vere & substantialiter unitae sunt duae naturae. Nec verum, est humanam naturam solam esse Christum, ac domicilium esse verbi assistentis. Inde urserunt pii has formas loquendi de unitate personae, Deum esse natum, passum &c. Etsi autem Nestorius negabat se cum Samosateno sentire, tamen suspicor eum re ipsa idem sensisse, sed in speciem aliter proposuisse vetus delirium involucris tectum.

Anno cccclii. Chalcedonensis synodus convocata est à Martiano Imperatore, in qua recte damnatus est Eutyches, qui negavit etiam duas naturas in Christo, ac contendit ipsam verbi naturam divinitus missam, editam esse per virginem, nec duas esse naturas unitas. Videtur & hic renovasse delyrium Samosateni, sed alio involucro propositum. Hoc iudicium synodi laudandum est.

Caeterum creverant iam in Ecclesia humanae traditiones. Ideo aliquos addidit haec synodus vitiosas constitutiones, non de dogma tibus sed de caeremoniis & cultibus extra scripturam, & tamen adhuc sunt verecundiores hae constitutiones, quàm aliae postea natae. In hac synodo primum facta est constitutio, quae prohibet nuptias monachis & virginibus, quae vota fecerunt, & excommunicat tales contrahentes connubia, quanquàm addit mitigationem, posse & hoc concedi iudicio Episcopi.

Verum multa politica utiliter tunc constituta sunt, ne Episcopi ipsi tenerent administrationem facultatum Ecclesiasticarum, sed ut Ecclesiae haberent Oeconomos, ne quis plura ministeria teneret. Item ne quis sine ministerio ordinaretur, Item ut in singulis provinciis Episcopi quotannis conveniant, & synodos habeant de praesentibus Ecclesiae controversiis.

Haec utilia decreta synodorum adversarii dissimulant, ac interim alia leviora proferunt, ut videatur nobis opponere veteris Ecclesiae antoritatem.

Fuerunt interim & aliae synodi, seu provinciales seu fre quentiores, in quibus convenerunt vicinarum provinciarum Episcopi. Talis fuit synodus Antiochena ante Nicenam, convocata adversus Samosatenum, quae pie & recte damnavit Samosateni impietatem. Talis item fuit synodus Gangrensis in Galatia vetus & pura, habet optima decreta contra superstitiones de coniugio, de cibis, de monachatu. Et apparet hanc synodum convenisse propter Montanum, Martionem, & similes, qui illas superstitiones valde auxerunt.

Secutae sunt aliae posteriores, ut Anchirana, quae habet hanc constitutionem memora bilem: Si diaconi in ordinatione non promiserint se victuros caelibes, retinendi sunt in ministeriis, etiamsi postea ducunt uxores, sed si promiserint, & postea tñ duxerint uxores, removendi sunt à ministerio. Habet & alios Canones de annis paenitentiae periculosos & superstitiosos.

Laodicena recte damnat Novatianos, sed errat taxans digamos etiam laicos, iubet eos prius puniri quàm admittantur ad communionem, prohibet etiam baptismum post duas septimanas quadragesimae. Caetera politica sunt honesta, ut cum prohibet nuptias cum haereticis. Haec synodus non longo intervallo secuta est Nicenam.

Sub Honorio Imperatore fuit Toletana prima synodus, quae continet multa capita utilia de doctrina. Nam pie recenset articulos de divinitate, & naturis Christi, & alios quosdam. Postea quaedam attexit politica, & caeremonias de chrismate, & de votis. Haec synodus prohibet diaconos evehi ad munus praesbyteri, si non abstineant à legitimis uxoribis. Item excommunicat parentes, qui filias votis obligatas, si nubant, parentum affectu complectantur. Item ipsas nuptas non admittit ad communionem, nisi discedentes a maritis.

Carthaginensis quinta, anno ccccxxxviii. habita, prohibet Episcopis, presbyteris, & diaconis consuetudinem legitimarum coniugum, ita paulatim cumulata est prohibitio. Antea diaconis concessa erat consuetudo cum uxoribus, ut testatur Anchirana synodus, postea secuta est prohibitio. Et hae constitutiones de caelibatu, subinde in omnibus synodis repetuntur, & adduntur acerbiores poenae, sicut quaedam Toletana Synodus constituit, ut facultates mulierum vendantur, si redeant ad viros.

Porro haec Cartaginensis synodus continet & aliam memorabilem constitutionem, de sacellis, & aris sanctorum, ubi non sunt eorum corpora condita. Has aras & sacella iubet Episcopos demoliri, aut si metuant tumultus, iubet eos in concionibus populum dehortari, ne ad illa loca accedant. Apparet aliquos crescentem superstitionem in cultu sanctorum voluisse prohibere.

Synodus Carthaginensis anni cccclvii egit de provocatione Episcoporum. Romanus Pontifex postulavit, ut concederetur provocatio, ubicunque aliquis ad Romanum provocasset, idque ut obtineret, commisit falsum, citavit commentitium decretum, quod affirmabat in eam sententiam editum esse in Nicena synodo. Postea ex Constantinopoli petitis exemplis deprehensa est vanitas, & repudiata petitio Romani Pontificis. Huic synodo interfuit Augustinus. Talibus artificiis Romani Pontifices viam sibi ad primatum struxerunt. Hoc exemplum monet, ne ita miremur antiquitatem, ut eam omnibus vitiis liberemus.

Carthaginensis quarta, decretum continet de precatione & oblatione pro mortuis, his verbis: Paenitentes, qui diligenter servarunt Canones paenitentiae, si casu moriantur ante communionem, commendetur eorum memoria precationibus & oblationibus. Illa aetas nondum habebat privatas missas, sed tamen paulatim superstitio creverat. Hic Canon non recipit mortuos, nisi diligenter servatis ritibus paenitentiae. Item, addit morem de oblationibus.

Tractavit causam gravissimam synodus Milevitana, cui interfuit Augustinus, & recte defendit piam doctrinam de peccato originali, de gratia & de iustificatione. Habet et politica quaedam, in quibus haec sunt memorabilia, vetar provocationem ad transmarinos Episcopos. Hoc decretum nunc ne Romanus quidem pontifex reciperet. Vetat item ab Imperatore peti iudices, non Episcopos. Id illis temporibus congruebat, nunc esset durum, de divortio etiam sanxit, ne persona innocens rursus contrahat matrimonium, & addit petendum esse, ut Imperator legem in eam sententiam ferat. Id quoque durius est. Nam Romae Fabiola contraxit aliud connubium, ut apparet ex Ieron.

Ea synodus confirmat & superstitionem de votis, concedit velari virgines ante vigesimum quintum annum contra veteres canones. Quanquàm igitur de doctrina tollerabiliter pronunciavit, tamen postea accedunt aliquae stipulae et superstitiosae constitutiones. Quare non omnia synodorum decreta sine delectu probanda sunt, et tamen fatendum est, pias synodos bene meritas esse, quia aliquos doctrinae Christianae articulos conservaverunt, et de his prodest tenere synodorum & antiquitatis testimonium.

## 14:17 On Ancient Ecclesiastical Writers
ON ANCIENT ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS.

These also have merit, especially insofar as they are witnesses of the ancient and first Church of the Apostles. For they confirm us by their testimony concerning the Trinity, concerning the natures in Christ, concerning the Baptism of infants, concerning the use of the Lord's supper, concerning the ordination of ministers, concerning the use of indifferent things, concerning the penance of the lapsed. Concerning all these articles, memorable examples of the Apostles are cited, which support us.

Furthermore, other writers were more diligent in other matters, and, as is human, they often inconsiderately pour forth absurd and false opinions, which, had they been admonished, they would undoubtedly have corrected. Often, when they did not think badly, they were nevertheless unable to say what they wanted with sufficient clarity. Often, on account of the custom of the times, they defended present traditions too harshly, and sometimes they even held some false opinions. Wherefore, not all the writings of the Fathers are to be approved without selection, and often they fight among themselves, nor is it rare for someone to disagree with himself. Wherefore the judgment ought to rest with the Apostolic scripture. But I submit examples.

Concerning Origen.

Origen, citing the examples and opinions of the Apostles and the ancient Churches, is a useful witness to posterity concerning some articles, concerning the Trinity, concerning the Two natures in Christ, concerning the baptism of infants, concerning original sin, concerning the use of the Lord's supper, and concerning certain others.

However, he mixed many false and absurd opinions into his writings, some of which even his own age disapproved. He imagines that before this world there were many worlds. He imagines that the punishments of the devils and the damned will cease. His own age also censured these.

In Romans, treating this proposition, We are justified by faith, not from works, he understands it κατασυνεκδοχὴν, by faith we are just, that is, by a perfect faith embracing all virtues: And he declares this, he says the same can be said of the other virtues, By mercy we are just, namely perfect, embracing the other virtues. To say this is nothing other than that men have the remission of sins on account of their works and on account of their virtues, and are just to be. And since he does not attend to what Paul is doing, what he calls faith, what that exclusive, Not of works, means for him, he adds confused and perplexed explanations, nor is he consistent with himself.

For sometimes he pours out some tolerable statement, but he soon corrupts it afterwards, such as that one Rom. iiii. The beginning of justification is from God. Faith, which believes in the one who justifies, and this faith when it has been justified, just as a root having received rain clings in the soil of the soul, so that when it has begun to be cultivated by the law of God, branches may rise in it, which may bear the fruits of works. Therefore, the root of righteousness is not from works, but from the root of righteousness, the fruit of works grows, namely that root of righteousness, by which God credits righteousness without works.

In iii. capite: Where is boasting? He seems now to be closer to the Pauline sentiment, he admits the exclusive, that men are justified by faith alone, and he alleges the Thief on the cross, and the woman in Luke: your faith has made you safe. But afterwards, explaining those things, he seems to want this, that a man at the beginning obtains the remission of sins by faith alone, afterwards he is righteous by other virtues, just as he himself says afterwards: Faith is credited for righteousness to him who is converted, but afterwards righteousness is credited for righteousness. Furthermore There is a wonderful variety and perplexity of the narration; even if it grants that a man, at the beginning, obtains remission by faith alone, yet if it afterwards imagines that those who are converted are without sin, satisfy the law, and are righteous on account of other virtues, it dissents from Paul and from the remaining divine scriptures, according to that saying: In thy sight shall no man living be justified Psalm 143:2. Likewise, If we say that we have no sin, etc. 1 John 1:8.

In chapter seven he clearly says that the saints represent another's person when they attribute sin to themselves, as in Daniel: Not in our justifications, but in your mercy will you hear us. He corrupts such sentences, and teaches confidence in one's own justice or despair. Chapter three he says: Without the law the justice of God is manifested, that is, without the natural law the new Evangelical laws have been handed down, such as that one: Let not the right hand know what the left is doing, this, he says, was a law previously unknown. Item, The law is spiritual, he understands it only concerning allegory, that is, ceremonies have an allegory, and he often inconveniently understands spirit, not concerning the motions of the holy spirit, but only concerning interpretation or allegorical thought.

Chapter VIII. That which was impossible to the law, because it was weak through the flesh. He transfers the flesh to the law, the flesh of the law was weak, that is, the ceremonies were impossible, etc. But Paul understands by flesh the nature of men, the law was weak through the flesh, that is, human nature could not be done. These passages show that Origen runs off the path, and does not attend to what Paul is doing.

I could collect many trivial things, as when he says that Peter excels the others, because it is said to him in the plural number, it shall be loosed in heaven. To the whole assembly of the Apostles it is said in the singular number, it shall be loosed in heaven. But I omit these futile things. Furthermore, it is profitable for the learned and those who apply judgment to read ancient writings, first because of historical testimonies, then because the comparison of them sharpens and exercises the studious. Thus the reading of Origen will also be profitable to those who have been rightly instructed beforehand, and hold the sum of Christian doctrine.

Concerning Dionysius.

There is one little book of Dionysius concerning the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy, which is useful on account of history. The others contain idle speculations. There, however, the ceremonies of the sacraments and the rites of the Church are handed down, and it appears that the ceremonies were still moderate at that time. Especially, however, the rites of the Mass are to be considered there, so that it may appear that the more recent ones in the Church of the Pope have departed far from the ancient form. Certain Psalms and readings from the Gospel were recited, prayers were said for the Church and the Republic. Afterwards, the presbyter standing at the altar recited the words of Christ concerning the Lord's Supper, then he distributed the sacrament to the people, and a thanksgiving followed. This was the rite of the mass, from which it is manifest that the mass was only a communion, and there were no private masses. Moreover, it is also to be wondered at that no mention is made of an oblation, nor does he even recount the rite of the one offering. It is especially useful to observe these things in Dionysius, so that we may oppose antiquity to those who defend the abuses of the masses.

He recounts baptism, chrism, communion, as I have said, the ordination of presbyters, and of those who made vows, and the anointing of the dead, where he narrates what the ceremonies of funerals were like, when the corpse had been placed in the temple, in the presence of the people some readings from the sacred scriptures concerning the resurrection were recited. Then the people were bidden to give thanks in prayers, because he had died piously in the acknowledgment of the Gospel. An exhortation was added, that everyone should pray for himself a pious end from this life. This custom was full of piety, and worthy of praise. For what greater benefits can be thought of, than in that immense struggle, to retain the knowledge of Christ, to be helped by Christ and to be saved. A more recent age has completely abolished this better ceremony, while retaining and accumulating worse ones.

Dionysius adds, however, that after this exhortation the presbyter departed, and poured oil over the corpse, and prayed that God would forgive him the infirmity which had remained in him after his conversion. Afterwards the corpse was buried in the earth. These were the only ceremonies of funerals then indeed, not yet was mention made of the dead in the Mass, much less was the body of the Lord offered for the dead. A later age added this profanation of the sacrament.

Thus far concerning Dionysius, in whom although the ceremonies are somewhat less vicious, nevertheless they are the beginnings of monasticism, and this is worthy of grave reproach, that he does not distinguish between sacraments divinely instituted, and human traditions. He speaks of Chrism just as he does of baptism, and equates πάρεργα ἔργοις, if I may so say. He even prefers the ordination of monks to the ordination of ministers, which is highly to be censured, since the ordination of ministers pertains to the preaching of the Gospel. But that ordination of monks is superstitious, and is done only for the sake of a forbidden worship, according to that saying: In vain do they worship me with the commandments of men. And yet there monasticism is called perfection. Therefore, let his testimonies be valid, as far as history is concerned, so that we may know what rites were then in use, but let not dogmas or laws be made from his descriptions.

Concerning Tertullian.

Tertullian rightly refuted Marcion and the remaining heretics of his faction. He contains useful testimonies concerning the Trinity, reciting not his own opinion, but the ancient one received from the Apostles. Against Praxeas there exists a clear testimony concerning the Word, that is, concerning the Son of God, that He is a person, even before He assumed human nature.

Furthermore, the ancients also censure certain of his errors, namely that he condemns second marriages, and argues ridiculously: It is not permitted to marry the wife of a deceased brother; he who marries a widow left by a Christian, marries the wife of a deceased brother: Therefore he does not act rightly.

He also plays with the kingdom of the Saints, which they imagined would last for a thousand years, in this bodily life, before the conflagration of the world, and before the final judgment, with some rising again gradually sooner, others later. This Jewish delusion must be utterly exploded from the Church.

In the little book on the soldier's crown he says many things about human rites, and declaims most harshly about custom, that it must be held as law. With these words badly twisted in the Church, as happens, huge errors would be confirmed in all ages, because the vigilance of men is never so great that some vicious customs do not creep in.

Tertullian, however, recounts quite childish customs, that after baptism one should not go to the bath for the first seven days: Item, that milk and honey should be offered to the baptized to taste. There, he says, we also make offerings for the dead, for birthdays on the annual day. Our adversaries now impiously twist this to masses for the dead. Why do they omit birthdays, if they attribute so much to the authority of Tertullian? But he is not speaking of the Lord's Supper. In truth, on birthdays and days of funerals, food and other gifts were brought into the temples for the poor. These they called offerings, and ἀγαπὰς, . And the custom was accepted from the heathens, but corrected somewhat. For the heathens used to give feasts even in temples, at birthdays and funerals, and afterwards the Nicene synod and others prohibited this pomp of birthdays.

Therefore, as has been said concerning the others, historical testimonies in Tertullian are useful, where he commemorates what the earlier Church thought. But his expositions and disputations are not to be received as dogmas, except insofar as they agree with Apostolic scripture.

Concerning Cyprian.

Cyprian lived around the year of the Lord 260. He contains useful testimonies concerning the Trinity, concerning the baptism of infants, concerning the use of the Lord's supper, and concerning the form of the election of Bishops, whom he writes were elected by the assembly of the Church, and that that election was approved by having some neighboring Bishops present.

But the ancients also criticized Cyprian, because he thinks that those baptized by Heretics are to be baptized again. He pours out absurd opinions sometimes while declaiming, when he exaggerates with immoderate hyperboles the cause which he has undertaken: As he writes quite harshly concerning canonical penalties, he says that absolution is not valid unless those penalties have been paid in full. This statement, how much inconvenience it has, is not obscure.

He also declaims vehemently about celibacy, although he does indeed mitigate that point, he orders those very people who had made vows to contract marriages, if they do not keep the promise. In the booklet on almsgiving he says that sins committed before baptism are remitted on account of the passion of Christ, but after baptism remission must be sought through alms. He repeats the same thing concerning the lapsed, that the benefit of Christ is consumed in baptism, afterwards remission must be sought through alms. These things are full of absurdity, which, having been admonished, he would undoubtedly have corrected. Therefore, not all of his sayings are to be held as dogmas.

Concerning the Supper of the Lord he is accustomed to use the words of oblation and sacrifice, just like the others, who say indiscriminately, we offer prayers, we offer bread, wine. We offer the body and blood of Christ, for that also is found in Cyprian. From this our adversaries take testimonies, to defend the profanation of the Supper of the Lord in the private mass etc.

Great is the force of custom, and following this men often speak improperly, as we now say mass, when is known to no one. The etymology of the name. Thus the ancients retained the terms of oblation and sacrifice, not caring much about the etymology or the proper meaning. And because Augustine saw that there was something inconvenient in these appellations, he himself softened it; he says that sacrifice is spoken of for the memory of a sacrifice, and oblation for the memory of an oblation. These are metonymies, as we say passover for the memory or sign of the passing over, but I do not wish to subtly interpret or excuse the customary locution of that time. For thus the people spoke, who sometimes receive an improper word.

Irenaeus clearly says that this oblation is an act of thanksgiving. The others felt the same, as the name of the Eucharist testifies. Wherefore they felt it to be a ceremony by which thanks are given. That has nothing inconvenient in it. For we receive it so that we may be reminded of the benefit given to us by Christ, and stir up faith, and then give thanks for that benefit, nor does it follow from that that this work must be done for others, must be applied to others, etc. The Fathers did not even think of these monsters. Therefore, when we read the name of sacrifice and oblation, let us understand either the sign of a sacrifice and oblation, or an act of thanksgiving; let us not invent applications for others.

Sometimes they call the oblation by one name, that whole business which is transacted there, namely the prayers and the Supper of the Lord. When this is done, let the prayers be understood to be the oblations.

Certain words are also read in Cyprian concerning the dead, which more recent writers badly distort, 'we offer sacrifices for them,' but he says this concerning the martyrs. For mention of them was made in the prayers, when thanks were being given to God, because He had helped them. Just as the Greek Canon says, 'we offer for the Patriarchs, Prophets, Apostles,' that is, we give thanks that from the beginning even until now You have chosen, redeemed, and sanctified the Church for Yourself, etc. This was the meaning of these words in the beginning; it was not requested that God should relax punishments for the dead. Afterwards, in time, evil opinions were added, and partly the former words were changed, and partly the form of the old words was retained, and posterity understood something other than what the earlier ones had understood.

Therefore, the testimonies of antiquity do not support the more recent abuses, which are partly foreign to present customs, and partly, if they have any vice, ought not to be opposed to the firm testimonies of Scripture, because the remaining ages also had their own inconveniences.

I answer these things most simply without sophistry regarding the words of oblation and sacrifice.

Concerning Basil.

In Basil there exist useful testimonies concerning the Trinity, and repentance against Novatus. In his sermon on humility he delivers an excellent sentiment concerning the justice of faith, which openly supports us. Without any sophistry he removes justification from good works, nor does he speak of ceremonial ones, but of all virtues, nor does he speak only of works before renovation, but of virtues in the renovated, and he commands us to believe that we are just by the sole confidence of mercy promised on account of Christ. His words are these:

But the Apostle says: He who glories, let him glory in the Lord, saying that Christ has been made for us wisdom from God, justice, sanctification and redemption, that as it is written, he who is to glory may glory in the Lord. For this is the perfect and entire glorying in God, when someone is not even puffed up on account of his own justice, but acknowledges that true justice is lacking to him, and that he is justified by faith alone in Christ, and Paul glories that he despises his own justice, but seeks through faith the justice which is through Christ, which is from God.

These words sufficiently show that Basil understood the righteousness of faith in such a way that it must be held that we are righteous, that is, accepted, by faith on account of Christ through mercy, not on account of our own virtues.

Furthermore, that Basil first established groups of monks, that example was harmful, and it has something of a defect, even if he himself at first did not have gross superstitions, and those groups were still a certain image of schools. There are also circulated certain books under his name which contain the rules of monks, some of which are undoubtedly supposititious and born a long time after Basil, for they are full of false opinions about celibacy and other forms of worship devised without the command of God, and they contain ridiculous trifles, such as a great heap of punishments or satisfactions, which he calls ἐπιτίμια, if a girl laughs in the choir, let her sit for two days in the vestibule, and similar nonsense, which if anyone wished to revive out of admiration for antiquity, he would truly be insane.

Concerning Gregory of Nazianzus.

Nazianzenus treated the article concerning the Trinity; he touches upon other dogmas lightly. He wrote the life of Cyprian, in which he narrates that a certain girl was loved by Cyprian before his conversion, who, invoking the virgin Mary, overcame the magical incantations of Cyprian.

This example is cited concerning the invocation of the saints. But even if it seems to be a fictitious fable, and later spread under the title of Nazianzen, nevertheless, even if it were a true history, it is not to be cited to confirm the invocation of the saints. For the errors of the pious are not to be opposed to the word of God, and in all ages even the pious in the Church have their infirmities.

They also allege from Basil and Nazianzen that, at the end of sermons about the saints, they are accustomed to address them, O Athanasius, pray for us. But even if these apostrophes can be excused by rhetorical figures, nevertheless it is possible that, according to the custom of their time, they then invoked the saints. For the invocation of the saints gradually crept into the Church at that time, and the errors of the times draw men so that they less disapprove of what is customary, and interpret it in good part, just as the force of rivers carries along those sailing with it. Nor, however, is the invocation of the saints to be approved for that reason. And after the custom grew, and now the impiety has been uncovered, it must be entirely removed from the Church.

Nor does Basil say anything about invocation; he only says that the memory of the saints is celebrated so that we may imitate their virtues, and he calls the saints helpers of our prayers, not because they are to be invoked, but because all the blessed in heaven pray for the Church and commend it to God.

Epiphanius writes that certain women, invoking the virgin Mary, were accustomed to carry her statue around. He condemns this whole business and calls it an idolatrous work. For Epiphanius contains refutations of ancient heresies, especially concerning the Trinity and a few other matters, which history I indeed judge should be read especially.

Concerning Chrysostom.

The age of Chrysostom had already received many vicious customs, which he himself, while recounting them, does not rebuke, just as he praises those approaching the monuments of the saints, and he also makes mention of prayer for the dead. He adorns the monastic life with immoderate and false praises. In the treatise on penance, when he collects many ways of obtaining the remission of sins, namely alms, tears, and other works, he nevertheless makes no mention of faith, about which it was necessary to speak, and that writing contains many false things, and

it is confused and perplexed.

The Greeks praised most highly the commentaries on Paul, where in the passages concerning justification and concerning faith the series of the Pauline disputation leads him to this point, that he often repeats this sentiment, That by faith we obtain the remission of sins on account of Christ, not on account of works. And he says expressly, That by faith not only is God loved, but in turn believers feel that they are loved by God, although in many ways they are guilty.

In this sentiment he sufficiently signified that he understands faith, not only as knowledge of history, but as the trust by which we believe that our sins are remitted to us, and indeed he distinguishes this faith from works, from not stealing, not killing, etc. And he says that this worship is superior. Although, however, his exposition is simpler and less impure than the Origenic one, nevertheless it itself also is obscure, nor does it everywhere agree with itself.

In chapter vii. he runs further outside the boundaries. He says that concupiscence and affections, unless they bring forth an external work, are not sins. But yet if anyone will read those commentaries attentively and with judgment, he will find many testimonies of many articles. And although there was darkness in the Church at that time, nevertheless it appears that he retained most of them this common opinion, That the remission of sins is given by faith for the sake of Christ, not for the sake of works. Therefore, although the ancients sometimes speak less conveniently, yet in other places it can be observed what they intended in reality.

Concerning the Supper of the Lord, it appears sufficiently from Chrysostom that there were no private masses. For he describes a presbyter standing at the altar, and calling the people to approach for communion.

In the booklet on the dignity of the priesthood, he learnedly distinguishes between civil and ecclesiastical power; he denies that the ecclesiastical has the power of coercing by corporal force.

Concerning Ambrose.

Ambrose touches upon many causes, namely concerning the Trinity, against the Novatians, and concerning justification. And although in the commentaries sometimes dissimilar opinions are found, which seem not so much to have been written by him as taken down by others, yet it is clear from his longer disputations that he held the same view concerning grace and justification that we teach.

The Epistle to Irenaeus concerning the statement of Paulinus, The law works wrath, Epistle xvii, testifies to this. Where he says thus: By the works of the law no one is justified, that is, through the law sin is known, but the guilt is not relaxed. Therefore, the Lord Jesus, coming, forgave the sin to all, which no one could avoid, and blotted out our handwriting by the shedding of his blood; this is what he says: Sin abounded through the law, grace abounded through Jesus, just as John says: Behold the lamb of God, who takes away the sins &c. Therefore let no one glory in works, because no one is justified by his deeds, but he who is just has it as a gift, because he is justified through Christ. Faith, therefore, is what liberates through the blood of Christ, because blessed is he to whom sin is remitted, and pardon is granted.

And similar sentiments are found in other places in this writer, as concerning the calling of the Gentiles. Item to the virgin Demetrias, where he says: Nor is a commandment given for any other reason, except that the help of the one commanding might be sought. Furthermore, under his title there exist certain preparations for the mass, and other vain things, which seem to be supposititious.

Concerning Jerome.

Jerome performed useful work for the Church in his versions, and although his expositions of the Prophets are thin, nevertheless the histories explanation taken from the ancients is useful. He wrote few things about dogmas; against Jovinian he strongly confirms false and superstitious opinions about human traditions. He disparages marriage, and attacks it with insulting speech, which is by no means worthy of a Christian. He collects poorly twisted sentences of scripture, as if they disparaged marriage, such as, If you live according to the flesh you shall die, and similar ones, and he expressly says that one marrying after second nuptials does not differ from a harlot. Likewise, that one must look not at what God grants, but what He wills, as if God did not will marriage. Finally, in the manner of a pagan, he collects common insults against the female sex and marriage, about which a Christian ought to think far otherwise, who knows that the cause of infirmity in both sexes is the corruption of nature, and yet that on account of God honor is to be attributed to the sex, and since God did not create this sex in vain, the work of God is to be acknowledged, and the divine ordinance is to be highly esteemed. Nor is the infirmity of minds less in men, in the businesses which have been entrusted to men. A Christian, however, for the sake of God bears and mitigates the weakness in companions of this life joined by God, and co-heirs of eternal of glory, and he knows that God wills that we care for them, as a part of the human race, and not despise them with diabolical pride. These things and others to this effect should have been said in a Christian disputation, rather than those scurrilous insults against the sex and divine ordination.

Concerning the distinction of foods, he praises rites instituted without the word of God, as if they were worship of God, indeed as if they were perfection. The statement he posits is ridiculous: If you wish to be perfect, it is good not to drink wine and not to eat meat, where he has badly twisted the saying of Paul, who, when he says: It is good not to eat meat, adds, if the example harms a brother. Since, however, it is necessary that such superstitions be reproved in the Church, for they beget many other errors, one must judge prudently concerning those things said inconsiderately.

In the dialogue against Pelagius, he correctly argues that renewal is not brought about only by the powers of free will, but that the aid of the Holy Spirit is necessary. He also correctly denies that the saints are without sin, and posits a memorable saying: We are righteous then, when we confess ourselves to be sinners, and our righteousness comes not from our own merit, but from the mercy of God. But afterwards he does not sufficiently state that he understands the sins of the saints concerning actual sins, such as the flames of lust, or of wrath, and the like, he does not understand it concerning interior and perpetual doubt, security, concupiscence. It is evident, therefore, that there are many not insignificant lapses in the writings of Jerome.

Concerning Augustine.

Augustine treated many necessary controversies, he refuted the Arians, Manichaeans, Donatists, and Pelagians. For philosophical opinions had already crept into the Church, which Pelagius confirmed, transforming the Gospel into philosophy, for he contended that there is no original sin, that men can satisfy the law of God, and by that external obedience merit the remission of sins, be righteous, and merit eternal life. He said nothing about faith in Christ, nothing about the help of the Holy Spirit. This doctrine of Pelagius was not Evangelical, but philosophical, just as the opinion of the scholastic doctors almost intends the same, except that these sew on something of monastic superstitions. And now again many are slipping into Pelagian opinions, which are plausible to reason.

Augustine therefore in his age the doctrine of the Gospel concerning grace, and faith in Christ, almost extinguished he restored, and rekindled it again. For this benefit the Church owes him very much. He speaks of original sin with much greater clarity than all the others. He also speaks more distinctly and correctly about free will, that by the powers of free will men can perform the external works of the law, and honest civil works. But without the Holy Spirit they cannot have spiritual motions, true fear of God, true trust, true patience, that is, the newness which must exist in those who are to be saved.

He hands down a useful distinction between the letter and the spirit, he teaches about gratuitous remission, he warns how Paul is to be understood when he says: No one is justified by the works of the law, namely that he does not only detract justification from ceremonies, but also from moral works. The Church had great need of this admonition. For Origen and many who followed him had scattered a false interpretation in the Church, that justification was only detracted from ceremonies, and they had feigned that men satisfy the law, and are righteous on account of works. Therefore Augustine expressly treats this question in the book On the Spirit and the Letter, and affirms that Paul speaks universally even about moral works when he denies that we are righteous by the law.
