Likewise he denies that men to satisfy the law Romans ch. viii.

It is of the greatest importance to remember this admonition of Augustine, and this passage of his, because since reason does not sufficiently perceive the magnitude of original sin and natural corruption, it easily slips into those opinions, so that you might think that the law is satisfied, and that men are righteous on account of their works. Thus, conversely, the righteousness of faith is obscured and lost, and true spiritual exercises are cast off, namely true invocation, which must rely on mercy alone. Just as we are now mocked by our adversaries, who wish to appear wiser, and shout that we foolishly exaggerate infirmity, and ridiculously strip justification from works, when nevertheless reason understands nothing else to be righteousness except obedience according to the law.

But the doctrine of the Gospel concerning sin, and also concerning the righteousness of faith, is a secret and peculiar wisdom of the true Church, which even few of the writers have acknowledged, and the sounder ones have acknowledged, some more obscurely, some more clearly; the Scotists and their like have utterly overwhelmed it. Therefore, after God has revealed these things again, let us diligently defend the doctrine that has been brought to light.

Furthermore, since the adversaries in turn do not consider how absurd it is to say that Christ has freed us only from ceremonial laws. Item, if liberation pertains only to ceremonial laws, it did not profit the Fathers before Moses. But it is necessary to establish that liberation from the law pertains to the whole Church from the beginning of the world until the end. These things are discussed more copiously, as I have said, in the booklet on the spirit and the letter.

Finally, those who understand it only concerning ceremonies are completely ignorant of what liberation from the law is. Just as all men after the fall of Adam are oppressed by sin, the wrath of God, death, the immense miseries of life, and eternal punishments, so are they all burdened by the law, which convicts of sin, accuses us, and kills with eternal terrors, as Paul says. Therefore, to be liberated from the law is to be liberated from that accusation, so that we are not guilty of the wrath of God and eternal death; it is not only to be liberated from rites or external spectacles, but much rather to be snatched from the law that terrifies, curses, condemns, and kills us. When, namely, another thing is proposed, on account of which we are pronounced righteous, namely, the Son of God, made a victim for us.

Thus Adam, Noah, Abraham, and all the elect before Moses were liberated from the law. They were accused by the law, they were exercised by horrible terrors and the sense of the wrath of God, and of the curse. But among these terrors they were raised up by the acknowledgment of mercy, promised on account of the coming Lord, and they established that they were pronounced righteous on account of the coming victim, not on account of the law. They knew that sins were not only external offenses, but an interior uncleanness, a horrible doubting about God, a raging and indignation against God in adverse circumstances, and other depraved impulses, and they knew that neither the sin itself and the infirmity of nature, nor the wrath of God, were taken away by any law. But they knew that they were snatched from such great miseries by the acknowledgment and trust of the promised savior. Thus they also are free from the moral law, namely, judging and killing them, and from the eternal wrath which the law denounces. They knew that in that natural knowledge gratuitous remission of sins was not proposed. Therefore they sought remission from elsewhere. But if they had felt that they would be righteous in such a way, when they were without vice, they would have succumbed in the agony of conscience, but they knew that the savior was promised for this reason, that they might establish that they pleased God, even if they were unworthy and unclean. Thus they felt that they were righteous, not on account of the law, but on account of the coming savior.

Deliverance from the law embraces these such great things, which secure men do not understand, who do not know what true repentance is, and finally who are not exercised by afflictions in invocation, and either have minds occupied with pleasures, or are delighted by their own opinions and despise the word of God, or bend or corrupt it to their own imaginations. Some more cunning adversaries, although they see that the interpretation of Augustine and our own is truly the sentiment of Paul and of the prophetic and apostolic scripture, nevertheless clamor against us, and cite the authority of Origen, Jerome, Chrysostom, and I know not whom, not because they truly and from the heart approve of them, but only to deceive the unskilled, so that they may not appear defeated.

For the adversaries do not bring to these contests a good conscience and a zeal for seeking the truth, but hatred of us, contempt for the Gospel, and a concern for defending their own authority. They judge that what the people think about Christ, and how the Churches are instructed, pertains nothing to them, and they are partly openly practicing sycophancy like Cochleus, Wicelius and their likes, and partly they are tyrants and satellites of tyrants, who on account of an opinion of wisdom or virtue govern the counsels of pontiffs, kings, and princes, since they are men ἄθεοι, who in general think that religions are fictitious to be, and in a wondrous way they please themselves in this name, because they dare to ἀντιπέρδειν πρὸς τὰς βροντὰς as he says in the Comedian. And such are the ones who are going to pronounce opinions in synods concerning the glory of Christ, whose name they think to be fabulous.

Therefore I exhort pious readers, First that they consider the kinds of doctrine, which ones set forth the opinion of prophetic and apostolic scripture simply and without sophistry. Next, when the Fathers are cited, which sayings of the Fathers are in agreement with the divine voice. For there is a great dissimilarity of the Fathers. Finally, as Paul commands to test the spirits, the will of both parties must be observed, and the sum of their counsel. The adversaries do this, not that they might amend anything, but that under any pretext whatsoever they might defend their tyranny, confirm, and fortify their wealth. Therefore kings and pontiffs oppose the marriage of priests, because they see that celibacy is more expedient for retaining power and wealth. In this way, since the marks of an impious will exist in certain manifest articles, it appears sufficiently that they are not moved by a good spirit, but are enemies of Christ and do not seek the truth in the other articles either. Wherefore let us constantly reject their judgments.

Psalm 42. He affirms that the reborn person is not righteous on account of works, but by faith, for thus he says: Truly fear, if you call yourself righteous, if you do not have that voice, from another psalm: Enter not into judgment with thy servant, for if you shall show judgment without mercy, where shall I go? If thou, O Lord, shalt mark iniquities, O Lord, who shall stand? Enter not into judgment with thy servant, for in thy sight shall no man living be justified. Therefore if no man living shall be justified in thy sight, because whoever lives here, however justly he lives, woe to him, if God shall enter into judgment with him. For also in another Prophet he rebukes the arrogant and the proud thus: Why do you contend with me in judgment? You have all forsaken me, says the Lord. Do not therefore contend in judgment, give effort to be righteous, and however much you shall be, confess yourself to be a sinner, and always hope for mercy, and in that humble confession securely address your soul that is troubling you and tumultuating against you. Why are you sad, O my soul, why do you trouble me? Perhaps you wished to hope in yourself, hope in the Lord, not in yourself, for what are you in yourself, what are you of yourself? Let Him be health in you, who received wounds on account of you, and he says hope in the Lord.

Psalm. xxxi. Who are the blessed? Not those in whom sin will not be found. For He finds it in all. For all have sinned and lack the glory of God. If therefore sins are found in all, it remains that they are not blessed, except those whose sins have been forgiven. The apostle therefore commended this thus: Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him for righteousness. Here he rightly adapts the saying about faith, and testifies that he understands faith, not only as knowledge of history, but as the confidence by which we trust that our sins are forgiven us on account of Christ. Nor indeed can anyone grasp the opinion of Paul, unless he understands the name of faith in this way. This is truly, as it is said, to err at the very threshold, to understand faith only as knowledge of history, not as confidence in promised mercy on account of Christ. Nor is it a wonder that the monks have wandered off the whole way in explaining Paul, because in this very place they have shamefully hallucinated. And now this darkness is especially an impediment to the adversaries, by which they are less able to receive the doctrine concerning faith, because they do not rightly understand the name of faith. Why do they not weigh such sayings of Augustine, such as this one, which I have just recited? Here he testifies that Paul intends this, that Abraham is pronounced righteous, who believed, not only concerning his posterity, but the remission of sins.

Such opinions, met with here and there in Augustine, sufficiently show that he thinks the same concerning grace and faith as we teach. Just as he also says concerning the spirit and the letter: From the law we fear God, but through faith we flee to mercy. Here he learnedly distinguishes the law and the Gospel.

Although, however, figures of speech sometimes occur in his writings that are not sufficiently explained or are inconvenient, these are to be pardoned on account of the times, because the custom of the common people had received certain figures, such as the naming of merit, and certain others, and the learned could not explode these. Furthermore, neither were the writers themselves sufficiently accustomed to accurate disputations, and how great the darkness was in the Church at that time can be estimated from the fact that the impious opinion of Pelagius was received with such applause that Augustine and a few others could not, without great struggles, explode it from the Churches again.

Furthermore, if anyone opposes the age of Augustine to us concerning ceremonies, let him know that not even to Augustine himself did all the rites and persuasions of his time please. For he complains that many superstitious opinions cling to the Church, that human traditions are preferred to the commandments of God, and that ceremonies have been so accumulated that the servitude of the Jews would have been more tolerable than that of the Church.

His words are these in Epistle 119 to Januarius. Yet they press down with servile burdens that very religion, which the mercy of God willed to be free with very few and most manifest sacraments of celebrations, so that the condition of the Jews, who were nevertheless subject to divine laws, not human ones, would have been more tolerable. And first concerning human rites he says, This whole class of things has free observances. Then he expressly commands that useless human rites be cut off. Therefore, Augustine does not so approve of the ceremonies of his time that he wishes the Church to be constituted according to that norm. For many things were received which not even he himself approves; indeed, he wishes them to be reproved and corrected; some he observes according to the custom of that time, just as we all forgive many things in present customs.

In his age, discourses about purgatory began to become frequent, which he neither refutes nor confirms; he only narrates, saying that some think thus, that the souls of the pious are purged after they have departed from their bodies. But in book 9 of the Confessions, he requests prayer for his deceased mother with these words. Inspire, O Lord, your servants, that they may remember my mother and father at your altar, and he asks for nothing more. Although this is said modestly by him, yet now it is wickedly twisted toward the offering of the sacrament for the dead, such as did not yet exist in the time of Augustine.

Vows were also customary at that time, and a question arose, whether marriages contracted after a vow ought to be dissolved. On this matter, the opinion of Augustine exists in the decrees 27. q. C. nuptiarum. Here, although Augustine attributed more to vows than was fitting, yet he pronounces that marriages contracted after a vow are not to be dissolved, and he affirms that they are truly marriages, because one person ought not to return to a vow with injury to the other, nor does the obligation become void between two persons, even if one has brought about a change of the prior purpose. These things he says in summary in that text. But the error concerning vows prevailed more than this mitigation of Augustine. Therefore, the constitutions that followed afterward tore apart marriages. Augustine saw that that tearing apart was vicious, but he did not sufficiently consider what of vice there was in the vows themselves, which was more obscure. For they were overcome by the common opinions of their age. Already the custom of making vows had been received. Great was the admiration of many for those living in that kind of life. But admiration hinders judgment. Therefore not was he debating whether vows were valid, since indeed many errors were implicit in them, they were held as acts of worship, as a singular merit of justice, as perfection, and likewise for most they were impossible. If he had refuted these first, he could have better prevented the breaking up of marriages.

It is evident, therefore, that many abuses had already clung to the Church in that age, some of which, although Augustine opposed them, he nevertheless took in good part, which, after they have been uncovered, ought not to be defended. Furthermore, even if the examples of the ancients were overlooked in their own time, they ought by no means to be adapted now to confirm greater abuses, so that the consequence is by no means valid: Augustine orders prayer to be made at the altar for his mother, Therefore masses for the dead are to be approved. Or, in Augustine's time some thought there was a purgatory, Therefore masses, indulgences, and other foundations devised for the dead are to be approved. For in Augustine's time these prodigious impieties did not yet exist, even if the seeds were gradually sown.

Concerning Gregory.

In the year 590, Gregory began his Pontificate, when 157 years had passed after the death of Augustine. Meanwhile, many had flowed into Italy. barbarous nations, Goths, Lombards, and their allies. And not only had the studies of letters fallen silent, and the Churches been neglected, but even those very barbarous nations, which held Italy, brought with them or easily received many superstitious opinions. Therefore, in a short time, abuses were greatly accumulated.

In that tearing apart of Italy, it seemed to be a peculiar happiness to be away from the republic, to live far off in some solitude, without a family, without children, not to witness the destruction of cities and the devastation of the fatherland. For it is miserable to say that which Aeneas says: And of which I was a great part. Therefore, modest men who had families congratulated the monks on their tranquility. Thus the admiration for monks grew, and more began to seek and love retreats.

Furthermore, barbarous men by nature admire new rites, which have the appearance of exceptional piety, and as it were of commerce with God. It is no wonder, therefore, that at that time both the gatherings of monks grew, and plausible opinions about that kind of works wandered more widely, and the light of the Gospel concerning true faith and true worships was extinguished.

The veneration of saints was also pleasing to the barbarians.

After it was once accepted to adorn these in the ethnic manner with statues and peculiar temples, the custom grew by the imitation of the powerful. And gradually so much impiety was added, that the veneration of the saints in these later centuries differed nothing from the manifest idolatry of the heathens. Anna and George were invoked no differently than Juno, Mars, or Hercules. People ran to the statues, and bishops confirmed such εἰδωλομανίαν with great authority, and doctors praised it. And in such cults was the sum of religion. Meanwhile, concerning the invocation of Christ, concerning faith, there was a huge silence.

Therefore, the principles of such great impiety had to be avoided, which indeed Gregory strongly confirmed, who instituted the public rite of the invocation of the saints, who ordered temples to be dedicated to their bones and dust.

Then also crept in the opinion concerning the offering of the body and blood of Christ to be made for the dead. This opinion brought forth a horrible profanation of the Sacrament.

Although, therefore, after the age of Gregory greater darkness followed, nevertheless, these errors then stuck in the Church. The false persuasion concerning monasticism, concerning works devised without the command of God, the invocation of the saints, and the offering of the body of Christ for the dead. These errors subsequently brought about a great ruin. Therefore, the age of Gregory cannot be the norm for reforming the Church, which, so that it may be perceived more clearly, I will first recount the more manifest errors of Gregory, then I will dispute a few things concerning the Lord's Supper. Gregory, in book 3 of his Epistles, in the Epistle to the Bishop of Catania in Sicily, commands that subdeacons or deacons should not use the company of the wives whom they had married before ordination, although the Sicilians had previously kept the Greek custom, and had not forbidden husbands the company of their wives. This lapse is sufficiently manifest. For no pious person can approve the breaking up of a legitimate marriage.

He narrates that there was a certain handsome man who preferred to leave the office of subdeacon than to lack the company of his wife. This man, whoever he was, was endowed with sounder judgment than those who were breaking up such marriages.

The sin of Gregory is increased because he wished this custom to be received in the Sicilian Churches, which up to that time had retained marriages in all Ecclesiastical ranks according to the decrees of the ancient synods, and did not burden deacons or others with vows. Why does Gregory take authority upon himself over foreign Churches? when indeed so tragically he declaims that he abhors the title of universal Bishop. Then, why does he there tear apart marriages, where Deacons were not burdened by vows, why here does he not fear the authority of superior synods. Since this lapse contains manifest impiety and tyranny, it sufficiently appears that the age of Gregory was not without great errors.

The same man is unjust toward those who had been educated in monasteries by the command of their parents, and afterwards, having become adults, sought another kind of life. Concerning these he answers that it is a crime for such persons to desert the monastic life. This harshness is to be reprehended not only because an injury was done to their age, but also because it greatly confirmed superstitious opinions concerning monastic observances.

I shall add a third error, not obscure. He is moved by specters, in order to approve the offering of the Sacrament for the dead. He narrates of two who served in baths after death, of whom one requested that the offering of the sacrament be made for him, so that he might be freed from those punishments. From these specters he takes dogmas in the Church against the manifest command of God. Deuterono. 18. Do not seek the truth from the dead. And Esaiae. 8. Whether the people He seeks the truth from God for the living, or from the dead. Therefore, whatever the state of souls may be after this life, nevertheless dogmas are not to be taken from specters. Furthermore, who does not see that it is poetic, what he says, that the pious after death have been made bathers. A similar fable is the invention about the daughters of Danaus, who draw water with sieves.

We do not establish this Catalog so that we might add refutations of errors, which exist elsewhere in sufficient numbers; I only wished to review the errors, so that it might appear that those are deceived who so admire the fathers, as if they had been ἀναμάρτητοι, and never dissented from the manifest divine scriptures. Although, therefore, the more learned Fathers sometimes advise something, nevertheless they are to be judged by the word of God.

Other refutations being therefore omitted, I will briefly add certain things concerning that offering for the dead: There is no need to ask whether there is a purgatory; this question pertains nothing to the offering. Even if there were a purgatory, nevertheless it is impious to offer the Sacrament for the dead. The reasons are many and most firm. First. It is impiety to institute a cult in the Church without a command of God; the application of the Lord's supper for others is done without any command and testimony divine: Therefore without any doubt this application is impious.

They confirm the major premise with very many sentences. You shall not have strange gods. In this commandment also strange forms of worship are prohibited. And to this pertains the saying, In vain do they worship me with the commandments of men. Likewise, Whatsoever is not of faith, is sin. Furthermore, acts of worship without the commandment of God cannot be done from faith, but the world does not understand how great a sin it is to invent acts of worship without the commandment of God, to depart from the word of God. Concerning this wickedness the prophets preach most of all, and they deplore the blindness of men, who with horrible audacity invent acts of worship and dogmas concerning the will of God, and do not retain the word and the acts of worship in which God has proposed His will to us. They themselves, blind, seek God in other ways. However, it is certain that Christ did not hand down the Sacrament so that it might be applied for the dead. What mention of the dead is made there? He commands the supper to be celebrated so that we may remember His death and His benefits. Are the dead present, so that they may remember together? But I will briefly add other reasons also. Second. The sentence is certain, which can in no way be shaken. The just shall live by his faith. Wherefore it is necessary for us to receive the remission of sins while alive, and it is impossible for it to happen to any for remission on account of a work, or the sacrifice of any little priest. Obscure and ambiguous causes require long disputes. This error concerning the oblation is refuted by arguments so clear and firm that they do not require a long explanation. The doctrine concerning the remission of sins is certain and clear. Remission happens to no one unless he receives it by his own faith. If anyone removes this opinion, he affects Christ with insult. Therefore, those who feign that that oblation merits remission for the dead affect Christ with insult.

Third. The use of the sacrament profits only those who, using it, remember the death and benefits of Christ. Therefore, it is impossible for that work to profit the dead, who neither use it themselves, nor add a remembrance there. The antecedent is manifest from the institution of Christ, because He commands to celebrate this mystery for a remembrance. Nor is anything else to be affixed to the institution. If anyone affixes more, if anyone transfers it to the dead, he impiously contaminates the institution of Christ.

Fourth. Scripture says openly: Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord: Rom. 8 the body is dead because of sin, but the Spirit lives because of justification, that is Those justified by the Spirit, as long as they carry around this body, in which the remnants of sin cling, are variously afflicted, so that in invocation faith, the knowledge of God, and spiritual newness may grow. But when the body is dead, the remnants of sin are abolished. And Paul explicitly adds that the spirit lives on account of justification. That life of the justified spirit is not dread, or a sense of the wrath of God, but is joy in the Holy Spirit, as Paul says. Therefore, there are no punishments of purgatory,

Christ says to the converted thief: Today you will be with me in Paradise, that is, in a tranquil and blessed life, not in punishments and dreads. Therefore, the souls of the just do not depart to torments, but to spiritual joy and to peace. In this life, the pious are exercised by horrible afflictions, because God by a wonderful counsel wills his Church to be subject to the cross, and to taste the afflictions of Christ. Thus Adam, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, David, Isaiah, Jeremiah, John the Baptist, and the other lights of the Church were in miseries, the magnitude of which no one can recount. Therefore Peter says: Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God. Although, therefore, such are the punishments of the pious while they live in the body, yet why should it be said that such afflictions exist after death? since these afflictions are destined for recognizing the remnants of sin in the flesh, and for repentance. But after death there is no place for repentance, as Paul clearly affirms. 2. Corinth: 3. Each one shall carry back those things which he did in the body. And the psalms teach this: The dead shall not praise you, O Lord. Item. For there is no one in death who is mindful of you. Therefore it cannot be affirmed that some are still exercised by those torments after death, in order to perform repentance.

If the adversaries say that those torments are not inflicted so that repentance may grow, but so that they may be satisfactions, this opinion is to be exploded much more. For the doctrine of satisfactions, which the sententiaries have fabricated, is false and impious. And indeed, into those disputes, as into a sink, very many lies flow together, concerning purgatory, concerning vows, concerning the oblation for the dead, and finally many other things. Since therefore the purgatory which they call such cannot be affirmed, it is impiety to institute an oblation for liberating the dead. Although even if there were a purgatory, the Lord's Supper could not be transferred to the dead.

But why do I dispute. Mention of purgatory arose from specters, then it was confirmed on account of profit, and now it is defended by Popes, Cardinals, Bishops, Canons, who are openly Epicureans, and most securely despise the judgment of God, and receive what they read concerning punishments after death as fables of the poets, concerning Ixion, Sisyphus, Tantalus, or similar ones, and they laugh at the foolishness of others, who affirm that God has proposed eternal punishments for the impious.

I omit therefore the disputation at present which the Greeks exhibited at the synod of Basel, an oration concerning purgatory, which today exists in the Phorcensis library, in which they discourse concerning the passage of Paul 1. Corinth. 3., which a more recent age has twisted toward purgatory, when it is established that he is speaking in that passage concerning repentance: He shall be saved, yet so as by fire, therefore he wishes the fallen one to be corrected by repentance. Wherefore he speaks concerning the present life, in which there is a place for repentance. Truly it is true what is said: Simple is the speech of truth. Since Paul speaks thus concerning repentance, this passage cannot be twisted to tortures after death.

Concerning the passage in the Maccabees there is also a most plain answer, The truth of things is not vitiated by the errors of those who have acted, says the jurisconsult. And Demosthenes against Aristocrates, reproving vicious examples, says, μή δὴ τους ἡμῖν ἐᾶτε λέγειν, ὡς γέγονεν, ἄλλ' ἐστὶ δίκαιον γενέσθαι. The Levitical sacrifices did not blot out sins before God, then nothing was instituted for the dead. Therefore it was an error to sacrifice for the sins of the dead, just as the Jews often received other vicious cults. For the nature of men is inclined toward superstition in all ages. Therefore, since that example fights against the scriptures, it is not to be cited to confirm superstitions in the Church. These are almost the principal things which are cited concerning purgatory. I have therefore included this disputation, so that it might appear more clearly that the lapse of Gregory, who confirmed the oblation for the dead, openly fights with the Apostolic scriptures.

Since this is so, the Canon of the Mass, as it is called, is also to be reprehended, in which it is said that an oblation is made to redeem the living and the dead. What audacity it was to transfer the Sacrament to the dead? when the institution speaks so clearly about the living, about the remembrance. Gregory writes that this Canon was composed by a certain scholastic, as he himself names him. But whoever was the author, who gathered this rhapsody, that cannot be denied, that the Latin Canon dissents from both Greek ones. Although neither do the Greek Canons agree among themselves. And they differ in significant places.

Thus far I have spoken concerning Gregory, nor do I wish of those following of the ages to add. For doctrine degenerated more afterwards. There was also added the tyranny of the Pontiffs, when Gregory still is ashamed of and strongly censures the title of universal Bishop, as several Epistles in book 4 testify.

I could add the complaints of the ancient writers concerning the greed and ignorance of the Bishops, which, if nothing else, yet warn of this, that the Church is by no means to be constituted according to the example and idea of that time. But in the Apocalypse of John, terrible images are proposed, which undoubtedly signify the times of the Church, and show that impious teachers would immediately rage in the Church, and would oppress the truth with tyrannical domination.

The histories of the synods also show how great a madness there was in very many Bishops, who, to defend impiety, incited Princes and the common people with wondrous arts, just as now the Pontiffs and Bishops attempt to incite the minds of kings to stir up civil war with all artifices.

Basil, at the end of his book on the Holy Spirit, with what a tragic complaint he deplores the fury and impiety of the Bishops of his time, relates that defense of evil dogmas is sought through seditions and slaughters. And he writes thus to the Italian and Gallic Bishops: ἀνατέτραπται μὲν γαρ τὰ τῆς εὐσεβέιας δόγματα, συγκέχυνται δὲ εὐσεβέιας θεσμοὶ, φιλαρχίαι δὲ τῶν μὴ φοβουμένων τὸν κύριον ταῖς προστασίαις ἐπιπηδῶσι, καὶ ἐκ τοῦ προφανοῦς λοιπὸν ἀθλὸν δυσσεβείας, ἡ προεδρία πρόκειται, ὥστε ὁτὰ χαλεπώτερα, βλασφημήσας, εἴς ἐπίσκοπον λαοῦ προτιμότερος, οἵχεται σεμνότης ἱερατικὴ, ἐπιλελοίπασιν οἱ ποιμαίνον του μετὰ ἐπιστήμης τὸ ποίμνιον του κυρίου .

That is, The dogmas of truth have been overturned, the laws of piety have been confounded, the ambition of those not fearing God seizes the governance of the Churches, nor is there access to honors except through impiety, so that whoever is most rabid and most audacious in lacerating pious and true dogmas, is judged most worthy of the honor of a Bishop. The gravity befitting Priests has perished, Pastors are lacking who might feed the flock of the Lord with erudition.

Thus he depicts the Bishops of his own time, to whose vices a more recent age adds commands and tyrannies.

Since, therefore, it is established that that age was not without vices, it must be conceded to the Church that it should consult the word of God concerning doctrine, just as the heavenly Father commands that we should hear the Son, and David says: Thy word is a lamp to my feet.

These things concerning the errors of the ancient writers, although I have omitted many absurdly spoken things, I have not collected for the purpose that anything should be detracted from their true praises. I believe that most of them were pious and excellent men, some even deserved very well, but not even they themselves wished their own sayings to be preferred to the doctrine of Christ. Furthermore, those who now oppose the authority of the ancients to us, greatly abuse their testimonies. Although in those times the seeds of errors were sown, yet such foul abuses had not yet pervaded the Church. There was in the beginning some sort of mention of the saints, how much impiety was added afterwards? Therefore, the declamation of Nazianzen is not to be cited, since his age was still ignorant of this recent Idolatry.

But why do the adversaries cite the authority of the Church, when they do not contend about doctrine, nor about religion, but about their own lusts and wealth, they do not wish their tranquility to be disturbed. This is the one and only cause why they desire to destroy us. For certain dogmas are clearer than the midday light. And yet in order to suppress these Manifest cruelty is exercised; they kill pious, learned, and good men, priests, on account of marriage. Where has this been read of any barbarity, that men are killed on account of honorable marriage? If they approve of the ancient Church, why do they not imitate the first times here? Or do they think that Ambrose or Augustine would have approved of this cruelty of punishments? They would truly have execrated this inhumanity, and openly testified that these Pontiffs, the authors of the cruelty, are not members of the Church, but organs of the Devil, and without any hesitation they would have undertaken the defense of the pious priests, women, children, and then of so many nations that are joined to this cause.

But after I have said what the true Church is, and it is established that we faithfully retain and defend the doctrine of the Catholic Church of Christ handed down in the Prophetic and Apostolic scriptures, and in the creeds, it is manifest that we truly think with the Catholic Church of Christ. I add this also, that the principal writers, Ambrose, Augustine, and a few others, think the same, if they are understood conveniently, and a few things are pardoned them, which did not then come into controversy.

Concerning the Liturgy, there is no doubt that there were neither private, nor venal, nor funeral Masses before Gregory. Nor did the invocation of the saints begin to be celebrated much before Gregory.

There is also the law concerning perpetual celibacy, quite recent, which is defended for no other reason than that celibacy is more convenient for maintaining wealth. And they do manifest injury to the word of God who affirm that the marriage of priests conflicts with divine law.

Concerning penance, concerning the remission of sins and justification, which we say men obtain by faith on account of Christ, not on account of works, concerning satisfactions, concerning the keys, concerning human traditions, concerning political matters, our people have disputed most things more clearly than the ancients, which nevertheless appears to be consistent with the perpetual opinions of those who were more learned and more experienced in spiritual matters, who indeed, if they had read this explanation and method, would have candidly approved it out of their piety, as I hear a distinguished Parisian theologian narrated, that from our explanation concerning justification, he first understood the opinion of Augustine more correctly.

I know that from the ancients many things can be excerpted that are fighting against our opinions. And each one extracts for his own inclination what seems convenient, just as from the same flowers bees gather honey, spiders poisons. But let sycophancies be absent from Ecclesiastical judgments. I do not appeal to all writers, but to the better ones, Ambrose, Augustine, and insofar as others agree with these, who, since they themselves sometimes said things that are fighting, will grant us pardon if we reprehend certain things, provided that we follow the manifest and certain opinion of divine scripture, and do not depart from the symbols, and hold what they themselves looked to and intended, but sometimes were unable to explain. For there is no doubt that this kind of doctrine which we profess is truly the very consensus of the Catholic Church of Christ, as the symbols, the sounder synods, and the more learned Fathers show. These things I have answered to the more moderate ones, who oppose to us the authority of the Church or of the Fathers.

However, a certain new kind of wise men arises, who, since they are ἄθεοι, wish to be moved by no religious contentions at all, they praise peace and concord, they execrate all who in any way sow discords, these as καθάρματα, and they judge that the plagues of the human race must be removed. This is the one philosophy of Popes, Cardinals, Kings, Canons, and very many who wish to be considered political men, who, to be sure, do not wish their leisure to be disturbed, do not wish their dignity to be undermined, and hate the doctrine which seems likely to harm their own advantages; in short, one has one reason, another has another. The one voice of all these in the councils of Kings is that no change should be granted, and that the concord of the Church and the authority of the ordinary power must be retained.

Then they have their rhetoricians, who deliver most vehement sermons to that effect, all of whom there is no need to name. For the writings of many are extant. But from all those, Omphalius recently stitched together a patchwork. In the beginning, he preaches like some Solon or Areopagite about the dignity of laws, he blames seditions, and he commemorates the contempt of laws, how sweet the harmony of order and εὐταξίας is in the republic, which laws bring about. Then, although he does not name a certain profession, he nevertheless shows sufficiently whom he is attacking, he declaims against us, who have shaken off certain tyrannical and impious laws of the Popes. But although I do not think that he says these things gratuitously, yet since the same things are said by many eminent and eloquent men, I shall not dispute what he is aiming at.

This whole type of sermon looks toward strengthening the minds of the powerful, so that no moderate and pious counsels may be heard, and then so that, inflamed, they may exercise unjust cruelty. But as David prayed that the counsels of Achitophel might not prevail, so we shall pray to God that the eloquence of these rhetoricians may not oppress the truth and glory of Christ. And since it is written: Out of the mouth of infants and sucklings you have perfected praise, we shall hope that God will not be wanting to us in refuting those calumnies, and in illustrating the glory of Christ.

I know that it can be said plausibly concerning the dignity of laws, concerning peace, concerning the common tranquility. I am not so unlearned in letters, nor so alien to the civil custom of life. I also feel that in the republic those burdens are to be forgiven for the sake of common tranquility which can be tolerated without impiety. Let these maxims be valid in that category: τό κακὸν εὖ κειμένον, μὴ κινητέον. And what Plato said, that the ways of a father who is delirious, just so the ways of a fatherland that is foolish, are to be tolerated. Those things are rightly said in their place concerning civil burdens, which are tolerated without impiety, but this Philosophy should not be transferred to the overwhelming of the glory of God. Errors of doctrine, and Idolatry must by no means be dissembled, just as Christ says: If anyone shall deny me, I will confound him. The first commandment, Thou shalt have no other Gods, is to be preferred far above all human things, the laws of men, empires, ordinary power, peace, country, and concord. There is nothing more august than these names, but nevertheless the name of God is to be preferred.

The Prophets and Apostles undoubtedly loved their country and the tranquility of their country as much as any others. And yet they were compelled to rebuke impious cults and depraved opinions. And indeed Christ professes that he brings a kind of doctrine, as it were a fire, which is to kindle huge discords. For it is necessary that struggles exist concerning the worship of God, because the Devil burns with a horrible hatred of God, and as much as he can he tries to destroy the word of God, and he incites impious men against God, and drags with him most flourishing empires; with these enemies Christ wages war.

Wherefore, since it is necessary for the pious to rebuke and abolish impious cults, they cannot but be the authors of changes; thus the Prophets and were the authors of the greatest changes.

Apostles. Although therefore political wisdom shrinks from the very name of change, and pious men, who certainly are not all foolish or fatuous, understand how many difficulties and dangers changes bring, nevertheless a Christian heart prefers the command of God, and with a lofty spirit receives all difficulties, and understands them to be ruled by Christ, to whom all things are subjected, as the Prophet says.

These things I answer briefly, not so much to the oration of Omphalius, as to the arguments of those wise men who in all councils preach about avoiding changes and about concord. And although men ἄθεοι mock this answer, nevertheless it is useful for the pious to consider these arguments, lest that species of wisdom deter minds from piety and from the profession of truth.

And I write these things especially for the sake of admonishing the youth. The impious, while they capture the minds of many with other allurements, riches, and other conveniences, then indeed also hold them ensnared by these persuasions: that changes are to be avoided, that it is fitting to favor the ordinary power, to protect the present form of the republic. How far these things are to be praised, Christians must be forewarned, lest they forget this commandment: You shall have no other gods

I grieve that some endowed with excellent talents conspire with the impious, and are torches for inciting Kings to cruelty, and to establishing impiety. That is a virtue worthy of great and excellent men, especially to contribute industry and authority to the glory of God. This scope ought to be proposed to all, that each one in his own place, as much as he can, may contribute some labor to the preservation of heavenly doctrine. Concerning other petty parasites, who write sycophantic booklets, I will not speak in this place, who are of that kind κολάκων, such as Dionysius the Sicilian used to keep, who would catch the spittle of the tyrant, and lick it, proclaiming it to be sweeter than nectar.

I return to those wise men, some of whom, feigning religion, after they see that the absurd superstitions of former times cannot be excused, attach softer interpretations to rites and decrees, so that they may rightly establish impiety, with the rites and vicious decrees preserved. Such is the book published at Cologne, under the title of reformation. I hear also that Cardinal Contarini in Italy is accustomed to say that the Lutherans do an injury to the Roman nobles, when they ascribe to them errors of common writers, such as the Legenda, Dormi secure, and similar works. The Roman leaders never thought so, nor did they approve of those absurdities. Thus, they now derive their errors from themselves. And I know that everywhere among the nations there are very many who, by this new artifice, hunt for the praise of singular wisdom, who are first of all unjust in this, that although they borrow most of the things corrected by us from our books, and adorn themselves with our feathers, so as to deceive the unwary, yet they return to us unjust δίδακτρα. For they do not cease to exercise cruelty against us, then they do not consider that this new Sophistry will be the extreme ruin of true religion.

If it is permitted for more petulant minds to invent glosses at their own discretion, what is to become of us? Idolatry is manifest in the worship of saints, in masses for the dead. And yet glosses are attached to retain rites that are vicious in themselves. Thus, a little later, perhaps they will excuse Egyptian superstitions. Far be from the Church this impious and pernicious Sophistry, which is a protestation contrary to the deed. Worship not instituted by the express word of God is vicious in itself, even if you attach whatever gloss you wish, just as the invocation of saints is vicious in itself, because it is not instituted divinely, and furthermore also on account of this cause, is vicious in itself. Because this very motion, even if you think otherwise, attributes to the saints the honor proper to God, which all hear.

I could recite many examples, but I cease, and I exhort the pious to execrate that nefarious Sophistry. Hezekiah not only corrected the superstitious opinions concerning the bronze serpent, but destroyed the statue itself. Thus it is piety to cast away with impious opinions the rites themselves, which are not proper political customs. Just as scripture commands Idols to be destroyed. So let the rites themselves of private masses, the Invocation of saints, the observance of Vows, Monastic dress, monastic sodalities, the bond of celibacy, distinctions of foods, & similar inept rites born from superstitions be taken away & abolished.

But why do I dispute? Those who paint vicious rites with this Sophistry do not truly act for this purpose, that they might remove errors from the Church, but that under any pretext whatsoever they might defend their own authority, and by art establish impiety. For depraved opinions easily sprout again if the rites themselves remain. It is necessary for the pious to be vigilant. For the Devil attacks the Gospel, not only openly inciting tyrants to cruelty, but also cunningly laying snares constructing [arguments] under the pretext of wisdom and pouring forth beautiful persuasions, against which the Holy Spirit so often warns us to be on our guard, as Paul says to Timothy, that impostor spirits would come, and says to the Colossians that human traditions would have the appearance of wisdom. Not only will manifest ravings be scattered, such as were most of the old and recent ones, as a little while ago the impostures of indulgences were manifest, but also crafty men will artfully paint false dogmas and impious rites, so that they may be received, loved, and retained with great applause. Does the impiety of Samosatenus not have the appearance of wisdom? Is the error of Pelagius not plausible to profane minds? Thus these have the appearance of wisdom. It is profitable for peace and tranquility to retain customary habits; therefore, let the more horrid opinions be plucked away and interpretations be feigned, εὐφημοτέραι let the rites themselves be retained. This seems to be said splendidly when something far different is being done.

These sycophancies are signified in the history of Christ, whom, when the lictors had blindfolded his eyes and had struck him with blows while mocking him, they ordered to prophesy by whom he had been struck. Thus those excusers of impious rites hold Christ and the Church in mockery. After they have devised some insipid gloss, they think they have now blinded the eyes of Christ, then they add blows, that is, they establish impiety, they incite Kings to cruelty, and they celebrate triumphs, as if they had now completely destroyed the truth. They take applause in their own theater, they are praised by the wicked, they are loved by kings, whose desires they serve. But God must be prayed to, that He may repress this kind of Sycophants.

Nicander says there is a kind of serpent, which he calls Haemorrhoids; they are small little beasts, of the length of one foot, but such is the force of their poison that from one struck by them bloody sweat breaks out over the whole body, so that blood flows copiously from the mouth, nostrils, ears, and bladder, so that the eyes shed bloody tears, so that the whole body burns with incredible inflammation. When a beast of this kind had killed the shipmaster of Helen in Egypt, the heroic woman crushed it with her foot, whence also the posterity of the Haemorrhoids is said to limp, having lost its spine. Furthermore, the outcome shows that this new Sophistry of interpreting traditions is a poison not unlike that of the Haemorrhoids in that although the unlearned are hostile to us, they fight with obstinacy and hatred, they do not fight with authority. These hemorrhoids, because of an opinion of doctrine, because of sophisms, and as Paul calls it, because of a show of wisdom, are in admiration, and they incite the minds of the powerful to suppress the truth. Inflamed by this poison, princes conceive the flames of hatred, they become bloody and furiously cruel. But Christ will not allow the light of the Gospel to be overwhelmed, as it is written: That which is from God will not be abolished. Therefore the Church, in which the true doctrine shines, will at length pluck out the thorns for those hemorrhoids. Those sophistical interpretations, and the cunning and cruel counsels of the impious, will not suppress the truth.

But as for the fact that some who are desirous of pious concord everywhere expect synods of the Pontiffs, and hope that these are remedies for the Church, or will correct vices, they are far deceived. For the Pontiffs and their conspirators and satellites will never cease to wage war against Christ; that I should think so, I am moved not only by human conjectures, which are many and not light. I am moved by the words of Christ, and then by the examples of all ages. For Christ denies that blasphemers are saved, who against conscience they attack the truth, they defend manifest εἰδωλομανίαν, and they have besprinkled themselves with the blood of the pious. Fury undoubtedly accompanies blasphemies and parricides, as the histories of Cain, Pharaoh, Saul, and the Jewish people testify. And God threatens blindness to blasphemers, as the Psalm says: Let their eyes be darkened. Therefore they increase their punishments daily, they bind Princes to themselves with impious treaties. Nor do they only rage openly, but they secretly lay snares for the life of pious Princes. Is it to be thought that these will admit moderate or pious counsels? And we have already experienced several times that most of those who feigned moderation, nevertheless in reality did nothing except to oppress us once ensnared, and to destroy the whole kind of doctrine. I know there are a few sounder ones in the colleges of the enemies, who deplore the obstinacy of the powerful, but the opinions of these are rejected as scholastic. Since these things are so, it is the duty of a pious mind, and one thinking of its own salvation, of the glory of Christ, to seek what is the true Church, so that it may join itself to this, so that it may be a part of this assembly, and of the flock of Christ, as Christ says: He who is not with me, is against me. Then let him know That the Church is by no means the tyrants and persecutors of Christ, and those who either assist or approve of cruelty. Concerning these, let us hold to the most certain rule of Paul: If anyone shall have taught another Gospel, let him be anathema. And when he says, let him be anathema, let us not think that he has used a light or common curse. When he names anathema, he signifies that God has cast out from the Church the enemies of true doctrine, and that they are to be fled from, as dire plagues, which God execrates. Let the good know that they are polluted by the society and company of these, and that they will pay heavy penalties for friendship and union with them. The Psalm says concerning this kind: He clothed himself with cursing like a garment, and it entered like water into his inward parts, and like oil into his bones. The contagion of this curse harms the others who are joined with them, who both attack the truth and exercise cruelty against the pious. Therefore, let us not think that this command has little importance: if anyone shall have taught another Gospel, let him be anathema. They are not Bishops, they are not members of the Church, but enemies of Christ, who are driven by furies, They do not think about the concord and peace of the Church but about establishing tyranny; they do not strive to heal the Churches, but they contrive civil wars, the devastation of Churches, the parricides of pious Priests, and of pious women. Therefore, the amendment of the Churches is not to be expected from them, but rather it should be considered that everyone should separate himself from them in opinion, mind, and will, flee their εἰδωλομανίαν, not listen to insults against true doctrine, not assist, not approve of their counsels, not confirm their power. Flee idolatry, says Paul. These precepts are not to be considered light. Therefore, let the true Church be sought; let us know that in her prayers are heard, in her let us know that there are members of Christ, to her let us know that the promises of the Gospel pertain. The promises do not pertain to the enemies of the Gospel, just as they do not pertain to the Jews, nor to the Mahometans, as God often testifies, and in Psalmo 16. the High Priest Christ says: I will not offer their libations, nor will I make mention of them with my lips. Whom would this so sad threat not move, so that he might flee the assembly opposing the true Church? Finally, divine scripture is full on both sides with such exhortations, which command to flee the enemies of true doctrine, and truly of the Church, and to embrace true doctrine, to love, to help, to adorn the true Church. Nor let us think that the Church is only a Platonic state. This assembly is the true Church in which the pure doctrine of the Gospel shines, in which the Sacraments handed down by God are rightly administered. In such an assembly it is necessary that there be some living members of the Church, who offer true worship to God, perform penance, call upon God with true faith, contribute zeal and effort to the propagation of the Gospel, show their confession, serve their calling, and finally perform pious duties commanded by God, are exercised by dangers of every kind, in which they exercise invocation and other good works. I affirm that this is the true Church, with which it is necessary for the pious everywhere in the world to be joined: in opinion, in will, and in confession. And I feel that such, by the benefit of God, are our Churches, which profess the pure doctrine of the Gospel, which is without any doubt, in agreement with the opinion of the Catholic Church of Christ. Would that good minds might consider how much it matters, not to be in the camps of the enemies of the Church, but to be a citizen of the true Church of Christ, for the sake of which God willed to make Himself known, for the sake of which all things he founded, which he sanctified with the blood of his son, in which he revealed himself through wonderful works by the Fathers Noah, Abraham, Joseph, Moses, David, Elijah, Elisha, the Apostles, and the remaining lights of the Church, finally which will have life and eternal glory, will enjoy the communion of God and the pious Angels. How great a glory and blessedness it is to be a companion of this assembly, to be seen in this host, which Christ leads, which pious Angels fly around, in which walk the Princes Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses, Elijah and the remaining men endowed with distinguished gifts. In this host you already hold a certain place if you do not assist, do not approve of the impiety and cruelty of the enemies of the Church, but embrace the true doctrine, confess it, and adorn it with pious morals. The Psalm says: Pray for the peace of Jerusalem. Blessed will be those who love her. O sweet and pleasant sentence, it exhorts all, that they may assist the Church with every kind of duty, that they may protect the purity of doctrine and consensus, that they may do good to the teachers, that they may commend the common salvation to God with prayers and vows, that they may ward off from there impious teachers and tyrants. I desire, however, from my heart, that political men consider the magnitude of these duties, who both ought to and can To help the Church. Let them look to posterity, to whom, just as they desire to leave a constituted republic, so much more ought they to hand down the true knowledge of God, uncorrupted religion, the pure Gospel, and rightly constituted Churches, just as Paul commands Timothy to guard the deposit faithfully, so that it may reach posterity whole and uncontaminated. We see the Popes, Bishops, and Canons affected by this care not at all; they fight about their wealth, not about doctrine. Therefore, let others in the schools, in the government of cities, take up this care. God especially demands this sacrifice from all, as Peter says: that we have been called to celebrate the benefit of God. This chief end of all counsels and actions ought to be proposed to the wise, that they may adorn the glory of Christ. For this duty, God promises huge rewards in this verse. Blessed shall they be who love the Church; He promises defense, success, and perpetual salvation to those who love the true Church. By this voice, let the pious rouse their spirits to the care of adorning the Church, and let them not only strengthen themselves against the threats of tyrants, but also fortify themselves against the Sophistry of those who falsely [use] the testimonies of antiquity and the Church to they cite the defense of impious dogmas, to refute which I have wished to instruct the studious somewhat.

Latin:

DE ECCLESIA-STICIS SCRI-ptoribus vetustis.

Hi quoque meriti sunt, praesertim quatenus sunt testes veteris & primae Ecclesiae Apostolorum. Confirmant enim nos suo testimonio, de Trinitate, de naturis in Christo, de Baptismo infantum, de usu cenae Domini, de ordinatione ministrorum, de usu indifferentium, de paenitentia lapsorum. De his articulis omnibus citantur memorabilia exempla Apostolorum, quae nobis patrocinantur.

Caeterum scriptores alii in aliis materiis fuerunt diligentiores, &, ut est humanum, saepe inconsiderate effundunt absurdas & falsas sententias, quas admoniti, haud dubie fuerant correcturi. Saepe cum non male sentirent, tamen non satis perspicue dicere potuerunt, quod volebant. Saepe propter temporum consuetudinem praesentes traditiones durius defenderunt, aliquas etiam falsas opiniones interdum habuerunt. Quare non sunt sine delectu omnia Patrum scripta probanda, & saepe ipsi inter sese pugnant, nec rarum est dissentire aliquem à seipso. Quare iudicium esse debet penes Apostolicam scripturam. Sed subiicio exempla.

De Origene.

Origenes citans Apostolorum & veterum Ecclesiarum exempla & sententias, est testis utilis posteritati de aliquot articulis, de Trinitate, de Duabus naturis in Christo, de baptismo infantum, de peccato originali, de usu caenae Domini, & de aliis quibusdam.

Caeterum miscuit suis scriptis multas falsas & absurdas sententias, quarum aliquas etiam ipsius aetas improbavit. Fingit ante hunc mundum fuisse plures mundos. Fingit diabolorum & damnatorum poenas cessaturas esse. Haec ipsius aetas etiam reprehendit.

In Rom. tractans hanc propositionem, Fide iustificamur, non ex operibus, intelligit eam κατασυνεκδοχὴν, fide sumus iusti, id est, perfecta fide complectente omnes virtutes: Idque declarat, dicitidem posse dici de caeteris virtutibus, Misericordia sumus iusti, scilicet perfecta, complectente caeteras virtutes. Hoc nihil aliud est dicere, quam homines propter opera & propter virtutes suas habere remissionem peccatorum, & iustos esse. Cumque non attendat, quid agat Paulus, quid vocet fidem, quid sibi velit illa exclusiva, Non ex operibus, addit enarrationes confusas & perplexas, nec sibi constat.

Interdum enim effundit aliquod tollerabile dictum, sed id postea mox corrumpit, quale illud est Rom. iiii. Initium iustificationis â Deo est. fides, quae credit in iustificantem, & haec fides cum iustificata fuerit, tanquàm radix imbre suscepto haeret in animae solo, ut cum per legem Dei excoli coeperit, surgant in eo rami, qui fructus operum ferant. Non ergo ex operibus radix iusticiae, sed ex radice iusticiae, fructus operum crescit, illa scilicet radice iusticiae, qua Deus acceptam fert iusticiam sine operibus.

In iii. capite: Ubi est gloriatio tua? Videtur iam propior esse Paulinae sententiae, admittit exclusivam, homines sola fide iustificari, & allegat Latronem in cruce, & mulierem apud Lucam: fides tua salvam te fecit. Sed postea declarans illa videtur hoc velle, hominem initio consequi remissionem peccatorum sola fide, postea iustum esse caeteris virtutibus, sicut ipse postea inquit: Fides reputatur ad iusticiam ei, qui convertitur, sed postea iusticia reputatur ad iusticiam. Porro mira varietas et perplexitas est enarrationis, etiamsi largitur hominem, initio sola fide consequi remissionem, tamen si postea imaginatur conversos, sine peccato esse, satisfacere legi, & iustos esse propter caeteras virtutes, dissentit à Paulo & à reliquis scripturis divinis, iuxta illud: Non iustificabitur in conspectu tuo omnis vivens. Item, Si dixerimus, quod peccatum non habeamus &c.

In capite septimo clare dicit, sanctos repraesentare alienam personam, cum sibi tribuunt peccatum, ut apud Danielem: Non in iustificationibus nostris, sed in misericordia tua exaudies nos. Tales sententias corrumpit, & docet fiduciam propriae iusticiae vel desperationem. Capite tertio inquit: Sine lege manifestata est iusticia dei, id est, sine lege naturali sunt traditae novae leges Evangelicae, Ut illa: Nesciat dextra quid faciat sinistra, haec, inquit, lex erat anteignota. Item, Lex est spiritualis, intelligit tantum de allegoria, id est, caeremoniae habent allegoriam, & saepe incommode spiritum intelligit, non de spiritus sancti motibus, sed tantum de interpretatione vel cogitatione allegorica.

Capite viii. Quod erat impossibile legi, quia infirmabatur per carnem: Transfert carnem ad legem, Caro legis erat infirma, id est, caeremoniae erant impossibiles &c. At Paulus carnem intelligit naturam hominum, Lex infirmabatur per carnem, id est, non poterat fieri humana natura. Hi loci ostendunt Origenem currere extra viam, nec attendere, quid agat Paulus.

Possem multa levia colligere, ut cum Petrum ait excellere caeteris, quia ei dicitur numero plurali, erit solutum in caelis. Ad totum coetum Apostolorum dicitur numero singulari, erit solutum in caelo. Sed haec futilia omitto. Caeterum eruditis & iudicium adhibentibus prodest vetera scripta legere, primum propter historica testimonia, deinde quia illorum collatio acuit & exercet studiosos. Ita proderit & Origenis lectio, iis qui antea recte instituti sunt, et summam Christianae doctrinae tenent.

De Dionysio.

Unus est libellus Dionysii de Ecclesiastica Ierarchia, qui propter historiam est utilis. Caeteri continent ociosas speculationes. Illic autem traduntur caeremoniae sacramentorum, & ritus Ecclesiae, et apparet mediocres adhuc fuisse caeremonias illo tempore. Praecipue autem ritus Missae ibi considerandi sunt, ut appareat recentiores in Ecclesia Papae procul recessisse à veteri forma. Psalmi quidam & lectiones ex Evangelio recitabantur, dicebantur preces pro Ecclesia et Repub. Postea presbyter stans ad aram, recitabat verba Christi de cena Domini, deinde distribuebat populo sacramentum, sequebatur gratiarum actio. Hic fuit ritus missae, unde manifestum est, missam tantum fuisse communionem, nec fuisse ullas privatas missas. Quin & illud mirandum est, quod nec mentio fit oblationis, ne ritum quidem recenset offerentis. Haec apud Dionysium praecipue prodest observare, ut antiquitatem opponamus iis qui defendunt abusus missarum.

Recenset baptismum, chrisma, communionem, ut dixi, ordinationem presbyterorum, & eorum qui vota faciebant, & unctionem mortuorum, ubi narrat quales fuerint caeremoniae funerum, cum cadaver in templo collocatum esset, praesente populo recitabantur aliquae lectiones ex sacris literis de resurrectione. Deinde iubebatur populus gratias agere in precibus, quod hic pie decessisset in agnitione. Evangelii. Addebatur adhortatio, ut sibi quisquè precaretur pium exitum ex hac vita. Hic mos fuit plenus pietatis, & laude dignus. Quae enim possunt maiora beneficia cogitari, quàm in illo ingenti agone, retinere Christi agnitionem, adiuvari à Christo & salvari. Hanc caeremoniam meliorem recentior aetas prorsus abolevit, retentis & cumulatis deterioribus.

Addit autem Dionysius, post hanc adhortationem abiisse presbyterum, & perfudisse oleo cadaver, & precatum esse, ut Deus ei condonaret infirmitatem, quae in eo reliqua fuisset post conversionem. Postea cadaver condebatur in terram. Hae tantum fu erunt funerum caeremoniae tunc quidem, nondum in Missa fiebat defunctorum mentio, multo minus offerebatur corpus Domini pro mortuis. Hanc prophanationem sacramenti posterior aetas addidit.

Hactenus de Dionysio, in quo etsi caeremoniae aliquanto minus viciosae sunt, tamen sunt initia monachatus, & hoc gravi reprehensione dignum est, quod non discernit inter sacramenta divinitus instituta, & humanas traditiones. De Chrysmate perinde loquitur, ut de baptismo, & aequat πάρεργα ἔργοις, ut ita dicam. Monachorum ordinationem etiam antefert ordinationi ministrorum, quod est valde vituperandum, cum ordinatio ministrorum pertineat ad praedicationem Eungelii. Illa vero monachorum ordinatio sit superstitiosa, & tantum fiat propter cultum prohibitum, iuxta illud: Frustra colunt me mandatis hominum. & tamen ibi monachatus vocatur perfectio. Ergo valeant eius testimonia, quod ad historiam attinet, ut sciamus qui ritus tunc suerint usitati, non fiant dogmata aut leges ex eius descriptionibus.

De Tertulliano.

Tertullianus recte confutavit Martionem & reliquos eius factionis haereticos. Continet utilia testimonia de Trinitate, recitans non suam sententiam, sed veterem acceptam ab Apostolis. Adversus Praxeam extat luculentum testimonium de verbo, hoc est, de filio Dei, quod sit persona, etiam antequàm adsumpsit humanam naturam.

Caeterum & veteres reprehendunt quaedam eius errata, vi delicet quod secundas nuptias damnat, & ridicule argumentatur: Non licet fratris mortui uxorem ducere, Ducens viduam relictam à Christiano, ducit fratris mortui uxorem: Ergo non recte facit.

Ludit etiam de regno Sanctorum, quod fingebant duraturum esse mille annos, in hac corporali vita, ante mundi conflagrationem, & ante novissimum iudicium paulatim aliis citius, aliis tardius resurgentibus. Hoc Iudaicum deliramentum prorsus explodendum est ex Ecclesia.

In libello de corona militis multa dicit de ritibus humanis, & durissime declamitat de consuetudine, habendam eam esse pro lege. His dictis in Ecclesia male detortis, ut fit, confirmarentur ingentes errores omnibus aetatibus, quia nunquàm tanta est vigilantia hominum, ut non obrepant aliquae viciosae consuetudines.

Recenset autem Tertulianus admodum pueriles mores, ne post baptismum primis septem diebus eatur in balneum: Item ut baptizatis praebeatur gustandum lac & mel. Ibi inquit, etiam oblationes pro defunctis, pro natalitiis annua die facimus. Id nunc impie detor quent adversarii nostri ad missas pro mortuis. Cur natales omittunt, si tantum tribuunt autoritati Tertuliani? Sed ille non loquitur de cena Domini. Verum in diebus natalibus & funerum adferebantur in templa cibi, & alia munera pauperibus. Haec vocabant oblationes, & ἀγαπὰς, & mos erat ab Ethnicis acceptus, sed nonnihil correctus. Nam Ethnici dabant epulas etiam in templis, in natalibus & funeribus, ac postea Nicena synodus & aliae prohibuerunt hanc pompam natalium.

Ergo ut de caeteris dictum est, testimonia historica in Tertuliano prosunt, ubi commemorat, quid senserit prior Ecclesia. Sed eius enarrationes & disputationes non recipiantur tanquàm dogmata, nisi quatenus consentiunt cum Apostolica scriptura.

De Cypriano.

Cyprianus vixit circiter annum Domini cclx. continet utilia testimonia, de Trinitare, de baptismo parvulorum, de usu cenae Domini, & de forma electionis Episcoporum, quos scribit electos esse à coetu Ecclesiae, & eam electionem comprobatam esse adhibitis ali quibus vicinis Episcopis.

Sed veteres etiam taxarunt Cyprianum, quod sentit baptizatos ab Hereticis, rursus baptizandos esse. Effundit inter declamandum interdum absurdas sententias, cum exaggerat immoderatis hyperbolis causam, quam instituit: Ut de poenis canonicis admodum duriter scribit, ait non valere absolutionem, nisi illae poenae fuerint persolutae. Hoc dictum quantum habeat incommodi, non est obscurum.

Vehementer etiam declamitat de caelibatu, etsi eum quidem locum mitigat, iubet contrahere coniugia illos ipsos, qui vota fecerant, si non servent promissum. In libello de eleemosyna inquit, peccata ante baptismum commissa remitti propter Christi passionem, sed post baptismum quaerendam esse remissionem per eleemosynas. Idem repetit de lapsis, consumptum esse beneficium Christi in baptismo, postea per eleemosynas quaerendam esse remissionem. Haec sunt plena absurditatis, quae admonitus haud dubiè correxisset. Non igitur dicta ipsius omnia pro dogmatibus habenda sunt.

De cena Domini solet uti verbis oblationis & sacrificii, sicut caeteri, qui dicunt promiscuè, offerimus orationes, offerimus panem, vinum. Offerimus corpus & sanguinem Christi, nam id quoque reperitur apud Cyprianum. Hinc adversarii nostri sumunt testimonia, ad defendendam prophanationem cenae Domini in missa privata &c.

Magna vis est consuetudinis, & hanc sequentes saepe improprie loquuntur homines, ut nunc missam dicimus, cum nulli nota sit nominis etymologia. Ita veteres retinuerunt vocabula oblationis & sacrificii, non admodum curantes etymologiam, aut propriam significationem. Et quia vidit Augustinus aliquid in his appellationibus esse incommodi, ipse leniit, sacrificium inquit dici pro memoria sacrificii, & oblationem pro memoria oblationis. Hae sunt metonymiae, ut dicimus pascha pro memoria, seu signo transitus, sed nolo argute vel interpretari, vel excusare, locutionem usitatam illius temporis. Sic enim populus loquebatur, qui interdum recipit impropriam vocem.

Irenaeus clare dicit hanc oblationem esse gratiarum actionem. Idem sentiebant caeteri, ut testatur nomen Eucharistiae. Quare senserunt esse caeremoniam, qua aguntur gratiae. Id nihil habet incommodi. Accipimus enim ut admoneamur beneficii nobis donati à Christo, & fidem exuscitemus, deinde agamus gratias pro eo beneficio, nec inde sequitur id opus pro aliis faciendum esse, aliis applicandum esse &c. Haec monstra ne quidem cogitarunt Patres. Ergo cum legimus nomen sacrificii & oblationis, intelligamus aut signum sacrificii et oblationis, aut gratiarum actionem, non affingamus applicationes pro aliis.

Interdum uno nomine vocant oblationem, totum illud negocium quod ibi agitur, videlicet orationes & cenam Domini. Hoc cum fit, orationes intellegantur esse oblationes.

Leguntur etiam apud Cyprianum de mortuis quaedam verba, quae recentiores male detorquent, sacrificia pro eis offerimus, sed haec dicit de martyribus. Horum enim fiebat mentio in precationibus, cum agerentur gratiae Deo, quod illos adiuvisset. Sicut Graecus Canon dicit, offerimus pro Patriarchis, Prophetis, Apostolis, id est, agimus gratias, quod Ecclesiam inde usque ab initio tibi elegisti, redemisti, sanctificasti &c. Haec fuit initio sententia horum verborum, non petebatur, ut mortuis Deus relaxaret poenas. Postea accesserunt tempore malae opiniones, & partim verba priora mutata sunt, partim retenta forma veterum verborum, aliud intellexit posteritas, quàm priores intellexerant.

Ergo testimonia antiquitatis non patrocinantur recentioribus abusibus, quae partim aliena sunt à praesentibus moribus, partim si quid habent vitii, non debent opponi firmis testimoniis scripturae, quia etiam reliquae aetates habuerunt sua incommoda.

Haec simplicissime sine sophistica respondeo ad verba oblationis & sacrificii.

De Basilio.

In Basilio extant utilia testimonia de Trinitate, & paenitentia contra Novatum. In concione de humilitate tradit egregiam sententiam de iusticia fidei, quae nobis aperte parrocinatur. Sine ulla sophistica detrahit iustificationem bonis operibus, nec loquitur de caeremonialibus, sed de omnibus virtutibus, nec tantum loquitur de operibus ante renovationem, sed de virtutibus in renovatis, ac iubet sentire quod sola fiducia misericordiae propter Christum promissae iusti simus. Verba eius haec sunt:

Dicit autem Apostolus: Qui gloriatur, in Domino glorietur, dicens, quod Christus nobis factus sit sapientia à Deo, iusticia, sanctificatio et redemptio, ur sicut scriptum est, gloriaturus in Domino glorietur. Haec est enim perfecta & integra gloriatio in Deo, quando ne quidem propter iusticiam suam aliquis effertur, sed agnoscit sibi deesse veram iusticiam, fide autem sola in Christum iustificari, & gloriatur Paulus se despicere suam iusticiam, quaerere autem fide per Christum iusticiam, quae ex Deo est.

Haec verba satis ostendunt Basilium sic intellexisse iusticiam fidei, quod sentiendum sit, nos fide propter Christum per misericordiam iustos, id est, acceptos esse, non propter proprias virtutes.

Caeterum quod Basilius primum instituit coetus monachorum, id exemplum nocuit, & aliquid habet vicii, etiamsi ipse primum non habuit crassas superstitiones, & illi coetus adhuc quaedam imago erant scholarum. Circumferuntur & libri quidam eius nomine, qui continent regulas monachorum, quorum aliqui haud dubie sunt suppositicii, & longo tempore post Basilium nati, suntenim pleni falsarum opinionum de caelibatu, & aliis cultibus excogitatis sine mandato Dei, et continent ridiculas nugas, ut magnum acervum poenarum seu satisfactionum, quas vocat ἐπιτίμια, si riserit puella in choro, sedeat biduo in vestibulo, & similes naenias, quas si quis vellet renovare admiratione antiquitatis, vere insaniret.

De Gregorio Nazi-anzeno.

Nazianzenus tractavit articulum de Trinitate, alia dogmata leviter attingit. Scripsit psit vitam Cypriani, in qua narrat, quandam puellam amatam esse à Cypriano ante conversionem, quae invocans Mariam virginem, vicerit magicas incantationes Cypriani.

Hoc exemplum citatur de invocatione sanctorum. Etsi autem videtur esse ficta fabella, & postea sparsa titulo Nazianzeni, tamen etiamsi vera esset historia, non est citanda ad confirmandam invocationem sanctorum. Nam errores piorum non sunt opponendi verbo Dei, & omnibus aetatibus etiam pii in Ecclesia habent suas infirmitates.

Allegant etiam ex Basilio & Nazianzeno, quod in fine concionum de sanctis, solent eos compellare, O Athanasi ora pro nobis. Etsi autem hae Apostrophae ex Rhetoricis figuris excusari possunt, tamen fieri potest, ut more sui temporis tunc invocaverint sanctos. Nam invocatio Sanctorum paulatim tunc in Ecclesiam irrepsit, & errores temporum trahunt homines, ut usitata minus improbent, & boni consulant, sicut impetus fluminum secum rapit navigantes. Nec tamen ideo approbanda est invocatio sanctorum. Ac postquam mos crevit, & iam retecta est impietas, prorsus ex Ecclesia tolli debet.

Nec Basilius de invocatione quicquam dicit, tantum ait celebrari memoriam sanctorum, ut eorum virtutes imitemur, & vocat sanctos adiutores precum nostrarum, non quod sint invocandi, sed quia omnes beati in caelo orant pro Ecclesia, & eam Deo commendant.

Epiphanius scribit mulieres quasdam invocantes virginem Mariam, solitas circumferre eius statuam. Hoc totum negocium damnat & vocat Idololatricum opus. Continet enim Epiphanius refutationes veterum haeresium, praecipue de Trinitate, & paucis aliis materiis. quam quidem historiam praecipue legendam esse censeo.

De Chrisostomo.

Chrisostomi aetas multos iam viciosos mores receperat, quos ipse recensens, non reprehendit, sicut laudat adeuntes monimenta sanctorum, facit & mentionem orationis pro mortuis. Monasticam immodicis & falsis laudibus ornat. In tractatu de paenitentia cum colligit multos modos consequendae remissionis peccatorum, scilicet eleemosynas, lachrymas & alia opera, tamen non facit mentionem fidei, de qua oportuit dici, ac scriptum illud plaeraque falsa continer, &

confusum ac perplexum est.

Graeci maxime laudaverunt commentarios in Paulum, ubi in locis de instificatione & de fide series Paulinae disputationis deducit eum eô, ut saepe repetat hanc sententiam, Quod fide consequamur remissionem peccatorum propter Christum, non propter opera. Et diserte dicit, Fide non solum diligi Deum, sed vicissim credentes sentire, quod à Deo diligantur, quanquàm multis modis rei sint.

In hac sententia satis significavit, se intelligere fidem, non tantum de noticia historiae, sed de fiducia, qua credimus nobis remitti peccata, & quidem hanc fidem discernit ab operibus, à non furando, non occidendo &c. Et dicit hunc cultum superiorem esse. Quanquàm autem eius enarratio simplicior est & minus impura, quàm Origenica, tamen ipsa quoque est obscura, nec ubique secum ipsa consentit.

In vii. cap. lóngius currit extra septa. Ait concupiscentiam & adfectus, nisi pariant externum opus, non esse peccata. Sed tamen si quis attente & cum iudicio leget commentarios illos, multa inveniet testimonia multorum articulorum. Et quanquàm tunc in Ecclesia caligo fuit, tamen apparet retinuisse plaerosque hanc communem sententiam, Quod fide propter Christum, non propter. opera donetur remissio peccatorum. Ideo etsi interdum minus commode loquuntur veteres, tamen in aliis locis quid reipsa voluerint, animadverti potest.

De cena Domini ex Chrysostomo satis apparet, nullas fuisse privatas misfas. Describit enim presbyterum stantem ad aram, & vocantem populum, ut accedat ad communionem.

In libello de dignitate sacerdotii erudite discernit civilem & Ecclesiasticam potestatem, negat Ecclesiasticam habere is cohercendi vi corporali.

De Ambrosio.

Multas causas attingit Ambrosius, videlicet de Trinitate, contra Novatianos, de iustificatione. Et quanquam in commentariis interdum dissimiles sententiae reperiuntur, qui non tam ab ipso scripti, quàm ab aliis excepti esse videntur, tamen perspicuum est ex eius longioribus disputationibus, sensisse eum de gratia et de iustificatione, quod nos docemus.

Id testatur Epistola ad Irenaeum de Paulino dicto, Lex iram efficit, Epistola xvii. Ubi sic inquit: Ex operibus legis nemo iustificatur, id est, per legem peccatum cognoscitur, sed culpa non relaxatur. Veniens igitur Dominus Iesus peccatum omnibus, quod nemo poterat evitare, donavit, & chirographum nostrum sui sanguinis effusione delevit, hoc est quod inquit: Superabundavit peccatum per legem, superabundavit gratia per Iesum, sicut Iohannes inquit: Ecce agnus Dei, qui tollit peccata &c. Ideo nemo glorietur in operibus, quia nemo factis suis iustificatur, sed qui iustus est donatum habet, quia per Christum iustificatus est. Fides ergo est, quae liberat per sanguinem Christi, quia beatus ille cui peccatum remittitur, & venia donatur.

Et similes sententiae aliquot reperiuntur in aliis locis apud hunc scriptorem, ut de vocatione gentium. Item ad Demetriadem virginem, ubi inquit: Nec ob aliud datur praeceptum, nisi ut quaeratur praecipientis auxilium.
