I have said these things so that I might admonish the reader concerning that principal particle and place it as if in a more illustrious position, because it teaches us that the kingdom of Christ is not a kingdom of destruction and perdition, but a kingdom of hope and salvation.

Latin:

Deus pacientiae.

Votum seu precatio est quae est παρασκευὴ ad conclusionem huius loci deusu caeremoniarum, precatur enim utrisque dari studium pacis & concordiae. Vocat Deum pacientiae, quasi dicat, deum patientium hoc est respicientem patientes & consolantem, sicut saepe alias scriptura dicit: Psalmo. 34. prope est dominus his qui tribulato sunt corde, et humiles spiritu salvabit. Psalmo. 10: Tibi derelictus est pauper, orphano tu eris adiutor. Psalmo. 12. Propter miseriam inopum & gemitum pauperum, nunc exurgam dicit dominus. Psalmo. 145. Allevat dominus omnes qui corruunt, & erigit omnes elisos. Psalmo. 50. Invoca me in die tribulationis & eripiam te &c. Has sententias & similes nobis inculcemus & ad nos quoque pertinere statuamus & talibus promissionibus fidem in nobis excitemus, alamus, atque confirmemus, Nam hoc exercitii genere fides alitur & corroboratur.

Ideo assumite vos mutuo, sicut & Christus assumpsit nos.

Haec est conclusio totius loci de usu caeremoniarum, in quo adhortatur gentes & Iudaeos ad concordiam. Et allegat exemplum Christi quod supra proposuit. qui cum sit filius Dei, tamen amantissime nos miseros & indignos complexus est, sua morte nos redemit, suo beneficio servat. Id exemplum iubet nos imitari, ut mutuo nos complectamur, nec propter dissimilitudinem rituum, tranquillitatem Ecclesiae & concordiam labefieri sinamus. Et quia tunc erat inter gentes ac Iudeos praecipue haec controversia de ritibus, iterum inculcat Iudaeis testimonia quae ostendunt Evangelium etiam ad gentes pertinere, quare Iudaei non debeant aspernari gentes, sed velut fratres & vere populum Dei complecti. Interim et gentes confirmat his testimoniis, ne dubitent Christi beneficia ad se pertinere. Citat autem inter caeteros locos & sententiam ex Esaia sumptam, quam suo more recitat iuxta translationem septuaginta interpretum. Neque tamen sententia Graecae lectionis ab Ebraica discrepat, ac ne verbis quidem multum dissonat. Ebraei sic legunt: Et erit illo die radix Iesse, quae stabit, ut sit signum populis, gentes eam requirent, & erit mors eius gloriosa. Quod hic legitur: Stabit ut sit signum populis, Graeci verterunt, erigetur ut imperet, gentibus. verbum enim Ebraicum quod hic signum vertimus, significat vexilla & trophaea & similia monumenta. Intelligit enim Christum ducem ac victorem fore, sub cuius vexillo tuti erimus, cuius praesidio tegemur ac defendemur adversus summa mala, peccatum, iram Dei, inferos, & adversus potentiam diaboli. Et quod Ebraeus habet: gentes eam requirent, idem est quod ait Graecus, gentes in eo sperabunt. Nam qui ab aliquo auxilium & salutem expetunt, sperant, & expectant concurrunt & confugiunt ad eum. id Ebraeus dixit, requirent eum. Ita si quis dextre interprtetur Graecam lectionem videbit sententiam cum Ebraica omnino congruere. Pulchre autem depingit haec sententia resurrectionem & regnum Christi. Quod enim dicit: Erit mors eius gloriosa, significat eum non periturum in morte, sicut alii règes cum moriuntur, amittunt regna. At hic rex per mortem occupabit regnum, & post mortem vere ac gloriose regnabit. Nam etiam post mortem erit signum populis, gentes ad eum concurrent auxilium & salutem ab eo expectabunt. Quare reviviscet post mortem, nec erit ociosus, sed defendet, gubernabit, & servabit eos qui ad ipsum confugient. Atque ita solent Prophetae subindicare Christi resurrectionem, quia testantur futurum ut perpetuo adorent eum homines: ut Psalmo. 72. Et timebunt eum donec erit sol & luna. Item: Tu es sacerdos in aeternum. Necesse enim erat Christum resuscitari ex morte, siquidem perpetuo regnaturus erat. Nam in hac mortali vita nullus rex perpetuo vivit, aut regnat. Deinde significatur hoc quoque, regnum Christi fore, non mundanum sed caeleste in quo divinitus res geretur, in quo Dei voluntas ad nos perferetur. Porro sententia tristis esset, si tale regnum describeret, in quo tantum proponerentur minae de iudicio Dei adversus homines. Iraque longe aliter hic describitur regnum Christi. Ingens consolatio in his verbis suavissime proponitur: In eo gentes sperabunt. Erit igitur regnum Christi, non regnum exitii & perditionis, sed regnum spei & salutis. Venit Christus non ut damnet, non ut perdat, sed ut servet ac restituat nos iam ante damnatos & adiudicatos morti.

Nam hoc regnum novum ideo constitutum est, ut sit potentius regno peccati & legis. Et cum lex antea edita sit, in qua ira Dei adversus peccatum ostensa est, non iam venit Christus ut legem afferat, in qua rursus condemnet nos, sed adversus illam condemnationem affert promissionem & consolationem. Itaque etsi terrent nos peccata nostra, tamen sciamus hunc Christum propositum esse ut speremus salutem. Hoc pontifice habemus Deum placatum. Hic dux teget nos adversus diabolum, adversus mortem, adversus mundi seviciam. Quare in omnibus afflictionibus ad hunc versiculum respiciamus: In eo gentessperabunt, & sciamus auxilium & salutem à Christo petendam & expectandam esse. Atque illud ipsum vult particula stabit ut sit signum populis, hoc est regnabit & ad ipsum, velut ad vexillum victoris respicient & confugient homines & hoc duce ac victore defendentur. Iam illud etiam indicat quale sit futurum regnum Christi cum ait sperabunt, significat enim nos hic spe sustentari. Quare interim in hoc mundo affligimur & duriter exercemur, & tamen defen dimur ac eripimur per Christum. Sed hic exiguus versiculus tam multa complectitur, ut enumerare omnia difficile sit, tantum abest ut explicare me posse confidam. Illud etiam adiiciendum est, quod describitur in regno Christi summus cultus esse, sperare in eum. Id egregium fidei praeconium est, quod Deus praecipue coli vult hac spe & fiducia misericordiae. & continet magnam consolationem. Cum enim hanc spem raequirat adversus iram profecto odit & prohibet desperationem. Praeterea tribuit hic versiculus Christo divinam potentiam, iubet invocare Christum non regnantem visibiliter. Iubet in eum sperare. Id certe est tribuere ei divinam potentiam quod exaudiat, quod sit efficax in nobis cum tamen non versetur nobiscum, visibili & mortali consuetudine. Sed non possum evolvere omnia quae hic Esaiae locus continet. Haec dixi ut de illa praecipua particula lectorem admonerem eamque velut in illustriore loco ponerem quod docet nos regnum Christi, non esse regnum exitii & perditionis, sed regnum spei ac salutis.

## 15:14
But I am certain, my brothers.

With this whole passage concerning the use of ceremonies completed, because it could appear that he had rebuked too vehemently, or certainly had noted both those abusing liberty and other morose persons who, through superstition, were more unfair and harsher toward good people using their liberty, he adds an excuse by which he again mitigates the entire assembly of that Church. For this excuse of liberty, in my judgment, pertains properly to this passage concerning the use of ceremonies in which, although the discourse is brief, yet if anyone observes the weight of the words, he will perceive that both parties are not gently chastised, namely, both those overly fierce ones who wish everything to be permitted to them everywhere, and those Timons who demand that ceremonies be observed with a certain superstitious and Jewish diligence: where if he offends anyone, he here again civilly placates him, and he does it in this way. Since an honorable opinion of him with whom we are dealing conciliates benevolence above all, he first attributes to them praise both of goodness and of doctrine, then he shows that he was led by duty, not so much to teach them as to admonish the learned. For the word of admonishing has less of offense. And when he has made mention of duty, he incidentally commemorates how widely he has spread the Gospel, and so that they may have faith in his doctrine, he also alleges the miracles which prove the doctrine. Which we ought to remember, so that we may know that we can safely assent to the doctrine of Paul, as to the word of God, and may certainly know that the doctrine of Paul has been approved by God.

Furthermore, here he again alludes to the common place concerning sacrifice, when he says that he sacrifices the Gospel etc. I said, however, above that a sacrifice is a work which we render to God, so that we may affect him with honor and confess that he is truly God, who hears us.

&c. But since the New Testament requires true knowledge of God and righteousness of heart: for it brings with eternal life, wisdom and eternal righteousness, it has sacrifices, not dead cattle, but living and perpetual things, that is, hearts which offer the knowledge of God, fear, faith, invocation, the preaching of the Gospel and of the benefits of God, thanksgiving, confession, patience, and similar motions obedient to the law of God, and these were signified in the Levitical ceremonies. But now the New Testament, because it does not contain shadows, but wisdom and righteousness of heart, does not have ceremonies which are sacrifices ex opere operato. In the Law, the Levites prepared the victims and slaughtered the cattle: but the priests offered them. So in the New Testament, the ministers of the Gospel both offer themselves and prepare other sacrifices. For when they teach the Gospel and preach the mercy of God, when they invoke God, when they give thanks, they truly sacrifice and offer praise to God, and confess him to be truly God and Savior, as it is written to the Hebrews: Through him let us offer the sacrifice of praise always to God, that is, the fruit of lips confessing his name. Then, when they teach, they also prepare other sacrifices. For those who believe the Gospel become also victims who are mortified, that is, they are terrified when sin is acknowledged, and they are vivified, they are raised up by the confidence of the mercy of God, and they acknowledge God, and thus they offer to Him invocation, thanksgiving, confession, patience, and similar virtues. These victims are acceptable to God on account of the high priest Christ, whom, having heard the Gospel, they apprehend as mediator. Hence it can easily be understood why he was delighted by this figure, ἱερουργοῦντα, τὸ εὐαγγέλιον, the Gospel-preaching sacrificer, for he wished to admonish what are the true victims of the new testament. And what he adds: that the offering of the Gentiles may become acceptable, although it seems to be said ambiguously, nevertheless the meanings are related to one another, so that the Gentiles offered through me, that is, prepared as victims, may become acceptable. Or in this way, that the Gentiles now offering, that is, believing and invoking God, may become acceptable. For the Gentiles themselves, prepared and, so to speak, consecrated, offer their own victims. And so the matter returns to the same thing, for he says in sum that he is everywhere spreading the Gospel, so that the Gentiles may acknowledge Christ, and become the people of God, and victims, and may invoke and celebrate God. But what he adds: sanctified in the Holy Spirit, he teaches again that in the new testament the duties that external sacrifices are not, nor do they please God by the work performed. For thus the offering of the Gentiles is accepted, he says, if it be sanctified by the Holy Spirit, that is, if the Gentiles offer spiritual customs, the fear of God, and trust in the mercy of God.

Let us observe here, however, the most honorable praises of the ministry of the word, namely that the preaching, narration, and treatment of the Gospel are necessary sacrifices of the New Testament. That ought to console both those teaching and those learning the Gospel amidst so many troubles which must be endured by both. Let the teachers know that this worship of God is necessary, let them know that it must be performed for the sake of the glory of God, let them know that it pleases God, even if some men hear the Gospel negligently, others despise it, and others even persecute it. Let those also who learn the Gospel remember that this study of learning the Gospel is a worship of God, which God both requires and approves. For we see how truly God commands this himself, when he says concerning his Son: Hear him. Wherefore it is necessary to perform this duty, this worship, to God. Therefore, even if we are engaged in other arts, nevertheless, just as farmers are commanded in the law to consecrate the first fruits of their labor to God, so we must consecrate a portion of our work and study to God. And although those who, after having been moderately versed in the humanities and other common disciplines, devote themselves entirely to the study of sacred letters are held in great contempt and hatred: yet let these also console themselves with this reason, that this kind of study is a necessary worship of God, and pertains to the glory of God, provided that it is treated piously. And if they will consider this, they will easily despise the judgments of those who flee Christian doctrine from afar as if it were a contagion, either because of a contempt for religion, or because other arts are more lucrative, and who mock all the rest who do not abstain from sacred letters entirely.

Latin:

Certus sum autem fratres mei.

Absoluto hoc toto loco de usu caeremoniarum, quia videri poterat vehementius obiurgasse, aut certe notasse tum abutentes libertate, tum alios morosos, qui per superstitionem iniquiores & asperiores erant bonis libertate utentibus, addit excusationem qua rursus mitigat universum coetum eius Ecclesiae. Nam haec excusatio libertatis, meo iudicio proprie pertinet ad hunc locum de usu caeremoniarum in quo & si brevis est oratio, tamen si quis observabit verborum pondera, sentiet non molliter utrosque castigari, videlicet, & praeferoces illos qui ubique sibi volunt omnia licere, & istos Timones qui caeremonias superstitiosa quadam & Iudaica diligentia observari postulant: ubi si quem, offendit, hic rursus civiliter placat, idque ita facit. Cum benevolentiam conciliet imprimis honorifica de eo, qui cum agimus, opinio, primum tribuit eis laudem & bonitatis, & doctrinae, deinde ostendit se officio adductum, non tam ut doceret eos, quam ut admoneret doctos. Nam verbum admonendi minus habet offensionis. Cumque officii mentionem fecit, obiter commemorat quam late sparserit Evangelium, & ut fidem habeant suae doctrinae, allegat & miracula quae comprobant doctrinam. quae meminisse debemus, ut sciamus nos tuto posse assentiri Pauli doctrinae, tanquam verbo Dei, ac certo sciamus Pauli doctrinam à Deo approbatam esse.

Caeterum hic iterum alludit ad locum communem de sacrificio, cum ait se sacrificare Evangelium &c. Dixi autem supra sacrificium esse opus quod nos Deo reddimus, ut cum honore afficiamus ac fateamur eum vere Deum esse, qui nos exaudiat.

&c. Cum autem novum testamentum requirat veram noticiam Dei, et iusticiam cordis: affert enim cum vita aeterna, sapientiam & iusticiam aeternam, habet hostias, non mortuas pecudes, sed res vivas, ac perpetuas, hoc est corda quae offerant noticiam Dei, timorem, fidem, invocationem, praedicationem Evangelii & beneficiorum Dei, gratiarum actionem, confessionem, patientiam, & similes motus obedientes legi Dei, Et haec significata sunt in caeremoniis Leviticis. Nunc autem novum testamentum, quia non continet umbras, sed sapientiam & iusticiam cordis, non habet caeremonias quae sint sacrificia ex opere operato. In lege Levitae praeparabant hostias, & mactabant pecudes: Sacerdotes vero offerebant. Ita in novo testamento ministri Evangelii, & offerunt ipsi, & alias hostias praeparant. Cum enim docent Evengelium & praedicant misericordiam Dei, cum invocant Deum, cum agunt gratias, vere sacrificant & offerunt Deo laudem, & fatentur eum vere esse Deum et salvatorem sicut ad Ebreos scriptum est: Per ipsum offeramus hostiam laudis semper Deo, id est fructum labiorum confitentium nomini eius. Deinde cum docent, praeparant etiam alias hostias. Nam hi qui credunt Evangelio fiunt etiam hostiae mortificantur hoc est perterre fiunt agnito peccato, & vivificantur, eriguntur fiducia misericordiae Dei, & agnoscunt Deum, itaque offerunt ei invocationem, gratiarum actionem, confessionem, patientiam & similes virtutes, Hae hostiae sunt acceptae Deo propter pontificem Christum, quem audito Evangelio apprehendunt tanquam mediatorem. Hinc facile intelligi potest, quare hac figura delectatus sit, ἱερουργοῦντα, τὸ εὐαγγέλιον, sacrificantem Evangelium, voluit enim admonere quae sint verae hostiae novi testamenti. Et quod addit: ut oblatio gentium fiat accepta, etsi ambigue dictum videtur, tamen sententiae inter se sunt affines, ut gentes oblatae per me, hoc est praeparatae tanquam hostiae, fiant acceptae. Aut hoc modo, ut gentes iam offerentes hoc est credentes & invocantes Deum, fiant acceptae. Nam & ipse gentes praeparatae & ut ita dicam consecratae offerunt suas hostias. Itaque res eodem redit, dicit enim in summa se ubique spargere Evangelium, ut gentes agnoscant Christum, & fiant populus Dei, & hostiae, ac invocent & celebrent Deum. Quod vero addit: sanctificata in spiritu sancto, iterum docet in novo testamento officia externa non esse sacrificia, nec placere Deo ex opere operato. Sic enim oblatio gentium est accepta, inquit, si sit sanctificata spiritu sancto, id est si gentes offerant spirituales morus, timorem Dei, & fiduciam misericordiae Dei.

Observemus autem hic honestissimas laudes ministerii verbi, quod videlicet Evangelii praedicatio, enarratio, tractatio sint sacrificia necessaria novi testamenti. Id consolari debet & docentes & discentes Evangelium inter tot molestias quae utrisque perpetiendae sunt. Doctores sciant hunc cultum Dei necessarium esse, sciant eum propter gloriam Dei praestandum esse, sciant eum Deo placere, etiamsi homines alii negligenter audiunt Evangelium, alii contemnunt, alii etiam persequuntur. Meminerint & hi qui discunt Evangelium, hoc studium discendi Evangelii cultum Dei esse, quem & requirit & approbat Deus. Videmus enim quam se vere hoc praecipiat Deus, cum ait de filio: Hunc auditae. Quare hoc officium, hunc cultum Deo praestare necesse est. Proinde etiam si in aliis artibus versamur, tamen, sicut agricolae sui laboris primitias Deo consecrare in lege iubentur, ita nos partem operae ac studii consecremus Deo. Et quanquam magno in contemptu atque odio sunt, qui postquam in literis humanioribus & aliis disciplinis communibus mediocriter versati sunt totos se dedunt studio sacrarum literarum: tamen hi quoque consolentur se hac ratione, quod hoc studii genus sit necessarius cultus Dei, & ad gloriam Dei pertineat, modo ut pie tractetur. Quod si considerabunt, facile contemnent iudicia istorum qui velut contagium procul fugiunt doctrinam Christianam, vel propter contemptum religionis, vel quia aliae artes magis quaestuosae sunt, ac caeteros irrident omnes, qui non abstinent à sacris literis omnino.

## 15:25
Now, however, I am setting out for Jerusalem to serve the saints.

When he was speaking of his own affairs, he mentioned his travels in passing, and added that he would also come to Rome at some time, after he had returned from Jerusalem, to which he now says he is setting out, in order to bring there money collected from various places to assist the Christians in Judea whose entire fortunes had been snatched away because of their profession of the Gospel. And under Claudius Caesar, in whose times this Epistle was written by Paul, there was a most grievous famine, in almost the whole world, and especially in the east. At such a time, Christians in Judea were especially in need of foreign help, because they had been despoiled of their own resources. Paul, however, distinguishes this alms collected for the needs of those who first taught the Gospel from other alms. For this is more truly a reward owed to teachers; therefore he says: They are their debtors. For if the Gentiles enjoy the spiritual goods of these men, they ought in turn to supply them with carnal goods. Paul therefore warns us in this place what we owe to the teachers of the Gospel, concerning which matter he preaches very copiously in other epistles. But since a certain iron age is now being lived in which those who teach and govern the Churches are treated most cruelly, I have thought that readers ought to be warned here, so that they may consider what is owed to the governors of the Churches, and likewise learn what grave punishments God has threatened to those who despise the priests and teachers of the Churches, and do not help them to the best of their ability. For Christ, when He says that the laborer is worthy of his hire, shows that a reward is owed to priests. Wherefore, since this duty is a debt, it is required of us more than other alms which are given freely. And in another place Christ adds a magnificent promise: Whoever shall have given to one of these little ones a cup of cold water only in the name of a disciple, amen I say he will not lose his reward. If we believe in Christ, let us declare our faith here, and with this hope let us treat priests more humanely and liberally, expecting that Christ will undoubtedly return grace to us in full measure. This kind of duty merits many and great rewards, both spiritual and corporal, public peace, the increase and defense of our resources, just as Paul teaches. 2. Corinth. 9. And on the contrary, the omission of this duty is punished with the most severe penalties, as it is written in Haggai, where God says that for this reason the crops were corrupted, and furthermore that other calamities had occurred, because the people neglected the temple and the priests. For these are the words: Because my house is neglected, and you are busy each one with his own house. For this reason the heavens have been restrained over you, so that they would not give dew, and the earth has been restrained so that it would not give its sprout &c. But what is happening now? In some places priests are slaughtered with more than Scythian cruelty, in others they are almost forced to perish from hunger, along with their wretched wives and small children. The people not only impart nothing of their own to them, but even the pensions which were donated to the Churches by the liberality of our ancestors to nourish both teachers and students of sacred letters he plunders the seed. In which matter there is a twofold evil. For both the present priests are killed by hunger, and because no one is supported from the public treasury who might learn the sacred letters, in a little while there will be a lack of men suitable for teaching the Churches. This matter threatens the destruction of the entire Christian religion. For how will religion be able to be preserved, without the study of letters, without suitable teachers? Thus those sacrilegious men are not only cruel toward the present priests, but they also attempt to destroy the entire Christian religion, as much as lies within them. The laws of the ancient Princes establish most atrocious punishments for sacrilege, not as the unskilled judge out of some superstition, as if God wished to be appeased and worshipped with gold: but because the most wise princes understood that for the studies of Christian doctrine to be preserved, the resources of the Churches must be retained. For it is in the interest of the republic, not only that provision be made for the sustenance of present priests, but also that Christian doctrine be propagated to posterity. That cannot be done otherwise, unless good talents destined for the studies of sacred letters are supported from the public treasury, so that there may remain for posterity those who can teach rightly. For it is necessary that these be supported from the public treasury just like soldiers, because while they devote their effort to this matter, they do not they can learn other profitable arts, for which reason they cannot have a livelihood, unless from the public. Therefore Paul spoke most gravely, comparing this order, both of those teaching and of those learning, with soldiers: No one serves as a soldier at his own expense. For he signifies that those who serve the Church must be nourished by public stipends. But we declaim these things in vain in these most miserable times in which the Christian religion lies oppressed by manifold tyranny. Good men, however, are to be admonished all the more of this, so that they may not be led by those examples to think too irreverently themselves about priests. For we have seen how much these examples harm the common people. Wherefore let us often set these things before ourselves, let us often inculcate these things to the people, that we deserve great rewards if we treat priests kindly, if we assist them, if we take care that the doctrine of Christ is faithfully propagated to posterity. And that those who are cruel to priests, who refuse to assist the studies of Christian doctrine, will pay horrible penalties to God. In turn, let priests also remember their duty, that they may teach rightly, that they may heal doubting consciences, that they may adorn the Gospel with the convenience of their morals, for those Epicureans who not only do not teach the Gospel, but sweetly mock all do not deserve to be called priests. religions, and meanwhile they hold sacred things for gain.

Latin:

Nunc autem proficiscor in Ierusa-lem ut serviam sanctis.

Cum de suo diceret, obiter commemoravit suas peregrinationes, & adiecit se Romam etiam aliquando venturum esse, postquam ex Ierosolyma redierit, quo nunc proficisci se dicit, ut eò pecuniam afferat passim collectam ad iuvandos Christianos in Iudaea quibus fortunae omnes ereptae erant propter Evangelii prosessionem. Et sub Claudio Caesare, cuius temporibus haec Epistola à Paulo scripta est, fame gravissime laboratum est, fere in toto orbe, maximeque in oriente. Tali tempore Christiani in Iudaea praecipue indigebant aliena ope, quia facultatibus suis spoliati erant. Discernit autem Paulus ab aliis elemosinis hanc collatam ad usus illorum qui primi docuerunt Evangelium. Nam haec est verius merces debita doctoribus, ideo ait: Debitores eorum sunt. si enim gentes fruuntur spiritualibus bonis istorum, debent eis vicissim carnalia bona suppeditare. Admonet itaque nos hoc loco Paulus, quid Evangelii doctoribus debeamus, qua de re saepe concionatur in aliis epistolis copiosissime. Cum autem ferrea quaedam aetas nunc agatur in qua crudelilissime tractantur hi qui docent & gubernant Ecclesias, duxi hic ad monendos esse lectores, ut quid debeat gubernatoribus Ecclesiarum considerent, discant item, quam graves poenas minatus sit Deus his qui sacerdotes et doctores Ecclesiarum contemnunt, nec pro virili iuvant. Christus enim cum inquit operarium mercede dignum esse, ostendit deberi sacerdotibus mercedem. quare hoc officium cum sit debitum magis requiritur à nobis, quam caeterae elemosinae quae gtatis dantur. Et alio in loco addit Christus magnificam promissionem : Quis quis potum dederit uni ex minimis istis calicem aquae srigidae, tantum in nomine discipuli amendico vobis non perdet mercedm suam. Si Christo credimus, hic declaremus fidem nostram, & hac spe humanius & liberalius tractemus sacerdotes, expectantes Christum haud dubie nobis cumulate redditurum esse gratiam. Hoc officii genus meretur multa & magna praemia, tum spiritualia, tum corporalia, pacem publicam, facultatum nostrarum incrementa & defensionem, sicut Paulus docet. 2. Corinth. 9. Et econtra huius officii praetermissio punitur gravissimis poenis, ut in Haggeo scriptum est. ubi Deus ideo corruptas esse segetes inquit, et praeterea alias calamitates accidisse, quia populus negligat templum & sacerdores. Haec enim sunt verba: Quia domus mea negligitur, & vos cumulatis unusquisque domi suae. Propter hoc super vos prohibiti sunt sunt caeli, ne darent rorem, & terra prohibita est ne daret germen &c. Quid autem nunc fit? sacerdotes alibi plusquam Scythica crudelitate trucidantur alibi pene coguntur fame perire, cum miseris coniugibus & parvis liberis. Populus non solum de suo nihil impertit eis, sed etiam pensiones quae liberalitate maiorum Ecclesiis donatae sunt ad alendos & doctores & scholasticos sacrarum litetarum soede diripit. Qua in re duplex malum est. Nam & praesentes sacerdotes fame necantur & quia nulli de publico aluntur qui discant sacras literas, paulo post defuturi sunt homines idonei ad Ecclesias docendas. Ea res interitum minatur universae religioni Christianae. Quomodo enim conservari religio poterit, sine literarum studiis, sine idoneis doctoribus? Ita sacrilegi isti, non solum erga praesentes sacerdotes crudeles sunt, sed etiam universam religionem Christianam, quantum in ipsis est delere conantur. Veterum Principum leges atrocissimas poenas in sacrilegia constituunt, non ut imperiti iudicant superstitione aliqua quasi Deus auro placari & coli velit: sed quod intelligebant sapientissimi principes ad studia doctrinae Christianae conservanda, Ecclesiarum facultates retinendas esse. Id enim reipub. interest, non solum ut praesentibus sacerdotibus curetur victus, sed etiam ut doctrina Christiana propagetur ad posteros. Id aliter fieri non potest, nisi de publico alantur bona ingenia destinata studiis sacrarum literarum, ut ad posteros reliqui sint, qui recte docere possint. Necesse est enim hos de publico ali sicut milites, quia dum huic rei operam dant, non possunt alias quaestuosas artes discere, quare victum, nisi de publico, habere non possunt. Ideo Paulus gravissime dixit comparans cum militibus hunc ordinem, tum docentium, tum discentium: Nemo militat suis stipendiis. Significat enim publicis stipendiis alendos esse hos qui Ecclesiae serviunt. Sed haec frustra declamamus his miserrimis temporibus quibus iacet opressa multiplici tyrannide religio Christiana. Boni tamen hoc magis admonendi sunt ne exemplis illis adducantur ut ipsi quoque parum reverenter sentiant de sacerdotibus. Vidimus enim quantum haec exempla vulgo noceant. Quare haec nobis ipsi saepe subiiciamus, saepe haec inculcemus populo, Magna nos mereri praemia, si sacerdotes benigne tractemus, eos iuvemus, si Christi doctrinam fideliter ad posteros propagari curemus. Et horribiles poenas Deo daturos esse istos, qui crudeles sunt in sacerdotes, qui recusant studia doctrinae Christianae iuvare. Vicissim & sui officii meminerint sacerdotes, ut recte doceant, ut conscientias ambigentes sanent, ut commoditate morum ornent Evangelium, non enim vocari sacerdotes merentur Epicurei isti qui non solum non docent Evangelium, sed suaviter irrident omnes religiones, & interim sacra in quaestu habent.

## 16:1 Argument
CHAP. XVI.

This chapter is almost entirely consumed with greetings. And it is useful to remember this example against certain hypocrites, who take away all offices of humanity from the saints, when indeed this courtesy has the significance of Christian love, and especially becomes teachers. At the end he warns not to admit or listen to pernicious teachers, and those sowing doctrine fighting against the Gospel. For just as a physician, when he has shown remedies, also orders one to beware of those things which seem harmful: So the Apostle, after he has handed down above the chief place of Christian doctrine, exhorts that they be circumspect and keep watch, lest any impious teachers creep up on them. And so that they may be able to beware more easily, he indicates the arts by which these impostors circumvent the unskilled. They deceive, he says, through χρηστολογίας κὰι εὐλογίας, χρηστολογίαι not however flatteries in the manners of the teachers and in the very kind of doctrine. For as far as manners pertain, those hypocrites diligently They know how to feign friendliness, ease, and patience; they know how to aptly play upon the affections of those with whom they deal. It is easy to find examples of this thing among monks. And at this time the Anabaptists, although they indeed teach many things that are not only false but also absurd and openly abhorrent to the whole nature of men, nevertheless capture the minds of men with that prodigious simulation of patience and modesty. Doctrine also has its flatteries somewhere, which itself also sometimes figuratively flatters the people, as when the common crowd is untimely relieved of the burdens of traditions. When ingenious men are loosened from the bonds of heavenly dogmas which seem absurd to reason.

εὐλογίαι signifies praises in Greek, but Paul, in the Hebrew manner, calls them εὐλογίας, that is, good imprecations and magnificent promises. For these most easily infatuate minds occupied by hope, fear, and other affections, as when riches are promised to the worshippers of Anna, when monks promise eternal life for their rites, when they promise happiness in all business for the sacrifice of the Mass. Against all snares of this kind, minds must be fortified with certain and firm knowledge of the word of God. As Peter says: You do well in attending to the prophetic word, as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts. May God therefore govern our hearts for the sake of our Lord Jesus Christ by the Holy Spirit, that we may retain the Gospel delivered from heaven, and may progress in the knowledge and trust of Christ, and that we may adorn the glory of the Gospel with all pious duties, and may He restore pious and perpetual concord to the Church. Amen. Thanks be to God.

THE END.

STRASBOURG AT THE HOUSE OF CRATO MYLIUS IN THE YEAR 1540 IN THE MONTH OF MARCH.

Latin:

CAP. XVI.

Hoc caput fere totum consumitur in salutationibus. Ac prodest hoc exenplum meminisse adversus hypocritas quosdam, qui omnia humanitatis officia sanctis adimunt, cum quidem haec comitas significationem habeat Christianae dilectionis, & vel praecipue deceat doctores. In fine admonet, ne admittant neve audiant perniciosos doctores, & serentes doctrinam cum Evangelio pugnantem. Ut enim medicus cum remedia monstravit, iubet etiam cavere ea quae videntur nocitura: Ita Apostolus postquam supra tradidit praecipuum locum doctrinae Christianae, hortatur ut sint circumspecti & advigilent, ne qui obrepant ipsis doctores impii. Et ut cavere facilius possint, artes indicat quibus imperitos isti impostores circumveniunt. Decipiunt, inquit, per χρηστολογίας κὰι εὐλογίας, χρηστολογίαι haud duautem blandiciae in moribus docentium & in ipso genere doctrinae. Etenim quod ad mores attinet, hypocritae isti gnaviter norunt simulare comitatem, facilitatem, patientiam, norunt apte alludere ad eorum afsectus, quibus cum agunt. Huius rei exempla facile est reperire apud monachos. Et hoc tempore Anabaptistae, cum quidem multa doceant non solum falsa, sed etiam absurda & palam abhorrentia à tota natura hominum, tamen animos hominum capiunt illa prodigiosa simulatione patientiae & modestiae. Habet alicubi suas blanditias etiam doctrina quae & ipsa figurate interdum adulatur populo, ut cum vulgus intem pestive levatur oneribus traditionum. Cum homines ingeniosi solvuntur vinculis dogmatum caelestium quae rationi videntur absurda.

εὐλογίαι significant graecis laudationes sed Paulus ebraico more εὐλογίας vocat benedictiones, hoc est bonas imprecationes, & magnificas promissiones. Nam hae facilime infatuant animos spe, metu, & aliis affectibus occupatos, ut cum Annae cultoribus promittuntur divitiae, cum Monachi promittunt vitam aeternam pro suis ritibus, cum promittunt felicitatem in omnibus negotiis pro sacrificio Missae. Adversus omnes huiusmodi insidias muniri oportet animos certa & firma cognitione verbi Dei. Sicut ait Pterus: Benefacitis attendentes prophetico sermoni, tanquam lucernae lucenti in loco caliginoso, donec illucescat dies & oriatur lucifer in cordibus vestris. Deus itaque gubernet corda nostra propter Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum Spiritu sancto, ut Evangelium de caelo traditum retineamus, & in agnitione & fiducia Christi proficiamus, et ut gloriam Evangelii omnibus piis officiis ornemus, & reddat Ecclesiae concordiam piam & perpetuam. Amen. Deo gratia.

FINIS.

ARGENTORATI APUD CRATONEM MYLIUM AN. M. D. X L. MENSE MARTIO.
